explain.label: explain2-track-1
explain.one_line: We test whether changing one small piece of DNA slides the point where a gene switch flips, without changing how sharply it flips.
explain.what: Engineers build tiny switches out of genes inside bacteria. Bacteria are single living cells, like the common lab germ E. coli. A switch works like a dimmer. When the incoming signal goes up, the output goes down. Each switch has two numbers. The first is the signal level where the output is halfway down. The second is how sharply it drops, like a gentle slope versus a cliff. Engineers can edit one short piece of DNA, called the dial. Its full name is the ribosome binding site. Think of it as a landing strip. The cell's protein-making machinery lands on it and starts reading the gene. A better landing strip means the cell makes more of a protein called a repressor. A repressor is a protein that turns another gene down. Our bet is simple. Editing the dial moves the halfway point left or right. It does not change the sharpness. Picture a curve on a graph. Sliding means the same S-shaped curve moves sideways. Changing shape means the S gets steeper or flatter. We bet on sliding. We use only public tables of switches that other people already measured. We do no new lab work. Before we test on fresh data, we write down what would count as failure.
explain.why: Suppose the bet holds. Then a designer can tune a switch with one simple edit. The designer can trust that the rest of the curve stays put. That saves a lot of trial and error. It also gives our project a clear rule to add to its law library. The law library is our list of rules that a computer has checked. It has no rule on this today. Suppose the bet fails. Then designers learn the edit has side effects. Either answer is useful. We do not claim the bet is true. The data so far say it is roughly true, but not exactly.

steps.text: Pick the switches. We use public tables of measured gene switches. They come from a free design tool called Cello. Cello is software that helps people design gene circuits. Each table lists many switches and their measured numbers.
steps.picture: Like starting from a printed catalogue of light dimmers with their test results.

steps.text: Find pairs of switches that differ only in the dial. In one table there are 10 such pairs.
steps.picture: Like finding two dimmers that are the same model except for the size of the knob.

steps.text: For each pair, compare how sharply the two drop. The biggest gap in the main table is about 16 percent. That is roughly one part in six.
steps.picture: Like checking whether two door hinges swing with the same snap. One is at most a sixth snappier.

steps.text: Compare where each one reaches halfway. These points differ by up to 7.7 times. So the dial really does something.
steps.picture: Like one dimmer needing a knob turn almost eight times bigger than the other.

steps.text: Prove the sliding idea with pure maths. A computer program that checks proofs line by line has confirmed it. The proof says this. If an edit only rescales the signal, the curve slides sideways and keeps its shape.
steps.picture: Like proving that a ruler slid along a table keeps the same gaps between its marks.

steps.text: Check the idea on a second, unrelated data set. It covers a different, well-studied bacterial protein. We redo the curve fitting for it.
steps.picture: Like asking a second shop whether their dimmers behave the same way.

steps.text: Work out the sharpness again ourselves. We start from the raw cell measurements. In those, a machine measures the glow of thousands of single cells, one by one. Our numbers agree closely with the published ones.
steps.picture: Like re-weighing a parcel on your own scale.

steps.text: Write down the pass and fail lines before opening any fresh data. The proposed lines are not yet frozen. That means they could still change.
steps.picture: Like calling your shot before you throw the dart.

steps.text: Test on the kept-back table. Report every miss, even if it hurts the idea.
steps.picture: Like showing the exam marks whether or not they are good.

explain.wrong_if: Here is the bet. We wrote it before looking at fresh data. Take pairs that differ only in the dial. Their sharpness should differ by no more than about 25 percent. That is one part in four. The halfway point should also move a lot in at least one pair. It should shift by about 6 times or more. For example, one switch might need a signal of 1 and its partner a signal of 6. If sharpness changes by more than 25 percent, we are wrong. If the halfway point hardly moves, we are wrong too. These lines are proposals and may still change. A pass line that is too loose is a problem. In our checks, pairs with nothing in common would also pass about half the time. So the lines must be tight.
could_go_wrong: The kept-back table is mostly the same switches measured again. So it is not a truly independent test.
We read the headers and part lists of the kept-back table. So we cannot promise it is untouched.
The edit does more than slide the curve. The flat top and flat bottom of the curve also move. For one gate, the top level was 3.9, 4.1 or 6.8, depending on the dial.
Sharpness depends on how the curve is fitted. The same data give different answers under different fitting methods.
Some of our planned pass lines are so loose that unrelated pairs would pass about half the time.
Yeast is a single-cell fungus, the kind used in bread and beer. Only one yeast pair qualifies. It differs in a second part as well. So yeast tells us nothing about the idea.
A rival explanation says proteins that tie each other up could change sharpness when the protein amount changes.
The second data set uses a different kind of signal. So it supports the idea but does not confirm it.

questions.q: What exactly is the dial, and how does it set the protein amount?
questions.a: The dial is a short stretch of DNA called the ribosome binding site. It sits just before the gene. The cell's protein-making machinery latches onto it before reading the gene. A stronger landing strip means the machinery starts more often. That gives more protein. A weaker one gives less.

questions.q: How do you know?
questions.a: We do not yet know. We re-ran the sums on public files and the numbers match. In the main table the sharpness gap is at most about 16 percent. That describes past data. It is not a proof for new switches.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We have not run the Cello fitting code. We have not run the full reshuffling test, which shows how much a number could wobble. We did not test whether predicted protein amounts match the halfway shifts. We have not read most of the original papers beyond their short summaries. We have not done any new lab work.

questions.q: Why does a dimmer picture fit?
questions.a: A gene switch turns its output down smoothly as the input rises. A dimmer does the same with light. The picture shows the two numbers that matter, the halfway point and the sharpness. The picture is a help, not a proof.

questions.q: Does the maths prove the idea?
questions.a: No. The proof says one thing. If the edit only rescales the input, the curve slides and keeps its sharpness. It says nothing about whether real DNA edits do only that.

questions.q: Why is the kept-back table a problem?
questions.a: About 15 of its 18 gate names also appear in the main table. About 13 of those have identical parts. So it is partly the same switches measured again. That is like grading a student on the same questions they practised.

questions.q: Did the earlier plan have errors?
questions.a: Two. It counted 9 matching pairs where there are 10. It also said two yeast switches differed in only one part. They also differ in the part that switches on their output.

questions.q: Is there another data set that agrees?
questions.a: Yes, partly. It covers a well-studied bacterial protein called the lac repressor. A lab chemical called IPTG acts as its signal. In two cases the halfway point moved 4.9 times and 17.5 times. The sharpness changed by at most 15 percent. A third case was too flat to judge.

questions.q: Is there a rival theory?
questions.a: Yes. One theory is about proteins that tie each other up and hold each other out of action. It says sharpness can depend on protein amount. We cannot say it is the strongest rival. That ranking would be our own judgement.

questions.q: What does 'move by 6 times' mean?
questions.a: It means the signal needed for the halfway drop gets about 6 times bigger or smaller. Say one switch flips halfway at a signal of 10. Its partner would then flip at about 60, or at about 1.7.

glossary.plain: A stretch of DNA that holds the recipe for one protein.
A small set of genes that turns an output up or down when a signal changes.
The long molecule in cells that stores the instructions for making proteins.
A tiny working part of a cell that does a job, such as switching a gene off.
A protein that turns another gene down.
Single-cell living things with no nucleus, such as the gut microbe E. coli.
A common lab bacterium that people use to build gene circuits.
A single-cell fungus, the kind used to make bread and beer.
The smallest living unit of an organism.
A short piece of DNA before a gene. The cell's protein-making machinery lands on it to start reading. A stronger one means more protein.
The signal level at which the output has dropped to the middle between its high and low levels.
How sharply the output changes as the signal rises. A cliff is steep. A gentle ramp is not.
The number that measures steepness of a switch curve. A bigger number means a sharper drop. In this text we just say sharpness.
A line on a graph that shows output against input.
How many times bigger or smaller a number gets. A 6-times shift means 10 becomes 60, or 10 becomes about 1.7.
Free software, plus its public tables, for designing gene circuits.
One gene switch that turns an input signal into an output signal.
Two gates that match in every part but one.
A public table that lists many gates and their measured values.
Data used to set up and tune our test before the real check.
Data that we keep unseen until the final test, so the test is fair.
To work out the curve numbers again from the raw measurements.
A way to measure the glow of thousands of single cells, one by one.
Reshuffling the data many times to see how much a number could wobble.
The DNA part that decides how strongly a gate's output gene is switched on.
A piece of DNA that tells the cell to stop reading a gene.
The flat top or flat bottom part of a curve.
A well-studied bacterial protein. A lab chemical called IPTG turns it off.
A lab chemical that acts as the signal for the lac repressor.
When one protein ties up another and holds it out of action.
A computer program that checks maths proofs line by line.
The project's list of rules that a computer has checked.
Parts in each hundred. 25 percent is one part in four.
A number we set in advance that the result must beat to count as a success.
The file format of the Cello tables. It is a plain data file.
A long code made from a file's bytes. If the file changes at all, the code changes. It lets you check you have the same file.
A kind of gut bacterium. One table covers it, but we did not open that table.

Removed the bare terms output promoter, terminator, plateau, ymin, z above 2 from the reading path (output promoter became 'the part that switches on their output'; plateau became 'flat top and bottom'). Glossary still defines them; ymin and z are in left_out only.
Added glossary entries for UCF, hash, and fold shift, and widened the 'steepness' and 'dial' entries; noted that orthogonal and allosteric appear only in source titles.
Added a concrete comparison to each number: 16 percent is about one part in six, 25 percent is one part in four, 7.7 times is almost eight times the knob turn.
Split long sentences across 'what', 'why', 'wrong_if' and the steps into short ones; spelled out abbreviations (RBS, DNA role, E. coli) on first use.
Explained 'not yet frozen' in the pass-and-fail step as 'could still change'.
Simplified the kept-back table Q&A comparison and the 'what have you not checked' answer (no bare 'bootstrap' or 'Cello fitting' jargon without explanation).
Merged the caveats about proteins that tie up each other and the second data set into plainer sentences; kept all eight caveats.

reader_unknown_words: Hill number (only half, explained as sharpness)
ribosome binding site (understood as the dial, but not the biology)
reader_could_not_follow: It also gives our project a clear rule to add to its law library.
A pass line that is too loose is a problem. In our checks, pairs with nothing in common would also pass about half the time.
A rival explanation says proteins that tie each other up could change sharpness when the protein amount changes.
Yeast is a single-cell fungus, the kind used in bread and beer. Only one yeast pair qualifies. It differs in a second part as well. So yeast tells us nothing about the idea.
The second data set uses a different kind of signal. So it supports the idea but does not confirm it.
reader_unanswerable: How much does the DNA edit change the maximum output level?
reading.reader_help: Say up front, in one plain sentence, what the practical goal is (building predictable gene circuits). Explain how a repressor makes the output fall as the signal rises, since the dimmer picture hides this. Cut jargon like law library, calibration, holdout and hash from the main text. Say why they bother testing at all if the data already roughly agree. Explain why a loose pass line passing unrelated pairs half the time matters. Draw the sliding versus steepening curves as an actual picture. Clarify the dial confusion: it appears to be both the dial and the landing strip for a reader. The text also moves between doing the test and doing a sanity check without saying which is which.

scout.summary: Scouted microbial self-organisation systems for the agree-phenotype / connect-mechanism / test-new-condition loop. Five candidates have a quantitative spatial phenotype plus a mechanistic model; for three of them I downloaded the actual measurement tables in this run and ran a first held-out check. Best: E. coli chemotactic range expansion (Cremer 2019 + Narla 2021) - 25 tabulated conditions of front speed and growth rate, public simulation code and parameter file, and a naive u^2 = k*growth-rate law fitted on 6 wild-type conditions already misses 6 held-out strains by 10 to 64 percent, so there is a real, non-trivial prediction to freeze. Runner-up: V. cholerae biofilm wrinkle wavelength vs agar stiffness (Yan 2019), which has all raw numbers public, a closed-form law, and bridges directly to the biomaterials/printing track (substrate stiffness is the control knob). Sectoring (Weinstein 2017) has excellent CC0 images and masks but every archive is 267 MB to 5.2 GB so I only fetched the READMEs. Synthetic stripe/Turing systems (Liu 2011, Karig 2018) have no public data that I could find.
scout.recommended: Chemotactic range-expansion front speed in soft agar (Cremer 2019 data with the Narla 2021 travelling-wave formula). It is the only candidate where I have the measured numbers for about 35 conditions in hand, public simulation code and parameters, and a first held-out check that already fails informatively (10 to 64 percent error for the simple scaling law), so a frozen prediction can be tested within two weeks; keep the biofilm wrinkling law as the runner-up because substrate stiffness links it to the biomaterials track.

candidates.name: Chemotactic range-expansion front speed in soft agar
candidates.system: Escherichia coli K-12 (wild type plus titratable-uptake strains Pu-ptsG, Pu-glpFK, glpK22) expanding in 0.25% soft agar with a low-concentration attractant (aspartate or serine) and a separate carbon source
candidates.phenotype_measured: Front (band) expansion speed u in mm/h, paired with batch growth rate in 1/h; also front position vs time and confocal radial density profiles (bulge shape)
candidates.why_it_fits: Mechanistic growth-expansion (Keller-Segel with growth) model with public Python code and a published parameter file; Narla 2021 gives a closed-form travelling-wave speed with stated dependencies (square root in growth rate, square root in background attractant over a_m, independent of uptake rate, a predicted attractant concentration of maximum speed). The source-data tables give 25 strain/carbon/attractant conditions plus a 10-point aspartate dose series that is non-monotonic, so there are several conditions that were not used to set the model parameters. All analysis is tabular: no image processing needed for the first test.

public_data.what: Nature source data, Extended Data Fig 1c: 25 conditions, mean expansion speed (mm/h), s.d., n, growth rate (1/h)
public_data.licence: publisher supplementary file, no explicit licence seen

public_data.what: Nature source data, Extended Data Fig 8: aspartate dose series (10 to 10000 uM) expansion speeds on glucose and glycerol, plus simulated speed vs concentration
public_data.licence: publisher supplementary file, no explicit licence seen

public_data.what: Simulation parameter sets (JSON blocks) for the growth-expansion model
Growth-expansion model simulation code (gp_chemotaxis.py, run_simulation.py, examplesim.par); repo tree listed, files not downloaded
public_data.licence: LICENSE file present, text not read

public_data.what: Narla travelling-wave solver and consolidated numerical data (all_data.mat is simulation output, not experiment); repo tree listed only
Raw confocal intensity scans of expanding populations (density profiles) - metadata fetched, archive NOT downloaded (over the 20 MB limit)

candidates.the_test: Freeze: (1) fit the single lumped coefficient k in u^2 = k * growth_rate on the 6 wild-type carbon-source conditions with 100 uM aspartate (rows 3-8 of ED Fig 1c); (2) separately freeze the full growth-expansion model with the published parameter file, changing only the measured growth rate per condition. Test on conditions not used in the fit: the 5 Pu-glpFK titration points (growth rate 0.22 to 0.74 /h), the 5 Pu-ptsG points, glpK22, the 6 serine conditions, and the aspartate dose series (speed peaks near 1000 uM then falls to 2.1 mm/h at 10 mM on glucose). Pass criterion written before running: full model within 15% on at least 80% of held-out conditions AND predicted aspartate concentration of maximum speed within a factor of 3 of the observed peak; the scaling law alone is expected to fail and is the control. Stretch: download the 168 MB confocal set and test the predicted bulge width.
candidates.biggest_risk: The published model parameters may already have been tuned against some of the 'held-out' conditions (the paper reports the model reproduces the dose curve), so the hold-out is weaker than it looks unless we refit from the wild-type subset only. Chemotactic coefficient changes with growth condition, which the simple law ignores. No new wet-lab condition is possible without a lab; the 'new condition' is new to our fit, not new to the world.
candidates.cost_and_time: Compute only, laptop scale. Tabular test: 2-3 days. Full simulation rerun across about 35 conditions: 1-2 weeks including reading the 132 kB simulation script.

candidates.name: Biofilm wrinkle wavelength versus substrate stiffness
candidates.system: Vibrio cholerae constitutive biofilm-former grown on agar plates of 0.4% to 3.0% agar (substrate shear modulus 0.14 to 67 kPa)
candidates.phenotype_measured: Radial wrinkle/blister wavelength lambda (um), with biofilm thickness h, residual-layer thickness, film modulus Gf and substrate modulus Gs measured per condition (n=3 each)
candidates.why_it_fits: Closed-form mechanical law that makes a number: bilayer theory lambda/h = 2*pi*(Gf/(3*Gs))^(1/3), with a trilayer correction that predicts wrinkling persists and lambda/h saturates when the substrate is stiffer than the film. Every raw triplicate is in a public spreadsheet. The control knob is substrate stiffness, which is exactly what a printed elastomer or hydrogel substrate would vary, so this candidate bridges to the biomaterials and physical-surrogate tracks. The law is simple enough to state formally.

public_data.what: eLife Source data 1: per-sample Gs, Gf, h, residual thickness and wavelength for 8 agar concentrations
eLife Supplementary file 1, Table S1 (mean +/- sd of the same quantities)
Fig 2 source data (wrinkle number vs radius and time, height line profile) and trilayer theory curves (lambda/hf vs stiffness ratio for 9 parameter sets)
MATLAB image-analysis scripts (repo tree listed)
public_data.licence: MIT-sized LICENSE file present (1067 bytes), text not read

public_data.what: Independent system for a transfer test: Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm wrinkling vs substrate surface energy under flow (Dryad, metadata fetched only)

candidates.the_test: Freeze the bilayer law with exponent 1/3 and fit only its prefactor on the three soft-substrate conditions where bilayer theory is valid (0.4, 0.5, 0.6% agar, Gf/Gs > 1.3). Predict lambda for the five stiffer conditions (0.7 to 3.0%), where bilayer theory says no wrinkling should occur. Then freeze the trilayer model with the measured residual-layer thickness ratio per condition and one fitted Gr/Gf, and predict the same five. Pre-registered expectation: bilayer under-predicts by more than 20% at 0.8% and 3.0% (my first pass below shows -22% and -30%); trilayer must bring all five within 10%. New-condition extension: predict the wavelength a film of the same Gf and h would show on a printable elastomer of known shear modulus, and compare with a physical thin-film-on-soft-substrate surrogate.
candidates.biggest_risk: Only 8 conditions, so a 3-train / 5-test split is thin and the trilayer model has enough freedom (Gr/Gf, hr/hf) to fit almost anything. The two public files disagree for 1.0% agar (spreadsheet triplicate mean 308.7 um, Table S1 says 334 +/- 17 um), so the data need a provenance note before freezing. Transfer to other organisms needs their Gf and h, which the Dryad set may not contain.
candidates.cost_and_time: Compute only. First test: 1-2 days. Trilayer linear-stability reimplementation: about 1 week. Physical surrogate on printed substrates: weeks, needs a lab or print partner.

candidates.name: Sector number and sector-boundary dynamics in colony range expansion
candidates.system: Four fluorescently labelled E. coli strains with different expansion velocities, radially expanding colonies on agar, imaged at day 8
candidates.phenotype_measured: Strain fractions vs length expanded, two-point angular correlation functions, relative rates of domain-wall annihilation vs coalescence, single-sector opening angle (wall velocity)
candidates.why_it_fits: The model (annihilating and coalescing random walkers on an inflating ring with deterministic selection bias) has only three measured inputs (R0, wall diffusion constant Dw, wall velocity vw) and predicts multi-strain outcomes; the authors already report one out-of-sample style check (unequal 10/10/80 inoculum predicted annihilation-coalescence difference about 0.51). The deposit includes raw images AND extracted masks and labelled domains, so the phenotype can be recomputed.

public_data.what: Zenodo mirror of Dryad deposit: 19 files, OME-TIFF images plus masks, labelled domains, homeland and radius fits for q=2, 3, 4 strain experiments and single-sector sweeps
public_data.size: 12.5 GB total; smallest image archive 267 MB (q2_eCFP_eYFP.zip)

public_data.what: README files describing folder layout (two fetched and read)
Open-access full text with parameter table

candidates.the_test: Freeze R0, Dw and vw from the two-strain and single-sector experiments only (q2 archives, 267 MB and 416 MB). Predict, with the random-walker simulation, the surviving sector count and the strain fractions at L = 6.5 mm for the four-strain experiment and for the unequal 10/10/80 three-strain inoculum, then measure both from the labelled-domain masks. Pass: predicted mean sector count within the replicate standard error (20 replicates each).
candidates.biggest_risk: Needs downloads of several hundred MB to GB that I was not allowed to make in this run, so I have not confirmed the masks open cleanly. The authors found selection effects were small at these sizes (kappa about 0.13 by my calculation), so the test may mostly confirm neutral theory, which is a weaker result.
candidates.cost_and_time: Compute only. 2-3 weeks including download and re-deriving sector counts from masks.

candidates.name: Reciprocal motility control: segregated vs co-localised two-strain rings
candidates.system: Two engineered E. coli populations that activate or inhibit each other's motility through quorum-sensing signals, spreading on semi-solid agar
candidates.phenotype_measured: Radial fluorescence intensity profiles (GFP, mCherry, darkfield) vs position in cm: ring spacing and phase offset between the two populations
candidates.why_it_fits: A motility-regulation field theory predicts that flipping the sign of the interaction turns out-of-phase rings into in-phase rings and extends to three populations. Radial profiles are public as source data, which makes ring spacing and phase directly measurable without images.

public_data.what: Nature Physics source data CSVs: radial GFP / mCherry / darkfield profiles
public_data.licence: publisher supplementary file; article itself is paywalled

public_data.what: Further source data spreadsheets (MOESM5, 6, 9, 10) downloaded but not parsed (legacy .xls)

candidates.the_test: Extract ring spacing and the GFP-mCherry phase lag from the mutual-activation profiles, fit the model's two interaction strengths, freeze, then predict the phase lag and spacing for the redesigned (co-localising) circuit and the three-population case and compare with their source-data profiles.
candidates.biggest_risk: The paper is paywalled (I read only the abstract and data statement) and the simulation code is 'available on reasonable request', so the model would have to be reimplemented from the earlier open theory. The prediction is mostly qualitative (in-phase vs out-of-phase), weaker than a number.
candidates.cost_and_time: Compute only. 3-4 weeks, dominated by reimplementing the model.

candidates.name: Engineered swarm ring patterns as input records
candidates.system: Proteus mirabilis with IPTG/arabinose-tunable swarming genes (cheW, umoD, flgM, fliA, lrp) forming centimetre-scale bullseye colonies

could_not_find: No public image or measurement data for the synthetic density-dependent-motility stripe system (Liu 2011): the paper is not open access and I found no Zenodo, Dryad or Figshare deposit; stripe wavelength vs inducer numbers were not retrievable.

No public data located for the synthetic stochastic Turing pattern (Karig 2018) or the Bacillus biofilm segmentation-clock rings (Chou 2022); Europe PMC returned no open full text for either, so I could not read their data statements.

No public quantitative dataset found for classic Bacillus colony morphology diagrams (branching vs compact as a function of agar and nutrient); Zenodo and Dryad keyword searches returned only unrelated records.

I did not download any raw image archive: Cremer confocal scans (168 MB), all Weinstein sector archives (267 MB to 5.2 GB), the Geisel wrinkling set (3.8 GB) and the Proteus repo data (61 + 74 MB) exceed the 20 MB limit, so those are marked fetched_ok=false and their contents are unverified beyond metadata and READMEs.

The exact closed-form speed expression in Narla 2021 (their Eq. 21) did not survive text extraction from the XML; I verified only its stated dependencies in prose. It must be transcribed from the PDF before freezing.

Cremer supplementary tables S9 and S10 (the paper's own tabulation of expansion speeds) were not fetched: the Europe PMC supplementary bundle returned a 162-byte stub. The source-data spreadsheets state that they carry the same data.
Curatolo 2020 article body and model equations are paywalled; simulation code is on request only. Four of its legacy .xls source files were downloaded but not parsed.
Licence terms for the Nature and Nature Physics supplementary files and for the daninolab GitHub repo were not stated anywhere I fetched.
Crossref rate-limited this run (HTTP 429) after two queries, so most DOIs were confirmed through Europe PMC rather than Crossref.
Whether the published growth-expansion parameters were tuned on the conditions I propose to hold out is not something I could determine from the text I read.

design.label: design-patterns
design.chosen: Chemotactic range-expansion front of E. coli in soft agar (Cremer 2019 data, Narla 2021 travelling-wave law, Cremer simulation code). I keep the scout's recommendation but change its test. The scout's pass rule (full simulation within 15% on 80% of conditions) is weak because the published parameters were probably tuned on those conditions. Reading the Narla full text I found that at fixed attractant concentration its closed form IS the scout's control law u^2 = k*r, and the already-seen data contradict two of its stated dependencies (exponent of speed on growth rate about 0.9 to 1.1 inside a titration series instead of 0.5; exponent on attractant about 0.3 instead of 0.5). So the design freezes mechanism-bridge and zero-parameter predictions against source-data sheets whose values nobody on this project has opened yet. Runner-up (biofilm wrinkle wavelength vs substrate stiffness) is not chosen: 8 conditions, the scout already computed its hold-out errors, and the trilayer model has enough freedom to fit anything.
design.one_paragraph: Phenotype agreed: front speed u (mm/h) and the radial density profile (bulge, trough, exponential back) of an expanding E. coli population. Mechanisms connected: single-cell swimming (diffusivity vs growth rate), attractant uptake rate, and receptor sensing limits feed a growth-expansion travelling wave. New conditions tested: uptake mutants, a two-attractant mixture, other strain backgrounds and GFP-plasmid strains, all in Cremer 2019 source-data sheets and a 168 MB confocal deposit whose numeric values were not opened in the scout run or in this design run (I printed header labels only). Six predictions are frozen in one git commit before any data module for those sheets exists. Two are zero-free-parameter (back-of-front e-fold length = u/r; bulge density proportional to 1/uptake), one is a bridge from single-cell data to the colony exponent, one is a composition rule for a mixture, one is a declared-seen diagnostic with a sensing-limit ablation, and one is a conditional print-and-grow test. What I already know from seen data, stated so nobody mistakes it for a blind result: the square-root law fitted on 6 wild-type rows (k = 16.91 mm^2/h) fails the titratable strains, the log-log slope of u on r is 1.12 in the Pu-glpFK aspartate series (0.90 without the zero-inducer point), and the slope of u on aspartate from 10 to 100 uM is 0.30 on glucose and 0.28 on glycerol (own calculations, script D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/scratch/design-patterns/calc.py on values in scratch/scout-patterns/dl/cremer/MOESM11.xlsx and MOESM22.xlsx).
design.model:
TWO MODELS, BOTH FROZEN.

M1, closed form (Narla, Cremer, Hwa 2021, PNAS, doi 10.1073/pnas.2105138118; equations transcribed in this run from the MathML of the Europe PMC full text PMC8640786, file scratch/scout-patterns/PMC8640786.xml; must be re-checked against the PDF before the freeze commit).
  Eq 1: d rho/dt = D_rho lap(rho) - div(v rho) + r rho (1 - rho/rho_c)
  Eq 2: v = chi0 grad(a)/(a + a_m)
  Eq 3: d a/dt = D_a lap(a) - mu rho a/(a + a_k), with a_k = a_m assumed
  Eq 21: c = (chi0 - D_rho) sqrt( r (a0/a_m) / (chi0 - D_rho + D_a) )
  Eq 23: same with phi = (chi0 - D_rho)/D_rho: c = D_rho phi sqrt( r (a0/a_m) / (D_rho phi + D_a) )
  Eq 22 (validity): a0/a_m >> 1 + D_a/(chi0 - D_rho)
  Eq 12: front rise rate lambda = c/(chi0 - D_rho)
  Eq 19: bulge amplitude beta = r a0/(mu a_m) (so density scales as 1/mu); Eq 40: trough density rho_min ~ beta a_m = r a0/mu
  Eq 36: behind the trough rho ~ exp(-lambda_G z) with lambda_G ~ r/c
  Eq 33: rho_max/rho_min ~ lambda c / r
  Eq 24: c = c_inf / sqrt(1 + (r a0/(mu rho_c)) (D_rho phi gamma/(D_rho phi + D_a)) (a0/a_m)); Eq 25: a0_max/a_m = sqrt( (mu rho_c/(r a_m gamma)) (1 + D_a/(D_rho phi)) ); gamma = 0.26 is the authors' own best-fit value for D_rho = 50 um^2/s (same full text).
  Stated dependencies: sqrt in r, sqrt in a0/a_m, independent of mu and of inoculum size.
  M1 parameters. FIXED from the published parameter file (scratch/scout-patterns/dl/cremer/MOESM3.txt, mainsimulation block): D_rho = 50.2 um^2/s = 0.1807 mm^2/h (D_chemotaxis_1 = 50.2e-12 m^2/s), D_a = 800 um^2/s = 2.88 mm^2/h (D_nutrients = 8.0e-10), a_m = 1 uM for aspartate (weber_offset_1 = 0.001 mM). Unit conversion: 1 um^2/s = 3.6e-3 mm^2/h. FITTED, one number: (chi0 - D_rho), on the 6 wild-type carbon-source rows at 100 uM aspartate (rows 3 to 8 of ED Fig 1c). Least squares through the origin gives k = u^2/r = 16.907 mm^2/h, then solve X^2*100/(X + 2.88) = 16.907 for X = chi0 - D_rho = 0.7874 mm^2/h = 218.7 um^2/s, so chi0 = 268.9 um^2/s and phi = 4.36 (calc.py). Check against the published file with no fitting: chi0 = 315 um^2/s gives X = 0.9533 mm^2/h and c = 4.87 mm/h at r = 0.9985/h, 12% above the measured 4.335 mm/h. For serine one extra number (a_m for serine) is fitted on the single wild-type glucose + serine row. HELD OUT of every fit: all strains other than wild-type HE206, all rows not at 100 uM aspartate, every profile, every sheet listed in the quarantine below.
  Derived sensitivity used in F1: d ln c / d ln D_rho at fixed phi = 1 - 0.5 X/(X + D_a) = 0.893 with the fitted X (0.876 with the published X).

M2, simulation (Cremer et al. 2019, Nature, doi 10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y; code github.com/jonascremer/chemotaxis_simulation, LGPL-3.0, gp_chemotaxis.py fetched and read in this run at scratch/design-patterns/dl_code/). Radial two-nutrient growth-expansion model, FiPy, run mode weber-log. The drift potential in the code (line 661) is log((1 + a/a_minus)/(1 + a/a_plus)) with a_minus = weber_offset_1 = 1 uM and a_plus = weber_offsetmax_1 = 0.03 mM = 30 uM. M1 has no upper sensing limit; M2 has one at 30 uM. That is the structural difference the dose test isolates. M2 parameters: the published mainsimulation block used unchanged; only lambda_1 (measured growth rate per condition) and n2_start (attractant concentration) vary. Nothing in M2 is refitted by us.

M0, control: u = sqrt(k r) with k = 16.907 mm^2/h, no mechanism. At fixed a0 this is algebraically M1 with constant motility, so M0 failing is M1-with-constant-motility failing.

DATA STATUS. SEEN by scout and designer (means only): ED Fig 1c (MOESM11, 25 rows) and ED Fig 8c dose series (MOESM22, 21 rows). QUARANTINED, values not opened (labels only, script scratch/design-patterns/hdr.py): MOESM13 Fig 3e (speed vs growth rate for GFP-plasmid strains HE274, HE484, HE486, with the authors' model curve), MOESM15 (other wild-type backgrounds HE21 and RP437; 5 mM aspartate as carbon; aspartate + serine mixture for 3 strains), MOESM16 (swimming speed, run time, diffusivity vs growth rate), MOESM21 (aspartate consumption per carbon source; uptake mutants gltJ, gltP, gltJP with relative uptake labels 1.02, 0.731, 0.687, 0.358; their speeds and density profiles), MOESM12/14/17/19/20 profile sheets, and the confocal archive doi 10.6084/m9.figshare.9639209 (168,455,158 bytes, CC BY 4.0, figshare API fetched). Limit of this claim: the paper's figures show all of it, and I cannot prove what a language model retained from the published paper; the quarantine is of the numeric source files.

CITATIONS (each DOI resolved in this run through the Europe PMC REST search): Cremer J et al. 2019 Nature doi 10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y verified=true; Narla AV, Cremer J, Hwa T 2021 PNAS doi 10.1073/pnas.2105138118 verified=true; Liu W, Cremer J, Li D, Hwa T, Liu C 2019 Nature doi 10.1038/s41586-019-1734-x verified=true (metadata only, data availability not checked; candidate independent-lab transfer set); Phan TV et al. 2024 PNAS doi 10.1073/pnas.2309251121 verified=true (title and metadata only: 'Direct measurement of dynamic attractant gradients reveals breakdown of the Patlak-Keller-Segel chemotaxis model'; not read, must be read before freeze because it may pre-empt F5); Yan J et al. 2019 eLife doi 10.7554/eLife.43920 verified=true (runner-up only).

LEAN BRIDGE. Law set 1.6.0 holds one pattern law (turing-ddi-linear-condition, candidate) and nothing on travelling fronts (source: agents/laws-patterns.json). Candidate statements this track would add, all elementary real analysis on Eq 21: c is strictly increasing in r and in a0; c does not depend on mu; 1/2 < d ln c/d ln D_rho < 1 at fixed phi; validity side-condition Eq 22. The formal statement proves algebra about the formula, not that a colony obeys it; the frozen predictions are what test that.

frozen_predictions.statement: The colony-level exponent of front speed on growth rate inside a carbon-uptake titration series equals s_pred = 0.5 + 0.893*alpha, where alpha is the log-log slope of single-cell diffusivity on growth rate measured in liquid (MOESM16, ED Fig 2 table, columns 'gr (1/h)' and 'diffusion (um^2/s)', ordinary least squares on all rows). No colony data enter s_pred. Assumptions frozen with it: soft-agar D_rho is proportional to liquid diffusivity and phi is constant.
frozen_predictions.number: Targets: s_obs = 1.12 for the Pu-glpFK aspartate series in ED Fig 1c (5 points, seen; 0.90 without the zero-inducer point) and the same slope computed on the unseen Fig 3e Pu-glpFK GFP-plasmid rows. Passing needs alpha between about 0.47 and 0.92. Constant motility (alpha = 0) gives 0.5.
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: abs(s_pred - s_obs) > 0.20 on either target, or alpha <= 0. If alpha is near 0 while s_obs stays near 1, growth-dependent motility is ruled out as the cause and the square-root growth law is simply wrong for these strains.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Input: MOESM16.xlsx (quarantined). Targets: MOESM11.xlsx rows 15 to 19 (seen) and MOESM13.xlsx sheet 'Figure 3e' (quarantined).

frozen_predictions.statement: Behind the density trough the profile rises exponentially toward the colony centre with e-fold length L_G = u/r (Eq 36), using only the measured speed and growth rate of that condition. Zero free parameters.
frozen_predictions.number: L_G = 4.75 mm for wild type on glycerol + 100 uM aspartate (3.675/0.7735) and 4.34 mm on glucose + 100 uM aspartate (4.335/0.9985).
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Fitted e-fold length outside +/-30% of the predicted value in either condition, or the log-density is not linear (R^2 < 0.90) over a window of at least 2 mm between the trough and the point where density reaches half its plateau. A failure says growth behind the front is not at the batch rate (nutrient or density limitation), which undercuts every use of batch r in the model.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Confocal profiles, folders confocal_glycerol_100uMaspartate and confocal_glucose_100uMaspartate in doi 10.6084/m9.figshare.9639209 (not downloaded), OD calibration from MOESM18 ED Fig 4a. Fallback if the archive is unusable: profile columns in MOESM12 and MOESM14.

frozen_predictions.statement: Across the aspartate-uptake mutants (wild type, gltP, gltJ, gltJ gltP) front speed does not depend on uptake rate, while bulge peak density scales as 1/uptake (Eq 19).
frozen_predictions.number: Speed: log-log slope on uptake = 0. Density: slope = -1, so the lowest-uptake strain (relative uptake 0.358 vs 1.02) has 2.85 times the wild-type peak density and the two intermediate strains 1.40 and 1.48 times (1.02/0.731, 1.02/0.687).
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: abs(speed slope) > 0.15, or density slope outside [-1.3, -0.7]. Speed passing is expected and only confirmatory (Narla states agreement with experiment); the density exponent is the part that can fail.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: MOESM21.xlsx sheets 'E7g' (strain, uptake, es) and 'ED7i,k' (position, OD profiles), both quarantined.

frozen_predictions.statement: New condition class, two attractants at once (aspartate + serine). Frozen primary rule: the faster single-attractant band sets the speed, u_mix = max(u_asp, u_ser). Named alternative: signals add, u_mix = sqrt(u_asp^2 + u_ser^2). Neither is derived in Narla 2021; both are my extensions and are labelled as conjectures.
frozen_predictions.number: Wild type on glycerol: primary 4.20 mm/h, alternative 5.58. glpK22: primary 5.85, alternative 7.66. Pu-glpFK: by inducer level, primary 2.01 / 2.77 / 4.17, alternative 2.39 / 3.75 / 5.83 at 10 / 50 / 800 uM inducer.
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Primary refuted if the measured mixture speed is outside +/-10% of the max-rule value for wild type or glpK22. If both land within 10% of the quadrature values the additive extension is adopted. Anything else (between, or below the slower band) means the single-attractant model does not compose and a two-band model is required.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: MOESM15.xlsx sheet 'ED Figure 1g' (quarantined); single-attractant inputs from MOESM11 rows 7, 14, 16, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25 (seen).

frozen_predictions.statement: Declared NOT blind: the dose data are seen. M1 predicts u proportional to a0^0.5 at low dose; the seen slope from 10 to 100 uM is 0.30 (glucose) and 0.28 (glycerol), so M1's attractant dependence is recorded as already refuted on seen data. Frozen claim about M2, which we have not run: with the published parameter file unchanged except lambda_1 and n2_start, M2 reproduces those slopes and the concentration of maximum speed on both carbon sources. Ablation: removing the upper sensing limit (weber_offsetmax_1 from 0.03 to 1000 mM) moves the simulated low-dose slope up by at least 0.10. My stated expectation: glucose passes, the glycerol peak fails.
frozen_predictions.number: Low-dose slope 0.30 (glucose) and 0.28 (glycerol). Observed maximum at 1000 uM on glucose (plateau 300 to 1000) and at 100 uM on glycerol.
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Simulated slope differs from observed by more than 0.10 on either carbon source, or simulated concentration of maximum speed is off by more than a factor of 3 on either. Ablation claim refuted if the slope moves by less than 0.10, in which case the sensing ceiling is not what flattens the dose response.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: MOESM22.xlsx ED Fig 8c (seen, 21 rows); 22 M2 runs plus 8 ablation runs.

frozen_predictions.statement: Only tested if a BSL-1 partner lab is found. In soft agar cast into a printed lattice of obstacles that lengthens diffusive paths by tortuosity tau for cells and attractant alike, Eq 23 with D_rho -> D_rho/tau and D_a -> D_a/tau gives u/u_open = tau^(-1/2). The naive path-length expectation is tau^(-1).
frozen_predictions.number: u/u_open = 0.82 at tau = 1.5 and 0.71 at tau = 2.0 (path-length rule would give 0.67 and 0.50).
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Measured ratio at tau = 2.0 below 0.60 or above 0.85. tau is measured independently from dye diffusion in the same lattice before any cells are plated.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: New measurement: time-lapse front position in a printed three-sector dish insert (see physical_build). Homogenisation needs pores much smaller than the bulge rise length, which M1 puts at about 0.18 to 0.22 mm (X/c with X = 0.787 or 0.953 mm^2/h, c = 4.335 mm/h); printable pores are larger than that, so a failure here may be a scale-separation failure and is reported as such.

steps: 1. Read before freezing: Narla 2021 PDF (confirm Eqs 12, 19, 21, 23 to 25, 33, 36, 40 as transcribed) and Phan 2024 (doi 10.1073/pnas.2309251121); note in the pre-registration anything that pre-empts F5. No source-data values are opened in this step.

2. FREEZE A (commit 1): PREREGISTRATION.md with the model section, the six predictions, thresholds, the fit recipe (k = 16.907 mm^2/h from MOESM11 rows 3 to 8), the seen/quarantined file list with SHA-256 of every downloaded file, and the exact cell ranges and regression recipe for alpha, slopes and e-fold fits. No data module in this commit.

3. Commit 2: analysis code only (parsers, fit functions, the Python 3 port of gp_chemotaxis.py), tested on synthetic profiles with known answers. The code is made to fail once on a planted wrong slope to show the check can fail.

4. FREEZE B (commit 3): M2 parameter files and the run matrix (22 dose runs, 8 ablation runs, 6 wild-type carbon runs as a sanity anchor), plus the port's regression check against the simulated curve already published in MOESM22 ED Fig 8b.
5. Commit 4: data modules for the quarantined sheets (MOESM13, 15, 16, 21). Run F1, F3, F4. Record pass/refuted per prediction in RESULTS.md; the pre-registration file is never edited.
6. Download the confocal archive (168 MB, CC BY 4.0) to C:/Temp or O:, run F2 and the profile half of F3.
7. Run M2 matrix, score F5 and the ablation.

8. Write the falsification map: which of M1's dependencies (r, a0, mu, D_rho, composition) survived. State the Lean candidates only for dependencies that survived or with the measured validity domain attached.
9. Optional stage C: if a partner lab exists, print the insert, measure tau by dye, then run F6.

10. Optional transfer: check data availability of Liu 2019 (doi 10.1038/s41586-019-1734-x) and, if speed and growth rate per evolved strain are public, pre-register a seventh prediction before opening them.
design.what_is_frozen_and_when: Freeze A, step 2, before any data module exists: model equations M0/M1, fixed parameters and their source file, the one fitted number (k = 16.907 mm^2/h, X = 0.7874 mm^2/h) and the rows it came from, the sensitivity coefficient 0.893, all six predictions with their numbers and refutation thresholds, regression recipes, and the quarantine list with file hashes. Freeze B, step 4, before any M2 run is scored: the M2 parameter files (published block, only lambda_1 and n2_start varied), the ablation definition, and the run matrix. Inputs that are frozen as a recipe, not a number, because their source is quarantined: alpha in F1 (computed from MOESM16 at step 5) and the uptake values in F3. Nothing is refitted after Freeze A. Results and any corrections go in RESULTS.md; the pre-registration stands as written. Declared in the pre-registration: F5 and the ED Fig 1c target of F1 use data already seen.
design.what_would_make_this_a_paper: A paper: (a) F1 passes, meaning a single-cell swimming measurement predicts the colony-level exponent with no colony fit, and F2 and the density half of F3 pass with zero free parameters. That is a law whose mechanism chain is checked link by link and whose algebra can be stated in Lean with a measured validity domain. Or (b) a clean split: F2/F3 pass while F1 and F5 fail. That would show the profile-shape relations hold but the published square-root dependencies on growth rate and attractant do not, on the authors' own data, with the sensing-ceiling ablation saying why. Either way the product is a pre-registered falsification map of a named travelling-wave law across about 60 public conditions, which is new. F4 adds a composition rule for mixtures that neither source paper states. F6 passing would be the strongest piece for the biomaterials route: a printed architecture changing a living front speed by a predicted factor. Merely confirmatory: M2 reproducing the dose curve on glucose (the authors showed this), the speed half of F3, and M0 failing on titratable strains (the scout already saw it).
risks: Blindness is partial. The paper's figures display the quarantined data, and F5 plus one F1 target use seen data. The pre-registration must say so; the claim is only that numeric source files were not opened.

Equations were transcribed from MathML with a home-made decoder. A sign or factor error in Eq 21 to 25, 36 or 40 would invalidate numbers; the PDF check in step 1 is mandatory. SI Appendix (Table S1 defaults, section S6 for gamma) was not fetched.
Parameter mapping between M2's file and M1 is my reading (xhi_1 as chi0, weber_offset_1 as a_m). It reproduces the measured glucose speed to 12% with no fit, which supports it but does not prove it.

F1 assumes soft-agar diffusivity scales with liquid diffusivity and phi is constant. If MOESM16 has too few rows or mixes strains, alpha will be poorly determined; report its confidence interval and call F1 inconclusive if the interval is wider than 0.4.
F2 needs a clean exponential stretch behind the trough. Radial geometry, time-dependence and carrying capacity may leave less than 2 mm; then F2 is inconclusive, not passed.

F3 has 4 strains, so the density exponent has 2 degrees of freedom. Sample sizes for many speeds are n = 1 or 2 (column K of MOESM11), so no standard deviation exists for several rows; thresholds are set on means.
The simulation code is Python 2.7 with FiPy; the port may change numerics. Mitigation: regression against the published simulated curve before scoring.

Licences: Nature supplementary files carry no explicit licence that I saw, so do not redistribute them on the dashboard; store hashes and parsed numbers with attribution. Code is LGPL-3.0 (LICENSE file read). Confocal deposit is CC BY 4.0.
Phan 2024 was verified by metadata only. If it already shows the Keller-Segel form failing in this system, F5 becomes a replication and must be framed that way.

F6 needs a wet lab the team does not have, resin leachables may inhibit growth or bind amino acids, and pore size is not well separated from the bulge width. I did not verify any resin's biocompatibility in this run.
Not found: any public dataset from a second laboratory with front speed and growth rate for the same system; Liu 2019 is a candidate whose data availability I did not check.
first_week: Day 1: read Narla PDF and Phan 2024; correct the equation transcription if needed; hash all files in scratch/scout-patterns/dl/cremer.
Day 2: write PREREGISTRATION.md from this design and commit it alone (Freeze A). Ask the Lean thread whether the four algebraic statements on Eq 21 fit the current law-set conventions.
Day 3: analysis code and synthetic-data tests (commit 2), including one planted failure per prediction.
Day 4: add data modules for MOESM13, 15, 16, 21; score F1, F3 (speed and sheet profiles), F4; write RESULTS.md.
Day 5: download the confocal archive, extract the two folders, score F2. Start the Python 3 port of gp_chemotaxis.py.
Days 6 to 7: finish the port, regression check, Freeze B, launch the 36-run M2 matrix; update the dashboard track with pass/refuted/inconclusive per prediction.
design.compute_needed: Laptop is enough. F1 to F4 are spreadsheet-scale. M2: each run is a 1D radial grid of 2000 cells, dt 0.5 s over 86,400 s (172,800 steps, from the published parameter block); 36 runs. I have not timed a run; if one exceeds about an hour on the Windows box, fan the 36 runs out on Modal CPU containers. No GPU and no cluster needed. Storage: 168 MB confocal archive on C:/Temp/<project> or O:, not D:.
design.physical_build: None is required for F1 to F5. Conditional build for F6: a Formlabs-printed insert for a 90 mm dish with three sectors, open (tau = 1), and two obstacle lattices designed for tau about 1.5 and 2.0, pores as small as the printer allows (a sibling agent's table, agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json, gives 0.2 mm minimum wall on Form 4). Print, post-cure, leach in water, measure tau per sector by dye diffusion, then a partner BSL-1 lab pours 0.25% soft agar with glycerol + 100 uM aspartate, inoculates wild-type K-12 at the centre and time-lapses the front. A second printed part, a dish holder with a dark-field light ring, makes the time-lapse reproducible. Without a lab this stays a frozen conditional prediction.

laws.label: laws-patterns
laws.lawset_version: 1.6.0 (lean/registry/lawsets/current.json -> lawset-1.6.0.json, created 2026-11-01T04:37:40.476Z, previous 1.5.0, 53 pinned laws). None of the pattern or cell-geometry laws relevant to this track is pinned in it: turing-ddi-linear-condition and the seven CellGeometry laws are status 'candidate' with introduced_in = null (proposed 2026-11-03 against 1.6.0, no later law set cut). Library read at git commit cb92aaf (2026-11-12).

existing.theorem_or_def: Delphi.Turing.turing_instability_iff (with structure TuringSystem, def D, def T, def WellMixedStable)
existing.status: candidate v1.0.0 (not in lawset 1.6.0; approval null; origin agent). proposals/turing-ddi-linear-condition/result.json: build ok, axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], 3/3 statement mutants rejected.
existing.statement_plain: For a two-species reaction-diffusion system linearised at a uniform steady state with Jacobian [[a,b],[c,d]] and diffusivities Du, Dv > 0: if the state is stable without diffusion (a+d < 0, ad-bc > 0), then some spatial mode with squared wavenumber q > 0 has negative mode determinant D(q) = Du Dv q^2 - (Dv a + Du d) q + (ad - bc) if and only if 2 sqrt(Du Dv (ad-bc)) < Dv a + Du d.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: File header 'What is not proved here': (1) nothing about organisms, i.e. that a tissue or colony is governed by such a system, or which chemicals u, v are; (2) nothing nonlinear: existence, selection and stability of the finite-amplitude pattern; (3) nothing about finite domains: on a bounded domain only a discrete set of q is admissible, so the continuum condition is necessary and not sufficient for a pattern on a given domain (header points to studio/lean/Admissible.lean, which is NOT in this repository). Registry scope.basis adds: two species, constant positive diffusivities, unbounded domain, no growth or mechanics.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: It is the only pattern-forming law in the library. For a two-morphogen synthetic circuit in a microbial lawn it splits the 6-parameter space (a,b,c,d,Du,Dv) into 'can pattern linearly' and 'cannot'. Any design whose measured or committed Jacobian and diffusivities give Dv a + Du d <= 2 sqrt(Du Dv det J) is eliminated as a deterministic Turing patterner before an experiment. My own corollary calculation (not in the file): with a > 0 > d the condition is equivalent to Dv/Du > ((sqrt(ad-bc) + sqrt(-bc))/a)^2; for the file's worked system (a=1,b=-2,c=2,d=-3) that is (1+2)^2 = 9, and the file uses Dv/Du = 10. So the law turns into a minimum diffusivity-ratio requirement on the two signals.

existing.statement_plain: With Du = Dv and the uniform state stable without diffusion, the mode determinant D(q) is strictly positive for every q >= 0, so no mode is unstable.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: a TWO-SPECIES result only; with three or more species Turing instability with equal diffusivities is possible (Marcon et al. 2016, doi:10.7554/eLife.14022), 'so this corollary must not be applied to larger networks'.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Eliminates the whole family 'two freely diffusing small-molecule signals of similar size (e.g. two acyl-homoserine lactones with near-equal diffusivity) produce a deterministic Turing pattern'. The design must either make the diffusivities differ, or add a third (possibly non-diffusing) node, in which case this corollary no longer applies and the library has no law at all.

existing.statement_plain: If the well-mixed state is stable, every mode q >= 0 has negative trace T(q) = (a+d) - (Du+Dv) q. If a mode has D(q) < 0, the characteristic polynomial lam^2 - T lam + D has a strictly positive real root (a growing mode).
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Same header as above. The link from 'positive root of the 2x2 characteristic polynomial' to 'a solution of the linearised PDE grows' is not stated in Lean; it is the standard separation-of-variables step and stays in prose.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: trace_neg_of_wellMixed rules out oscillatory (Hopf/wave) onset within this model class: any design claim of a travelling or oscillating pattern arising from a two-species system that is stable when well mixed cannot rest on this model. exists_pos_growth_of_D_neg is what justifies reading D(q) < 0 as 'the pattern grows'.

existing.statement_plain: A concrete system J = [[1,-2],[2,-3]], Du = 1, Dv = 10 is stable without diffusion (trace -2, det 1) and unstable at q = 1/4: D(1/4) = 10/16 - 7/4 + 1 = -1/8 (numbers from the file). It satisfies 2 sqrt(10) < 7.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: None beyond the model; it is a non-vacuity witness, dimensionless, not a biological parameter set.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Template for the positive side of the loop: a frozen design is entered as a TuringSystem with rational numbers and norm_num shows it is inside the patterning region. From the proof's minimiser q* = (Dv a + Du d)/(2 Du Dv), my calculation for this system gives q* = 7/20 and a fastest-determinant wavelength 2 pi / sqrt(q*) = 2 pi / 0.5916 = 10.6 length units; that wavelength statement is NOT a theorem in the file (see missing).

existing.statement_plain: Three walls of equal positive tension balanced at a point meet pairwise at exactly 120 degrees; cell size does not enter. junction_inner is the general Neumann triangle T3^2 = T1^2 + T2^2 + 2 T1 T2 cos(angle(u,v)) for unequal tensions.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header 'What is assumed, not proved': walls are fluid films of uniform tension in static equilibrium; the force balance at a junction is the whole model; nothing is said about how a tissue reaches equilibrium or whether a given epithelium is one.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: For close-packed microbial monolayers or foams of cells where interfaces behave as tensioned films, it fixes the vertex angle distribution: a predicted spatial pattern with equal-tension triple vertices at angles other than 120 degrees is eliminated; with unequal tensions junction_inner converts measured angles into tension ratios (a measurable design variable for adhesion-engineered strains). It does not apply to rigid rod-shaped cells, which are not fluid films.

existing.statement_plain: A straight-walled polygonal cell whose every corner is a 120 degree junction has exactly six sides; fewer than six sides force a mean corner sharper than 120 degrees, more than six a blunter one.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: about a single convex polygon with straight sides; curved walls between unequal cells (partitionCurvature in the Thompson module) are outside it.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Narrows the admissible tilings of a 2D colony or spot lattice: a design that asks for a regular straight-walled non-hexagonal cell tiling under equal tension is eliminated; non-hexagonal cells must have curved walls, i.e. pressure differences.

existing.statement_plain: In any trivalent closed lattice on a sphere the mean number of sides per face is 6 - 12/F, strictly below six; a trivalent closed lattice of only pentagons and hexagons has exactly twelve pentagons.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: consequences of Euler's formula and handshaking, 'true of every such lattice and therefore uninformative about which lattice an organism builds'. Sphere topology and trivalent vertices are hypotheses carried in the structures.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: A topological budget for patterns on closed surfaces (spherical colonies, cysts, droplets, hollow aggregates): any claimed spot or cell lattice on a sphere with all-hexagonal neighbours is eliminated; twelve five-fold defects (net) are forced. On a flat plate it gives no constraint.

existing.statement_plain: Equal discs on the hexagonal lattice cover pi/(2 sqrt 3) of the plane, between 0.9068 and 0.9070 (bounds proved in the file), more than the square lattice's pi/4.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: compares two lattice arrangements only; does NOT prove the hexagonal arrangement is the densest of all packings of equal discs (Thue 1910, Fejes Toth 1940), 'that theorem is not formalised here'.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Gives the areal coverage of an ideal hexagonal spot or coccoid-cell lattice, so a design claiming a hexagonal lattice of round colonies or cells with coverage outside (0.9068, 0.9070) at contact is eliminated. It cannot yet be used as an upper bound on coverage for arbitrary arrangements (optimality missing).

existing.statement_plain: Four walls of equal positive tension balanced at a point and meeting at equal angles meet at arccos(-1/3), strictly between 90 and 120 degrees; without the equal-angle assumption the six pairwise cosines sum to -2.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Same header as tripleJunction_120: fluid films of uniform tension in static equilibrium.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: The 3D analogue for biofilm or aggregate interiors: fixes the admissible junction geometry of a 3D cellular foam pattern; weaker relevance to a plate-based spatial-pattern experiment.

existing.status: proved; no registry entry (module moved into this repo 2026-11-12, commit cb92aaf); claim ids thompson1917-ch07-06 and ch07-04
existing.statement_plain: Two cells in a medium with cell-medium tensions T1, T2 and cell-cell tension T3: if T3 exceeds both, the external angle is below 120 degrees; if T3 >= T1 + T2, equilibrium forces T3 = T1 + T2 and the cells touch only at a point. The wall between two cells of radii r1, r2 has curvature 1/r1 - 1/r2, zero exactly when the cells are equal.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: The module has no 'assumed' section; its header only names the topics (Laplace pressure, liquid cylinders, triple junctions, bee's cell, Errera). The assumptions are the hypotheses of each theorem: planar junction (EuclideanSpace R (Fin 2)), unit wall directions, static force balance, uniform tension per interface.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Gives a tension-ratio criterion for whether two cell types or droplets adhere over an area or only touch: an adhesion-patterning design (engineered adhesins sorting two strains) that needs a flat shared interface is eliminated if the committed interfacial tensions satisfy T3 >= T1 + T2.

existing.status: proved; no registry entry; claim id thompson1917-ch05-12
existing.statement_plain: A liquid cylinder of radius r0 is unstable to a varicose undulation of wavelength L longer than its circumference 2 pi r0: at constant volume the undulated surface has less area than the cylinder.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: No header assumptions section. From the definition's docstring: the perturbation is r(z) = a + eps cos(2 pi z / L) at constant volume and the area is replaced by an upper bound using sqrt(1 + r'^2) <= 1 + r'^2/2; surface energy is the only energy (no viscosity, no growth, no dynamics, no fastest-growing wavelength).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: The only other wavelength-threshold instability in the library. For a pattern made by break-up of a fluid-like filament or streamer of cells or matrix into beads, it eliminates bead spacings shorter than the circumference: spacing L <= 2 pi r0 cannot arise from this mechanism.

existing.status: proved; no registry entry; claim ids thompson1917-ch08-01, ch08-02
existing.statement_plain: For a box-shaped cell the plane bisecting wall of least area cuts across the longest axis; for a box a x b x c with c <= b <= a <= 2b the next division is at right angles to the first.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: No header assumptions section. Model: cell is a rectangular box, the new wall is a plane bisector, and the cell chooses the least-area wall (Errera's rule is the hypothesis, not a theorem about cells).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Constrains division-plane sequences and hence lineage geometry in a growing microcolony: under Errera's rule an elongated cell cannot divide lengthwise. Weak for this track because rod-shaped bacteria place the septum by other mechanisms; usable only as a named hypothesis.

existing.theorem_or_def: ThompsonLaws.Hygromorphs.diffusiveTime, diffusiveTime_scale, diffusiveRate, diffusionMode, diffusionMode_heat, diffusionMode_boundary, diffusionMode_decay
existing.status: proved; no registry entry; claim id hygromorph-response-time
existing.statement_plain: The diffusive time across thickness h is h^2/D and scales as k^2 when h is scaled by k. The function exp(-pi^2 D t / h^2) sin(pi x / h) satisfies the 1D heat equation u_t = D u_xx, vanishes at x = 0 and x = h, and decays at rate pi^2 D / h^2.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: 'Formalizations of the mathematical core of the claims' of the plant hygromorph claim set; no assumptions section. Model: pure diffusion with constant D, one dimension, fixed-concentration boundaries, a single eigenmode (not a general solution, no uniqueness).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: This is the only place in the library where a diffusion PDE is actually differentiated in Lean, so it is the reusable proof pattern (HasDerivAt on exp * sin) for a reaction-diffusion mode lemma. It also bounds signal equilibration time: a design that needs a morphogen to equilibrate over distance h in time much less than h^2/(pi^2 D) is eliminated under pure diffusion.

existing.status: proved; no registry entry; claim ids darwin1859-ch03-01, ch03-02
existing.statement_plain: Unchecked geometric growth N0 r^t with r > 1 exceeds any bound K in finitely many generations, and reaches a target M within log(M/N0)/log(r) generations.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: 'What is proved is that the conclusion follows from the assumptions, not that any population satisfies them.' Discrete generations, constant multiplier, no density dependence, no space.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Supplies only the well-mixed growth clock (time to reach a quorum threshold density). It has no spatial term; there is no logistic growth, no carrying-capacity ODE and no front in the library. Useful as the growth half of a future Fisher-KPP statement.

existing.statement_plain: A rate scaled as X0 Q10^((T - Tref)/10) has ratio Q10^((T2 - T1)/10) between two temperatures; the log ratio is linear in T2 - T1.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header 'Named hypotheses: the Q10 form itself (an empirical rule, not a theorem of physics)'. The registry scope and constants were sourced for fish muscle, not microbes.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: The only accepted, pinned law that can serve the 'test a new condition' step: if growth rate r and kinetic rates are committed to a Q10, a temperature shift fixes the ratio of rates, and (once a wavelength or front-speed law exists) the predicted change in pattern scale. Using it for bacteria needs a microbial Q10 source; none is in the registry.

existing.theorem_or_def: Delphi.Constraints.ne_of_lt_intervals, Delphi.Constraints.cubeLaw_rules_out', Delphi.Constraints.exponent_rules_out (and the other *_rules_out lemmas: kimura_rate_rules_out, fisher_rules_out, twofold_rules_out, ...)
existing.statement_plain: For each formalised law, a lemma that derives False from the law plus a candidate's committed intervals, with a last hypothesis that is a decidable arithmetic fact about the committed numbers.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: 'an elimination is only as strong as the law's own assumptions'; 'A candidate that does not commit to those assumptions is not eliminated: the checker reports cannot rule, never passes'; 'Nothing here says a surviving candidate is possible.'
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: This file imports Kimura, Favored, Fisher, MaynardSmith and Thompson only. It has NO lemma for Turing or CellGeometry, and the registry entry for turing-ddi-linear-condition has constraints: []. So today no pattern design can be eliminated by a generated certificate; the constraint lemma has to be written first (see missing).

existing.statement_plain: Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection in partial-change form for one haploid locus: the change in mean fitness under one round of selection times mean fitness equals the variance in fitness.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: one locus, finitely many types, haploid or clonal, discrete generations, fitnesses held fixed (no frequency dependence, no environmental change).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Listed to prevent a naming error: this is NOT the Fisher-KPP front-speed law. I searched every .lean file under lean/ for KPP, front speed, wave speed, travelling/traveling, logistic, chemotaxis, quorum, colony, biofilm: no hits. There is no travelling-wave or range-expansion law in the library. For this track Fisher.lean only constrains competition between strains in a well-mixed culture.

Companion: equal_diffusivity_rules_out: Du = Dv and (exists q >= 0, D S q <= 0) -> False.

missing.source: Turing 1952, doi:10.1098/rstb.1952.0012 (verified=true, fetched https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1098/rstb.1952.0012 in this run). Interval form is my own derivation from turing_instability_iff.

missing.law: Unstable band, critical wavenumber and pattern wavelength
missing.statement_math: With m = Du Dv, P = Dv a + Du d, Delta = ad - bc and P^2 > 4 m Delta: {q > 0 : D(q) < 0} = (q-, q+), q+- = (P +- sqrt(P^2 - 4 m Delta)) / (2m). At onset (P^2 = 4 m Delta) the critical squared wavenumber is q_c = sqrt(Delta/(Du Dv)) and the wavelength is lambda_c = 2 pi / sqrt(q_c). Fastest-growing mode: argmax over q of lam_+(q) = (T(q) + sqrt(T(q)^2 - 4 D(q)))/2.
missing.why_needed: The track's observable is a spacing (stripe or spot period). The existing theorem only says 'some q is unstable'; it does not say which, so no predicted wavelength can be compared with a plate image and no wavelength claim can be ruled out.
missing.difficulty: easy for the band and q_c (roots of a quadratic; the proof of turing_instability_iff already uses the minimiser P/(2m)); moderate for the fastest-growing mode (maximising an expression with a square root needs calculus on lam_+(q)).
missing.source: Murray, Mathematical Biology (2003), doi:10.1007/b98869 (verified=true, Crossref book record resolved in this run; I did not open the chapter text, so the formulas above are standard results re-derived by me, unverified against the page). Turing 1952 doi:10.1098/rstb.1952.0012 (verified=true).

missing.law: Critical diffusivity ratio and the self-activation requirement
missing.statement_math: Under WellMixedStable: (exists q > 0, D(q) < 0) implies exactly one of a, d is positive; and if a > 0 > d then instability iff Dv/Du > ((sqrt(ad - bc) + sqrt(-bc)) / a)^2. My derivation: put s = sqrt(Dv/Du) in Dv a + Du d > 2 sqrt(Du Dv Delta), giving a s^2 - 2 sqrt(Delta) s + d > 0, whose larger root is (sqrt(Delta) + sqrt(Delta - ad))/a and Delta - ad = -bc. Check against the file's witness: (1 + 2)^2 = 9 < 10.
missing.why_needed: Diffusivity ratio is the quantity a circuit designer can actually choose (signal size, matrix binding, degradation). This form converts the iff into a one-number design requirement and into a necessary sign structure for the network (one self-enhancing species), which eliminates network topologies before any parameter is measured.
missing.difficulty: easy: algebra over reals with one square root; needs bc < 0 derived from a > 0 > d and det > 0.
missing.source: Derived by me from lean/Delphi/Turing.lean (calculation shown). Background reference: Gierer and Meinhardt 1972, doi:10.1007/BF00289234 (verified=true via Crossref); Diego et al. 2018, doi:10.1103/PhysRevX.8.021071 (verified=true via Crossref) for topology-only conditions.

missing.law: Finite-domain mode admissibility (minimum domain size)
missing.statement_math: On [0, L] with zero-flux boundaries the admissible squared wavenumbers are q_n = (n pi / L)^2, n in N. A linearly growing non-uniform mode exists iff exists n >= 1 with q- < (n pi / L)^2 < q+. Corollary: L < pi / sqrt(q+) implies no pattern. Number of half-wavelengths n satisfies L sqrt(q-)/pi < n < L sqrt(q+)/pi.
missing.why_needed: A colony, droplet or microfluidic chamber is a bounded domain. The file header itself says the continuum condition is 'necessary and not sufficient' on a bounded domain and points to studio/lean/Admissible.lean, which is not in this repository. This is the law that makes domain size a testable new condition (shrink the chamber, the pattern must vanish or lose a stripe).
missing.difficulty: easy to moderate: the algebraic statement is easy; proving that cos(n pi x / L) are the Neumann eigenfunctions and satisfy the linearised PDE follows the diffusionMode_heat pattern in ThompsonLaws/Hygromorphs.lean (moderate, vector-valued).
missing.source: Murray 2003, doi:10.1007/b98869 (verified=true as a record; formulas re-derived, not checked against the page). Crampin, Gaffney and Maini 1999, doi:10.1006/bulm.1999.0131 (verified=true via Crossref) for the growing-domain extension.

missing.law: Mode-growth bridge from the 2x2 algebra to the linearised PDE
missing.statement_math: If lam and v != 0 satisfy (J - k^2 diag(Du, Dv)) v = lam v, then w(x,t) = exp(lam t) cos(k x) v solves w_t = J w + diag(Du, Dv) w_xx; hence D(k^2) < 0 gives a solution whose amplitude grows without bound.
missing.why_needed: Today 'D(q) < 0' is interpreted as instability only in the docstring. Without this lemma a certificate eliminates a statement about a quadratic, not about a reaction-diffusion system; the bridge is what lets the registry say the law is about patterns.
missing.difficulty: moderate: HasDerivAt for R^2-valued functions and second derivatives in x; the scalar version exists (diffusionMode_heat), the vector version is bookkeeping.
missing.source: Turing 1952, doi:10.1098/rstb.1952.0012 (verified=true).

missing.law: Fisher-KPP front speed (range expansion of a colony)
missing.statement_math: For u_t = D u_xx + r u (1 - u/K): (i) linear dispersion: u = exp(-s (x - c t)) solves u_t = D u_xx + r u iff c = D s + r/s, hence c >= 2 sqrt(r D) with equality at s = sqrt(r/D); (ii) monotone travelling waves with 0 < u < K exist iff c >= c* = 2 sqrt(r D); (iii) compactly supported initial data spread at exactly c*.
missing.why_needed: Colony radius versus time is the cheapest spatial readout in a microbial experiment, and expanding-front systems lay down their stripes at the front, so spacing depends on front speed. The task brief assumed this law exists; it does not (no hit for KPP, front, wave speed, logistic anywhere under lean/). With it, a design committing r, D and a front speed outside the bound is eliminated, and a change in r (temperature via q10_ratio, nutrient) predicts the new speed as sqrt of the ratio.
missing.difficulty: easy for (i) (AM-GM on D s + r/s plus one HasDerivAt); hard for (ii) and (iii): phase-plane existence and the parabolic comparison principle are not in Mathlib.
missing.source: Fisher 1937, doi:10.1111/j.1469-1809.1937.tb02153.x (verified=true via Crossref: 'The wave of advance of advantageous genes', Annals of Eugenics 7:355-369). Aronson and Weinberger 1978, doi:10.1016/0001-8708(78)90130-5 (verified=true via Crossref) for (iii). Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov 1937 has no DOI I could resolve: verified=false. Experimental scope for bacterial colonies: Wakita et al. 1994, doi:10.1143/JPSJ.63.1205 (verified=true as a record; content not read).

missing.law: Chemotactic (Keller-Segel) aggregation threshold
missing.statement_math: rho_t = Dr rho_xx - chi (rho c_x)_x, c_t = Dc c_xx + alpha rho - beta c, uniform state (rho0, alpha rho0 / beta). Mode matrix [[-Dr q, chi rho0 q],[alpha, -Dc q - beta]] has negative trace and determinant q (Dr Dc q + Dr beta - chi rho0 alpha), so some q > 0 is unstable iff chi rho0 alpha > Dr beta, and the unstable band is 0 < q < (chi rho0 alpha - Dr beta)/(Dr Dc). (My derivation, shown.)
missing.why_needed: Most real microbial spatial patterns (aggregates, spots, travelling bands) come from directed motility, not from two diffusing morphogens. TuringSystem has diagonal diffusion only, so it cannot express a cross-diffusion term; a design based on chemotaxis is currently outside every law ('cannot rule'). The threshold makes cell density rho0 the experimental knob: below Dr beta/(chi alpha) no aggregation.
missing.difficulty: easy for the linear threshold (same quadratic-in-q machinery, here the determinant is linear after factoring q); hard for anything nonlinear (blow-up, band profile).
missing.source: Keller and Segel 1970, doi:10.1016/0022-5193(70)90092-5 (verified=true via Crossref); Keller and Segel 1971, doi:10.1016/0022-5193(71)90051-8 (verified=true via Crossref). Range-expansion context: Cremer et al. 2019, doi:10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (verified=true as a record; content not read).

missing.law: Density-dependent motility instability (stripe formation in engineered expanding populations)
missing.statement_math: rho_t = (mu(rho) rho)_xx + g rho (1 - rho/rho_s). Linearising the flux term at rho0: delta_t = (mu(rho0) + rho0 mu'(rho0)) delta_xx, so the uniform state is diffusively unstable iff mu(rho0) + rho0 mu'(rho0) < 0, i.e. d ln mu / d ln rho < -1. (My derivation, shown; short-wavelength regularisation and the signal equation h_t = Dh h_xx + alpha rho - beta h are needed for a finite wavelength.)
missing.why_needed: This is the mechanism of the best-characterised synthetic stripe-forming bacterial system, so it is the most likely concrete circuit for this track. A law here would constrain how steeply motility must fall with density for any stripe to appear, and eliminate designs whose measured motility-density curve is too shallow.
missing.difficulty: easy for the sign condition (one derivative); moderate to hard for the wavelength, which needs the coupled signal equation and a regularising term.
missing.source: Liu et al. 2011, doi:10.1126/science.1209042 (verified=true via Crossref); Fu et al. 2012, doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.198102 (verified=true via Crossref); Cates et al. 2010, doi:10.1073/pnas.1001994107 (verified=true via Crossref); Curatolo et al. 2020, doi:10.1038/s41567-020-0964-z (verified=true via Crossref). I resolved the records only and did not read the papers in this run; that they use exactly this equation is unverified background.

missing.law: Morphogen decay length and band-detect ring position
missing.statement_math: Steady state of c_t = D c_xx - k c with c(0) = c0, c -> 0: c(x) = c0 exp(-x / ell), ell = sqrt(D/k). A band-pass receiver responding for theta_lo <= c <= theta_hi lights exactly on ell ln(c0/theta_hi) <= x <= ell ln(c0/theta_lo); ring width = ell ln(theta_hi/theta_lo), independent of c0.

The law gives two eliminations: ring width cannot depend on sender strength, and ring radius shifts by ell ln 2 per doubling of c0. The library has diffusive time h^2/D but no decay length.
missing.difficulty: easy: exp satisfies the ODE (HasDerivAt), logs of positive reals; uniqueness of the bounded solution is moderate.

The closed-form ring formulas are my derivation from the stated model, not taken from the paper. Related: Payne et al. 2013, doi:10.1038/msb.2013.55 (verified=true as a record; content not read).

missing.statement_math: For n species with Jacobian J and D = diag(D1..Dn), Di >= 0: the uniform state is unstable at q iff J - q D has an eigenvalue with positive real part. For n = 3 with one immobile species, give the Routh-Hurwitz conditions on the characteristic cubic of J - q D and show a system with D1 = D2 > 0, D3 = 0 that is stable at q = 0 and unstable at some q > 0.
