explain.label: explain2-track-4
explain.one_line: We will print 21 spinning seed models, drop them in water, and test whether a published computer model or a simple rule better predicts how fast they sink.
explain.what: Some trees make fruit with two curved wings. When it falls, the fruit spins like a helicopter blade. Scientists call this spinning fall "autorotation". It just means the fruit turns by itself as it drops. Researchers 3D-printed copies of such fruit. They dropped the copies in a tall tank of water. We want to write down our guesses first. Then we will print 21 new shapes and drop them. We have two guesses to compare. The first is a published computer model. It cuts each wing into thin strips and adds up the push of the water on every strip. The second is a much simpler rule, built by the earlier designer. It is a short formula with one number you can adjust. The test measures how fast each model sinks at a steady speed. It does not measure sideways gliding. So far this is only a plan. We have no new results.
explain.why: Spinning fruit fall slowly. So wind can carry the seeds away from the parent tree. If we can predict the best wing curve, we learn how a simple shape gets good flight. This test also checks a published model. We write our guess before we look, so nobody can say we tuned it afterwards. A miss would be useful too. We do not claim this will help medicine or machines yet.

steps.text: Download the public data and the model code from the research group. Both are free to reuse under the MIT licence.
steps.picture: Borrowing a recipe book that the cook says anyone may copy.

steps.text: Redo the earlier arithmetic from scratch. Every number we checked came out the same, apart from tiny rounding.
steps.picture: Adding up a restaurant bill a second time and getting the same total.

steps.text: Write down what the computer model predicts for each of 21 new wing shapes. Then seal the file. Sealing means saving it so it cannot be changed. We do this before any drop happens. For example, an invented prediction might read: 'this shape sinks at 8 centimetres per second'.
steps.picture: Calling the score before the match starts.

steps.text: Write down what the simple rival rule predicts for the same shapes. It is the earlier designer's own rule. It is not a proven law.
steps.picture: Asking a second friend to guess the score too.

steps.text: Print the 21 shapes. Each differs in how curved the wings are. Each also differs in the tilt of the wing root. The root is the spot where the wing joins the seed. Tilt is the angle of that join.
steps.picture: Baking 21 loaves, each with a slightly different shape.

steps.text: Drop each shape in a tall water tank and time its steady sinking speed. That is the constant speed it reaches once it stops speeding up. Repeat the drops, because copies of the same shape differ by a few percent. We do not yet know how many repeats we will do.
steps.picture: Dropping the same stone many times to see how much the timing wobbles.

steps.text: Compare the sealed guesses with the measured speeds. Say the invented guess was 8 centimetres per second and the tank gave 7. We then ask whether that 1 centimetre gap is bigger than the usual scatter between copies. Count a win only if it is.
steps.picture: Two runners are only separate if they finish further apart than the stopwatch error.

steps.text: Publish the result, including a miss. We also plan a second test with a flat plate that really glides sideways.
steps.picture: Telling the team both the wins and the flops.

explain.wrong_if: Here is our bet, written before we look. The model should pick the right wing curve. It should also put the shapes with a tilted root in the right order of speed. We call the model wrong if it misses by more than the usual scatter between copies of one shape. If the simple rule does as well, the strip model adds nothing. Old public data already hint at this. We fitted the simple rule to ten sets of old data. That means we adjusted it afterwards to match them. Its average miss was 0.055. The model's was 0.088. The miss is measured as a ratio, so smaller is better. Think of about 5.5 percent against 8.8 percent. These were fits to old data. They were not guesses made in advance.
could_go_wrong: The test measures sinking speed, not sideways gliding. So our glide-distance rule does not apply to it.
The published model is partly tuned. Its drag was reduced and its weight set to 1.2 grams. So it was not a pure prediction.
Copies of one shape differ by a few percent. That can make a close contest end in a tie.
The simple rival rule is the earlier designer's own construction. It may be a weak or unfair opponent.

At a root tilt of 15 degrees, the model and the rival differ by only about 6.5 percent. Two repeat rounds of the same shape at zero tilt already differ by about 7 percent. So the gap we want to see is no bigger than the noise.
The published experiments used only two tilts, 0 and 35 degrees. So there is no data at all for 15 degrees.
One of our planned checks may be too easy. It might pass whatever happens, so it would prove nothing. We could not find the file that sets it, so we cannot say for sure.
The public data could change if the repository owner updates it.

questions.q: How do you know the earlier numbers are right?
questions.a: We downloaded the files again. We checked their fingerprints, which are short codes that change if the file changes. Then we re-ran the sums. The results matched, apart from tiny rounding. That shows the numbers were read correctly. It does not show the physics idea is right.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We have not printed or dropped a single new fruit. We have not tested a tilt of 15 degrees in water. We did not re-run every computer simulation the reviewers used. Some of the test design files we could not find.

questions.q: Why drop things in water instead of air?
questions.a: The researchers used a tall tank of water. The flow in water behaves like fast air around a larger seed. Water also makes the fall slow enough to time.

questions.q: How many times is each shape dropped?
questions.a: We do not know yet. The plan only says the drops are repeated. The number is not fixed in the facts we have.

questions.q: What does the wing fold number mean, and what does tilt do?
questions.a: The fold value is a number for how curved the wing is. The tilt is the angle where the wing joins the seed. In the public data, the same fruit shape sank at 0.1011 metres per second with no tilt. At a 35 degree tilt it sank at 0.0676 metres per second. That is about 10 centimetres per second against 7. The first is a slow walk across a kitchen. So tilting the root made the fruit sink about 1.5 times slower.

questions.q: Is this about gliding?
questions.a: No. A spinning fruit sinks nearly straight down. We read our glide-distance rule as giving zero for it, so it says nothing here. That is why we also plan a flat-plate glider test. A flat plate is a thin sheet that can drift sideways as it falls.

questions.q: Do real fruits match the best curve?
questions.a: Partly. We have data on 27 wild fruits, meaning fruits gathered from trees outside the lab. Their average fold value was 1.8, with about 10 percent measurement error. That sits near the model's best value for one tilt. The tilt of each real fruit was not reported, so we do not know more.

questions.q: Does wind carry real fruit as far as a simple sum says?
questions.a: No. A simple wind-drift sum came out about 4 to 8 times too far for twelve tropical fruit species. The middle value was about 7 times. Real fruits land much closer to the tree. We do not use this sum in the test.

questions.q: Why does the glide rule matter at all?
questions.a: It is a side thread and does not change the test. Our project keeps a list of rules, and each rule has a maths proof checked by a computer. One rule links wing shape to gliding. Long, thin wings glide further, but only up to a limit. It assumes a standard simple drag model. So it is a limit, not a measurement.

questions.q: Who disagrees on why spinning seeds fall slowly?
questions.a: One account says a small whirl of air sticks to the front edge of the wing and adds lift. The other fits a simple curve to measurements. The model we chose uses the curve, not the whirl.

tracks.title: A new biomaterial, printed on Formlabs

scout.summary: Five printable, passive architectures whose geometry is fixed by a law already in the Lean library (ThompsonLaws at upstream commit cb92aaf, 2026-11-12). The strongest is a vat-printed humidity bilayer flap made from two Formlabs elastomers: the Timoshenko law plus the 0.2 mm minimum wall leaves only a soft passive layer (Flexible 50A or Silicone 40A) under a Flexible 80A V2 active layer, and predicts normalised curvature kappa*h/d_eps = 1.5 at a thickness ratio of about 1.8. I checked the bound against public data I downloaded: in six beech bilayer configurations (ETH dataset, 3 KB CSV) the measured kappa*h/d_eps peaks at 1.50-1.53 against the bound of 1.5, and falls to 0.91 at equal thickness, as the law says. Second is a hollow strut with a lattice or powder core, where the law gives one inner/outer radius ratio k* = sqrt(1-q). The other three (diffusion-clocked flaps, Murray manifold, self-buckling column) are weaker on data or on discriminating power. Main gaps: no humid-air swelling number exists for any Formlabs resin (only full-immersion figures), the 3/2 bound theorem is derived on paper but is not yet in the Lean file, and no public dataset was found for vat-printed hygromorphs, hollow printed struts or Plateau-junction lattices.
scout.recommended: Run the printer-limited hygromorph flap (candidate 1). It is the only candidate where the law, the printer's 0.2 mm wall limit and the resin catalogue together cut the design space to two material pairs and one thickness ratio, and the same bound already reproduces public wood-bilayer data to within about 2% at the optimum; it also plugs straight into the Marom-Buehler pipeline as a new machine backend, and its prints double as the timing test of candidate 3.

candidates.name: Printer-limited hygromorph flap (two-elastomer vat-printed bilayer)
candidates.system: Bilayer strip or shading flap, 60 x 5 mm, total thickness 0.8 mm: Formlabs Flexible 80A V2 as the swelling layer on Flexible 50A (or Silicone 40A) as the non-swelling layer. Printed as two parts on a Form 4 and bonded with uncured resin plus post-cure (single-job two-material printing was not found by the sibling materials agent).
candidates.phenotype_measured: Equilibrium curvature kappa (1/m) from an edge-on photo and circle fit, reported as the dimensionless kappa*h/d_eps; plus free linear swelling strain d_eps of single-layer coupons.
candidates.why_it_fits: The law removes most of the catalogue. Timoshenko curvature is kappa = f(m,n)*d_eps/h, with f <= 3/2 and equality at thickness ratio m = n^(-1/2). With Flexible 80A as the active layer (secant modulus about 5.8 MPa), a stiff passive layer needs a wall far below the 0.2 mm printable minimum: Tough 1000 would need 0.058 mm and Rigid 10K 0.019 mm at h = 0.8 mm. Forced to 0.2 mm they reach only f = 0.86 and f = 0.15. Only a passive layer softer than or similar to the active one lands at the optimum with both walls printable: Flexible 50A (n = 0.31, passive 0.514 mm, active 0.286 mm) or Silicone 40A (n = 0.138, passive 0.583 mm, active 0.217 mm). That is a non-obvious, checkable design rule for a partner who builds bio-based printed skins and has no passive responsive element yet. It also extends the Marom-Buehler pipeline to a new machine backend (their only instance is filament printing), which their repo names as the extension path.

public_data.what: Source data for the 4D-printed cellulose shading system (Cheng 2024): shade-coverage photos and bilayer tracking. Metadata and the zip file listing were read by range request; the archives themselves were not downloaded (over 20 MB). The 40 MB archive holds 190 entries, mostly JPEG photos.
Formlabs Flexible 80A V2 technical data sheet: stress at 50% elongation, and mass and volume change after water immersion.
public_data.licence: manufacturer data sheet, no open licence

candidates.the_test: Week 1: print 1 mm coupons of Flexible 80A V2, Flexible 50A and Silicone 40A. Measure free linear strain after 24 h at 30% and 90% RH (salt jars) and after 24 h immersion; measure modulus in tension. Freeze the prediction from those numbers before any bilayer is printed. Week 2: print bilayers at h = 0.8 mm with passive/active ratio m = 0.4, 0.8, 1.8 and 3.0 (n = 5 each) plus a Tough 1000 control at 0.2/0.6 mm. Frozen prediction with n = 0.31: f = 0.78, 1.25, 1.50 at m = 0.4, 0.8, 1.8, and f = 0.86 for the Tough 1000 control. If d_eps is 1%, that is 33, 53 and 64 degrees of arc on a 60 mm strip. Pass: the largest curvature is at m = 1.8, no specimen exceeds kappa*h/d_eps = 1.5 beyond measurement error, and each measured f is within 20% of the prediction. Fail on any of the three.
candidates.biggest_risk: The swelling in humid air may be too small to see. The only published figures are for full immersion (+3% volume after 1 day, +7% after 1 week), and humid-air uptake is unknown. Second risk: the two resins may not bond, or the elastomer modulus may change when wet, which is the reported reason Timoshenko over-predicts soft printed bilayers by up to about 4 times in the literature read by the sibling hygromorph agent.
candidates.cost_and_time: About 3 weeks. Three resin cartridges, a humidity jar set and a balance; no cluster compute. Lean work: add the f <= 3/2 theorem (one AM-GM inequality).

candidates.name: Cored hollow strut at the law-fixed radius ratio
candidates.system: Circular strut for a lightweight space-truss or lattice module: solid wall with a low-density core (gyroid lattice core in resin, or trapped unsintered powder in an SLS nylon tube). Inner/outer radius ratio k set by the core-to-wall density ratio q.
candidates.phenotype_measured: Mass (g) at matched bending stiffness EI from three-point bending, reported as the mass factor mu = mass / mass of the solid rod with the same EI.
candidates.why_it_fits: HollowTube.lean proves that with a core of density q times the wall, mass at fixed stiffness is minimised at exactly k* = sqrt(1-q), with mass factor sqrt(q(2-q)), and that a buckling bound t/R >= lambda moves the optimum to min(k*, 1-lambda). One measured number (q) therefore fixes the cross-section. For q = 0.19, k* = 0.90 and the strut is 41% lighter than a solid rod of equal stiffness; for q = 0.52, k* = 0.69 and the saving is 12%. The partner's large printed pieces sit on space trusses and their stated gap is a verified structural envelope with less mass.

public_data.what: Raw compression curves for gyroid and nine other TPMS lattices at several relative densities (Doyle 2025). Nine gyroid files downloaded and analysed here to get the core stiffness scaling.
public_data.size: 91 CSV files, 17.9 MB total; 2.1 MB downloaded

public_data.what: Photogrammetry of 3D-printed cylindrical shells buckling under axial compression, relevant to the local-buckling bound lambda. Found by search only; not downloaded (over 20 MB).

candidates.the_test: Measure q first (weigh a printed core block). Print five struts of equal design stiffness (same I as a 5 mm radius solid rod, span 120 mm) at k = 0, 0.5, 0.7, k*, 0.95, three of each. Weigh, then three-point bend to get EI. Frozen prediction for q = 0.19: mass factor 1.00, 0.82, 0.69, 0.59 (at k* = 0.90), 0.62. Pass: the k* strut is the lightest, its mass factor is within 10% of sqrt(q(2-q)), measured EI of all five agree within 10%, and the 0.95 strut is heavier than the k* strut or fails by wall buckling first.
candidates.biggest_risk: The model counts the core as dead mass with no stiffness. A real lattice core adds some stiffness and also props the wall against buckling, so the measured optimum may sit at a thinner wall than k*. At k* = 0.90 the wall is 0.65 mm on a 6.5 mm outer radius, near the printable limit for a drained resin part.
candidates.cost_and_time: About 2 weeks. One rigid resin or one nylon powder build, a balance and a bench test frame.

candidates.name: Diffusion-clocked flaps (response time set by active-layer thickness)
candidates.system: The same bilayer flap as candidate 1, printed with active-layer thickness 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 mm so that neighbouring flaps open in sequence with no control hardware.
candidates.phenotype_measured: Time to half of final curvature (hours) after a humidity step, from time-lapse photos.
candidates.why_it_fits: Hygromorphs.lean already has the diffusive time h^2/D and the slowest-mode decay rate pi^2*D/h^2, so doubling the active thickness predicts four times the response time. The Marom-Buehler paper predicts and measures only final angles, so a timing test exercises the part of their dynamical framework that has no data yet. For a facade, timing is the design variable that decides whether a flap follows a passing shower or only the daily cycle.

public_data.what: Same beech bilayer time series as candidate 1: curvature at 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 24, 48 h for six configurations that share one active-layer thickness (4.1 mm).

candidates.the_test: Measure D for Flexible 80A V2 from coupon mass uptake versus square root of time. Print flaps with active layer 0.2, 0.4, 0.8 mm at the optimal ratio, n = 5 each; step from 30% to 90% RH; record half-times. Frozen prediction: half-times in the ratio 1 : 4 : 16, absolute value from the measured D. Pass: fitted exponent of half-time against active thickness between 1.7 and 2.3. The plant-tissue literature read by the sibling physics agent reports 1.3-1.5, so a result below 1.7 would be a real finding that surface transport, not bulk diffusion, sets the clock.
candidates.biggest_risk: Dense photopolymer may take days at 0.8 mm; the sibling physics agent estimated 11-160 h at 0.4 mm for dense filament polymers. The test would then run for weeks, and creep could mask the end point.
candidates.cost_and_time: 2 to 4 weeks, mostly waiting; shares all prints with candidate 1.

candidates.name: Murray-law branching manifold for passive irrigation or wicking
candidates.system: Four-generation symmetric bifurcating channel tree printed in clear resin, channel radii following r_parent^x = sum of r_child^x, for a passively fed green wall or evaporative cooling element.
candidates.phenotype_measured: Flow rate at a fixed gravity head (mL/min) for trees of equal total channel volume, giving hydraulic resistance.
candidates.why_it_fits: MurrayCubic.lean proves the cube law from minimum pumping-plus-volume cost and generalises it: the junction exponent is (b+c)/a for any cost law, 3 for Poiseuille flow with a volume cost and 5/2 for a wall-surface cost. The law therefore fixes every radius in the tree from the inlet radius alone.

public_data.what: Code and digitised data for capillary-driven branching networks tested against Murray's law (digitised from Zhang and Lorente 2023). Downloaded and unpacked; contains zl_fig7_data.csv and a Python network model.

candidates.the_test: Print three trees with exponent x = 2, 3 and 4, equal segment lengths, equal total channel volume, smallest channel at least 0.5 mm. Measure flow at a fixed 100 mm water head, five repeats. Frozen prediction (my calculation for a four-generation symmetric tree): relative resistance 240 : 200 : 210, so the x = 3 tree carries 20% more flow than x = 2 and 5% more than x = 4. Pass: x = 3 has the highest flow and the x = 2 to x = 3 ratio is 1.20 within 0.05.
candidates.biggest_risk: The optimum is shallow. The predicted difference between x = 2.5 and x = 3 is only 3%, below what printed-channel roughness and residual resin allow, so the test can reject area-preserving branching but cannot pin the exponent. Architectural value is indirect.
candidates.cost_and_time: About 2 weeks; one clear resin cartridge and a graduated cylinder.

candidates.name: Self-buckling column series (Greenhill height limit in soft resin)
candidates.system: Free-standing vertical cylinders printed in Silicone 40A or Flexible 80A V2 at radius 0.5, 1 and 2 mm and a range of heights: a tabletop model of slender tree-like pavilion columns.
candidates.phenotype_measured: Critical height (mm) at which a column of given radius can no longer stand upright under its own weight.
candidates.why_it_fits: Magnitude.lean defines Greenhill's critical height as C*d^(2/3) and proves a column stands if and only if its diameter exceeds (h/C)^(3/2); LimbBoneSimilarity.lean carries the matching elastic-similarity exponents. The law fixes the slenderness of every member in a scaled family from one constant. Soft resins bring the critical height into the build volume, which stiff resins do not.

public_data.what: Tallo global tree allometry database (height and stem diameter for individual trees), the natural comparison set for the 2/3 exponent. Record metadata fetched; the 49 MB CSV was not downloaded (over 20 MB).

candidates.the_test: Print columns at each radius in 5 mm height steps around the predicted limit, clamp the base, release and record standing or buckled. Frozen prediction for Silicone 40A (assumed modulus 0.8 MPa, density 1100 kg/m3): critical heights 33, 53 and 83 mm at radius 0.5, 1 and 2 mm; the ratio between the largest and smallest must be 4^(2/3) = 2.52 whatever the modulus. Pass: fitted exponent of critical height against diameter between 0.60 and 0.73.
candidates.biggest_risk: Weakest link to a partner need: it validates a scaling rule but does not produce a new material. The absolute heights depend on a modulus Formlabs does not publish, and printed slender elastomer columns may come out bent, which lowers the apparent limit.
candidates.cost_and_time: About 1 week; one elastomer cartridge.

measured_numbers.quantity: Normalised curvature kappa*h/d_eps of beech bilayers at 48 h, for passive fraction r = 0.12, 0.17, 0.22, 0.34, 0.43, 0.49 (law says at most 1.5)
measured_numbers.source: Own calculation (scratch/scout-biomaterial/retro_beech.py) from the downloaded CSV (doi 10.3929/ethz-b-000275694): curvature 4.31, 4.51, 4.26, 3.18, 2.05, 1.57 per m; thickness h1 = 0.6-3.9 mm on h2 = 4.1 mm (Table 1 of doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0205607); d_eps = (0.0019 - 0.0001) per % moisture times the measured moisture drop of 7.7-8.3 points. The swelling coefficients are the paper's nominal beech values, which the paper itself treats as uncertain to 10%, so 1.53 is not a violation.

measured_numbers.quantity: Time to half of 48 h curvature, same six beech configurations (all share a 4.1 mm active layer; total thickness 4.7-8.0 mm)
measured_numbers.value: 3.5 to 3.7 h in all six
measured_numbers.source: Own linear interpolation (scratch/scout-biomaterial/calc2.py) of the downloaded CSV, doi 10.3929/ethz-b-000275694. Curvature at 24 h is 86-97% of the 48 h value, so the 48 h value is not full equilibrium.

measured_numbers.quantity: Flexible 80A V2 after deionised-water immersion (ASTM D471 slab)
measured_numbers.value: +8% mass, +3% volume at 1 day; +9% mass, +7% volume at 1 week
measured_numbers.source: https://media.formlabs.com/asset/af9d9268-d8c4-4019-9ccd-bd3af926c67e/-ENUS-Flexible-80A-V2-TDS.pdf, read by pdftotext in this run. The table columns came out misaligned in extraction; I assigned rows by counting two rows per solvent in the listed order, and the result matches the sibling materials agent's reading.

measured_numbers.quantity: Implied isotropic linear swelling strain of Flexible 80A V2 in water
measured_numbers.value: 0.99% at 1 day, 2.28% at 1 week
measured_numbers.source: Own calculation: (1.03)^(1/3) - 1 and (1.07)^(1/3) - 1. Immersion only; humid-air strain is not published.

measured_numbers.quantity: Flexible 80A V2 stress at 50% elongation, post-cured (used for a secant modulus of about 5.8 MPa)
measured_numbers.value: 2.9 MPa
measured_numbers.source: Same Formlabs data sheet, line 'Stress at 50% Elongation 1.5 MPa / 2.9 MPa'. Secant modulus = 2.9 / 0.5, own estimate. Moduli for Flexible 50A (1.8 MPa), Silicone 40A (0.8 MPa), Tough 1000 (932 MPa) and Rigid 10K (10 GPa) are taken from D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json, not re-fetched by me.

measured_numbers.quantity: Optimal layer thicknesses at h = 0.8 mm with a Flexible 80A active layer
measured_numbers.value: Flexible 50A passive: 0.514 / 0.286 mm (printable). Silicone 40A passive: 0.583 / 0.217 mm (printable). Tough 1000 passive: 0.058 mm (not printable; f = 0.86 at 0.2 mm). Rigid 10K passive: 0.019 mm (not printable; f = 0.15 at 0.2 mm).
measured_numbers.source: Own calculation (scratch/scout-biomaterial/calc.py): m_opt = n^(-1/2), f from the Timoshenko coefficient in upstream/leanbio/lean/ThompsonLaws/Hygromorphs.lean; 0.2 mm minimum wall from spec-formlabs-materials.json.

measured_numbers.quantity: Predicted curvature bound for the 0.8 mm flap
measured_numbers.value: 18.6 per m (radius 54 mm, 64 degrees on a 60 mm strip) at 0.99% strain; 42.8 per m (radius 23 mm) at 2.28% strain
measured_numbers.source: Own calculation: kappa = 1.5 * d_eps / h (calc.py).

measured_numbers.quantity: Hollow strut optimum for core density ratio q = 0.19, 0.28, 0.45, 0.52
measured_numbers.value: k* = 0.900, 0.849, 0.742, 0.693; mass saving against a solid rod of equal stiffness 41%, 31%, 16%, 12%
measured_numbers.source: Own calculation (calc.py) from k* = sqrt(1-q) and mu* = sqrt(q(2-q)), theorems massFactor_deriv_eq_zero_iff and massFactor_at_optimum in upstream/leanbio/lean/ThompsonLaws/HollowTube.lean.

measured_numbers.quantity: Gyroid lattice compressive stiffness at relative density 0.19, 0.28, 0.52 (three specimens each) and fitted scaling exponent
measured_numbers.value: about 40-45, 85-91, 382-421 MPa; exponent 2.25
measured_numbers.source: Own analysis (calc.py) of nine CSV files from doi 10.5281/zenodo.14725395: steepest 40-point tangent of stress against extension/anvil height below 6% strain, no machine-compliance correction, so absolute values are rough. The base material was not confirmed from the record.

measured_numbers.quantity: Relative hydraulic resistance of a four-generation symmetric tree at fixed channel volume, junction exponent x = 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4
measured_numbers.source: Own calculation (calc2.py): radii r_i = r_0 * 2^(-i/x), resistance sum of 2^(-i) / r_i^4, rescaled to equal volume.

measured_numbers.quantity: Greenhill self-buckling height of a uniform Silicone 40A cylinder, radius 0.5, 1, 2 mm
measured_numbers.source: Own calculation (calc.py): L = (7.84 * E * r^2 / (4 * rho * g))^(1/3) with E = 0.8 MPa (secant estimate) and rho = 1100 kg/m3 (assumed). The coefficient 7.84 is unverified background.

measured_numbers.quantity: Marom-Buehler printed filament bilayers, measured against predicted angle
measured_numbers.value: 35.3 +/- 3.1 vs 36.4 deg (humidity bend); 41.3 +/- 2.2 vs 41.3 deg (humidity twist)
measured_numbers.source: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/spec-marom-buehler-deep.json (sibling agent's reading of arXiv:2604.26367); I confirmed the arXiv record and the repo but did not re-read the paper text.

could_not_find: Any humid-air (relative humidity, not immersion) swelling strain or water diffusivity for a Formlabs resin. The only figures are full-immersion mass and volume change, so every curvature and timing number for candidate 1 and 3 is conditional on coupon measurements.

Any public dataset for a vat-printed (SLA or DLP) humidity-driven bilayer. Zenodo, Figshare, the Stuttgart data repository and Europe PMC searches returned none; one unreviewed 2026 Zenodo report on humidity-responsive photopolymer actuators exists (10.5281/zenodo.23202170) but it carries no licence and I did not read its PDF.

The 3/2 curvature bound as a Lean theorem. Hygromorphs.lean has the Timoshenko coefficient, its derivation from beam equilibrium and the equal-layer case, but not the general bound or the optimum m = n^(-1/2); those rest on the sibling physics agent's paper derivation and my numerical use of it.
The numeric files inside the Cheng 2024 Figshare deposit. Both archives exceed the 20 MB download limit; from the zip directory the smaller one is mostly photographs.

Measured moduli for the beech layers in the ETH dataset as plain numbers (they are in a figure), so the retrodiction tests the bound and the position of the optimum, not a parameter-free Timoshenko prediction.

Any public dataset of printed hollow or cored struts in bending, or of plant stems with wall and pith dimensions plus stiffness. The cylinder-buckling Dryad set (463 MB) and a maize stalk set (1.3 GB) were seen in search but not downloaded.
The base material and specimen density definition for the gyroid compression files; the Zenodo record does not state them and I did not obtain the paper's full text.

A candidate with usable public data for Plateau junction geometry (120 degree struts) in a printed lattice. Cells.lean and Mechanics.lean have the 120 degree junction and the isotropic three-strut stiffness theorems, but my searches found no dataset, so I did not rank one.
The article that the Murray capillary Zenodo archive supports, and a DOI for Greenhill's 1881 paper; the Greenhill coefficient used is unverified background.
Whether the partner practice has any stated need for humidity-responsive parts. The sibling partner agent lists passive responsive skins as an inferred gap, not a quoted one.

design.label: design-biomaterial
design.chosen: Candidate 1, the vat-printed two-resin swelling bilayer (Formlabs Flexible 80A V2 as the swelling layer), kept as the scout recommended, but with the test rebuilt, because the scout's version could hardly fail and had four design faults. (1) Its central pass rule was the ceiling kappa*h/d_eps <= 1.5. The reported failures of this law in soft bilayers are all over-predictions, so a soft bilayer sits under the ceiling whether or not the law holds. I keep the ceiling as one prediction and move the weight to predictions that separate two rival input models. (2) The scout fixed the optimum at thickness ratio 1.8 from dry datasheet moduli. The same data sheet reports that Flexible 80A V2 loses 28 Shore A points after one day in water (https://media.formlabs.com/asset/af9d9268-d8c4-4019-9ccd-bd3af926c67e/-ENUS-Flexible-80A-V2-TDS.pdf, chemical compatibility table; my row count, the sibling materials agent read 26). Through the Gent hardness relation (unverified background formula) that is a 3.6 to 3.8-fold drop in modulus, which moves the predicted optimum from m = 1.8 to about m = 0.9 and flips the direction of the thin-active versus thick-active asymmetry (own calculation, D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/scratch/design-biomaterial/calc.py). So wet-state and dry-state inputs make opposite, checkable predictions. (3) A 60 x 5 x 0.8 mm strip of these elastomers cannot hold its shape in air: my elastogravity length is 20 to 28 mm for the soft pairs and the linear cantilever sag of a 40 mm strip is 14 to 39 mm (calc.py). Curvature must be read with the strip on edge under water. (4) Flexible 50A, the scout's passive layer, itself takes up 0.7% water in the 24 h cube test (D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json), so the differential strain is unknown until both resins are measured. I also raise total thickness from 0.8 to 1.0 mm so the 0.2 mm wall limit allows thickness ratios from 0.25 to 4. Runner-up not chosen: the cored hollow strut. Its model counts the core as dead mass, which is already known to be wrong in one direction, so a miss would be hard to interpret.
design.one_paragraph: Print thirty 40 x 4 x 1.0 mm bilayer strips of Flexible 80A V2 (swelling layer) on Flexible 50A (backing) at five thickness ratios m = h_backing/h_active = 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 (six strips each), plus six strips backed by 0.2 mm of Tough 1000, soak them in deionised water for 7 days and read curvature from blinded photographs. Before any bilayer exists, measure on single-resin coupons the free swelling strain (at each active-layer thickness), the small-strain modulus dry and wet, and the layer thicknesses. The Timoshenko law in the Lean library then gives every curvature with no fitted parameter. Two input models are frozen as rivals: M_wet uses moduli measured in the swollen state (my primary prediction) and M_dry uses dry moduli (what a datasheet-driven design uses, and what the scout used). With datasheet placeholders they disagree by a factor of 2.0 at m = 0.25 and 1.5 at m = 4, and they put the peak at different levels (m = 1 against m = 2), so the experiment picks one or rejects both. The pre-registration is two git commits before any bilayer data exist: Freeze A (model, prediction function, analysis script, thresholds) before any resin is opened, and Freeze B (the numeric prediction table computed mechanically from the coupon data) before any bilayer is printed. Nothing here has been measured yet. Every number below marked provisional comes from data sheets and my calculation and will be replaced at Freeze B.
design.model:
LAW (already in Lean, read at upstream/leanbio commit cb92aaf, file lean/ThompsonLaws/Hygromorphs.lean, def timoshenkoCoefficient and theorem bilayerCurvature_ofEquilibrium):
  kappa = f(m, n) * d_eps / h,   f(m, n) = 6 (1+m)^2 / [ 3 (1+m)^2 + (1 + m n)(m^2 + 1/(m n)) ]
  m = h_p / h_a (backing over active thickness), n = E_p / E_a (backing over active modulus), h = h_p + h_a, d_eps = eps_a - eps_p (free linear swelling strain of active minus backing).
CEILING AND OPTIMUM (not yet in Lean; to be added before Freeze A is closed): f(m, n) <= 3/2 for all m, n > 0, with equality iff m^2 n = 1. Proof: f <= 3/2 is equivalent to 2m <= m^3 n + 1/(m n), which is AM-GM because (m^3 n)(1/(m n)) = m^2. I re-derived this and checked it on a 201 x 301 log grid (maximum 1.500000, calc.py). Lean statements to prove (written here, NOT compiled by me): theorem timoshenkoCoefficient_le_ceiling (h m n : Real) (hh : 0 < h) (hm : 0 < m) (hn : 0 < n) : timoshenkoCoefficient h m n <= 3 / (2 * h); theorem timoshenkoCoefficient_eq_ceiling_iff ... : timoshenkoCoefficient h m n = 3 / (2 * h) <-> m ^ 2 * n = 1; and a house-style lemma bilayer_ceiling_rules_out that concludes False from a candidate committing to |kappa| * h / |d_eps| >= c with c > 3/2, plus one generated certificate per stiff-backed candidate (m >= 1/4 forced by the 0.2 mm wall at h = 1 mm, n given as an exact rational, claimed normalised curvature above the computed f).
ASYMMETRY IDENTITY (own algebra, follows from f(m, n) = f(1/m, 1/n)): A := kappa(m=4)/kappa(m=1/4) = f(4, n)/f(1/4, n) equals 1 iff n = 1, is above 1 iff the backing is softer than the active layer, and does not depend on d_eps. A is a one-number read-out of the effective modulus ratio.
TWO RIVAL INPUT MODELS, BOTH FROZEN. M_wet (primary): n = E_p,wet / E_a,wet, moduli measured on coupons taken from the same bath at the same time as the curvature reading. M_dry (rival): n = E_p,dry / E_a,dry at the dry reference state. Everything else is identical.
PARAMETERS. Fitted on bilayer data: none. Measured on single-resin coupons before any bilayer is printed (inputs, not fits): eps_a(h_a, t) and eps_p(h_p, t) for coupons whose thickness equals each layer thickness (0.2, 0.33, 0.5, 0.67, 0.8 mm), at t = 24 h, 72 h, 7 d of immersion and at the dry reference; E dry and wet at 0 to 5% strain by dead-weight extension; water diffusivity D from mass uptake against sqrt(t). Measured per bilayer specimen before soaking: h_p and h_a from the cut face of a sacrificial twin, baseline curvature kappa_0. Held out: every bilayer curvature. The response is d_kappa = kappa(7 d) - kappa_0, reported as f_meas = d_kappa * h / d_eps.
PROVISIONAL INPUTS (placeholders, replaced at Freeze B). Secant moduli at 50% elongation: Flexible 80A V2 5.8 MPa, Flexible 50A 1.8 MPa, Silicone 40A 0.8 MPa; Tough 1000 tensile modulus 932 MPa (D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json; the elastomer values are that agent's estimates, no modulus is published). Wet Flexible 80A V2: 5.8 / 3.84 = 1.51 MPa, from 83A to 55A with the Gent relation E = 0.0981(56 + 7.62336 S) / (0.137505 (254 - 2.54 S)) MPa, which gives 11.38 and 2.97 MPa (formula is unverified background; only the ratio is used). Backing assumed not to soften (unknown). Free strain of Flexible 80A V2 in water: 0.99% at 1 day and 2.28% at 1 week, the cube roots of +3% and +7% volume (https://media.formlabs.com/asset/af9d9268-d8c4-4019-9ccd-bd3af926c67e/-ENUS-Flexible-80A-V2-TDS.pdf; the table is misaligned in text extraction and rows were assigned by counting two per solvent, so treat as medium confidence).
PROVISIONAL PREDICTION TABLE for the Flexible 50A backing, h = 1.0 mm (calc.py, calc_out.json). Layer thicknesses backing/active in mm: 0.20/0.80, 0.33/0.67, 0.50/0.50, 0.67/0.33, 0.80/0.20. M_wet (n = 1.19): f = 1.03, 1.37, 1.50, 1.29, 0.89 at m = 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4; peak level m = 1; A = 0.87. M_dry (n = 0.31): f = 0.50, 0.93, 1.37, 1.50, 1.33; peak level m = 2; A = 2.65. Tough 1000 control, 0.2 mm on 0.8 mm (m = 0.25): f = 0.61 under M_wet (n = 616), 1.13 under M_dry (n = 161); the law's optimum would need a 0.04 to 0.07 mm Tough layer, below the 0.2 mm wall. Optional second pair, Silicone 40A backing: M_wet (n = 0.53) f = 0.70, 1.14, 1.46, 1.45, 1.19, A = 1.69; M_dry (n = 0.138) f = 0.27, 0.60, 1.12, 1.47, 1.46, A = 5.42. Size of the signal at the optimum for h = 1 mm on a 40 mm strip: 14.9 per m, 34 degrees of arc, 2.95 mm sagitta at d_eps = 0.99%; 3.0 per m, 6.9 degrees, 0.6 mm at d_eps = 0.2%.
ERROR BUDGET (own estimate, calc.py; assumes coupon length read to 0.02 mm on 60 mm, thickness to 0.01 mm, circle fit to 3%, six coupons): total relative error on f_meas is 3.7% at d_eps = 1%, 5% at 0.5%, 10% at 0.2%. The 20% and 30% windows below are therefore 4 to 8 standard errors wide at d_eps >= 0.5% and too tight below 0.3%, which is why there is a signal gate.
WHAT IS ALREADY SEEN. The scout tested the ceiling on six public beech-bilayer configurations (measured kappa*h/d_eps = 1.35, 1.50, 1.53, 1.36, 1.04, 0.91; scout file, from doi 10.3929/ethz-b-000275694). That is a retrodiction on seen data and is not counted as a test here. No Formlabs bilayer data exist to have been seen.

frozen_predictions.statement: No configuration exceeds the Lean ceiling: the mean normalised response f_meas = d_kappa*h/d_eps of every one of the six configurations (five thickness ratios plus the Tough 1000 control) is at most 1.5. This is the weakest prediction and is expected to pass; it is listed because it is the machine-checked statement.
frozen_predictions.number: f_meas <= 1.5 in all 6 configurations
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Any configuration mean exceeds 1.65 (1.5 plus 10%, about two to three standard errors at d_eps >= 0.5%). A violation would mean the coupon strain is not the strain the layer sees in the bilayer (for example through-thickness cure gradient or anisotropic swelling), since the inequality itself is a theorem.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Blinded circle fits of edge-on photographs of strips lying on edge under water at 7 d, minus baseline curvature; d_eps from thickness-matched single-resin coupons in the same bath; h by twin cross-section. n = 6 per configuration.

frozen_predictions.statement: The asymmetry index A = f_meas(m=4)/f_meas(m=0.25) for the Flexible 50A pair equals the value computed from WET moduli, not the value from dry moduli. Provisional: A = 0.87 (below 1, thick-active strip bends more) under M_wet against 2.65 (above 1) under M_dry.
frozen_predictions.number: A = f(4, n_wet)/f(0.25, n_wet); provisional 0.87; rival 2.65
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Measured A lies outside [A_wet/1.3, 1.3*A_wet] (provisional 0.67 to 1.13). M_dry is declared the better model if measured A is closer to A_dry than to A_wet on a log scale. Declared in advance: if coupons give n_wet and n_dry within a factor 1.5 of each other, this prediction does not discriminate and is reported as such, not as a pass.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: The 12 strips at m = 4 and m = 0.25 (0.8/0.2 and 0.2/0.8 mm), same soak, same imaging; wet and dry small-strain moduli of both resins from dead-weight extension of coupons.

frozen_predictions.statement: Among the five printed thickness ratios the largest mean response is at the level nearest n_wet^(-1/2). Provisional: m = 1 (equal layers, 0.5/0.5 mm); the dry-modulus model says m = 2.
frozen_predictions.number: argmax level = level nearest n_wet^(-1/2); provisional m = 1 (M_dry: m = 2)
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: The observed maximum is at a different level AND exceeds the mean at the predicted level by more than two pooled standard errors. Tie rule frozen now: if the predicted f at two adjacent levels differ by less than 5% (for example Silicone 40A wet: 1.46 at m = 1, 1.45 at m = 2), either level counts.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: All 30 strips of the pair, five levels, n = 6 each; per-specimen measured m is used to assign levels.

frozen_predictions.statement: With no parameter fitted to bilayer data, each of the five configuration means is within 20% of f(m, n_wet). Provisional values 1.03, 1.37, 1.50, 1.29, 0.89 at m = 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4. Equivalently, the single modulus ratio n_eff that best fits the five means lies within a factor 2 of the tensile n_wet. (Published printed bilayers needed a fitted ratio 4 to 17 times the measured one, per the sibling agent's reading of doi 10.3390/biomimetics6040058.)
frozen_predictions.number: |f_meas/f_pred - 1| <= 0.20 at each of 5 levels; n_eff/n_wet in [0.5, 2]
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Two or more of the five means fall outside 20%, or n_eff/n_wet is outside [0.5, 2]. Reported separately: the common scale factor s = mean(f_meas/f_pred); s below 0.8 with a correct shape points at the strain input, a wrong shape points at the modulus input or at the beam assumptions.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Same 30 strips; one-parameter least-squares fit of n to the five means done by the analysis script committed at Freeze A.

frozen_predictions.statement: A stiff backing at the thinnest printable wall is worse than a soft backing at its optimum. For the Tough 1000 control (0.2 mm on 0.8 mm Flexible 80A V2) f = f(0.25, n_T,wet), provisional 0.61, so the best soft-backed level beats it in normalised response by rho = f_best/f_Tough, provisional 2.46 (the dry-modulus model says 1.33). The raw-curvature ranking, which also depends on how much the Flexible 50A backing swells, is computed and frozen at Freeze B and may go either way.
frozen_predictions.number: rho = 1.5 / f(0.25, n_T,wet); provisional 2.46 (M_dry: 1.33)
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Measured rho is outside [0.7*rho_pred, 1.3*rho_pred] (provisional 1.7 to 3.2), or the Tough control's f_meas is at or above the best soft-backed f_meas (rho <= 1).
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Six Tough 1000-backed strips against the six strips at the best soft-backed level; d_eps for the Tough pair is the Flexible 80A V2 coupon strain minus the Tough 1000 coupon strain (data sheet: 0.0% water uptake, D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json).

frozen_predictions.statement: Conditional arm, the one that matters for a building skin. The law does not care how the water arrives: at 90% relative humidity the normalised response at each level equals the immersion value once the strain and the moduli measured at 90% RH are used. Run only if the coupon differential strain between 30% and 90% RH is at least 0.3%; otherwise the arm is recorded as 'not testable with stock resins', which is itself the finding that the partner demonstration needs a different active resin.
frozen_predictions.number: f_meas(90% RH)/f(m, n at 90% RH) between 0.8 and 1.25 at m = 0.5, 1, 2
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Any of the three levels falls outside 0.8 to 1.25 after equilibration (curvature change under 5% between readings 48 h apart).
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: A second set of 18 strips (three levels, n = 6) in a sealed saturated-salt jar with a logged humidity sensor, read on edge on a low-friction sheet; coupons in the same jar. Strip length cut to 20 mm for this arm because of gravity.

steps: 1. FREEZE A (git commit, before any resin is opened). Commit a pre-registration folder holding: PREREG.md with the model, the six predictions and thresholds exactly as written here; predict.py containing f(m, n), the asymmetry index, the level-assignment and tie rules (seed: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/scratch/design-biomaterial/calc.py); analyze.py that takes blinded photos and coupon CSVs and prints the verdicts, run once on synthetic images to show it can return 'refuted'; the provisional table; the gates G1-G3 below. Record the commit hash on the dashboard. The commit goes in the project repository by whichever thread owns track 5; I wrote nothing there.

2. Lean (parallel, laptop). Add the ceiling theorem, the equality condition and the rules_out lemma to a new module next to ThompsonLaws/Hygromorphs.lean, with generated certificates for the stiff-backed candidates. Check with #print axioms. If the proof is not closed by Freeze B the paper may still cite the law but the dashboard must say 'derived on paper, numerically checked, not machine-checked'.

3. Coupons. Print (or cast, see step 5) single-resin coupons 60 x 4 mm of Flexible 80A V2 and Flexible 50A at 0.2, 0.33, 0.5, 0.67, 0.8 mm, Tough 1000 at 0.2 mm, six each, plus 1 mm dog-bone strips for modulus. Wash, post-cure to the data-sheet schedule, then pre-leach: 48 h in water, dry to constant mass at the dry reference (sealed jar, logged 30 +/- 5% RH). Record cure dose.

4. Coupon measurements. Length by flatbed scan at 2400 dpi and mass on a 0.1 mg balance at 0, 1, 3, 7 d of immersion and in a 90% RH jar; small-strain modulus dry and wet by hanging weights and photographing extension; D from mass against sqrt(t).

5. Fabrication route trial. Route R1: print the two layers as separate sheets and bond green-to-green with a wiped film of the active resin, clamp between glass, post-cure. Route R2: print the backing as a tray whose pocket depth equals the active thickness, fill with active resin, level, cover with release film, cure. Make 10 x 10 mm pieces only; peel by hand and section to read bond-line thickness. Rule: trial pieces may be soaked for the peel test, but they are 10 mm squares and are never photographed or measured for curvature.

6. Gates, evaluated on coupon data only. G1 signal: differential strain (80A minus 50A, 0.33 mm coupons, 7 d immersion) at least 0.3%; if not, go down the frozen fallback ladder: Silicone 40A backing, then Tough-only family, then isopropanol as the stimulus (labelled solvent swelling), then an open-mode PEG-acrylate active resin. G2 bond: at least one route survives a hand peel after a 24 h soak, with a bond line under 0.05 mm. G3 thickness: printed layer thickness within 15% of nominal at 0.2 mm; if not, drop the m = 0.25 and m = 4 levels to 0.3 mm walls (m = 0.43 and 2.33) and say so in Freeze B.

7. FREEZE B (git commit, before any bilayer strip is printed). Commit the raw coupon CSVs, the chosen route, pair, levels and read-out time, and the numeric prediction table produced by running predict.py unchanged on those CSVs for both M_wet and M_dry. From here no number or threshold changes.

8. Build. Print 30 strips (five levels, n = 6) of the chosen pair and 6 Tough-backed controls, 40 x 4 x 1.0 mm, plus one sacrificial twin per level for cross-sections. A script assigns random ID codes; the key file is committed encrypted or held by a second person.

9. Test. Pre-leach and dry as for coupons, photograph baseline curvature on edge, immerse with fresh thickness-matched coupons in the same bath, photograph on edge under water at 24 h, 72 h and 7 d. Method check on two spare strips first: the on-edge reading must not change by more than 5% when the dish is tapped.

10. Analysis and FREEZE C. Run analyze.py on blinded files, commit the output, then unblind. Report each prediction as passed, refuted or not discriminating, for M_wet and M_dry side by side, with the 24 h and 72 h readings as secondary.

11. Conditional and exploratory work, labelled as such: the humid-air arm (P6); a horizontal-cantilever-in-air photograph of the best soft-backed and the Tough-backed strip to show the gravity limit (not frozen; my linear estimate is 14 to 25 mm sag at 40 mm for the soft pair against 1.7 to 3.5 mm for the Tough-backed strip); a response-time series for the scout's candidate 3 using the same prints.

12. Hand-off. Dashboard entry with all three commit hashes; a small demonstration flap for the partner sized below the measured elastogravity length; a note to the Marom-Buehler pipeline owners with the measured resin inputs so the design can be re-run through their code as a second machine backend.
design.what_is_frozen_and_when: Freeze A, day 1, before any resin is opened: the law and its two input models (M_wet primary, M_dry rival); predict.py and analyze.py; the six predictions with their windows (1.65 ceiling; factor 1.3 on A; peak-level rule with the 5% tie rule; 20% per level and factor 2 on n_eff; 0.7 to 1.3 on rho; 0.8 to 1.25 for humid air); specimen geometry (40 x 4 x 1.0 mm, m = 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, n = 6); read-out (7 d immersion, on edge, baseline subtracted, thickness-matched coupons); gates G1-G3 and the fallback ladder; the rule that a non-discriminating P2 is not a pass; the provisional datasheet table, marked provisional. Freeze B, about day 14 (the 7 d coupon reading falls on day 13), after coupons and before any bilayer strip is printed: raw coupon data; chosen fabrication route, pair and levels; the numeric prediction table for both models, generated by the unchanged predict.py. Freeze C, after the 7 d reading: analysis output on blinded files committed before unblinding. Never changed after Freeze A: thresholds, the form of f, which model is primary. Allowed to change only at Freeze B and only by the written rules: input numbers, the two extreme thickness levels under gate G3, the material under gate G1.
design.what_would_make_this_a_paper: Paper-grade, outcome 1: M_wet passes P2 to P5 with no fitted parameter while M_dry misses by the predicted factors (about 2 at m = 0.25, 1.5 at m = 4, and the peak one level off). That would show, in a material class with no published humidity or water bilayer that I or the sibling agents found (a limited search), that the reported over-prediction of Timoshenko in soft printed bilayers is an input-state error and not a failure of the law; together with a machine-checked ceiling and optimum and Lean certificates that remove the stiff-backed designs under the 0.2 mm wall, this is a worked case of a formal law plus a printer constraint cutting a catalogue to one geometry, which is the claim the contracting route needs. Paper-grade, outcome 2: both models are refuted with n_eff far outside the factor-2 window even though strain and modulus were measured thickness-matched and wet. That reproduces the published anomaly in a third material class while ruling out the usual explanation, and points at a named hypothesis of the Lean derivation (perfect bond, uniform strain through each layer, linear response). That is a useful negative result and a reason to formalise the next law (large rotation or graded swelling). Merely confirmatory: only P1 passes; or the peak is 'somewhere in the middle' with P2 not discriminating because wet and dry moduli turned out similar; or agreement is reached only after fitting n or a scale factor. Not a result at all: gate G1 fails and the fallback uses isopropanol. That still demonstrates the pipeline, but it must be described as solvent swelling and the humid-air question stays open. For the contract rather than the paper, the decisive number is the coupon strain between 30% and 90% RH: at or above 0.3% a stock-resin facade flap is plausible, below it the offer to the partner is the method plus an open-mode hydrogel active layer.
risks: Signal too small. The two Formlabs figures for water uptake disagree by about ten times: +8% mass for Flexible 80A V2 in the ASTM D471 slab test (https://media.formlabs.com/asset/af9d9268-d8c4-4019-9ccd-bd3af926c67e/-ENUS-Flexible-80A-V2-TDS.pdf) against 0.7% for 'Flexible 80A' in the 24 h cube test (sibling chemistry agent, formlabs.com/support/solvent-compatibility). It may be V1 against V2 or cube against slab; I could not tell. Mass +8% with volume +3% is also odd. Gate G1 and the fallback ladder exist for this.

The backing swells too. Flexible 50A takes 0.7% water in the cube test, so the differential may be much smaller than the 80A strain. Silicone 40A (<0.1%) is the clean backing but may not bond to a urethane-acrylate resin; untested.

Not at equilibrium. The data sheet volume change more than doubles between 1 day and 1 week. Mitigation: thickness-matched coupons in the same bath, 7 d primary read-out, and a plateau check. My diffusion guess (D about 1e-11 m2/s, 90% in 4 h for a 0.8 mm layer) assumes a 2 mm test slab, which I did not verify.

Gravity and friction. Elastogravity length 20 to 28 mm for the soft pairs (calc.py, moduli provisional); a strip read flat or hanging gives a wrong curvature. On-edge underwater reading reduces weight to about 9% but adds bottom friction; the tap check in step 9 is the control.

Thin elastomer walls. The 0.2 mm minimum is published for Grey V5 only; no figure exists for elastomers (D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json). Gate G3 handles a miss, at the cost of a narrower m range and weaker P2.

Bond line and residual stress. A resin bond film adds a third layer, and post-cure shrinkage gives a built-in curvature. Baseline subtraction handles the second; the first is limited by the 0.05 mm rule and reported.

Width effect. Elastomers have Poisson ratio near 0.5, so a strip wider than about sqrt(h/kappa) (5 to 18 mm over the expected strain range, calc.py) bends more than the beam law says, by up to (1 + nu). 4 mm is inside the limit except at the highest strain; a 2 mm-wide spare set at the peak level is the check.

Modulus measurement is low-tech. Dead-weight extension of a wet elastomer strip is perhaps 10% accurate; n enters P2 strongly (A goes from 0.87 to 1.34 as n goes from 1.18 to 0.7). The factor-1.3 window on A already allows for roughly 15% error in n; a borrowed tensile frame would tighten it.

Leaching and ageing. Uncured monomer leaves in the first soak and the resin keeps curing in light. Pre-leach, fixed cure dose and storing in the dark limit this; a dry-wet-dry cycle on six strips measures what remains.

The provisional wet modulus rests on a hardness-to-modulus formula I did not verify and on a garbled table row. If the real softening is small, M_wet and M_dry coincide, P2 stops discriminating, and the study becomes a plain zero-fit test (P3 to P5).

Novelty claim is from a limited search by sibling agents (no vat-printed humidity bilayer found; liquid-driven DLP precedents exist, doi 10.1002/marc.201600625 and 10.1021/acsami.8b02444). A patent and database check is needed before saying 'first'.
first_week: Day 1: write PREREG.md, predict.py and analyze.py from this design; run analyze.py on synthetic arcs with a planted 30% error to see it report 'refuted'; commit as Freeze A and post the hash. Order or locate cartridges and tanks for Flexible 80A V2, Flexible 50A and Tough 1000 (Silicone 40A optional), a 0.1 mg balance, a humidity logger, salts and jars. Ask Formlabs support for the D471 slab thickness, the thin-wall limit for the elastomers, and whether the cube-test 0.7% figure is for V1 or V2.
Day 1 to 3 (parallel): prove the ceiling and equality theorems in Lean on the laptop against upstream commit cb92aaf; add the rules_out lemma and two certificates; run #print axioms.

Day 2: print coupon builds (one build per resin): 60 x 4 mm strips at 0.2, 0.33, 0.5, 0.67, 0.8 mm, six each, plus modulus strips and the 10 x 10 mm bond-trial sheets and trays. Wash and post-cure to the data sheets.
Day 3: measure as-printed thickness of every coupon (gate G3). Start pre-leach soak. Make the R1 and R2 bond-trial pieces from spare sheets.
Day 5: dry coupons to constant mass in the 30% RH jar; take dry length scans, masses and dry modulus.
Day 6: start the immersion series and the 90% RH jar; read mass and length at 1 h, 4 h, 24 h (gives D and the first strain number). Section the bond-trial pieces and read bond-line thickness.

Day 7: first decision meeting on coupon data only: is the 24 h differential strain on track for gate G1 (0.3%), which route bonds, do the 0.2 mm walls print. Wet modulus at 24 h. The 3 d and 7 d coupon readings follow in week 2, then Freeze B.
design.compute_needed: Laptop only. predict.py and analyze.py are stdlib Python plus an image circle fit (seconds per photo). The Lean addition is one small module on the existing toolchain (minutes to build). No Modal credits and no cluster are needed. Optional and not part of the frozen test: a nonlinear two-layer finite-element check of the 1 to 2% strain case, which would fit on the laptop.
design.physical_build: Formlabs Form 4, stock resins, no Open Material licence for the main test. Resins: Flexible 80A V2 (active), Flexible 50A (backing), Tough 1000 (stiff control); Silicone 40A optional second backing. Builds: (a) coupon set, about 70 strips 60 x 4 mm at five thicknesses plus modulus strips and bond-trial pieces; (b) main set, 30 bilayer strips 40 x 4 x 1.0 mm at backing/active = 0.20/0.80, 0.33/0.67, 0.50/0.50, 0.67/0.33, 0.80/0.20 mm, 6 Tough-backed strips at 0.20/0.80 mm, 5 sacrificial twins, 6 spare 2 mm-wide strips; (c) conditional humid-air set, 18 strips cut to 20 mm; (d) one demonstration flap for the partner, sized after the results. Each bilayer needs two prints and a bond (route R1) or a printed tray plus a cast-and-cured second resin (route R2), because single-job two-resin printing was not found for this printer. Bench items: Form Wash and Form Cure, 0.1 mg balance, flatbed scanner (2400 dpi), camera on a copy stand, low-force thickness gauge or USB microscope for cut faces, glass dishes, sealed jars with saturated salts and a humidity logger, small weights for the modulus test, deionised water. Total elapsed time about 5 weeks: two for coupons, one for building and pre-leaching the strips, 7 days for the soak, a few days for analysis.

existing.statement_plain: For a bonded two-layer strip (thicknesses h1, h2; moduli E1, E2; eigenstrains e1, e2), force balance, moment balance and interface strain compatibility force exactly one curvature: kappa = (1/h) * 6(1+m)^2 / (3(1+m)^2 + (1+mn)(m^2 + 1/(mn))) * (e1 - e2), with h = h1+h2, m = h1/h2, n = E1/E2.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: The file header states no assumed/not-proved section; it says only that the file formalises 'the mathematical core of the claims in claim-sources/plant-hygromorph-mechanics/claims/key-claims.json'. Assumptions sit in the theorem hypotheses: Euler-Bernoulli strip per unit width, linear elasticity, perfect bonding, uniform eigenstrain per layer, positive h and E. Small strain, no edge or plate (Poisson) effects and no viscoelastic relaxation are not stated anywhere and are my reading.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: This is the forward map for a printed two-resin (or resin plus swelling layer) actuator: once the two moduli, the two thicknesses and the swelling mismatch are committed, the curvature is fixed. A design that claims a different curvature for the same four inputs is eliminable. It turns a 4-parameter free design into a 1-dimensional surface in (h, m, n, mismatch, kappa).

existing.statement_plain: Curvature is linear in the mismatch; zero mismatch gives zero curvature; for equal thickness and modulus kappa = (3/2) * mismatch / h; the coefficient is positive for positive h, m, n, so the layer that swells more is on the convex side.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Same file; no header assumptions section. Positivity of h, m, n is a hypothesis.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Fixes the bending direction (a design whose active layer is on the wrong face is ruled out by sign alone) and gives the scaling test for the print: halving total thickness at fixed ratios doubles curvature; doubling the swelling strain doubles curvature. Both are one-print falsifiable.

existing.statement_plain: The response time of a layer of thickness h and diffusivity D is h^2/D; scaling thickness by k scales it by k^2. The slowest mode exp(-pi^2 D t/h^2) sin(pi x/h) solves the 1-D heat equation with zero boundary values and decays on h^2/(pi^2 D).
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: No header assumptions section. Model is 1-D Fickian diffusion with constant D and fixed-concentration faces; that swelling tracks concentration is not stated or proved.

Combined with the curvature law (kappa ~ 1/h) it gives a speed-versus-stiffness trade the design cannot escape by geometry alone; D must be measured for the chosen resin.

existing.statement_plain: A stimulus-response system is a state space X (real normed space), a stimulus space E and a vector field f(x, e). existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header, 'What is not proved here': 'Nothing about organisms', 'Nothing nonlinear', 'Nothing about finite domains ... the continuum condition proved here is necessary and not sufficient for a pattern on a given domain'. Two-species only.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Only if the biomaterial is meant to self-pattern (reaction-diffusion in a gel or frontal curing): two reagents with equal diffusivity in the matrix cannot pattern. Peripheral to a directly printed geometry.

missing.law: Timoshenko curvature ceiling (optimal bilayer)
missing.statement_math: For all h, m, n > 0: timoshenkoCoefficient h m n <= 3/(2h), with equality iff m^2 n = 1 (E1 h1^2 = E2 h2^2). Hence |kappa| <= (3/2)|d_eps|/h. Proof sketch (mine): the bound is equivalent to (1+mn)(m^2 + 1/(mn)) >= (1+m)^2, i.e. m^3 n + 1/(mn) >= 2m, which is AM-GM since (m^3 n)(1/(mn)) = m^2.
missing.why_needed: The existing file gives the forward map but no bound, so nothing can be ruled out without committing every parameter. This inequality is the first real *_rules_out for the track: any printed bilayer claiming curvature above 1.5 * mismatch / thickness is impossible whatever the two resins are, and the optimum fixes the thickness ratio from the modulus ratio.
missing.difficulty: easy: one AM-GM step after field_simp; positivity and nlinarith should close it.
missing.source: Timoshenko 1925, 'Analysis of Bi-Metal Thermostats', J. Opt. Soc. Am. 11:233, doi:10.1364/JOSA.11.000233 (verified=true, resolved at api.crossref.org in this run). The bound statement and proof sketch are my own calculation from the definition in lean/ThompsonLaws/Hygromorphs.lean, not copied from the paper.

missing.law: Printed bilayer mean and Gaussian curvature from anisotropic swelling
missing.statement_math: For a bilayer with print-path angle theta between layers and swelling strains (alpha_par, alpha_perp): mean curvature H and Gaussian curvature K are closed-form functions of (alpha_par - alpha_perp), layer thicknesses, moduli ratio and theta; twist-only at +phi/-phi, saddle at 90 degrees.
missing.why_needed: The repo has the strain kinematics (shearStrain_mismatch) but stops before curvature. Without the strain-to-shape map a twisting or doubly curved print cannot be predicted or eliminated.
missing.difficulty: hard: needs classical laminate plate theory (2x2 tensor version of the Timoshenko balance) and, for the narrow-to-wide strip transition, a nonlinear energy argument that Mathlib has no ready scaffolding for.
missing.source: Sydney Gladman, Matsumoto, Nuzzo, Mahadevan et al. 2016, 'Biomimetic 4D printing', Nat. Mater. 15:413-418, doi:10.1038/nmat4544 (verified=true, Crossref). Armon, Efrati, Kupferman, Sharon 2011, 'Geometry and Mechanics in the Opening of Chiral Seed Pods', Science 333:1726-1730, doi:10.1126/science.1203874 (verified=true, Crossref). Reyssat and Mahadevan 2009, 'Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers', J. R. Soc. Interface 6:951-957, doi:10.1098/rsif.2009.0184 (verified=true, Crossref).

missing.law: Cellular-solid stiffness and strength scaling (Gibson-Ashby)
missing.statement_math: E*/E_s = C1 (rho*/rho_s)^n and sigma*/sigma_s = C2 (rho*/rho_s)^p, with (n, p) = (2, 3/2) for bending-dominated and (1, 1) for stretch-dominated open-cell lattices. As a law: given the regime, log-log slope of modulus against relative density is exactly n.
missing.why_needed: A Formlabs proof of concept will almost certainly be a lattice or foam. This is the law that turns 'resin modulus plus relative density' into 'part modulus', and it is the main lever for a new architected biomaterial. Nothing in the repo relates relative density to stiffness.
missing.difficulty: easy as a named hypothesis with ratio and log-slope theorems (same shape as CubeLaw / PowerLaw in lean/Delphi/Flight.lean); hard if the exponents are to be derived from beam theory on a unit cell.
missing.source: Gibson and Ashby 1982, 'The mechanics of three-dimensional cellular materials', Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 382:43-59, doi:10.1098/rspa.1982.0088 (verified=true, Crossref). The exponent values are unverified background: I resolved the DOI but did not read the full text in this run.

missing.law: Maxwell rigidity count (bending versus stretching topology)
missing.statement_math: For a pin-jointed frame with b struts and j joints in 3-D: M = b - 3j + 6. M < 0 implies a mechanism (bending-dominated when joints are rigid); M >= 0 is necessary for stretch-dominated behaviour. In 2-D: M = b - 2j + 3.
missing.why_needed: It is a purely combinatorial, decidable test on a lattice unit cell, exactly the kind of check the kernel can discharge with decide, and it selects which Gibson-Ashby exponent applies. It would let the pipeline eliminate unit cells before any simulation.
missing.difficulty: easy for the count and the classification as a definition plus decide on concrete cells; moderate to prove the necessity statement from rank-nullity of the equilibrium matrix.
missing.source: Deshpande, Ashby, Fleck 2001, 'Foam topology: bending versus stretching dominated architectures', Acta Mater. 49:1035-1040, doi:10.1016/S1359-6454(00)00379-7 (verified=true, Crossref). Formula as stated is unverified background (full text not read in this run).

missing.law: Two-phase composite bounds (Voigt-Reuss, Hashin-Shtrikman)
missing.statement_math: For phases with moduli E1 <= E2 and volume fractions f1 + f2 = 1: (f1/E1 + f2/E2)^(-1) <= E_eff <= f1 E1 + f2 E2. Hashin-Shtrikman tightens this for isotropic composites, e.g. bulk modulus K_HS- = K1 + f2 / (1/(K2 - K1) + 3 f1/(3K1 + 4G1)).
missing.why_needed: A 'new biomaterial' from existing resins is a composite or a multi-material print. These bounds are the hard walls of property space: any claimed effective modulus outside them is eliminable with norm_num, and the gap between the bounds is what experiment has to resolve.
missing.difficulty: easy for Voigt-Reuss as an interval lemma (weighted AM-HM); hard for Hashin-Shtrikman if derived variationally, easy if stated as a named hypothesis with the interval lemma.
missing.source: Hashin and Shtrikman 1963, 'A variational approach to the theory of the elastic behaviour of multiphase materials', J. Mech. Phys. Solids 11:127-140, doi:10.1016/0022-5096(63)90060-7 (verified=true, Crossref). The explicit HS expression is unverified background.

missing.law: Thin-shell local buckling coefficient for the hollow tube
missing.statement_math: Axial or bending wall stress at local buckling of a thin cylinder: sigma_cr = E t / (R sqrt(3(1 - nu^2))), so the floor in HollowTube is lambda = t/R >= sqrt(3(1 - nu^2)) sigma / E; with a compliant core the coefficient rises as a function of core-to-wall modulus ratio.
missing.why_needed: constrained_optimum leaves lambda = C sigma / E with 'C a free constant'. Until C is supplied the optimum min(sqrt(1 - q), 1 - lambda) cannot be evaluated for any resin, so the hollow-tube law cannot yet rule out a single printed tube.
missing.difficulty: easy to add as a named constant with the resulting instance of constrained_optimum; hard to derive from Donnell shell equations in Lean.
missing.source: Karam and Gibson 1995, 'Elastic buckling of cylindrical shells with elastic cores - I. Analysis', Int. J. Solids Struct. 32:1259-1283, doi:10.1016/0020-7683(94)00147-O (verified=true, Crossref). The classical coefficient 1/sqrt(3(1 - nu^2)) is unverified background.

missing.law: Euler column buckling for lattice struts
missing.statement_math: P_cr = pi^2 E I / (K L)^2; for a solid circular strut of diameter d: sigma_cr = pi^2 E d^2 / (16 K^2 L^2). Strut slenderness L/d is bounded above by pi sqrt(E / sigma_design) / (4K).
missing.why_needed: Sets the maximum strut slenderness of any printed lattice under compression; together with the printer's minimum strut diameter it bounds cell size from above. Greenhill in Magnitude.lean covers self-weight only, with the constant bundled.
missing.difficulty: easy as algebra from P_cr (a rules_out lemma is one div_lt_iff step); moderate to derive P_cr as the first eigenvalue of y'' + (P/EI) y = 0 (the sine-mode machinery in diffusionMode can be reused).
missing.source: No source fetched in this run (verified=false). Standard textbook result; treat the formula as unverified background until a DOI is attached.

missing.law: Elastic similarity derived, and registered
missing.statement_math: If members of a family are sized to keep the same safety factor against self-weight buckling (h_crit = C d^(2/3)) then d ~ L^(3/2); with M ~ d^2 L this gives L ~ M^(1/4), d ~ M^(3/8).
missing.why_needed: The registry entry elastic-similarity is a 'gap' with no module, while LimbBoneSimilarity.elastic_similarity_exponents only does the arithmetic after assuming d ~ M^(3/8). Linking greenhill_stands_iff to the exponents closes the gap and gives the track a second, non-isometric scale-up family to test against printed size series.
missing.difficulty: easy: rpow algebra on two existing definitions, then propose.mjs to register.
missing.source: McMahon 1973, 'Size and Shape in Biology', Science 179:1201-1204, doi:10.1126/science.179.4079.1201 (verified=true, Crossref). Registry gap: lean/registry/laws/elastic-similarity.json ('not formalised: R7 and R9 use isometric sections').

missing.law: Stereolithography working curve (cure depth)
missing.statement_math: C_d = D_p ln(E / E_c) for exposure E > E_c, where D_p is the resin's penetration depth and E_c its critical exposure; C_d is strictly increasing in E and a layer bonds only if C_d >= layer thickness.
missing.why_needed: This is the one law that ties the design space to the Formlabs process: it bounds printable layer thickness, minimum feature and the through-thickness cure gradient that itself creates a bilayer (and so a built-in curvature via the Timoshenko map). Without it, 'printable on a Formlabs machine' is not a formal constraint.
missing.difficulty: easy: Real.log monotonicity; D_p and E_c enter as named per-resin hypotheses in the style of lean/Delphi/Empirical.lean.
missing.source: Bennett 2017, 'Measuring UV curing parameters of commercial photopolymers used in additive manufacturing', Addit. Manuf. 18, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2017.10.009 (verified=true: DOI and title returned by a Crossref bibliographic search in this run; full text not read, so the equation itself is unverified background). No Formlabs resin D_p or E_c values were fetched.

missing.law: Resin property envelope as named empirical hypotheses
missing.statement_math: For each usable resin i: a structure ResinBand_i with fields E_lo <= E <= E_hi, sigma_lo <= sigma_u <= sigma_hi, rho band, elongation band, minimum wall t_min, minimum strut d_min; each with a source field.
missing.why_needed: Every existing theorem here is conditional on sigma_max, E, rho, t. With no sourced numbers the checker can only answer 'cannot rule' (the registry says of Laplace that it 'is proved with no instance'). The ten-material list has to be entered as data before any certificate can be instantiated.

missing.source: Not fetched in this run (verified=false). Must come from the manufacturer's technical data sheets, fetched by whichever agent owns the materials table; I supply no property numbers.

missing.law: Equilibrium swelling of a crosslinked network (Flory-Rehner)
missing.statement_math: ln(1 - phi) + phi + chi phi^2 + (V1 / (v_c)) (phi^(1/3) - phi/2) = 0 determines the equilibrium polymer fraction phi; linear swelling strain eps = phi^(-1/3) - 1 increases as crosslink density falls.
missing.why_needed: The Timoshenko map needs the swelling mismatch as an input. This law supplies it from chemistry (crosslink density, solvent quality), which is where the 'chemistry side' of the track connects to the mechanics. Without it the mismatch is a free parameter.
missing.difficulty: moderate: existence and uniqueness of the root on (0, 1) and monotonicity in crosslink density by the intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity; no closed form.
missing.source: Flory and Rehner 1943, 'Statistical Mechanics of Cross-Linked Polymer Networks II. Swelling', J. Chem. Phys. 11:521-526, doi:10.1063/1.1723792 (verified=true, Crossref). The equation as written is unverified background.

missing.law: Snap-through threshold of a doubly curved shell
missing.statement_math: There is alpha_c > 0 such that the elastic energy of the shell as a function of mean curvature has two minima iff snapParameter L kappa h > alpha_c (bistable), one otherwise.
missing.why_needed: snapParameter_threshold_mono takes alpha_c as an arbitrary real. Without existence and a value, a printed snapping element can only be ranked, not accepted or eliminated.
missing.difficulty: hard for the shell energy; moderate if reduced to the one-degree-of-freedom quartic energy, where bistability is a discriminant condition.
missing.source: Forterre, Skotheim, Dumais, Mahadevan 2005, 'How the Venus flytrap snaps', Nature 433:421-425, doi:10.1038/nature03185 (verified=true, Crossref).

missing.law: Murray-type law for a non-living porous material
missing.statement_math: For a hierarchical pore network with mass loss fraction X through pore walls: r0^alpha = (1/(1 - X)) sum_i r_i^alpha, alpha = 3 for laminar flow and alpha = 2 for diffusion- or ion-limited transport.
missing.why_needed: junction_law covers any cost k Q^a / r^b + m r^c, but its 'maintenance' term is metabolic. A printed material needs the version whose second term is a material or surface cost and which allows wall exchange; otherwise the cubic law is applied outside its stated premise.
missing.difficulty: moderate: reuse vesselCost_lt and junction_law with flow not conserved (Q0 = (Q1 + Q2)/(1 - X)); the alpha = 2 case needs a separate diffusive conductance model.
missing.source: Zheng et al. 2017, 'Bio-inspired Murray materials for mass transfer and activity', Nat. Commun. 8, doi:10.1038/ncomms14921 (verified=true, Crossref). Murray 1926, 'The Physiological Principle of Minimum Work', PNAS 12:207-214, doi:10.1073/pnas.12.3.207 (verified=true, Crossref). The formula with X is unverified background (abstract-level recall, full text not read in this run).

missing.law: Material index for minimum-mass stiff members
missing.statement_math: At fixed bending stiffness and length, mass of a solid beam of free section is proportional to rho / E^(1/2); of a plate of free thickness, rho / E^(1/3); of a tie, rho / E. So material A beats B for a beam iff E_A^(1/2)/rho_A > E_B^(1/2)/rho_B.
missing.why_needed: HollowTube optimises shape at fixed material. Choosing among ten resins (or a resin against a lattice of it) needs the companion ordering on materials, otherwise 'which resin' stays outside the formal loop.
missing.difficulty: easy: algebra with rpow and one monotonicity lemma.
missing.source: Wegst and Ashby 2004, 'The mechanical efficiency of natural materials', Philos. Mag. 84:2167-2186, doi:10.1080/14786430410001680935 (verified=true, Crossref). Index forms are unverified background.

missing.law: Flaw-tolerance length scale for hierarchical composites
missing.statement_math: A brittle platelet of thickness h with surface energy gamma, modulus E and theoretical strength sigma_th fails at sigma_th regardless of cracks iff h <= h* = alpha^2 gamma E / sigma_th^2 (alpha a geometry constant).
missing.why_needed: It is the published design rule behind nacre-like and bone-like architectures, and it gives a feature-size ceiling to compare with the printer's resolution floor: if h* is below the minimum printable feature for a resin, flaw-tolerant architecture is ruled out for that resin on that printer.
missing.difficulty: easy as a Griffith-criterion inequality (sigma_f = alpha sqrt(gamma E / h) capped at sigma_th); hard if Griffith itself is to be derived.
missing.source: Gao, Ji, Jager, Arzt et al. 2003, 'Materials become insensitive to flaws at nanoscale: Lessons from nature', PNAS 100:5597-5600, doi:10.1073/pnas.0631609100 (verified=true, Crossref). Formula form is unverified background.

missing.law: Interface crack deflection criterion
missing.statement_math: A crack reaching an interface deflects along it rather than penetrating iff G_interface / G_bulk < f(Dundurs alpha), a fixed function of elastic mismatch.
missing.why_needed: Decides whether a multi-material layered print toughens (deflects) or fails through. It is a single inequality on two measurable toughnesses, so it suits a rules_out lemma for layered designs.
missing.difficulty: easy as a named-hypothesis inequality with the threshold supplied as data; hard to derive the function f.
missing.source: He and Hutchinson 1989, 'Crack deflection at an interface between dissimilar elastic materials', Int. J. Solids Struct. 25:1053-1067, doi:10.1016/0020-7683(89)90021-8 (verified=true, Crossref). I give no threshold number: I did not read the full text in this run.
