laws.elimination_pattern: There are two layers, and the names matter: the *_rules_out theorems live in lean/Delphi/Constraints.lean (and in Empirical, Genotype, Perturb and Hydrostatics), while the files in lean/Delphi/Certificates contain no theorem named *_rules_out at all; they contain generated instances named elim_<candidate>_<constraint id>. A *_rules_out lemma takes the law as a named hypothesis, then the candidate's commitment as hypotheses (usually intervals a <= x <= b), then one last decidable arithmetic side condition, and concludes False (or the negation of the law); the Constraints.lean header says 'Every lemma concludes False from the law plus the candidate's commitment'. Real example, lemma: 'theorem cubeLaw_rules_out' {W : ℝ → ℝ} {k : ℝ} (h : CubeLaw W k) {L₁ L₂ a b c d : ℝ} (h₁ : 0 < L₁) (h₂ : 0 < L₂) (hr : a ≤ W L₂ / W L₁ ∧ W L₂ / W L₁ ≤ b) (hℓ : c ≤ L₂ / L₁ ∧ L₂ / L₁ ≤ d) (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hne : b < c ^ 3 ∨ d ^ 3 < a) : False'. Real example, certificate (lean/Delphi/Certificates/Eliminations.lean): '/-- Candidate `giant-insect-mass`, constraint C7. -/ theorem elim_giant_insect_mass_C7 : ∀ (W : ℝ → ℝ) (k L₁ L₂ : ℝ), Delphi.CubeLaw W k → 0 < L₁ → 0 < L₂ → ((100 : ℝ) ≤ W L₂ / W L₁ ∧ W L₂ / W L₁ ≤ (100 : ℝ)) → ((100 : ℝ) ≤ L₂ / L₁ ∧ L₂ / L₁ ≤ (100 : ℝ)) → False := fun W k L₁ L₂ h h₁ h₂ hr hℓ => Delphi.Constraints.cubeLaw_rules_out' h h₁ h₂ hr hℓ (by norm_num) (by norm_num)'. So a certificate is the lemma with the candidate's numbers written as exact rationals, everything physical still universally quantified, and the only proof obligations discharged by norm_num (or decide +kernel for the combinatorial ones); it is generated, with the header 'Do not edit; regenerate', by lean/eliminate/eliminate.mjs from a candidates JSON, and that generator is not in this repository. A candidate that does not commit to the law's assumptions is not eliminated: the checker reports 'cannot rule', never 'passes'. This track would add a module such as lean/Delphi/ConstraintsMaterial.lean with lemmas of the same shape, for example hoop_rules_out {P r t σmax : ℝ} (hr : 0 < r) (ht : 0 < t) (hσ : Delphi.Physiology.hoopStress P r t ≤ σmax) (hclaim : σmax * t / r < P) : False := absurd (Delphi.Physiology.hoop_pressure_limit hr ht hσ) (not_le.mpr hclaim), and bilayer_curvature_rules_out once the 3/(2h) ceiling is proved. A certificate file lean/Delphi/Certificates/EliminationsBiomaterial.lean would then hold one elim_<design>_<id> per rejected design, with the resin's datasheet strength, the wall and the radius as rationals and norm_num closing the inequality; resin numbers must enter as named hypotheses with a source, never as axiom, and each new law goes through lean/registry/propose.mjs with a non-vacuity witness before it can colour a verdict.

explain.label: explain2-bm-science
explain.one_line: We test whether printed two-layer plastic strips can curl with damp air, using a maths limit that a computer has checked.
explain.what:
A pine cone scale is two layers stuck together. When the air dries, one layer shrinks more than the other. The scale bends open. We ask if a 3D printer can make strips that do the same with ordinary printing plastic.

Here is a plain example. Take a strip 40 millimetres long and 0.8 millimetres thick. That is about as long as your thumb and eight hairs thick. Say one layer grows 0.1 to 0.3 percent more than the other when it soaks up water. That is our own estimate, not a measurement. The best possible bend is then a circle about 20 to 60 centimetres wide. The tip of the strip moves only about 1 to 4 millimetres.

Where does "best possible" come from? An engineer named Timoshenko published a bending formula in 1925. A computer program that accepts only complete proofs has confirmed one limit in it. The limit says a strip can never curl tighter than 1.5 times the mismatch, divided by its thickness. The mismatch is how much more one layer lengthens than the other, as a fraction of its length. A mismatch of 0.2 percent is written 0.002. We use the limit to rule out hopeless designs on paper before we print anything.
explain.why:
Plants move with no motor and no power. A printed part that did this could be useful. Printing a strip and then waiting days to see nothing happen wastes time. A rule that rules out hopeless designs saves that time.

The limit is not new. A 2015 paper by Holstov had already drawn it on a graph. What is new is that a computer has now proved it. We do not know yet if a real printed strip will follow the formula. We have not printed one.

Real pine cones show what is possible. A cone scale 1 millimetre thick bends about 1.3 per centimetre between dry and soaked air. That is a circle about 8 millimetres wide. Printing plastic swells far less than a cone does, so our strips would bend much more gently.

steps.text: Write down the bending formula for two layers. Check it against the original 1925 paper.
steps.picture: Checking a recipe against the cookbook it came from.

steps.text: Ask a proof-checking program to confirm the formula can never give more than 1.5 times the mismatch over the thickness.
steps.picture: A strict referee who rejects any argument with a gap.

steps.text: Test the checker. Feed it a proof with a gap and a false claim. It must refuse both.
steps.picture: Trying a fake banknote on the till to see if it spots it.

steps.text: Compare the formula with a computer model of a flat strip. The two agreed to about seven decimal places.
steps.picture: Measuring the same table with two different rulers.

steps.text: Gather real numbers from pine cones. These are layer thickness, stiffness, and how long they take to move.
steps.picture: Timing a real runner before setting the race rules.

steps.text: Estimate how fast water soaks into printing plastics. We model a layer 0.2 to 0.8 millimetres thick. That is two to eight hairs thick.
steps.picture: A sponge that dries one thin layer at a time.

steps.text: List which designs the limit rules out. Also list which plastics swell too little to bother with.
steps.picture: Crossing off holiday plans that you cannot afford.

steps.text: Print real strips and measure them in damp and dry air. This step is still to do.
steps.picture: Finally taking the cake out of the oven to taste it.

explain.wrong_if: Here is the bet, written before we looked. We say a printed two-layer strip will never curl tighter than 1.5 times the mismatch divided by its thickness. If we measure a real strip that curls tighter, we are wrong. We also bet that thin layers react faster, by roughly the square of the thickness. So a layer half as thick should be about four times quicker. If it is not much faster, we are wrong about that part. And if a stiff printed layer on a soft one curls far less than the formula says, the formula is not useful here.
could_go_wrong: The formula is for a thin ribbon. A wide sheet behaves differently. It can curl about 30 to 50 percent tighter, but only in one direction.
Water soaks into printed plastic very slowly. A demonstration could take days instead of minutes.
The formula says nothing about speed. It also ignores creep, which is slow sagging under a steady push. It does not cover how well the two layers stay glued.
Printing plastics may swell too little to give a bend you can see.
Two documents from Formlabs, a company that makes 3D printers, disagree on how much one resin swells in water. They probably describe two versions of it.
Heat may bend a strip more than damp air does. That would confuse the test unless we vary both.
We could not read three of the original papers in full. Some of what we say about them is second-hand.

questions.q: What is the mismatch, and how is it measured?
questions.a: It is how much more one layer lengthens than the other, as a fraction of its length. If one layer grows 1 millimetre per metre more, the mismatch is 0.001, or 0.1 percent. No one has measured it for printed strips in damp air. Our numbers are estimates.

questions.q: What would a real strip look like?
questions.a: Our example is 40 millimetres long and 0.8 millimetres thick, with a mismatch of 0.1 to 0.3 percent. The tightest possible bend is a circle about 20 to 60 centimetres wide. The tip would move about 1 to 4 millimetres. A real strip would bend less than this. Nobody has printed or measured one yet.

questions.q: How do you know the limit is true?
questions.a: A proof-checking program accepted it, using only the three standard starting rules of maths. It also rejected a false version that said 7/5 instead of 3/2. A 2015 paper had also shown the same limit on a graph.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We have not printed or measured any strip. We could not read some original papers in full. We did not test wide sheets, big swelling, creep or glue between layers. The speed numbers for plastics are our own estimates.

questions.q: Is this a new discovery?
questions.a: No. The limit was already known from graphs. The new part is that a computer has proved it.

questions.q: Do real pine cones reach the limit?
questions.a: Close, but not quite. By our own arithmetic they reach about 82 to 97 percent of it.

questions.q: Why not use a stiffer partner layer to curl more?
questions.a: Because the best bend needs balance. A stiffer layer must be made thinner to balance a softer one. When the two are balanced, the stiffness difference no longer changes the result. Only the mismatch and the total thickness set the limit. So a stiffer partner cannot beat it.

questions.q: Does ordinary printing plastic swell much in water?
questions.a: Mostly little. A one-centimetre cube of two Formlabs resins gains about 0.7 percent in weight in a day. That is about a sixth of a drop of water for a cube weighing 1.2 grams. One other resin sheet gained 8 percent in a day. So it depends on the resin and the test.

questions.q: How fast could a printed strip move?
questions.a: Our model says a layer 0.2 to 0.4 millimetres thick of a stiff stock resin takes about 9 to 38 hours to soak. A layer 0.8 millimetres or thicker could take days. These are model results, not measurements. We do not know of any measured soaking speed for these resins.

questions.q: Does the formula match what others measured?
questions.a: It follows the trends. But it predicts a bend about four times tighter than printed soft humidity strips actually made. So the formula gives the best case, not the typical case.

explain_more.label: explain2-bm-making
explain_more.one_line: We want to make a plastic strip that curls on its own when damp, like a pine cone scale. First we must measure how much the plastic swells.
explain_more.what: Our goal is a window shade that moves by itself when the air gets damp, with no motor. Picture a pine cone. Each scale is two layers stuck together. When one layer swells more than the other, the scale bends. We want to copy that with 3D-printed plastic. We would stick one layer that swells when wet onto one layer that hardly swells. Wet the strip and it curls, like a leaf curling as it dries. A written rule, worked out by the engineer Stephen Timoshenko in 1925, says how far such a strip can bend. It was first written for thermostat strips made of two metals that bend when heated. The rule depends on how much the wet layer grows and how thick the strip is. We have planned five things to print. The first is a small strip, about as long as a paper clip (30 by 3 by 1 millimetres). The last is a small shade module, a single slat about as long as your hand (120 millimetres). Before any of that, we must soak small test strips and measure how much each plastic swells. Nobody has published that number for these plastics.
explain_more.why: Buildings use motors and sensors to open and close shades. A shade that moves with the damp in the air would need no power. A rule that predicts the bend lets a designer plan such a part before printing it. First we must learn whether the rule works for cheap, common printer plastics. Nobody has measured how much these plastics swell in damp air. Every prediction rests on one data sheet from the maker. We do not know yet if the idea works. The first test is small. It costs about a thousand dollars in materials, if the lab borrows the big machines. That is roughly the price of a decent laptop. We soak the strips in liquid water, not damp air, for a practical reason. Water gives the biggest swelling, so it is the easiest first test. Damp air will swell the plastic less. If it swelled only one tenth as much, our louver (slat) would turn about 6 degrees instead of about 58. So the water test only shows whether the idea can work at all. Damp air must be tested next.

steps.text: Print flat test strips from several Formlabs plastics. The Form 4 printer holds one plastic at a time, so each plastic is a separate print.
steps.picture: Like baking one flavour of cookie per tray.

steps.text: Rinse the strips in rubbing alcohol (isopropanol, a cleaning liquid). Dry them, then bake them under light. Weigh them again and again until the weight stops dropping. That means no more liquid is left inside.
steps.picture: Like weighing laundry on the line until it stops getting lighter.

steps.text: Measure each strip's length and thickness before it gets wet. Use a fixed camera with a ruler in the picture.
steps.picture: Like marking a child's height on a door frame, always from the same spot.

steps.text: Soak the strips in water and weigh them at set times. Use a fine scale and wipe each strip the same way every time. A thin film of water on the surface can weigh as much as the water inside.
steps.picture: Like weighing a sponge: squeeze it the same way each time.

steps.text: Measure the length again after soaking. On a 40 millimetre strip, the length changes by about 2 parts in 1,000. That is about 80 micrometres, roughly the width of one human hair.
steps.picture: A strip as long as a pencil stub that grows by one hair's width.

steps.text: Glue or print a swelling layer onto a layer that hardly swells. Note the thickness of each.
steps.picture: Like pressing a damp paper towel onto a dry plastic ruler.

steps.text: Wet the two-layer strip and photograph its curl from the side. Fit a circle to the curve. The size of that circle tells us how tight the bend is.
steps.picture: Like tracing a round plate to find its size.

steps.text: Compare the measured bend with the bend the written rule predicts from the swelling numbers.
steps.picture: Like checking a recipe's promised cooking time against your oven.

explain_more.wrong_if: Our bet, written before we look: a strip with measured layer swelling and thickness will curl to within a fifth of the rule's prediction. For the first strip, the prediction is a curl with a radius of about 41 millimetres. A 41 millimetre radius is a circle a little wider than a bottle cap's diameter, times about two. We ran many computer trials with our best guesses for the unknown inputs. Nine out of ten trials landed between 28 and 83 millimetres. We are wrong if the real curl is far outside that range. We are also wrong if the plastic swells too little to see.
could_go_wrong: The swelling numbers come from one data sheet. It does not say how thick the tested slab was.
The plastics may swell much less in damp air than in liquid water. Then the strips may barely bend. Our notes say we have no data on damp air at all.
The two layers may not stick to each other well. Nobody has measured that bond.
Alcohol left inside a strip after rinsing could be mistaken for swelling in water.
The signal is tiny, about 80 micrometres (one hair's width) on a 40 millimetre strip. A cheap ruler or caliper cannot measure it.

The rule assumes the layers are stuck together perfectly and that the bends are small. The real strip may break both assumptions. A bend that is too tight, or a join that slips, would make the rule fail.
Thick layers soak slowly. Doubling the length makes the wait four times longer. A shade one metre wide could need about 184 days (our estimate, from 54 to 660) to finish bending.
We estimated, not measured, how stiff the plastic is when wet. A wrong guess may shift the predicted bend.

questions.q: How do you know the bend rule is right?
questions.a: We re-ran the project's check script and an independent solver. They agree to about one part in a billion. That shows the maths is consistent. It does not show that real plastic obeys the rule.

questions.q: How do you know these plastics swell at all?
questions.a: One data sheet for Flexible 80A V2 says it gains 8 percent in mass and 3 percent in volume in one day in water. Other Formlabs plastics gain under 1 percent in their cube test. One older soft one gains 2.3 percent.

questions.q: Why test in liquid water if the shade will sit in damp air?
questions.a: Water is the strongest case, so it is the easiest first test. If the strip cannot bend in water, it will not bend in air. Damp air will swell the plastic less. We have no measurement of how much less. If it swelled one tenth as much, the slat would turn about 6 degrees instead of about 58. Damp air is the next test, not this one.

questions.q: What would the shade look like?
questions.a: Our biggest planned part is one slat, 120 millimetres long, about the length of your hand. Wet in water, we predict it turns about 58 degrees (likely range 30 to 85). That is roughly like tilting a door a bit more than halfway open. A real shade would be many such slats. We have not designed one, and we have not built anything yet. Large slats are a problem. A long, soft slat held sideways also sags under its own weight more than it curls.

questions.q: What are the five things you plan to print?
questions.a: One: a small strip, 30 by 3 by 1 millimetres. Two: a row of ten fingers of different widths, to test how the bend changes with width. Three: tiles of growing width, up to 60 millimetres, to see when a strip becomes a plate that the rule does not cover. Four: a tree that splits twice, with thick and thin branches, to see if all turn by the same angle. Five: the 120 millimetre slat. The first three look possible with stock plastics in under a week. Fourth is riskier because its thinnest branch is 0.2 millimetres thick. The fifth can be tested in water only.

questions.q: Has anyone built a damp-air bending part from printed resin before?
questions.a: Partly. A 2024 paper printed a polyurethane ink that folds in under one second in humid air. Polyurethane is a stretchy plastic. That ink is not a Formlabs plastic, and its bend was not compared with the rule. We found no part checked against a law whose maths a proof assistant has verified. A proof assistant is software that checks maths step by step. That is only what our search found. It does not prove no such part exists.

questions.q: Why is the swelling so hard to measure?
questions.a: The change is tiny and surface water confuses scales. It needs a fine scale, a fixed camera and a fixed routine.

questions.q: Would alcohol work better than water?
questions.a: Alcohol makes the soft plastic gain about 39 percent in a day. A hard plastic gains under 0.1 percent. That is far stronger. But the strips would stretch too much for the simple rule.

questions.q: Can I repeat this at home?
questions.a: Partly. A phone and a kitchen scale can show whether a strip curls. They cannot give numbers good enough to test the rule. Proper kit costs one to two thousand dollars. Buying every core item new would cost $9,017 to $11,524. We think most of that can be borrowed, which leaves $920 to $1,231 to buy. Some printer-setting costs are separate. Formlabs sells a mode for using other makers' resin (Open Material Mode) for $875 per printer.

questions.q: How fast would it bend?
questions.a: A 0.4 millimetre layer would settle in hours to about a day. The 120 millimetre slat would take about 2.7 days in water, and likely between under 1 day and 10 days. Both estimates assume a slab thickness the data sheet never states. They are our estimates, not measurements.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We have not printed or soaked any strip. We have not measured swelling in damp air, bond strength, or wet stiffness. Several prices came from search snippets only.

explain_more.label: explain2-bm-contract
explain_more.one_line: Short answer: a printed, damp-bending shade probably cannot go on tall flats in England, and nobody we found pays for a design rule alone. So we offer a London design studio measurements, not promises.
explain_more.what:
We want to offer a London design studio a small first sample. It is a printed strip made of two plastic layers. One layer swells in damp air and the other does not, so the strip curls. A curling strip could open or close a window shade with no motor.

We would also offer a design rule. The rule says how far a two-layer strip can possibly curl. It is simple: the curl can never be more than 1.5 times the size mismatch between the layers, divided by the strip's thickness. Think of a cheap oven thermostat. Its two metals grow by different amounts when warm, so the strip bends. Our strip does the same with damp instead of heat.

An old textbook formula already hints at this limit. A 2015 paper (Holstov) plotted it with numbers. What we add is a proof. We used a free maths-checking program called Lean. It is a theorem prover: software that checks a proof one tiny step at a time and refuses any gap. That means a person can trust the sums without redoing them. But Lean checks only the maths of a model. It does not show that a real printed strip will behave that way. That is why the sample must be measured.

Before building anything, eight research helpers read building rules, safety sheets, grant lists and patents. A patent is a legal right to an invention. This page sums up what they found about the contract side. It covers what the part must pass, what it costs to handle, who pays, and who owns what.

We do not know who "we" will be on the offer. We do not know if the team is a company or a university group. We also do not know what the sample will cost to make. The studio's making arm, called Fab.Pub, lists a minimum budget of 250 pounds (about the price of a good bicycle lock set) and no other fees. That is all we found.
explain_more.why:
Many clever building ideas fail on boring questions. Will it burn? Is it safe to print? Who pays? Does someone already own the idea? Asking these first saves months of work.

It also stops us from saying things we cannot prove. Nobody has yet measured an energy saving from a damp-air shade. The best real example only measured how much shade it made. A fair offer should say that plainly. It should offer measurements the studio lacks, not big promises.

explain_more.wrong_if:
Before looking, we wrote down a bet. Nobody will pay for the design rule alone. And no printed resin will pass the fire rules for tall homes. A resin is a liquid plastic that hardens under light.

We would be wrong if a firm showed it pays for design rules alone. We would be wrong if a printed resin earned the top fire grade. We would also be wrong if someone measured a real energy saving from a damp-air shade. The helpers looked for all three and found none. But they could not search everywhere. So "we found none" is not the same as "none exists".
could_go_wrong: The helpers searched limited sources. So 'nobody has done this' may only mean 'we did not find it'.
The patent scan was only partly checked. The checkers could not open two key patent pages, so we leave those claims out.
The swelling figure for one bendy resin came from a scrambled data sheet. Nobody has re-measured it in damp air.
The strip may bend more from heat than from damp. That could hide the effect we want to show.
Grant lists change fast. Most European grants need an applicant based in Europe.
We do not know whether the team is a company or a university group. That decides which grants fit.
No patent lawyer has looked at anything. So who owns what is still open.
The studio prints with robot arms and plant-based plastic, not with resin or powder. So our samples only prove the shape idea, not a finished product.
Lean proves the maths of our model. It does not prove a printed strip will behave that way. Only measuring a real strip can show that.

questions.q: How do you know?
questions.a: Each helper saved the pages it read and wrote down exact quotes. A second set of readers then rechecked the main claims. We only use claims they could confirm, in full or in part. The rest are listed under 'left out'.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We have not tested any printed strip yet. We did not read paid standards or the full text of some papers. We did not check Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland. No lawyer or fire engineer has reviewed this.

questions.q: Could a printed plastic part be used as a shade on a tall block of flats in England?
questions.a: Probably not. Take homes with a floor at 18 metres or higher. That is roughly six floors up. There, outer wall parts must be nearly non-burning. Shading slats are not exempt. Shading lower than 4.5 metres from the ground, about the height of a double-decker bus, falls outside that rule.

questions.q: Can we say the part is fire safe?
questions.a: No. A real fire grade needs large test pieces. A desk print is too small to be graded. The printer maker publishes only a small-scale plastic burn rating called UL 94. The English fire guide does not use it. The guide never mentions it.

questions.q: Who would pay for this?
questions.a: Clients pay for finished installations. Public grants pay for early proof work. Window and shade makers join public projects but offer help, not cash. We found nobody who pays for a design rule alone. We may have missed some.

questions.q: Is the idea patented by someone else?
questions.a: Many nearby ideas are patented. So we cannot claim 'a plate that curls in damp air'. Some patents on wood versions are narrow. One live patent from MIT and a printer firm is the nearest to a resin-printed damp-swelling part. Its first and widest sentence is narrower than first thought. The first scan found no patent that pairs a computer-checked proof with print design. But a lawyer must confirm that.

questions.q: Is it safe to make?
questions.a: With care, yes. All 14 resin sheets we checked mark the liquid as a skin allergy risk. That means repeated skin contact can cause a lasting allergy. Two resins also carry a warning for harm to unborn children or fertility. We would leave those out of any public sample. The washing liquid, rubbing alcohol, catches fire easily. So we need gloves, goggles and fresh air.

questions.q: Can we call it green or recyclable?
questions.a: No. The printer maker says cured resin and used powder cannot be recycled. It calls one powder partly plant-based but gives no percentage. New European Union rules limit vague claims like 'biobased' from 27 September 2026.

questions.q: Who is the team, and what does the studio get?
questions.a: We do not know yet whether the team is a company or a university group. The studio would get a small printed sample, measurements of how it curls, and the design rule with its proof. It would not get a finished building product.

questions.q: How much will the sample cost?
questions.a: We do not know. The studio's making arm lists only a minimum budget of 250 pounds and no other published fees.

questions.q: Why does the rule need a proof at all?
questions.a: An earlier paper plotted the same limit using numbers, but a plot is not a proof. A proof says no choice of layers can ever beat the limit. The program Lean checks that with no gaps. The limit applies to the maths model, so the real strip must still be measured.

loop: stay on the latest law set

scout.summary: The public law library (fractastical/leanbio, head cb92aaf, pushed 2026-11-12, CI green) is pinned at law set 1.6.0 (53 laws, cut 2026-11-01). Since late October it gained: the versioned registry and eight law sets 1.0.0-1.6.0; seven perturbation laws (five accepted in 1.5.0); Hydrostatics (Boyle v2); the four machine-discovered disc-* flying-fish laws (fin-ratio gap >=0.406 vs <=0.389, pectoral allometry exponent 1.017-1.099, wing-loading band 37.0-46.4 N/m2 with n=4, and a contested mass exponent); E3 v2 (aerobic ceiling 0.0458 -> 0.0833 W); then, after 1.6.0, Turing.lean (2 Nov), CellGeometry.lean (3 Nov), Crystals.lean (7 Nov) and on 12 Nov twelve ThompsonLaws modules (Hygromorphs, HollowTube, MurrayCubic and others) and four DarwinLaws modules. Three things the team should know before reusing the framework. (1) Eleven law files in the registry (turing-ddi-linear-condition, seven cell-geometry laws, three crystal laws) are in NO law set: 1.6.0 does not pin them, and the ThompsonLaws/DarwinLaws theorems have no registry entries of their own. (2) Upstream Constraints.lean carries 14 of the 33 *_rules_out lemmas in the application repo; vmin_rules_out and aerobic_flight_rules_out are absent, so EliminationsFlier, EliminationsTff and EliminationsPhysiology cannot compile upstream as shipped, and by static import analysis the default build covers 26 modules and leaves 21 unbuilt (including Flight, Perturb, Physiology, Scaling, Empirical, Genotype, Hydrostatics, HollowTube, MurrayCubic and all eight Eliminations* certificates); 39 of the 46 laws in 1.6.0 that name a Lean module point at a module the green CI does not build. (3) The application repo's own registry is at 1.8.1, not 1.6.0: 1.7.0 rescoped E3 and fick-principle because under 1.6.0 they fire red on a real flying fish making an ordinary unpowered glide, and 1.8.0 narrowed five scopes to fix a third wild-type false positive; staying on 1.6.0 keeps those known false positives. The certificate pattern is reusable as is: a lemma concluding False from a law plus a candidate's committed interval, instantiated by eliminate.mjs with exact rationals and closed by norm_num, with three verdicts (eliminated, consistent, cannot rule). Existing theorems map onto track 2 (Turing: equal diffusivities cannot pattern), track 3 (Laplace and hoop pressure limits, Murray junction exponent), track 4 (glide range, wind glide, v_min) and track 5 (Timoshenko bilayer curvature, hollow-tube mass factor, snap parameter); track 1 has no dose-response law in the library. I did not run a Lean build.
scout.recommended: Run the glide energy-budget certificate first: it has a measured polar, a lemma already written, data I could fetch, and a pre-computable set of verdicts (22.3 m at 10 m/s, 50.1 m at 15 m/s), and it hands track 4 its mechanical model. Doing it forces the two repairs every other track needs anyway, restoring the missing *_rules_out lemmas upstream and deciding honestly whether verdicts are stamped 1.6.0 or a newer set.

candidates.name: Glide energy-budget certificate (range <= L/D x (h + v^2/2g)) against published flying-fish glides
candidates.system: Exocoetidae gliding flight: Cypselurus hiraii wind-tunnel models (Park and Choi 2010), CFD model (Deng 2019), field and aquarium launch speeds (Makiguchi 2013)
candidates.phenotype_measured: Single-glide horizontal distance (m) given launch speed (m/s), launch height (m) and maximum lift-to-drag ratio
candidates.why_it_fits: It is the one flying-fish test with a measured polar, a model that outputs a number, and a lemma already written for it (Delphi.Constraints.glide_range_rules_out and Delphi.Perturb.wind_glide_rules_out in the application repo; perturb-wind-glide and flight-climb-glide-law are accepted in 1.6.0). It doubles as track 4's mechanical model. My calculation with measured L/D 4.37: a 10 m/s sea-level launch allows at most 22.3 m, 15 m/s allows 50.1 m, 20 m/s allows 89.1 m; so the often-quoted '50 m glide' is ruled out for a 10 m/s launch and sits exactly on the bound at 15 m/s, and Deng's 13.2 m height needs at least 16.1 m/s.

candidates.the_test: Write four candidates in the eliminate.mjs schema, each committing launch speed, launch height, L/D max and claimed range as exact rationals: (a) 50 m from a 10 m/s launch at L/D 4.37; (b) 50 m at 15 m/s; (c) Deng's 45.4 m and 13.2 m apex at his L/D 4.7; (d) Kawachi's modelled 80 m, which assumes L/D 15.7 against the measured 4.37. Run eliminate.mjs, compile the generated certificate, and record eliminated / consistent / cannot-rule per row. Then repeat (a) with Park and Choi's ground-effect allowance (drag down 14% at h/b 0.33 over water) through glide_range_le_groundEffect, and with a headwind through wind_glide_rules_out. Pre-register the expected verdicts before running. On 1.6.0, declare each row an unpowered glide and confirm E3/C14 do not turn it red; if they do, that is the documented 1.6.0 false positive and must be reported, not hidden.
candidates.biggest_risk: The field distances and speeds are second-hand (Makiguchi and Park and Choi quote older film and observation work I could not fetch), so an 'eliminated' row may indict the quoted number rather than the fish. glide_range_rules_out exists only in the application repo's Constraints.lean, not upstream, and the bound treats kinetic energy as extra height, which is my reading and must be checked against the lemma's actual hypotheses.
candidates.cost_and_time: About one week: one day to restore the lemma upstream or run against the application repo, two days for candidates and certificates, two days for ground-effect and wind variants. No compute beyond a Lean build.

candidates.name: Port the *_rules_out certificate pattern to tracks 1-5 on law set 1.6.0
candidates.system: fractastical/leanbio (Lean 4.35.0, Mathlib v4.35.0) plus the application repo's lean/eliminate pipeline
candidates.phenotype_measured: Per track, one committed design quantity checked against one proved law: diffusivity ratio (track 2), wall stress or junction radius exponent (track 3), glide range or minimum speed (track 4), bilayer curvature or tube mass factor (track 5)
candidates.why_it_fits: The pattern is generic: every lemma concludes False from the law plus a committed interval, and eliminate.mjs fills in exact rationals. Theorems already proved cover four of five tracks: Delphi.Turing.no_instability_of_equal_diffusivity and turing_instability_iff; Delphi.Physiology.laplace_pressure_limit and hoop_pressure_limit; ThompsonLaws.MurrayCubic.murray_junction and junction_law; Delphi.Flight.glide_range_le; ThompsonLaws.Hygromorphs.bilayerCurvature and snapParameter_threshold_mono; ThompsonLaws.HollowTube.massFactor_at_optimum. None of the Turing, Thompson or Darwin theorems has a *_rules_out wrapper yet, and none is pinned by 1.6.0.

candidates.the_test: Step 0: restore the 19 missing lemmas to upstream Constraints.lean (or build against the application repo) and add the Eliminations* modules to a build target so CI actually checks them. Step 1: for each of tracks 2-5 write one wrapper, for example turing_rules_out (well-mixed stable, Du = Dv, claimed growing mode -> False), laplace_rules_out (claimed lumen pressure above 2 t sigma_max / r -> False), murray_rules_out (junction radii off r0^3 = r1^3 + r2^3 beyond a stated band -> False), bilayer_rules_out (claimed curvature outside the Timoshenko value for the committed thickness and modulus ratios -> False). Step 2: one candidates.json per track with one design that must be eliminated and one that must survive; run eliminate.mjs; compile. Step 3: run propose.mjs on each new law (build, no sorry or axiom, witness, joint consistency, mutants rejected) and record that they are candidate, non-binding, and outside 1.6.0 until a new law set is cut. Track 1 gets an explicit 'cannot rule: no dose-response law formalised' row.
candidates.biggest_risk: Keeping the label '1.6.0' while using laws 1.6.0 does not pin (Turing, cell geometry, crystals, every Thompson and Darwin theorem) would misstate provenance; either cut a new law set or say each verdict is 'against unreleased law file X at commit cb92aaf'. Second risk: 39 of 46 module-backed laws in 1.6.0 sit in modules the default build skips, so 'CI green' currently says little about them.
candidates.cost_and_time: Two to three weeks for four wrappers, four candidate files and the build fix; no data cost.

candidates.name: Davenport's pectoral-length ceiling (76-79% of standard length) tested on museum morphometrics
candidates.system: Exocoetidae and other Beloniformes, 109 museum specimens (Daane et al. 2021 Data S1, sheet A)
candidates.phenotype_measured: Pectoral fin length divided by standard length, per specimen
candidates.why_it_fits: Davenport gives a mechanistic ceiling with a number: the wing's leading edge sits at 24% of standard length and the fin cannot exceed 76% (2003) or 78-79% (1992) without fouling the tail beat. The registry already holds the floor (disc-flying-fish-fin-ratio-gap, >= 0.406); the ceiling is the missing other side and is a natural new *_rules_out. My check on the cached sheet: 49 flying fish span 0.406-0.823; the 14 with SL >= 15 cm span 0.656-0.757, all under 0.76; three specimens exceed 0.76 and two exceed 0.79, all Hirundichthys rondeleti under 6.1 cm SL.

candidates.the_test: State the law as 'adult flying fish (SL >= 15 cm): pectoral/SL <= 0.76' with a rules_out lemma, run propose.mjs for joint consistency with the 0.406 floor and for mutant rejection, and score it on specimens not used to set the threshold: the three Zootaxa Cypselurus revisions found on Zenodo carry per-species morphometric tables. Report the juvenile exceedances as a scope boundary, and decide before looking at new data whether the 0.76 or the 0.79 reading is the one being tested.
candidates.biggest_risk: Only three flying-fish species are in the sheet and the adults-only cut (n = 14) was chosen by me after seeing the data, so the 15 cm threshold is post hoc; the independent tables were found but not opened in this run.
candidates.cost_and_time: About one week, no compute.

candidates.name: Wing-loading allometry: Davenport's exponents against the registry's four-specimen band
candidates.system: Exocoetus obtusirostris growth series (Davenport 1992) versus Cypselurus hiraii models (Park and Choi 2010)
candidates.phenotype_measured: Wing loading (N/m2) as a power of standard length; mass and lateral fin area exponents
candidates.why_it_fits: Davenport reports mass ~ SL^2.981, lateral fin area ~ SL^1.834 and wing loading ~ SL^1.236, which predicts how the registry's 37.0-46.4 N/m2 band must move with size; the band rests on four stuffed specimens of one species. It also bears on the contested disc-heterurus-mass-exponent (0.981 from 14 fish over a narrow length range) against Davenport's 2.981.

public_data.what: Davenport 1992 abstract with the three exponents
Fish 1990 abstract: six genera, fin area and span scaling (no numbers in the abstract)

candidates.the_test: Use allometry_consistency_rules_out (application repo) on the triple (2.981, 1.834, 1.236): mass exponent minus area exponent is 1.147 by my subtraction, not 1.236, so either the wing-loading area differs from 'lateral fin area' or the triple is inconsistent; resolve from the full text, then rescope disc-measured-wing-loading-band to a stated length range.
candidates.biggest_risk: The specimen tables are behind a paywall; with abstracts alone the 1.147 versus 1.236 gap cannot be resolved.
candidates.cost_and_time: Days once the full text is in hand; blocked until then.

candidates.name: Printed flying-fish planform as a passive-glide surrogate
candidates.system: A rigid printed model of the Park and Choi L3 planform, compared with published robotic and wind-tunnel models
candidates.phenotype_measured: Glide ratio and minimum airspeed of a physical model
candidates.why_it_fits: It ties track 6 to the Formlabs print and to track 4. The law set predicts numbers for it: with W = 0.5886 N, S = 0.012688 m2 and C_Lmax 0.78, wing loading is 46.4 N/m2 and v_min is 9.85 m/s (my calculation, air density 1.225 kg/m3), and the glide ratio should not exceed 4.37 out of ground effect.

public_data.what: Saro-Cortes et al. 2022 abstract: modular robotic model, wind tunnel at Reynolds number 30,000, pelvic-fin position and pitch trade lift against pitch stability
Chen et al. 2023 abstract: robotic flying fish exits water at 1.55 m/s (5.9 body lengths per second), crossing time 0.233 s

candidates.the_test: Print the L3 planform at full scale and at a lighter wing loading, launch from a fixed-speed catapult at a measured height, film from the side, and compare range with the certificate's bound; a model that out-ranges the bound falsifies either the measured L/D or the lemma's assumptions.
candidates.biggest_risk: A v_min near 10 m/s is too fast for a hand launch indoors, a resin print will not match a 60 g fish's mass distribution, and I found no public raw force data for any of the robotic models.
candidates.cost_and_time: Three to six weeks including printing and a launch rig; outside what this scout could verify.

could_not_find: Any public raw dataset of flying-fish glide trajectories (tracked distance, speed, height per flight). Zenodo returned taxonomy papers and a copy of Deng 2019; Dryad returned one unrelated dataset; Figshare returned nothing relevant. Every field distance and speed I have is quoted second-hand.
Park and Choi 2010 full text in this run: the publisher returned 403 and the Wayback copy returned a bot challenge. Its numbers come from the project's cached PDF, not a fresh fetch.
The Daane 2021 Data S1 workbook in this run: the PubMed Central link returned a download interstitial. The fin-ratio numbers come from the project's cached CSV extract.
Full texts of Davenport 1992, 1994 and 2003, Fish 1990 and Kawachi 1993 (paywalled). The specimen-level wing-loading tables that would resolve the 1.147 versus 1.236 exponent gap are in those.
The primary film and observation sources behind '10 m/s leap, 50 m glide, 400 m with taxiing, 8 m height'. They predate DOIs or I did not locate one; I cite none of them.
A dose-response or reporter-response law in the library: grep for Hill, dose-response and Michaelis found nothing relevant, so track 1 has no theorem to wrap.

A compiled confirmation. I did not run lake build; the claim that three upstream certificates cannot compile rests on the missing lemma names, and the built/unbuilt module split rests on a static import walk.
Why upstream Constraints.lean is the shorter version: whether the 19 lemmas were dropped deliberately in the 9 November split or left behind is not recorded in the commit messages I read.

Registry entries for the ThompsonLaws and DarwinLaws theorems moved in on 12 November: the three ported laws that mention them point at Delphi modules, and no law file names a ThompsonLaws or DarwinLaws module directly.

design.label: design-flyingfish
design.chosen: Energy-height glide certificate with a stall floor: the scout's recommended glide energy-budget test, tightened and given three tests that can fail
design.one_paragraph: I keep the scout's first candidate but change what is tested. As the scout wrote it, the test is arithmetic on second-hand field numbers and cannot fail; one row of it (50 m from 8 m at L/D 4.37) is already a compiled certificate in the application repo (lean/Delphi/Certificates/Eliminations.lean, elim_pure_glide_field_distance_C15). The scout's own flagged doubt is real: the proved lemma glide_range_le has only potential energy W*h on the left-hand side, and nothing in the library treats launch speed as height. The design adds the missing piece as one new wrapper, and adds the stall floor the library already proves (vmin_le): a lifting glide cannot spend kinetic energy below the minimum speed. That changes the numbers a lot. With the measured polar of Park and Choi's model L3 the stall floor is 9.85 m/s, so a 10 m/s launch buys 0.65 m of level glide, not the scout's 22.3 m, and a single 50 m glide needs at least 17.0 m/s with the full ground-effect allowance. The bound is a theorem only while lift equals weight; for a lofted launch it is a modelling claim, and that is where it can be wrong. Three tests can fail: (1) the trajectories in Deng 2019's full text, cached in the project but with launch conditions not yet recorded in physics/glide-data.csv and not opened by me; (2) the logged aquarium leaps of Makiguchi 2013, which at 3.87 to 5.15 m/s sit far below the stall floor and so must be short ballistic hops; (3) a Formlabs-printed glider launched at measured speed, shared with track 4. The same package (pre-registration file, candidates file, three verdicts, wild-type false-positive audit) is the kit the other tracks reuse. One conflict to settle: the workflow says stay on law set 1.6.0 while the request says use the latest of everything. Upstream leanbio pins 1.6.0 and the application repo is at 1.8.1; I stamp every verdict with both and report the known 1.6.0 false positives instead of hiding them.
design.model:
QUANTITIES. W weight (N); S reference area (m2, pectoral + pelvic + body planform, the area Park and Choi's coefficients use); rho air density; C_Lmax; (L/D)max; delta ground-effect drag reduction (0 away from the surface); v0 launch airspeed; v1 airspeed at the end of the lifting glide; h0, h1 heights at start and end; x horizontal air distance; w along-track wind (positive = tailwind); g = 9.81 m/s2.

EQUATIONS.
(M1) Stall floor, already proved (Delphi.Scaling.vmin_le, present upstream): lift = W and C <= C_Lmax imply v^2 >= vmin^2 = 2W / (rho S C_Lmax).
(M2) Energy balance over the lifting glide: W (h0 - h1) + (W / 2g)(v0^2 - v1^2) = (1 - delta) Dbar x + loss, loss >= 0, where Dbar is the path-mean drag. Pointwise L = W and L/D <= (L/D)max give Dbar >= W / (L/D)max.
(M3) Define energy height H = (h0 - h1) + (v0^2 - vmin^2) / 2g. Then x <= (L/D)max H / (1 - delta). This is the existing Delphi.glide_range_le_groundEffect (Flight.lean, present upstream) instantiated with h := H, plus M1 for v1 >= vmin. The new Lean work is one wrapper, glide_energy_range_rules_out, concluding False from M1, M2 and a claimed x above the bound. No new physics is assumed in the proof; the physics is in the hypothesis lift = W.
(M4) Wind: ground distance = x (1 + w/u) for airspeed u, through the existing Delphi.Perturb.wind_glide_rules_out (present upstream).
(M5) Below the stall floor the wings carry at most the fraction f = v^2 / vmin^2 of the weight, so a leap at speed v and launch angle theta is airborne at most T = 2 v sin(theta) / (g (1 - f)).

SCOPE, STATED AS A HYPOTHESIS NOT A THEOREM. M3 is proved only for lift = W. A lofted launch has a near-ballistic arc where the wings are unloaded and drag is only parasitic, so distance per unit energy lost can exceed (L/D)max. My check: at 10 m/s, model L3, C_Dmin 0.055: D = 0.5 x 1.225 x 100 x 0.012688 x 0.055 = 0.043 N against W = 0.589 N, a ratio of 13.8, above 4.37. So whether M3 survives a lofted trajectory is an empirical question, and prediction P2 tests it.

PARAMETERS AND WHERE THEY COME FROM (none fitted to the test data).
- Model L3 (Cypselurus hiraii): mass 0.06 kg, areas 0.006377 + 0.001837 + 0.004474 = 0.012688 m2, C_Lmax 0.78, (L/D)max 4.37. Source: physics/glide-data.csv row 'Table 1 model L3; Table 2' in the application repo, the project's reading of Park and Choi 2010; I did not re-fetch the full text.
- delta = 0.14 at h/b 0.33 over water. Source: scout's reading of physics/prior-art/raw/wb-park-choi-2010.pdf; also used as 7/50 in the existing certificate.
- rho = 1.225 kg/m3: the value already used in the compiled certificate elim_glider_below_minimum_speed_C9 (49/40); standard sea-level air, unverified background.
- Deng 2019 model: (L/D)max 4.7, C_Lmax 1.03, one trajectory with 45.4 m distance and 13.2 m height. Source: abstract as recorded in the scout file; I verified only the DOI.
- Cheilopogon heterurus doederleini: mass 0.226 kg and wing area 0.0225 m2 (Kawachi 1993 as quoted by Deng, second-hand, physics/glide-data.csv theory row); leap speed 3.87 to 5.15 m/s, pitch at leap 20.0 +- 3.3 degrees (Makiguchi 2013 as recorded in physics/glide-data.csv).

MY CALCULATIONS (script: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/scratch/design-flyingfish/calc.py).
- L3: W = 0.06 x 9.81 = 0.5886 N; W/S = 46.39 N/m2; vmin^2 = 2 x 46.39 / (1.225 x 0.78) = 97.10; vmin = 9.85 m/s.
- Level launch at the surface, x <= 4.37 (v0^2 - 97.10) / 19.62: 10 m/s gives 0.65 m (0.75 m with delta 0.14); 15 m/s gives 28.5 m (33.1 m); 20 m/s gives 67.5 m (78.4 m). Without the stall floor the same formula gives the scout's 22.3, 50.1 and 89.1 m.
- Launch airspeed needed for a 50 m single glide: sqrt(97.10 + 19.62 x 50 / 4.37) = 17.9 m/s; with delta 0.14, sqrt(97.10 + 19.62 x 50 x 0.86 / 4.37) = 17.0 m/s.
- Deng: apex 13.2 m needs v0 >= sqrt(19.62 x 13.2) = 16.09 m/s; 45.4 m at L/D 4.7 needs v0 >= sqrt(19.62 x 45.4 / 4.7) = 13.77 m/s.
- Cheilopogon: W/S = 0.226 x 9.81 / 0.0225 = 98.5 N/m2; vmin = 12.5 m/s at C_Lmax 1.03 (14.4 m/s at 0.78); at 5.15 m/s f = 26.5 / 156.2 = 0.170; T = 2 x 5.15 x sin(23.3 deg) / (9.81 x 0.830) = 0.50 s; horizontal reach 5.15 x cos(23.3 deg) x 0.50 = 2.37 m.

FITTED VERSUS HELD OUT. Literature tests: nothing fitted; the held-out data are Deng's launch conditions and Makiguchi's per-leap durations, neither recorded in the project's data file and neither opened by me (I counted keywords in Makiguchi's text: 'duration' 29 times, 'airborne' twice, so the numbers are probably there, but I did not read them). Physical test: the printed glider's own (L/D)max and vmin are fitted on steady trimmed drop glides; the catapult level launches are held out.

CITATIONS (DOI resolved at api.crossref.org in this run; title and authors matched). Park and Choi 2010, 10.1242/jeb.046052. Deng, Zhang, Liu, Mao 2019, 10.1088/1748-3190/ab23e6 (open copy: Zenodo record 8382768, cc-by-4.0, 1,550,487 bytes, listed by the Zenodo API in this run, not downloaded). Makiguchi et al. 2013, 10.3354/ab00494 (PDF fetched, 212,919 bytes, https://www.int-res.com/articles/ab2013/18/b018p105.pdf). Kawachi, Inada, Azuma 1993, 10.1006/jtbi.1993.1113 (title only; its content is known to me second-hand). Socha et al. 2015, 10.1139/cjz-2014-0013 (pointer for non-equilibrium gliding; full text not read).

frozen_predictions.statement: Every flight trajectory Deng 2019 reports that reaches an apex of 13.2 m starts at an airspeed of at least 16.1 m/s, and every reported trajectory satisfies apex <= v0^2 / 2g.
frozen_predictions.number: v0 >= 16.1 m/s for the 45.4 m, 13.2 m trajectory
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Any reported launch airspeed for that trajectory is below 16.1 m/s, or any reported apex exceeds v0^2 / 19.62 by more than 2%. A refutation means either the abstract's numbers are being misread or the simulated fish has a thrust or wind term the abstract does not mention; either way the Deng row leaves the candidate table.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Deng et al. 2019 full text, trajectory section (physics/prior-art/raw/pdf2-deng-2019.txt in the application repo, or Zenodo record 8382768). Opened only after the pre-registration commit.

frozen_predictions.statement: The quasi-steady bound holds on lofted trajectories: for every trajectory Deng reports, distance / (4.7 x v0^2 / 19.62) is at most 1.00, and the best one reaches at least 0.30 of it.
frozen_predictions.number: ratio in [0.30, 1.00]; if v0 is exactly 16.1 m/s the ratio is 45.4 / 62.0 = 0.73
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Any ratio above 1.00 (the certificate then eliminates a trajectory that a 3-degree-of-freedom model flies, so the lemma's lift = weight hypothesis is unsafe for lofted launches and the law's scope must be narrowed to level glides in a new version). Or the best ratio is below 0.30 (the bound is too loose to constrain a design).
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Same Deng table, plus our own 3-degree-of-freedom integrator run on Deng's polar as a cross-check of the reading.

frozen_predictions.statement: The aquarium leaps logged by Makiguchi 2013 at 3.87 to 5.15 m/s are ballistic hops, not glides: no leap is airborne longer than 0.50 s.
frozen_predictions.number: airborne time <= 0.50 s (0.43 s at the mean pitch of 20.0 degrees); horizontal reach <= 2.4 m
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Any logged leap is airborne longer than 0.50 s. Then one of three inputs is wrong and each is worth knowing: the leap speed estimated from tail-beat frequency is too low, the live fish's C_Lmax is well above the 0.78 to 1.03 of stuffed and simulated models, or the wing area quoted from Kawachi is too small. If the paper reports no per-leap airborne time, the verdict is 'cannot test', recorded as such.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Makiguchi et al. 2013 Tables and Results (open PDF, fetched, values not read). Accelerometer-derived durations.

frozen_predictions.statement: Certificate verdicts, fixed before any build: (a) 50 m single glide from a 10 m/s launch, L3 polar, delta 0.14: eliminated. (b) the same at 15 m/s: eliminated (bound 33.1 m). (c) the same at 20 m/s: consistent (bound 78.4 m). (d) Kawachi's 80 m at its own L/D 15.7: cannot rule (no launch speed committed) and flagged as an input conflict with the measured 4.37. (e) a 0.65 m glide from 10 m/s: consistent. (f) mutant: (L/D)max raised to 8 in row (b): consistent, showing the verdict depends on the measured polar.
frozen_predictions.number: 6 of 6 verdicts as listed; minimum launch airspeed for 50 m is 17.0 m/s
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Any generated certificate fails to compile, any verdict differs from the list, or propose.mjs accepts a mutant of the wrapper (stall floor dropped, or inequality reversed). This row checks the pipeline and my arithmetic; a failure is a bug report, not a finding about fish.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: eliminate.mjs output and lake build of the generated certificate module against leanbio at commit cb92aaf.

frozen_predictions.statement: Printed glider, level catapult launches at three speeds above its measured vmin: no flight exceeds (L/D)max_measured x (h0 + (v0^2 - vmin_measured^2) / 2g), and the best flight at each speed reaches at least half of it.
frozen_predictions.number: 0 of at least 30 flights above 1.10 x bound; best flight per speed >= 0.50 x bound
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: More than 1 of 30 flights lands beyond 1.10 x bound (the 10% is the allowance for speed and tape error), which would mean launch pitch-up converts speed to range better than a lift = weight glide and the scope must be narrowed. Or the best flight at every speed is under 0.50 x bound, which would mean the bound is true but useless as a design constraint for track 4.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: Phone video at 240 frames per second for launch speed over a marked 0.5 m gate; tape for landing distance; (L/D)max and vmin fitted beforehand on at least 10 trimmed drop glides that are not part of the 30.

frozen_predictions.statement: Wild-type audit: with the rows for real fish declared as unpowered glides, law set 1.8.1 turns none of them red on an accepted law; law set 1.6.0 turns them red on E3 and C14 (the false positive documented in lean/registry/CHANGELOG.md under 1.7.0).
frozen_predictions.number: 0 accepted-law violations under 1.8.1; E3 and C14 red under 1.6.0
frozen_predictions.refuted_if: Any accepted law other than E3 or C14 is red on a real-fish row under 1.6.0, or any accepted law is red under 1.8.1. Either is a new false positive and goes to the registry as a contest. If 1.6.0 shows no red at all, the changelog's account is wrong for these rows and that is reported too. This is a control, expected to confirm.
frozen_predictions.data_or_measurement: The declared-claim checker (lean/eliminate/browser-check) run once per law set on the same candidates file.

steps: 1. Pre-registration commit. Write tracks/flyingfish/PREREG.md containing the model above, the six predictions with thresholds, the candidates file with exact rationals, and the SHA-256 of the two unopened sources (pdf2-deng-2019.txt and the Makiguchi PDF). Commit before any Lean file, integrator or data extract exists. FREEZE 1.

2. Provenance check. Confirm which law ids in lawset-1.6.0.json cover Flight.glide_range_le_groundEffect, Scaling.vmin_le and Perturb.wind_glide_rules_out (flight-climb-glide-law 1.0.0 and perturb-wind-glide 1.0.0 are in the set; the vmin owner needs reading). Record leanbio commit cb92aaf and application repo commit 09d9868.

3. Wrapper. In a standalone lake package under tracks/flyingfish/lean that requires leanbio at cb92aaf, write glide_energy_range_rules_out from glide_range_le_groundEffect and vmin_le. Build Delphi.Flight, Delphi.Scaling and Delphi.Perturb explicitly, since the scout's static analysis says the default target skips them. Check no sorry and no added axiom.

4. Certificates. Run the six P4 candidates through an eliminate.mjs copy pointed at the new wrapper; compile; score P4. Run the wrapper through propose.mjs as a candidate law, with two mutants that must be rejected.
5. Wild-type audit (P6) under 1.6.0 and 1.8.1, both stamped on every row.
6. Open Deng. One person extracts the trajectory table into a CSV with page locators; a second checks it. Score P1 and P2. Run our own integrator on Deng's polar only after scoring.
7. Open Makiguchi. Extract per-leap durations and speeds; score P3.

8. Physical calibration. Print the glider, weigh it, measure area from the CAD, fit (L/D)max and vmin on trimmed drop glides. Commit those two numbers and the resulting bound per launch speed. FREEZE 2.
9. Physical test. 30 catapult launches; score P5.

10. Hand-over kit. Publish the PREREG template, candidates schema, three-verdict runner and wild-type audit under tracks/framework/ for tracks 1 to 5, with the mapping the scout found (Turing, Laplace and hoop, Murray, bilayer curvature) and an explicit 'cannot rule: no dose-response law' row for track 1. Update the dashboard's track 6 panel with scored predictions, including any that failed.
design.what_is_frozen_and_when: FREEZE 1 (step 1, before any code or data extraction): the model equations, every parameter value with its source, the six predictions and thresholds, the candidates file, the statement of the wrapper lemma, the two law sets and two commits the verdicts are stamped with, and hashes of the unopened Deng and Makiguchi files. FREEZE 2 (step 8, after calibration glides, before any catapult launch): the printed glider's mass, area, fitted (L/D)max and vmin, the launch speeds, the bound at each, and the rule for discarding a flight (wing strike, visible stall at release, speed gate missed). Nothing in FREEZE 1 may be edited after step 1; corrections go in a dated addendum that keeps the original text. Honest limit: the Deng full text is already in the project cache, so its blindness rests on discipline and on the fact that no launch speed appears in physics/glide-data.csv; whoever writes the commit must not have read that section.
design.what_would_make_this_a_paper: A paper-grade result is a prediction failing in a way that changes a law. The strongest is P2 or P5 failing high: a lofted launch beating the lift = weight bound would show that the certificate needs a scope clause, give a measured size for the excess, and make a case study of a machine-checked law being narrowed by a pre-registered test, which is the claim the whole framework rests on. P3 failing is also publishable in a small way: it would say the tail-beat speed estimate or the stuffed-model C_Lmax is off for live fish, and would name which. A second route to a paper is the positive one only if it is quantitative: all six hold and the stall-floor bound is tight (P2 ratio and P5 best flights above about 0.7), because then the pair of numbers 0.65 m at 10 m/s and 17.0 m/s for 50 m is a new, checkable statement that taxiing is required rather than helpful, and the same wrapper becomes track 4's design constraint. Merely confirmatory: P4 and P6 passing (pipeline works, known false positive reproduced), P1 passing (energy conservation in someone else's simulation), and all predictions passing with loose ratios near 0.3.
risks: The stall-floor numbers rest on one stuffed specimen (model L3) at a chord Reynolds number of 2.0e4 and a tunnel speed of 12 m/s. A live fish with cambered, tensioned fins may have a higher C_Lmax; at C_Lmax 1.03 the L3 floor drops from 9.85 to 8.57 m/s (my calculation: sqrt(97.10 x 0.78 / 1.03)) and the 10 m/s bound rises from 0.65 m to 5.9 m. The qualitative conclusion survives; the 0.65 m does not.
Every field distance and speed is second-hand, as the scout said. The design therefore makes no pass or fail claim on field numbers; the 17.0 m/s figure is an implication, not a tested prediction.

P3 may be untestable: I confirmed only that the word 'duration' appears 29 times in Makiguchi's text, not that per-leap airborne time is tabulated. Body pitch at leap is also not the trajectory angle.
The Cheilopogon wing area (0.0225 m2) is Kawachi's value quoted by Deng; I could not check it against Kawachi's paper, for which Crossref gives a title and no abstract.
Deng's blindness is by discipline, not by access (see the freeze note).

Law-set labelling. The wrapper is new and is in no law set; a verdict from it must be stamped 'candidate wrapper over flight-climb-glide-law 1.0.0, leanbio cb92aaf', never '1.6.0' alone. The workflow asked for 1.6.0 and the request asked for the latest of everything; I resolved it by reporting both 1.6.0 and 1.8.1, and this needs a human decision.

Build risk. Nobody has run lake build on upstream; the claim that Flight, Scaling and Perturb are outside the default target is the scout's static analysis. If they fail to build at cb92aaf, step 3 falls back to the application repo's lean/ and the provenance stamp changes.
Folder ownership. lean/ in the application repo belongs to another thread, so the wrapper lives in tracks/flyingfish/lean and reaches the registry only as a proposal.

Physical test: a resin print is heavy and brittle. If the glider's vmin comes out above about 8 m/s the catapult launches need a long hall and survive few landings; P5 would then be run with fewer than 30 flights and must be reported as underpowered.
Overlap with track 4, which owns the passive glide surrogate. P5 should be run once, by track 4, against this track's frozen bound.
first_week: Day 1: write and commit tracks/flyingfish/PREREG.md and candidates.json (FREEZE 1). Hash the two unopened sources. Ask the lean thread whether glide_energy_range_rules_out should go upstream or stay a track-local proposal.
Day 2: standalone lake package against leanbio cb92aaf; fetch the Mathlib cache; build Delphi.Flight, Delphi.Scaling, Delphi.Perturb; record what actually builds. Write the wrapper.
Day 3: generate and compile the six P4 certificates; run propose.mjs with two mutants; score P4. Run the wild-type audit under both law sets; score P6.
Day 4: open Deng; two-person extraction of the trajectory table; score P1 and P2. Open Makiguchi; score P3 or record 'cannot test'.

Day 5: 60-line 3-degree-of-freedom integrator as a cross-check on the Deng reading; send the glider CAD to print; write the tracks/framework/ kit README and the dashboard panel with every scored row, passes and failures alike.
design.compute_needed: Laptop only. One Lean 4.35.0 plus Mathlib v4.35.0 build using the prebuilt Mathlib cache (several GB of disk: put .lake on D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work or reuse the existing junction, since C: is nearly full); certificate modules compile in minutes. The integrator is a few seconds of Python. No Modal credits and no GPU cluster are needed.
design.physical_build: One Formlabs-printed flying-fish glider, built once and shared with track 4. Planform from Park and Choi's model L3: pectoral span 0.261 m, standard length 0.203 m (physics/glide-data.csv). The span exceeds a desktop resin printer's bed in one piece (unverified background), so print a hollow body and the two pectoral and two pelvic fins as separate flat plates about 0.7 mm thick that slot in at a fixed incidence, in a tough or durable resin rather than a rigid brittle one; the resin choice should come from the materials agent's list. Target all-up mass 30 g, giving W/S = 0.294 / 0.0127 = 23 N/m2 and, if the fish's C_Lmax 0.78 carried over, vmin about 7.0 m/s (my calculation: sqrt(2 x 23.2 / (1.225 x 0.78))); the real values are measured in calibration, not assumed. Add a nose ballast pocket for trim. Launcher: elastic catapult on a level rail 1.0 m above the floor with a 0.5 m marked speed gate. At a 10 m/s launch the placeholder bound is 4.37 x (1.0 + (100 - 48.6) / 19.62) = 15.8 m, so a sports hall or long corridor is needed. Measurements: phone video at 240 frames per second for speed, tape for distance, kitchen scale for mass. If a hall is not available, the literature tests P1 to P4 and P6 stand on their own.
