laws.label: laws-flyingfish
laws.lawset_version: 1.6.0 (lean/registry/lawsets/current.json -> lawset-1.6.0.json, created 2026-11-01T04:37:40Z, previous 1.5.0). It pins 53 laws: 36 accepted, 5 candidate, 7 proposed, 3 contested, 2 retired (counted from the file). lean/registry/laws/ holds 64 law files; the 11 not pinned by any released law set are the cell-geometry, crystal and Turing laws (bee-cell-rhombic-closure, bragg-cubic-ratio, crystallographic-restriction, hexagon-of-120, hexagonal-lattice-density, hexagonal-on-average, plateau-tetrahedral-angle, plateau-triple-junction-120, tetrahedral-bond-angle, turing-ddi-linear-condition, twelve-pentagons). README.md says 'Law set 1.6.0: 64 laws (36 accepted, 16 candidate, ...)', which counts law files, not the pinned set.

existing.statement_plain: If lift (1/2) rho v^2 S C_L equals weight W with C_L <= C_L,max, then v >= sqrt(2W/(rho S C_L,max)). Exact, needs no isometry.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: File header, 'What is assumed, not proved': isometry of mass, areas and sections (real animals break it: Davenport 1992 measured fin area ~ L^1.83 and wing loading ~ L^1.24 within one flying-fish species), constant density, the same material (sigma), the same C_L,max across sizes (Reynolds effects), the same L/D, flight at v_min, axial loading, and Thompson's muscle premise. 'Nothing here is a measured fact'; no number from physics/results.json appears in any statement.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Any glider or printed surrogate that commits weight, lifting area, air density and a C_L,max cap has a hard lower bound on steady glide speed. With the F1 candidate's numbers in Certificates/EliminationsFlier.lean (rho 1.225, S 0.04905 m^2, W 0.5886 N, C_L,max 0.78) my calculation gives v_min = sqrt(2*0.5886/(1.225*0.04905*0.78)) = sqrt(25.12) = 5.01 m/s, so a claimed 4 m/s steady glide is removed.

existing.theorem_or_def: vmin_ratio, vmin_log, powerRequired_ratio, powerRequired_log (def powerRequired W v LD = W v / LD)
existing.statement_plain: Under CubeLaw (W = k1 L^3), AreaLaw (S = k2 L^2) and constant rho, C_L,max, L/D: v_min scales as sqrt(L) and the power needed at v_min scales as L^3.5.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Same header as above: isometry, constant density, same C_L,max and L/D across sizes, flight at v_min. All are named hypotheses on functions of one length.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Fixes how speed and power must change when the fish (or a surrogate) is scaled isometrically: a design claiming a 2x scale-up with unchanged glide speed, or power growing as L^3, is inconsistent. For a printed surrogate at a different scale it tells which speed ratio to expect before the test.

existing.statement_plain: Under isometry, area ratio is (L2/L1)^2 and weight per lifting area ratio is L2/L1.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Isometry of mass and area and constant density are named hypotheses (CubeLaw, AreaLaw). Registry README: C2a, C7b, C8e, C9c, C8c are evaluated against one specimen (Cypselurus hiraii, Park and Choi 2010 Table 1 model L3) and so scoped to Exocoetidae.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Wing loading must rise linearly with size for an isometric family; a scaled design that keeps wing loading constant has to declare non-isometric fins, which then moves it under the measured-allometry laws (E1, flight-allometry-law).

existing.statement_plain: With breaking load = sigma * A and A ~ L^2, the static safety factor F_break/W = sigma k3/(k1 L) falls as 1/L; above L_max = sigma k3/(k1 n) the member cannot carry n body weights.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Same material sigma, isometric section, axial loading (header).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Gives a maximum size for any fin spar or body section at a committed material strength; for a printed surrogate, sigma is the resin's strength, so the same lemma bounds the scale at which a load factor n can be carried.

existing.theorem_or_def: SectionModulusLaw, LeverLaw, bendingStress, bendingStress_ratio_body, bendingSafety_eq, bending_cannot_carry, bendingStress_ratio_sheet, bendingStress_log_sheet
existing.statement_plain: Bending stress F*l/Z with lever ~ L and section modulus ~ L^3: for a body-like load (~L^3) stress grows as L and there is a size limit; for a sheet-like load (~L^2) the exponent is lower.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Isometric section modulus and lever arm, same material; header notes bones thicken with size in real animals.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: The fin acts as a cantilever carrying lift; this bounds root bending stress versus size and is the only structural law currently available for the pectoral fin or a printed fin.

existing.status: accepted theorem; the premise law is retired (superseded by aerobic-power-bound)
existing.statement_plain: If power available scales as L^3 (fixed mass-specific muscle power) and power required as L^3.5, a size exists above which required exceeds available.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Thompson's muscle premise (p constant) is a contested named hypothesis; the size's value needs f, p, L/D, rho, C_L,max, 'which no proof supplies'.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Existence-only upper size limit for powered flight; superseded in practice by powerLaw_crossover and the aerobic bound.

existing.theorem_or_def: PowerLaw, powerLaw_ratio, powerLaw_log, powerLaw_div, cubeLaw_powerLaw, vmin_powerLaw_log
existing.statement_plain: For mass ~ L^bW and lifting area ~ L^bS with constant rho and C_L,max, the v_min exponent is (bW - bS)/2.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header, 'What is assumed, not proved': every law is a named hypothesis on functions of one linear dimension or positive reals; the power-law forms and their exponents are assumed; 'No number from physics/ appears in a statement.'
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: With the Davenport exponents quoted in the file (2.981 and 1.834) my calculation gives a v_min exponent of (2.981-1.834)/2 = 0.5735 rather than the isometric 0.5; a design that commits three mutually inconsistent exponents is removed (the C13 check).

existing.statement_plain: A steady unpowered glide from height h with L/D <= (L/D)max covers at most h*(L/D)max; with drag reduced by a fraction delta near the surface, at most h*(L/D)max/(1-delta). Climb rate is at most (P_avail - P_req)/W.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: steady gliding with lift equal to weight and no thrust; 'ground effect, updraft and taxiing thrust are outside, which is why the field glide distances exceed the bound'; power balance with non-negative losses; delta (Park and Choi 2010 measured 0.09 to 0.14 for a flying-fish model) enters only as a candidate input.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: This is the central glide law for the track: any single-glide distance claim above h*(L/D)max/(1-delta) is removed. It is also the law a passive surrogate test checks directly (release height, measured distance). It has no initial kinetic-energy term, so it under-bounds a fish leaving the water fast (see missing law 2).

existing.theorem_or_def: aerobicPower, aerobic_le_Ca, aerobic_le_metabolic, sustained_le, sustained_flight_requires, climb_le_aerobic
existing.statement_plain: Sustained mechanical power is at most eta*E*Q*Ca (efficiency x oxycaloric equivalent x cardiac output x arterial O2 content); sustained flight at speed v needs W v/(L/D) <= eta*E*Q*Ca.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: O2 delivery is Q(Ca-Cv) (Fick), mechanical power at most eta times metabolic power, 0<=Cv<=Ca, 0<=eta<=1, 'sustained power is aerobic (anaerobic bursts are outside)'. fick-principle 1.1.0 adds a scope note: use a taxon-appropriate MO2max or Q.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Removes sustained powered flight from the design space. My calculation from the committed numbers in Certificates/EliminationsPhysiology.lean: required 0.5886*10/4.37 = 1.347 W against supply 0.15*19.342857*0.06564129*0.18723338 = 0.0357 W, a 38x shortfall, matching the CHANGELOG's '38x with the original snapper proxies'.

existing.registry_id: (part of flight-allometry-law module; not separately registered)
existing.statement_plain: If demand ~ L^b1 and supply ~ L^b2 with b2 < b1, there is a size above which supply < demand.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Power-law forms and exponents are hypotheses.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Size ceiling for any supply exponent below 3.5; lets the track replace the retired muscle premise with a measured supply exponent.

existing.theorem_or_def: Atmosphere, vminAt, demandAt, supplyAt, Feasible, vmin_mono, demand_mono, supply_anti, feasible_downward_closed, ceiling, infeasible_at_ground_infeasible_everywhere, demand_anti_area
existing.statement_plain: With air density and O2 partial pressure both falling with height, v_min and power required rise and aerobic supply falls; feasible heights form an interval down to the ground; a design infeasible at the ground is infeasible everywhere; larger lifting area lowers demand at fixed height.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: the atmosphere is a monotone named hypothesis with no numbers; arterial content is a monotone function of PO2 ('Nothing here formalises the Hill equation, the Bohr shift, the Root effect, or any compensation'); haematocrit, ventilation and cardiac output held fixed; temperature, humidity and wind not in it. The size of the effect is data: about 30% more required capacity over 0 to 5000 m (physics/flier/tff/tff.json, as quoted in the header).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Tells the track that altitude cannot rescue a design that fails the oxygen budget at sea level, and that the only trade available is lifting area against demand at one height.

existing.statement_plain: A steady glide from height h with airspeed u, sink s and along-track wind w (positive tailwind) covers exactly (u/s) h (1+w/u) over the ground and at most (L/D)max h (1+w/u).
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: 'pure kinematics, no source needed'; sign convention w positive for tailwind; headwind no stronger than airspeed (-u <= w).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Removes ground-range claims that exceed the wind-corrected bound; for a surrogate flown outdoors or in a tunnel it is the correction that must be applied before comparing with glide_range_le.

existing.statement_plain: In the barometric troposphere density falls with height and v_min is proportional to 1/sqrt(rho), so v_min rises with height.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: rho(h) = rho0 (1 - beta h/T0)^n with n > 0 as a named hypothesis (Narayanan and Osechas 2022, PMID 36501962: T0 288.15 K, lapse 6.5 K/km); constants recorded in lean/perturb-sources.json, which is not in this repo.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: A design evaluated at altitude must use the density there; a claimed v_min below the density-corrected value is removed.

existing.statement_plain: Sustained power is zero outside [CTmin, CTmax] and at most P_ref*Q10^((T-Tref)/10) inside.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: the thermal performance curve (Schulte 2015, PMID 26085663) and the Q10 rule (Rome et al. 1992, PMID 1556515: scup red muscle 71 W/kg at 10 C, 134 W/kg at 20 C, Q10 1.88) are named hypotheses; a scup proxy, not a flying-fish measurement.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Removes designs that claim swimming or launch power outside the thermal window or above the Q10-scaled reference.

existing.status: accepted (v1.1.0 carries approval role carried-forward-pending-review per CHANGELOG 1.6.0)
existing.statement_plain: No design holds station in a current above U_crit, or in a current whose drag power rho Cd A U^3/2 exceeds eta*E*Q*Ca.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: ground speed = U_swim - U_current; sustained swimming at most U_crit (Plaut 2001, PMID 11733165); drag power paid by aerobic power. v1.1.0 scope note: aerobic only below about 0.8 U_crit.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Bounds the sustained underwater phase. It does not bound the burst that precedes take-off, which is anaerobic (see missing law 4).

existing.theorem_or_def: WaterColumn, WaterColumn.pressure, bladder_volume_eq, bladder_volume_anti, secretion_ratio, closed_bladder_rules_out, seaWater, freshWater, oneAtmPer10m, seaWater_gradient_lt_oneAtmPer10m
existing.statement_plain: With P(d) = p0 + rho g d and P V constant, a closed swim bladder has volume V(0) p0/(p0 + rho g d) at depth d; a larger claimed volume is ruled out.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: p0, rho, g > 0 are fields of WaterColumn; Boyle's law (fixed gas amount, fixed temperature, quasi-static) is the hypothesis hboyle. Version 1.0.0 (Perturb.closed_bladder_rules_out, 1 atm per 10 m) is superseded but still compiled.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Constrains buoyancy claims for the underwater approach to the surface; candidate status means a violation is flagged, not red.

existing.statement_plain: Daily energy conservation eps*dm = a*I - (R + Act + s*a*I): a design whose activity cost exceeds assimilated intake net of SDA loses mass; a claimed mass gain above the balance is ruled out.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: energy conservation carried as hypothesis hbal; SDA fraction from Bihun et al. 2024 (PMID 38881304, walleye) and McLeod and Clark 2016 (PMID 27191721, larval clownfish) - other species, not flying fish.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Limits how many flights per day a design can afford once a per-flight energy cost is committed.

existing.statement_plain: Under a linear osmolyte-depth hypothesis no teleost lives below 8200 m.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header states the hypothesis is contradicted by observation (a snailfish filmed at 8336 m); lean/registry/lean/P3bContested.lean compiles the contradiction. Rows give amber, never red.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Not relevant to a surface glider; listed because it is the registry's worked example of an observation contesting a law, which this track's experiment loop must be able to do.

existing.statement_plain: Within one flying-fish species fin area grows more slowly than L^2 and wing loading faster than L; hence AreaLaw cannot hold with that exponent.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: observations are fields of a structure, never axioms. Davenport 1992 on Exocoetus obtusirostris: area exponent 1.834, wing loading 1.236, mass 2.981; 'The three fits are separate regressions and are NOT mutually consistent (1.236 against 2.981 - 1.834 = 1.147)'.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Stops the track from scaling a flying fish isometrically: a design that uses AreaLaw for the fins contradicts E1 inside Exocoetidae.

existing.statement_plain: With a fitted mass exponent in [2.90, 3.02], a scaled design's weight ratio lies between r^2.90 and r^3.02 for length ratio r >= 1.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: six fitted field rows of five species in physics/length-weight.csv, excluding the Hirundichthys affinis male row at 2.208 'which is named and left out'. Scoped to Exocoetidae adults (registry README).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Removes scaled designs whose mass does not follow the measured band; certificate elim_mass_exponent_2_2_claimed_as_a_flying_fish_fit_E2 rules out an exponent of 276/125 = 2.208.

existing.theorem_or_def: TeleostAerobicV2, TeleostAerobic.toV2, aerobicCeilingV2_le, no_aerobic_flight_above_ceiling_v2, teleostAerobicV2_nonvacuous (v1: TeleostAerobic, aerobicCeiling_le, no_aerobic_flight_above_ceiling)
existing.status: accepted, approval role carried-forward-pending-review (no person has reviewed v2, per CHANGELOG 1.6.0)
existing.statement_plain: eta <= 0.23, oxycaloric <= 19.35 J/ml and O2 delivery Q*Ca <= 0.0187 ml/s at 0.06 kg give an aerobic ceiling of at most 0.0833 W; sustained flight needing more is ruled out.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Law file: zebrafish MO2max (Palstra et al. 2010, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0014483, resolved via Crossref in this run) scaled from 0.43 g to 60 g with a mass exponent of -0.10 to -0.13; efficiency from Gladman and Askew 2024 (PMC11583979, not fetched by me). Cross-taxon transfers; valid only at 0.06 kg; high-performance pelagic teleosts were not fetched.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: The strongest elimination on the track: required 1.3473 W (the number committed in elim_real_fish_sustained_flight_any_teleost_E3) against 0.0833 W is a 16.2x shortfall by my calculation (1.3473/0.0833), matching the CHANGELOG's '16x on the new envelope'. Sustained flapping flight is out; only burst-launched gliding survives.

existing.statement_plain: With no O2 uptake in air, mean aerobic power over a flight of duration t is at most E*S/t for an O2 store S.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Header: gills do not ventilate in air (physiology/index.js self-test). Docstring: 'Nothing here bounds anaerobic (burst) power, which is what a flying fish is understood to use.'
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Caps airborne aerobic power by flight duration; certificate elim_one_minute_powered_flight_on_the_store_E4 removes a one-minute powered flight on a 1 ml store.

existing.registry_id: E5 (and candidates disc-flying-fish-fin-ratio-gap, disc-pectoral-length-allometry in lean/registry/proposals/<id>/law.lean)
existing.status: E5 accepted but deliberately not a constraint; the two disc laws are candidate
existing.statement_plain: Pectoral length / standard length of 49 flying-fish specimens lies in [0.406, 0.823], median 0.687; measured non-flying beloniforms are at most 0.389 (n = 60); pectoral length scales as SL^b with b in [1.017, 1.099].
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Law file E5: 'A statement about the RECORD. A design outside the range is outside everything measured, which is weaker than impossible'; preserved museum specimens, lengths only: no mass, no fin area, no glide data (Daane et al. 2021 Data S1, doi 10.1016/j.cub.2021.08.054, resolved via Crossref in this run).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Flags designs with fin ratio outside the measured band and gives the gap 0.389 to 0.406 that a transitional or engineered design would have to cross; it is the natural target interval for an experiment, not an elimination.

existing.statement_plain: Measured wing loading W/(A_pectoral + A_pelvic + A_body) lies between 37.025 and 46.375 N/m^2 (n = 4).
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: File caveats: 'stuffed specimens of one species (Cypselurus hiraii); n is tiny; model M has pelvic fins folded (A2 = 0); a record bound, not an impossibility' (Park and Choi 2010 Table 1 via physics/glide-data.csv).
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Gives the wing-loading band a surrogate should sit in to be comparable with the measured fish; candidate status means out-of-band is flagged grey, not red.

existing.statement_plain: An intervention lethal at or before the stage at which a phenotype is scored cannot yield that phenotype.
existing.assumptions_outside_kernel: Death and scoring times come from genotype/interventions.json (not in this repo); instantiated only where both times are stated in hours.
existing.how_it_constrains_this_track: Removes genetic levers for fin size that kill before fins can be measured (ezh2 at 48 hpf; wls at 288 h against rays scored at 1080 h).

laws.elimination_pattern: A certificate has two layers. The library layer is a lemma named *_rules_out that takes (a) the law's own hypotheses, (b) the candidate's commitment as equalities or intervals, and (c) one last decidable arithmetic fact, and concludes False; it is proved by citing the positive theorem and closing with linarith. A real example from lean/Delphi/Perturb.lean: `theorem wind_glide_rules_out {u s h w x LDmax : ℝ} (hu : 0 < u) (hs : 0 < s) (hh : 0 ≤ h) (hw : -u ≤ w) (hLD : u / s ≤ LDmax) (hx : x = (u + w) * (h / s)) (hbig : LDmax * h * (1 + w / u) < x) : False := by have := glide_ground_range_le hu hs hh hw hLD hx; linarith`. The generated layer (lean/Delphi/Certificates/Eliminations*.lean, namespace Delphi.Constraints.Eliminations, written by lean/eliminate/eliminate.mjs from a candidates JSON, header 'Do not edit; regenerate') has one theorem per candidate named elim_<candidate>_<constraint id>; it instantiates the lemma with the candidate's numbers as exact rationals and discharges the arithmetic with `by norm_num`, for example `theorem elim_flier_F1_too_slow_C9 : ∀ C : ℝ, 0 < C → C ≤ (39 / 50 : ℝ) → Delphi.lift (49 / 40 : ℝ) (4 : ℝ) (981 / 20000 : ℝ) C = (2943 / 5000 : ℝ) → False := fun C hC hCm hlift => Delphi.Constraints.vmin_rules_out (by norm_num) (by norm_num) hC hCm (by norm_num) hlift (by norm_num)`. Finite-data certificates (anatomy graph, codon table, staging) use a Boolean checker plus a soundness theorem and `by decide +kernel` instead. Per lean/Delphi/Constraints.lean, a candidate that does not commit to the law's assumptions is reported 'cannot rule', never 'passes', and surviving means only 'not ruled out by these theorems'. Empirical inputs are fields of a structure passed as an argument, never an axiom, and each structure needs a non-vacuity witness. For this track: first restore the C8 to C16 lemmas (missing law 1), then add e.g. `glide_energy_rules_out` for missing law 2, write a candidates JSON with the surrogate's mass, area, launch speed, height and claimed distance as rationals, generate `elim_<surrogate>_<id>`, and run the new law through propose.mjs (build, axiom check, witness, joint consistency, mutants) so it enters as candidate; a measured surrogate glide that beats the bound is then recorded with contest.mjs rather than deleted.

explain.label: explain2-track-6
explain.one_line: We test whether a computer-checked rulebook can say if a claimed flying fish glide breaks the laws of physics.
explain.what: We are building a referee for animal claims. A claim might be "a fish glided 50 metres". The referee checks the claim against rules of physics. A proof program has checked those rules step by step. The referee gives one of three answers: ruled out, not ruled out, or cannot tell. It never says "proved". Our test case is the flying fish, because researchers measured fish bodies in a wind tunnel. The newest glide test is only a plan with bets written down first. It has no result yet.
explain.why: Claims about animals are often repeated from paper to paper. Nobody redoes the sums. This project is for catching that. When we reopened the sources, almost every number held. But one headline pair of numbers came from two different simulated flights. A referee that checks the sums is useful. It should also say plainly what it cannot judge. It could be used on many other animals later. For example, a long glide seen at sea may include paddling on the water. Our simple rule does not cover that, so the referee says "cannot tell".

steps.text: Measure the fish. Researchers put stuffed fish models in a wind tunnel. Air blew past them at 12 metres per second, about 43 kilometres per hour. They recorded how much lift and drag the body makes. Lift is the upward push of air. Drag is the backward pull of air.
steps.picture: Holding a paper plane out of a car window and feeling it pull up and back.

steps.text: Work out the slowest speed that keeps the fish up. We used a model fish of 0.06 kilograms, about the weight of a large egg. We combined its weight with the best lift number from the tunnel. The answer is 9.85 metres per second. That is about the speed of a fast cyclist. Below it, the fish drops. This is called the stall speed.
steps.picture: A bicycle that wobbles and falls once you go too slowly.

steps.text: Work out a distance limit. A fish that launches fast can trade its speed for distance, like a cyclist coasting off a hill. The best lift-to-drag ratio found was 4.37. That means the air gives 4.37 units of lift for every 1 unit of drag. The rule is: distance = 4.37 x (launch speed squared minus stall speed squared) / (2 x 9.81). The number 9.81 is how fast gravity speeds things up.
steps.picture: Coasting downhill: the faster you start, the farther you roll.

steps.text: Try the rule on real numbers. Launch at 10 metres per second. Speed squared is 100. Stall speed squared is about 97.1. The gap is 2.9. Then 4.37 x 2.9 / 19.62 gives 0.646 metres. That is about the length of your arm. So a 10 metres per second launch buys less than one metre of glide at the same height. To glide 50 metres, half a football pitch, the same rule needs a launch of about 17 metres per second. That is about 61 kilometres per hour, a car in town.
steps.picture: Rolling a toy car off a very low ramp: it stops within an arm's length.

steps.text: Write the rule as a proof. A proof program, this one called Lean, checks every step of the logic. It checks that the distance limit really follows from the numbers we typed in. It does not check that the numbers are right. Those come from measurements and papers.
steps.picture: A strict teacher who marks each line of a sum, but does not know if you copied the starting numbers correctly.

steps.text: Write down bets before looking. For example, a launch at 10 metres per second should buy under 1 metre of glide at the same height. Each bet says which result would count against us.
steps.picture: Writing your guess in a sealed envelope before the race.

steps.text: Re-check the sources. We downloaded the original papers and data. We redid the sums with a short program anyone can rerun.
steps.picture: Checking a restaurant bill line by line.

steps.text: Look for rival explanations. Long flights might have another cause. One example is the fish beating its tail on the water surface, which gives it extra push.
steps.picture: A long jumper who seems to leap far, but took a running start you did not count.

steps.text: Report the answer in three ways only. The referee says ruled out, not ruled out, or cannot tell. "Not ruled out" never means "possible" or "true".
steps.picture: A court that can say guilty, not guilty, or not enough evidence, but never "innocent for sure".

explain.wrong_if: We bet that the stall speed and the distance limit hold for a fish that glides with no tail paddling. We would be wrong if a careful, measured glide with no extra push went clearly farther than the limit allows. We would also be wrong if a fish like our model could fly slower than 9.85 metres per second. We have a second bet. A live fish leaping from an aquarium at 3.9 to 5.2 metres per second, about a brisk jog, should not glide far at the same height. If a measured long glide came from such a launch, that bet would fail.
could_go_wrong: Every wind tunnel number comes from stuffed fish models. A live fish may behave differently.
The distance rule only works if the fish is neither climbing nor sinking. A fish pushed upward, for example by rising air, could go farther than the rule says.
Field distances such as 50 metres were reported by others. They were not measured by us. We found no public raw record of real glide tracks.
The simulation paper gives a 45.4 metre distance and a 13.2 metre height. These came from different runs, so it is easy to misread them as one flight.
The aquarium paper gives take-off speeds but not how long each leap lasted. So one planned test cannot be done with it.
Paddling on the water may explain long flights. The simple rule cannot judge those.
Some of our own bets would have come true whatever the data showed. Passing them tells us little. They add less than they seem to.
The proof program checks the logic only. The numbers fed into it can still be wrong or out of date.

questions.q: How do you know?
questions.a: We reopened the original papers and reran the sums with short programs. Almost all numbers matched. Anyone can rerun them using the commands listed below.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We did not rerun the proof program ourselves for the newest proof. We found no public raw glide-track data. We did not read every figure in the simulation paper.

questions.q: Is the glide test finished?
questions.a: No. It is a plan with bets written first. We found no results for it yet.

questions.q: What is this project for?
questions.a: It is for checking animal claims against physics, and saying plainly when a check is not possible. The flying fish is only the first test case.

questions.q: What does the proof program prove?
questions.a: It proves that the rule's steps follow from each other. For example, it proves that a given stall speed and lift-to-drag ratio lead to a given distance limit. It does not prove that the measured numbers are right.

questions.q: How does 4.37 become a distance limit?
questions.a: Take launch speed squared minus stall speed squared. Multiply by 4.37. Divide by twice the pull of gravity, which is 19.62. For a 10 metres per second launch this gives 0.646 metres.

questions.q: Does "not ruled out" mean the claim is true?
questions.a: No. It only means our rules could not knock the claim down.

questions.q: Why would a fish glide farther than the rule allows?
questions.a: It may paddle its tail on the water first, which adds push. The rule leaves that out. So a longer distance seen at sea does not mean a law of physics is wrong.

questions.q: How slowly can the model fish fly?
questions.a: About 9.85 metres per second, about the speed of a fast cyclist. That uses a 0.06 kilogram fish and the best lift number measured in the tunnel.

questions.q: How fast do live fish leap in an aquarium?
questions.a: They were estimated at 3.9 to 5.2 metres per second, about a brisk jog. That is well below the 9.85 floor. But it is a different fish from the model.

questions.q: Why does a simulation headline need care?
questions.a: Its 45.4 metre glide and 13.2 metre height came from two different runs. All the runs began at 20 metres per second, about 72 kilometres per hour.

glossary.plain: Software that checks each step of a maths argument and refuses it if any step is missing. It checks the logic, not the measurements.
A tube where fast air blows over a model so we can measure the forces on it.
The upward push that air gives a moving wing or body.
The backward pull of air that slows something moving.
Lift divided by drag. A ratio of 4.37 means 4.37 units of lift for each unit of drag. A higher number means a farther glide.
The slowest speed at which the body still gets enough lift to stay up. Below it, the fish drops.
Moving through the air without flapping or any push.
A glide that stays at about the same height instead of sinking.
A computer model that imitates what would happen in real life.
Skimming along the water surface with the tail beating, which gives extra push.
Pushed upward, for example by rising air.
Reported by others in an older paper, not measured by the people now quoting it.
A result we write down before looking, so we can later see if we were wrong.
A measure of speed. 10 metres per second is about 36 kilometres per hour, the pace of a fast cyclist.
A jump out of the water made by a live fish in a tank.
Our name for the checker that tests claims against rules.
A label our check program prints when a number we recomputed does not match the paper's number.

reading.reader_help: Say upfront what the project output actually is (a tool? a report?). Explain why a speed-squared difference gives distance. Spell out the inconsistent "bets" and why some are empty. The "ruled out" verdict is never shown on a worked example, so show one claim going through all three outcomes. The 'what you did not check' items are vague. Also, the 65 of 67 checks claim is unexplained, and the verdict on the flying fish claim itself is never given.

specialists.topic: Gaps in bio-based and bio-inspired materials for architecture, 2025-2026 (label: spec-architecture-gaps)
specialists.summary: Every bio-based family surveyed is held back by the same short list: moisture, missing long-life data, and missing standards. Mycelium composites are insulation-grade only (compressive 0.03-4.44 MPa, water uptake around 300%, expected life under 50 years, no standard test methods). Living building materials reach mortar-like strength (about 3-5 MPa) but the cells die when the material dries at room humidity. PHB is brittle (2-15% strain) with a narrow processing window; I found no verified creep or outdoor-durability numbers for PLA or PHA in buildings. Engineered timber is the only mature family (covered by EN 16351 and ANSI/APA PRG 320); its limits are rolling shear (about 1.5 MPa for softwood CLT) and adhesive delamination in fire. For passive responsiveness, the strongest evidence is the 4D-printed cellulose shading in Freiburg: 424 modules, over a year outdoors, shade coverage swinging from 50% to about 90% with weather, full actuation within 30 minutes. But its authors state that the indoor-climate benefit has not been quantified, and only 170 actuation cycles were tested. The only energy numbers I could verify for passive bio-based envelopes are modelled, not measured: 20-60% cooling-energy savings for radiative-cooling wood. The most addressable gap for a small computational team with desktop SLA/SLS printers is therefore the missing link between passive actuator geometry and a measured building-performance number, followed by multilayer actuator design, durability protocols, printed scaffolds for weak bio-fills, and bio-based resins. One caveat for the printing plan: Formlabs Nylon 11 Pro absorbs only 0.4% water, so it can serve as the passive restraining layer or scaffold but not as the moisture-driven active layer. Not found or not verified: bacterial cellulose and algae facade numbers, PLA creep data, and any measured (not simulated) energy saving from a power-free bio-based facade.

findings.claim: Mycelium-based composites have compressive strength of 0.03-4.44 MPa and flexural strength of 0.05-4.40 MPa, which restricts them to non- or semi-structural uses.

Uncompressed mycelium composites have density 59-318 kg/m3, water absorption around 300% and thermal conductivity 0.05-0.07 W/mK; water uptake ranges from 6% to 436% depending on species and substrate.

The 2025 review names the adoption barriers for mycelium composites as low mechanical strength, weathering susceptibility, scalability, limited lifespan (under 50 years) and lack of standardised manufacturing and testing methods.

Mycelium is much less combustible than PLA in micro-scale calorimetry: peak heat release 67 W/g versus 375 W/g for PLA, with 23 wt% char versus 0.6 wt%. In cone calorimetry at 50 kW/m2 the mycelium composite peaked at about 180 kW/m2 against 200 kW/m2 for the substrate alone.
P3HB is brittle (2-15% strain, >35 MPa yield stress, 60-80% crystallinity) and its thermal processing window is narrow; high cost is also named as an obstacle.

A 2023 review of biopolymers for cladding (PLA, PHA, PHB, starch, cellulose, PBS) states that research on their application and limitations as building cladding is limited. I read only the Crossref abstract; the publisher page returned 403, so its property tables are not included.

CLT is standardised (EN 16351 in Europe, ANSI/APA PRG 320 in North America) and has been used up to 18 storeys. Rolling shear is the mechanical bottleneck: about 1.5 MPa for softwood CLT, 0.5 MPa for spruce against 2.8-3.1 MPa for two hardwoods.
In fire, heat reaching CLT adhesive layers can degrade the adhesive and cause delamination, after which the char layer no longer protects the section.

Delignified, densified wood reached 404.3 MPa strength and cools below ambient passively; the authors' building model gives 20-60% cooling-energy savings, largest in hot dry climates. This is a modelled figure, not a measured building result.
Wood-based radiative coolers degrade under UV; a 2025 coated variant kept 4.5 C of daytime cooling after 720 h of UV exposure with solar reflectance 0.958, emittance 0.95 and strength 47 MPa.

A chitosan-cellulose composite (FLAM) costs about 2 USD/kg, with Young's modulus 0.26 GPa and density 0.37 g/cm3, and was extruded at large scale through a 7 mm nozzle; the same paper puts common PLA and ABS filament at 20-30 USD/kg.
Sand-gelatin living building materials reach 3.0-4.8 MPa compressive strength and 1.4-2.3 MPa modulus of rupture across the tested groups.

In the original cyanobacterial living building material, no cells stayed viable at 20 C and 24% RH because the hydrogel lost about 80% of its water; viability held only at 4 C and above 50% RH. Trehalose was later shown to preserve viability at low humidity without changing mechanical properties. The first statement is Qiu et al.'s account of Heveran et al. 2020; I did not read Heveran's full text.

Bioprinted cyanobacterial living building material kept cells viable for 14 days and was stronger in compression than cell-free scaffolds; a December 2025 protocol paper says published methods are still fragmentary.

Hemp-lime has compressive strength 0.09-0.57 MPa, thermal conductivity 0.087-0.10 W/mK and an average moisture buffer value of 2.78 g/m2 %RH, which the authors class as excellent passive humidity buffering.

The Freiburg 4D-printed cellulose shading system used 424 self-shaping modules, ran outdoors for more than a year, and moved between 50% shade coverage (humid nights, winter) and about 90% (hot dry summer days) with no power or sensors.

Those bilayers complete a full transformation between 30% and 90% RH within 30 minutes and were tested for 170 actuation cycles; the authors say this cycle count is small against a building lifetime and that UV degradation and wear need further study.
The same study evaluated shade coverage only and states that quantifying the improvement in indoor climate regulation is future work. No measured energy or comfort number exists for this system.
The printed shading covered about 9.3 m2 of facade. My calculation: 5.5 kg of actuating filament divided by the reported 0.59 kg/m2 = 9.3 m2 (check: 0.7 kg restricting filament / 0.07 kg/m2 = 10 m2).
Its manufacturing was cheap and desktop-scale: four FFF printers, 25-32 minutes per module, 17 days in total, 7% reprint rate, cellulose powder at 1.52 EUR/kg.
A 2023 systematic review of hygroscopic adaptive facades finds most papers study the material's response to moisture and fabrication methods rather than building performance.
Pine cone scales actuate as multilayers, not bilayers: finite-element models using a simplified bilayer underestimated the measured bending, and the tissues show pronounced sorption hysteresis.
A bacterial-spore hygromorph bilayer has been aggregated into a bench-top humidity-responsive ventilation panel; it has had pilot testing only.

Bio-based isosorbide methacrylate resins for vat printing reach Tg above 200 C and 2-2.8 GPa modulus but are brittle (fracture energy 26-37 J/m2, raised to about 100 J/m2 by copolymerisation). A 2026 review reports about 10 MPa tensile strength for a fully bio-based filled system.

Formlabs Nylon 11 Pro Powder: 46 MPa tensile strength (XY), 1580 MPa modulus, HDT 178 C at 0.45 MPa but only 50 C at 1.8 MPa, 0.4% water absorption, UL 94 HB at 3 mm. The page does not state bio-based content. A literature SLS PA11 (castor-derived) measured 45 MPa and 925 MPa.
A passive thermochromic hydrogel window interlayer switches at 32.6 C with 78.89% luminous modulation; it is not bio-based and its abstract gives no building energy figure.

Mamou-Mani's Conifera installation (2019) used 700 3D-printed PLA and PLA-wood-pulp modules. This comes from design-press search snippets, not a page I opened, and the outlets disagree on print time (two versus four months).

A news report describes a power-free shape-memory-alloy facade device with simplified-model cooling savings of 9.1% (tropical monsoon) to 17% (hot desert). I could not find the underlying paper or DOI.

recommendations: Gap 1 (most addressable): no one has tied passive hygromorphic shading geometry to a measured or simulated energy or comfort number. The Freiburg team reports shade coverage only. Build a design-to-performance model (humidity and temperature in, curvature and shade coverage out, then solar gain) and validate it on a printed bench-scale array with logged irradiance behind it. This is computation plus desktop printing and gives the first number of its kind.

Gap 2: multilayer actuator design. Pine cone scales bend more than bilayer models predict, and current printed facades use simple bilayers. Use the constraint framework to design graded or multilayer mesostructures and print the passive restraining architecture on SLA/SLS. Caveat: Nylon 11 Pro absorbs only 0.4% water, so the active swelling layer must be a separate hygroscopic material (cellulose-filled filament, veneer or hydrogel) bonded to the printed part.

Gap 3: durability evidence. Only 170 cycles and limited UV data exist against a decades-long service life. A small rig cycling printed coupons between 30% and 90% RH with UV exposure, reporting curvature drift per 1,000 cycles, would fill a gap the field itself names. It needs time and a humidity chamber, not scale.

Gap 4: printed architected scaffolds or formwork for weak, wet bio-fills. Mycelium (0.03-4.44 MPa, ~300% water uptake) and hemp-lime (0.09-0.57 MPa) need a load path and water shedding. Computationally designed PA11 lattices or shells that carry load and drain, with the bio-fill providing insulation and humidity buffering (MBV 2.78), can be prototyped at tile scale. The fire rating of the printed part (UL 94 HB) is a limit to state up front.

Gap 5 (hardest for a small team): tough, high-bio-content resins for vat printing. Isosorbide systems reach Tg above 200 C but remain brittle. This is chemistry-led and needs a printer that accepts third-party resin, so treat it as a partner topic, not a first project.

Do not promise energy savings to a partner yet. The only verified savings figure for a passive bio-based envelope (20-60%) is modelled for radiative-cooling wood, not measured, and not for a moving skin.
Before quoting bacterial cellulose, algae-facade or PLA creep numbers anywhere, run a dedicated fetch: none could be verified in this run.

specialists.topic: Physics: design equations for a printed self-shaping bilayer, beyond the textbook formula (label spec-bilayer-physics)
specialists.summary: Design equations for a printed hygromorph bilayer strip, with sources and arithmetic. (a) Curvature follows Timoshenko: kappa = f(m,n) d_eps/h, f = 6(1+m)^2/[3(1+m)^2+(1+mn)(m^2+1/(mn))]; the project Lean file already encodes and derives this. I show (AM-GM proof plus numerical check) that f is maximised at m = n^(-1/2) with f = 3/2 for every modulus ratio, so at the optimum R = h/(1.5 d_eps) independent of n; using equal layers at n=10 costs 34 % of the curvature. (b) Response time tau ~ h^2/D: measured filament diffusivities of 0.001-0.015 mm^2/h give 11-160 h at 0.4 mm and 170-2560 h at 1.6 mm, versus minutes for porous plant-like layers at D ~ 1e-9 m^2/s; measured pine-scale exponents are 1.3-1.5, below 2. Filament swelling strains are only 0.15-0.25 %. (c) Own beam-theory results: M_block = E w h^2 d_eps/8, F_block = 3 E w h^2 d_eps/(16L), work density 0.0352 E d_eps^2, peak stress E d_eps/2; pine cone scales measure 2.2-3.6 N and 42-107 N mm. (d) A plate cannot hold bilayer curvature in two directions once width exceeds about sqrt(h/kappa) = h/sqrt(1.5 d_eps) (2.3-29 mm over the table); wide sheets roll in one direction at roughly (1+nu) times the beam curvature (consistent with the published 3/4 mean-curvature result); the numerical prefactor of the transition was not retrieved. (e) Direction is steered by orienting the swelling anisotropy (fibre/microfibril angle, print path) and by ribs or slits; off-axis orientation converts bending to twist. (f) Creep gives a permanent offset but little loss of stroke in wood bilayers; printed-polymer creep data were not found. Table: R = 133/53/27/13 mm (h=0.4 mm), 267/107/53/27 mm (0.8 mm), 533/213/107/53 mm (1.6 mm) at 0.2/0.5/1/2 %, identical for n=1 and n=10 at optimal m. Distinguishing the law from a 20 % error needs about +-0.1 mm on tip deflection (or +-0.3 deg) in the hardest case, easily met by imaging, but needs thickness to ~3 % and free swelling strain to ~5 % (4 um on 40 mm at 0.2 %), which is the real bottleneck. Scratch: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/scratch/spec-bilayer-physics/ (calc.py, calc_out.json, build.py).

findings.claim: (a) Timoshenko bilayer curvature: kappa = f(m,n)*d_eps/h with f = 6(1+m)^2 / [3(1+m)^2 + (1+mn)(m^2 + 1/(mn))], m=h1/h2, n=E1/E2, h=h1+h2, d_eps = free differential strain between layers. The project Lean file already encodes exactly this coefficient (timoshenkoCoefficient) and derives it from two-layer beam equilibrium (bilayerCurvature_ofEquilibrium). The same structure appears as Eq. 3 of Rueggeberg & Burgert 2015 (equation text partly garbled in the XML I fetched). Original source Timoshenko 1925 was DOI-verified but its text was not read.

(a) Optimal thickness ratio: f is maximised at m* = n^(-1/2) (i.e. h1/h2 = sqrt(E2/E1): the stiffer layer is the thinner one) and the maximum is f = 3/2 for EVERY n. Proof (own derivation): f <= 3/2 <=> (1+m)^2 <= (1+mn)(m^2+1/(mn)) <=> 2m <= 1/(mn) + m^3 n, which is AM-GM with equality iff m^2 n = 1. Confirmed numerically for n = 1, 2, 5, 10, 100 (m_opt = 1, 0.7071, 0.4472, 0.3162, 0.1; f_max = 1.5 each). Consequence: at the optimum, kappa = 3 d_eps / (2h) and the predicted radius does not depend on the modulus ratio at all, so the n=1 and n=10 columns of the requested table are identical in R and differ only in layer thicknesses. The Lean file has only the m=n=1 case (bilayerCurvature_symmetric = 3/2*d_eps/h); the general optimum/upper-bound theorem is not there.

(a) Cost of ignoring the optimum: with equal layer thicknesses (m=1) f falls to 1.4545 (n=2), 1.25 (n=5), 0.9959 (n=10), 0.2105 (n=100), i.e. a 34 % curvature loss at n=10. The optimum is flat: f stays within 5 % of 1.5 for m in [0.635, 1.576] at n=1 and [0.172, 0.505] at n=10. Independent cross-check: Reyssat & Mahadevan quote f about 1.3 for the pine cone scale at m about 1, n about 5; my formula gives f(1,5)=1.25.

(b) Diffusion-limited response time scales as tau ~ h^2/D. Reyssat & Mahadevan state tau ~ h^2/D with D ~ 1e-9 m^2/s for water in the molecular pores of plant tissue, giving tau ~ 1000 s for an active layer of ~1 mm; with a bottleneck of size l_b the law becomes tau ~ h_a*l_b/D. Their measured pine-scale fits are sub-quadratic: drying tau = 96*h_a^1.5 min and wetting tau = 29*h_a^1.3 min (h_a in mm), so the pure h^2 law is an upper-exponent idealisation and evaporation/boundary transport matters. Groenquist et al. also state diffusion time is proportional to squared diffusion path for wood bilayers. The Lean file encodes diffusiveTime h D = h^2/D and the slowest-mode rate pi^2 D/h^2.

(b) Implication at printable thickness for dense thermoplastics: measured Fickian water diffusivities of 3D-printing filaments are 0.001-0.0151 mm^2/h (2.8e-13 to 4.2e-12 m^2/s; Nylon 0.001, PEKK 0.00245, PET-G 0.00335, PC 0.00472, PLA grades 0.0078-0.0151). h^2/D then gives: 0.1 mm -> 0.66-10 h; 0.4 mm -> 10.6-160 h; 0.8 mm -> 42-640 h; 1.6 mm -> 170-2560 h; 2 mm -> 265-4000 h (divide by 4 if both faces are exposed and the whole thickness must equilibrate). With a porous/wicking active layer at D~1e-9 m^2/s (3.6 mm^2/h) the same thicknesses give 10 s, 160 s, 640 s, 43 min, 67 min. So a dense printed bilayer thicker than ~0.4 mm actuates over days to months; hour-scale actuation at 0.4-2 mm needs a porous, fibre-filled or gel-like active layer roughly 2-3 orders of magnitude more diffusive than neat filament polymer.
findings.value: 0.4 mm: 10.6-160 h (dense polymer) vs 160 s (porous, D=1e-9 m^2/s)

findings.claim: (b) Achievable differential strain in off-the-shelf filament polymers is small: Aniskevich et al. report maximal moisture swelling of 0.15-0.25 % for most of 12 filaments (up to 0.5 % stated in the abstract), swelling linear in moisture content. That puts dense-thermoplastic bilayers at the 0.2 % row of the table (R = 133-533 mm), whereas plant tissue reaches far larger strains (pine cone active cells ~20 % longer wet than dry; hygroscopic coefficient 0.001 per %RH) per Reyssat & Mahadevan.
findings.value: filament swelling 0.15-0.25 %; pine tissue up to ~20 %

findings.claim: (c) Blocking moment and force (own derivation from beam theory, equal-modulus optimum n=1, m=1): composite EI = E w h^3/12, so the moment that holds the strip flat is M_b = EI*kappa = E w h^2 d_eps/8; the tip force that returns a cantilever of length L to zero tip deflection is F_b = 3 EI kappa/(2L) = 3 E w h^2 d_eps/(16 L). Force scales as h^2 while curvature scales as 1/h, so thickness trades stroke for force. Illustrative numbers with an ASSUMED E = 2 GPa, w = 10 mm, L = 40 mm, d_eps = 1 %: h = 0.4/0.8/1.6 mm -> M_b = 4/16/64 N mm, F_b = 0.15/0.60/2.4 N. For general n the Lean-derived equilibrium (P*h/2 = (E1 I1 + E2 I2) kappa) should be used; I did not tabulate n=10 forces.
findings.value: M_b = E w h^2 d_eps/8; F_b = 3 E w h^2 d_eps/(16 L)

findings.claim: (c) Work density (own derivation): maximum work into a matched linear load is F_b*delta_free/4 with delta_free = kappa L^2/2, giving W/V = (3/16) EI kappa^2/(w h) = (27/768) E d_eps^2 = 0.0352 E d_eps^2, independent of thickness and length. With the ASSUMED E = 2 GPa: 0.28, 1.76, 7.0, 28 kJ/m^3 at d_eps = 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2 %. Peak layer stress at the interface for n=1, m=1 is E d_eps/2 (2, 5, 10, 20 MPa for the same cases), which sets the delamination/yield check.
findings.value: W/V = 0.0352 E d_eps^2; sigma_max = E d_eps/2

findings.claim: (c) Measured natural benchmark: pine cone scales 1.1-1.5 mm thick generate blocking forces of 2.2-3.6 N and blocking moments of 42-107 N mm on wetting, with force rates of 0.16-0.38 N/min; bimetal-strip theory agrees fairly well but over-predicts; restrained swelling stress of wetted spruce (tangential) is quoted as about 1.2 MPa (Le Duigou & Castro 2016). My illustrative 1.6 mm, 1 % case (2.4 N, 64 N mm) is the same order.

(d) Plate versus strip: a uniform isotropic bilayer mismatch asks for the same curvature in every direction (a spherical cap), which has non-zero Gaussian curvature and therefore requires in-plane stretching. Scaling (own derivation): a cap of curvature kappa over width w needs stretching strain ~ (kappa w)^2, energy/area ~ E h kappa^4 w^4; bending energy/area ~ E h^3 kappa^2; they balance at w ~ sqrt(h/kappa). Narrower than this the strip can double-curve; wider, it must become (nearly) developable and bend in ONE direction only, with stretching confined to edge layers. Armon et al. use exactly this dimensionless width, w*sqrt(kappa0/t), for seed-pod strips (narrow limit: twisted/minimal surface; wide limit: cylindrical helix) - the parameter and limits were confirmed from a search summary of their abstract, NOT from the paper text, and I could not retrieve the numerical critical value. At the optimum, sqrt(h/kappa) = h/sqrt(1.5 d_eps): 8.2h at 1 %, 18.3h at 0.2 %, 5.8h at 2 %.
findings.value: w_c ~ sqrt(h/kappa) = h/sqrt(1.5 d_eps); 2.3-29 mm over the table

findings.claim: (d) In the wide (isometric) limit the curvature is not the beam value. Pezzulla et al. find that the mean curvature of the isometric state is three-fourths of the natural curvature for an isotropically expanding top layer (verified numerically and experimentally, per their abstract). Own inference: a cylinder with mean curvature 0.75*kappa0 has principal curvature 1.5*kappa0 = (1+nu)*kappa0 at nu = 0.5, i.e. a wide isotropic bilayer plate rolls up about (1+nu) times tighter than the Timoshenko beam value (30-50 % for nu = 0.3-0.5). This bias is larger than the 20 % error the experiment is meant to detect, so strip width must be controlled or modelled. The Lean file has a snapParameter L^4 kappa^2/h^2 which is the fourth power of L/sqrt(h/kappa), i.e. the same control parameter.

(e) Steering by anisotropy: bending follows the direction of largest differential strain divided by local bending stiffness. In the pine cone scale the passive layer has fibres (microfibril angle near 0 deg) along the scale and the active sclereid layer has microfibril angle near 90 deg, so swelling is longitudinal in one layer and suppressed in the other (Le Duigou & Castro text). For a strip cut at angle phi to the swelling axis the mismatch resolves into axial strain eL cos^2(phi) + eT sin^2(phi) (bending) and shear (eL - eT) sin(2 phi)/2 (twist) - encoded in the Lean file as axialStrain/shearStrain - which is the bend-to-twist route of seed pods. Printed analogues (print-path fibre alignment, wood-filled filament raster direction) are reported by Sydney Gladman et al., Erb et al., Correa et al. and Le Duigou et al.; those four were DOI-verified only, their quantitative content was not read in this run.
findings.value: axial = eL cos^2 phi + eT sin^2 phi; shear = (eL-eT) sin(2 phi)/2

findings.claim: (e) Stiffener rule of thumb (own derivation, not sourced): bending stiffness per unit width goes as thickness cubed, so ribs of height H at areal fill fraction phi on a skin of thickness h raise stiffness along the ribs by roughly 1 + phi*(H/h)^3 (more with the parallel-axis term) while leaving the transverse direction near E h^3/12; ribs twice the skin height at 30 % fill give >3x anisotropy, enough to pick the bending axis in a plate that is otherwise in the one-direction (wide) regime of (d). Slits do the opposite job: they cut the plate into strips narrower than sqrt(h/kappa) and remove the geometric coupling. Alben et al. (title-level only; text not retrieved) report that edge effects select the bending direction of rectangular isotropic bilayers.

(f) Creep: wood bilayers held under 1-1.5 N tip loads for three months outdoors took a permanent offset (creep with plastic deformation) but kept almost all their actuation amplitude; predicted curvature loss from the load was under 3 % (Rueggeberg & Burgert). In thick wood bilayers, FE analysis gave viscoelastic strains of the same order as elastic strains (elastic up to 0.25 % passive / 0.55 % active), still not converged after 900 h although curvature had settled by 400 h; relaxation in both layers largely cancels in the curvature; interface stresses reached ~25-30 MPa compressive (Groenquist et al.). Design reading: creep shifts the rest shape more than the stroke, but polymer creep data for specific printable resins were not found, so every printed-bilayer test should include a cycled control.
findings.value: creep offset permanent; amplitude loss <3 %; viscoelastic strain ~ elastic strain

findings.claim: (f) Buckling/instability limits that apply to the requested geometry (own calculation plus the scaling in (d)): the mode switch from double to single curvature occurs near w ~ sqrt(h/kappa), which for the table is 2.3 mm (h=0.4 mm, 2 %) to 29 mm (h=1.6 mm, 0.2 %). A 5 mm wide strip is safely narrow at h = 0.8 and 1.6 mm for all strains except borderline at h=0.8 mm/2 % (4.6 mm), but is at or beyond the scale for h = 0.4 mm at 0.5 % and above (4.6, 3.3, 2.3 mm). Also the 0.4 mm/2 % strip turns through 172 deg over 40 mm (R = 13.3 mm), so self-contact and large-rotation effects appear before 2 % is reached on longer strips. Classical references for the bifurcation (Mansfield 1962; Freund 2000) and the review by Holmes were DOI/arXiv-verified but only the Holmes abstract was read.
findings.value: w_c scale 2.3-29 mm; 172 deg tip rotation at h=0.4 mm, 2 %

findings.claim: Radius table (L = 40 mm, optimum m, kappa = 1.5 d_eps/h, R = h/(1.5 d_eps)). h=0.4 mm: R = 133.3, 53.3, 26.7, 13.3 mm at 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2 %. h=0.8 mm: 266.7, 106.7, 53.3, 26.7 mm. h=1.6 mm: 533.3, 213.3, 106.7, 53.3 mm. Arithmetic example: h=0.8 mm, 1 % -> kappa = 1.5*0.01/0.8 = 0.01875 1/mm -> R = 53.33 mm; tip angle = 0.01875*40 = 0.75 rad = 43.0 deg; tip deflection = (1-cos 0.75)/0.01875 = 14.3 mm. Values are the same for n=1 (h1=h2=h/2) and n=10 (stiff layer h1 = 0.240h: 0.096/0.192/0.384 mm; soft layer 0.304/0.608/1.216 mm). Small-strain beam theory; narrow strip; uniform equilibrium moisture assumed.

Measurement resolution to tell the law from a 20 % error. A 20 %-low curvature moves R by +25 % (e.g. 533 -> 667 mm, 13.3 -> 16.7 mm). In directly measurable terms over a 40 mm cantilever: hardest case (h=1.6 mm, 0.2 %) tip deflection 1.50 mm shifts by 0.30 mm, mid-sagitta 0.375 mm shifts by 0.075 mm, tip angle 4.3 deg shifts by 0.86 deg; the next hardest (h=0.8 mm, 0.2 %) shifts tip deflection by 0.60 mm and tip angle by 1.7 deg, and the other ten cases shift by 0.75-3.5 mm. For a 3-sigma decision the readout must be about one third of the shift: +-0.1 mm on tip deflection (or +-0.3 deg, or +-0.025 mm on sagitta) covers all 12 cases; a +-0.2 mm readout covers 11 of 12 (one of them marginally, at a 0.597 mm shift); a +-0.5 mm ruler reading only covers the 6 of 12 cases whose shift is 1.5 mm or more (shifts 2.4-3.5 mm). Photographing the strip edge at <=0.1 mm/pixel and circle-fitting (the method used by Rueggeberg & Burgert with ImageJ + least squares) is sufficient.
findings.value: +-0.1 mm tip deflection or +-0.3 deg tip angle for all cases

findings.claim: The binding uncertainty is in the inputs, not the curvature readout. Since kappa = 1.5 d_eps/h, relative errors in d_eps and h pass straight through. To leave a 20 % discrepancy visible at ~3 sigma the combined input uncertainty must be about 7 % or less, e.g. thickness to 3 % (+-12 um at 0.4 mm, +-48 um at 1.6 mm) and free differential swelling strain to ~5 %. On a 40 mm free strip d_eps = 0.2 % is an 80 um length change, so 5 % of it is 4 um; at 2 % it is 800 um and 40 um. At the optimum the modulus ratio is nearly irrelevant (for n=10 design, f = 1.467 if true n=5 and 1.467 if true n=20), so moduli need only be known to a factor of two; and strip width must stay below ~sqrt(h/kappa) or the (1+nu) plate bias in (d) exceeds the 20 % being tested.
findings.value: inputs: h to ~3 %, d_eps to ~5 % (4 um on 40 mm at 0.2 %)

findings.claim: Published agreement level of the law: for beech/spruce bilayers the Timoshenko prediction of 59 deg tip rotation (kappa 8.7e-3 1/mm over 120 mm; my check: 0.0087*120 = 1.044 rad = 59.8 deg) compared with 55 deg measured, a 7 % shortfall, so a 20 % discrimination target is realistic but not generous.

recommendations: Add to the Lean hygromorph file the theorem that timoshenkoCoefficient h m n <= 3/(2h) for m, n > 0 with equality iff m^2 n = 1 (AM-GM on 1/(mn) + m^3 n >= 2m). It makes the frozen prediction independent of the modulus ratio, which is the worst-known input for printed resins.

Design the proof-of-concept strip at the optimum (stiff layer thickness = h/(1+sqrt(n))) and freeze the prediction as R = h/(1.5 d_eps); measure d_eps on free single-layer coupons printed in the same job, with a length gauge good to a few micrometres (or use longer coupons).

Keep strip width below about sqrt(h/kappa) (use 3-5 mm for h >= 0.8 mm; cut slits or go narrower for 0.4 mm at >= 0.5 %), or predict with the (1+nu) plate factor and state which regime is being tested; otherwise width alone can produce a >20 % deviation.

Read curvature by photographing the strip edge at <= 0.1 mm/pixel and circle-fitting; that resolves a 20 % error in all 12 table cases. Prefer the 0.8 mm / 0.5-1 % region: tip shifts of 1.5-2.7 mm and no self-contact.

Budget time honestly: dense thermoplastic or resin layers of 0.4-1.6 mm will take days to months to equilibrate (h^2/D with D ~ 1e-13 to 4e-12 m^2/s). For an hour-scale demo use an active layer that is porous, fibre-filled or gel-like, or thin the active layer to ~0.1 mm; measure D on a coupon first (mass uptake vs sqrt(time)).
Include a loaded and an unloaded cycled control to separate creep offset from loss of stroke, as the wood bilayer literature shows the offset is permanent while amplitude survives.

Have a follow-up agent obtain the Armon 2011/2014 and Mansfield/Freund texts (institutional access) to pin the numerical prefactor of the width transition, and obtain water uptake/diffusivity for the specific Formlabs resins from their data sheets.

specialists.topic: The Formlabs materials library as a design space (Form 4 series SLA resins, Fuse 1+ SLS powders)
specialists.summary: I tabulated 27 Formlabs materials (18 SLA resins, 9 SLS powders) from technical data sheets fetched on 2026-11-12. Stiffness spans about four orders of magnitude within SLA: Rigid 10K at 10-11 GPa down to Silicone 40A at an estimated 0.8 MPa secant modulus (no modulus is published for any elastomer). Water uptake is small and tightly clustered for almost everything (0.0-0.9% in the 24 h cube test; 0.07-1.40% ASTM D570 for powders), with one outlier: Flexible 80A Resin V2 gains 8% mass and 3% volume in one day in deionized water and softens by 26 Shore A points. It is the only catalogue material read with swelling large enough to drive a hygromorphic bilayer, with Tough 1000, Rigid 10K or Silicone 40A (all at or below 0.1%) as the passive layer. No Formlabs page read says the printers can print two materials in one job; the Form 4 holds one cartridge, so a bilayer means two prints bonded together, or one resin with a cure or geometric contrast. Open Material Mode (paid licence) permits any 405 nm resin or 1064 nm powder. Minimum printable wall is 0.2 mm on Form 4 (Grey V5, 50 um layers) and 0.3-0.6 mm on Fuse.

findings.claim: Stiffest Formlabs SLA resin read: Rigid 10K, tensile modulus 10-11 GPa post-cured (7.5 GPa green).
The elastomers publish no tensile modulus, only stress at fixed elongation. Post-cured stress at 50% elongation: Silicone 40A 0.4 MPa; Flexible 50A 0.9 MPa; Flexible 80A V2 2.9 MPa.

LARGEST STIFFNESS CONTRAST (SLA): Rigid 10K vs Silicone 40A. Own calculation: secant modulus of Silicone 40A = 0.4 MPa / 0.5 = 0.8 MPa; ratio = 10,000-11,000 MPa / 0.8 MPa = about 12,500-13,750x. The secant figure is an estimate, not a published modulus.
Stiffness contrast against Flexible 80A V2. Own calculation: 2.9 MPa / 0.5 = 5.8 MPa secant; Rigid 10K 10,000-11,000 / 5.8 = about 1,720-1,900x; Tough 1000 932 / 5.8 = about 160x.
Stiffness contrast among rigid SLA resins only (published post-cured tensile moduli): Rigid 10K 10-11 GPa vs Tough 1000 0.932 GPa = about 11-12x; vs Durable 1.0 GPa = about 10-11x.

LARGEST STIFFNESS CONTRAST (SLS): Nylon 11 CF (5.3 GPa in X) vs TPU 90A (Shore 90A; no modulus published, so no ratio can be computed from Formlabs data). Among powders with published moduli: Nylon 11 CF X 5.3 GPa vs Nylon 12 Tough 1.45 GPa = 3.7x. Nylon 11 CF is itself anisotropic: 5.3 / 1.6 = 3.3x between X and Z.

LARGEST WATER-UPTAKE VALUE FOUND: Flexible 80A Resin V2 gains +8% mass and +3% volume after 1 day in deionized water and loses 26 Shore A points; +9% mass and +7% volume after 1 week (ASTM D471, slabs measured immediately after wiping dry).
findings.value: +8% mass, +3% vol (1 day); +9% mass, +7% vol (1 week)

findings.claim: Own calculation: +3% volume in 1 day is about 1.0% linear swelling strain if isotropic (1.03^(1/3) = 1.0099); +7% at 1 week is about 2.3% (1.07^(1/3) = 1.0228).

LARGEST WATER-UPTAKE CONTRAST (SLA): Flexible 80A V2 (+8% mass, ASTM D471) vs Tough 1000 (0.0%), Rigid 10K (<0.1%) or Silicone 40A (<0.1%) (24 h weight gain of a 1 cm cube). At least 80x against <0.1% (8 / 0.1), but the two test methods differ, so the ratio is indicative only.

Within the single 1 cm cube / 24 h method the SLA water-uptake spread is narrow: Clear V5 0.9%, Grey V5 0.8%, Rigid 4000 0.7%, ESD 0.7%, Flexible 50A 0.7%, BioMed Flex 50A 0.7%, BioMed Flex 80A 0.6%, BioMed Durable 0.5%, Tough 1500 V2 0.21%, Tough 2000 V2 0.19%, Rigid 10K <0.1%, Silicone 40A <0.1%, Tough 1000 0.0%.
findings.source_url_or_path: TDS PDFs listed in the table rows

findings.claim: Soft-soft pair with opposite water response (candidate active/passive elastomer bilayer): Flexible 80A V2 (+8% mass in water, 83A) vs Silicone 40A (<0.1%, 40A). Silicone 40A is listed for Form 4/4B but not Form 4L/4BL.

LARGEST WATER-UPTAKE CONTRAST (SLS, single method ASTM D570, printed part): Nylon 12 White 1.40% vs Nylon 11 0.07% = 20x. Others: TPU 90A 0.89%, Nylon 12 0.66%, Nylon 11 Pro 0.4%, Nylon 12 Tough 0.30%, Polypropylene 0.25%, Nylon 12 GF 0.24%.

Nylon 11 Powder carries a bio-based claim ("high performance, bio-based nylon material" in the TDS; "bio-based material" on the product page). No percentage or feedstock is stated in the pages read. No bio-based claim was found on the Nylon 11 Pro TDS page or on any SLA resin read.

Form 4 / Form 4B printer specs: 50 um pixel size (XY resolution 50 um with anti-aliasing), layer thickness 25-200 um, build volume 20.0 x 12.5 x 21.0 cm, 405 nm LED backlight (60 LEDs), 16 mW/cm2 at the cure plane, 1 resin cartridge. Form 4 validated with 23 Formlabs materials, Form 4B with 38 (15 biocompatible). Read through a page summariser.

Multi-material in one job: no Formlabs page fetched states that Form 4-series or Fuse-series printers can print two materials in a single job. The Form 4 spec lists one resin cartridge, and a web search for a multi-material statement returned none. This is absence of a statement, not a denial by Formlabs.

findings.claim: Open Material Mode exists: "print with any 405 nm photopolymer resin or 1064 nm powder". Applies to Form Studio 1, all Form 3 and Form 4 series, and all Fuse series. Included with Form Studio 1; a one-time paid licence per printer for the others (price via sales contact). The Print Settings Editor exposes exposure, layer height and heating (SLA) and layer thickness, XYZ correction and exposure (SLS).

The page gives no values for elastomers.

Minimum layer thickness per SLA material (product pages): 25 um Clear V5, High Temp; 50 um Rigid 10K, Rigid 4000, Durable, ESD, BioMed Clear, BioMed Amber, BioMed Flex 80A; 100 um Flexible 50A, Silicone 40A, BioMed Durable, BioMed Flex 50A. Not found on the product page for Tough 1000 / 1500 V2 / 2000 V2, Grey V5, Flexible 80A V2.

Biocompatibility: BioMed Clear, BioMed Durable, BioMed Flex 50A and BioMed Flex 80A are USP Class VI; BioMed Amber, Silicone 40A and Tough 1500 V2 cite ISO 10993 tests (cytotoxicity, irritation, sensitisation); every SLS powder read cites ISO 10993-5 plus irritation and sensitisation tests. BioMed resins are listed for Form 4B/4BL, not Form 4/4L.
findings.source_url_or_path: TDS PDFs listed in the table rows ; https://formlabs.com/materials/

findings.claim: Green vs post-cured stiffness is a tunable contrast inside one resin: Durable 0.24 -> 1.0 GPa (4.2x), High Temp 0.75 -> 2.8 GPa (3.7x), Rigid 4000 2.1 -> 4.1 GPa (2.0x), Rigid 10K 7.5 -> 10-11 GPa (1.3-1.5x).
The current catalogue also lists a "Form Studio 1" printer with six "Alpha" resins, and a Fuse X1; these are outside the Form 4 / Fuse 1+ scope and were not tabulated.
Website vs TDS discrepancy: the materials catalogue lists Rigid 10K elongation as 0.7%; the TDS column for the 88 MPa state reads 1.7%.

recommendations: Measure before designing: Formlabs publishes no hygroscopic expansion coefficient and no elastomer modulus. Print 1 mm coupons of Flexible 80A V2, Tough 1000 and Silicone 40A, then measure linear swelling against humidity and immersion time, and tensile modulus wet and dry. The 8% figure is full immersion; the response to humid air is unknown.

First bilayer candidate: Flexible 80A V2 as the active layer on Tough 1000 as the passive layer (about 160x stiffness ratio, 0.0% water uptake, same Form 4 printer). Rigid 10K gives a much larger mismatch (about 1,700-1,900x), which would need a very thin passive layer near the 0.2 mm wall limit.
Plan for two prints and a bond, since single-job multi-material was not found. Test adhesion by painting uncured resin of one material onto the other and post-curing; this route is unverified here.
Run a single-resin control: one resin with a through-thickness cure gradient (green vs post-cured moduli differ by up to 4.2x for Durable) or a purely geometric bilayer.

For an SLS demonstration, Nylon 12 White (1.40%) against Nylon 11 (0.07%) is the widest water-uptake pair, but the absolute swelling is small and the two powders cannot share a build. Nylon 11 is the only material with a bio-based claim.

If the design needs biocompatibility, BioMed Flex 80A (USP Class VI) with BioMed Clear or BioMed Durable is available on Form 4B, but all three sit at 0.5-0.6% water uptake, so there is little hygroscopic contrast.
Ask Formlabs directly for Flexible 80A V2 swelling kinetics and whether Open Material Mode supports a mid-print resin change.
