findings.claim: Mycelium-bound composite research mostly sits at TRL 3-5, while packaging and insulation applications reach TRL 7-9.
findings.evidence_quote: Most MBC research currently resides between TRL 3 and TRL 5, where laboratory validation and early prototyping dominate

findings.claim: A 2026 quantitative synthesis reports mycelium compressive strength of 0.05-1.2 MPa, narrower than the 0.03-4.44 MPa range in the 2025 review used in the earlier file; both are reported, they come from different review sets.
findings.evidence_quote: A comparative synthesis of reported data reveals significant variability in compressive strength (0.05-1.2 MPa) and elastic modulus

findings.claim: Full-scale EN 13501-1 reaction-to-fire testing is rarely done for mycelium composites; the cited exception tested mycelium-Miscanthus panels for fire resistance (not reaction-to-fire class) and reached EI 15. This confirms and strengthens the earlier 'no fire classification' gap.
findings.evidence_quote: Full-scale testing in accordance with the BS EN 13501-1 standard [25] is rarely used for MBCs owing to its high cost, complexity, and large sample size.

findings.claim: The only Euroclass figure for a mycelium insulation I found is a company statement on an accelerator profile (Mykor: Euroclass B, REI 60-120); no test report was seen. A search summary also mentioned a Euroclass E for another product, which I could not verify and do not use.
findings.evidence_quote: with greater fire performance rating of Euroclass B and resistance REI of 60-120

findings.claim: Mycelium panel production cost is quoted by a review as about 0.83 USD per cubic foot (secondary estimate); converted by me to 29.3 USD/m3.
findings.evidence_quote: Mycelium panel production is estimated at $0.83 per cubic foot

findings.claim: The 2025 review names low strength, weathering susceptibility, scalability, under-50-year life and lack of standard test methods as barriers for mycelium (confirms the earlier file).
findings.evidence_quote: including low mechanical strength, weathering susceptibility, scalability issues, limited lifespan (<50 years), and a lack of standardised manufacturing/testing methods

findings.claim: PLA property ranges and price in the Nature Communications 2026 comparison table: Tg 55-80 C, modulus 0.3-3.8 GPa, tensile 10-80 MPa, price 2-3 USD/kg.
findings.evidence_quote: PLA Chemical industrial synthesis 6–9 weeks >1.5 years 55–80 0.3–3.8 10–80 NA 37 80% 2–3

findings.claim: PHA property ranges and price in the same table: Tg -10 to 15 C, modulus 0.4-3.8 GPa, tensile 15-45 MPa, price 3-8 USD/kg. Column mapping is mine from the table header.
findings.evidence_quote: PHA Bacterial extraction 1–4 months 1–6 months -10−15 0.4–3.8 15–45 NA 55–72 47.8% 3–8

findings.claim: A techno-economic study cited by an algal-bioplastic review puts algal PHA at 7-9 USD/kg, uncompetitive with petroleum plastic.
findings.evidence_quote: estimated PHA production cost between $7 and to 9 per kg, which is still uncompetitive compared to petroleum-derived plastic

findings.claim: Printed pure PLA lost most of its strength in 12 weeks of simulated UV: about 28 MPa initially and below 10 MPa after 12 weeks (coupon FDM test, laboratory lamp, not outdoor). A 10 percent coffee-ground filler kept 24-25 MPa. My retention bound is at most 36 percent (10/28).
findings.evidence_quote: after 12 weeks of UV degradation, there is a significant reduction in strength to below 10 MPa, indicating significant disruption of the polymer chain due to photo-degradation

findings.claim: Lab creep studies of printed PLA exist (ASTM D2990 coupons, desktop FDM printer) but I found none at facade temperature and humidity, so a building creep number for PLA remains unverified (absence of evidence from this search only).
findings.evidence_quote: The geometry of creep test specimens follows the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM D2990) standards.

findings.claim: North American CLT market price has been steady at about 42-44 USD per cubic foot over two years, which I convert to 1483-1554 USD/m3 (35.315 ft3 per m3); for an assumed 100 mm panel that is 148-155 USD/m2 (assumption, not from the source).
findings.evidence_quote: Prices have held fairly steady during the last 2 years at around $42 to $44 dollars

findings.claim: A 2019 techno-economic model gives CLT mill-gate minimum selling prices of 536 USD/m3 (large plant) and 652 USD/m3 (small plant), versus 600-742 USD/m3 literature values.
findings.evidence_quote: has a minimum selling price of $536/m3.

findings.claim: CLT is covered by EN 16351:2021 and ANSI/APA PRG 320-2019; weak rolling shear is the cited limit for large-span heavy-load use.
findings.evidence_quote: the weak transverse layer rolling shear performance limits the application of CLT in large-span heavy-load structures

findings.claim: Embodied-carbon data are missing for most emerging structural materials; engineered wood and reused steel reach 3-5 percent of primary steel's cradle-to-gate EC in the authors' beam case (stored carbon excluded).
findings.evidence_quote: Only 18% (37 out of 204) of the emerging structural materials reviewed had EC values; less (11%) had embodied energy values.

findings.claim: Bacterial cellulose fibres/ideal material are reported at 15-138 GPa modulus, 60-90 percent crystallinity.
findings.evidence_quote: BC has a crystallinity of up to 60% to 90% and a young’s modulus of up to 15 to 138 Gpa

findings.claim: Measured bulk BC sheets are far weaker than the fibre figure: crude dry BC 180.3 MPa modulus, 11.6 MPa strength; crude fresh hydrated BC 3.1 MPa modulus, 1.2 MPa strength (a 58x drop, my ratio 180.3/3.1). This is a biomedical-materials study, not an architectural element.
Lab-scale BC production cost fell from 0.25-0.27 to 0.07-0.08 EUR per g with flour-based nitrogen substitution, i.e. 70-270 EUR/kg dry.
findings.evidence_quote: the maximum reduction was observed for BY-BC at 50% substitution (from 0.25 to 0.07 €/g; 72.00%)

findings.claim: BC bioplastic commercialisation is described as just beginning and held back by cost.
findings.evidence_quote: BC’s adoption as a biodegradable bioplastic is still in its infancy of commercialization, primarily constrained by high production costs.

findings.claim: The architecture-specific BC literature I found is conceptual: a 2021 paper proposes BC as structural and membrane material and says mechanical enhancement for structural use is ongoing; the abstract gives no strength or durability numbers.
findings.evidence_quote: the current study is part of the ongoing research on enhancing the mechanical properties of bacterial cellulose in order to use it for structural applications

findings.claim: Algae facades are pumped glass-panel photobioreactor systems; the BIQ house has 129 flat-panel glass PBRs and is called very complex, and in an LCA of a column PBR cultivation electricity caused almost all CO2.
findings.evidence_quote: BIQ house is very complex, consisting of 129 flat panel glass PBRs, making even the cleaning and maintenance cost higher than in this study.

findings.claim: A microalgae-derived bio-cement block received ASTM C129 and C90 certification in February 2023 (company press coverage); it is non-living, so it refines the earlier view that bio-based mineral materials are lab-only.
findings.evidence_quote: Prometheus Materials has been awarded ASTM C129 certification for non-loadbearing concrete masonry units (CMU) and ASTM C90 for loadbearing CMUs for its bio-cement product.

findings.claim: Among microbial mineralisation (MICP) uses, self-healing concrete is the most commercially mature and geotechnical uses are TRL 5-7; the review lists long-term durability data, scale-specific cost and monitoring protocols as gaps.
findings.evidence_quote: The self healing concrete application is the most advanced toward commercial maturity, and there are products available from Basilisk, Evonik and BioMason.

findings.claim: Chitosan-cellulose FLAM costs about 2 USD/kg with 0.26 GPa modulus; at high chitosan content the composite shrinks during drying and loses integrity. I found no moisture, weathering or outdoor-durability data in the paper text (confirms the earlier file).
findings.evidence_quote: high amounts of chitosan (>17%) produce strong internal forces as the polymers loses water and shrinks, undermining the integrity of structure

findings.claim: The Freiburg 4D-printed cellulose shading evaluated shade coverage only; the authors say quantifying indoor-climate improvement is future work (no energy or comfort number exists for it).
findings.evidence_quote: While we have focused on evaluating the 4D-printed shading elements through analysis of shade coverage in this study, it will be important to quantify the improvement of indoor climate regulation in future work.

findings.claim: Only 170 actuation cycles were tested, which the authors call small against a building's lifetime; UV exposure marginally lowered curvature at low RH.
findings.evidence_quote: The number of cycles tested is still small compared to the entire lifetime of a building

findings.claim: Freiburg manufacturing figures: 18.25 printer-hours per m2 of facade, 5.5 kg actuating and 0.7 kg restricting filament in total (0.59 and 0.07 kg/m2), cellulose powder at 1.52 EUR/kg; implied area 5.5/0.59 = 9.3 m2.
findings.evidence_quote: Using four 3D-printers (working 10 hours per day), the rate of 4D-printing manufacturing is 18.25 hm −2

findings.claim: Only 10.3 percent of studies in a 2026 systematic map of biomimetic interior-comfort strategies report statistically validated findings and half are review- or concept-led (interior comfort field, not facades; used as an indicator of weak evidence stratification).
findings.evidence_quote: only 10.3% of studies report statistically validated empirical findings, whereas 50.0% remain review-based or concept-led.

findings.claim: CORRECTION of spec-resin-chemistry.json ('every current SLA resin gains under 1% mass in water ... Flexible 80A 0.7%'): the Flexible 80A V2 datasheet shows +8 percent mass and +3 percent volume after 1 day in deionized water and +9 and +7 percent after 1 week (ASTM D471 slabs). The 0.7 percent row is the older 'Flexible 80A Resin' in the 1 cm cube table; there is no V2 row there. spec-formlabs-materials.json had this right.
findings.evidence_quote: Deionized Water 1 day -26 +8% +3% 94% 89%

findings.claim: Using the project's 3/2 ceiling and isotropic linear strain from the 3 percent volume change (0.99 percent), a Flexible 80A V2 layer bonded to a non-swelling layer would bend to a radius of about 67 mm at 1 mm total thickness after one day of immersion (11.7-134.7 mm over the cases in the table). Immersion, not humid air; swelling would need to be re-measured in air.

Reconfirmed from Formlabs' 24 h table: Elastic 50A V2 gains 39.2 percent in isopropyl alcohol and 0.7 percent in water; Rigid 10K gains under 0.1 percent in both. This confirms the earlier 39 percent versus under 0.1 percent claim (and the warning that 163.9 is the xylene column).
findings.evidence_quote: Results are reported as weight gain percentage after 24 hours of exposure to solvent.

findings.claim: DISAGREEMENT on polyamide moisture strain: the earlier file estimated 0.2-0.45 percent hygroscopic strain for PA12 (from mass uptake, calibrated on PA6.6); a 2021 hot-pressed PA11/PA12 durability paper states water or moisture causes no hardness or dimension change. I could not find dimension data in its text, and it is hot-pressed sheet, not sintered. Neither is a measurement on Fuse powders.
findings.evidence_quote: absorbed water or moisture does not cause plasticization; thus, neither hardness nor dimension changes.

findings.claim: Waste-based bioplastic wall-cladding tiles were tested for acoustics, mechanics and heat but only for non-load-bearing interior use; the authors list long-term durability and fire resistance as future work.
findings.evidence_quote: Future research directions include evaluating long-term durability, fire resistance, and advanced formulations to expand the applications of bioplastic cladding in modern architecture.

findings.claim: Independent numerical re-check of the project record: the Timoshenko coefficient f(m,n) peaks at exactly 1.5 at m = n^(-1/2) for n = 0.1, 1, 2, 5, 10, 50 (grid maximum 1.5 in each case), and equal layers at n=10 give f = 0.9959, a 33.6 percent loss. The earlier file rounded this to 34 percent.

key_claims.claim: The best passive bio-based skin has no building-performance number and a short durability record, so the open gap is the link from actuator geometry to measured or simulated solar gain and cycle life.
key_claims.evidence_quote: While we have focused on evaluating the 4D-printed shading elements through analysis of shade coverage in this study, it will be important to quantify the improvement of indoor climate regulation in future work.

key_claims.claim: Among stock Formlabs SLA resins, Flexible 80A V2 is the one with large water uptake (+8 percent mass, +3 percent volume in 1 day, immersion), which contradicts the earlier blanket 'under 1 percent' statement and is the only catalogue resin with swelling big enough for a hygromorph layer; humid-air constants remain unpublished.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Deionized Water 1 day -26 +8% +3% 94% 89%

key_claims.claim: Mycelium and other living or fungal materials lack a verified reaction-to-fire class and are research-stage (TRL 3-5) beyond insulation and packaging, so they are the wrong first target for a small computational team.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Full-scale testing in accordance with the BS EN 13501-1 standard [25] is rarely used for MBCs owing to its high cost, complexity, and large sample size.

key_claims.claim: Embodied-carbon data are missing for most emerging structural materials, so a transparent carbon sheet for the proof of concept is a real, computation-only contribution.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Only 18% (37 out of 204) of the emerging structural materials reviewed had EC values; less (11%) had embodied energy values.

recommendations: Pitch the new biomaterial as a law-constrained printable hygromorph (bilayer with the 3/2 ceiling built in) rather than a mycelium, bacterial-cellulose, algae or living material; those need fire, biosafety or growth infrastructure the team does not have.

Do gap 1 first (humid-air swelling constants and response time for Flexible 80A V2, Silicone 40A, Rigid 10K, Nylon 11 and a hydrogel resin if open mode is licensed); it unlocks gaps 2 and 3 and settles the PA12 disagreement.
Never quote an energy saving, a fire class, or a PLA creep life for the printed demonstrator; report curvature, cycles and modelled shading only, labelled as such.
Quote bacterial-cellulose stiffness only as wet versus dry bulk-sheet numbers (3.1 versus 180 MPa), not the 15-138 GPa fibre figure.

For the practice conversation, offer gap 4 (a carbon and provenance sheet with a script) alongside the physical samples, since the practice's own PLA carbon-saving figures disagree across sources (project record).
Before relying on the Flexible 80A V2 number, re-measure it in humid air and on a printed Form 4 coupon; the TDS slab was wiped wet after immersion and the table was scrambled in text extraction.

A source-stated TRL for bacterial cellulose, algae facades, chitosan or passive skins: the TRL values for those rows are my judgement from the evidence described, labelled as such. Only mycelium and MICP TRLs are source-stated.

Humid-air (RH) swelling coefficient or diffusivity for any Formlabs resin or powder; the PA11/PA12 dimensional-change statement is from a hot-pressed sheet abstract and I did not find the data behind it.
PLA or PHA creep, hydrolysis and weathering numbers at real facade temperature and humidity; PLA UV data are from a laboratory lamp on FDM coupons.
Moisture, weathering and outdoor-durability data for chitosan-cellulose composites; cost and standards for living building materials.

ICC-ES or European Technical Assessment status of any mycelium or microalgae-cement product (EOTA ETA database and ICC-ES reports were not queried); the Prometheus ASTM certification comes from trade-press coverage, not the certificate.
Values read from figures: the Mass Timber Performance Index chart and the Freiburg shade-coverage curves were not read as numbers beyond what the text states.
Measured (not modelled) energy or comfort saving for any power-free bio-based responsive facade: none found, consistent with the earlier file.

Coverage bias: most full texts came through Europe PMC and are open access; Crossref was rate-limited (HTTP 429) on rapid queries so some searches were slower; OpenAlex was not used, per the rules. MDPI/Elsevier paywalled literature on PLA and BC mechanics was therefore mostly unread.
The practice's own statements on UV, creep, moisture and fire were not re-searched; the buyer entries rely on the project-record file spec-partner-architecture.json for the practice's needs.

fleet.label: bm-bilayer-theory-verified
fleet.topic: The bilayer equations, each read in its original paper
fleet.summary: I read Timoshenko 1925 (J. Opt. Soc. Am. 11, 233-255, public-domain scan on the Internet Archive; the publisher site blocks automated fetches with a captcha, which I did not bypass), Stoney 1909 (Internet Archive scan), the Freund-Floro-Chason 1999 paper (open preprint, the companion of Freund 2000), Reyssat & Mahadevan 2009 (equation images), and Pezzulla et al. 2016 (arXiv). RESULT 1: Timoshenko's printed eq.(4) is the project's f(m,n) exactly, as are R&M eq.2.6 and Freund-Floro-Chason eq.(6) with E replaced by E/(1-nu). Timoshenko 1925 does not state the ceiling 3/2 or the optimum m^2 n = 1; those are the project's own results, which I re-proved symbolically (3/2 - f = 3(m^2n-1)^2/(2(m^4n^2+4m^3n+6m^2n+4mn+1))) and by a 2.4-million-point grid. His own remark that the modulus ratio does not matter is limited to n between 1/2 and 2 at equal thickness (3 percent). RESULT 2 (assumptions): the formula is for a narrow strip, linear, perfectly bonded, plane sections, no Poisson ratio. For a wide plate Timoshenko himself replaces E by E/(1-nu) and f is unchanged (a sphere, while the sag is below about h/2). Plane-strain E/(1-nu^2) enters only after the plate flips to a cylinder, where the curvature is (1+nu) times the strip value (+30 to +50 percent); I derived this symbolically and it is confirmed by Pezzulla et al. (L+N = kappa_o(1+nu)) and by Alben's discrete model. Three independent criteria put the strip/plate boundary at a plate diameter of 2.0, 2.2 and 4.2 times sqrt(h/kappa). Stoney's 1909 equation is the thin-film limit of the same f. RESULT 3 (printed, wet, soft strips): the modulus ratio is a second-order risk at the optimum (a factor-2 error costs 2-3 percent of curvature; softening of the wet layer to 50 percent costs 2-3 percent), while large swelling strain, creep, the adhesive joint and anisotropic swelling are not covered by the theory and are not sized because no sources were found. Diffusion limits speed: tau ~ h^2/D (R&M), and for the only measured D of printable polymers (0.001-0.015 mm^2/h) my model gives a 90 percent curvature response at 0.72 a^2/D, 2-460 h for active layers of 0.2-0.8 mm. No diffusivity for any Formlabs resin exists in the sources found. RESULT 4 (honest gaps and one contradiction): Armon 2011, Alben-Balakrisnan-Smela 2011 and Freund 2000 could not be read in the original (abstracts only), so their equations and critical values are not reproduced. Two Formlabs documents disagree on Flexible 80A water uptake (0.7 percent in an older cube-table row versus +8 percent mass in the V2 datasheet), so the project-record sentence that stock resins gain under 1 percent in water holds for the cube table but not for Flexible 80A V2.
fleet.lay_summary: A strip made of two layers bends when one layer swells more than the other, like a bimetal thermostat. The project's formula for how tightly it bends turns out to be the same one Timoshenko printed in 1925, so the maths is on solid ground. That formula is for a thin ribbon, though; a wide sheet behaves differently and rolls up about 30 to 50 percent tighter, in one direction only. It also says nothing about how fast the bending happens, and water creeps into ordinary plastics very slowly: a layer a few tenths of a millimetre thick can take hours to days, like a damp sponge that dries one thin layer at a time. Several things in a printed, soft, wet strip (big swelling, creep, the glue between layers) are outside the formula, and I could not find numbers for them. I also could not read three of the original papers in full, and two Formlabs documents disagree on how much one resin swells in water, most likely because they describe two versions of it.

glossary.plain: Two layers bonded together so that a difference in how they expand makes the strip curl.
How tightly something bends: one divided by the radius of the circle it follows.
How stiff a material is: the force needed to stretch it by a given fraction.
How much a material gets thinner sideways when you stretch it lengthwise; about 0.3 to 0.5 for plastics and rubbers.
Two simplifications for a flat body: free to thin sideways (plane stress) or held from stretching sideways (plane strain); the stiff modulus then becomes E/(1-nu^2).
The stiffness of a sheet pulled equally in two directions, E/(1-nu).
The stretch a layer wants to have by itself (from swelling or heat) if nothing held it.
Same in every direction / different in different directions, like wood grain.
A ribbon that can only bend one way versus a sheet that must stretch if it tries to bend two ways at once.
The moment a wide sheet stops forming a bowl and flips to rolling up like a scroll.
The line inside a bent beam that is neither stretched nor squeezed.
How fast water spreads through a material; time to soak a layer of thickness h is about h squared divided by D.
Following the simple law that water moves from wet to dry in proportion to the difference.
A standard model of rubbery materials that stay accurate at large stretches.
Standard test recipes for fluid immersion, water absorption and tensile strength.
3D printing by light-curing liquid resin / by laser-fusing powder.
Technical data sheet from the manufacturer.
A computer program that does algebra exactly, used here to prove formulas.

findings.claim: PRINTED FORM. Timoshenko 1925 eq.(4), read from the page image (journal p.235): 1/rho = 6(a2-a1)(t-t0)(1+m)^2 / { h [ 3(1+m)^2 + (1+mn)(m^2 + 1/(mn)) ] }, with m = a1/a2 (thickness ratio of the two layers), n = E1/E2 (modulus ratio), h = a1+a2 total thickness, width taken as unity, a1,a2 the expansion coefficients, t-t0 the uniform temperature rise. No Poisson ratio appears.
findings.evidence_quote: the following general equation for the curvature of a bi-metal strip will be obtained,  [eq.(4) follows; transcribed by me from the page image because the OCR of the equation is garbled]

findings.claim: AGREEMENT WITH THE PROJECT. The project's f(m,n) is algebraically identical to Timoshenko's printed eq.(4): the Lean definition copies the same expression (with the 1/h factor folded in). I also re-derived the strip curvature from Timoshenko's own equilibrium conditions (axial forces equal, moment Ph/2 = M1+M2, equal strain at the interface) with sympy; it matches the printed f with residual exactly 0. R&M 2009 eq.2.6 and Freund-Floro-Chason eq.(6) (with M for E) are the same function (see below).

CONVENTIONS. Timoshenko uses m = a1/a2 and n = E1/E2 with layer 2 the high-expansion layer on the convex side; Reyssat & Mahadevan use m = h_p/h_a and n = E_p/E_a (passive/active) with alpha = alpha_a - alpha_p. f(m,n) = f(1/m,1/n) exactly (sympy residual 0), so swapping which layer is called 1 changes nothing; only the sign of curvature depends on which layer expands more.

findings.claim: STATED ASSUMPTIONS (Timoshenko 1925). Narrow strip of unit width; cross-sections stay plane and perpendicular to the curved axis (Euler-Bernoulli, no shear deformation); uniform temperature; difference of expansion coefficients constant; perfect weld; no friction at supports; isotropic layers implicit (one E and one alpha per layer). He calls these 'ideal conditions' and says they are 'not far removed from real conditions'. No explicit thin-layer or small-strain statement is made; the algebra is linear in strain.
findings.value: narrow strip; plane sections; constant delta-alpha; perfect bond
findings.evidence_quote: it was assumed that the difference in the coefficients of expansion remained constant during heating, that the friction at the supports could be neglected and that the width of the strip could be considered as being very small.

findings.claim: Timoshenko's own plane-section assumption, page 234.
findings.evidence_quote: The following analysis has been made on the assumption that cross-sections of the strip originally plane and perpendicular to the axis remain plane during bending and become perpendicular to the curved axis of the strip.

findings.claim: TIMOSHENKO'S OWN REMARK ON MODULUS RATIO IS NARROWER THAN 'THE MODULUS RATIO DROPS OUT'. He prints the special case m=1: 1/rho = 24(a2-a1)(t-t0)/[h(14+n+1/n)] (eq.5), = (3/2)(..)/h at n=1 (eq.6), = (48/33)(..)/h at n=1/2 or 2 (eq.7), and concludes n has no substantial effect because (6) and (7) differ by about 3 percent. That holds only for n within 1/2..2 at equal thickness. At m=1, n=10 the coefficient is 0.9959, 33.6 percent below the ceiling. The project's statement (modulus ratio drops out) is correct only at the optimum m^2 n = 1; Timoshenko does not claim more. My sympy/numpy check reproduces 24/(14+n+1/n), 3/2, 48/33 and the 3.03 percent difference.
findings.evidence_quote: The difference between (6) and (7) is only about 3 per cent.

findings.claim: THE CEILING 3/2 AND THE OPTIMUM m^2 n = 1 ARE NOT STATED IN TIMOSHENKO 1925. I searched the OCR of the whole article (pp.233-255) for optimum, maximum, minimum, greatest; 'maximum' appears only for stresses. So the ceiling and optimum are the project's derivation (Lean-checked), not a quotation of Timoshenko. (OCR of equations is imperfect, so a printed statement in an equation line could have been missed.) Independent proof of mine: 3/2 - f = 3(m^2 n - 1)^2 / (2 (m^4 n^2 + 4 m^3 n + 6 m^2 n + 4 m n + 1)), which is >= 0 with equality iff m^2 n = 1 (sympy factorisation). Brute-force over 2,404,601 (m,n) points on 1e-3..1e3 gives max f = 1.5000000000000002; argmax m = n^-1/2 for n = 0.1...100.

PHYSICAL MEANING OF THE OPTIMUM (own identity). m^2 n = 1 is the same as E1 a1^2 = E2 a2^2, i.e. the stiffness-weighted first moment about the interface vanishes: the interface is the neutral axis of the unloaded composite. That is why at the optimum the curvature depends only on the first moment of the eigenstrain and not on n, and (finding below) why the response-time curve is identical for n=1 and n=10.

PLANE STRESS / PLANE STRAIN IN THE ORIGINAL. Timoshenko treats the wide plate himself (section 4, p.242): uniform heating bends a plate into a sphere (equal curvatures), which needs only E -> E/(1-sigma) in each layer (sigma = Poisson ratio, equal for both materials). The final equations contain only the ratio of moduli, so eq.(4) and (6) 'remain without any change'. So the plate formula is NOT E/(1-nu^2); it is the biaxial modulus E/(1-nu) and the coefficient f is unchanged. He also states a limit: the small-deflection plate result holds while the deflection is less than about half the plate thickness; beyond that the mid-surface strain (stretching) matters.
findings.value: E -> E/(1-sigma); f unchanged; valid for sag < h/2
findings.source: https://archive.org/download/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3.pdf (PDF pages 41-50 = journal pp.233-242; doi 10.1364/JOSA.11.000233) (journal p.242, PDF page 50)
findings.evidence_quote: If the deflections are small, say less than a half of the thickness of the plate, this strain in the middle surface of the plate can be neglected without any essential error

findings.claim: WHERE E/(1-nu^2) DOES ENTER (own derivation, sympy, linear 3-D elasticity, plane stress through thickness). If a wide plate is forced to a CYLINDER (curvature in one direction only, as happens beyond the sphere-to-cylinder bifurcation), the layers see plane-strain-like constraint: effective modulus E/(1-nu^2) and effective eigenstrain (1+nu)*eps. For equal Poisson ratio in both layers the cylinder curvature is exactly (1+nu) times the strip (Timoshenko) curvature, independent of m and n; the sphere is exactly 1.0 times. For nu = 0.3, 0.35, 0.4, 0.5 the factor is 1.30, 1.35, 1.40, 1.50. If the layers have different nu (0.35 stiff, 0.49 soft, n=10, m=1) the factor is 1.56 relative to the beam value. The ceiling 3/2 therefore becomes (1+nu)*3/2 for a wide cylindrically-curved plate (2.25 at nu=0.5), not a violation but a different regime.
findings.value: kappa_cyl/kappa_beam = 1+nu (equal nu); sphere/beam = 1; unequal nu example 1.56

findings.claim: INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF (1+nu) 1: Pezzulla et al. minimise a plate energy for a sheet with dome-like natural curvature in the large-stretch (isometric) limit and obtain L+N = kappa_o(1+nu) with Gaussian curvature K=0, where kappa_o is the curvature of the beam cut from the sheet; for nu=1/2 the mean curvature is 3/4 kappa_o. A cylinder (N=0) therefore has L=(1+nu)kappa_o. Experiments (PVS bilayer disks) and neo-Hookean finite-element runs on several shapes collapse onto the three-fourths law.
findings.evidence_quote: The minimization gives L + N = κo(1 + ν) and K = 0, a solution solely in terms of the principal invariants of the curvature tensor

findings.claim: INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF (1+nu) 2: Alben's discrete bilayer model (equal layers of thickness h, equal moduli, lattice Poisson ratio nu=1/3) gives an analytic cylindrical state eps_x = eps_a/2, eps_y = 0, kappa = eps_a/h, and his mesh simulation reports curvature 8.5-10.5 against 10. Minimising his printed energy eq.(7) with sympy gives kappa = 4 Cs eps_a h/(8Cb+3Cs h^2), which equals eps_a/h for his constants (Cs h^2 = 8 Cb). Timoshenko's beam value for equal layers is 0.75 eps_a/h, and (1+nu)*0.75 = (4/3)*0.75 = 1.0, so his cylinder equals (1+nu) times the beam value exactly. In the thin-membrane limit (Cb->0) the same formula gives (4/3) eps_a/h.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1110.1007 (S. Alben, Bending of bilayers with general initial shapes; NOT the Nano Letters paper) ; D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-bilayer-theory-verified/alben_eq7_check.py
findings.evidence_quote: For the parameters in this simulation, ϵx = 0.05; ϵy = 0; κ = 10.

findings.claim: WHEN IS A PRINTED STRIP 'NARROW'? Three independent criteria all scale as sqrt(h/kappa) and agree within a factor of about 2 on the plate diameter D above which the strip value fails: (i) Timoshenko p.242 sag kappa D^2/8 < h/2 gives D < 2.0 sqrt(h/kappa); (ii) Freund-Floro-Chason's linearity limit S = K = kappa R^2/(4 h_s) < 0.3 gives D < 2.19 sqrt(h/kappa); (iii) Pezzulla's sphere-to-cylinder bifurcation for a disk gives R_c = 2.112 sqrt(h/kappa), D_c = 4.22 sqrt(h/kappa) (sag 2.2 h at bifurcation). Holmes' review states the same scaling kappa_n ~ h/l^2. At the optimum kappa=1.5 eps/h, so sqrt(h/kappa)=h/sqrt(1.5 eps): 2.3-29 mm over the table (h 0.4-1.6 mm, eps 0.2-2 %), confirming the earlier agent's range; Pezzulla critical disk diameters are 9.8-123 mm over the same grid.

findings.claim: PRIOR GAP CLOSED, WITH A CAVEAT: spec-bilayer-physics could not retrieve the numerical prefactor of the sphere-to-cylinder transition. Pezzulla eq.(6) gives it for convex disks: kappa_ob (curvature scaled by 1/h) = sqrt((20+14*sqrt2)/27) * gamma^2 = 1.2141 gamma^2, gamma = h/S, shape factor S = ((2/9) * integral r^4 dA / A)^(1/4); for a disk S = (2/27)^(1/4) R = 0.5217 R. I read the equation from the PDF text layer (symbols partly garbled) and recomputed the constants; I could not compare against the figure. For a long strip the shape factor is dominated by the LENGTH (L^4/360 for L>>w), so eq.(6) is a sphere-vs-cylinder criterion for a convex sheet, not a strip-width criterion. findings.claim: STONEY 1909, as printed. A steel rule (102 mm long, 12 mm wide, 0.32 mm thick) is coated with nickel of thickness t on one side. Taking moments gives neutral axis at b = (2/3)d, then P t = (1/6) E d^2 / r, and with r = l^2/(8z): P = (4/3) E d^2 z /(t l^2) (eq.1), for a very thin film. A correction for finite film thickness (assuming film and rule have the same modulus) gives P = (4/3) E (d^2 + t d) z /(t l^2) (eq.2). E is the plain Young's modulus (no Poisson ratio); the formula is a one-way strip result. Own check: sympy reproduces eq.(1) from P t = E d^2/(6r).
findings.value: P = E d^2/(6 r t) (thin film, strip); 1/r = 6 P t/(E d^2)
findings.evidence_quote: This equation is only true when the film of nickel is very thin;

findings.claim: STONEY'S STATED LIMITS. Film 'very thin'; thickness of the rule neglected against r in the first derivation; the thick-film correction assumes the film has the same modulus as the substrate; no Poisson ratio, no plane strain, no nonlinear range. The modern equibiaxial form sigma_f = E_s h_s^2 kappa/(6(1-nu_s) h_f) is a later restatement for plates (quoted in Injeti et al.), not Stoney's printed equation.
findings.value: thin film, uniaxial E; modern form uses 1/(1-nu)
findings.evidence_quote: neglecting the thickness of the rule, which is small in comparison with r

findings.claim: TIMOSHENKO REDUCES TO STONEY FOR A THIN FILM. Taking a1 -> 0 in kappa = eps f/(a1+a2): kappa -> 6 eps (E1/E2)(a1/a2)/a2, which is Stoney's 1/r = 6 P t/(E d^2) with P = E_film*eps (sympy limit = 6). So Stoney's equation is the thin-film limit of the project's f; the project's f is exact in thickness ratio within beam theory, so Stoney's 'film must be thin' limit does not apply to it.
findings.value: lim f/(6 m n) = 1 as m->0

findings.claim: FREUND-FLORO-CHASON (1999) eq.(6), the plate generalisation of Stoney for arbitrary thickness and modulus ratio, is Timoshenko's f: kappa = (6 eps_m/h_s) h m [ (1+h) / (1 + h m (4+6h+4h^2) + h^4 m^2) ], h = h_f/h_s, m = M_f/M_s with biaxial modulus M = E/(1-nu). Substituting h = a1/a2, m = E1/E2 gives Timoshenko's kappa with residual exactly 0 (sympy). The difference between the two is therefore only (a) M instead of E and (b) circular plate versus narrow strip.
findings.value: FFC eq.(6) = Timoshenko eq.(4) with E -> E/(1-nu)

findings.claim: FFC STATED ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS (the Stoney formula's six assumptions): (i) thicknesses small against lateral size; (ii) film much thinner than substrate; (iii) homogeneous, isotropic, linear-elastic substrate and isotropic film; (iv) edge effects inconsequential, quantities uniform in the plane; (v) no through-thickness stress; (vi) infinitesimal strains and rotations. They relax (ii) and (vi). Stoney with equal moduli at h_f/h_s = 0.1 is 'in error by 30 percent' (printed); my evaluation of their eq.(6) gives kappa/kappa_Stoney = 0.7513 = 1/(1+h)^3, i.e. Stoney overestimates by 33.1 percent. Nonlinear (rotation-stretching) effects set in for normalised mismatch strain S = (3/2) eps R^2 h_f M_f/(h_s^3 M_s) above roughly 0.3; the nonlinear law is S = K[1+(1-nu_s)K^2], K = R^2 kappa/(4 h_s). For R/h_s=100, h_f/h_s=0.01, equal moduli, S=0.3 corresponds to eps_m about 0.002.

findings.claim: FREUND 2000 (J. Mech. Phys. Solids 48, 1159) ITSELF WAS NOT READ: paywalled, no open copy found; Crossref confirms the DOI and Elsevier licence only. What I report about 'Freund on bilayer plates' comes from the 1999 companion paper by the same author (open preprint) and from search-result summaries of the 2000 abstract (nonlinear range, S about 0.3, bifurcation from axisymmetric to asymmetric). Treat the 2000 paper's content as second-hand.

REYSSAT & MAHADEVAN 2009: eq.(2.5) is delta-kappa = alpha delta-phi f(m,n)/h and eq.(2.6) is f(m,n) = 6(1+m)^2/[3(1+m)^2+(1+mn)(m^2+1/(mn))] exactly as Timoshenko, with m = h_p/h_a, n = E_p/E_a, total h = h_p+h_a, linear hygrometric expansion coefficients assumed independent of humidity. I read the equation images (rsif20090184e5.jpg, e6.jpg), which closes the earlier agent's gap that the printed equations were images not captured. They say f(m,n)=0 as n -> 0 or infinity, and that for m=1 f varies by under 10 percent for n in 0.3-3.5 (my numbers: f(1,0.3)=1.361, f(1,3.5)=1.349, 9.3 and 10.0 percent below f(1,1) and the ceiling respectively: agreement within rounding) and under 20 percent for n 0.3-5 (computed 16.7 percent).
findings.evidence_quote: we adapt the theory of bimetallic thermostats to hygrometry sensors (Timoshenko 1925), as the actuation mechanism of pine cone scales relies on the same principle, with humidity replacing temperature.

findings.claim: PINE CONE CHECK. R&M take m about 1, n about 5 (moduli from Dawson et al. 1997) and state f(m,n) is about 1.3; the printed formula gives f(1,5) = 1.25 (4 percent lower than the rounded 1.3). Their text says the strain of the active cells along the axis is alpha = 0.001 per percent relative humidity, with no significant radial strain (an extreme natural case of anisotropic swelling).
findings.evidence_quote: the thickness ratio m = hp/ha ≃ 1, while the length of the active zone La ≃ 10ha

findings.claim: DIFFUSION-LIMITED ACTUATION TIME, original statement. R&M: imbibition time scale tau ~ h^2/D; for molecular pores D ~ 1e-9 m^2/s, active-layer thickness 1 mm gives tau ~ 1000 s; with a bottleneck of size l_b, tau ~ h_a l_b/D. Their measured pine-scale fits are sub-quadratic: drying tau = 96 h_a^1.5 min, wetting tau = 29 h_a^1.3 min (h_a in mm), which they attribute to strong strains (up to 20 percent) coupled to transport and a bottleneck. So h^2/D is a scaling, not a law, even in the source.
findings.value: tau~h^2/D; D~1e-9 m^2/s -> ~1000 s at 1 mm; exponents 1.3-1.5 measured
findings.evidence_quote: For molecular pores, D ∼ 10−9 m2 s−1, the thickness of the active layer ha ∼ 1 mm and τ = ha2/D ∼ 1000 s

findings.claim: MEASURED D FOR DENSE PRINTABLE POLYMERS (re-checked). Aniskevich et al. Table 3 (1.75-2.8 mm filament cylinders, up to 97 percent RH): D = 0.001 (Nylon), 0.00245 (Antero), 0.00247 (CPE), 0.00335 (PET-G), 0.00399 (Ultem), 0.00472 (PC), 0.00782 (PLA LAVA), 0.0151 (PLA T-W) mm^2/h, with time to reach 80 percent of equilibrium moisture 360 h (Nylon), 92 h (PC), 27 h (PLA T-W) and up to 550 h (Koltron). This confirms the earlier agent's range 0.001-0.0151 mm^2/h. Several grades have concentration-dependent D, so these are order-of-magnitude inputs, and none is a Formlabs material.

CURVATURE RESPONSE TIME (own calculation, linear bilayer with a diffusing eigenstrain). Active layer (thickness a) exposed on its free face only, bonded face sealed, eigenstrain proportional to local concentration. Curvature reaches 63 percent at D t/a^2 = 0.198, 90 percent at 0.724, 99 percent at 1.67, never overshoots; mass uptake reaches 90 percent at 0.861; the slowest mode is 4/pi^2 = 0.405. At the optimum m^2 n = 1 the normalised curve is identical for n=1 and n=10 (interface = neutral axis); for n=3, m=1 it is faster (t90 = 0.542). In real units with measured D (0.0151-0.001 mm^2/h): a = 0.2 mm -> t90 = 1.9-29 h; a = 0.4 mm -> 7.7-116 h; a = 0.8 mm -> 31-463 h. This agrees with the earlier agent's h^2/D table (0.4 mm: 10.6-160 h) after the factor 0.72.
findings.confidence: medium (model assumes sealed bond face, Fickian constant D)

findings.claim: KINETICS AND STIFFNESS ARE COUPLED AT THE OPTIMUM (own consequence of m = n^-1/2). If the swelling layer is the STIFF one (n = E_active/E_passive > 1) the optimum makes it the thin one (n=10: active = 24 percent of total thickness, 0.19 mm of 0.8 mm), which is also the fast layer. If the swelling layer is the SOFT one (n < 1, hydrogel or elastomer) the optimum makes it the thick one (n = 0.1: active = 76 percent of total), and the t ~ a^2/D penalty grows. This matters for the Flexible 80A (active, soft) against rigid (passive) pairing considered by the earlier agents.

ASSUMPTION AUDIT 1, NARROW VS WIDE (sizes). A printed strip is 'narrow' only if its width is below roughly 2-4 sqrt(h/kappa) (previous finding). Wider, three things change: it stays spherical (curvature = beam value, Timoshenko p.242) while the sag is below about h/2; then it bifurcates to a cylinder along the long side whose curvature is (1+nu) times the beam value, 30-50 percent more for nu 0.3-0.5 (own derivation, Pezzulla, Alben), and up to 1.56 for dissimilar Poisson ratios (0.35 vs 0.49 example). A cylinder also means the strip cannot curve across its width (relevant to a doubly curved architectural panel).

ASSUMPTION AUDIT 2, END ZONES AND THE JOINT. Timoshenko says the shear (and, for different moduli, normal) stresses at the ends of the strip cannot be found elementarily, are 'local' within a distance of the order of the thickness, and 'may be of the same order' as the normal stresses, so the bond between two materials matters. Size for a 40 mm strip at h = 0.8 mm: 2 x 0.8/40 = 4 percent of the length is end zone (own arithmetic). Two separately printed layers bonded with adhesive add a third layer that Timoshenko's two-layer theory does not contain; I did not quantify it.
findings.value: end zone ~ h each end; ~4 % of a 40 mm strip at h=0.8 mm
findings.source: https://archive.org/download/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3/sim_optical-society-of-america-journal_1925-09_11_3.pdf (PDF pages 41-50 = journal pp.233-242; doi 10.1364/JOSA.11.000233) (journal p.238, PDF page 46)
findings.evidence_quote: they are of “local” type and are concentrated near the ends of the strip along a distance, the magnitude of which is of the same order as the thickness h of the strip.

findings.claim: ASSUMPTION AUDIT 3, ANISOTROPY OF PRINTED PARTS (what is published). Formlabs' Nylon 12 powder datasheet gives one tensile modulus (1850 MPa) but elongation at break 11 percent in X/Y and 6 percent in Z; its Nylon 11 CF powder gives tensile modulus 5.3 / 2.8 / 1.6 GPa for X / Y / Z (3.3x between X and Z). For SLA the only source found is Formlabs' own blog test (Form 2, Clear Resin, ASTM D638 Type IV bars at 15-degree build angles), which says strength and Young's modulus stay 'roughly constant' with build angle: SLA parts are 'isotropic for all intents and purposes', but one printer, one resin, vendor-authored. No source gives anisotropy of HYGROSCOPIC SWELLING in a printed part. In beam theory only the modulus and swelling strain along the strip axis enter, so for a strip whose axis lies in the build plane the Z properties do not matter; off-axis raster or fibre orientation adds bend-twist coupling (the Lean file's axial/shear strain relations) that I did not size because the in-plane shear modulus is unknown.
findings.value: Nylon 11 CF E = 5.3/2.8/1.6 GPa (X/Y/Z); Nylon 12 elongation 11/6 %
findings.evidence_quote: Tensile Modulus | 5.3 GPa | 2.8 GPa | 1.6 GPa

findings.claim: SIZE OF AN ANISOTROPY OR WET-STIFFNESS ERROR IN THE MODULUS RATIO (own calculation). Because f is flat at its optimum, misjudging n costs little: design for m = n0^-1/2 and the true n is 2x or 0.5x n0 -> f is 2.2-3.0 percent below 3/2 (n0 = 10 ... 1); 3.3x or 0.3x -> 6.8-9.3 percent. Moisture softening of only the active layer to 65 percent of dry modulus (the earlier record's Grey V5 figure, not rechecked) costs 0.9-1.2 percent; to 50 percent, 2.2-3.0 percent; to 30 percent, 6.9-9.3 percent. Formlabs' Flexible 80A V2 datasheet shows -26 Shore A points after one day in deionized water, so softening is real for that resin. So the modulus ratio is a second-order uncertainty provided the thickness ratio was chosen at the optimum.

WET, SOFT, LARGE-STRAIN (not sized). The Timoshenko/Stoney/FFC algebra is linear and small-strain. The hydrogel-type printable resins in the earlier record swell 3.5-74 percent linearly (Maennel 2020, from spec-resin-chemistry; not re-fetched here), far outside it. Pezzulla et al. had to use incompressible neo-Hookean finite elasticity with large distortions (stretch lambda up to about 1.15 in their Fig.2b) and a 1-D finite-strain beam model for kappa_o(lambda,m,n); I could not read the plotted values and did not build a finite-strain bilayer, so the size of the correction is unknown. Creep and hysteresis of printed polymers under humidity cycling were also not sized. Expect the largest departures from f for exactly the large-swelling, soft materials the project wants.
findings.evidence_quote: using a Neo-Hookean incompressible material model [21] implemented in the commercial software COMSOL Multiphysics

findings.claim: ARMON ET AL. 2011 (Science 333, 1726): ONLY THE ABSTRACT COULD BE READ. Full text is behind a 403 and not in Europe PMC or arXiv. Abstract (Europe PMC): Bauhinia seed pod valves turn from flat to helical; strips cut from tissue and from composite elastic materials show helical configurations with sharp transitions; modelled by 'incompatible elasticity' as a thin strip with a flat intrinsic metric and saddle-like intrinsic curvature. I therefore cannot print the equation, its stated assumptions (thin, small strain, isotropy) or the dimensionless width parameter from the original. From a secondary source: Pezzulla et al. cite Armon for approximate expressions of the natural metric and curvature of a pre-stretched bilayer. Armon et al. 2014 (Soft Matter, abstract only) add 'dimensionless parameters' and 'quantitative predictions for the twisted-to-helical transition'. The earlier agent's w*sqrt(kappa0/t) and its limits (from a search summary) remain unverified by me.
findings.confidence: high (that I could not read it)
findings.evidence_quote: we modeled the pod as a thin strip with a flat intrinsic metric and a saddle-like intrinsic curvature.

findings.claim: ALBEN, BALAKRISNAN & SMELA 2011 (Nano Lett. 11, 2280): ONLY THE ABSTRACT COULD BE READ (not open). Claim: for thin rectangular bilayers with one isotropically strained layer, bending prefers the long edge because doubly curved regions at the curled edges lower the energy; the energy difference between 'spiral' and 'cigar' shapes grows with aspect ratio. It is consistent with Pezzulla's 'longest length' rule and with Alben's separate arXiv paper (not the Nano Letters paper), but I did not see the paper's equations or assumptions.
findings.confidence: high (that I could not read it)
findings.evidence_quote: We find that the bending direction is determined by the existence of doubly curved regions at the curled edges, which lower the energy.

findings.claim: DESIGN CONSEQUENCE OF THE BIFURCATION FOR STEERING: a wide isotropic bilayer always rolls along its long side (Pezzulla: bending along the longest length when several symmetry planes exist; Alben 2011 abstract: long edge), so a printed panel that must curl across its short side needs anisotropic swelling or stiffness (print path or fibre orientation) or slits, not just a different aspect ratio. This restates the earlier agent's point (e) with two primary-text confirmations.
findings.value: isotropic wide sheet bends along its longest length
findings.evidence_quote: If multiple planes of reflection symmetry exist for a particular shape, bending will occur along the longest length of the disk

findings.claim: DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN FORMLABS DOCUMENTS (relevant to 'stock resins gain under 1 percent in water'). Formlabs' Flexible 80A Resin V2 datasheet (ASTM D471 slabs, wiped dry) lists deionized water, 1 day: -26 Shore A, +8 percent mass, +3 percent volume; 1 week: +9 percent mass, +7 percent volume. Formlabs' solvent-compatibility page (1 cm cube, 24 h, parsed by the earlier agent from saved HTML, which I re-read) lists a row 'Flexible 80A Resin' (no V2; separate rows exist for Elastic 50A V1 and V2) with water 0.7 percent. spec-resin-chemistry ('under 1 percent for every current resin') and spec-formlabs-materials (+8 percent) are each faithful to one Formlabs source. Sibling reports of this programme (bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json, bm-formlabs-all-resins.json; not independently verified by me) read the 0.7 percent row as the OLDER formulation (its IPA value 11.7 percent matches the V1 sheet), and bm-diffusion-kinetics.json argues the two cannot be the same resin because D >= 6.3e-12 m^2/s would give about 3.8 percent in a 1 cm cube at 24 h. I therefore agree that the project-record sentence is true for the cube table but wrong for Flexible 80A V2, with the residual doubt that no V2 cube value was measured. If that sibling inversion is right (D about 9.3e-12 m^2/s = 0.0335 mm^2/h for an ASSUMED 2 mm slab), my t90 = 0.724 a^2/D gives 0.86 h (a = 0.2 mm), 3.5 h (0.4 mm), 13.8 h (0.8 mm): hours, not days, for that one resin.

findings.claim: NO WATER DIFFUSIVITY FOR ANY FORMLABS OR OTHER VAT-PHOTOPOLYMER RESIN WAS FOUND, again. A second search (Europe PMC, web) found only saturation uptakes and a paper that cites ISO 62's option to fit D without reporting values; the epoxy-SLA literature calls uptake non-Fickian. The earlier gap stands, so every real-unit time above uses the FDM filament D as a bracket, not a measurement of the project's material.

CONFIRMED FROM THE EARLIER FILES (spec-bilayer-physics.json): f(1,10)=0.9959 and a 34 percent loss (mine 33.6); f(1,5)=1.25; optimum m=n^-1/2 and ceiling 3/2; 0.4 mm dense-polymer times 10.6-160 h as h^2/D; filament D range; 2.3-29 mm width scale. key_claims.claim: The project's f(m,n) is Timoshenko's printed eq.(4) (also R&M eq.2.6, and Freund-Floro-Chason eq.(6) with E -> E/(1-nu)); it is a narrow-strip, linear, perfectly-bonded, plane-section result with no Poisson ratio, and Timoshenko 1925 does NOT state the ceiling 3/2 or optimum m^2 n = 1 (those are the project's derivation, here re-proved: 3/2 - f = 3(m^2n-1)^2/(2(m^4n^2+4m^3n+6m^2n+4mn+1))).
key_claims.evidence_quote: the following general equation for the curvature of a bi-metal strip will be obtained,  [eq.(4) on journal p.235, transcribed from page image]

key_claims.claim: Plane stress versus plane strain: for a wide plate Timoshenko himself substitutes the biaxial modulus E/(1-nu) and f is unchanged (sphere, valid while sag < h/2). Beyond the sphere-to-cylinder bifurcation (diameter above about 4.2 sqrt(h/kappa) for a disk) the curvature becomes (1+nu) times the strip value (+30 to +50 percent), confirmed by my sympy derivation, Pezzulla et al. (L+N = kappa_o(1+nu)) and Alben's model. So E/(1-nu^2) matters only in that cylindrical regime, and the strip result is safe for strips narrower than about 2 sqrt(h/kappa).

key_claims.claim: Diffusion-limited actuation: tau ~ h^2/D in the original (R&M), with measured sub-quadratic fits (exponents 1.3-1.5). With the only measured D for printable dense polymers (0.001-0.0151 mm^2/h, FDM filaments, none Formlabs), my model gives a 90 percent curvature response at 0.72 a^2/D: 1.9-29 h at a = 0.2 mm, 7.7-116 h at 0.4 mm, 31-463 h at 0.8 mm. No D for any Formlabs resin exists in the sources found.

key_claims.claim: Armon 2011, Alben-Balakrisnan-Smela 2011 and Freund 2000 (JMPS) could not be read in the original (only abstracts, or a companion paper); statements about their equations, assumptions and critical values are second-hand and labelled so.

recommendations: Keep f(m,n) and the 3/2 ceiling, but state its regime next to every curvature prediction: narrow strip (width below about 2 sqrt(h/kappa), i.e. 2-29 mm for the planned table), linear and small strain, perfectly bonded. Quote Timoshenko 1925 eq.(4) as the source of f, not of the optimum.

Cite the optimum m^2 n = 1 and the 3/2 ceiling as the project's own result (Lean plus the factorised identity 3/2 - f = 3(m^2n-1)^2/(2(...)) in this report), because Timoshenko's paper does not contain them; if a reviewer asks for a printed source, none was found.

For wide architectural panels, predict the curvature with the plate model, not the strip: sphere (strip value) while the sag is below about h/2, then a cylinder along the long side at (1+nu) times the strip value (+30 to +50 percent). To curl across the short side, add anisotropy (print path, fibre or rib orientation) or slits.

Because kinetics scale as a^2/D and the optimum makes a soft active layer the thick one (m = n^-1/2), prefer a STIFF active layer or a thin soft one with a fast-water route; do not pair a thick soft swelling layer with a rigid passive layer if hour-scale actuation is wanted.

Close the two biggest measurement gaps with one bench step each before designing around them: (a) weigh a Flexible 80A V2 cube and a 0.4 mm strip in water over 1, 6, 24, 168 h and fit D and the saturation (resolves the 0.7 versus 8 percent conflict and supplies the missing D); (b) measure the free swelling strain of each layer separately with a ruler or calipers (the real bottleneck for testing the 20 percent claim).

For the Lean track (read-only here, so a suggestion): add (i) the neutral-axis identity E1 a1^2 = E2 a2^2 <=> m^2 n = 1, (ii) the closed form 3/2 - f = 3(m^2n-1)^2/(2(...)), (iii) the invariance of f under E -> E/(1-nu) for equal nu and under m,n -> 1/m,1/n, and (iv) the (1+nu) cylinder theorem; all four were proved symbolically here.
Retrieve Armon 2011, Alben-Balakrisnan-Smela 2011 and Freund 2000 through a library or the authors' pages before any partner document cites their equations or critical widths.

fleet.label: bm-bioinspired-generative-design
fleet.topic: Generative and agentic design tools that could sit in the pipeline (Bioinspired123D, SciAgents, other open tools) and where a verified-law filter (Timoshenko ceiling, hollow-tube, Murray) could remove candidates before printing
fleet.summary: Bioinspired123D (Luu and Buehler, 2026; Apache-2.0 code, weights on Hugging Face) turns a text prompt into a Blender Python script. It has 12 base scripts in three families (helical, cellular, tubular), a 3B-parameter finetuned model (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct base) and an image-only vision-model critic. It outputs Blender geometry; the authors exported STL by hand and printed in ABS, PLA and PETG on FDM machines. The repo has no STL exporter, no units, no moduli, no layer or bilayer concept, and no manufacturability check (the paper says minimum feature size, overhang and build volume 'are not explicitly enforced'). Its validation is a script-generation benchmark (base 0%, base+retrieval 18%, finetuned 54%, finetuned+retrieval 60%), not a physical measurement. SciAgents (Ghafarollahi and Buehler 2024; Apache-2.0) is different: it takes keywords, walks a knowledge graph with an AutoGen/AG2 agent team and outputs a text research hypothesis (README example: 8,100 words). It emits no geometry. Other open tools: Marom/Buehler CategoryTheoryDesign (Apache-2.0; Grasshopper plus Python, Timoshenko bilayer to G-code, 4 FFF specimens measured, no resin or SLA profile); Silkworm (Grasshopper to G-code, no licence declared, last push 2015); two ETH-lineage truss inverse-design codes (MIT; output nodes and connectivity); svVascularize (Murray exponent 3.0 as a built-in growth parameter, tube solids); LLMto3D and C33D (LLM to Rhino/Grasshopper code or STEP). None of the tools surveyed applies a proven law as a hard pre-print filter. The nearest thing is the 'verify' step of CategoryTheoryDesign, which checks two evaluations of the same Timoshenko formula against each other within a tolerance (epsilon 0.05), not against a ceiling. The data-flow recommended here puts a 'law gate' between candidate generation and STL export: candidates.json goes to the project's existing lean/eliminate/eliminate.mjs, which already writes a three-state ledger (eliminated, consistent, cannot-rule) and Lean certificates. What exists: the ceiling theorem (HygromorphCeilingCheck.lean), HollowTube.lean and MurrayCubic.lean, and the eliminate.mjs machinery. What must be written: constraint entries and rules_out wrappers for these three laws (grep finds no bilayer, hollow-tube or Murray constraint in lean/constraints.json), an extractor from generator output to candidates.json, a physical-units and materials layer (none of the generators has one), a mesh/printer check, and a Formlabs path (PreForm takes STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP, not G-code). I wrote and ran a Python prototype of the gate on 9 synthetic candidates: it eliminates 4, leaves 3 consistent (not ruled out, not shown feasible) and returns 2 'cannot rule'; it is not Lean-checked and its candidates are not measurements. I confirmed the ceiling numerically (max f = 1.5 over a 121x121 log grid, exact 3/2 at m^2 n = 1) and the earlier '34 percent' loss for equal layers at n = 10 (33.6 percent). A critical gap for the filter: no hygroscopic strain d_eps exists for any Formlabs resin (earlier record), so the Timoshenko gate can only be applied in normalised form (kappa*h/d_eps <= 1.5) until coupons give d_eps.
fleet.lay_summary: Some new AI tools can turn a sentence like 'a spiral plywood-like structure' into a 3D shape that can be printed. We looked at the main ones and found that none of them knows any physics: they check that the shape looks right, not that it obeys a law of mechanics. Another tool reads the scientific literature and proposes research ideas as text, so it cannot make a shape at all. We propose a simple checkpoint between the AI and the printer, like a bouncer at a door: before anything is printed, a short program asks whether each design breaks a proven rule, for example 'no two-layer strip can bend more than a fixed amount'. Designs that break a rule are thrown out for free, saving resin and printing time. Most of the pieces for the bouncer already exist in the project; what is missing is the plumbing that carries the AI's shapes to it and the real material numbers it needs.

findings.claim: The project already has an elimination engine: eliminate.mjs reads candidates.json and writes a ledger with three states and Lean certificates. Present at delphisci/lean/eliminate/eliminate.mjs (61,252 bytes, sha256 146cd55e...). The earlier laws-biomaterial.json said the generator was 'not in this repository'; it is present in this delphisci tree (that statement may have referred to the leanbio upstream).
findings.evidence_quote: Checks candidates against the formalised constraints and writes a ledger with three states per (candidate, constraint): eliminated, consistent, cannot-rule.

findings.claim: lean/constraints.json has no constraint for Timoshenko, bilayer, hygromorph, Murray or hollow-tube (grep -i returned nothing); its quantities are cube-law, flight, physiology and genotype quantities. So the three laws cannot yet be called through eliminate.mjs.

The ceiling theorem sits in tracks/lean/HygromorphCeilingCheck.lean as a copy that carries the two definitions and is meant to be pasted into lean/ThompsonLaws/Hygromorphs.lean; the earlier law inventory lists 'Rules-out wrappers for the theorems that already exist' as missing.
findings.evidence_quote: theorem timoshenkoCoefficient_le (h m n : ℝ) (hh : 0 < h) (hm : 0 < m) (hn : 0 < n) : timoshenkoCoefficient h m n ≤ 3 / (2 * h)

findings.claim: Own check of the project's ceiling: over a 121x121 log grid (m, n from 1e-3 to 1e3) the maximum of h*coefficient is exactly 1.5, reached at m^2 n = 1; exact Fraction arithmetic at m=1/k, n=k^2 for k=1,2,3,5,10 gives 3/2. Equal layers at n=10 give 0.99585, a loss of 33.6 percent against 1.5. This confirms the earlier record's '34 percent'.

Prototype gate result (Python, not Lean-checked, synthetic candidates): 9 candidates give 4 eliminated, 3 consistent, 2 cannot-rule; one of the consistent ones is a junction, because 1^3 = 1 vs 2*0.8^3 = 1.024 (2.4 percent off, inside the 10 percent tolerance). A normalised curvature of 1.53, from the earlier beech retro-calculation, comes out 'cannot rule' because it exceeds 1.5 by 2 percent, below the 10 percent input tolerance.
findings.source: Own run of law_filter_prototype.py (exit 0); beech 1.53 value from D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/scout-biomaterial.json
findings.value: tolerance 0.10; ceiling check uses exact rationals

findings.claim: Hollow-tube law inputs for a gate: mass at fixed bending stiffness is rho*sqrt(4 pi I)*mu(k) with mu(k) = (1 - k^2 + q k^2)/sqrt(1 - k^4); interior optimum k* = sqrt(1-q), mu(k*) = sqrt(q(2-q)); with wall floor t/R >= lambda the optimum is min(sqrt(1-q), 1-lambda). Form 4 supported-wall floor 0.2 mm (project record).
findings.evidence_quote: An interior critical point exists iff 0 < q < 1; it is k* = sqrt(1 - q), the unique global minimiser, with mu(k*) = sqrt(q(2 - q)).

findings.claim: Gap that blocks an absolute Timoshenko gate: no hygroscopic expansion coefficient or diffusivity for any Formlabs resin exists in the record, so kappa <= 1.5*d_eps/h cannot be evaluated in absolute units; only the normalised kappa*h/d_eps <= 1.5 can, once d_eps is measured on coupons. I found nothing in this survey to contradict that earlier finding.

key_claims.claim: None of the surveyed generators (Bioinspired123D, SciAgents, CategoryTheoryDesign, Silkworm, truss codes) applies a proven law as a hard pre-print filter; Bioinspired123D explicitly does not enforce printer limits and its critic is image-based.
key_claims.evidence_quote: printer-specific constraints such as minimum feature size, overhang limits, and build-volume restrictions are not explicitly enforced during generation.

key_claims.claim: Bioinspired123D outputs Blender scripts and has a dimensionless, material-free parameter space (12 base scripts); STL was exported by hand and printed on FDM machines, so a layer assigning units, materials and layer structure must be written before any bilayer or tube law can act on it.
key_claims.evidence_quote: selected designs generated by Bioinspired3D and Bioinspired123D were exported from Blender as STL files and fabricated via 3D printing.

key_claims.claim: The project already owns the elimination machinery (eliminate.mjs, three-state ledger, Lean certificates) and the three law statements, but lean/constraints.json has no entry for any of them, so the missing piece is constraint entries and rules_out wrappers plus an extractor, not a new engine.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Checks candidates against the formalised constraints and writes a ledger with three states per (candidate, constraint): eliminated, consistent, cannot-rule.

key_claims.claim: Formlabs printers are fed STL/OBJ/3MF/STEP through PreForm, so Grasshopper/Silkworm G-code pipelines (the Mamou-Mani route) do not reach a Form 4 or Fuse 1+ without a new export module; CategoryTheoryDesign's README says a new process needs its own S_*.py and machine_*.py and no SLA profile exists.

fleet.dataflow: NOTE: this schema has no dedicated field, so the data-flow is in recommendations[0..] and below. Named files; E = exists, W = must be written. (1) brief.md [W, one page: stimulus, layer materials, printer Form 4 or Fuse 1+, wall floor 0.2 mm]. (2) SciAgents or a human writes hypothesis.md [E]; Bioinspired123D writes cand_NNN.py + render_NNN.png [E]; CategoryTheoryDesign Grasshopper writes bilayer parameters [E, FFF only]. (3) extract_params.py [W]: runs each cand_NNN.py in headless Blender, reads parameters and the mesh, applies materials.json [W: Formlabs moduli, wall floor, d_eps once measured; moduli exist in spec-formlabs-materials.json, d_eps does not] and writes candidates.json in the eliminate.mjs schema {candidates:[{id, problem, description, source, accepts[], commits{}}]}. (4) lean/constraints.json + lean/Delphi/Constraints.lean [W: entries and *_rules_out wrappers for timoshenko ceiling, hollow tube, Murray junction, each with 'accepts' assumption flags]. (5) node lean/eliminate/eliminate.mjs candidates.json --out ledger.json --lean Certificates/EliminationsBiomaterial.lean [E]: writes ledger.json (eliminated/consistent/cannot-rule) and EliminationsBiomaterial.lean certificates. (6) survivors.json = candidates whose verdict is not 'eliminated' [W, 10 lines]. (7) export_stl.py [W]: Blender export of survivors to cand_NNN.stl, plus mesh_check.py [W: watertight, wall >= 0.2 mm, overhang 5 mm, per Form 4 design spec]. (8) PreForm [E, external] opens STL/OBJ/3MF; Form 4 prints one resin per job so a bilayer is two prints bonded (project record). (9) coupons.csv [W]: measured curvature vs time and humidity feed back as d_eps and as the test of the ceiling.
recommendations: Insert the law gate between candidate generation and STL export, as in the data-flow above: cand_NNN.py -> extract_params.py -> candidates.json -> lean/eliminate/eliminate.mjs -> ledger.json -> survivors.json -> export_stl.py -> PreForm. Reuse eliminate.mjs rather than writing a second engine; the prototype law_filter_prototype.py is a throwaway to show the three-state logic.

Write, in this order: (a) paste HygromorphCeiling into lean/ThompsonLaws/Hygromorphs.lean and add bilayer_curvature_rules_out; (b) hollow_tube and murray_junction rules_out wrappers; (c) three constraint entries in lean/constraints.json with explicit assumption flags (Euler-Bernoulli strip, linear elastic, perfect bond, uniform eigenstrain; laminar volume-cost for Murray; fixed bending stiffness for the tube) so candidates that do not commit to them read 'cannot rule', never 'passes'. All of this is outside the read-only scope of this task and is a proposal only.

Do not rely on Bioinspired123D as the bilayer generator: it has no layers, units or materials. Use it, if at all, for the tubular and cellular families, where a hollow-tube or wall-floor gate can act once Blender units are mapped to millimetres; ask the authors or inspect the 12 base scripts for the unit convention (not determined here).

For the Mamou-Mani Grasshopper route, add a Formlabs output module to CategoryTheoryDesign (new S_sla.py replacing the bilayer expression, new machine module that writes two STL/3MF parts instead of G-code), after checking its Apache-2.0 NOTICE obligations. Do not build on Silkworm: no licence and last updated 2015.

Run the gate in normalised form (kappa*h/d_eps <= 1.5 with a 10 percent d_eps tolerance, as in the prototype) until coupon measurements give d_eps for the chosen resin pair; otherwise the Timoshenko check cannot be evaluated in absolute units.

Expect the gate to be weak early: a candidate with unknown d_eps, or one that does not state its assumptions, lands in 'cannot rule'. Log the fraction of cannot-rule outcomes; if it stays above half, the gate is not yet saving prints.

glossary.plain: Free 3D modelling software that can be driven by Python scripts.
A visual-programming add-on for the Rhino 3D program that architects use to make parametric shapes.
A simple 3D file format that stores a surface as triangles; most printers accept it.
Line-by-line movement instructions for a filament or pellet printer; Formlabs printers do not use it.
Formlabs' free program that prepares a 3D file for their printers.
A large language model, an AI that writes text or code.
A setup where several AI programs take turns, check and repair each other's work.
A map of concepts joined by labelled links, built here from scientific papers.
The standard formula for how far a strip of two glued layers bends when one layer swells more than the other.
The proven maximum bend: curvature can never exceed 1.5 times the swelling difference divided by total thickness.
How little material a tube needs for a given stiffness when part of its middle is empty.
A rule that the cube of a parent channel's radius equals the sum of the cubes of its two daughters' radii.
The small program that checks a computer-written mathematical proof step by step.
A small machine-checked proof that one specific design breaks a specific law.
The three answers of the filter: provably impossible; not ruled out; or not enough information to say.
How stiff a material is.
The difference in swelling between the two layers of a strip.
Printing by squeezing melted plastic filament through a nozzle.
Printing by shining light into a vat of liquid resin to harden it layer by layer.
Printing by melting plastic powder with a laser.
Giving the AI a few relevant example documents to read before it answers.
A cheap way to retrain a small slice of a large AI model.
A 3D surface with no holes, so a slicer can tell inside from outside.
