fleet.label: bm-biopolymer-films
fleet.topic: Chitin, silk fibroin, cellulose nanocrystals and other biopolymer actuators: hygromorphic films, measured strain and curvature, and combination with a printed backing
fleet.summary: Survey of humidity-driven films from silk, chitosan, cellulose nanocrystals, gelatin and similar. The largest in-plane humidity strain in a cast, stiff, bulk-scale biopolymer film is regenerated silk fibroin at 5.0 to 7.3 percent (10 to 90 percent RH), against roughly 0.2 to 1 percent for stock Formlabs resins (about 1.0 percent linear for Flexible 80A V2 by my conversion of its data-sheet 3 percent volume gain). An 8 um silk layer on 25 um polyimide changes curvature by 13 to 21 cm^-1 and bends in 13 to 44 s, but silk has only been bonded to polyimide, not to printed resin or nylon. Bacterial peptidoglycan swells 27 to 50 percent in thickness with GPa modulus and a glue composite survived 180,000 cycles in about 3 s, but those strains are through-thickness AFM values on nanometre films. Cellulose films swell little (NFC 0.06 to 0.09 percent; CNC 0.04 percent per percent moisture, 0.30 across aligned CNC) and bend only when very thin; chitosan composites bend (3.91 cm^-1; more than 140 degrees in 3 s for a carboxymethyl chitosan/MXene film) without a published strain; for gelatin I could not read any numbers. Two earlier claims: I confirm the Formlabs cube table (Rigid 10K under 0.1 percent water and IPA, Elastic 50A V2 39.2 percent IPA) and I confirm, by reading the data-sheet table by coordinates, that Flexible 80A Resin V2 gains 8 percent mass and 3 percent volume in 1 day in water, which contradicts a blanket reading of 'every SLA resin under 1 percent'. A consistency check against the project's 3/2 curvature ceiling: no measured silk curvature exceeds it, and the sulfonated-silk value would be 92 percent of it if its free strain were about 5 percent.
fleet.lay_summary: Some natural materials swell when the air gets humid, and a thin strip with a swelling layer glued to a non-swelling layer curls like a drying leaf. The plastics Formlabs sells swell by only about a fifth of a percent to one percent, so they curl very little. Silk protein cast as a thin film swells by 5 to 7 percent while staying a hard solid, and an 8-micrometre silk coat on a plastic strip (thinner than a hair) curled to a radius under a millimetre in under a minute. Cellulose and chitosan films swell less or have been measured less well, and for gelatin I could not read the numbers. The catch is speed: the thicker the swelling layer, the slower it moves, so silk works as a thin coating on a printed backing and nobody has yet tested that backing with a Formlabs part. The first step would be a cheap bench test, a silk coating on a printed strip, before anything is shown to an architect.

findings.claim: Cast regenerated Bombyx mori silk fibroin films (methanol-treated, freestanding, RH swung 10% to 90%) shrink and swell in length by 5.0 to 7.3 percent. This is the largest in-plane humidity strain I found in a stiff, cast, bulk-scale biopolymer film, and it is 5 to 36 times the 0.2 to 1 percent estimated for stock Formlabs resins.
findings.value: WR strain 5.02 +/-1.05 % (0% PEO), 5.02 +/-0.51 (10%), 5.74 +/-1.01 (20%), 5.93 +/-0.93 (40%), 7.29 +/-0.83 % (60% PEO porogen), 10-90 %RH, linear, n=5; Æ in the quote is the PDF-text-extraction form of +/-

findings.claim: How silk strain was defined: change in film length between 10 percent and 90 percent RH divided by original length, from image analysis over three RH cycles, on 3 mm x 10 mm freestanding films.
findings.evidence_quote: The WR strain is defined as a ratio of deformation (the change in length in response to 10% and 90% RH) to the film’s original length, determined by ImageJ software

findings.claim: Silk/polyimide bilayers (silk cast on a 25 um polyimide film) bend in 13 to 44 s and straighten in 22 to 40 s when RH is alternated between 10 and 90 percent. This is the response time for an 8 um silk layer.
findings.evidence_quote: all silk/polyimide bilayer films took similar time to bend within 13–44 seconds and straighten within 22–40 seconds in response to rapid RH changes

findings.claim: Silk-on-polyimide bilayer with 8 um regenerated silk on 25 um polyimide: the change in curvature between dry and hydrated state is 13 cm^-1 for unmodified silk and 21 cm^-1 after sulfonating its tyrosine residues, i.e. radii of curvature of 0.77 mm and 0.48 mm. For comparison, beech/spruce wood bilayers in the project record reach 0.0087 mm^-1 = 0.087 cm^-1, so these silk bilayers curve 150 to 240 times more tightly (at 33 um instead of about 5 mm total thickness).
findings.value: delta kappa 13 -> 21 cm^-1; h_silk 8 um; h_PI 25 um; 10-90 %RH in 10 min steps
findings.evidence_quote: This difference increased from 13 cm-1 to 21 cm-1 (Figure 1c,d), and raised WR energy density from 1.6 MJ m-3 to 3.5 MJ m-3

findings.claim: Thickness of the silk bilayer in the tyrosine paper: 8 um silk layer on 25 um polyimide (the text prints 3x4x0.025 mm), humid-chamber dried (>90% RH) overnight.
findings.evidence_quote: depositing an 8 µm thick layer of RSF onto 3x4x0.025 mm polyimide films (CAPLINQ)

findings.claim: Silk water-responsive actuation energy density (work per volume, from bilayer curvature) is 1.6 MJ/m3 for methanol-treated silk, 3.0 to 3.1 MJ/m3 for nanoporous silk and 3.5 MJ/m3 for tyrosine-sulfonated silk; mammalian skeletal muscle is quoted at 8 kJ/m3 in one paper and 0.8 kJ/m3 in the other (the two papers disagree by 10x).
findings.source: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10422709 (Soft Matter 2023, doi 10.1039/d2sm01601j) ; https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10616826 (Soft Matter 2025, doi 10.1039/d5sm00040h; accepted manuscript)
findings.evidence_quote: there is a range of porosities that result in silk’s optimal water-responsive energy density at 3.1 MJ m

findings.claim: Silk processing for a cast hygromorph layer: degum cocoons by boiling in 0.02 M sodium carbonate 30 min, dissolve in 9.3 M lithium bromide at 60 C for 2 h, dialyse, cast, dry overnight in a humid chamber (about 90% RH), then immerse in 99.9% methanol for 10 min to lock in beta-sheets; optional PEO porogen is leached in water for one day. Plasma-treated polyimide was the backing.
findings.value: Na2CO3 0.02 M 30 min; LiBr 9.3 M 60 C 2 h; methanol 99.9% 10 min; PEO leach 1 day; plasma 30 s
findings.evidence_quote: Both freestanding and bilayer films were immersed in a 99.9% methanol solution (Sigma-Aldrich) for 10 min.

findings.claim: Tyrosine paper uses a two-step methanol stabilisation (99.9% then 90%, 10 min each) and a diazonium coupling in aqueous silk solution, then dialysis; this is a wet-chemistry route that needs a lab.
findings.evidence_quote: The dry films were immersed in 99.9% methanol (Sigma-Aldrich) for 10 min, followed by immersion in 90% methanol for 10 min, to stabilize the β-sheet structure

findings.claim: Bacillus subtilis peptidoglycan (PG, a sugar-peptide cell-wall polymer) swells in thickness by 50.1 percent (cortex PG) and 27.2 percent (cell-wall PG) when RH rises from 5 to 90 percent, as measured by environmental AFM on nanometre-thick layers. This is the largest humidity strain I found in a stiff polymer, but it is a through-thickness AFM value on 70 to 150 nm layers, not an in-plane value on a bulk film.
findings.value: cortex PG height +50.1 %, volume +65.2 %; cell wall PG height +27.2 %, volume +45.8 %; 5->90 %RH; layer thickness 70.6 nm and 153 nm at 5 %RH
findings.evidence_quote: cortex PG shows a height change of 50.1% and a volume change of 65.2%

findings.claim: Peptidoglycan is stiff: Young's modulus 4.91 GPa at 5 percent RH falling to 1.77 GPa at 90 percent RH (factor 2.8 softening).
findings.evidence_quote: Young's moduli are 4.91 GPa at 5% RH and 1.77 GPa at 90% RH

findings.claim: Peptidoglycan mixed with a commercial craft glue gives a castable composite (1.33 GPa dry, 0.47 GPa at 90% RH) that bends coated Mylar, silicone and PDMS films within about 3 s and survived 180,000 bend/straighten cycles with a reported degradation of 5.17e-5 percent per cycle.
findings.value: E=1.33->0.47 GPa; relaxation tau 2.34 s bend / 2.12 s straighten on Mylar; 180,000 cycles
findings.evidence_quote: the PG/adhesive‐coated Mylar film can respond to RH changes within ≈3 s (Figure 5f ), and bend and straighten over 180, 000 cycles without significant performance degradation

findings.claim: Peptidoglycan headline performance: 72.6 MJ/m3 energy density, 9.1 MW/m3 power density, up to 27.2 percent deformation within 110 ms, actuation pressure about 354.6 MPa. Inside the paper the cortex PG measurement is 59.9 MJ/m3 and the 27.2 percent belongs to cell-wall PG, so the abstract mixes two samples.
findings.evidence_quote: PG can deform as much as 27.2% within 110 ms, and its actuation pressure reaches ≈354.6 MPa.

findings.claim: Bacillus spore monolayers on microcantilevers and elastomer sheets give hygromorph actuators with energy density above 10 MJ/m3 (two orders above synthetic water-responsive materials); mutants roughly doubled it.
findings.evidence_quote: the mechanical response of Bacillus spores to water gradients exhibits an energy density of more than 10 MJ m(-3), which is two orders of magnitude higher than synthetic water-responsive materials

findings.claim: Spider dragline silk fibres can shrink up to 50 percent in length with about two-fold radial swelling at high RH or when wetted (background statement in a Science Advances paper, not measured in this survey); the same paper measures humidity-driven twist up to 255 deg/mm (N. pilipes) between 40 and 100 percent RH. Fibres, not films, so not directly printable.
findings.value: up to 50 % length; twist 255 deg/mm (N. pilipes), 127 deg/mm (A. versicolor)
findings.evidence_quote: dragline silk can shrink up to 50% in length concomitantly with radial swelling (about twofold increase of the diameter)

findings.claim: Nanofibrillated cellulose (NFC) films 8 um thick bend with a steady-state curvature of 0.3 to 0.75 cm^-1 when a 10 to 40 percent RH difference is imposed across the thickness, reaching steady state in tens of seconds. The paper's own estimate of the swelling that explains this is only 0.06 percent (8 um) and 0.09 percent (48 um): cellulose films bend because they are thin, not because they swell a lot.
findings.evidence_quote: the swelling ratio of the 8-µm NFC film is estimated to be only about 0.06%; whereas for the 48-µm film, the swelling ratio is about 0.09%

findings.claim: NFC curvature falls steeply with thickness: about 0.2 cm^-1 at 38 um, minimal at 48 um, and paper of 60 um bends little. This is a gradient-driven (RH differs on the two faces) bend, not a bonded bilayer.
findings.evidence_quote: a thickness of ≈38 µm showed only moderately small bending of about 0.2 cm−1, and the one with thickness of ≈48 µm exhibited only a minimal curvature

findings.claim: Cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) film hygroscopic swelling coefficient: 0.040 percent strain per percent moisture content for self-organised (isotropic) films, and for shear-oriented films 0.02 (parallel) and 0.30 (perpendicular to alignment). Measured by digital image correlation from 0 to 97 percent RH. The wood bilayer coefficient in the project record (beech 3.2e-3 per percent moisture content = 0.32 percent per percent) is about equal to the perpendicular CNC value.
findings.evidence_quote: Self-organized CNC films showed isotropic swelling, CHS ∼0.040 %strain/%C. By contrast, shear-oriented CNC films exhibited an anisotropic swelling, resulting in CHS ∼0.02 and ∼0.30 %strain/%C, parallel and perpendicular to CNC alignment, respectively.

findings.claim: Converting CNC film coefficients to a strain needs the moisture-content change, which I did not retrieve. Illustration only, with an ASSUMED 10 wt percent change: isotropic CNC 0.4 percent, shear-oriented perpendicular 3 percent. The assumed value is unverified background, not a finding.

CNC on polyurethane bilayer (70 um CNC layer with glucose additive on 70 um polyurethane/silver nanoparticle elastomer): horizontal bending angle rises from 0 to 70.5 deg in 60 s of moisture absorption, and in the vertical orientation 0 to 144.2 deg in 14 s; recovery 71 to 80 s; 5000 bend cycles without loss.
findings.value: 70.5 deg / 60 s (horizontal); 144.2 deg / 14 s (vertical); revert 80 s / 71 s; 5000 cycles; layers 0.07 +/-0.01 mm each
findings.evidence_quote: the horizontal bending angle of the actuator increases from 0° to 70.5° as the moisture absorption time increases from 0 to 60 s, and then it takes 80 s to revert to its original position

findings.claim: The CNC/PU film has a coffee-ring cracking problem: pristine CNC layers crack within hundreds of bend cycles; adding glucose gives crack-free films after 5000 cycles. Humidity step magnitude (RH values) is not stated in the main text I read; actuation force 299.4 Pa at a bending angle of 76.5 deg.
findings.evidence_quote: after subjected to 5000 bending cycles, the actuator still exhibited stable actuating performance, revealing excellent structural stability

findings.claim: Chitosan (82.7 percent deacetylated, from crab-shell chitin) / 50 wt percent multiwalled carbon nanotube cast films, 20 to 40 um thick, bend away from a moist source and back towards a dry one; 100 cycles with no obvious fatigue; 25 x 4 x 0.04 mm strips. No curvature or strain value is given in the main text I read.
findings.evidence_quote: (film length = 25 mm, width = 4 mm, and thickness = 40 μm) in response to moist and dry stimuli by adsorption and desorption of water molecules

findings.claim: Chitosan films on a carbon nanotube/PDMS layer give a humidity-driven curvature of 3.91 cm^-1 (3.84 cm^-1 with near-infrared light); the PDMS supplies the mechanical support. Thickness, RH step and cycle count are not in the abstract and I could not read the full text.
findings.evidence_quote: for an ultra-large actuation curvature (3.91 cm-1 in humidity actuation, 3.84 cm-1 in light actuation)

findings.claim: Carboxymethyl chitosan (a chitosan derivative) / MXene composite film with a thickness gradient bends beyond 140 degrees within 3 s under a 40 percent RH difference across the film, with over 1000 self-oscillation cycles; tensile strength 39.9 MPa. The MXene is an inorganic conductive filler, so this is not a pure biopolymer film.
findings.value: >140 deg in 3 s; dRH 40 %; >1000 cycles; tensile 39.9 +/-0.9 MPa
findings.evidence_quote: with a bending angle exceeding 140° within 3 s

findings.claim: Gelatin: the only gelatin-specific hygromorph paper located is Kumar, Siraj and Satapathy, Materials Advances 2024, 'Vapor selective and controlled actuation of gelatin-based soft actuators'. The publisher blocked every automated fetch, so I could read only the title and a one-line abstract and obtained no curvature, strain, thickness, response time or cycle numbers. A search-engine summary mentioned about 7 mN lifting force under water vapour and 25x own weight under ethanol vapour; I could not verify that from the page.
findings.evidence_quote: Soft actuators with multi-vapour responsiveness demonstrating distinct movement.

findings.claim: Chitin: no humidity-actuated film made directly from chitin or chitin nanofibres was found (Europe PMC title search for chitin AND actuator/humidity/moisture returned 3 unrelated records). Chitosan, its deacetylated form, is the only chitin-derived polymer with humidity actuators located.

Formlabs cube test (1 cm cube, 24 h) confirms the earlier agents: water uptake of Rigid 10K is under 0.1 percent, Flexible 80A Resin 0.7, Elastic 50A V2 0.7, Clear Resin V5 0.9, and isopropyl alcohol uptake of Elastic 50A V2 is 39.2 percent versus under 0.1 for Rigid 10K. Acetic acid 5 percent (chitosan's solvent is 1 percent acetic acid): Rigid 10K under 0.1, Elastic 50A V2 1.5, Flexible 80A 0.9. Methanol is not in the Formlabs table.

findings.claim: CONTRADICTION with a blanket reading of the earlier resin-chemistry file ('every current SLA resin gains under 1 percent mass in water at 24 h'): that holds for the 1 cm cube table (which has a row for Flexible 80A Resin, not V2), but Formlabs' own Flexible 80A Resin V2 data sheet (ASTM D471 slabs) gives +8 percent mass and +3 percent volume after 1 day in deionised water and +9 percent mass, +7 percent volume after 1 week, with 26 Shore A points softening. I confirm this figure of the spec-formlabs-materials file by reading the table cells by coordinates. The two Formlabs tests use different specimens, so 0.7 and 8 are not the same quantity.
findings.value: Flexible 80A V2, DI water: 1 day +8 % mass +3 % volume -26 Shore A; 1 week +9 % mass +7 % volume -27 Shore A
findings.evidence_quote: Flexible 80A Resin V2 TDS ASTM D471, label Deionized Water spans these two rows (y=396 and y=405): 1 day -26 +8% +3% 94% 89% ; 1 week -27 +9% +7% 101% 88%

findings.claim: Own calculation: the best stock soft resin (Flexible 80A V2, 3 percent volume gain in 1 day) corresponds to about 1.0 percent linear swelling if isotropic ((1.03)^(1/3)-1), 2.3 percent after 1 week. Silk's 5.0 to 7.3 percent in-plane strain is 5 to 7 times that, and 25 to 36 times the 0.2 percent estimated for the Clear/Rigid pair.

Own calculation with the project-record Timoshenko ceiling kappa_max = 1.5 d_eps / h: for a 1 mm bilayer, 1 percent differential strain gives at best 15 m^-1 (radius 67 mm), silk's 5.02 percent gives 75 m^-1 (radius 13 mm), 7.29 percent gives 109 m^-1 (radius 9 mm). For 0.3 mm total thickness: 50, 251 and 365 m^-1.

Own check of the 3/2 ceiling against measured silk curvature: for the 33 um silk/polyimide bilayer, 13 cm^-1 requires a differential strain of at least 13e2 x 33e-6 / 1.5 = 2.9 percent and 21 cm^-1 requires at least 4.6 percent. Using the free-film strain of unmodified silk (5.02 percent, different films and batch) the ceiling is 22.8 cm^-1, so the unmodified bilayer reaches 57 percent of it. The 21 cm^-1 sulfonated-silk value would be 92 percent of the ceiling if that silk strained about 5 percent; its free-film strain was not reported, so this is a consistency check, not a test. No measured curvature exceeds the ceiling.

Own scaling estimate (diffusion-limited, tau proportional to h^a with a = 1.3 to 2): the 13 to 44 s bend time of an 8 um silk layer becomes 6 to 114 min for a 100 um silk layer and 2 to 190 h for a 1 mm layer. Silk is therefore a thin-coating technology; a thick silk layer would be as slow as the printed resins.

key_claims.claim: Cast silk fibroin films strain 5.0 to 7.3 percent in length between 10 and 90 percent RH, far above the 0.2 to 1 percent of stock resins (and above the roughly 1 percent linear equivalent of the best soft resin, Flexible 80A V2).

A silk-on-backing bilayer works with a thin silk layer: 8 um silk on 25 um polyimide gives a 13 to 21 cm^-1 curvature change and bends in 13 to 44 s. The only backing tested is polyimide; no printed resin or nylon backing has been tested.
key_claims.evidence_quote: This difference increased from 13 cm-1 to 21 cm-1 (Figure 1c,d), and raised WR energy density from 1.6 MJ m-3 to 3.5 MJ m-3

key_claims.claim: Cellulose by itself is not a large-strain material: nanofibril film swelling is about 0.06 to 0.09 percent and the CNC isotropic coefficient 0.040 percent per percent moisture; only shear-aligned CNC across the alignment (0.30) approaches wood-like values.
key_claims.evidence_quote: the swelling ratio of the 8-µm NFC film is estimated to be only about 0.06%; whereas for the 48-µm film, the swelling ratio is about 0.09%

key_claims.claim: The statement that stock Formlabs resins gain under 1 percent in water holds for the 1 cm cube table but not for Flexible 80A Resin V2 on its own data sheet (ASTM D471: +8 percent mass, +3 percent volume in 1 day).

recommendations: Run one bench coupon before any design work: cast regenerated silk fibroin (target 10 to 50 um) on a post-cured Rigid 10K strip 0.2 to 0.4 mm thick (IPA-wipe, optionally plasma), methanol-stabilise, and measure curvature at 30, 60, 90 percent RH. Compare with the 3/2 ceiling: for a 0.3 mm total thickness and 5 percent strain it is about 250 m^-1 (radius 4 mm).

Keep the active layer thin. Time grows roughly as thickness to the power 1.3 to 2, so 8 um bends in under a minute but a 1 mm silk layer would take hours to days (own scaling estimate). Design the printed part as the stiff, thin backing, not as the swelling layer.

Do not put Elastic 50A or Silicone 40A through the methanol step: Elastic 50A takes up 39 percent IPA and Silicone 40A 5.9 percent, against under 0.1 percent for Rigid 10K (Formlabs table), and methanol is untested. Rigid 10K is the safest backing; chitosan (cast from 1 percent acetic acid) is gentler, since 5 percent acetic acid costs Rigid 10K under 0.1 percent.

Measure, do not borrow, the silk modulus and free strain on your own films, and check whether the 21 cm^-1 sulfonated silk is near the 1.5 d_eps / h ceiling; this gives a second, independent test of the Lean-checked bound on a real biopolymer.

Treat cellulose as a stiffening or anisotropy tool, not as the motor: NFC and isotropic CNC swell 0.04 to 0.09 percent; only aligned CNC across the alignment (0.30 percent per percent moisture) approaches wood.
Obtain the gelatin paper (Kumar 2024) through a library or by contacting the authors before claiming anything about gelatin.

glossary.plain: A material or shape that changes shape when the air gets more or less humid.
Two layers stuck together, one that swells and one that does not, so the pair bends.
The structural protein of silkworm silk, which can be dissolved and cast into films.
A plastic-like sugar polymer made from the shells of crabs and shrimp (from chitin).
Tiny rod-shaped crystals of plant cellulose that can be dried into a film.
The sugar-and-protein mesh that forms the wall of bacteria.
How tightly something bends: one divided by its radius of bend.
How full of water vapour the air is, from 0 to 100 percent.
How much a length grows, as a percentage of the original length.
How much work a material can do per cubic metre when it swells.
A liquid plastic that a laser or light hardens layer by layer.
Plastic powder melted into shape by a laser, such as nylon.
A proven upper limit: a two-layer strip cannot curve more than 1.5 times the strain difference divided by its thickness.
A short alcohol bath that makes silk film stop dissolving in water.
Cleaning a solution by letting small salts pass out through a membrane.

fleet.label: bm-buehler-materials-corpus
fleet.topic: What Buehler's materials papers say about design rules
fleet.summary: I clustered the 493 track-5 papers of the Buehler corpus (my keyword rules give 12 clusters; the largest are silk and filaments 118, collagen and bone 74, printed or machine-learning-designed hierarchical composites 70, and hierarchy, flaw-tolerance and size-effect work 69) and read abstracts or full texts for 15 of them, including 12 deep-dive papers: open-access full texts for the silk torsion, tendon, silica hierarchy, spider web, silk/HAP/chitin and plant-AI papers, and the two MIT PhD theses that contain the printed composite work. Result 1: the corpus is a source of design logic, not of resin or moisture numbers. None of 795 abstracts mentions vat-photopolymer, powder-bed or Formlabs printing (abstract-level; only 319 of 493 track-5 works have abstracts), 16 mention humidity-type stimuli, and no paper gives a hygroscopic expansion coefficient or diffusivity for a printed polymer. This confirms the earlier agents' gaps and does not fill them. Result 2: the printed composites traced to a printer (Dimas and Gu theses; Mirzaeifar 2015 says only multimaterial printing) came from Objet Connex single-print two-material jetting (VeroWhitePlus/VeroMagenta against TangoBlackPlus, moduli 2187 and 0.53 MPa, ratio 4126 by my arithmetic; nominal ratio about 1500 and effective 45-60 after interface mixing per Dimas), which Form 4 and Fuse 1+ cannot do. Result 3: four ideas transfer: stiffness ratio and soft/stiff topology as governing variables; a computational filter followed by a few printed tests (printed ML design about 25x tougher than the stiff material, 100,000 candidates screened); a formal reduction before printing with a test beyond the model (Brommer 2015); and humidity as a gated, hysteretic stimulus (silk threshold 68-70 % RH, five-cycle sweeps) with a coating that freezes a face (paraffin wax). Not transferable: molecular and nanometre rules (including the exponential defect-tolerance law, simulated at 27 x 70 micrometres), crystal misorientation, protein-sequence mechanisms, and the fabrication routes (jetting, PDMS ink writing at 160 C, nanofibril casting, mycelium growth). Deepening: with Buehler-style contrast (n = 1700-4100) the project's Timoshenko coefficient at equal thickness is only 0.4-0.9 % of the 3/2 ceiling and the optimum thickness ratio is 41-64, so the stiffness ratio that helps fracture hurts curvature. Cross-check of earlier agents: Flexible 80A V2 gains 8 % mass in 1 day in water by its own ASTM D471 data sheet, so "under 1 %" holds for the Formlabs solvent table (which lists only the older Flexible 80A at 0.7 %) but not for that resin; the 39.2 % IPA uptake of Elastic 50A V2 against under 0.1 % for Rigid 10K is confirmed on the re-fetched page.
fleet.lay_summary: Markus Buehler's group has written hundreds of papers on how bone, silk and shell get strong from their structure, and we searched them for rules that could guide a printed material that bends when the air turns damp. Almost none of the papers are about humidity, and none used the resin or powder printers that Formlabs sells; their printed samples came from a different machine that can spray a hard and a soft plastic in the same print. What carries over is the method: let a computer throw out bad designs, print only a few, test them, and write the rule you want to keep as a precise statement. One of our own calculations adds a warning: if the hard and soft plastics differ by a thousand times in stiffness, a two-layer strip of equal thickness curls about a hundred times less than the best possible, like a thermostat strip made of two metals that are far too unequal. So the demonstration should pick its two materials, and their thicknesses, together.

findings.claim: Spider dragline silk twists by more than 300 deg/mm when humidity rises past a threshold of about 70 % RH, independent of spider species (Liu et al. 2019, Buehler co-author). Natural protein fibre, not a printable resin.
findings.evidence_quote: We demonstrate that spider dragline silk exhibits a humidity-induced torsional deformation of more than 300°/mm. When the relative humidity reaches a threshold of about 70%, the dragline silk starts to generate a large twist

findings.claim: Measured thresholds for the three species: N. pilipes 68 %, A. versicolor and N. edulis around 70 %; the RH was cycled 40 -> 100 -> 40 % five times. Below threshold the fibre stays still, so the response is a gate, not a smooth ramp.
findings.evidence_quote: The threshold of RH for torsional actuation of the N. pilipes silk was 68%, as observed in the experiments

findings.claim: The twist is only partly reversible: when RH falls below threshold the N. pilipes silk keeps its twist, the other two species reverse it only slightly or noticeably. This is a hysteresis a bilayer law cannot represent.
findings.value: N. pilipes: twist maintained on drying
findings.evidence_quote: the twist deformation of the N. pilipes dragline silk was maintained, whereas the A. versicolor and N. edulis dragline silks reversed the twist slightly or rather noticeably

findings.claim: Tested fibres were micrometre-scale: N. pilipes 121 mm long and 3.1 +/- 0.1 um diameter; A. versicolor 87.9 mm long and 6.7 +/- 0.1 um. The result therefore says nothing about millimetre-thick printed sections, where diffusion time scales with thickness squared.
findings.evidence_quote: Torsional actuation of N. pilipes spider dragline silk (121 mm in length, 3.1 ± 0.1 μm in diameter)

findings.claim: Dragline silk is described as shrinking up to 50 % in length while its diameter roughly doubles at high humidity (supercontraction); the sign of axial strain is opposite to ordinary swelling.
findings.evidence_quote: dragline silk can shrink up to 50% in length concomitantly with radial swelling (about twofold increase of the diameter)

findings.claim: Molecular simulation attributes the twist to proline in the MaSp2 protein; this is a sequence-level mechanism with no direct analogue in an acrylate resin.
findings.evidence_quote: molecular simulations of MaSp1 and MaSp2 proteins in dragline silk reveal that the unique torsional property originates from the presence of proline in MaSp2

findings.claim: Giesa et al. 2017: dragline silk shrinks by up to 50 % along its axis in high humidity, and in-silico point mutations of polar or charged residues suppress or even reverse that supercontraction while keeping the mechanical properties. Simulation plus in situ mechanical and Raman tests; abstract only read.
findings.evidence_quote: they shrink along the main axis by up to 50% when exposed to high humidity, a phenomenon called supercontraction

findings.claim: Removing water from tendon collagen shortens the molecule and generates tensile stress from several MPa to almost 100 MPa, against about 0.3 MPa for contractile muscle (Masic et al. 2015, Buehler co-author). A measured upper bound on water-driven actuation stress in a natural polymer.
findings.evidence_quote: shortening of the molecule that translates into tensile stresses in the range of several to almost 100 MPa, largely surpassing those of about 0.3 MPa generated by contractile muscles

findings.claim: The paper converts relative humidity to osmotic pressure with the relation Pi = R T / v_m ln(RH) (v_m the molar volume of water), so the humidity stimulus can be expressed as a pressure on the polymer.
findings.evidence_quote: To allow the quantitative control of the osmotic pressure acting on the collagen fibre, we studied it in a chamber with controlled relative humidity (RH) that was then converted to osmotic pressure

findings.claim: Clamped tendon fibres built up 106 +/- 16 pN per molecule at 5 % RH. This is collagen, not a synthetic polymer.
findings.evidence_quote: Hindering the strain by clamping the fibre is, however, accompanied by a remarkable stress generation that reaches 106±16 pN per molecule at 5% RH

findings.claim: Ling et al. 2018: a designed-in-silico, self-assembled silk-nanofibril / hydroxyapatite / chitin-nanofibril nacre-like film reached 281 +/- 14 MPa strength and 22 +/- 2 MJ/m3 toughness at the 4:16 SNF/HAP:CNF ratio, 2-3x natural nacre strength.
findings.evidence_quote: the strength and toughness of 4:16 SNF/HAP:CNF nanocomposites reached 281±14 MPa and 22±2 MJ m −3

findings.claim: The same films were programmed into water-driven grab-and-release actuators because of their gradient structure and the water sensitivity of each component. This is the closest Buehler paper to a designed hygromorph bilayer; I could not read an actuation angle, curvature, RH or time from the main text, so no actuator number is reported.
findings.evidence_quote: these SNF/HAP:CNF nanocomposites can be programmed into "grab-and-release" actuators due to the gradient structure of the nanocomposites as well as the high water sensitivity of each of the components

findings.claim: Films were cast to about 10 um thickness at about 25 C and 50 % RH: a nanometre-fibril, water-cast process with no route onto a Form 4 or Fuse 1+.
findings.evidence_quote: allowed to dry at ~25°C and 50% relative humidity to give membranes of an approximate thickness of 10 μm

findings.claim: Sen and Buehler 2011 (atomistic-to-mesoscale simulation of silica): over up to four hierarchy levels the defect tolerance rises exponentially to about a hundred micrometres with no added material or mechanism; the base silica is brittle and sensitive to nanometre defects.
findings.evidence_quote: Over a range of up to four hierarchy levels, we find an exponential increase in the defect-tolerance approaching hundred micrometers without introducing additional mechanisms or materials.

findings.claim: The trade-off is stated: the biocalcite-like layout (soft nanoporous silica inclusions) gains defect tolerance at the cost of lower fracture strength than the bone-like layout. The soft phase here is a nanoporous form of the same silica, i.e. contrast made by porosity, not by a second chemistry.
findings.evidence_quote: the biocalcite-like structure shows a higher defect-tolerance at the cost of a lower fracture strength

findings.claim: Simulated geometry is micrometre scale (platelets 8.4 x 2.4 um by 100 nm; structure 27 x 70 um), and nothing was fabricated. The exponential law is a simulation result at a length scale 100-1000x below Form 4 or Fuse resolution.
findings.evidence_quote: The overall size of the structure considered here is 27 μm by 70 μm and 100 nm out-of-plane.

findings.claim: Dimas, Bratzel, Eylon, Buehler 2013: composites emulating bone, sponge and nacre topologies were printed in multi-material 3D printing at micrometre resolution from brittle base materials, and the soft/stiff topology alone raised fracture performance; model and test agree. Printed and tested.
findings.evidence_quote: The reported findings confirm that specific topological arrangements of soft and stiff phases as a design mechanism enhances the mechanical behavior in composites.

findings.claim: Dimas and Buehler 2014: the stiffness ratio of the two constituents is named as an important feature determining composite properties; DIC strain fields of printed composites were compared with simulation and plotted on Ashby diagrams.

findings.evidence_quote: We elucidate the role of stiffness ratio variations of composite constituents as an important feature in determining the composite properties.

findings.claim: Thesis chapter of the same work (simulation): one composite designed at minimal cost has a toughness modulus eight times that of its constituents while keeping over 80 % of the Young modulus of the stiffest phase.

OWN CALCULATION (calc.py): the Timoshenko coefficient f(m,n) is invariant under (m,n) -> (1/m,1/n) (max difference 2e-16 over a test grid) and a 400 x 301 log-grid search finds maximum f = 1.5000000000000002, so the 3/2 ceiling in the project record is reproduced numerically.

OWN CALCULATION: with the Buehler-style stiff/soft contrast an equal-thickness bilayer is nearly useless. f(1,n) = 0.0058 for n = 4126 (VeroMagenta/TangoBlackPlus, Gu thesis moduli), 0.0138 and 0.0126 for n = 1724 and 1897 (Rigid 10K / Flexible 80A V2 with the project's 5.8 MPa secant estimate), i.e. 0.4 % to 0.9 % of the 1.5 ceiling; at n = 50 (Dimas effective ratio) it is 0.375 (25 %), at n = 10 it is 0.996 (66 %, matching the earlier "34 % loss").

OWN CALCULATION: reaching the ceiling at such contrast needs m = n^(-1/2), a thickness ratio of 64 (n = 4126), 41.5-43.5 (n = 1724-1897), 7.1 (n = 50) or 3.2 (n = 10). With a 0.2 mm thin layer (Form 4 minimum wall in the project record) the thick layer would be 12.9, 8.3-8.7, 1.41 or 0.63 mm. The modulus ratio drops out of the curvature at the optimum, but it sets how thick the part must be. Timoshenko assumes small linear strain; the earlier agents note it over-predicts soft printed bilayers, so these are upper bounds.

OWN CALCULATION: osmotic pressure Pi = -(R T / v_m) ln(RH) at 25 C with v_m = 18.0 cm3/mol (water molar volume; unverified background constant): 166 MPa at 30 % RH, 95 MPa at 50 %, 49 MPa at 70 %, 14.5 MPa at 90 %, 7.1 MPa at 95 %, 1.4 MPa at 99 %, 0.41 MPa at 99.7 %. The thermodynamic driving pressure at room humidity is far above the roughly 0.3 to 100 MPa stresses Masic reports, so the limit on a printed layer is its sorption isotherm and stiffness, not the pressure.
findings.value: 49 MPa at 70 % RH; 0.4 MPa at 99.7 % RH

key_claims.claim: The Buehler corpus does not close the project's evidence gap: no abstract among the 795 fetched works mentions vat-photopolymer, powder-bed or Formlabs printing, only 16 mention humidity-type stimuli, and none reports a hygroscopic expansion coefficient or diffusivity for a printed polymer (abstract-level; 319 of 493 track-5 works have abstracts). Every printed-composite result I could trace to a printer (Dimas and Gu theses) used single-print multi-material jetting (Objet Connex), which Form 4 and Fuse 1+ do not offer; Mirzaeifar 2015 says only "advanced multimaterial 3D printing".
key_claims.source: own counts (corpus_stats.py) over buehler-corpus.json and buehler.json; https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/79497 (L. Dimas MIT thesis 2013)
key_claims.evidence_quote: All specimens used in the study are printed at Objet Inc., in Billerica, MA, USA using an Objet Connex500TM multi-material 3D printer.

key_claims.claim: What transfers is design logic: stiffness ratio and soft/stiff topology as governing variables, a computational filter followed by printed tests (printed ML-chosen design about 25x tougher than the stiff material), a formal reduction before printing (Brommer), and humidity as a gated, hysteretic stimulus tested by RH sweeps and cycles. Molecular, crystallographic and nanometre-scale rules do not transfer.
key_claims.evidence_quote: the ML-designed hierarchical composite is approximately 25 times tougher than the stiff material and approximately 40 times tougher than the soft material.

key_claims.claim: Buehler-style hard/soft contrast is incompatible with an equal-thickness hygromorph bilayer: with moduli 2187 and 0.53 MPa (ratio 4126) the Timoshenko coefficient at equal thickness is 0.0058, 0.4 % of the 3/2 ceiling, and the optimum thickness ratio is 64; for the Rigid 10K / Flexible 80A V2 pair (ratio about 1700-1900, project estimate) it is 41-44. This is my arithmetic on the project's Lean-checked formula, not a Buehler result.

recommendations: Treat the Buehler corpus as a source of design logic and test protocol, not of numbers: it contains no resin-moisture data, no hygroscopic expansion coefficient, no diffusivity, and (abstract-level) no vat or powder-bed printing. The coupon measurements the earlier agents asked for are still needed.

Use the corpus precedent to frame the proof of concept: Dimas, Gu and Brommer each close the loop model -> print -> test, and Brommer adds a test beyond the model. Our novelty is the machine-checked bound as the first filter, which no paper in this corpus has (abstract-level).

Choose the bilayer stiffness ratio on purpose. At n of about 1700-4100 (Buehler-style hard/soft jetting contrast) the optimum thickness ratio is 41-64 and an equal-thickness strip loses over 99 % of the curvature ceiling; prefer a soft/soft pair or measure wet moduli first, then fix m = n^(-1/2) within the 0.2 mm minimum wall.

Copy the Liu 2019 test protocol: sweep RH in steps, look for a threshold, cycle at least five times and record hysteresis; add a one-face wax or sealant coating coupon (Luu 2025) to confirm the passive layer.

Test the porosity-as-soft-phase idea (my inference from Sen & Buehler: soft nanoporous inclusions in the same silica) on a single material: SLS PA12 or SLA rigid coupons with lattice-density gradients, compared against the Timoshenko-type prediction. Not reported by any Buehler paper on Formlabs hardware.

Obtain the full text of Ling 2018 supplementary information and the Dimas 2014 / Gu 2018 papers through the library before any number from them is used in a claim; this report relied on abstracts plus the two MIT theses for those.

glossary.plain: A material or part that changes shape when the air gets more or less humid.
How full of water vapour the air is, as a percentage of the most it can hold at that temperature.
How many times stiffer one material is than another; 1000 means one is a thousand times harder to bend.
Two thin layers stuck together; if one swells more than the other the pair curls, like the metal strip in an old thermostat.
A proven upper limit on how tightly a two-layer strip can curl for a given swelling difference; the project checked it by computer.
Structure built in levels, like fibres twisted into threads twisted into rope.
How well a material keeps its strength when it has cracks or flaws.
How much energy a material soaks up before it breaks.
A printer that sprays two different plastics in the same print; the Formlabs printers named here use one material per print.
A fast statistical stand-in for a slow computer simulation, used to rank many designs.
A branch of mathematics about how structures map to one another while keeping chosen features.
The pull a material exerts on water; drier air means a stronger pull.
Two 3D-printing methods: light-cured liquid resin (SLA) and laser-fused powder (SLS).
Measuring how a surface stretches by comparing photos before and during a test.
Computer simulation that follows individual atoms.
