Numerical values of tau_m, tau_L, tau_T, tau_Delta, m0, m_eq(u) in the paper or the repo: none exist; the code never integrates dynamics.

The slider settings (RH_ref, RH, T_ref, T_cur) behind Table 3, and per-specimen angle data and the measurement method: not in the paper or repo; ct_design.gh slider state is in a binary format I did not decode. Three of the four predicted angles are not reproduced by a single sensible step under the .gh panels; the setup guide's panels differ from the .gh panels, so the discrepancy may come from stale panels rather than from the model.
The four actuation videos (.mov) were not downloaded or viewed, so my bend-crosstalk estimate (27.3 and 17.0 degrees) is unchecked against the specimens.
The journal (JMPS) full text: only the Crossref record and arXiv v2 were read; the published version may differ.

A plate-theory derivation of the twist curvature for the +/-45 laminate: neither the paper nor the repo gives it, and I did not derive it (the panels hold one scalar E per material, not laminate stiffnesses).
Mamou-Mani: nothing about the architecture practice was researched in this task (other agents' files spec-partner-architecture.json cover it).

glossary.plain: A branch of mathematics about things and the rules that carry one thing into another, used here as a bookkeeping language for design steps.
One of those carrying rules, such as 'average these fibres into one layer'.
The test that a carrying rule respects time: running then summarising equals summarising then running.
A strip made of two glued layers that bends when one layer swells or expands more than the other.
A material that changes shape when the humidity changes, like a pine cone scale.
A century-old formula that tells how much a two-layer strip bends for a given mismatch in swelling.
A proof written for a computer program (Lean) that checks every logical step, so a mistake cannot slip through.
A proven upper limit: however you choose the layer thicknesses and stiffnesses, the strip cannot bend more than 1.5 times the mismatch divided by its thickness.
Ordinary desktop 3D printing that melts a plastic thread and lays it down line by line.
How long a material takes to settle after its surroundings change.
The list of movement instructions a 3D printer follows.

recommendations: Correct the project's working description before citing the JMPS paper: it formalises the pine cone only. Awns, pods, flytrap and nacre are motivation with no equations; cite Forterre 2005, Elbaum 2007 and Armon 2011 for those.

WHAT A JOINT PAPER ADDS (1, a rejected design): the authors' own future-work text promises a simulation condition that 'returns rejected candidates ... with an explicit interface failure' but shows only four successes. The Lean theorem bilayer_rules_out is a real rejection rule (no candidate with kappa above 1.5*d_eps/h can pass). A joint paper can show a candidate rejected by a checked theorem, which their pipeline never does.

WHAT A JOINT PAPER ADDS (2, a correction the authors can accept): state the hypotheses their Proposition A.25 needs (tau_L=tau_T=tau_Delta, equal laminar moisture) and replace 'F is parameter substitution' by a statement that allows a time-rescaling, since conjugacy fixes tau. Prove both in Lean with the explicit counterexample. This turns 'verified by construction' from a slogan into a theorem with stated side conditions.

WHAT A JOINT PAPER ADDS (3, a design rule): the machine-checked ceiling shows their printed pairs are already at 97.8 to 98.2 percent of the geometric maximum, so the only lever left is the eigenstrain mismatch and the response speed. Pair that with a first-order-insensitivity-to-modulus result at m^2 n = 1 (formalisation rank 6) as a robust-to-infill design window.

WHAT A JOINT PAPER ADDS (4, dynamics): their objects are dynamical but only equilibrium angles were measured. Predict and measure actuation TIME versus thickness (tau proportional to h^2, which Lean already has as diffusiveTime) on printed strips. For Formlabs resins the project record says no water diffusivity or hygroscopic coefficient was found and stock resins gain under 1 percent mass in water, so the stimulus for a first demonstration is likely a solvent (isopropanol uptake: Elastic 50A 39 percent against under 0.1 percent for Rigid 10K, project record) or heat, not humidity. This is a hypothesis to test, not a result; Delta_eps for that pair is unmeasured.

WHAT A JOINT PAPER ADDS (5, a new Spec): the repo names 'SLA' and a new machine profile as an extension path but has none. A resin or powder-bed Spec needs exposure, layer, orientation and post-cure instead of raster angle; vat parts have no raster anisotropy, so the mismatch must come from material pairing, cure gradient or geometry. That forces a new tissue-level object and reduction, which is the scientifically new part. Neither the JMPS paper nor the MRS review addresses SLS.

WHAT A JOINT PAPER ADDS (6, the twist coefficient): derive the +/-phi laminate twist from laminate stiffnesses and prove in Lean whether the repo's reuse of the bending coefficient is right; report the bend crosstalk that two-material twist specimens carry (27.3 degrees by my estimate, to be checked on the videos).

Before building on Table 3, ask the authors for the slider settings, the per-specimen angles, and which of the two panel sets (guide vs .gh) produced the predictions. Pre-register the predicted angle and time before any Formlabs print, in line with this project's freeze-then-test habit.
Treat n=3 to 4 specimens and 'within one s.d.' as modest evidence; a joint paper should report all specimens and a stated acceptance tolerance.

Do not describe the Lean files as 'the paper formalised': they check the flat-space Dyn, the Timoshenko algebra and the strain projections, plus items (ceiling, derivation from equilibrium, mapsSolutions, diffusion, snap) that the paper does not contain.

fleet.label: bm-clients-and-market
fleet.topic: Who would pay, and for what: buyers, partners and procurement routes for a law-constrained printable responsive material
fleet.summary: Who would pay, and for what: the evidence supports three payers and one gap. (1) Clients pay for finished installations: Mamou-Mani's pages name Hyundai Motor (through the artist's Tate Modern commission), Neko Health, COS, Hermes (via RDAI) and Buro Happold as sponsors or clients, and its fabrication arm Fab.Pub (a Therme Group joint venture) has a public material-intake route and a GBP 250 minimum budget, but no published fees. (2) Public funders pay for proof-of-concept research: NSF SBIR/STTR (Phase I ceiling USD 335,937 and Phase II USD 2,239,578 as of 16 Oct 2026; my sample of 118 NSF awards has medians near USD 305k and USD 1.25m), UK Knowledge Transfer Partnerships (GBP 8,500 per month of eligible cost, 12-36 months; round one of 2026-27 closed), and the Royce industrial collaboration programme. Innovate UK Smart grants, named in the brief, are closed. (3) Manufacturers take part rather than pay: Warema and Schueco were 'external partners' in a ministry-funded Fraunhofer ISE project, Fraunhofer ISE says manufacturers commission facility tests, and Schueco's start-up programme offers non-financial help. Gap: no firm was found that pays for a law-constrained material or verified rule as such; Foster + Partners and ZHA have in-house research and a 2017 Autodesk passive-facade study but no buying evidence. Formlabs offers Open Material Mode (from USD 875, free to accredited education), in-kind consumables for student groups and a certified-materials track, but no sponsored-research programme. Contradictions with earlier files: Open Material Mode price (store page 'from $875' vs a reseller listing of about USD 3.7k in bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json); Smart grants closed; SBIR Phase I top is USD 335,937 on one sbir.gov page and USD 323,000 on another.
fleet.lay_summary: We looked for people who might pay for a printable material that follows proven rules. We found plenty of people who pay for finished installations, such as a car maker backing an art commission in a London gallery, a health clinic and a fashion brand. We found almost no one who pays for the material or the rule on its own. The likely first money is public: grants in the US and UK that pay universities and small companies to prove an idea. Big window and shade makers join those public projects but say they offer help, not cash. Think of it as selling a seed sample to a garden designer: she may plant it, but a research fund will pay for growing it.

recommendations: Treat the proof of concept as a sample plus a verified design rule, not a product. Nothing read shows anyone paying for a rule as such; the documented money is installation fees, public grants and test fees. The project record's thin-bilayer limit (about 0.2-0.9 mm total thickness for stock-resin humidity actuation, bm-passive-facades-evidence.json) points to interior, installation and demonstrator uses first, not full-scale shading.

Approach Fab.Pub through its public material-intake route with a hand-scale sample, a one-page rule sheet (the 3/2 ceiling and what it permits) and a request for a joint test pathway. Ask Mamou-Mani what a paid prototype or joint pilot would cost, since no fee is published.

Choose the money route by who the applicant is. US for-profit: NSF Project Pitch under Advanced Materials sub-topic 5 (Structural and Infrastructural Materials), roughly USD 305k Phase I; check the current solicitation and deadline on seedfund.nsf.gov. Team with a university: STTR. UK company plus university: a KTP in a later round (round-one 2026-27 closed) or Royce ICP. Smart grants are not available.

For a UK university-company deal use a Lambert Toolkit agreement as a starting point; the contract-research model lets the sponsor control publication. Settle background IP first, since the earlier IP scan found the responsive-printed-object field crowded.
To get manufacturer evidence without selling to them, price a Fraunhofer ISE CONTINENT characterisation request, or join a publicly funded consortium as Warema and Schueco did.

Do not plan on Formlabs money. Ask for in-kind resin only if a student or accredited academic partner is the applicant, and use free Open Material Mode through an educational partner if a non-Formlabs resin is needed.

fleet.label: bm-competing-approaches
fleet.topic: Competing and complementary approaches to printed passive shape change, and what a sceptical reviewer would say about the Lean-constrained humidity bilayer
fleet.summary: Four of the five alternatives are real and measured but none is a drop-in rival to a passive, reversible, humidity-driven element. (1) Shape-memory polymers are far faster and stiffer: Ding 2017 reports transformation in about 20 s with a 1 GPa/1 MPa pair, and a Formlabs Clear resin printed on a Form 2 recovers at 0.306 deg/s with about 5 N force; but both need heat (62 C and 120 C tested) and are one-shot. (2) A thermal bilayer is the same Timoshenko law with a different driver (his 1925 paper is about bimetal thermostats), and stock Formlabs resins already give a large mismatch: Tough 1000 at 161.6-168.2 and Rigid 10K at 41-48 micrometre/m/C, so 0.45-0.51 percent differential strain over 40 K (own calculation), 2.3-2.5 times the 0.2 percent humidity estimate of earlier agents, with a printable thickness ratio (0.29-0.31) and no thin-wall problem; its weaknesses are that Tough 1000 softens at 40-45 C and nobody has measured such a bilayer. Bloom (14,000 thermobimetal tiles on 414 panels) is the built precedent but gives no curvature numbers. (3) Fibre-aligned hydrogels bend through 20-720 degrees in 1-280 minutes in the literature range but are soft (kPa to 100 kPa) and wet-only. (4) Kirigami and auxetics (tracking to +/-1.0 degree, over 300 cycles) are geometries that need an external strain, so they complement rather than replace a bilayer. (5) Snap-through beams act in 0.6-108 s once a swelling threshold is crossed, but the numbers are solvent-triggered. The three hardest objections: (a) the law is a 1925 formula with a 2015-published maximum that over-predicts printed soft bilayers about 4 times, and Lean certifies only the algebra; (b) strain and speed in humid air are unmeasured and the estimated t90 is a day and a half for 0.4 mm; (c) temperature is a bigger and faster driver of these resins than humidity, so the proposal needs a temperature-by-humidity factorial before any claim. Each has an experiment with a pass/fail rule in the findings and recommendations. Confirmed or corrected from earlier agents: Flexible 80A V2 gains 8 percent mass and 3 percent volume in 1 day (contradicts the blanket under-1-percent claim); its hardness drop is 26 not 28 points; the 3/2 ceiling is prior art (Holstov 2015).
fleet.lay_summary: The team wants a printed panel that bends by itself when the air gets damp, like a pine cone. We looked for rivals. A plastic that remembers its shape can snap into a curve in about twenty seconds, but only when warmed and only once. Two layers of plastic that expand by different amounts when warm, like the strip in an old thermostat, can be made from the same Formlabs resins the team already plans to use, and our arithmetic says warmth would bend them more than damp air would. Cut-and-fold sheets and snap-through strips can move a lot, but they need something else to push them. A fair critic would say three things: the maths is old and over-promises for soft plastics, nobody has measured how fast or how far these resins swell in damp air, and ordinary heat from the sun may swamp the effect. We lay out one test for each worry, with a pass or fail rule agreed before any panel is printed.

glossary.plain: Two thin layers stuck together that expand by different amounts, so the pair bends like a bimetal strip.
A 1925 formula giving how tightly a two-layer strip curls from the mismatch in swelling and stiffness of its layers.
The curl can never exceed one and a half times the strain mismatch divided by strip thickness, however stiff the layers.
A proof-checking program that confirms a mathematical argument has no gaps.
A plastic that can be bent and frozen in a new shape and then springs back to its first shape when warmed.
The temperature where a hard plastic turns soft and rubbery.
How much a material grows per degree of warming.
A soft, jelly-like plastic that soaks up a lot of water and swells.
Cut-and-fold paper art; a cut sheet that pops into 3D when pulled.
A structure that gets fatter sideways when you stretch it.
A sudden flip of a buckled strip from one curved shape to its mirror image.
How long water takes to soak through a layer until it is 90 percent of the way to full.
The measured curl divided by the largest curl the law allows; 1 means perfect, small means the law over-promises.
A resin 3D printer that cures liquid with light, and a powder 3D printer that melts nylon with a laser.
The temperature at which a plastic bar sags under a standard load.
How stiff a material is.

findings.claim: SMP bilayers print on a commercial multimaterial inkjet machine (not a Formlabs printer) and reach the programmed curved shape within seconds of immersion in 62 C water; this is the strongest measured speed among the alternatives.
findings.evidence_quote: They transformed into their permanent configuration within a few seconds, depending on the specific sample.

findings.claim: In the same paper the whole transformation was complete after about 20 s.
findings.evidence_quote: After ~20 s, the samples had completed the transformation

findings.claim: Stiffness of the SMP/elastomer pair: glassy SMP about 1 GPa, elastomer about 1 MPa. A 1000-fold modulus contrast, with the stiff layer being the thermally-triggered one.
findings.evidence_quote: At room temperature, the SMP is glassy with a modulus of ~1 GPa, which is two to three orders of magnitude stiffer than the elastomer ( E ~ 1 MPa)

findings.claim: Glass transitions of that pair are 62 C (SMP) and 8 C (elastomer), so activation needs a surface hotter than normal ambient; a sun-heated dark facade could reach it but the paper tested only warm-water immersion.
findings.evidence_quote: temperatures of the SMP and elastomer are 62°C and 8°C, respectively

findings.claim: The deployed shape is one-shot: after heating, the curved permanent shape stays largely unchanged on further cooling and heating (reprogramming needs a separate mechanical heat-and-fix step). A passive reversible daily cycle is therefore NOT what this SMP route delivers.
findings.evidence_quote: remains largely unchanged upon further cooling and heating

findings.claim: Authors of the SMP printing paper (Ge 2016) state the speed and stiffness advantage over hydrogels: SMP modulus MPa to GPa and response seconds to minutes, against hydrogels at kPa to 100 kPa and response of tens of minutes to days.
findings.evidence_quote: faster response rates (in the scale of seconds to minutes depending on actuation temperature)

findings.claim: Same paper, hydrogel side of the comparison: hydrogel response is limited by solvent diffusion on a time scale of tens of minutes, hours or days.
findings.evidence_quote: the solvent diffusion based slow response rates in the time scale of a few ten minutes, hours, and even days

findings.claim: Ge 2016 printed methacrylate SMP networks with failure strain above 300 percent on a projection microstereolithography system, a vat-photopolymer route like Formlabs SLA but a research machine with micron resolution.
findings.evidence_quote: failure strain which is more than 300% and larger than any existing printable materials

findings.claim: A Formlabs vat printer HAS been used for shape memory: Clear resin (named FLGPCL02) printed on a Form 2, 6 x 19 x 115 mm bars, programmed and recovered at 120 C. Average recovery speed was 0.306 deg/s at 0.1 mm layers and 0.308 deg/s at 0.025 mm layers.
findings.evidence_quote: The average recovery speed for the samples with 0.1 mm layer thickness was calculated at 0.306 degrees/second

findings.claim: Recovery force of those Formlabs Clear SMP bars: 5.34 N (0.025 mm layers) and 4.76 N (0.1 mm layers), a 4.5 to 5.8 N range across print orientations.
findings.evidence_quote: The average recovery force for samples with 0.025mm layer thickness was calculated as 5.34 N

findings.claim: Own arithmetic: at 0.306 deg/s a 90 degree programmed bend takes about 294 s (90/0.306) to recover, but only at 120 C; the test furnace temperature was well above the glass transition, so the study shows the Formlabs resin is a working SMP, NOT that it can be triggered by a sun-warmed facade. The study does not state the resin Tg.
findings.evidence_quote: the temperature was raised to 120°C (above the glass transition temperature)

findings.claim: The bimetal law and the humidity-bilayer law are the same law: the formula the project calls Timoshenko is from his 1925 bimetal-thermostat paper; the driver changes (thermal mismatch alpha*dT instead of swelling strain) but the Lean-checked ceiling kappa*h/d_eps <= 3/2 applies unchanged with d_eps = delta-alpha * delta-T.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1364/JOSA.11.000233 (Crossref record: "Analysis of Bi-Metal Thermostats", J. Opt. Soc. Am. 1925; text not read, paywalled)

findings.claim: Bloom (Los Angeles, 2011): a built thermobimetal canopy. Its responsive surface is made of 14,000 thermobimetal tiles supported on 414 hyperbolic-paraboloid panels; each tile curls a specified amount above 70 F (21.1 C) or when the sun hits it, no power. The page gives no curl angle, thickness or response time.
findings.evidence_quote: Each individual piece automatically curls a specified amount when the outdoor ambient temperature rises above 70˚F or when the sun penetrates the surface.

findings.claim: Resolving an apparent conflict: earlier-in-session snippets said 14,000 tiles and a review said 414 panels; both are on the same page (14,000 tiles on 414 panels), they are not rival counts.
findings.evidence_quote: Composed of 414 hyperbolic paraboloid-shaped stacked panels

findings.claim: A 2025 review of adaptive shading states the trade-off in general terms: passive smart-material systems are simpler and more sustainable but often lack responsiveness to dynamic conditions.
findings.evidence_quote: passively actuated systems use smart materials that respond to environmental stimuli, offering simpler and more sustainable operation, but often lack responsiveness to dynamic conditions

findings.claim: Formlabs data sheet, Tough 1000: thermal expansion (0-150 C) 161.6 (green) and 168.2 (post-cured) micrometre/m/C; the micro sign is lost in the PDF text extraction and the table columns are scrambled, so the green/post-cured mapping is my reading.

Formlabs data sheet, Rigid 10K: thermal expansion (0-150 C) in the metric column reads 48, 41, 47 and 46 micrometre/m/C across four conditions (mapping scrambled); imperial column 23-27 microinch/in/F, which x1.8 gives 41-49, consistent.

Tough 1000 softens near ambient-plus: heat deflection temperature at 0.45 MPa is 40.4 C (green) and 44.6 C (post-cured). A 20-60 C thermal swing therefore crosses its softening range, so the modulus ratio n (and the optimum thickness ratio) change during the swing and a CTE averaged over 0-150 C probably overstates the glassy-range value.

Own calculation: stock Formlabs pair Tough 1000 (high CTE, soft, active) on Rigid 10K (low CTE, stiff, passive) has a differential CTE of 113.6-127.2 micrometre/m/C, i.e. 0.45-0.51 percent differential strain over a 40 K swing (0.23-0.25 percent over 20 K). At the 3/2 ceiling and h = 1 mm this is kappa = 6.8-7.6 per m (radius 131-147 mm); at h = 0.4 mm and 40 K, 17-19 per m (radius 52-59 mm).

Own calculation: for that pair n = E_passive/E_active = 10-11 GPa / 0.932 GPa = 10.7-11.8, the optimum passive/active thickness ratio is m = n^-1/2 = 0.29-0.31 (e.g. 0.23 mm Rigid 10K on 0.77 mm Tough 1000 for h = 1 mm, both above the 0.2 mm Form 4 wall minimum), and an equal-thickness pair already reaches f = 0.93-0.97 of the 1.5 ceiling. Unlike the humidity pair, the stiff layer is the passive one, which is printable.
findings.source: own calculation: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-competing-approaches/calc.py (output calc_out.json) ; moduli from agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json (not re-fetched)

findings.claim: Confirms and sharpens the earlier agents: the thermal differential strain of this stock pair (0.45-0.51 percent over 40 K) is 2.3-2.5 times the 0.2 percent humidity differential that spec-resin-chemistry.json ESTIMATED for 24 h. The 0.2 percent is itself an estimate, never measured.

Anisotropic-hydrogel route (Gladman 2016): composite hydrogel inks with cellulose fibrils aligned along the print path give localized, programmable anisotropic swelling; flat prints fold into complex 3D shapes on immersion in water, with an inverse-design theory. I could read only the abstract, so no curvature or time numbers.
findings.evidence_quote: we printed composite hydrogel architectures that are encoded with localized, anisotropic swelling behaviour controlled by the alignment of cellulose fibrils along prescribed four-dimensional printing pathways

findings.claim: Hydrogel bilayer actuators across the literature span bending angles of 20-720 degrees with actuation times of 1-280 minutes (review, Figure 2a).
findings.evidence_quote: The bending angle of bilayer actuators can range from 20 to 720° with actuation times varying from 1 to 280 min

findings.claim: Hydrogels are soft (kPa to about 100 kPa per Ge 2016), so a hydrogel on a stiff Formlabs resin is mechanically dead under the Timoshenko law (project record bm-hydrogels.json: f = 0.0000-0.11 at m = 1; not re-derived here). This limits fibre-reinforced hydrogels to wet or very humid use and to elastomer partners.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/srep31110 (PMC4976324, Europe PMC full text) ; agents2/bm-hydrogels.json
findings.evidence_quote: the low modulus of hydrogels ranging from ∼kPa to ∼100 kPa

findings.claim: Anisotropy by aligned fibres can also be printed in silicone: PDMS with 15 vol percent glass fibres (direct ink writing) swells anisotropically in solvent, and a cellulose-fibril hydrogel does so in water (Jiang 2019).
findings.evidence_quote: Using 3D printable fibrous composites, we fabricate structures with geometries near bifurcation points

findings.claim: Kirigami with a measured outcome: cut thin-film solar cells on a Kapton sheet tilt their facets when stretched, tracking the sun to within +/-1.0 degree of the predicted direction. The motion is a function of applied uniaxial strain, i.e. the cuts are a transformer and need an external driver.
findings.evidence_quote: we show tracking to within ±1.0° of the predicted pointing vector

findings.claim: Same kirigami trackers survived more than 300 cycles without appreciable performance loss, a durability figure that no humidity-bilayer source I read matches (wood: about a dozen loops; printed cellulose: 170 cycles per project record).
findings.evidence_quote: no appreciable decrease in performance after >300 cycles

findings.claim: Conventional trackers raise yearly energy by 20-40 percent over fixed arrays, which is what the kirigami tracker is benchmarked against.
findings.evidence_quote: conventional trackers can provide an increase in yearly energy generation between 20 and 40% compared with non-tracking solar arrays

findings.claim: Buckling-induced kirigami: a perforated sheet under uniaxial tension buckles out of plane into 3D patterns; stretching far leaves permanent folds. Again the input is tension, not humidity. I read the abstract only; no tilt/strain numbers retrieved.
findings.evidence_quote: under uniaxial tension the ligaments buckle out of plane, inducing the formation of 3D patterns whose morphology is controlled by the load direction

findings.claim: Own reading of the kirigami and auxetic literature in this run: kirigami and auxetics are geometries that convert an in-plane strain into out-of-plane motion; I found no source in which one is driven by humidity or temperature alone. They are therefore COMPLEMENTS to a bilayer (strain amplifier) rather than substitutes. Hypothesis, not tested here.

Swelling-triggered snap-through (Jiang 2019): printed fibrous-composite beams near a bistable/monostable boundary snap when anisotropic swelling crosses a bifurcation; actuation time is programmable from 0.6 to 108 s for millimetre-scale structures, with no electronics.
findings.evidence_quote: The actuation time can be programmed by varying structural parameters (from 0.6 to 108 s for millimeter-scale structures)

findings.claim: The snap time quoted above is the time after the trigger crosses a threshold; the slow step is still diffusion. The authors say conventional swelling actuation can take many minutes due to diffusion limits, and the snap gives a fast, large-amplitude output from a slow stimulus.
findings.evidence_quote: This forces a key geometric parameter to pass through a bifurcation, triggering rapid and large-amplitude self-actuation.

findings.claim: Isotropic PDMS in the same paper swells 42 percent linearly in toluene; the glass-fibre composite is the anisotropic one. The 0.6-108 s numbers come from solvent-triggered PDMS/glass-fibre and hydrogel beams, not from humid air.

Prior art for the ceiling: Holstov, Bridgens and Farmer (2015) plotted the Timoshenko factor f(m,n) over many stiffness ratios and wrote that its maximum stays at 1.5, reached at a different thickness ratio each time. The Lean kernel proof is new; the number is not. (Agrees with agents2/bm-wood-cellulose-hygromorphs.json, contradicts spec-hygromorph-4d.json which called it the project's own derivation.)
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136)
findings.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

findings.claim: Speed benchmark for a wood humidity bilayer: 1 mm rotary-cut veneer on 0.2 mm fibreglass reached 80 percent of the curvature change in about 2 h 15 min in both directions.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136)
findings.evidence_quote: 80% of the total curvature change in both the transfer from dry conditions to humid and vice-versa is achieved in approximately 2 hours 15 minutes

findings.claim: Timoshenko prediction vs measurement in printed soft humidity bilayers (Dingler 2021, PEDOT:PSS on PDMS): measured peak curvature of the 54 micrometre bilayer was about one third of the 17 micrometre one (1.2 per mm).
findings.evidence_quote: A maximum curvature of 1.2 mm –1 was reached, which is about three times the value of the 54 µm bilayer at r.H. = 90%.

findings.claim: Predicted peaks in the same paper: 5.3 per mm for the 17 micrometre film (with humidity-dependent modulus) and 1.6 per mm for the 54 micrometre film. Own arithmetic: 5.3/1.2 = 4.4 and 1.6/(1.2/3) = 4.0, so the formula over-predicts the maximum by about 4 times. The authors themselves say the calculation "nicely predicts the trends", so this is an over-prediction of size, not of shape.
findings.evidence_quote: The maximum curvature predicted from a humidity dependent E PDOT:PSS is 5.3 mm –1

findings.claim: Humidity changes the modulus of the active layer itself: PEDOT:PSS storage modulus fell by a factor of 2.4 from lowest to highest humidity (about 130 to 54 MPa), the reason the law must be fed wet-state, not dry, moduli.
findings.evidence_quote: This leads to a decrease in E' by a factor of 2.4 from lowest to highest humidity.

findings.claim: Dingler et al. name the cause: an inherent linear assumption in the Timoshenko equation, with rotations that become large; they suggest large-rotation beam models or finite elements. (Strictly, curvature from small material strain does not need small rotation, so the stated cause is not the whole story; the humidity-dependence of E and the wide-plate geometry also matter.)
findings.evidence_quote: It has to be noted, however, that there is an inherent linear assumption in the Timoshenko equation.

findings.claim: For filament-printed wood-PLA bilayers, even the extended model could not reproduce observed values because non-linear material behaviour is not in the model (Krueger 2021).
findings.evidence_quote: Although the observed experimental values could not be reproduced computationally, because the potentially non-linear material behavior is not accounted for in the model

findings.claim: Dingler 2021 overall verdict is more favourable than the over-prediction suggests: calculated curvatures follow the experimental trends.
findings.evidence_quote: Overall, the analytically calculated curvatures nicely predict the trends of the experimental actuators.

findings.claim: CONFIRMS bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json and CONTRADICTS the blanket claim in spec-resin-chemistry.json that every SLA resin gains under 1 percent water: Flexible 80A Resin V2 data sheet (ASTM D471 slabs, wiped dry, no conditioning) gives, for deionized water, +8 percent mass and +3 percent volume after 1 day and +9 percent mass and +7 percent volume after 1 week. Column mapping: 12th of 18 solvents (acetone, xylene, IPA, TPM, butyl acetate, ethanol, acetic acid, HCl, NaOH, bleach, H2O2, deionized water ...), values read by position, so confidence is medium.
Volume row of the same table, same column mapping: deionized water +3 percent (1 day) and +7 percent (1 week); the neighbours are H2O2 +6/+9 and isooctane +122/+164.

Hardness row, same mapping: deionized water -26 (1 day) and -27 (1 week) Shore A points. This CONFIRMS the later correction (-26, in bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json) and CONTRADICTS the -28 used in design-biomaterial.json.
Test condition for those numbers: slabs are measured immediately after wiping dry with no conditioning, so the values include surface water and no drying hysteresis is represented.
findings.evidence_quote: Rectangular slabs, used for hardness, mass, and volume change, are evaluated immediately after wiping dry without a conditioning period.

findings.claim: Own arithmetic from that table: 3 percent volume is 0.99 percent isotropic linear swelling after 1 day, 7 percent is 2.28 percent after 1 week (1.03^(1/3) and 1.07^(1/3)). Isotropy is assumed, not measured.

Rigid 10K takes up under 0.1 percent IPA in 24 h (1 cm cube), CONFIRMING the passive-layer claim for that solvent; the water row of the same table is scrambled in the PDF text and I could not read it. I did not re-check the 39 percent IPA figure for Elastic 50A.
findings.evidence_quote: Isopropyl Alcohol < 0.1

findings.claim: Own calculation of one-face-exposed 90 percent equilibration time t90 = 0.848 h^2/D (coefficient from agents2/bm-diffusion-kinetics.json, not re-derived here). With D = 1e-12 m2/s (stock rigid methacrylate resin, earlier agents' literature value, not re-verified): 9 h at 0.2 mm, 38 h at 0.4 mm, 151 h (6 days) at 0.8 mm, 603 h (25 days) at 1.6 mm. With D = 6e-12 (Flexible 80A V2-class, inferred by an earlier agent from Formlabs 1 d/1 wk mass gains): 1.6 h at 0.2 mm, 6.3 h at 0.4 mm, 25 h at 0.8 mm. With D = 1e-10 (hydrogel): 5.7 min at 0.2 mm, 23 min at 0.4 mm, 1.5 h at 0.8 mm.

findings.claim: Own calculation: a 21-fold speed gap between the SMP route and the hydrogel hinge that Ding 2017 uses as comparator (about 20 s versus about 7 min for 36 degrees at 0.8 mm; different geometries and stimuli, so indicative only).
findings.evidence_quote: it takes about 7 min to achieve a bending angle of 36°

findings.claim: Own calculation, arc swept by a strip at the 3/2 ceiling: for d_eps = 0.5 percent, h = 1 mm and L = 100 mm the strip bends through 43 degrees; for d_eps = 1 percent, h = 0.4 mm, L = 100 mm through 215 degrees. Large rotations therefore arise for thin humid strips, which is where Dingler says linear theory strains.

OBJECTION 1 (the model and the novelty). Reviewer: "The proposal rests on a 1925 bimetal formula whose 3/2 maximum was already published in 2015 (Holstov). It over-predicts printed soft humidity bilayers about 4 times (Dingler) or cannot be reproduced at all (Krueger). A Lean proof of an inequality inside that formula says nothing about whether it describes a Formlabs resin, and the Lean file I read proves the bound and equality when m^2 n = 1, not the converse that the optimum is only there." BEST RESPONSE: Concede the novelty claim is narrow (a kernel-checked, assumption-explicit bound), and reframe: the bound is a hard upper filter, it can only err on the side of excluding designs, and an over-prediction means efficiency eta = kappa_measured*h / (1.5*d_eps_measured) is below 1, never above. Report eta and the position of its maximum as the scientific result. The wet modulus, not the dry datasheet value, must set n (Dingler: modulus fell 2.4-fold from 10 to 90 percent RH). Keep the claim to "eta <= 1 and the maximum sits near n_wet^-1/2". EXPERIMENT THAT SETTLES IT: Measure d_eps (free swelling strain, coupon of the same thickness as each layer) and wet and dry modulus on single-layer coupons BEFORE printing any bilayer; freeze predictions; print 5 thickness ratios x >=5 strips at fixed total thickness; read curvature in the same bath/chamber. Pass: measured eta within +/-20 percent of f(m,n_wet)/1.5 at every ratio and the argmax within one step of n_wet^-1/2. Falsified if any strip exceeds eta = 1 beyond measurement error (the model or measurement is wrong) or the best strip stays below eta = 0.5 (the law is uninformative for these resins).
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136) ; https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202007982 (PMC11469309) ; https://doi.org/10.3390/biomimetics6040058 (PMC8544213) ; Lean file D:/Users/ashenoy00000/.antigravity-ide/ScienceClaw/delphisci/tracks/lean/HygromorphCeilingCheck.lean (read only; theorems timoshenkoCoefficient_le, timoshenkoCoefficient_eq_of_optimal, bilayer_rules_out)
findings.evidence_quote: the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

findings.claim: OBJECTION 2 (strain and speed: the physical premise). Reviewer: "No humid-air swelling coefficient or diffusivity exists for any Formlabs resin. Estimates put the differential strain near 0.2 percent per day and the t90 of a 0.4 mm layer at about 38 hours, of 0.8-1.6 mm at 6-25 days. An SMP bilayer moves in seconds, a thermal bilayer in minutes, a snap element in under two minutes, hydrogels in minutes to hours. An architectural element that needs weeks is not an element." BEST RESPONSE: The speed gap is real and cannot be argued away for stock rigid resins; it can be narrowed by design: layers of 0.2 mm (9 h), a Flexible 80A V2-class active layer (D of about 6e-12 gives 1.6 h at 0.2 mm; measured 1 percent linear swelling per day when immersed) or a hydrogel layer (minutes to hours). Slow can be a feature for a seasonal or diurnal element, as with the 2 h 15 min wood hygromorph. State plainly that the two numbers on which everything rests (d_eps in air and D) are unmeasured, and make measuring them the first deliverable. EXPERIMENT: sorption isotherm and kinetics at 23 C, RH steps 30, 60, 90 percent, on 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 mm coupons of Flexible 80A V2, Tough 1000, Rigid 10K, Nylon 11 and Nylon 12 (gravimetry plus optical length to 5 micrometres per 40 mm, plus the same coupon edge-on for curvature when bonded); fit D from the t^0.5 slope. Go/no-go rule written in advance: continue the humidity route only if the differential strain between the best active/passive pair is >= 0.3 percent for 30 to 90 percent RH AND t90 <= 24 h at <= 0.4 mm; otherwise switch to the hydrogel or thermal route.
findings.source: own calculation: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-competing-approaches/calc.py (output calc_out.json) ; https://media.formlabs.com/asset/af9d9268-d8c4-4019-9ccd-bd3af926c67e/-ENUS-Flexible-80A-V2-TDS.pdf ; https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1602890 (PMC5389747) ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-08055-3 (publisher PDF at raney.seas.upenn.edu) ; https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136)

findings.claim: OBJECTION 3 (wrong stimulus and confounding). Reviewer: "Temperature moves these resins more than humidity does. Formlabs' own data give a Tough 1000 / Rigid 10K CTE gap of 114-127 micrometre/m/C, i.e. 0.45-0.51 percent over 40 K against the 0.2 percent humidity estimate, so on a real facade your humidity bilayer will mostly be a thermal bilayer, and a thermal bilayer needs no new material (Bloom is built). Water also plasticises, leaches residual photoinitiator and hydrolyses acrylates, and no humidity-driven shading has a measured energy or comfort benefit." BEST RESPONSE: Accept the physics. The Lean law is driver-agnostic, so restate the proposal as a Lean-bounded bilayer characterised under BOTH drivers, with the thermal response as the control and possibly the better sun-tracking driver (shade is needed when hot). What humidity adds is a stimulus uncorrelated with surface temperature at night and in rain, and the potential to use a bio-based polymer; the case for it is climate-dependent (project record: tracks need for shade in dry-summer cities, fails in humid ones). Durability claims must wait for the cycle and creep data. EXPERIMENT: climate-chamber factorial on identical strips: T = 20, 40, 60 C crossed with RH = 30, 90 percent, with the strip held edge-on, plus 100 humidity cycles and a 7-day creep hold (90 percent RH versus 30 percent). Fit d_eps = delta-alpha*dT + delta-beta*dRH and report each term. Pass for the humidity route: the humidity term is at least half the thermal term over a 20 K daily swing, curvature after 100 cycles is within 10 percent of cycle 1, and mass loss from leaching stays below the swelling signal (dry-wet-dry mass check). Otherwise the honest conclusion is that the thermal bilayer is the better stock-resin design.

key_claims.claim: The Timoshenko 3/2 ceiling is prior art (Holstov 2015 plotted it and wrote that the maximum stays at 1.5); the new element is only the kernel-checked proof, and the Lean file read proves the bound and equality when m^2 n = 1, not the converse.
key_claims.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136)
key_claims.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

key_claims.claim: The formula over-predicts the maximum curvature of printed soft humidity bilayers by about 4 times (5.3 vs 1.2 per mm; 1.6 vs about 0.4 per mm), although it follows trends.
key_claims.evidence_quote: A maximum curvature of 1.2 mm –1 was reached, which is about three times the value of the 54 µm bilayer at r.H. = 90%.

key_claims.claim: Stock Formlabs resins give a larger and faster-driven thermal bilayer mismatch than the estimated humidity one: Tough 1000 CTE 161.6-168.2 vs Rigid 10K 41-48 um/m/C is 0.45-0.51 % over 40 K (own calculation), against 0.2 % estimated for humidity; so a temperature-by-humidity factorial is required before any humidity claim.
The strongest alternatives are faster but not drop-in: SMP bilayers move in about 20 s but need heat and are one-shot; kirigami needs external strain; hydrogel bilayers need 1-280 min and are soft.
key_claims.evidence_quote: They transformed into their permanent configuration within a few seconds, depending on the specific sample.

recommendations: Run the three experiments in the findings (OBJECTION 1-3) in this order: coupon sorption/CTE/modulus first (objection 2 and the inputs for 1), then the T x RH factorial (objection 3), then the bilayer thickness-ratio sweep (objection 1). Write the pass/fail thresholds into the pre-registration before any bilayer is printed.

Add a thermal-only control (20-60 C at fixed RH) to EVERY humidity test; without it a humidity result on these resins is uninterpretable because thermal strain is of the same size or larger (0.45-0.51 % per 40 K vs the 0.2 % estimate).

Print a stock-resin thermal bilayer as a cheap second arm: Tough 1000 (about 0.77 mm) on Rigid 10K (about 0.23 mm) at h = 1 mm; measure curvature versus temperature 20-60 C. It needs no Open Material Mode, tests the Lean ceiling with a driver that is fast, and is the fallback if the humidity go/no-go fails. Check first that the two parts bond (no bond data in any source read).

Treat SMP as an assembly or deployment feature, not as the daily actuator: a Formlabs Clear flat print that is heated and programmed once could be a one-shot deployable pavilion element. Do not claim passive operation without finding or tuning a resin with Tg inside the facade surface range (not found for any Formlabs resin in this run).

Report efficiency eta = kappa_measured*h/(1.5*d_eps_measured) and the thickness ratio of its maximum for every bilayer, wet-state modulus included; state in the proposal that the 3/2 number is prior art (Holstov 2015) and the contribution is the machine-checked bound plus the printer-constraint filter.
Keep kirigami and snap-through as strain-amplifier ideas only after a bilayer gives measured strain; do not claim them as humidity-driven.

fleet.label: bm-diffusion-kinetics
fleet.topic: Time to equilibrate: diffusion, poroelasticity and thickness scaling
fleet.summary: Equilibration time of a polymer layer is t = c h^2/D with fixed constants: for a one-face-exposed active layer (the bilayer case) t50 = 0.197, t90 = 0.848 and t99 = 1.78 h^2/D; for two exposed faces divide by 4. My own laminate calculation shows an optimal hygromorph bilayer reaches 99 % of its final curvature at 1.65 h_a^2/D whatever the modulus ratio, and reproduces the project's 3/2 ceiling numerically. Measured water D spans four decades: 1.4e-13 to 5e-12 m2/s for dense polyamide, TPU and filament thermoplastics (Aniskevich 2023, PA11 Oliver-Ortega 2018, TPU 2026), 1.5e-12 to 1.1e-11 for dimethacrylate resins (Sideridou 2011), 4e-11 to 2e-10 for hydrogels and PEG-acrylates (PNAS 2022; arXiv 2406.15224), 6e-10 to 1e-9 for PDMS and porous tissue. No D has been published for a Formlabs resin, but Formlabs' own 1 day / 1 week mass gains imply D about 3e-12 (Grey V5, M_inf about 3.7 %, assumed 3.2 mm bars) and at least 6e-12 m2/s (Flexible 80A V2, assumed 2 mm slabs); the earlier '<1 % in 24 h' cube numbers are therefore far from equilibrium (a 10 mm cube at D = 1e-12 reaches 19 % of plateau in 24 h). D is not constant: it varies 2-4x with humidity in half the filaments and 21x with water content in PA6, which makes drying about 2.5x slower than wetting. Case II (front moving at constant speed, t ~ h) needs relaxation slower than diffusion in a glassy polymer plasticised by a strong penetrant; I found no measured Case II water data for any Formlabs material, only pseudo-Fickian or sub-Fickian reports (PA11 n = 0.27-0.31; epoxy SLA anomalous). Demonstration verdict (one face, t90): hours need D >= 1e-11 (Flexible 80A V2-class, hydrogel or PEG-acrylate layer, 0.2-0.8 mm; 0.2 mm Flexible 80A about 1 h); stock rigid resins at 0.2-0.4 mm need 9-38 h, at 0.8-1.6 mm 6-25 d; dense nylon or TPU at 0.8 mm or more need 3 weeks to many months.
fleet.lay_summary: A thin plastic strip that curls when it gets wet cannot curl faster than water can soak into it. The soaking time grows with the square of the thickness: a strip twice as thick takes four times as long, like a thick sponge versus a thin cloth. Stiff 3D-printed plastics and nylon soak up water very slowly, so a half-millimetre strip can take days or weeks to finish moving, while a soft rubbery print or a jelly-like layer finishes in an hour or a few hours. Formlabs' own one-day test numbers look small mostly because one day is too short for a thick block to fill up, not because the plastic cannot absorb more. So a demonstration that finishes in an afternoon needs a thin layer, 0.2 to 0.8 millimetres, of a soft or water-loving material, and a stiff nylon or resin strip is a week-long experiment.

glossary.plain: How quickly water spreads through a material; larger means faster, in square metres per second.
The ordinary slow spreading of water in which the soaking time grows with thickness squared.
A sharp wet front that moves into a glassy plastic at a steady speed, so time grows with thickness, not thickness squared.
A plastic that is hard and stiff (glassy) or soft and stretchy (rubbery) at the temperature of use.
The time for the layer to fill to 50, 90 or 99 percent of its final water content.
Water can enter only through one side because the other side is glued to a layer that water does not enter.
Soften a plastic by letting a small molecule such as water get between the chains.
Two bonded layers, one of which swells in water, so the strip bends like a bimetal strip.
The point where the material has taken up all the water it will take at those conditions.
A sponge-like material whose swelling speed is set by water flowing through its pores while the network deforms.
A rule that diffusion speeds up by a fixed factor for each rise in temperature; the activation energy sets the factor.
Technical data sheet published by the manufacturer.

findings.claim: Fickian slab: the fractional uptake of a plane sheet of thickness l with both faces held at the bath concentration depends only on x = D t / l^2. The half-time is x50 = 0.04918, the 90 % time x90 = 0.2120, the 95 % time x95 = 0.2823 and the 99 % time x99 = 0.4453. Short-time law M_t/M_inf = 4 sqrt(D t/(pi l^2)). Single slowest-mode time constant tau = l^2/(pi^2 D).
findings.source: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-diffusion-kinetics/diffusion_kinetics.py (series of Crank eq. 4.14, reproduced by an independent finite-volume solve that gives x50 = 0.04918 as well)
findings.evidence_quote: D was calculated at low times of immersion, when M t / M ∞ ≤ 0.5, as: (3) M t M ∞ = 4 L · ( D π ) 1 2 · t 1 2

findings.claim: Thickness scaling: for a layer exposed on both faces the half-time is t50 = 0.0492 h^2/D; for an active layer exposed on ONE face only (the other face bonded to an impermeable passive layer, the bilayer case) the effective sheet thickness is 2h, so t50 = 0.197 h^2/D, t90 = 0.848 h^2/D, t99 = 1.78 h^2/D. Doubling h quadruples every time.

Measured thickness exponents in a porous hygromorph are below 2: wetting time varies as h^1.3 and drying time as h^1.5 in pine-cone scales, against the Fickian h^2 estimate (tau = h_a^2/D ~ 1000 s for D ~ 1e-9 m2/s and h_a ~ 1 mm).
findings.evidence_quote: the shrinking (drying) time varies as τ d = 96 h a 1.5 min and the swelling (wetting) time varies as τ d = 29 h a 1.3 min (where h a is in mm)

findings.claim: Hydrogel swelling time is proportional to thickness squared; the cooperative diffusion coefficient follows from tau = h^2/(pi^2 D) with D = (K_os + 4 mu/3)/f (osmotic and shear moduli over network-solvent friction).
findings.evidence_quote: Our previous study confirmed that τ is proportional to the square of the sample thickness, following cooperative diffusion ( 27 ). We estimated the cooperative diffusion coefficients, D , from the relation τ = h ∞ 2 π 2 D

findings.claim: Water D in 12 FFF filaments (97 % RH and lower, room temperature, cylinders of 1.75 or 2.8 mm diameter): Nylon 0.001, Antero 0.00245, CPE 0.00247, PET-G 0.00335, Ultem 0.00399, PC 0.00472, PLA Lava 0.00782 up to PLA T-W 0.0151 mm2/h, i.e. 2.8e-13 to 4.2e-12 m2/s. Confirms the earlier agent's range.

In those filaments the moisture swelling strain is small (0.15-0.25 % for most), and the Nylon filament shrank by 2.43 % in humid air, so a polyamide filament is not a safe stand-in for a swelling layer.
findings.evidence_quote: Most materials had a maximal swelling ability of 0.15−0.25%, which was not dependent on their structure and composition.

findings.claim: Concentration dependence of D, filaments: D was independent of humidity for six of twelve filaments, fell about four-fold with moisture for four and rose 2-3-fold for PLA Lava and PET-G.
findings.evidence_quote: For the other six materials, the diffusion coefficient changed with the moisture concentration in the atmosphere. The dependence significantly (four times) decreased for four materials, including ABS White

findings.claim: Concentration dependence of D, polyamide 6 in water: the FE-model input table gives D = 2.58e-9 at zero water, 7.34e-9 at 30 000 ppm, 2.42e-8 at 65 000 ppm and 5.51e-8 at 89 000 ppm, a factor 21.4 between dry and near-saturated (own division). The unit printed in the table header is garbled ('[m/s 2]'), so only the unit-free ratio is used.

Consequence of a D that rises with water content (own finite-volume simulation, D = D0 exp(beta c), D ratio 21.4): the half-time for wetting is 0.114 times the constant-D0 value and the half-time for drying 0.279 times, so drying takes 2.46 times longer than wetting; for a ratio of 100 drying is 4.05 times slower. A wet/dry cycling demonstration is therefore limited by the drying half-cycle and a single D from the wetting curve under-predicts it.

Dimethacrylate photopolymers (the chemistry class of SLA resins): water diffusion coefficient 1.52e-8 cm2/s (TEGDMA) up to 11.01e-8 cm2/s (Bis-GMA), i.e. 1.5e-12 to 1.1e-11 m2/s (own unit conversion, x1e-4). The abstract says D was highest in water, so these are read as the water values; the disc thickness is not in the abstract.
findings.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21783239/ (10.1016/j.dental.2011.06.007), abstract via Europe PMC search API
findings.evidence_quote: The diffusion coefficient for all resins was higher in water than in ethanol/water solution or ethanol. Bis-GMA-resin showed the highest diffusion coefficient (11.01 × 10⁻⁸cm² s⁻¹)

findings.claim: In dimethacrylate resins the volume increase depends linearly on the amount of water or ethanol absorbed, so swelling strain equilibrates on the same clock as mass uptake.
findings.evidence_quote: The volume increase was found to depend linearly on the amount of water or ethanol absorbed.

findings.claim: Flexible TPU (60A-98A, FDM, immersed in 0.9 % NaCl up to 96 h): Fickian D from the initial uptake 1.40e-13 to 3.40e-12 m2/s, equilibrium uptake up to ~1.8 %; the authors flag the lowest value (TPU 98A) as possibly an artefact of very low initial absorption.
findings.evidence_quote: Diffusion coefficients ranged from 1.40 × 10 −13 to 3.40 × 10 −12 m 2 s −1 , with no monotonic dependence on hardness.

findings.claim: Neat PA11 (hot-pressed, immersed in water): D = 4.95e-13 m2/s at 23 C and 22.0e-13 m2/s at 40 C, M_inf 1.43 % and 1.58 %; the n exponent is 0.305 and 0.272, below the Fickian 0.5 ('pseudo-Fickian').

Temperature: from the two PA11 points the apparent activation energy is 67.7 kJ/mol (own Arrhenius calculation) and D rises 4.44-fold from 23 to 40 C; extrapolating the same line to 50 C gives a ten-fold speed-up (extrapolation beyond the data, treat as indicative). A warm bath is therefore a 4-10x accelerator for a polyamide demonstration, at the cost of a different strain/modulus state.
findings.value: Ea 67.7 kJ/mol; x4.44 (23->40 C); x9.9 (->50 C, extrapolated)

findings.claim: Water in PDMS elastomer: D about 6-8e-10 m2/s (value quoted second-hand in a Sylgard-184 chip paper, which says the pervaporation time scales as H^2/D); the older figure D ~ 1e-9 m2/s comes from a web-search snippet of Randall & Doyle 2005 that I did not open. PDMS equilibrates in minutes at 1 mm but takes up very little water.
findings.evidence_quote: τp ∼ H2/Dwp , Dwp ≃ 6–8 × 10-10 m2 s-1 being the diffusion coefficient of water in PDMS

findings.claim: Polyampholyte hydrogel (45 wt% water, 1.1-1.3 mm thick): cooperative swelling diffusivity 8.8e-11 to 1.7e-10 m2/s, roughly 10-100x faster than dense photopolymer resins.
findings.evidence_quote: The cooperative diffusion coefficient of swelling, D sw , increases slightly from 8.8 × 10 −11 to 1.7 × 10 −10 m 2 /s by increasing C MBAA from 0 to 5.0 mol%

findings.claim: Printed PEG-acrylate type gels (PEGDA-700/PEGMEMA, 2 mm dry slabs photocured in glass moulds) swell to equilibrium in hours: exponential time constant tau of about 61 min or less for 5-40 mol% PEGDA, about 120 min for 1 mol% PEGDA-700 and about 190 min for 10k-PEGDA; curves reach their plateau by ~3-6 h. Own D = l^2/(pi^2 tau) with l = 2 mm gives 3.6e-11 to 1.1e-10 m2/s (lower bound; swollen thickness is larger, 3 mm gives up to 2.5e-10).
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.15224 (arXiv:2406.15224), p. 13 and Fig. 2 (value symbols checked on the rendered page image); sample size p. 7
findings.evidence_quote: When PEGDA-700 is employed, the 1:99 formulation experiences a much larger time to reach equilibrium (τ ≃120 minutes) than the formulations with higher PEGDA-700 content (all τ ≤61 minutes).

findings.claim: Stock photopolymer: low-cost acrylate LCD resins as 60 x 60 x 1 mm plates in seawater: R3 +12.37 % in 2.5 d then 13.49 %; R2 (4.3 %) stable within 4 d; R1 (3.4 %) not saturated until after 8 d. Own inversion with x95/x99 for both-face exposure: D about 4e-13 to 2e-12 m2/s (R1 4.1e-13 to 6.4e-13, R2 8.2e-13 to 1.3e-12, R3 1.3e-12 to 2.1e-12).
findings.evidence_quote: While resin R2 stabilized within four days, resin R1 did not reach saturation until after eight days.

findings.claim: Formlabs Grey V5 tensile bars (ASTM D638 Type 4, DI water): mass 101.38 % after 1 day and 103.23 % after 1 week, modulus 88.63 % and 65.29 %. This resolves the earlier agent's 'scrambled table' doubt: the values sit in the MASS column and the DI Water row by word coordinates (pdf read with PyMuPDF).

First kinetic parameters for a Formlabs resin: a two-point Fickian inversion of the Grey V5 bars (ratio 3.23/1.38 = 2.34, below sqrt7 = 2.65, so the curve is bending to a plateau) gives x = D t/l^2 = 0.0279 at 1 d, equilibrium uptake M_inf about 3.7 % (the bars would be 38 % saturated at 1 d and 88 % at 1 wk) and D = 3.3e-12 m2/s for an ASSUMED 3.2 mm bar (1.3e-12 at 2 mm, 5.2e-12 at 4 mm; the TDS does not state bar thickness). Cross-check: the same D and M_inf predict 1.17 % for a 10 mm cube at 24 h against Formlabs' 0.8 % (Grey V5) and 0.9 % (Clear V5).
findings.source: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-diffusion-kinetics/diffusion_kinetics.py (inputs from the Formlabs TDS above and https://formlabs.com/support/solvent-compatibility/)

findings.claim: Formlabs Flexible 80A V2 slabs (ASTM D471) in DI water: +8 % mass and +3 % volume at 1 day, +9 % mass and +7 % volume at 1 week (confirmed by word coordinates: the 'Deionized Water' label sits between the 1-day and 1-week lines). Because 8 to 9 % is close to a plateau, a Fickian inversion gives D = 9.3e-12 m2/s, and D >= 6.3e-12 m2/s allowing for the integer rounding of the percentages, for an ASSUMED 2 mm slab (thickness not stated in the TDS); D scales with thickness squared (2.3e-12 if the slab were 1 mm).

The two Formlabs numbers for 'Flexible 80A' water uptake cannot be reconciled by kinetics: with D >= 6.3e-12 m2/s a 1 cm cube should reach 42 % of its plateau in 24 h, i.e. about 3.8 % mass for a 9 % plateau, against 0.7 % reported in the cube table. So the 'Flexible 80A Resin' row and 'Flexible 80A V2' are most likely different formulations (the earlier agents left V1 versus V2 open); this supports reading V2 as the swelling material only if the V2 cube value is measured.

Confirmed: Elastic 50A V2 gains 39.2 % mass in isopropanol in 24 h (acetone 43.4 %, TPM 45.6 %, water 0.7 %) while Rigid 10K gains <0.1 % in isopropanol and water (1 cm cubes). Interpreting the cube as 3-D Fickian with a 43-50 % plateau, D of isopropanol in Elastic 50A is about 3.6e-11 to 6.7e-11 m2/s (own estimate), so a 0.4 mm layer is within 90 % in about 34-62 min on one face: a rubbery elastomer takes up its solvent roughly 10-60x faster than stock glassy resins take up water (solvent and water differ, so indicative only).
findings.source: https://formlabs.com/support/solvent-compatibility/ (HTML table parsed, saved at D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/data/bm-diffusion-kinetics/solvent.html); inversion in D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-diffusion-kinetics/diffusion_kinetics.py

findings.claim: Why '<1 % in 24 h' is not an equilibrium number: a 10 mm cube reaches only 7 % (D=1.4e-13), 19 % (1e-12), 51 % (1e-11) and 96 % (1e-10 m2/s) of its equilibrium uptake in 24 h; a 3 mm cube 23 %, 53 %, 97 % and 100 %. For Grey V5 the fitted equilibrium is about 3.7 %, four times the 24 h cube value. Earlier records state the 24 h figure is short-time; this puts numbers on how short.
findings.value: 10 mm cube, 24 h: 19 % of plateau at D=1e-12

findings.claim: Sintered PA12 (SLS) saturates fast compared with dense PA12: 8 x 8 mm cylinders gained mass 'sharply in the first 36 h' and reached 5.47 % (CF/PA12: 4.6 % after 24 h). Own apparent-D bracket 1.3e-11 to 3.0e-11 m2/s if 90-99 % was reached at 36-72 h (the curve could not be read numerically). This is mostly open pores filling, not polymer-matrix diffusion, and the 5.5 % is 3-4x the dense PA12 saturation (1.6 %) in the earlier record.
findings.evidence_quote: Δ m of PA12 sample increases sharply in the first 36 h as the samples were immersed into water. With further prolonged immersed time, the Δ m increases slowly and reaches a saturation state with Δ m of 5.47%.

findings.claim: Hot-pressed PA11 and PA12 (dense) took 'around two months' to reach water saturation (1.5 % in water, 0.8 % in humid air); specimen thickness for the durability series is not stated (sheets 1 mm, bulk 4 mm), so no D is derived.
findings.evidence_quote: After around two months, both PAs had the same saturation level for water and moisture absorption, i.e., 1.5% and 0.8%, respectively.

findings.claim: Epoxy-based stereolithography parts show anomalous (non-Fickian) water uptake that looks pseudo-Fickian, fitted by dual-sorption, diffusion-relaxation and dual-Fickian models. Quoted from a web-search extract of the Loughborough repository page; the page itself returned 403/anti-bot, and Crossref gives no abstract, so I did not read the paper or any D value.
findings.evidence_quote: Moisture transport in three different epoxy-based stereolithography materials has been investigated using mass uptake experiments. The results show that anomalous (non-Fickian) diffusion occurs to varying degrees in all three materials, the characteristic uptake appearing to be pseudo-Fickian.

findings.claim: Fickian (Case I) uptake is linear in the square root of time; the exponent n in M_t/M_inf = K t^n is 0.5 for Fick, 1 for Case II, in between for anomalous transport. Fickian behaviour needs polymer relaxation much faster than diffusion (rubbery state); Case II needs diffusion much faster than relaxation, typical of glassy polymers with strongly plasticising penetrants; anomalous when the two rates are comparable.
findings.source: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC7023388/fullTextXML (10.3390/polym12010138) and PMC11359223 (10.3390/polym16162265); classical sources Alfrey-Gurnee-Lloyd 1966, Thomas-Windle 1982 and Ritger-Peppas 1987 are DOI-verified only, not read
findings.evidence_quote: (1) Case I (Fick’s diffusion, n = 0.5). Polymer relaxation is much faster than water diffusion, and the diffusion is followed by an instantaneous response of the system, resulting in Fick’s behavior.

findings.claim: Which polymers: rubbery polymers are typically Fickian, many glassy polymers are Fickian at low solubility, Case II appears in glassy polymers with highly absorbent liquids when the absorbed liquid plasticises the polymer.
findings.evidence_quote: Rubbery polymers typically demonstrate Fickian diffusion due to their rapid response to environmental changes. Additionally, many glassy polymers also display Fickian diffusion under conditions where liquid solubility levels are relatively low.

findings.claim: Case II is a moving front: the dissolution/swelling front propagates as a wave into the undissolved glassy polymer, so the penetration time scales with distance (t ~ h / v, front speed v) rather than distance squared. A crossover length h* = D/v separates the two regimes (own scaling, no measured v for any Formlabs resin exists in what I found).
findings.evidence_quote: this frontal dissolution process in glassy miscible polymer films closely resembles the phenomenology of Case II non-Fickian diffusion commonly observed in the dissolution of glassy polymers by solvents

findings.claim: Water also plasticises the glassy resins, which couples D to the state of the network: Grey V5 bars keep only about 65 % of dry modulus after one week in water, PA6.6 falls to about 21 %. A swollen layer is softer, so the bilayer's n changes during the experiment, but the optimum curvature (3/2) does not depend on n.
findings.source: https://formlabs-media.formlabs.com/filer_public/dd/7f/dd7f3de9-55ae-4c82-ac52-408a4b5df64d/clear_resin_v5_tds___formlabs.pdf (modulus column); earlier agent spec-resin-chemistry.json for PA6.6

findings.claim: Bilayer curvature kinetics, own laminate calculation (active layer on one face, Fickian eigenstrain profile, bonded passive layer impermeable): at the optimum m^2 n = 1 the curvature reaches 50 %, 90 % and 99 % of its final value at 0.091, 0.719 and 1.65 h_a^2/D, identical for modulus ratios n = 1, 0.1, 0.01. Uptake itself needs 0.197, 0.849 and 1.78 h_a^2/D. Curvature leads mass uptake early (bending is dominated by the outer, wettest fibre) but equilibrium time is within 8 % of the uptake time. Away from the optimum the thickness ratio m shifts these (m = 2: 0.036, 0.528, 1.46; m = 0.5: 0.142, 0.789, 1.72).
findings.value: curvature t99 = 1.65 h_a^2/D at m^2 n = 1

findings.claim: Independent numerical check of the project record's 3/2 ceiling: the same laminate code run with uniform eigenstrain returns kappa h/d_eps = 1.500000 at (m,n) = (1,1), (3.162, 0.1), (10, 0.01) and (0.316, 10), all with m^2 n = 1, and equals the Timoshenko formula f(m,n) at (1, 0.1) = 0.99585 and (0.5, 3) = 1.49309. This confirms the formula numerically; it is not the Lean proof.

Verdict for a demonstration (one-face exposed active layer, t90): D ~ 1e-10 to 1e-9 m2/s (hydrogel, PEG-acrylate, porous or PDMS) finishes in minutes to hours at every thickness 0.2-1.6 mm (1.6 mm: 6 h at 1e-10). D ~ 1e-11 (Flexible 80A V2 class, Bis-GMA) gives 57 min (0.2 mm), 3.8 h (0.4), 15 h (0.8) and 2.5 d (1.6). D ~ 1e-12 (stock rigid acrylate resins, PET-G, PC) gives 9 h, 38 h, 6.3 d and 25 d. D ~ 3e-13 (PA11/PA12-class, nylon, TPU) gives 1.3 d, 5.2 d, 21 d and 12 weeks.
findings.value: hours: D>=1e-11 and h<=0.8 mm; days: D~1e-12 and h<=0.8 mm; weeks: D<=5e-13 and h>=0.8 mm

findings.claim: Printable thickness floors from the project record: 0.2 mm on Form 4 (Grey V5) and 0.3-0.6 mm on Fuse. At those floors one-face t90 is 1.8 d for 0.3 mm and 7.1 d for 0.6 mm of dense PA11 (D = 4.95e-13; 0.848 x h^2/D, e.g. 0.848 x (0.6e-3)^2 / 4.95e-13 = 6.2e5 s), and 9.4 h for 0.2 mm of a stock rigid resin at D = 1e-12.

key_claims.claim: Time to equilibrium scales as h^2/D with fixed constants: for an active layer exposed on one face (bilayer) t50 = 0.197, t90 = 0.848, t99 = 1.78 h^2/D; for both faces exposed multiply by 1/4. recommendations: Demonstration thickness: print the swelling layer at 0.2-0.4 mm and choose a high-D material (Flexible 80A V2 or a PEG-acrylate/hydrogel resin in Open Material Mode); expect 1-4 h for 0.2-0.4 mm Flexible 80A V2 at D about 1e-11 and minutes to an hour for PEG-acrylates. A stock rigid-resin or nylon active layer is a week-scale experiment.

Make the first measurement the one that is missing: immerse thickness-matched coupons (0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 mm, both faces open) and weigh at 1, 4, 24, 72 h and 7 d; fit D from the sqrt(t) slope and the plateau. This replaces my assumed-thickness inversions and also gives n, which decides Fickian versus relaxation-limited.
Report the exposure geometry and use h_eff = 2 h for a one-face bilayer; treat the time to read curvature as 1.65 h_a^2/D (99 %), not h^2/D.
If time is the constraint, warm the bath: PA11 data imply about 4x per 17 C (extrapolated about 10x at 50 C), but check the strain and modulus at that temperature separately.
Plan for drying being 2-4x slower than wetting if D rises with water content; time the dry half-cycle separately.
Do not read the Formlabs 24 h cube percentages as saturation values; use the 1 week figure or your own plateau.

could_not_find: A directly measured water diffusion coefficient for any Formlabs resin or powder. The values here are my own inversions of Formlabs' 1 day and 1 week mass gains and depend on an assumed specimen thickness (3.2 mm bars for Grey V5, 2 mm slabs for Flexible 80A V2); neither thickness is stated in the TDS. If the true thickness differs, D scales with its square.

Water D for Formlabs Nylon 11/12, TPU 90A (SLS). PA11 (hot-pressed), TPU (FDM) and sintered PA12 data are used as analogues; laser-sintered parts differ in porosity and crystallinity. The 2024 Villani paper on sintered PA12 (10.1007/s40964-024-00826-3) was behind an access redirect, so the earlier agent's snippet D = 4.34e-11 vs 4.17e-12 m2/s is still unconfirmed.

Any measured Case II front speed or anomalous-diffusion exponent n for water in a Formlabs resin or a printed SLA photopolymer. Ashcroft/Altaf 2012 (epoxy SLA) reports anomalous uptake but I could not read the paper (repository 403/anti-bot page) and have no D values from it.

Primary reading of the classical Case II and swelling-kinetics papers (Alfrey 1966, Thomas-Windle 1982, Ritger-Peppas 1987, Tanaka-Fillmore 1979, Crank's book): DOIs resolve in Crossref but the texts are paywalled; the n = 0.5 and 1 definitions are taken from open-access reviews, and the Crank slab constants are reproduced by my own numerics.

The diffusion coefficient in the PDMS paper is quoted second-hand (arXiv:2401.05139 citing its ref. 33) and the Randall & Doyle 2005 figure (~1e-9 m2/s) came from a search-tool snippet that I did not open; both are medium confidence.

Sideridou 2011 specimen thickness and test temperature (abstract only), so the dimethacrylate D range cannot be tied to a thickness; I also could not confirm from the abstract which medium each listed D belongs to beyond the statement that D was highest in water.

Thickness of the PA11/PA12 durability specimens in Bahrami 2021 (1 mm sheet or 4 mm bulk), so no D from the 'two months' saturation; the Zheng 2022 sintered-PA12 uptake curve was a figure whose values I could not read, so its apparent D is a bracket from an assumed 90-99 % at 36-72 h.
Swollen thickness and exact equilibrium swelling of the PEGDA/PEGMEMA gels; D from tau used the dry 2 mm thickness (lower bound) and 3 mm (upper), not a measurement.

Whether the Formlabs Flexible 80A (cube table) and Flexible 80A V2 (TDS) are different resin versions; kinetics alone cannot explain the factor of about 5-10 between 0.7 % and 8 %, so this remains open (the earlier agents left it open too).
Humid-air (not immersion) diffusivities of any stock Formlabs resin; all Formlabs data are full-immersion, and Aniskevich shows D itself shifts 2-4x with humidity level for half of the filaments.
Crossref check of the Bahrami 2021 DOI (10.3390/polym13203553) was not run in this session; it is marked verified=false although it was printed in the Europe PMC XML that I read.

confirmed: Flexible 80A V2 +8 %/+9 % mass and +3 %/+7 % volume in DI water (spec-formlabs-materials.json), now by word coordinates
Grey V5 bars +1.38 % (1 d), +3.23 % (1 wk) with modulus 88.63 % and 65.29 % (spec-resin-chemistry.json): the 'scrambled table' mapping is correct
Elastic 50A V2 39.2 % in isopropanol vs <0.1 % for Rigid 10K (24 h, 1 cm cubes)
Aniskevich filament D 0.001-0.0151 mm2/h and swelling 0.15-0.25 % (spec-bilayer-physics.json)
Low-cost acrylate resins take 2.5 to >8 days to saturate (1 mm plates; spec-resin-chemistry.json)
deepened: No D for any Formlabs resin was found: still no direct measurement, but two derived estimates now exist (Grey V5 about 3e-12, Flexible 80A V2 >= 6e-12 m2/s, thickness assumed)
'Under 1 % in 24 h': the number is right but is a kinetic snapshot; equilibrium for Grey V5 is about 3.7 % (4x higher)
spec-bilayer-physics.json used tau = h^2/D: for a one-face layer this is within 18 % of t90 (0.848 h^2/D) but overstates both-face t90 by 4.7x; exact constants are now given
contradicted_or_qualified: design-biomaterial.json 'D about 1e-11 m2/s, 90 % in 4 h for a 0.8 mm layer' is a both-faces-open number (t90 = 0.212 l^2/D = 3.8 h); for a one-face bilayer layer it is 15.1 h. The D itself is consistent with my Flexible 80A V2 estimate (9e-12, >= 6e-12), but it rests on an unverified 2 mm slab.

The earlier note that Flexible 80A uptake differs ten-fold between cube table (0.7 %) and TDS (8 %) cannot be explained by diffusion kinetics (predicted cube value >= 3.8 %), which favours a resin-version difference.

fleet.label: bm-formlabs-all-resins
fleet.topic: Every Formlabs resin and powder, as a design space
fleet.summary: Fetched 2026-11-12 (UTC): the Formlabs materials catalogue, the solvent-compatibility table, the data-sheet index, 57 product pages, 54 English technical data sheets (TDS, PDF; 7 more are web-format TDS pages) and 18 safety data sheets (all saved with URL, date, byte size and sha256 in data/formlabs-tds/MANIFEST.tsv). The table has 48 rows: 23 current Form 4-family SLA resins (including casting, ceramic and colour bases), 7 Form 4B medical resins, 10 legacy or Form 3-only resins, and 8 powders (Nylon 12, 12 White, 12 Tough, 12 GF, 11, 11 CF, TPU 90A, and Polypropylene, which is no longer on the catalogue); Nylon 11 Pro and the six Alpha resins are in findings (web-format TDS). Per material: tensile and flexural modulus, UTS, elongation, Shore, HDT, density where published, 24 h cube water and IPA uptake, biocompatibility standards, minimum layer thickness, printers and the post-cure recipe from the TDS footnotes, state by state (green and post-cured). Main results. (1) Earlier agents are confirmed on the cube table (all current resins 0.0-0.9% water in 24 h; Elastic 50A V2 39.2% IPA vs Rigid 10K <0.1%) but one claim must be narrowed: Flexible 80A Resin V2 gains +8% mass and +3% volume in 1 day in water (+9%/+7% in 1 week) in its own TDS slab test, so "stock resins gain under 1%" is false for that resin, and the 0.7% quoted for Flexible 80A in the cube table is the V1 row. (2) The Grey V5 one-week water figures (+3.23% mass, modulus to 65%) are now read cleanly and confirmed. (3) Flexible 50A is the renamed Elastic 50A V2. (4) Chemistry: all Form 4 resins except Silicone 40A are methacrylate/urethane-methacrylate (SDS), so acrylate pairs can co-cure; Silicone 40A is polysiloxane with no bonding evidence. (5) Ranking: the best pairs are Flexible 80A V2 (active) with Rigid 10K, Rigid 4000, Tough 2000 V2, Grey/Clear V5 or Tough 1000 (passive); applying the project 3/2 law with the 0.2 mm wall limit, the printable curvature is best with soft partners (Flexible 50A 26.6 /m, Silicone 40A 20.1 /m at 1 day) because the optimum thickness ratio n^(-1/2) is impractical for stiff partners (8.3 mm of Flexible 80A V2 over 0.2 mm of Rigid 10K). (6) Gaps: no humid-air swelling, no diffusivity, no elastomer moduli, no measured adhesion, slab thickness of the 80A V2 test unstated. All swelling-based curvature numbers are own calculations with stated assumptions and should be replaced by coupon measurements.
fleet.lay_summary: Formlabs sells about sixty liquid resins and a handful of nylon powders for its 3D printers. We downloaded the official data sheets for all of them and lined up how stiff each one is and how much water or alcohol it soaks up. Almost all of them barely drink water, less than one percent of their weight in a day, so they would hardly change shape in humid air. One soft resin is the exception: it swells about three percent in volume after a day in water, which is enough to make a thin strip bend. Think of a strip of wet paper stuck to a strip of plastic: the paper swells, the plastic does not, and the pair curls. The best pairs are that soft resin glued to a stiff one from the same chemical family. Nobody has published how strongly two Formlabs materials stick to each other, or how fast humid air gets into them, so the next step is a small printed test strip, not more reading.

glossary.plain: a printer that hardens liquid resin layer by layer with a violet light
a printer that fuses nylon or rubber powder layer by layer with a laser
the maker's technical data sheet (properties) and safety data sheet (ingredients)
how stiff a material is: the force needed to stretch or bend it a little; bigger means stiffer
a rough stiffness taken as stress at a fixed stretch divided by that stretch; used here where no modulus is published
hardness scales from pressing a pin in; A for rubbers, D for hard plastics
heat deflection temperature: the temperature at which a loaded bar starts to sag
freshly printed and washed, versus after extra light and heat that finishes hardening it
taking up water or solvent so the part gets heavier and bigger
isopropyl alcohol, the liquid used to wash printed resin parts
two thin layers of different materials bonded together; if one swells it bends the pair
how tightly a strip bends, in 1/metre; 20 per metre means a circle of radius 5 cm
the two chemical families here: plastic-like acrylics that cure together, versus silicone, which sticks poorly to other things
a paid Formlabs setting that lets the printer run non-Formlabs resin or powder
a simple model of how rubber stretches, used to correct the rough stiffness estimate

findings.claim: RANKING (a) modulus contrast, SLA pairs, top 6. Method (script pairs.py, saved): 19 materials = 12 Form 4-family SLA resins with full TDS plus 7 Fuse powders, 171 unordered pairs. (a) modulus contrast = ratio of post-cured tensile moduli; elastomers have no published modulus, so secant = stress at 50% elongation / 0.5 (own estimate: Flexible 80A V2 5.8, Flexible 50A 1.8, Silicone 40A 0.8, TPU 90A 12.2 MPa). (b) swelling contrast = absolute difference of 24 h water mass gain in percentage points (1 cm cube table; Flexible 80A V2 uses its +8% slab value; "<x" read as x). (c) adhesion class 3 = both resins are (meth)acrylate photopolymers on the same Form 4 (SDS), 1 = polysiloxane vs acrylate, SLA vs SLS, or two powders (no co-print). Combined = sum of the three tie-averaged ranks (lower is better).
