could_not_find: Equilibrium swelling and wet modulus for any hydrogel printed on a Form 3 or Form 4 (the only Formlabs print is Form 2 PEGDMA; Form 3 appears in other papers only as the maker of mould or spacer parts). The definition and units of Burke's 'swelling ratio' 41.7 did not extract.

Any peer-reviewed measurement of a HEMA/pHEMA vat-printed gel's swelling ratio, equilibrium water content or modulus. The pHEMA equilibrium water content of roughly 40% from contact-lens literature is unverified background and I did not use it.
A measured water diffusivity or time to equilibrium for printed PEGDA or GelMA layers at 0.1-1 mm: the only measured D is for a polyampholyte gel, so tau figures are order-of-magnitude.
Per-sample bending radii of the GelMA bilayer (only the 11-20 mm range is in text; per-sample values are in Fig. 5a), so my 11 mm prediction cannot be compared sample by sample.
Hydrogel fatigue numbers for printed PEG or GelMA actuators (cycles to failure, threshold toughness): the review says few studies go beyond 10 cycles.
Drying-crack thresholds (critical thickness, humidity, rate) for printed hydrogels; only the arXiv mechanism papers and APS meeting abstracts (seen as search snippets, not opened) were found.
Numerical swelling for PEGDA/PPGDMA (Zhao 2018) and the polyurethane/sodium acrylate cuff (Hiendlmeier 2023): full texts paywalled, as in the earlier agents.
Whether a water-based hydrogel resin is safe for the Form 4 resin tank film, cartridge or wiper, and whether Form 4 can pause mid-print for resin exchange; Open Material Mode price. No source found.
Quantitative leachable (TPO, LAP, absorber) amounts from printed hydrogels into water; only a wash-time result for one resin (Warr 2020).

A Springer paper (J. Mater. Res., doi 10.1557/s43578-021-00411-2) that a search linked to PEGDA on a Form 2 could not be opened (access redirect), so I did not use it; an acrylamide/PEGDA700 + cellulose nanocrystal Form 2 paper named in a search snippet was not located in Europe PMC.
Primary figures for Nichol 2010 (moduli and swelling are in figures); I used Yue 2015's restatement of them.

My use of the Timoshenko formula assumes small-strain linear elasticity and a swollen modulus; hydrogels at 7% to 70% strain and with time-varying modulus violate this, and no measurement of f for hydrogels on stiff resins exists.

fleet.summary: PRELIMINARY SCAN ONLY: not legal advice, not a freedom-to-operate opinion, not a patentability opinion. Run 2026-11-12. Google Patents refuses curl and WebFetch (HTTP 503) from this network, but pages and the search endpoint worked from a real Chrome tab, so every row in the table below was read from its Google Patents page (claim 1, assignee, dates, machine-derived status); EP 4019251 B1 was also read from the EPO publication server. Compared with the earlier agent (agents/spec-ip-landscape.json), which worked from the USPTO search only: (a) the three Harvard / MIT-Harvard applications it left as 'grant not determined' are all Abandoned; (b) the three building-scale wood-bilayer families whose claims it could not read are now read, and all three are narrow: ETH/Empa WO2018033422 claims a lever-coupled shading device and is Ceased; Stuttgart EP4019251 B1 (granted 2026-03-25, opposition window still open) and the Empa/ETH/Stuttgart German national phase DE112019001411 claim pre-conditioning layers at one humidity so the glued part self-shapes at a target climate; none covers a printed resin or powder element; (c) the granted MIT/Stratasys US 11155025 B2 claim 1 is narrower than the earlier summary implied (two joints in series, a planar member, members that touch to limit curvature) but it is the live patent nearest a resin-printed differential-swelling part and runs to about 2034-02-25. CROWDED: printed stimulus-responsive objects in general (MIT/Stratasys), hygromorphic coatings and composites (MIT, NTU, USAF), hydrogel 4D printing (Harvard, now abandoned, UT, CityU, Accenture), wood bilayer building parts (ETH, Empa, Stuttgart), and, as prior ART rather than live rights, the bilayer mechanics themselves: the ETH specification already cites Timoshenko 1925, states that an optimum thickness ratio exists (0.2-0.3 for wood) and reports measured curvature changes. OPEN, by keyword: zero Google Patents documents combine a theorem prover or proof assistant with material, geometry or additive-manufacturing design (queries listed in the table); the nearest are a 2010 Microsoft design-space exploration patent (expired, software architectures) and a 2020 PARC satisfiability-solver manufacturing planner (live, integrated circuits), plus a granted Toyota computational design method for shape-morphing structures (live), which shows that design-method claims in this field are grantable. WHAT THE TEAM COULD PLAUSIBLY CLAIM, if it files before public disclosure (counsel to confirm grace-period rules): (1) a design-and-verification METHOD in which candidate geometries or layups are released to a printer only with a machine-checked proof that they satisfy stated laws (most open, but must show a concrete technical effect); (2) a certified FILE FORMAT binding geometry, material assignment and a proof (open, but data-structure claims face eligibility objections); (3) a specific GEOMETRY found by the constrained search with a measured, unexpected response (narrow); (4) a COMPOSITION (least likely, since stock Formlabs resins are the vendor's formulations and hygromorphic compositions are heavily claimed). 'License your patent' presupposes a patent the team may not hold: no filing by the team was searched for by name or found. Limits: Google's status labels are machine-derived and not authoritative; no Espacenet, Patentscope, CNIPA, JPO or CPC-class search was possible; Formlabs's own patents were not searched; absence of keyword hits is not proof of absence.
fleet.lay_summary: This is a first look, not legal advice, at who already owns ideas close to ours. Plenty of people have patented things that bend or curl when they get wet or when the air gets damp, including MIT, Harvard, two Swiss universities and Stuttgart, so we cannot claim 'a plate that curls in humidity' as ours. Several of the best-known older filings have already lapsed or been dropped, which makes them public knowledge anyone may use rather than fences. What we did not find anywhere is a patent that uses a computer-checked proof to decide which shapes are allowed to be printed, a bit like a spell-checker that refuses to print a design unless the maths is signed off. If the team files on that method before showing it publicly, that is where something ownable might sit; the team does not yet hold such a patent, so there is nothing to license today. A patent lawyer must check all of this before anyone relies on it.

glossary.plain: A quick keyword look at patent records, not the thorough professional search a lawyer would order.
A lawyer's formal opinion on whether making or selling something would infringe someone else's live patent; this report is not one.
The set of filings in different countries that all stem from one first application.
The first and usually broadest sentence in a patent that says exactly what is protected.
The earliest filing date, used to decide who was first.
Anything made public before a filing date, including old patents and papers, which can block a later patent.
Labels meaning the owner no longer holds an enforceable right; Google's labels are automatic and can be wrong.
Changing shape when the humidity changes.
Two glued layers that swell by different amounts, so the pair curls like a bimetal strip.
3D printing something designed to change shape later, time being the fourth dimension.
Software that checks a mathematical proof step by step so no gap can slip through.
A cheap early patent filing that fixes a date while the full application is prepared.
A fixed period after a European patent is granted in which anyone may ask the patent office to revoke it.
Two kinds of 3D printing: SLA hardens liquid resin with light, SLS fuses plastic powder with a laser.

findings.claim: The ETH/Empa specification states Timoshenko's 1925 result as prior knowledge: for each stiffness ratio an optimum thickness ratio exists, and for wood it is 0.2-0.3. The thickness-ratio optimum of a hygro-bilayer is therefore published, patent-document prior art (it is an optimum, not the 3/2 ceiling).
findings.evidence_quote: For each stiffness ratio, there exists an optimum thickness ratio to achieve the same maximum bending (Timoshenko, Analysis of Bimetal thermostat, 1925).

findings.claim: The same specification reports measured curvature changes for beech 4 mm + spruce 0.8 mm bilayers going from 85% to 35% RH in 24 h: 0.00818 mm^-1 (plain beech), 0.00971 (horizontal strips), 0.01011 (diagonal strips).
findings.evidence_quote: The homogenous (the sample were the beech was not milled) had a MC loss of 31 % and a change of curvature of 0.00818 mm"1.

findings.claim: Own calculation using the project-record ceiling kappa*h/d_eps <= 3/2: the plain beech/spruce bilayer (h=4.8 mm, dkappa=0.00818 mm^-1) needs a differential free strain of at least 0.00818*4.8/1.5 = 0.0262 (2.6%); strips give 3.1% and 3.2%. This is consistent with the patent's stated layer difference of at least 3%, and f(m=0.2,n=25)=1.5 shows the patent's 0.2-0.3 thickness ratio sits at the ceiling when the modulus ratio is about 25 (m^2 n = 1); that modulus ratio is not stated in the patent and I did not verify it.

University of Stuttgart EP 4019251 B1 is granted (mention of grant 2026-03-25), Active, with only an EP family listed; claim 1 is a method that obtains target climate data (RH2, T2), selects layer type/orientation/thickness, pre-conditions at a different RH1/T1, bonds, and relies on the part changing to a final shape in the target climate. Opposition may be filed within nine months of the grant mention, i.e. to about 2026-12-25 (my arithmetic).

findings.claim: Literature check: arXiv API totalResults is 0 for 'theorem prover' AND 'material design', 'proof assistant' AND 'additive manufacturing', 'Lean 4' AND 'metamaterial', and 'proof assistant' AND '4D printing'; Crossref queries returned only software/hardware verification and generic additive-manufacturing standards. The closest published work is Lean formalisation of chemical physics (Bobbin 2024), not a design gate.

Hygromorphic building-element research is very active and public: a 2025 paper on rice-husk 4D-printed hygromorphic building skin and a 2026 chapter on a simulation framework for porosity-driven hygromorphic bilayers both resolve in Crossref, as does the 2024 Nature Communications weather-responsive 4D-printed shading paper. These are prior art against broad claims on printed hygromorphic facade elements.

Google Patents returned zero documents for hygroscopic 'shape-changing' facade panel 3D printed, and only five for 'hygromorphic' AND '3D printing' (MIT US9931829, CMU US20220322599, Accenture EP3988317, Purdue US20260001811, IIT EP4783825): printed hygromorphic building elements are thinly patented by keyword, with the heavy prior art in papers.

recommendations: Ask a patent attorney about a provisional filing BEFORE the paper, repo or live dashboard publicly discloses the law-constrained design pipeline; public disclosure can be prior art against later filings in most jurisdictions (grace-period rules differ; counsel to confirm).

Frame any claim as a design-and-verification method with a concrete technical effect (for example a slicer or printer that refuses to build without a valid machine-checked certificate, or a measured property guaranteed by the certified bound), not as a humidity bilayer. A certified file format needs a technical-effect hook to survive eligibility objections.

Do not describe the proof of concept as a 'new material composition' if it uses stock Formlabs resins or powders; a specific verified geometry with a measured, unexpected response is the more defensible physical claim.

fleet.label: bm-lay-analogies
fleet.topic: Plain-language explanations that are also correct
fleet.summary: Nine plain-language explanations were written, each with a 3-6 sentence paragraph, an everyday comparison, a note on where the comparison breaks, a one-line common wrong idea and its source; all quoted evidence was checked word for word against the pages and PDFs fetched in this run (quote_check.json; a doctored control quote correctly fails). Topics: pine cone opening (Reyssat and Mahadevan 2009: opens dry, closes wet, dead tissue works, active cells change length about 10 % between dry and saturated air), bilayer as bimetal strip, what a Lean law is, proof versus simulation, why a ceiling rules out designs, what 0.7 % water uptake means, why thin is faster, why a stiffer partner does not curl more, and why Elastic 50A swells in alcohol but not water. New beyond the earlier files: (1) the 3/2 ceiling is readable in the 1863 bimetal formula, kappa = 3/(2a) x mismatch/h with a = 1 + (square) >= 1, which I showed equals the project coefficient to 7e-16 over 200,000 random cases, so a layperson can see the ceiling without Lean; Holstov 2015 had already plotted it, so it is not a new discovery, only a newly proved one. (2) I re-ran the Lean check (5 theorems, 0 errors, 0 sorryAx) and two false versions (ceiling 7/5), which Lean refuses. (3) 0.7 % water uptake is 7 mg per gram, about a sixth of a drop for a 1.2 g cube; I estimate 0.09-0.28 % length change, and a bilayer magnifies a stretch by 0.75 L/h = 37.5 (tip moves 1.3-4.2 mm on a 40 mm, 0.8 mm strip at best). (4) CONTRADICTION: the earlier claim that every current Formlabs SLA resin gains under 1 % in water is false for Flexible 80A V2 (+8 % mass in 1 day, ASTM D471 slab); the 0.7 % is the cube test on a differently named resin row; the sibling file bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json reached the same correction and I confirm it from the PDF. (5) The 39 % isopropanol figure is Elastic 50A V2 (V1 is 25.6 %), confirmed against Rigid 10K <0.1 %. (6) The thin-is-faster rule is a 4x law only ideally; pine cones measure exponents 1.3-1.5, and bimetal heat is 19 million times faster than water in dense resin, which is where the bimetal analogy fails most. No measured humid-air swelling or water diffusivity exists for any Formlabs resin; all such figures here are labelled estimates.
fleet.lay_summary: A pine cone is made of two layers stuck together. When the air dries out, one layer shrinks and the other does not, so each scale bends open. Printed plastic can do the same thing if two layers swell by different amounts, but plastic swells far less than a pine cone does. We checked, with a computer program that accepts only complete proofs, that a two-layer strip can never curl tighter than a fixed limit set by its thickness and how much it swells. That means we can rule out some shapes on paper before wasting a print. Thin strips respond faster, but the time falls with the square of the thickness, so a strip half as thick is about four times quicker in theory and about two and a half times in real cones.

glossary.plain: Two layers stuck face to face, as in the scale of a pine cone.
Two metals bonded together that bend when heated because they expand by different amounts.
How much more one layer lengthens than the other, as a fraction of its length.
How sharply a strip bends: one divided by the radius of the circle it follows.
A limit that no choice of layers can beat; here, 1.5 times the mismatch divided by the strip's thickness.
A computer program that checks mathematical proofs step by step and refuses incomplete ones.
A proof covers every case at once; a simulation only checks the cases it tries.
How much heavier a part gets when it absorbs water, as a percent of its starting weight.
Slow spreading of water into a material; D says how fast, in square metres per second.
How hard a material pushes back when you stretch or bend it.
A material that changes shape when humidity changes.
Liquid plastic hardened by light in a printer (Form 4 uses this).

findings.claim: Pine cones open when dried and close when wetted.
findings.evidence_quote: Using the pine cone as an example that opens when dried and closes when wet

findings.claim: Fallen pine cones are dead and still open and close repeatedly with humidity, so no living process is needed.
findings.evidence_quote: But when dead fallen dry cones are moved into a humid environment, they close and open again when dried, an experiment that may be repeated many times.

findings.claim: The cone scale works through a two-layer structure: an active outer layer of long thick-walled cells that lengthen when humid and shorten when dry, and an inner passive layer that responds much less.
findings.evidence_quote: closely packed long parallel thick-walled cells respond by expanding longitudinally when exposed to humidity

findings.claim: Reyssat and Mahadevan state the scale tissue behaves like a bimetallic strip, with humidity replacing temperature.
findings.value: bimetal analogy used by the cone researchers
findings.evidence_quote: Consequently, the tissue behaves like a thermally actuated bimetallic strip that curves in response to temperature changes because of the differential expansion of the constituent strips that are glued together.

findings.claim: Measured hygrometric expansion coefficient of the cone's active cells is 0.001 per percent relative humidity; over 0 to 100 percent RH that is a length change of about 10 percent (own multiplication).
findings.evidence_quote: the hygrometric expansion coefficient of the cells that characterizes the strain per relative humidity α = 0.001 ± 0.0001

findings.claim: The authors expect a curvature change of about 1.3 per cm for a 1 mm thick scale going from zero to saturated humidity, which gives a scale-opening angle of roughly 75 degrees.
findings.evidence_quote: Δκ ∼ 1.3 cm −1 (for h ∼ 1 mm and Δϕ = 100, i.e. relative humidity changing from zero to saturation)

findings.claim: Cone researchers built a paper-and-plastic copy that curls on drying and straightens on wetting (everyday model of the cone).
findings.evidence_quote: we also build bilayer hygromorphs of a thin layer of plastic attached to paper which curl upon drying and straighten on wetting

findings.claim: A bimetal strip converts temperature change into mechanical displacement, and the sideways displacement is much larger than the lengthways expansion of either metal (the bend amplifies a small stretch).
findings.evidence_quote: The sideways displacement of the strip is much larger than the small lengthways expansion in either of the two metals.

findings.claim: The classical (1863, Villarceau) bimetal curvature formula is kappa = 3/(2a) x (mismatch strain)/h with a = 1 + (E1 h1^2 - E2 h2^2)^2 / (4 E1 h1 E2 h2 h^2). Because a is 1 plus a square, a >= 1, so kappa <= 1.5 x mismatch / h, with equality when E1 h1^2 = E2 h2^2. This is the project's 3/2 ceiling and its optimum m^2 n = 1 in older notation.

The project's coefficient f(m,n) equals 1.5/a of the Villarceau form to rounding error: largest absolute difference 6.7e-16 over 200,000 random thickness and stiffness pairs spanning four decades each.

CONTRADICTS the idea that the 3/2 ceiling is new: Holstov, Bridgens and Farmer (2015) plotted f(m,n) for many stiffness ratios and wrote that its maximum stays at 1.5. What the project adds is the kernel-checked proof and the closed-form optimum. (Confirms the sibling file bm-wood-cellulose-hygromorphs.json; also shows the ceiling is visible in an 1863 formula.)
findings.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

findings.claim: Holstov et al. warn equal layer thickness costs response in their fibreglass-and-wood example: up to 60 percent. My recomputation with n=30 gives f(1,30)=0.545, a 63.7 percent loss against 1.5.
findings.evidence_quote: If the layers were of equal thickness, for the same overall thickness of the composite the response would be reduced by as much as 60%.

findings.claim: When one layer is infinitely stiffer than the other (stiffness ratio 0 or infinity) there is no bending; and at equal thickness the coefficient changes by less than 10 percent when the stiffness ratio varies from 0.3 to 3.5 (my calculation: 0.86 percent).
findings.value: f=0 at n->0 or inf; <10 % change n=0.3..3.5
findings.evidence_quote: In the limit where n is 0 or +∞, one of the layers is infinitely more rigid than the other, and f ( m,n ) = 0: no bending occurs.

findings.claim: With a stiffness ratio of 10 and equal thickness the coefficient is 0.9959, 66.4 percent of the 1.5 ceiling (a 34 percent loss); at the optimal thickness ratio m = n^-1/2 it is exactly 1.5 for every n tested (0.001 to 10000).

The Lean kernel check of HygromorphCeilingCheck.lean, re-run 2026-11-12 with the project's check.sh (toolchain leanprover/lean4:v4.35.0), reports errors=0, sorryAx=0, and five theorems each depending only on propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The theorem bilayer_rules_out says any claimed curvature above 3/2 x mismatch / h cannot be reached.
findings.evidence_quote: theorem bilayer_rules_out (h m n Δε κ_claimed : ℝ) (hh : 0 < h) (hm : 0 < m) (hn : 0 < n)

findings.claim: Lean refuses a false version of the law: with the ceiling stated as 7/5 instead of 3/2 (value 1.4 instead of 1.5) Lean gives 'error: linarith failed to find a contradiction', and a version with a 'sorry' placeholder is listed as depending on sorryAx. A failure to prove is a refusal, not itself a disproof; the disproof of 7/5 is that the optimum gives exactly 3/2 (theorem bilayerCurvature_optimal).
findings.evidence_quote: error: linarith failed to find a contradiction

findings.claim: Lean's own documentation says an interactive prover requires every step to be justified down to basic axioms, in contrast to automated reasoning systems that can trade soundness for power.
findings.evidence_quote: every rule of inference and every step of a calculation has to be justified by appealing to prior definitions and theorems, all the way down to basic axioms and rules

findings.claim: Lean's documentation notes that verifying a real system requires first describing it in mathematical terms, so the proof covers the description, not the object (basis of the 'where the analogy breaks' note for E3).
findings.value: description step is outside the proof
findings.evidence_quote: formal verification requires describing hardware and software systems in mathematical terms

findings.claim: Sampling 2,000,000 random thickness and stiffness combinations (log-uniform, 1e-3 to 1e3) gave a maximum coefficient of 1.4999999999740508, never above 1.5, and the best sample had m^2 n close to 1; this is evidence, not proof.
Euler's polynomial n^2+n+41 gives a prime for each n from 0 to 39 (40 passes) and first fails at n=40 with 1681 = 41 x 41; a worked example of tests passing then failing.

Ceiling arithmetic R_min = h / (1.5 x mismatch): h=0.8 mm and 0.2 percent mismatch give R_min=266.7 mm; a 50 mm radius at h=0.8 mm needs at least 1.067 percent mismatch; at h=0.4 mm it needs 0.533 percent.
Formlabs' solvent table is a 24-hour weight-gain test on printed 1 cm cubes that were washed and post-cured: it is neither an equilibrium value nor a size change.
findings.evidence_quote: Formlabs measures resistance to solvents by observing, measuring, and weighing printed cubes (originally measuring 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm) before and after immersion in a solvent for 24 hours.

findings.claim: Confirms the earlier record: on the current Formlabs page Elastic 50A Resin V2 shows 39.2 percent in isopropyl alcohol and 0.7 percent in water; Rigid 10K shows <0.1 percent in both. Column order from the page header (Isopropyl Alcohol is the 10th solvent, Water the 18th).
Same row for Rigid 10K Resin (both IPA and water <0.1 percent).

Elastic 50A Resin V1 on the same page takes up 25.6 percent IPA and 2.3 percent water, so the '39 percent' belongs to V2 and V1 is the Formlabs resin with the highest water gain in that table among the rows read.

The row labelled plain 'Flexible 80A Resin' shows 0.7 percent in water and 11.7 percent in IPA (same 24 h cube test). This is the '0.7 percent' in the earlier record; the page does not state a version.

CONTRADICTS the earlier claim (spec-resin-chemistry.json) that every current Formlabs SLA resin gains under 1 percent mass in water. The Flexible 80A V2 data sheet (ASTM D471 full immersion) lists deionized water at 1 day: hardness -26 Shore A points, mass +8 percent, volume +3 percent; 1 week: mass +9 percent, volume +7 percent. Different resin version and method from the 0.7 percent cube; both are real. (Same correction was already made by the sibling file bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json; confirmed here from the PDF.)

Caution on the Flexible 80A V2 volume column: for isooctane the table gives +56 percent mass but +164 percent volume at 1 week, more than simple mass-additivity allows (about +90 to +100 percent using an assumed resin density 1.1 to 1.21 and isooctane density 0.69, both unverified background); for water volume (+3 %) is below mass-additivity (about +9 %). So strain derived from the volume column is uncertain; I use 0.12 percent length per percent mass only as a low-end figure.
Clear Resin V5 density is 1.21 g/cm3 (ASTM D792); used as a stand-in density for a printed Formlabs resin cube (about 1.2 g for 1 cm^3). Density of Elastic 50A and Flexible 80A was not read.
findings.evidence_quote: Density 1.21 g/cm3

findings.claim: A 0.7 percent uptake is 7 mg of water per gram of resin, about 8.5 mg in a 1.21 g cube; at 0.05 mL per drop (and 1 g/mL water, unverified background) that is 0.14 drop per gram and 0.17 drop per cube; 8 percent would be 80 mg per gram, 1.6 drops.
findings.evidence_quote: In this usage, a drop is typically considered to be approximately 0.05 mL.

findings.claim: Wikipedia itself warns a drop is not a fixed volume, which limits the drop comparison to an order of magnitude.
findings.evidence_quote: The volume of a drop is not well defined

findings.claim: Estimated length change for 0.7 percent mass gain: low 0.087 percent (using 0.124 percent length per percent mass from the Flexible 80A V2 1-day volume +3 %, cube-root) and high 0.282 percent (ideal volume mixing, resin density 1.21 / 3 = 0.40 per percent mass). On 40 mm that is 0.035 to 0.113 mm. Both are estimates; no measured strain exists for a Formlabs resin in the sources read.

At the ceiling with a perfectly passive partner, a 40 mm long, 0.8 mm thick strip with those mismatches reaches radius 616 to 189 mm and a tip deflection of 1.3 to 4.2 mm; tip deflection divided by elongation is about 0.75 L/h = 37.5 in both cases.

Reyssat and Mahadevan: with a diffusion constant of about 1e-9 m2/s and a 1 mm active layer, tau = h^2/D is about 1000 s; but the measured fits are drying 96 h_a^1.5 min and wetting 29 h_a^1.3 min (h_a in mm), so the real exponents are 1.5 and 1.3, not 2.
findings.evidence_quote: the shrinking (drying) time varies as τ d = 96 h a 1.5 min and the swelling (wetting) time varies as τ d = 29 h a 1.3 min (where h a is in mm)

findings.claim: Reyssat and Mahadevan's order-of-magnitude statement of the square law.
findings.evidence_quote: For molecular pores, D ∼ 10 −9 m 2 s −1 , the thickness of the active layer h a ∼ 1 mm and τ = h a 2 / D ∼ 1000 s

findings.claim: Doubling thickness multiplies the time by 4 in the ideal square law, by 2.83 for the measured pine drying exponent (1.5) and 2.46 for the wetting exponent (1.3).

Time to 90 percent of final water for a layer open on one face is 0.848 h^2/D (50 percent: 0.197, 99 percent: 1.78), from the Crank slab series, solved by bisection in calc.py (matches sibling file bm-diffusion-kinetics.json). For D = 1e-12 m2/s: 0.2 mm 9.4 h; 0.4 mm 37.7 h; 0.8 mm 150.8 h (6.3 days); 1.6 mm 603 h (25 days). For D = 1e-11: 0.94, 3.8, 15.1, 60.3 h. For D = 1e-9: 34 s, 2.3 min, 9 min, 36 min.

A water diffusion coefficient of 0.85e-12 m2/s was reported for 3D-printed PMMA dental resin (37 C, a non-Formlabs resin); the sibling file recomputed about 2.6e-13 from the same paper's medians. I found no measured water diffusivity for any Formlabs resin, so 1e-12 is an order of magnitude, and times could be about 3 times longer.
findings.evidence_quote: Diffusion coefficient was calculated and values as D = 1.02–1.15 × 10 −12 m 2 /s for milled and 0.85 × 10 −12 m 2 /s for printed materials were obtained.

findings.claim: Thermal diffusivity of AISI 1010 steel is 18.8 mm2/s and of nylon 0.09 mm2/s. Heat reaches 90 percent equilibrium across 1 mm of steel in 0.045 s (0.848 x 1^2 / 18.8), against about 9.8 days for water in a 1 mm dense resin at D=1e-12 m2/s: a ratio of 1.9e7 in diffusivity.
findings.evidence_quote: Steel , AISI 1010 (0.1% carbon) 18.8

findings.claim: Force and stroke trade against thickness: curvature falls as 1/h while blocking force rises roughly as h^2 (project record, own beam-theory derivation in spec-bilayer-physics.json, not re-derived here), so thin is faster but weaker.

Project record, not re-derived here: six beech bilayers from the ETH dataset reach kappa x h / mismatch of 1.35, 1.50, 1.53, 1.36, 1.04, 0.91; the 1.53 uses nominal swelling coefficients, so it signals uncertainty, not a counter-example to the ceiling.

Readability check of the nine explanation paragraphs (Flesch-Kincaid grade, own implementation with a syllable heuristic) is reported in readability.json; none exceeded 11 (range 6.3 to 10.6, mean 9.4); this is a rough machine estimate, not a reader test.

key_claims.claim: A pine-cone scale is a two-layer structure that opens when dried and closes when wetted, and dead fallen cones keep doing this, so the explanation needs no living process.
key_claims.evidence_quote: But when dead fallen dry cones are moved into a humid environment, they close and open again when dried, an experiment that may be repeated many times.

key_claims.claim: The curl ceiling kappa <= 1.5 x mismatch / h is both Lean-checked (this run: 5 theorems, 0 errors, 0 sorryAx) and visible in the classical 1863 bimetal formula, where kappa = 3/(2a) x mismatch/h and a = 1 + a square >= 1; it is not new (Holstov 2015 plotted it) but its proof is.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

key_claims.claim: Formlabs' 0.7 % is a 24-hour weight gain of a 1 cm cube for the rows Flexible 80A and Elastic 50A V2, not an equilibrium value and not a size change; Flexible 80A V2 gains +8 % mass in one day by another method, so no single 'water uptake of Formlabs resins' exists.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Formlabs measures resistance to solvents by observing, measuring, and weighing printed cubes (originally measuring 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm) before and after immersion in a solvent for 24 hours.

key_claims.claim: Diffusion time scales as thickness squared in the ideal case (4x for double thickness), but pine-cone data give exponents 1.5 (drying) and 1.3 (wetting), so real strips are 2.5 to 4 times faster when half as thick.
key_claims.evidence_quote: the shrinking (drying) time varies as τ d = 96 h a 1.5 min and the swelling (wetting) time varies as τ d = 29 h a 1.3 min (where h a is in mm)

table.name: E1-pine-cone: Why a pine cone opens when it dries
table.fields: explanation=Each scale of a pine cone is two layers stuck together. The outer layer is made of long, thick-walled cells that get longer when they take up moisture and shorter when they dry. The inner layer hardly changes size. When the air dries, the outer layer shrinks and the inner one does not, so the scale is forced to curve outward and the cone opens. When the cone gets wet, the outer layer lengthens again and the scales close. Fallen cones are dead wood, so no living cell is doing the work: it is purely swelling and shrinking of dry material. | everyday_comparison=A strip of plastic tape stuck along one side of a sheet of paper: the paper takes up and loses moisture, the tape does not, and the sheet curls. | where_it_breaks=The paper-and-plastic version was built by the cone researchers as a copy (it curls on drying and straightens on wetting), so it is a fair model of the mechanism. It breaks on size and speed: the cone's cells change length by about 10 percent between dry and saturated air (0.001 per percent of relative humidity x 100 [calc]), far more than a stock printed resin manages (a few tenths of a percent), and the cone opens more slowly than it closes (drying time 96 h_a^1.5 min against wetting 29 h_a^1.3 min, h_a in mm). | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: the cone is alive and opens on purpose when it senses rain or warmth. Right: it opens when DRY and closes when WET, and it does so even when dead. | sentences=6

table.name: E2-bilayer-bimetal: Why two layers that swell unequally bend, like a bimetal strip
table.fields: explanation=A bimetal strip is two metals bonded face to face that expand by different amounts when heated. The layer that wants to grow longer cannot slide past its partner, so the whole strip bends, with the longer-growing layer on the outside of the curve. A water-driven bilayer works the same way, except moisture instead of heat makes one layer change size. Only a difference in change is needed, so the second layer can simply stay put, as the inner layer of a pine-cone scale does. The bend is much larger than the tiny stretch that causes it, because a long thin strip turns a small length difference into a large sideways swing. The same equation, worked out by Timoshenko in 1925 for thermostats, is used for both. | everyday_comparison=Two runners on a curved running track: the runner in the outer lane has a longer path, so if two lanes are tied together the longer one must sit on the outside of the bend. A thermostat or dial thermometer is the real-world example. | where_it_breaks=The track picture gives the direction of the bend but not how much. The big break is speed: heat spreads through 1 mm of steel in about 0.05 s (thermal diffusivity 18.8 mm2/s [calc]), but water creeping into a dense resin (D about 1e-12 m2/s) needs about 10 days for the same 1 mm, roughly 19 million times slower [calc]. Also, in a thermostat both metals expand; in a hygromorph usually one layer does the swelling and the other is a passive partner. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: one layer must grow while the other shrinks. Right: only a difference in change is needed; one layer can stay the same size. | sentences=6

table.name: E3-lean-law: What a 'law' in Lean is
table.fields: explanation=Lean is a computer program that checks mathematical proofs. A 'law' in this project is a statement typed into Lean, for example: for any two layers of any thickness and any stiffness, the curl per unit of swelling mismatch can never exceed 3/2 divided by the total thickness. Lean accepts the statement only if there is a chain of steps in which every step follows from earlier results, down to a few basic rules. If one step is missing, Lean refuses, and our check script also fails if a placeholder called 'sorry' was left in. On 12 Nov 2026 we ran the project's file: five theorems, no errors, no placeholders [calc: lean_check_out.txt]. | everyday_comparison=A strict referee who redoes every line of your arithmetic and will not accept 'it is obvious'. | where_it_breaks=A referee of the sums does not know whether you wrote down the right problem. Lean checks the mathematics of the formula we typed in; it cannot check that the formula describes a real printed strip. The Lean file's formula was matched by us to two independent published forms (Reyssat 2009 and the 1863 form on Wikipedia, identical to 1e-15 over 200,000 random cases [calc]), but that match is a human check, not a Lean check. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: 'checked by Lean' means the physical strip is guaranteed to behave that way. Right: it guarantees the maths of the model; the real strip must also meet the model's assumptions (thin, elastic, small bend, well-bonded layers). | sentences=5

table.name: E4-proof-vs-simulation: Why a proof differs from a simulation
table.fields: explanation=A simulation tries particular cases and reports what happened. A proof shows something is true for every case at once, including ones nobody tried. We sampled 2 million random layer combinations and the largest curl coefficient found was 1.49999999997, never above 1.5 [calc]. That is strong evidence, but it is not a guarantee. The Lean proof reduces to the fact that a squared number is never negative, so no combination can beat 1.5. Tests can pass for a long time and then fail: the formula n x n + n + 41 gives a prime number for every n from 0 to 39 and fails at n = 40, where it gives 1681 = 41 x 41 [calc]. | everyday_comparison=Trying a million keys in a lock versus showing from the lock's design that no key of this shape can open it. | where_it_breaks=A proof only speaks about the model; a simulation or a real print can reveal that the model itself is wrong, which no proof can. For the strip, the published bilayer data are consistent with the proved ceiling (six beech bilayers peak at 1.50-1.53 against 1.5 [rec]) and the 1.53 slightly above the bound shows measurement uncertainty, not a broken proof. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: a plot or simulation that never crosses the limit has proved the limit. Right: Holstov et al. (2015) plotted the maximum as 1.5 for many stiffness ratios; the Lean proof is what turns the observation into a certainty. | sentences=6
table.source: Holstov 2015 (doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136; open copy https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076) ; own calculation calc.py ; HygromorphCeilingCheck.lean

table.name: E5-ceiling-rules-out: Why a ceiling on curl lets a design be ruled out before printing
table.fields: explanation=The proven ceiling says the curl of a two-layer strip, measured as 1/radius, can never exceed 1.5 times the swelling mismatch divided by the total thickness, however the layers are chosen. So if you know how much your materials can swell, you can work out the tightest possible curl before printing anything. A 0.8 mm strip whose layers differ in swelling by 0.2 percent can never curl tighter than a circle of radius 267 mm, a circle about half a metre wide [calc]. To curl to a 50 mm radius the same strip needs at least 1.07 percent mismatch [calc]. A design asking for more is ruled out on paper, which saves a print, a cure and a week of soaking. | everyday_comparison=A fuel tank and the best possible mileage: no engine can drive farther than tank size times the best mileage physics allows, so you can rule out a 2,000 km trip on 10 litres before building the car. | where_it_breaks=The ceiling is an upper bound for an idealised two-layer strip, not a promise: real strips reach less (the six beech bilayers scored 0.91 to 1.53 of the 1.5 limit [rec]; a cellulose-acetate film reached 65 percent of it [rec]). It does not cover other structures such as lattices, gradients, or wide plates that curve in two directions, and it rests on the swelling mismatch being known, which for Formlabs resins nobody has measured. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: you must print and test to learn whether a shape is possible, or that the 3/2 ceiling is a new discovery. Right: with a known swelling mismatch, a lower limit on the radius is arithmetic; the ceiling itself was already seen in 2015 and its closed form follows from a 1863 formula. | sentences=5

table.name: E6-water-uptake-0.7pct: What a water uptake of 0.7 percent means
table.fields: explanation=Water uptake of 0.7 percent means 100 g of plastic gained 0.7 g of water. A 1 cm cube of printed resin weighs about 1.2 g, so it takes in roughly 8 mg, less than a fifth of a drop [calc]. The water squeezes in between the plastic's molecules and makes the part slightly bigger, by our estimate 0.09 to 0.28 percent in length, about 0.04 to 0.11 mm along a 40 mm strip [calc]. Alone that is invisible, but a thin bilayer magnifies it about 37 times: the tip of a 40 mm long, 0.8 mm thick strip could move 1.3 to 4.2 mm at best [calc]. And 0.7 percent is Formlabs' 24-hour cube test, not the final amount, and it describes one resin: the Flexible 80A V2 data sheet reports +8 percent mass in one day. | everyday_comparison=A sixth of a drop of water inside a 1.2 g cube; or, scaled up, half a kilogram of water gained by a 70 kg person. | where_it_breaks=The drop sits on a surface in the picture, but the real water is inside the plastic. A 'drop' is not a fixed volume (about 0.05 mL by convention). Mass percent is not length percent: the conversion is 0.12 to 0.40 percent of length per percent of mass [calc], and we have no measured value for any Formlabs resin in humid air. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: 0.7 percent is nothing, so the plastic cannot change shape (or is waterproof). Right: small swelling matters once a thin bilayer amplifies it, but it is also small: a 0.2 percent mismatch caps a 0.8 mm strip at a 267 mm radius. | sentences=5

table.name: E7-thin-is-faster: Why a thin strip is faster than a thick one
table.fields: explanation=Water spreads into plastic slowly, like ink spreading through still water, and the time it takes grows with the square of the distance it must travel. Make the layer twice as thick and, in the ideal case, it takes four times as long; make it half as thick and it takes a quarter. For a dense resin with a water diffusivity of about 1e-12 m2/s, a 0.2 mm layer reaches 90 percent of its final water in about 9 hours, 0.4 mm in about 38 hours, 0.8 mm in about 6 days, and 1.6 mm in about 25 days [calc]. A porous pine-cone layer is about a thousand times quicker (D near 1e-9 m2/s), so a 1 mm layer needs minutes to a couple of hours. The price of being thin is strength: the force a strip can push with falls roughly as the thickness squared [rec]. | everyday_comparison=Thin fries cook through much sooner than thick wedges, because heat also spreads by the same square-law. | where_it_breaks=Real objects are not ideal: for pine-cone scales Reyssat and Mahadevan measured exponents of 1.5 for drying and 1.3 for wetting, not 2, so doubling thickness slows the cone by 2.5 to 2.8 times, not 4 [calc]. Cooking adds surface effects and evaporation, so the fries comparison is only the same family of mathematics, and was not tested here. The 1e-12 diffusivity is an order of magnitude from printed dental resin (0.85e-12 m2/s); no value for a Formlabs resin has been measured, so the times could be 3 times longer or shorter. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: half as thick means twice as fast. Right: between 2.5 and 4 times as fast, because the time grows faster than the thickness. | sentences=5

table.name: E8-stiffer-is-not-better: Why a stiffer partner layer does not bend the strip more (the modulus ratio drops out)
table.fields: explanation=You might expect a much stiffer passive layer to push the strip into a tighter curl. It does not. The best possible curl is the same, 1.5 times the mismatch divided by the thickness, whatever the stiffness ratio, provided you adjust the thicknesses. The recipe is that the stiffer layer is made thinner, by the square root of the stiffness ratio; equivalently stiffness x thickness squared is equal in both layers. If you ignore the recipe you lose curl: with a 10 times stiffness gap and equal thicknesses you get only 66 percent of the maximum [calc]. Make one layer infinitely stiffer than the other and the strip does not bend at all. | everyday_comparison=A seesaw: a heavy child sits closer to the pivot so that weight times distance balances. | where_it_breaks=The seesaw is our own gloss on the rule 'stiffness x thickness squared equal': the rule comes from algebra (m squared x n = 1), not from the seesaw. When the layers are about equally thick, stiffness hardly matters (Reyssat: f changes by under 10 percent for stiffness ratios 0.3 to 3.5; we get 0.9 percent at equal thickness [calc]). | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: stiffer partner, more bend. Right: the match between thickness and stiffness sets the bend, and the ceiling does not depend on the stiffness ratio. | sentences=6

table.name: E9-liquid-matters: Why Elastic 50A drinks 39 percent isopropanol but under 1 percent water
table.fields: explanation=How much a plastic swells depends on the liquid as much as the plastic. In Formlabs' 24-hour soak test, Elastic 50A V2 gained 39.2 percent of its weight in isopropyl alcohol but only 0.7 percent in water, while Rigid 10K gained under 0.1 percent in both. The stiff resin has little room for any liquid, and the soft rubbery one lets some liquids in and others hardly at all. The practical lesson is that a water-driven design must be checked against every liquid the part meets, including a cleaning bath. The older Elastic 50A V1 took up 25.6 percent isopropanol and 2.3 percent water in the same test. | everyday_comparison=Salt dissolves in water but not in cooking oil: whether something gets in depends on the pairing. | where_it_breaks=The resin does not dissolve; the cured network swells and holds the liquid, so 'dissolving' is the wrong picture. The reason one liquid gets in and another does not is general chemistry, not shown in the sources I fetched. | common_wrong_idea=Wrong: if it ignores water it ignores every liquid. Right: water uptake and alcohol uptake are separate numbers. | sentences=5

recommendations: Always say 'mass percent in a 24 h cube test' when quoting a Formlabs water uptake, and never 'water uptake of Formlabs resins' as one figure: Flexible 80A V2 is +8 % in a day.

When explaining the ceiling to the architecture practice, show the 1863 formula (a = 1 + square) beside the Lean proof: a layperson can see that no choice beats 1.5, and credit Holstov 2015 for the numerical observation.
State the limits of Lean every time it is mentioned: it proves the maths of the model, not that a printed strip will behave.
Measure it: coupon strips of Rigid 10K and Flexible 80A V2 weighed and measured at 24 h, 1 week and equilibrium would turn every labelled estimate here (strain per percent mass, D) into data.

If a hands-on demo is wanted for visitors, use the paper-and-tape curl or a real pine cone in a bowl of water (cone closes, then reopens on drying) as the opening act before showing the printed sample.

fleet.label: bm-lean-materials-laws
fleet.topic: Which materials laws can be formalised in Lean next, and prove two
fleet.summary: Two easy textbook laws were written and kernel-checked with the project script (check.sh): (1) Voigt-Reuss ordering, reuss_le_voigt for two phases with equality exactly when f(1-f)(E1-E2)^2 = 0, plus an n-phase version via Jensen for x^-1; (2) Euler buckling of a strip, P_cr = pi^2 E (b t^3/12)/(K L)^2, strictly increasing in thickness, strictly decreasing in length, scaling as t^3 and 1/L^2 (and s^2 under uniform scaling), with critical stress depending only on t/(K L). Both: errors=0, sorryAx=0, only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound. One extra also passed: the Timoshenko ceiling 3/(2h) is attained only on m^2 n = 1 (the project record proved 'at most' and 'equal when m^2 n = 1', not the converse). A negative control with sorry correctly failed. One first attempt failed (two errors in the Euler file) and was fixed. The statements prove facts about the formulas; they do not derive the formulas from elasticity (Mathlib at the pinned rev has no elasticity vocabulary: 0 files). Ratings: easy = Voigt-Reuss (done), Euler monotonicity (done), Gibson-Ashby as named-hypothesis exponent algebra, I = b t^3/12 by integral_pow, Poisson-ratio window, Griffith inequality, cure-depth log curve; moderate = Hashin-Shtrikman closed-form ordering, Gibson-Ashby exponents from strut geometry, Euler eigenvalue derivation, Calladine count via rank-nullity, Weibull size effect, Flory-Rehner; hard = Voigt/Reuss as physical bounds (energy principles), Laman, laminate-plate-theory bending with twist, diffusion-coupled transient bending. Hollow tube and Timoshenko swelling bending are already in the library. This confirms laws-biomaterial.json's difficulty ratings (no material disagreement) and adds items it lacked. Water-uptake premise: 'under 1 percent' fails for Flexible 80A V2 (+8 percent mass, per later project files, not re-fetched by me).
fleet.lay_summary: A law of materials is only as trustworthy as the arithmetic behind it, so we asked a proof-checking program to confirm that arithmetic. We tested two simple laws. The first says a mix of stiff and soft material is stiffer when the parts are forced to stretch together, like planks side by side, than when they share the same pull, like layers stacked end to end. The second says a thin ruler squeezed from its ends gives way at a load that grows very fast with thickness (eight times for double) and drops fast with length. Both checks passed, and a deliberately sloppy proof was rejected, so the checker is doing its job. The checker confirms the formulas are consistent; it does not prove that a real printed part follows them, which still needs measurement.

fleet.topic: Mamou-Mani Architects: what they build and how
fleet.summary: Fetched about 30 pages of the practice's own site, 19 Fab.Pub pages and 7 press pieces on 2026-11-12 as raw HTML (sha256 in data/mamou-mani/manifest.tsv) and extracted 77 verbatim-checked findings. The portfolio is larger and more varied than the earlier spec-partner-architecture record: about 30 listed projects from Cloud Capsule (2014) to Tate Modern (2025-26), in four material families: (a) PLA bioplastic printed on robot arms (Conifera 700 modules, Altostrata 12 modules, The Roe 30 x 20 kg modules, RIVA 3 x 1.9 m single print, Harmonic Tides, WOW!House); (b) timber and rattan (Galaxia 60 m x 20 m, 18,000 screws at 1.8 kN each; THK Tower 96 t ulin; Concordia; Catharsis); (c) sheet metal and ceramics (Smile, IWAN, Hermes facade, RIVA exterior); (d) sand (Sandwaves, 58 x ~160 kg). Fab.Pub has moved beyond PLA: recycled PETG (Neko Health Monolith Wall, 260 panels, 12 x 7.5 m, >800 robot-hours) and bamboo-filled PLA/PETG compounds (Tate), plus a named flame-retardant blend Fab.Shield. Philosophy in their words: designs 'emerge from the constraints of reality rather than through ego-led geometry'; the architect as 'a gardener'; circularity 'begins before a material is selected'. Pipeline: Rhino/Grasshopper, the open-source Silkworm G-code plugin (four co-authors), Dassault 3DEXPERIENCE, genetic algorithms, WASP printers (2018), robot arms and a shipping-container Mobile Factory. Material limits they state: PLA composts only industrially (60 C, 100% humidity, about a month), PLA is costlier than petroleum plastic and 'not very well researched', sand is weak, budget and time dominate temporary work. Moisture is almost unaddressed; fire is solved by additives with no published class; durability evidence is anecdotal (Conifera outdoors, WOW!House 3 years). Their sustainability numbers disagree: PLA carbon saving 68% (Dezeen 2019), 80% (several), 73.7% (computed from Aurora LCA), 75.5-83.7% (computed from the Altostrata per-kg figures); toxicity 30x vs 50x. Contradictions with earlier files are listed in findings F04, F13, F38, F39 and in recommendations. Not found: any item called Triumphant Fantasia, any Mamou-Mani project called Spiral (Galaxia is the spiral Burning Man temple), any measured water uptake, expansion or diffusivity, any fire class.
fleet.lay_summary: Mamou-Mani is a London architecture studio that designs shapes with computer code and then has them made, often by 3D printing in plant-based plastic. Think of a giant Lego-like canopy of 700 printed bricks, or a 60-metre timber temple built from ordinary planks and 18,000 screws and then burned on purpose. The studio says openly that its plastic has a built-in tension: it should last, yet it should also be able to rot away when you want it to. It publishes almost no hard numbers on water, sun or fire resistance, and one strength test is quoted in a unit that makes no physical sense. That gap is where a new, carefully measured material could be useful to them.

findings.evidence_quote: Computational architecture, circular design and digital fabrication.

findings.claim: Altostrata (2023) dimensions and module count (own page)
findings.value: 30 m long; 12 modules; up to 2.7 m high
findings.evidence_quote: It is 30M long and made of 12 bespoke modules reaching 2.7M high

findings.claim: Altostrata structural evidence is one in-house pull test with ARUP and Fab Pub, reported in a unit that is not a force ('500 kg.m2'); the page gives no mass, load case, specimen or failure mode
findings.evidence_quote: Our in-house tests with ARUP and Fab Pub have proven a resistance to pull forces of 500 kg.m2.

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS earlier agent spec-partner-architecture ('no direct statement by the practice on UV, creep or moisture'): the Altostrata page does claim weather resistance, in one qualitative sentence with no data
findings.evidence_quote: the large-scale utilisation of bio-plastics, engineered to endure outdoor environments and resist weathering conditions.

findings.claim: The practice states the durable-vs-biodegradable tension itself, on its own project page (2023)
findings.evidence_quote: There often lies a deep contradiction between sustainable and biodegradable.

findings.claim: Moisture statement (new): the practice says humidity speeds PLA biodegradation; this is the only moisture sentence on any practice page, and it concerns end-of-life composting, not in-service water uptake
findings.evidence_quote: Warm temperatures, high humidity and small particle sizes will make biodegradation even faster.

findings.claim: Altostrata page gives per-kg embodied carbon for PLA vs petroleum plastic; own calculation of the saving: 1-0.49/2 = 75.5 % and 1-0.49/3 = 83.7 %, so the '80 %' headline sits inside that range
findings.evidence_quote: Bioplastics can be 80% more effective at reducing energy needs

findings.claim: Toxicity multiplier is inconsistent across the practice's own statements: 30x less toxic when heated (Altostrata page, Fab.Pub) vs 50x less toxic fumes (founder to Dezeen, 2019)
findings.evidence_quote: PLA is up to 30 times less toxic than petroleum-based plastics when heated.

findings.claim: Practice admits PLA is under-researched (Altostrata page)
findings.evidence_quote: PLA although widely used in 3D printing is not very well researched compared to Pet-based polymer

findings.claim: The Roe tree (Jan 2023 - Feb 2024): thirty PLA modules, compounded with fireproof materials for interior use
findings.evidence_quote: Composed of thirty 3D-printed modules in PLA bioplastics, compounded with fireproof materials for interior use.

findings.claim: The Roe module mass and print time; own calculation 30 x 20 kg = 600 kg and 30 x (15-20 h) = 450-600 robot-hours
findings.evidence_quote: each weighing around 20 kg and taking 15-20 hours to print using a large-scale printer attached to a robotic arm.

findings.claim: NEW: RIVA (King's Cross, 2025) interior piece is PLA with a non-toxic fire retardant, the practice's largest single print (3 m x 1.9 m); the exterior piece is folded aluminium with a lattice hinge
findings.evidence_quote: The interior piece was 3D printed robotically from a blend of fermented sugar and non-toxic fire retardant.

findings.claim: NEW (partly contradicts 'no named fire product' in spec-partner-architecture): Fab.Pub names a flame-retardant blend, Fab.Shield, but publishes no test class or data
findings.evidence_quote: Fab.Shield Flame-retardant blend developed for architectural performance requirements.

findings.claim: Fab.Pub says custom PLA blends are designed around fire safety and compliance; no fire classification is published
findings.evidence_quote: Our custom PLA blends are designed with performance, fire safety, and regulatory compliance in mind.

findings.claim: Fab.Pub claims PLA is mechanically stronger than ABS and PETG 'under standard conditions' (the qualifier is the only stated mechanical limit)
findings.evidence_quote: PLA is mechanically stronger than common 3D-printing plastics like ABS and PETG under standard conditions.

findings.claim: NEW durability evidence: Conifera modules were left outdoors at the studio 'to prove the longevity of PLA' (journalist visit June 2022); no duration, climate data or measured property change is given
findings.evidence_quote: Outside are more Conifera modules, deliberately exposed to wind and rain to prove the longevity of PLA

findings.claim: Wallpaper* states the industry's doubt about PLA durability (journalist's words, not the practice's)
findings.evidence_quote: the architecture and design industries have been slow to embrace PLA because of doubts over its durability.

findings.claim: Fab.Pub is a joint venture of Mamou-Mani and Therme Group, formed summer 2021 (Wallpaper*)
findings.evidence_quote: in summer 2021, the group formed a joint venture with the architect to run Fab.Pub

findings.claim: NEW durability evidence (2024): WOW!House PLA installation reused and reinstalled for three years 'and it hasn't changed' (founder interview; no measurement)
findings.evidence_quote: The Wow House installation, for example, has been reused and reinstalled for three years now, and it hasn't changed.

findings.claim: Founder names the durable-vs-biodegradable contradiction and calls PLA 'a nice middle ground'
findings.evidence_quote: there is a contradiction between the idea of sustainable or durable and biodegradable, which is the opposite.

findings.claim: Founder: PLA still costs more than petroleum plastic (Therme interview, 6 Mar 2024)
findings.evidence_quote: Though it remains more expensive than petroleum plastics

findings.claim: Founder cites an ARUP-commissioned report: PLA 80% less carbon, 60% less carcinogenic when burnt; he adds he is not 100% sure on these points
findings.evidence_quote: PLA uses 80% less carbon, is 60% less carcinogenic when it is burnt

findings.claim: Design philosophy in his words (1): emergence from constraints
findings.evidence_quote: Designs emerge from the constraints of reality rather than through ego-led geometry.

findings.claim: Design philosophy (2): bottom-up parametric design
findings.evidence_quote: with parametric design you bring the shapes in from the bottom up, guided by parameters.

findings.claim: Design philosophy (3): architect as gardener, direct test loop
findings.evidence_quote: you could be more like a gardener as an architect, growing beautiful, natural things, and evolving them

findings.claim: Studio website philosophy: tools guided by mathematics and natural systems
findings.evidence_quote: guided by mathematics and natural systems

findings.claim: Studio website: circularity and physical evidence stance
findings.evidence_quote: Circularity begins before a material is selected.

findings.claim: Studio website: AI/generative tools stance
findings.evidence_quote: AI and generative tools become valuable when they remain connected to material behaviour, fabrication and human judgement.

findings.claim: Galaxia (Burning Man 2018): 60 m wide, 20 m high, 20 timber trusses, 200 volunteers, 18,000 screws, 6 months off site plus 1 month assembly
findings.evidence_quote: 60 m span · 20 m high · 20 timber trusses · 200 volunteers · 18,000 screws · 6 months off site

findings.claim: Galaxia engineering rule: the engineers supplied a per-screw capacity and the architecture was derived from it
findings.evidence_quote: A screw resists 1.8 kilonewtons, these are your loads, deal with it.

findings.claim: Galaxia cost limit, in their words
findings.evidence_quote: We had to fundraise every penny.

findings.claim: Founder on durability as a goal (Galaxia was burned by design)
findings.evidence_quote: We are taught that the Greek ruins are the ultimate architecture because they lasted.

findings.claim: Sandwaves (Riyadh, Diriyah Season; page says 2019, Dezeen reported 20 Jan 2020): 58 sand-printed elements, 'largest sand-printed installation to date'
findings.evidence_quote: The Sandwaves is the largest sand-printed installation to date

findings.claim: Sandwaves material limit stated by founder: sand is weak so members are thick, ~160 kg each; own calculation 58 x 160 kg = 9,280 kg
findings.evidence_quote: Sand isn’t a particularly strong material, which led us to design very thick structural members; each piece weighed around 160 kg.

findings.claim: Conifera (Milan Design Week 2019, COS): 700 interlocking printed modules; no mass or strength on the practice's own page
findings.evidence_quote: Mamou-Mani designed a sequence of 700 interlocking, 3D-printed modules

findings.claim: Software pipeline for Galaxia (Jan 2018): Rhino + Grasshopper for parametric modelling, Silkworm to G-code, renderers Maxwell/Keyshot/V-Ray
findings.value: Rhino, Grasshopper, Silkworm, Maxwell, Keyshot, V-Ray
findings.evidence_quote: Rhino and Grasshopper 3D will be initially used for parametric modeling. The resulting 3D models will then converted to G-Code using Silkworm

findings.claim: Silkworm enables non-planar slicing and variable extrusion (founder, 2018): printer parameters become design parameters
findings.evidence_quote: We have also used varying e-values to under extrude or over extrude in a specific location or do non-planar slices

findings.claim: NEW: named printers for the Galaxia mandala: WASP4070 at Fab.Pub (prototype) and WASP3MT in Reno (final); PLA filament Excelfil from Voltivo. Fills a gap in spec-partner-architecture ('printer models not found')
findings.evidence_quote: prototypes of the mandala will be 3D printed at the Fab.Pub using a WASP4070 3D printer, while the final design will be fabricated on a WASP3MT

findings.claim: Silkworm authorship confirmed on the practice's own Food Ink page: four co-authors including Andrei Jipa (spec-partner-architecture listed three; upgrades its 'medium' confidence)
findings.value: co-written with Adam Holloway, Karl Kjelstrup-Johnson, Andrei Jipa
findings.evidence_quote: a Grasshopper3D plugin we co-wrote with Adam Holloway, Karl Kjelstrup-Johnson and Andrei Jipa

findings.claim: Studio website: Silkworm described as a Grasshopper/Rhino to G-code plugin
findings.evidence_quote: Silkworm is a plugin that translates Grasshopper and Rhino into GCode for 3D Printing.

findings.claim: Cable robot 'Polibot' developed in-house for the ARUP 'DNA of Making' installation (founder, 2018)
findings.evidence_quote: it is a cable robot that we have developed as part of our installation

findings.claim: Aurora (Design Museum, 2021) LCA: PLA 2333.89 kgCO2 vs ABS 8890.42 kgCO2; own calculation saving 6556.53 kg = 73.7 %
findings.evidence_quote: AURORA IN PLA: 2333.89kgCO2 AURORA IN ABS: 8890.42kgCO2

findings.claim: Aurora: modules are printed, broken down and reprinted on site; designed on Dassault 3DEXPERIENCE
findings.evidence_quote: structure comprised of 3D-printed modules that are printed, broken down and re-printed on site

findings.claim: Carbon claim for PLA vs ABS/petroleum is 68% (Dezeen 2019), 80% (Aurora page, Wallpaper* 2023, Therme 2024, WOW!House page), 73.7% (computed from Aurora LCA), 75.5-83.7% (computed from Altostrata page): sources disagree and none is an independent LCA
findings.evidence_quote: It’s 68 per cent more carbon efficient in terms of carbon emissions than conventional plastic.

findings.claim: Composting conditions stated by the founder (Dezeen 2019): industrial 60 C, 100% humidity, about a month; home about six months
findings.evidence_quote: You need 60 degrees Celsius and 100 per cent humidity and then it decomposes within a month.

findings.claim: Take-back loop: crush, pelletise, reprint (founder, 2024); compounds mostly sugar-based biomaterial mixed with wood-based pigments
findings.evidence_quote: take back” scheme where [the client returns the structure to us] and we crush it, turn it into pellets, and then put them in the printer.

findings.claim: Fab.Pub take-back is conditional: only 'for suitable Fab.Pub-produced parts' and 'where its condition and material specification allow'
findings.evidence_quote: For suitable Fab.Pub-produced parts, our Take-Back Scheme provides a route to return products at the end of use.

findings.claim: Wooden Waves (BuroHappold, London, 2015): untreated FSC-style certified plywood with laser-cut lattice hinges; more than 100 prototypes
findings.evidence_quote: More than 100 prototypes were developed.

findings.evidence_quote: 1kg of PLA bioplastic printed at high speed and high temperature with custom infill.

findings.claim: Cloud Capsule (London, 2014): 2 m micro-pavilions on a Delta Tower printer, light diffusion modelled in Radiance
findings.evidence_quote: these 2 metre high micro-pavilions demonstrate measured changes in the levels of light diffused through their forms.

findings.claim: Whale Shark time limit stated as a constraint
findings.evidence_quote: we were given only four months from concept to completion

findings.evidence_quote: basalt was hard to keep consistent in colour and flow.

findings.evidence_quote: The project reused and reconfigured modules developed through earlier research, including Altostrata

findings.evidence_quote: Catharsis is made of a total of 60 timber modules assembled through metal hinges developed with our engineers.

findings.evidence_quote: the studio uses sugarcane-derived PLA, which he considers suboptimal as the manufacturer grows the plant in Thailand

findings.evidence_quote: using a mix of PLA and brass powder

findings.claim: Fab.Pub material library: Fab.Pure Clear PLA, Fab.Grain wood+bioplastic, Fab.Shield flame-retardant, Fab.Stone chalk-filled, Fab.Zen bamboo-filled, Fab.Lava mineral-reinforced (under development), Fab.Roast coffee-waste
findings.evidence_quote: Mineral reinforcement Under development. Fab.Lava Mineral-reinforced material under development for strength and texture.

findings.claim: Mamou-Mani Ltd is registered in England and Wales, France and Spain and is a Circularity in Practice signatory
findings.evidence_quote: Mamou-Mani Ltd - Registered in England & Wales, France and Spain | Circularity in Practice Signatory

key_claims.claim: The practice itself states the central design contradiction: durable use versus biodegradability. PLA is chosen as a 'middle ground' that only composts industrially (founder, Frederic 2024, Dezeen 2019; Altostrata page 2023).
key_claims.evidence_quote: there is a contradiction between the idea of sustainable or durable and biodegradable, which is the opposite.

key_claims.claim: No quantitative moisture, UV, creep or weathering data are published by Mamou-Mani or Fab.Pub. Durability evidence is qualitative: Conifera modules left outdoors, WOW!House reused 3 years 'hasn't changed', Altostrata 'engineered to ... resist weathering'. The only moisture sentence concerns composting.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Outside are more Conifera modules, deliberately exposed to wind and rain to prove the longevity of PLA

key_claims.claim: Fire is handled by additives per project (Roe 'compounded with fireproof materials', RIVA 'non-toxic fire retardant', Fab.Shield blend) and no fire class or test result is published.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The interior piece was 3D printed robotically from a blend of fermented sugar and non-toxic fire retardant.

key_claims.claim: The only structural test on any practice page is one in-house pull test reported in an invalid unit (500 kg.m2); the founder concedes PLA is 'not very well researched'. A machine-checked, unit-correct property envelope would be new to them.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Our in-house tests with ARUP and Fab Pub have proven a resistance to pull forces of 500 kg.m2.

recommendations: Lead with their own sentence: 'there is a contradiction between the idea of sustainable or durable and biodegradable' (Frederic 2024; also the Altostrata page). Propose a material whose stability and decay are both specified and measured.

Offer what they lack: a unit-correct datasheet (modulus, strength, water uptake, expansion per % moisture, softening temperature) with test methods. Their only structural number is '500 kg.m2' and they say PLA is 'not very well researched'.

Moisture is the open ground: the practice has never published uptake or movement of its PLA blends, and their wood-, bamboo- and paper-filled blends (Fab.Grain, Fab.Zen, Paper PLA) are exactly the class known to be hygroscopic. Ask whether they treat that movement as a defect. A bilayer with the proved 3/2 curvature ceiling is a deliberate use of it.

Design the proof of concept to match their module culture: interlocking modules, reversible joints (cable ties, slotted shells, male/female connections), translucent or filled finish for backlighting, lattice infill tuned for weight, stiffness and light (as they did for the Tate platforms). Deliver the Grasshopper definition.

Match the process gap honestly: they print on robot arms with pellets and filament (PLA, PETG, filled blends), not resin or powder. Formlabs prints prove geometry and mechanism; a second step on Fab.Pub's extruder is needed to show their loop (crush, pelletise, reprint). Their stated minimum is GBP 250 and 2 weeks.
Do not quote their carbon percentages as fact; cite the Aurora LCA figures with the computed 73.7% and note the three other values.
Questions to ask them directly: fire classification of Roe/RIVA modules; the meaning of '500 kg.m2'; what Conifera modules did after outdoor exposure; whether Fab.Shield has a test report.

fleet.label: bm-mycelium-living-materials
fleet.topic: Mycelium and engineered living materials: could a living layer be the swelling layer of a humidity bilayer printed on Formlabs machines?
fleet.summary: Particulate mycelium composites (the usual product) are a poor swelling layer. They are stiff only to 0.03-4.44 MPa compressive, take up 6-436 % water, shrink 2.78-17 % on drying, swell 205-244 % through the thickness but under about 7 % in plane, vary a lot from specimen to specimen, and some batches fail (contamination, disintegration). The Buehler-corpus 'robust myco-composite' (Shen 2024) is a paste-printed (2 mm layers) chitosan/cellulose/coffee body colonised for 14 days; it reaches 160 MPa modulus and 0.72 MPa strength, but the mycelium weakens the substrate and acts as a hydrophobic skin (contact angle 117 to 138 degrees) and a weld. It is a skin or protective layer, not a large-swelling layer, and nobody has grown it on a Formlabs resin. Two living layers do have measured humidity strain in air and could be the active layer of a bilayer. (1) Nie 2026: a Trametes versicolor film made of two grown layers (0.22 and 0.30 mm), E = 23.7 MPa with PVA and glycerol, 374.9 mg/g moisture uptake at 85 % RH, volume expansion 9.27 % vs 3.38 % (30 to 85 % RH), bends in 8 min. (2) Wang 2017: dried microbial cells, 1 micrometre on 200 micrometre latex, volume linear in RH, fitted modulus 70 MPa, response in seconds, 100 cycles. My own calculation (linear Timoshenko, project-record f(m,n) with ceiling 3/2): both are far softer than Formlabs rigid resins, so they only work against a soft elastomer (Silicone 40A, Flexible 50A, Flexible 80A V2) where the optimum active/passive thickness ratio is 0.18-0.50 and f is 1.40-1.49. Against Rigid 10K the optimum needs a 20-fold thicker active layer and f falls to about 0.01. Predicted curvature is an upper bound: about 56 1/m linear, 13-15 1/m after the 3.8-4.4x derating the project record gives for soft films. Blockers: contamination, batch variability, no building-product standard or fire class, a living layer that must be added after printing (SLS sintering and SLA post-cure would kill it), plasticiser in the Nie film, 1-year dormancy limit, and no data on adhesion or growth on photopolymer resins.
fleet.lay_summary: Mushroom 'roots', called mycelium, can be grown into a leathery sheet, and some of those sheets curl when the air gets damp, like a pine cone. We looked for a living layer that could bend a printed strip when humidity changes. The usual mycelium building blocks, grown on sawdust, swell a lot but mainly in thickness and they are weak and inconsistent, so they are a poor choice. Two other options look better: a mushroom-root film grown in a dish, and a hair-thin coat of dried bacteria. Both swell a few percent in damp air, far more than the printing plastics do, and the bacteria coat reacts in seconds. They are soft, so they only bend a printed strip well if the strip is a rubbery printing resin, not a hard one. The big unknowns are keeping the living layer clean and consistent and getting it approved for buildings.

glossary.plain: The root-like thread network of a fungus, which can be grown into a solid material.
A material where mycelium grows through and glues together another material such as sawdust or a printed frame.
Two thin layers stuck together; if one swells more than the other, the strip curls.
A number up to 1.5 that says how well a two-layer strip turns a swelling difference into bending; the project proved the 1.5 limit.
Stiffness: how much force it takes to stretch or bend a material by a given amount.
How damp the air is, as a percentage of the most water vapour the air can hold.
Swelling in the thin direction (making a board fatter) versus swelling along the surface (what makes a strip curl).
A fungal protein that coats surfaces and makes them repel water.
Letting mycelium grow onto a printed object from a bed of living mycelium instead of mixing it into the ink.
A film whose two faces are different, named after the two-faced Roman god.
'Generally recognised as safe': a US food-safety status for an organism.
Unwanted bacteria or moulds taking over the culture.
Two 3D-printing methods: curing liquid resin with light, or fusing plastic powder with a laser.
A scale for how hard a rubbery material feels; lower is softer.

findings.claim: Shen et al. (MIT, Buehler group) print a chitosan/cellulose/coffee-ground biocomposite and colonise it with mycelium by indirect inoculation; the colonised composite has Young's modulus 160 MPa and tensile strength 0.72 MPa, reported as the strongest mycelium composite to date.
findings.source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38315077 (published abstract, Mater. Horiz. 2024, 10.1039/d3mh01277h); body text from arXiv v2 https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12151 because the RSC page returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare) in this run
findings.evidence_quote: We found that our method yields the strongest mycelium composite reported to date with a modulus of 160 MPa and tensile strength of 0.72 MPa

findings.claim: In that paper mycelium colonisation WEAKENS the printed substrate (printed uncolonised composite is about 340 MPa stiffness and 4.2 MPa tensile strength), so the living phase is a skin and a welding agent, not a reinforcement.
findings.value: uncolonised printed ~340 MPa / 4.2 MPa vs colonised 160 MPa / 0.72 MPa
findings.evidence_quote: In comparison to the uncolonized biocomposite, growth of mycelium actually weakens the material.

findings.claim: Printed uncolonised composite: approximate stiffness 340 MPa and tensile strength 4.2 MPa.
findings.evidence_quote: At approximate stiffness of 340 MPa and tensile strength of 4.2 MPa for the printed composite

findings.claim: Typical mycelium composites, per Shen et al., have ultimate tensile strength up to 0.20 MPa and modulus up to 7.13 MPa, in the range of lightweight foams.
findings.evidence_quote: The upper limits of reported ultimate tensile strength and modulus of mycelium composites measure 0.20 MPa and 7.13 MPa respectively

findings.claim: Colonisation time on the printed substrate is typically 14 days (indirect inoculation on a bed of living mycelium); Ecovative substrate is pre-incubated 5 days.
findings.evidence_quote: until fully colonized as indicated by development of a full mycelium skin around the sample, typically a period of 14 days

findings.claim: The mycelium skin raises water contact angle from 117 to 138 degrees; the skin loses only 4.5 degrees in 30 s, which the authors attribute to hydrophobins.
findings.evidence_quote: resulted in the formation of a smooth “skin” with improved hydrophobicity as measured by an increase in water contact angle from 117º to 138º (Fig. 5a)

findings.claim: Colonised composite absorbs less water and swells less in volume than non-colonised composite over 24 h submersion, though it first swells quickly; the numbers are only in Fig. 5c and could not be read from the text.
findings.evidence_quote: the fully colonized composite exhibited lower water absorption and volume swelling than non-colonized samples after being submerged for 24 hours

findings.claim: Shen et al. printed with 2.5 mm extrusion width and 2 mm layer height, about 25 to 40 times coarser than Form 4 SLA layers (50-100 um), so the route is a paste printer, not a Formlabs printer.
findings.value: 2.5 mm width; 2 mm layer; 0.5 mm resolution
findings.evidence_quote: 2.5 mm extrusion width, 2 mm layer height, and 0.5 mm system resolution

findings.claim: Mycelium bridged gaps of up to 8 mm between printed biocomposite regions ('bio-welding'), used to make foldable containers and mycelium textiles.
findings.evidence_quote: In preliminary experiments, mycelium was found to be capable of bridging gaps up to 8 mm between regions of printed biocomposite.

findings.evidence_quote: the algorithm proposed an innovative hierarchical mycelium-based composite based on integrating path sampling with principles extracted from

findings.claim: Mycelium-bound composites (particulate substrate) reach only 0.03 to 4.44 MPa compressive strength.
findings.evidence_quote: MBC compressive strength ranges from 0.03 to 4.44 MPa

findings.claim: Water uptake of mycelium-bound composites depends strongly on species and substrate: 6 % (Ganoderma lucidum on beech sawdust) to 436 % (T. versicolor on rapeseed straw).
findings.evidence_quote: T. versicolor absorbs 26.8% and 30.3% water in wheat straw and flax, respectively, but 436% in rapeseed straw.

findings.claim: Drying shrinkage of mycelium composites is reported between 2.78 % and 17 %, wood-like and wider than plastics (0.3-2.5 %).
findings.evidence_quote: which reported MBC shrinkages between 2.78% and 17%

findings.claim: Bamboo-sawdust composites shrank 3.14-5.83 % against 9.80-16.66 % for corn-pericarp composites across fungal species (2024 study quoted by the review).
findings.evidence_quote: MBCs made from bamboo sawdust had lower shrinkage (3.14% to 5.83%) than those made from corn pericarp (9.80% to 16.66%) across various fungal species
