Contamination is a measured failure mode: flax-dust and straw-dust samples grew slowly and were systematically contaminated, so they were dropped from testing.
findings.evidence_quote: A slow growth and systematic contamination for all flax dust (FD) and straw dust (SD) samples was observed.

findings.claim: Typical incubation for moulded composites is about 10 days, starting at about 70 % water, then oven-drying to stop growth.
findings.evidence_quote: A 10-day incubation period allows mycelium facilitating substrate cohesion, forming a 3D network of fungal and plant fibres.

findings.claim: 2026 hemp-hurd mycelium composites (P. ostreatus, G. applanatum; 14 d in mould, hot-pressed 100 C) take up 309 to 356 % water in 2-72 h at 40 C (formulation 2) and swell through thickness by 205 to 244 %.
findings.evidence_quote: Formulation 2 exhibited the highest water uptake, increasing from 309 ± 49% after 2 h to a maximum mean value of 356 ± 28% after 72 h

findings.claim: Swelling is almost entirely through-thickness: width and length change stays below about 7 %, so in-plane (bilayer-relevant) swelling is far smaller than the headline numbers, and wet integrity is poor (some formulations fell apart).
findings.evidence_quote: In contrast, in-plane dimensional changes were limited, with width and length changes generally remaining below approximately 7%.

findings.claim: Best mean compressive stress 5.7 MPa; best flexural stress 4.6 MPa with flexural modulus 627 MPa, but with very large scatter (SD 285 MPa on the modulus).
findings.evidence_quote: The highest mean maximum compressive stress was 5.7 ± 1.2 MPa, whereas the highest mean maximum flexural stress and flexural modulus were 4.6 ± 2.1 MPa and 627 ± 285 MPa, respectively.

findings.claim: One formulation (no. 5) disintegrated during handling and could not be tested, showing batch-level failure.
findings.evidence_quote: the resulting material exhibited insufficient macroscopic cohesion and disintegrated during handling, preventing reproducible specimen preparation.

findings.claim: Mycelium grown 21 days on 3D-printed wood-PLA gyroid scaffolds gives yield strength 7.29 MPa (50 % porosity) and thermal conductivity 0.012 W/mK (90 % porosity); colonisation raised yield strength by 50-78 % at 70-90 % porosity.
findings.evidence_quote: of 7.29 ± 0.65 MPa for 50% porosity MBC

findings.claim: In the gyroid work the printed scaffold is dip-coated in a nutrient (peptone-malt-agar) solution before inoculation and grown 21 days; 40 mm cubes at 70 % porosity were covered in 14 days.
findings.evidence_quote: The fungus is then inoculated and grown for 21 days.

findings.claim: Fomes fomentarius growth on FDM PLA and PLA/hemp bars has only a minor effect on PLA's tensile properties; autoclave pre-treatment can significantly weaken the printed material.
findings.evidence_quote: The results indicate that mycelial colonization has a minor impact on the mechanical properties of PLA

findings.claim: Luo et al. 2025 print a mycelium-inoculated paste ('Mycofluid', coffee grounds 54.9 wt %, brown-rice flour 13.7 %, water 24.7 %) and show living mycelium can fuse separate prints.
findings.evidence_quote: Notably, we demonstrate how living mycelium can fuse separate prints, enabling complex geometries that are otherwise challenging to 3D print as one part.

findings.claim: Dense pure-mycelium sheets from S. commune dikaryons reach tensile strength up to 47.29 MPa and Young's modulus 0.69-2.06 GPa (monokaryon: 4.62-7.77 MPa and 0.38-0.64 GPa), i.e. polymer-film territory.
findings.evidence_quote: The highest σ was recorded for S139 and P351, with 47.29 MPa and 47.16 MPa, respectively.

findings.claim: Liquid-culture pure-mycelium materials from three species: tensile strength 4.5-6.3 MPa, elongation at break 0.8-1.6 %, Young's modulus 408-710 MPa; species matters little.
findings.evidence_quote: The Young’s modulus of the PMMs also showed relatively small differences ranging between 408 and 710 MPa.

findings.claim: Pure-mycelium fibrous materials from Ganoderma lucidum and Pleurotus ostreatus were all hydrophobic, with water contact angle above 120 degrees; grown on cellulose they are stiffer.
findings.evidence_quote: All the developed fibrous materials were hydrophobic with water contact angles higher than 120°.

findings.claim: Nie et al. 2026 (Nat. Commun.) grow Trametes versicolor mycelium membranes that are intrinsically two-layered (aerial layer A, nutrient-side layer B); plasticised with 10 % PVA + 10 % glycerol the optimised film has E = 23.7 MPa, elongation 36 %.
findings.evidence_quote: with proper E (23.7 MPa), enough EG (36%) and T (1.0 MJ·m −3 ) values

findings.claim: That mycelium film takes up 374.9 mg/g moisture at 25 C and 85 % RH (5 cycles), i.e. about 37 % of its dry mass, reversibly.
findings.evidence_quote: average moisture uptake of 374.9 mg·g −1 (25 °C, 85% RH) in 5 consecutive cycles

findings.claim: Micro-CT between 30 % and 85 % RH gives bulk (volumetric) moisture expansion 9.27 % for layer A and 3.38 % for layer B, a 2.7-fold contrast between the two grown layers.
findings.evidence_quote: Bulk moisture expansion rate ( ε b ) was higher for layer A (9.27%) than layer B (3.38%)

findings.claim: Layer thicknesses of the Janus film are 0.22 mm (A) and 0.30 mm (B), so the film is about 0.5 mm thick; a 5 x 25 mm strip bends within 8 min when RH goes from 20 % to 85 %.
findings.evidence_quote: For layer A and B, average thickness was measured as 0.22 and 0.30 mm, respectively.

findings.claim: Strips programmed by geometry and glycerol give bending angles from -19.0 to +43.2 degrees (reversible, RH-dependent).
findings.evidence_quote: a library of bending angles, (−19.0 ± 10.3)° to (43.2 ± 10.7)° was achieved

findings.claim: Dormant mycelium films are re-activatable but the dry storage period must be limited to within 1 year to keep spores alive; fresh membranes hold >90 % water and need a 20-day culture.
findings.evidence_quote: To maintain the livingness of spores in macerates, the dry storage period should be limited within 1 year.

findings.claim: The authors cite earlier work (Sinha et al., Adv. Mater. 2025) on humidity-responsive living S. commune films but say it lacked demonstrations and mechanism; Nie's own film was made with a plasticiser, so it is not pure mycelium.
findings.evidence_quote: The humidity-responsive behavior observed in living Schizophyllum commune films by Sinha et al. provides promising inspiration.

findings.claim: Wang et al. 2017 (Sci. Adv.) made true bilayers: a 1 um cell layer (E. coli, B. subtilis, yeast) on a 200 um latex sheet bends at 15 % RH and flattens at 95 % RH.
findings.value: cell layer 1 um on latex 200 um; 15 % -> 95 % RH
findings.evidence_quote: The top layer is composed of E. coli cells (1 μm thick), and the bottom layer is a latex sheet (200 μm thick). It bends at 15% RH (A) and becomes flat at 95% RH (B).

findings.claim: Cell-layer modulus fitted from the Stoney-type model is 70 MPa; single-cell volume is linear in RH (AFM), V/V_wet = 0.345 RH + 0.667 with V_wet taken at 95 % RH.
findings.evidence_quote: The fitted elastic modulus of the cell layer is 70 MPa

findings.claim: From that volume law the linear (1/3-power) strain of the cell layer is -10.3 % between 15 % and 95 % RH and -5.3 % between 30 % and 70 % RH (own calculation).
findings.source: own calculation: scripts/bm-mycelium-living-materials/bilayer_candidates.py (uses the formula quoted above)

findings.claim: Films respond within a few seconds and showed no change in bending after 100 dry-wet cycles (fabric samples).
findings.evidence_quote: biohybrid films that can reversibly change shape and biofluorescence intensity within a few seconds in response to environmental humidity gradients

findings.claim: The garment used B. subtilis (US FDA GRAS status); the E. coli shoe prototype was flagged as not GRAS, to be replaced by GRAS species before commercialisation.
findings.evidence_quote: The garment used B. subtilis , which has the status of GRAS given by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

findings.claim: Co-cultured mycelium + bacterial-cellulose films reach tensile strength 195.62 MPa and toughness 11.51 MJ/m3; haze is tuned from 16.0 to 78.5 % by culture duration (4-8 days).
findings.evidence_quote: the films achieve simultaneous high tensile strength (195.62 ± 9.06 MPa)

findings.claim: A Cordyceps militaris living fungal textile keeps metabolic activity, accepts yeast and Aspergillus co-cultures, and degrades almost completely in 41 days.
findings.evidence_quote: Environmental assessments confirm near-complete morphological degradation within 41 days.

findings.claim: Living building material (hydrogel + sand + bacteria): earlier prototype had no viable cells at 20 C and 24 % RH after about 80 % water loss, but adding 200 mM trehalose kept cells viable after 12 days at about 15 % RH, with 1-4 MPa compressive strength.
findings.value: no viable cells at 24 % RH (old); viable at ~15 % RH with trehalose; 1-4 MPa
findings.evidence_quote: Non-saturated (gel/sand = 0.13) and saturated (gel/sand ratio = 0.3) LBMs with 200 mM trehalose show viable cells after curing for 12 days under ambient conditions (22°C and RH of approximately 15%).

findings.claim: Mycelium is far less flammable than PLA or PMMA in micro-scale calorimetry (peak heat release 67 W/g vs 375 and 446 W/g; char 23 wt %), but this is a material test, not a building fire classification.
Variability and contamination are the stated reasons mycelium cannot yet reach industrial product certification.
findings.evidence_quote: The lack of consistency and reproducibility of a specific material profile, therefore, prevents the scaling up of mycelium in both size and quantity to reach an industry-standard level of product certification.

findings.claim: Fungal material production carries long cycles, contamination risk and multi-step processing like other fermentation industries.
findings.evidence_quote: These variables include long production cycles, the risk of contamination

findings.claim: Mycelium composites do not fit the European construction-product regulation and CE-marking route; the benchmark harmonised standard for an equivalent panel is EN 13986.
findings.evidence_quote: This misalignment poses challenges particularly in comparing MBCs with other construction materials whose performance and standard basic requirements are determined by the Construction‐products regulations (CPR)

findings.claim: Many studies omit the fungal species used, which prevents reproduction.
findings.evidence_quote: However, many studies fail to specify the fungal species used in composite production, thus hindering reproducibility due to the omission of mycelium network details

findings.claim: A 2026 opinion paper on living architecture names system stability, environmental variability, biosafety and regulatory constraints as the open challenges for engineered living materials in buildings.
findings.evidence_quote: it also introduces challenges related to system stability, environmental variability, biosafety, and regulatory constraints.

findings.claim: Numerical check of the project-record ceiling: over a 161 x 161 log grid of (m, n) the maximum of f is 1.5000 and it is reached where m^2 n = 1; f is also unchanged under (m, n) -> (1/m, 1/n), so it does not matter which layer is called 1.

recommendations: Do not use particulate mycelium-bound composite as the swelling layer: swelling is through-thickness, scatter is large (627 +/- 285 MPa flexural modulus), and wet integrity fails. Use mycelium, if at all, as a thin hydrophobic skin on the passive side.

If a living layer is wanted, make the PASSIVE layer a soft Formlabs elastomer (Silicone 40A, Flexible 50A or Flexible 80A V2), not Rigid 10K: with E_active about 24-70 MPa the optimum thickness ratio (m^2 n = 1) is only reached against a soft partner. Target active layer about 18-50 % of the passive thickness for a mycelium film, or at least 10-30 um of dried cells on 0.2 mm elastomer.

First experiment (cheap, reproducible): a dried B. subtilis or yeast cell layer sprayed on a 0.2 mm printed Flexible 50A strip, cycled 30 to 70 % RH in a salt-solution chamber; measure curvature and compare with the derated prediction (derate the linear-theory number by 3.8-4.4x). Second: a Nie-type Trametes film (needs a mycology lab) laminated to Silicone 40A.
Add the living layer AFTER printing and post-cure; do not put it through SLS sintering or SLA UV post-cure. Test fungal growth and adhesion on cured resin coupons first, since no literature exists.

For the architecture pitch, present the living layer as a research option with a non-living, certifiable fall-back (the elastomer bilayer, or dried-cell or killed-mycelium film) because no standard, fire class or CE route exists for mycelium products.

fleet.label: bm-natural-benchmarks
fleet.topic: Nature's benchmarks: pine cone, wheat awn, seed pod, Venus flytrap
fleet.summary: Natural benchmarks collected from open full texts and abstracts, with every quote re-extracted verbatim by script. PINE CONE is the only well-measured Timoshenko-type bilayer: Reyssat & Mahadevan (2009) m ~ 1, n ~ 5 (n from Dawson 1997, not read), cells ~20 percent longer wet, alpha = 0.001, response 29 min wetting and 96 min drying at 1 mm, predicted angle ~75 degrees against up to 100 observed. Eger et al (2022) measure layers of ~1.0 mm (active) and ~0.5 mm (passive), moduli 35->25 MPa (active) and 800->200 MPa (passive), +22 percent versus +1 percent length on wetting, 12-24 degree angles, 4.5 wt percent water uptake. Le Duigou & Castro (2016) give blocking forces 2.2-3.6 N and say bimetal theory fits 'fairly well' but over-predicts unless modulus is halved. My calculation (calc.py) puts these natural bilayers at 82-97 percent of the proved 3/2 ceiling from measured m and n (98-100 percent for P. pinaster only if n = 5 is assumed), never demonstrably at the exact optimum m^2 n = 1; the engineered paper/polymer strip of Reyssat & Mahadevan is at 98.8 percent. This CONTRADICTS the earlier files' adoption of m ~ 1, n ~ 5 as the pine-cone state: Eger's data give m ~ 0.5 and n = 8-23 (transverse indentation caveat). AWNS: Erodium and Pelargonium coil from tilted cellulose in a single layer (tilt 20 to 10 degrees; Erodium gruinum 46 mN, 528 uN m; Pelargonium 5.1 mN, 20.7 uN m; model within 16-25 percent for Erodium, 2.8x too high for the Pelargonium moment). Wheat awn: only the mechanism and a daily-humidity-cycle timescale; no numbers readable. PODS: Bauhinia has fibres at 45 degrees in two crossed layers and a dimensionless-width rule, but no thickness/modulus/angle values were readable (paywall); sesame capsule has an active parenchyma that shrinks to 30 percent of wet thickness with assumed stiffness ratios 20:5:0.1. FLYTRAP: closes in ~100 ms (up to 900 ms by one measure) by snap-buckling, reopens in 28-31 h; it is not a Timoshenko bilayer and is 10^4 times faster than diffusion allows at 1 mm. Theory agreement is stated qualitatively in every paper I could read; no percent error is reported except the Le Duigou modulus correction and the Ronzan model/measured ratios.
fleet.lay_summary: A pine cone opens when it dries because its scales are made of two layers that shrink by different amounts, like a strip of two metals that curls when heated. We gathered the measured sizes and speeds: the swelling layer is about a millimetre thick, the stiff layer about half that, and the scale needs roughly half an hour to an hour or two to move. A mathematical result already checked by computer says no two-layer strip can bend more than a fixed amount, and real pine cones get within about 80 to 97 percent of it, not exactly to it. Other plants do different tricks: the Venus flytrap snaps shut in a tenth of a second like a popper toy, and the cranesbill seed twists into a corkscrew from tilted threads in a single layer. Some numbers we wanted, such as those for wheat bristles and the twisting seed pod of the orchid tree, sit behind paywalls and could not be read.

findings.claim: Pine cone cell strain: single-cell ESEM shows the active-tissue cells of Pinus coulteri are about 20 percent longer wet than dry; the strain-humidity fit is eps = 0.0011*phi + 0.0033 (phi = humidity, as printed; unit of phi not stated in the caption).

findings.claim: Pine cone hygroscopic expansion coefficient alpha = 0.001 +/- 0.0001 (strain per unit relative humidity) measured on single cells, said to agree with macroscopic data (Harlow 1964). Taken as per percent RH this gives 0.113 strain over 0-100 %RH (my arithmetic, calc.py), about half the '~20 percent' length change quoted for wet versus dry.

Pine cone bilayer geometry and modulus ratio used by Reyssat & Mahadevan: passive/active thickness ratio m ~ 1, active-zone length ~10 h_a, and n ~ 5 taken from Dawson et al. 1997 (the Dawson text itself could not be fetched), giving f(m,n) ~ 1.3.

key_claims.claim: Pine-cone benchmark numbers for an engineered bilayer to match: active layer ~1 mm and passive ~0.5 mm; differential length strain ~21 percent in liquid water (22 percent vs 1 percent), ~11 percent over 0-100 %RH by the cell-level fit; response 29 min wet / 96 min dry at 1 mm (minutes to hours); water uptake only ~4.5 wt percent at 80 %RH.

key_claims.claim: Timoshenko-type theory fits the natural pine cone only 'fairly well' and over-predicts unless wet (about 50 percent lower) moduli are used; the same direction as the pine fibre modulus falling 800 -> 200 MPa when wet. An engineered design must be predicted with wet-state moduli.

key_claims.claim: Flytrap and Erodium are not Timoshenko bilayers: the flytrap closes in ~100 ms by snap-buckling (water transport takes minutes), and the Erodium coil comes from a single layer of tilted cellulose (20 to 10 degrees). The ceiling applies to pine cone, sesame and the paper strip; the others are analogies only.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The rapid closure of the Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) leaf in about 100 ms is one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.

glossary.plain: A material that changes shape when its moisture content changes, like a pine cone.
Two layers stuck together, one that swells and one that resists, so the strip curls.
How tightly a strip is bent: one over the radius of the circle it makes.
Thickness of the passive (restraining) layer divided by thickness of the active (swelling) layer.
How much stiffer the passive layer is than the active layer.
How stiff a material is: the force needed to stretch it, per area, per fraction stretched.
Units of stiffness or pressure: a million or a billion pascals; rubber is a few MPa, wood about 10 GPa.
How much something stretches or swells, as a fraction of its size (0.1 means 10 percent).
The proved upper limit: a two-layer strip can never bend more than 1.5 times its swelling mismatch divided by its thickness.
A quick flip from one curved shape to the opposite one, like a hair clip or a popper toy.
The direction the stiff cellulose threads in a cell wall run, relative to the cell's length.
Pressing a tiny hard tip into a surface to measure how stiff it is.
How full of water vapour the air is, as a percent of its maximum.
Percent of the dry weight that is water.
The push a bending strip makes when held in place so it cannot move.
The bristle on a grass or cranesbill seed that twists or bends with humidity.
The two kinds of woody plant cells in a pine scale: swelling ones and stiff fibre ones.
A rough time for water to soak through a layer of thickness h; grows with the square of the thickness.
A fingerprint of a file: any change to the file changes it.

recommendations: Use the pine cone as THE benchmark and state it in the proposal as numbers: active layer ~0.5-1 mm, passive layer ~0.5 mm (m ~ 0.5), length strain mismatch ~10-21 percent, water uptake ~4.5 wt percent at 80 %RH, response of minutes at 0.3-1 mm (29/96 min wet/dry at 1 mm), angular change 12-100 degrees depending on species and humidity range, and 102-cycle durability (Ulrich). Quote the ceiling as 'natural cones reach 82-97 percent of the proved 3/2 limit'.

Design to the thickness ratio, not the modulus ratio: for a measured n the optimum is m = 1/sqrt(n) (n=5: 0.447; n=8: 0.354; n=22.9: 0.209). Nature's m ~ 0.5 with n 8-23 implies pine cones are slightly thick on the passive side; an engineered strip can beat them by tuning m.

Predict with WET-state moduli. Both Le Duigou (50 percent reduction needed) and Eger (fibre 800 -> 200 MPa) show the dry-modulus model over-predicts. This supports the 'M_wet' arm already frozen in the earlier design-biomaterial.json.

Do not present the flytrap or Erodium as Timoshenko benchmarks. Use them only as analogies: flytrap = snap through (a hair clip flipping, 100 ms, 10^4 times faster than diffusion allows), Erodium = corkscrew from tilted threads, Bauhinia = a wrung towel twisting from two crossed layers, sesame = a soft cushion drying on a stiff shell, pine cone = a bimetal thermostat run by water instead of heat.

Close the gaps with a library copy: Dawson 1997 (n, alpha, units), Armon 2011 and its supplementary material (pod thickness, modulus, helix angle), Elbaum 2007 (awn modulus, bending angle). Until then keep these as second-hand and say so.

Compare engineered strain honestly: the earlier agents found stock resins and filaments swell 0.15-0.5 percent (filaments) or under 1 percent mass in 24 h (Formlabs resins). Pine active tissue changes length by 11-22 percent with ~4.5 wt percent water; the engineered bilayer should be benchmarked on strain per mass of water and on time, not only on final curvature.

fleet.topic: Reproducibility pack: parts list, files and costs
fleet.summary: Reproduction pack for the first bilayer swelling experiment on Formlabs hardware, with prices read from official Formlabs store pages on 2026-11-12. Bought new, the core kit costs about $9.0k to $11.5k: $5,133 is read directly from Formlabs and Adafruit pages (Form 4 Basic $2,625, Form Wash V2 $699, Form Cure V2 $999, two extra tanks $238, three 1 L resins $547, two humidity sensors $25), $3.4k to $4.7k comes from search-result snippets (mostly the 0.1 mg balance at $2.8k to $3.7k) and $0.4k to $1.7k from unverified guesses. Most of it can be borrowed (printer, wash, cure, balance, scanner, microscope, camera); the unavoidable purchases are resin, tanks, IPA, sensors, salts and small items, about $920 to $1,230. It contradicts an earlier file on one point: Open Material Mode has an official price, $875 for the Form 4, not about $3.7k. It amends the design: a 90 %RH salt jar is not a clean fixed point, so use NaCl (75 %RH) and K2SO4 (about 97 %RH). Instrument needs follow from the signal: a 40x4x1 mm strip weighs about 174 mg, so a 0.1 mg balance gives 0.3 % error at 8 % uptake and a 1 mg balance 2.9 %; length needs optical measurement at about 10 um per pixel with a certified scale, thickness about 2 um pixels. Included: a file-naming and logging convention with a tested validator, a pinned open-source Python stack that resolves under Python 3.14, and SHA-256 manifests of every saved page. The step most likely to differ between labs is conditioning each layer to a defined dry reference mass after the IPA wash: Flexible 80A V2 takes up about 45 % IPA by mass in a day, nobody has measured drying rates, and Formlabs gives two different wash times. PreForm is free but not open source.
fleet.lay_summary: This is a shopping list and instruction sheet so another lab can repeat our first test without asking us anything. The test needs a resin 3D printer, a rinse-and-bake station, a very fine scale and a way to hold air at a known dampness. Bought new it costs about as much as a small used car, but most of it can be borrowed from a university lab or makerspace, leaving about a thousand dollars of materials to buy. The step most likely to go differently from lab to lab is getting each printed strip properly dry after its alcohol rinse, because the soft rubber-like resin soaks up almost half its weight in alcohol and nobody has measured how fast it dries. If one lab leaves a trace of alcohol inside, it will read that as the strip swelling in water. So every lab should first record a drying curve, like weighing laundry until it stops getting lighter.

findings.claim: Humidity fixed points of saturated salts at 25 C (Greenspan 1977, Table 2, read from OCR of the NIST PDF): MgCl2 32.78 +-0.16, K2CO3 43.16 +-0.39, Mg(NO3)2 52.89 +-0.22, NaCl 75.29 +-0.12 %RH. K2SO4 is 97.59 (20 C) and 97.00 (30 C) in Table 3, so about 97.3 at 25 C by my linear interpolation.

Salt-jar temperature coefficients from Greenspan Table 3 (20 to 30 C): MgCl2 -0.063, NaCl -0.038, K2SO4 -0.059 %RH per C, so a +-2 C room gives at most +-0.13 %RH; the jar is not the weak link, the sensor is.

DEVIATION from design-biomaterial.json: its 90 %RH jar is not one of the clean saturated-salt points I could read; the readable wet points are NaCl 75 %RH and K2SO4 about 97 %RH. Use those (or log the real RH with a sensor) and call the target RH nominal.

Adafruit SHT45 board is $12.50 with stated accuracy +-1.0 %RH, +-0.1 C, so it cannot separate a 75 % jar from 74 % by itself; the salt jars (+-0.12 to +-0.4 %RH) are the better reference than the sensor.

Items I flag as commonly borrowable are $8,096.52-10,293.04 of that, leaving $919.98-1,231.20 to buy. Buying only the Formlabs chain new and borrowing the rest: about $5,243-5,554 (own arithmetic).
Resin demand is tiny against the 1 L minimum: total part volume of the planned ~170 strips is 16.9 mL (supports, rafts and tank fill not counted, unknown), 1.7 % of one cartridge.

Balance need: a 40x4x1 mm Flexible 80A V2 strip weighs about 174 mg (1.09 g/cm3). At 8 % uptake (14 mg) a 0.1 mg balance reads uptake to 0.3 % and a 1 mg balance to 2.9 %. At 0.1 % uptake (0.17 mg) even 0.1 mg gives 23 % error; reading 0.1 % to 5 % needs 0.82 g of material on a 0.1 mg balance (8.2 g on a 1 mg one). A 1 mg balance suffices for the swelling candidate, not for proving a passive layer inert on strip-sized coupons.

Length need: 0.2 % strain on 40 mm is 80 um, so the project target of 5 % of that is 4 um; 2400 dpi scanning is 10.6 um/pixel, a 4056-px camera over a 60 mm field is 14.8 um/pixel, a 10 um-step caliper has a difference sd of 4.1 um before contact error on a soft elastomer. So use optical measurement with sub-pixel edge fitting and a certified scale, not callipers; the Flexible 80A V2 1-day strain of about 1 % (400 um) is easy with anything.
Thickness need: 3 % of a 200 um layer is 6 um, so cut-edge images need pixels of about 2 um or finer; callipers cannot do this.

Rough conditioning-time estimate (assumption-laden): with water D >= 6e-12 m2/s (bm-diffusion-kinetics), t90 for a 1 mm slab with both faces open is about 9.8 h and drying about 25 h at 2.5x slower; for 0.2 mm about 0.4 h and 1 h. IPA D is not measured. This conflicts with the minutes-scale scaling (low confidence) in bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json unless IPA moves much faster than water, so it must be measured as a dry-down curve.

recommendations: RUN ORDER FOR A LAB STARTING FROM NOTHING (design says about 5 weeks): (1) install PreForm and record versions; (2) borrow what bom.csv flags Y; (3) buy resin, tanks, IPA, salts, sensors; (4) set up the jars and log RH for 48 h before any specimen goes in; (5) check the balance with check weights and the scanner or camera with a certified scale; (6) run the dry-down curve below before any swelling measurement; (7) then follow agents/design-biomaterial.json.

FOLDER LAYOUT: BM1/PREREG.md; BM1/CAD/ (STL or 3MF per build plus the .form project file); BM1/RAW/<batch>/ (camera DNG, scanner TIFF, edge images, named by naming.py); BM1/LOGS/ (measurements CSV, humidity CSV, one file per day, LF line ends, equipment.csv for printer firmware, PreForm version, resin lot and tank id); BM1/MANIFEST.tsv from naming.py manifest. Git for text files, the manifest for binaries.

FILE NAMES: BM1_<batch P##>_<specimen S### or bilayer B###>_<MASS|IMG|SCN|EDG|RHL|NOTE>_<DRY|R##|H2O|IPA|PRE|WSH>_t####h_<UTC YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ>.<csv|json|dng|tif|png|txt>. Example BM1_P01_S003_IMG_H2O_t0024h_20261113T143000Z.dng. Validate with naming.py check; log columns utc,batch,specimen,quantity,value,unit,uncertainty,instrument,operator_code,rh_pct,temp_c,note validated by naming.py log-check.

LOGGING RULES: UTC always; one reading per row; instrument id, operator code, RH and temperature on every row; raw values never overwritten, corrections appended as new rows; every photograph carries the scale target and a grey card in frame.

LENGTH PROTOCOL: scan or photograph at fixed height with the certified scale in the frame; edge position by sub-pixel fit (scikit-image) with a hand cross-check in Fiji on 10 percent of images; callipers only as a gross sanity check on elastomers.

FLAGGED STEP most likely to differ between labs: conditioning each printed layer to a defined dry reference mass after the IPA wash and post-cure (solvent age and time, drying time and RH, and the criterion for constant mass). Why: Flexible 80A V2 takes up about 45 % mass of IPA in a day (data sheet via project record) against 6.9 % for Tough 1000 and under 0.1 % for Rigid 10K; Formlabs prefers fresh solvent for the second wash and rates one IPA refill at 120 prints; the project record has a 10 min versus 5 + 5 min wash disagreement for the same resin; no leaching or drying rate is measured (my estimate is 1 to 25 h depending on thickness). Leftover solvent or leachable monomer would be read as water gain or swelling. Runner-up: UV dose, because a lab without Form Cure V2 will not reproduce the cure. Control: record a dry-down mass curve for 3 strips per resin, define constant mass as under 0.05 % change over 24 h at 22 +-2 C and 33 %RH (my proposed threshold, not from a source), use fresh IPA for the second wash, and log solvent batch and age.

AMENDMENTS TO THE EARLIER DESIGN: wet jar 97 %RH (K2SO4) or 75 %RH (NaCl) instead of 90 %RH; the Flex Build Platform ($339) is optional; Open Material Mode is $875, not about $3.7k, so the hydrogel fallback is cheaper than bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json said.

IF NO FORMLABS PRINTER IS ACCESSIBLE: ask a makerspace to print the two layers and hand them over unwashed (or washed to your protocol) with resin lot numbers. The Fuse path (about $49.8k before powder) is not realistic to reproduce in-house; keep it as an outsourced option.

fleet.label: bm-passive-facades-evidence
fleet.topic: Does passive humidity response actually help a building?
fleet.summary: Short answer: there is a real but narrow performance case, and humidity-driven shape-changing shading has no measured building benefit yet. (1) Humidity-driven SHADING: the best example (Freiburg, 424 printed cellulose modules, 13-month mock-up) measured only shade coverage (about 90 % on hot dry summer days, 50 % at night); the authors call the indoor-climate benefit future work. No energy, comfort or daylight number was found for any humidity-driven shading or cladding element. (2) The sign logic depends on climate. My own calculation on 2023 hourly weather for nine cities shows relative humidity tracks the need for shade in dry-summer climates (Madrid, Phoenix: element mostly closed, 0.95-0.98, in overheating sunny hours if it responds within an hour) and fails in humid ones (Singapore: mostly open in 98 % of those hours; Houston, Mumbai, Sydney 38-50 %). Slow, thick elements lose much of the benefit (Dubai 0.78 falls to 0.54 when the lag goes from 1 h to 24 h). (3) The only passive humidity-responsive building element with in-service numbers is humidity-controlled ventilation: 30 % cut in airflow-for-energy and 35-50 % fan energy in about 30 occupied dwellings (manufacturer-authored), 14-27 % heating savings in independent simulation, up to 11.6 kWh/m2 primary energy in a Warsaw simulation, but ineffective on upper floors without fans, and always relative to a constant-flow reference. (4) Passive humidity-BUFFERING materials give small energy effects (under 3 kWh/m2 in most of 15 Chinese cities; up to 19 % in a Beijing simulation) and larger comfort effects (up to 85 % in a simulated library with printed tiles). (5) Passive TEMPERATURE-responsive elements have the best short measured numbers (wax-louver tile 3.1x and 2.6x; hydrogel window -6.95 C) but only days of testing, and a 264-hour hydrogel life. (6) The strongest argument for passive devices is that motorised facades fail from maintenance (Institut du Monde Arabe non-functional within six years, secondary source). Design implication from the project record: curvature = 1.5 x strain / thickness and response time grows with thickness squared; with the earlier agent's estimated 0.2-0.95 % differential strain for stock Formlabs resins, only bilayers about 0.2-0.9 mm thick (total) could reach the curvature Freiburg measured, so a thick architectural-scale SLA or SLS part would be too slow and too weak for humidity actuation. Missing: annual simulation or test-cell comparison with measured actuation, hot-humid tests, multi-year weathering, cost and maintenance data, and any independent field test of hygromorphic shading.
fleet.lay_summary: A building shade that opens and closes by itself when the air turns damp or dry sounds clever, because it needs no motor. But nobody has yet measured whether such a shade really lowers a building's energy bill or makes rooms more comfortable. The best real example, in Freiburg, Germany, closed about 90 percent on hot dry afternoons, and the team said the indoor benefit still has to be measured. My own weather check suggests the trick works where hot days are dry, like Madrid or Phoenix, and backfires where hot days are also damp, like Singapore, because the shade would stay open. Think of a curtain that closes when the air is dry: fine in a desert, useless in a rainforest. The one damp-sensing part with real in-home data is a ventilation vent that opens wider when a bathroom gets humid; its saving looks real, but the measurements came mostly from the maker. So the honest answer is a narrow case, for dry-summer climates and thin parts, not yet proven by tests.

findings.claim: The best-documented humidity-responsive passive facade shading (Freiburg livMatS, 4D-printed cellulose bilayers) has no measured indoor-climate, energy or comfort result; the authors measured only shade coverage and defer the building benefit to future work.
findings.evidence_quote: it will be important to quantify the improvement of indoor climate regulation in future work

findings.claim: The 13-month outdoor monitoring in that study (June 2022 to July 2023, RH 10-91 %) was done on a tessellated mock-up of the facade system; the 424 final modules were deployed on the building afterwards. This refines an earlier agent's wording that the 424 modules themselves ran outdoors for more than a year.
findings.evidence_quote: installed in a mock-up of the facade system and evaluated for 13 months under the full range of daily and seasonal weather effects

findings.claim: Measured shade coverage in summer: nearly 90 % on hot, sunny, low-RH days (RH about 25 %) and 50 % at night and early morning; in winter the modules stay open and close only from 50 % to 65 % on warmer, drier days.
findings.evidence_quote: During hot and sunny days, the RH is typically low at around 25%, and the 4D-printed modules reach nearly 90% shade coverage

findings.claim: The control logic works because, in Freiburg's dry hot summers and humid cold winters, relative humidity is an indirect proxy for the need for shade.
findings.evidence_quote: creating an indirect but reliable link between the need for shading and the behavior of hygromorphic materials in response to RH

findings.claim: The authors list hot-humid tropical and cold-dry climates as untested.
findings.evidence_quote: exploring applications in different building systems and climate zones, such as hot and humid tropical or cold and dry tundra climates

findings.claim: Durability evidence for the cellulose bilayer is short relative to a building: 170 lab actuation cycles at RH 30-90 %, a UV chamber test with small curvature loss, and the 13-month mock-up. The authors state the cycle count is small against a building's lifetime.
findings.evidence_quote: The number of cycles tested is still small compared to the entire lifetime of a building

findings.claim: Actuation speed of the printed cellulose bilayer: full transformation between 30 % and 90 % RH within 30 minutes, fast enough to follow diurnal humidity swings.
findings.evidence_quote: The bilayers reach a full transformation between two RH extremes of 30% and 90% within 30 minutes

findings.claim: At 80 % RH the printed cellulose bilayers average a curvature of 0.0155 1/mm (15.5 1/m) regardless of temperature.
findings.evidence_quote: At 80% RH, all bilayers are observed with an average curvature of 0.0155 mm

findings.claim: Manufacturing yield at facade scale: 30 of 424 modules reprinted at print stage (7 %), 6 more replaced after cycle testing (1.4 %).
findings.evidence_quote: after which only six modules were re-printed and replaced (1.4% failure rate)

findings.claim: A 2023 systematic review of hygroscopic adaptive facades (El-Dabaa and Abdelmohsen) concludes that most studied papers focus on the material's response and facade implementation, not on measured building performance.
findings.evidence_quote: most of the studied papers focus on the response behaviour of programmable materials to variation in moisture content and the implementation of hygroscopic design in adaptive

findings.claim: The 2013 review of climate adaptive building shells (Loonen et al.) concluded the concept is not yet mature.
findings.evidence_quote: it was found that the concept of CABS cannot yet be considered mature

findings.claim: A 2025 shading study states the trade-off of passive actuation: simpler and more sustainable, but often less responsive to dynamic conditions than motorised systems.
findings.evidence_quote: offering simpler and more sustainable operation, but often lack responsiveness to dynamic conditions

findings.claim: Motorised adaptive facades have failed in service: the Institut du Monde Arabe's 240 motor-controlled apertures became non-functional within six years because of maintenance demand (as reported by a 2025 review citing its ref 12; the primary source was not read).
findings.evidence_quote: it gradually failed, becoming non-functional within six years

findings.claim: The same review reports that GSW Headquarters (1999) blinds still operate after 25 years but need more maintenance than conventional buildings.
findings.evidence_quote: which, while still operational after 25 years, requires more maintenance than conventional buildings

findings.claim: Field monitoring of humidity-controlled ventilation in occupied Paris-area dwellings (heating season 2007-2008, mechanical exhaust with humidity-sensitive inlets and grilles) measured an average 30 % cut in airflow-for-energy versus the French constant-airflow reference (55 % if extrapolated to statistical average occupancy). The authors work for the manufacturer (Aereco), so this is not independent.
findings.evidence_quote: The measured savings on the airflow for this project have been evaluated at 30% in average (55% if extrapolating to the statistical average occupancy in France).

findings.claim: Same monitoring: fan electricity cut by 35-50 % versus the constant-flow reference.
findings.evidence_quote: the energy consumption of the fan has been reduced between 35% to 50% in comparison with the French reference for a constant airflow ventilation system

findings.claim: The humidity-sensitive grille behaves seasonally: mostly closed in the cold season, wider open in the hot season. That saves heating losses; my inference (not measured there) is that it admits more outdoor air in warm humid weather, which would not help cooling or latent load.
findings.evidence_quote: the grille is mainly closed in cold season; in hot season the grille aperture opens wider

findings.claim: Internal inconsistency in the manufacturer paper: its abstract says more than 4.5 million dwellings are equipped with humidity-controlled ventilation, its introduction says more than 7 million. Both are unverified manufacturer claims.
findings.evidence_quote: more than 7 million dwellings are already equipped today only considering humidity controlled ventilation

findings.claim: Independent-group simulation (Belgian universities, CONTAM, detached house, self-regulating inlets): the humidity-controlled system increases heating-energy savings up to 27 % for very airtight buildings and 14 % for average airtightness, relative to the constant-flow system; adding moisture buffering changed energy demand by only 0.75 %.
findings.evidence_quote: System C+ increases the energy savings up to 27% for very airtight buildings and 14% for buildings with an

findings.claim: Simulation in Warsaw (Dfb climate): humidity-sensitive demand-controlled ventilation in an eight-floor block saved up to 11.64 kWh/m2 of primary energy, but operation on the higher floors was ineffective and needed supplementary fans; savings depend on the electricity source (1.07 vs 5.18 kWh/m2).
findings.evidence_quote: However, the operation of the system on higher floors was found to be ineffective.

findings.claim: Simulation of five interior finishes in 15 Chinese cities: moisture-buffering materials cut HVAC load by under 3 kWh/m2 in most cases; benefit is clear in mild climates and weak in humid areas, and the effect can worsen indoor humidity.
findings.evidence_quote: the reduction is limited, within 3 kWh/m 2 , in most simulated cases

findings.claim: A simulated gypsum-based humidity-control material gave a maximum energy-saving rate of 19.31 % in Beijing, strongest where day-night temperature and RH differences are large. Simulation only.
findings.evidence_quote: The maximum potential energy-saving rate in Beijing can reach up to 19.31%.

findings.claim: Binder-jet 3D-printed superhygroscopic geopolymer tiles in a simulated 15-person library room improved annual hygrometric comfort by up to 85 % (a comfort metric, not energy), moisture buffering value above 14 g m-2 %RH-1. Dynamic hygrothermal simulation, not a measured building.
findings.evidence_quote: The use of 3D-printed, geopolymer tiles for surface finishing in a library hosting 15 people was shown to improve annual indoor hygrometric comfort by up to 85%

findings.claim: Measured outdoor test of a passive wax-motor louver tile in insulated boxes (Santa Barbara, July and September): 3.1x less daytime heat input than a fixed black tile and 2.6x less night heat loss than a fixed white tile. A small tile, a short test, numbers read from the arXiv version of the Device 2024 paper.
findings.evidence_quote: our device reduced the energetic cost of cooling by 3.1x and heating by 2.6x compared to non -switching devices

findings.claim: Actuator hysteresis is a design-critical number: a prior two-way shape-memory-polymer radiative switch had a high switching band and large hysteresis, which the arXiv authors call impractical for regulating daily temperature fluctuations.
findings.evidence_quote: This makes it impractical for use in regulating daily temperature fluctuations

findings.claim: Thermochromic PNIPAm hydrogel window coating, two-day outdoor test in a self-built insulated test box (Wuhan, ambient about 41 C, 718 W/m2): average daytime indoor temperature 6.95 C below ordinary glass (43.15 vs 51.44 C), 384 kJ/m2 per day estimated saving. Short test, one site.
findings.evidence_quote: The PHPF group exhibited an average temperature reduction of 6.95

findings.claim: Same hydrogel window: dehydration forces a PVDC encapsulation, and even so the service life is extended only to 264 hours.
findings.evidence_quote: extending its service life to 264 hours without compromising optical functionality

findings.claim: Own calculation on 2023 hourly weather for nine cities: if a passive shade is fully closed at RH 30 % and fully open at RH 90 % (the range tested by Cheng 2024) and responds within an hour, it is, averaged over hours with T>=24 C and sun >=300 W/m2, 0.95 closed in Madrid and 0.98 closed in Phoenix.

recommendations: Do not claim an energy or comfort benefit for a humidity-driven shape-changing element in the proposal; claim a demonstrated, measured shape change and a test plan. The literature has no such number to borrow.

Pitch it for climates where hot hours are dry (Mediterranean, arid, continental summers). Avoid hot-humid claims. In temperate-humid London (mean RH 79.7 % in the 2023 calculation) a pure-RH shade is weak (selectivity 0.37 at 1 h lag, 0.28 at 6 h); a temperature-coupled design, as Freiburg's has, helps.

Design for thickness: keep total bilayer thickness well under 1 mm if resin differential strain is 0.2-1 %, or pick a much higher-swelling pair (hydrogel-resin pairs in earlier files) and accept durability risk (a hydrogel window lasted 264 h even when encapsulated).

A credible proof of concept is two matched boxes or a small test cell (static vs responsive) logging indoor temperature and illuminance for months, plus a humidity-buffering or humidity-vent element as a second, lower-risk demonstration that has published building numbers.

Treat humidity-sensitive ventilation and moisture-buffering tiles as the evidence-backed neighbours of the idea; the printed-tile Nature Communications study shows printed passive humidity elements are publishable.

fleet.label: bm-poc-designs
fleet.topic: Five concrete proof-of-concept objects with predicted numbers
fleet.summary: Five printable proof-of-concept objects were designed around the verified law kappa = f(m,n) d_eps / h (ceiling 3/2 at m^2 n = 1), with all numbers produced by saved scripts (run_all.py, about 6 s, seeded, bit-identical on rerun). The law itself was re-checked two ways: the project's check script re-run unchanged, and an independently written layered-beam solver that matches f(m,n) to 1e-9; a laminate-plate calculation shows the small-deflection plate curvature equals the beam curvature exactly (equal Poisson ratio), which contradicts the earlier '(1+nu)' inference; the extra factor can only arise after buckling (Pezzulla abstract: isometric mean curvature three quarters of natural, i.e. at most 1.5 x for a cylinder). Materials: the only stock Formlabs resin with a water response big enough to drive a bilayer is Flexible 80A V2 (+3 % volume in 1 day, +7 % in 1 week, ASTM D471), giving 1-3 % linear strain by my arithmetic; partners are soft (Flexible 50A, Silicone 40A) because stiff partners (Tough 1000, Grey V5, Rigid 10K) reach only 59, 33 and 11 % of the ceiling at printable thickness and the highlighted Elastic 50A / Rigid 10K pair only 6 %. Predictions (median, 5th-95th percentile over the stated strain, modulus, thickness and diffusivity ranges): object 1, a 30 x 3 x 1 mm strip, final R = 41 mm (28-83), tip deflection 10.5 mm, settling 8 h; object 2, a ladder of ten fingers, tests the f(m) fall-off (f(0.8)/f(0.4) = 0.55) and kappa proportional to 1/h (slope -0.99); object 3, a width ladder up to a 60 mm tile, crosses from the strip regime (width/thickness 3) to the plate regime outside the verified law and predicts between 1.0 and 1.5 x the strip curvature; object 4, a three-generation Y-tree, predicts the same turning angle (35 deg) in every generation but settling times in the ratio 15 : 1 trunk to twig (Fickian 16, front-driven 4); object 5, a 120 mm louver blade module, turns 58 deg (30-85) and settles in 2.7 days (0.8-10) in water, but time grows as L squared (about 184 days at 1 m) and a horizontal soft blade sags more than it curls. Before calibration the strain prior dominates the uncertainty (73-88 % of variance) and moduli barely matter; after a coupon calibration the predicted/true curvature has a 99 % band of about 0.8-1.3. New practical findings: strips must be photographed submerged (self-weight sag of a 30 mm strip in air is comparable to the signal), the IPA wash gives 29 % linear stretch and must precede bonding, and Formlabs' own mass and volume rows imply diffusivities that differ by 6.8x. Feasible with stock resins in under a week: objects 1-3 (bond quality is the risk), object 4 with risk (0.2 mm active twig), object 5 in water only. None of this is a measurement: every strain and modulus is a derived prior, and the first experiment is the coupon calibration.
fleet.lay_summary: The idea is a two-layer strip: one layer swells when it gets wet and the other does not, so the strip bends like a drying leaf. A checked rule says how much it can bend: the best two-layer strip curls to a radius of about two-thirds of its own thickness divided by how much the wet layer grows. We worked out five things to print, from one little strip up to a small window-shade module, and for each we predict how far it bends and how long it takes to get wet through. For the first strip the prediction is a curl of about 41 millimetres radius within a working day in water, with a plausible range of 28 to 83. The honest catch is that nobody has measured how much the Formlabs resins swell, so the first step is to soak small test strips and measure them, and only then compare the bends with the rule. Think of a wet sponge cloth versus a thick sponge: doubling the thickness makes the soaking four times slower, so a real building-sized shade made of these plastics would take months.

findings.claim: The project's own ceiling script, re-run unchanged and read-only today, reports that f(m,n) <= 3/2 survives a grid, exact-rational checks along m^2 n = 1, and 4000 hill-climbs from random starts.
findings.evidence_quote: VERDICT: the ceiling holds in every check

findings.claim: My own layered-beam solver (Euler-Bernoulli, plane stress, perfect bond, written independently of the project's closed form) reproduces the project's f(m,n) to 1e-9 at seven (m,n) points, and f is unchanged when the two layers are relabelled (m,n)->(1/m,1/n).

Curvature of an optimal bilayer (m^2 n = 1) settles to within 10 % of its final value at 0.719 h_a^2/D and reaches 99 % at 1.653 h_a^2/D, identical for passive/active modulus ratios 0.1, 1 and 10; one-face uptake t50/t90/t99 = 0.197/0.848/1.781 h^2/D. This independently confirms the numbers of the earlier diffusion-kinetics agent (bm-diffusion-kinetics.json: 0.719 and 1.65), using a different closed-form moment method.

CONTRADICTS the earlier inference (spec-bilayer-physics.json, finding d: 'kappa_cyl ~ (1+nu) kappa_beam') as a statement about small-deflection plates: for isotropic layers with equal Poisson ratio and an isotropic eigenstrain, classical laminate (plate) theory gives kappa_plate / kappa_beam = 1.000000 exactly, for any modulus ratio. A factor above 1 can only appear after the plate leaves the spherical shape (buckling into a cylinder).

The post-buckling factor is bounded, from a source abstract, at 3/2: Pezzulla et al. state the mean curvature of the isometric state is three fourths of the natural curvature. A cylinder has mean curvature kappa_cyl/2, so kappa_cyl = 1.5 kappa_natural (my arithmetic, assuming 'natural curvature' means the spherical-state principal curvature, which I could not confirm from the full text). The tile (object 3) is therefore predicted between 1.0 and 1.5 times the strip law once w^2 kappa/h is well above 1.
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.05259 (arXiv export API record saved: data/bm-poc-designs/arxiv_1509.05259.xml; DOI 10.1039/C6SM00246C)
findings.evidence_quote: We find that the mean curvature of the isometric state is three fourth's the natural curvature, which we verify by numerics and experiments.

findings.claim: Flexible 80A V2 (Formlabs data sheet, ASTM D471 slabs, deionized water): +8 % mass and +3 % volume after 1 day; +9 % mass and +7 % volume after 1 week. I re-fetched and re-read the PDF today. This is the only Formlabs water-swelling datum large enough to drive a bilayer, and it contradicts the blanket 'stock resins gain under 1 % in 24 h' of the earliest agents (that statement holds only for the 1 cm cube table).
findings.confidence: high (numbers); medium (row/column reading, from text order of the PDF)
findings.value: 1 day +8 % mass +3 % volume; 1 week +9 % mass +7 % volume

findings.claim: Linear strain implied by those volume changes if swelling is isotropic: 1.03^(1/3)-1 = 0.99 % (1 day) and 1.07^(1/3)-1 = 2.28 % (1 week); an upper end of 3.2 % follows from ideal mixing of 9 % water mass (0.09 x 1.09/1.00 = 9.8 % volume) into resin of solid density 1.09 g/cm3. These three numbers are the strain prior of every prediction here.
findings.confidence: medium (isotropy and ideal mixing are assumptions)
findings.evidence_quote: Solid Density 1.09 g/cm3

findings.claim: DEEPENS bm-diffusion-kinetics.json: inverting the same two Formlabs points with a two-face Fickian slab gives very different diffusivities depending on whether the MASS pair (8 -> 9 %) or the VOLUME-derived strain pair (0.99 -> 2.28 %) is used: D = 9.3e-12 m2/s versus 1.4e-12 m2/s for an assumed 2 mm slab (factor 6.8), with equilibrium strain about 2.5 % from the volume pair. The slab thickness is not stated in the data sheet, so both scale as thickness squared. The strain (volume) pair is the relevant one for bending, and it is the slower; the earlier agent used only the mass pair.
findings.evidence_quote: Rectangular slabs, used for hardness, mass, and volume change, are evaluated immediately after wiping dry without a conditioning period.

findings.claim: Moduli used are own secant estimates from the data sheets' stress-at-elongation rows: Flexible 80A V2 post-cured 2.9 MPa at 50 % (5.8 MPa secant), 4.7 MPa at 100 %; Flexible 50A 0.9 MPa at 50 %, 1.7 MPa at 100 % (1.7-1.8 MPa); Silicone 40A 0.4 MPa at 50 %, 1.0 MPa at 100 % (0.8-1.4 MPa). They are not tensile moduli; Formlabs publishes none for these elastomers.
findings.evidence_quote: Stress at 50% Elongation 1.5 MPa 2.9 MPa | Stress at 50% Elongation 0.5 MPa 0.9 MPa | Stress at 50% elongation 0.4 MPa

findings.claim: Flexible 80A V2 hardness is 68 Shore A green and 83 post-cured, and drops 26 Shore A points after 1 day in water. Using the Gent Shore-to-modulus relation (UNVERIFIED BACKGROUND, from memory) this is about 11.4 MPa dry and 3.2 MPa wet, a wet/dry ratio of 0.28; I used it only to bracket the wet modulus (prior 4.3-11 MPa dry x 0.28-1.0).
findings.evidence_quote: Shore A Hardness 68 83

findings.claim: Water uptake of the candidate passive partners in Formlabs' 24 h, 1 cm cube table: Flexible 50A 0.7 % (isopropanol 39.2 %), Silicone 40A under 0.1 % (isopropanol 5.9 %), Rigid 10K under 0.1 %. Cube mass at 24 h is not an equilibrium value and gives no strain, so the passive layer's own water strain is a prior (Flexible 50A 0-0.8 %, Silicone 0-0.05 %), not a measurement.

findings.claim: Print constraints used: Flexible 50A and Silicone 40A have a stated minimum layer thickness of 100 micron on their product pages and both list Form 4; Flexible 80A V2 test parts were printed on a Form 4 at 100 um settings; Form 4 build volume 20.0 x 12.5 x 21.0 cm; Fuse 1+ 30W build volume 165 x 165 x 300 mm. Every object below fits (largest footprint about 150 x 60 mm), and every layer thickness is a multiple of 0.1 mm.
findings.evidence_quote: Compatible Printer Form 4, Form 4B, Form 3, Form 3B, Form Studio 1 Print Technology SLA Biocompatibility Skin Contact Minimum Layer Thickness 100 micron | 20.0 × 12.5 × 21.0 cm | 165 x 165 x 300 mm

findings.claim: Silicone 40A's data sheet washes parts in 80 % isopropanol / 20 % butyl acetate and post-cures at 60 C submerged in water. A silicone that is washed in a solvent mix is not a drop-in partner to be washed after bonding; bond strength to acrylate resins is not documented anywhere I read.
findings.evidence_quote: washed in a Form Wash for 20 minutes in 80% Isopropyl Alcohol / 20% Butyl Acetate

findings.claim: Which partner reaches the ceiling at printable thickness (total 1.0 mm, every layer >= 0.2 mm, nominal moduli): soft partners do, stiff partners do not. Flexible 80A V2 (wet 3.0 MPa) with Flexible 50A gives f = 1.495 (99.6 % of 3/2) and with Silicone 40A f = 1.493; with Tough 1000 f = 0.88 (59 %), Grey V5 0.50 (33 %), Rigid 10K 0.16 (11 %). The optimum stiff layer would be 0.054 mm (Tough 1000) or 0.017 mm (Rigid 10K), below any printable wall.
findings.source: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-poc-designs/run_all.py step 4 (results.json: partner_table_h1mm); moduli from the data sheets (Tough 1000 932 MPa, Grey V5 2500, Rigid 10K 10 000 are post-cured tensile moduli in the sibling file bm-formlabs-all-resins.json, not re-read by me)

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS the design appeal of the pair the earlier agents highlighted (Elastic/Flexible 50A at 39 % isopropanol against Rigid 10K at under 0.1 %): the numbers are confirmed, but with a 10 GPa passive layer of at least 0.2 mm the best achievable f is 0.096, i.e. 6.4 % of the ceiling, and the strain (about 29 % linear for the softer resins) lies far outside the small-strain domain of the law.
findings.confidence: medium (modulus of 50A is a secant estimate)

findings.claim: Hazard for post-processing: Flexible 80A V2 gains +45 % mass and +113 % volume in isopropanol in one day, a linear stretch of 28.7 %. Silicone 40A gains 5.9 % mass (about 2.7 % linear by ideal mixing with an ASSUMED density 1.1 g/cm3). A bonded Flexible 80A / Silicone stack placed in the wash would curl to R of about 3 x its thickness (small-strain law, outside its domain), so each layer must be washed and dried BEFORE bonding and the bonded stack must never be washed.
findings.confidence: medium (data sheet numbers high; silicone strain assumed)
findings.value: linear stretch 80A V2 28.7 %, Si 40A 2.7 %, R = 3.0 h

findings.claim: OBJECT 1 prediction (30 x 3 mm strip, 0.4 mm Flexible 80A V2 over 0.6 mm Flexible 50A plus a 0.02-0.10 mm bond line, immersed in water at room temperature): final radius R = 41 (27.6-83.3) mm (median, 5th-95th percentile), tip deflection 10.5 (5.35-14.8) mm, tip angle 41.9 (20.6-62.2) deg, time to settle within 10 % of final 7.6 (2.1-30) h. With Silicone 40A as passive layer: R = 33.6 (25-54.2) mm, tip deflection 12.5 (8.09-15.9) mm, settling 8.3 (2.6-28) h. Effective kappa h / d_eps = 1.45 (1.3-1.49) (A) and 1.48 (1.37-1.5) (B), never above 3/2.
findings.confidence: medium (conditional on the strain prior; no hygroscopic measurement exists)
findings.value: A: R 41.0 mm; B: R 33.6 mm

findings.claim: Before calibration the prediction is dominated by the unmeasured swelling strain: squared Spearman correlation with log curvature is 0.73 (pair A) and 0.88 (pair B) for the active layer's strain, 0.20 / 0.00 for the passive strain, and at most 0.006 for either modulus. This is the law's 'modulus drops out' in practice, with a limit: at the nominal 0.4/0.66 mm stack, over a 3 x 3 grid of E_a (1.2, 3, 11 MPa) and E_p (1.2, 1.7, 2.5 MPa) f ranges from 1.22 to 1.50 (6 of 9 points at or above 1.41), the worst corner (E_a 1.2 MPa with E_p 2.5 MPa) being 18 % below the ceiling (f_tim values computed from the project script); the moduli explain under 1 % of the variance.

Prediction power after calibration: if the free strains of both layers are read from 30 mm coupons (+-0.02 mm), layer thicknesses from callipers (+-0.02 mm) and the bond line from a microscope (+-0.01 mm), but moduli stay at their central values, the ratio predicted/true curvature has a 95 % interval of 0.87-1.20 (pair A) and 0.90-1.16 (pair B), and a 99 % interval of 0.80-1.31 and 0.86-1.24. A measured curvature outside the 99 % interval refutes 'kappa = f d_eps / h with coupon-measured inputs' for that build (subject to a defect check and n >= 6 replicate strips).
findings.confidence: medium (own calculation; excludes physics outside the law)

findings.claim: Gravity makes air-photography of these soft strips unreliable: a 30 mm cantilever sags 4.6 (3-7.2) mm (A) and 6.6 (4.3-10) mm (B) under its own weight in air, comparable to the predicted tip deflection (10.5 / 12.5 mm), but only 0.19 (0.12-0.29) / 0.6 (0.39-0.91) mm when submerged (net density about 90 kg/m3 against water). Strips should therefore be photographed in the bath (flat-window cuvette), or kept under 20 mm in air. This contradicts the earlier recommendation to photograph 40 mm strips in air (spec-bilayer-physics.json), which was written without a self-weight term: at 40 mm the sag is about 3.2 times larger still (L^4).
findings.source: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-poc-designs/run_all.py step 8 (object1 sag_air_mm, sag_water_mm; formula q L^4/(8 D), densities 1.09 and 1.01 g/cm3 from the data sheets, silicone 1.1 assumed)

findings.claim: Camera is not the limiting error: a circle fit to a photographed silhouette with 0.03 mm edge noise (about half a 0.05 mm pixel) recovers curvature with relative standard deviation 0.1-0.51 % for R = 20-100 mm over a 30 mm arc.
findings.confidence: high (own simulation; real lens distortion not modelled)

findings.claim: OBJECT 2 prediction (ratio ladder at 1.0 mm total, active thickness 0.2-0.8 mm in 0.1 mm steps): kappa h / d_eps peaks near an active thickness of 0.41 mm (90 % interval 0.32-0.52) for pair A and 0.35 mm (0.26-0.45) for pair B. Predicted shape ratios f(0.8)/f(0.4) = 0.55 (0.3-0.89) (A) and 0.41 (0.22-0.69) (B); f(0.2)/f(0.4) = 0.79 (0.58-0.98) (A). The curve is flat near the top (rungs 0.3-0.5 within about 10 % of each other), so the ladder tests the fall-off at the ends, not the exact peak.

OBJECT 2 thickness ladder at fixed layer ratio (total 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 mm): the law predicts kappa proportional to 1/h; the fitted log-log slope per simulated build is -0.993 (-1.02--0.874) (A) and -0.998 (-1.03--0.933) (B) against the ideal -1; settling time grows from 2.1 (0.5-9.3) h (0.5 mm) to 30 (8.5-1e+02) h (2.0 mm) for pair A, with 99 % of simulated builds settled inside 7 days at 2.0 mm.

OBJECT 3 (tile width ladder, 60 mm long, 1.0 mm thick; widths 3, 6, 12, 24, 60 mm): the strip-validity parameter Omega = w^2 kappa / h is 0.2 (0.1-0.32) at 3 mm (strip law valid, Omega < 0.3 in 92 % of builds), 0.82 (0.4-1.3) at 6 mm (transition), 3.3 (1.6-5.1) at 12 mm, and 81.6 (40.1-128) at 60 mm, i.e. a continuous 60 mm tile is far into the plate regime that the verified law does not cover. Strip-law radius 41.5 (27.8-82.1) mm; if a wide tile buckles to a cylinder with 1.5 times the curvature the radius would be 27.7 (18.5-54.7) mm and the edge rise 14.7 (8-19.4) mm against 10.4 (5.4-14.7) mm. Scaling guesses for the critical width c x sqrt(h/kappa): 3.3 / 6.6 / 13.3 mm for c = 0.5 / 1 / 2 (prefactor unknown). Design target that follows for a NEW biomaterial: at the optimum, settling takes 0.719 h_a^2/D, so a 2 mm active layer that must settle in one hour needs D >= 8.0e-10 m2/s, about 80 times the best stock-resin estimate here (1e-11) and of the order of the porous plant-tissue value 1e-9 m2/s quoted (second hand, not re-read by me) by Reyssat & Mahadevan. recommendations: Run experiment 0 first (1 day): print free coupons of every layer (30 x 3 x 0.4 mm Flexible 80A V2, 30 x 3 x 0.6 mm Flexible 50A and Silicone 40A), wash and dry them, record dry length and mass, immerse in deionized water at a controlled temperature, and log length (+-0.02 mm) and mass (0.1 mg) against sqrt(time) for 7 days. This yields the missing strain, D and slab-independent data and shrinks the object 1 uncertainty from a factor 2-3 to about +-15 %.

Decide the bond method before anything else (it is the single point of failure and nothing documented exists): wash and fully dry both layers first, bond with a thin film of liquid Flexible 50A, shim the bond line to 0.05 mm, flash-cure; peel-test and microscope-section three samples; try the Silicone 40A pair only as an experiment.
Photograph strips submerged in a flat-window tank, or keep any in-air strip under 20 mm; never wash a bonded stack in isopropanol.

Print order: day 1 coupons plus object 1 and 2 layers (both resin tanks), day 2 bond, days 2-6 soak and measure; object 3 shares the same layers; make object 4 only after the 0.2 mm active layers have printed cleanly; object 5 blades are the same layers at 1.2/1.8 mm.

Ask Formlabs (support) for the slab thickness, humid-air (RH) mass and dimension data and the DMA storage modulus of Flexible 80A V2; this removes the 6.8x diffusivity ambiguity and the wet-modulus guess.

For the new biomaterial the law implies four floors: differential strain >= 2 %, diffusivity >= 8e-10 m2/s for a 2 mm layer settling in an hour, an equivalent modulus of about 0.5 GPa for a 1 m horizontally cantilevered blade, and a bondable inert partner at a thickness ratio near sqrt(E_passive/E_active). Stock Formlabs resins meet the first only marginally and miss the second by about two orders of magnitude.

Offer the practice the scaling law and the proof-of-concept as 'what the law forbids' (time ~ L^2, sag ~ L^4/h^2, wide plates leave the law) before the material claim; humid-air performance of any Formlabs resin is not yet evidenced.

could_not_find: Any measured hygroscopic strain, humid-air (RH) swelling, or water diffusivity of any Formlabs resin or powder. The strain prior comes from two volume figures in one data sheet (isotropy assumed, slab thickness unstated); the diffusivity prior spans a 6.8x disagreement between the mass and the volume rows of the same sheet.

Any bond strength or bond-line data between Flexible 80A V2 and Flexible 50A or Silicone 40A (silicone to acrylate adhesion is undocumented), and whether a Form 4 job can carry two resins; the one-resin-per-job statement is relayed from bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json and I did not re-verify it with the manual.

A tensile or storage modulus for Flexible 80A V2, Flexible 50A or Silicone 40A. The data sheet has a DMA storage-modulus curve for 80A V2 (1 Hz, 0.1 % strain) but it is a figure and I could not read values; my moduli are secant estimates from stress at 50-200 % elongation, and the wet modulus rests on the Gent Shore-to-modulus relation, which is unverified background from memory.
Equilibrium water strain of the passive partners (Flexible 50A, Silicone 40A); only 24 h cube mass is published, so passive strain is a prior (0-0.8 % and 0-0.05 %).

The numerical prefactor of the strip-to-plate transition (Armon 2011 full text not read) and the full text of Pezzulla et al. (only the abstract), so the x1.5 bound for a buckled tile is an arithmetic reading of the abstract, and whether it depends on Poisson ratio is unknown.

A finite-strain (large-deformation) bilayer model; I did not implement one, so the isopropanol regime (29 % linear stretch) is only flagged as a hazard and not predicted, and the 1-3 % water regime carries an unquantified finite-strain error of the order of the strain itself.
Print times, cartridge availability, lead time and cost of Flexible 80A V2, Flexible 50A and Silicone 40A for the team's printers; the under-a-week claim assumes the resins are on hand.
Concentration-dependent or Case II water transport in these elastomers: the model uses a constant Fickian D; the passive-layer swelling lag is a mean-strain approximation.

Gravity sag is a first-order small-deflection formula and breaks down where the sag exceeds the blade length (the horizontal 120 mm blade); it only shows gravity dominates. Densities of Silicone 40A (assumed 1.1 g/cm3) and of the 50A/80A in water are unverified.
Any physical measurement: nothing was printed or tested; every number in this report is a prediction from data-sheet-derived priors.

glossary.plain: Two thin sheets stuck face to face; if one grows and the other does not, the pair bends.
How tightly something is curved; the radius is the size of the circle the bend would draw (small radius, tight curl).
How much a material stretches or grows, as a fraction of its length (1 percent means 1 mm per 100 mm).
How stiff a material is: how much force it takes to stretch it a given amount.
How fast water spreads into a material; the soaking time is the thickness squared divided by this number.
Growth of a material because liquid has soaked into it.
The liquid plastic a Formlabs printer hardens with light, layer by layer.
A rubbery plastic that stretches a lot and springs back.
A small test piece printed alongside the real parts and measured on its own.
Running the same calculation thousands of times with inputs drawn at random from their plausible ranges to see how wide the answers spread.
The range that holds the middle 90 out of 100 simulated outcomes.
The ordinary kind of spreading in which soaking time grows with thickness squared.
A sharp soaking front moving at constant speed, so soaking time grows only with thickness.
A picture taken with the strip under water, where buoyancy cancels almost all of the strip's weight.
Rubbing alcohol, used to wash printed parts; some resins swell enormously in it.

fleet.label: bm-polyamide-sls
fleet.topic: Polyamide 11 and 12 (SLS) and TPU: moisture, swelling, kinetics
fleet.summary: Polyamide SLS parts and TPU hold little water from humid air and respond slowly. Sintered PA12 (EOS PA 2200 sheet) holds 0.52 wt% at 23 C/50 % RH, 1.33 wt% at 96 % RH and 1.93 wt% in 100 C water; dense PA12 saturates at 1.6 % and dense PA11 at 0.8 % (50 % RH) and 1.9 % (immersion) per Arkema ISO 62; Formlabs lists 0.66 % (Nylon 12), 0.07 % (Nylon 11, 2021 TDS) and 0.89 % (TPU 90A) by ASTM D570. A TPU (Estane 87A) isotherm goes 0.25, 0.53, 0.91, 1.35 wt% at 20, 40, 60, 80 % RH. The 5.5-10.5 % uptakes reported for immersed sintered PA12 are mostly pore filling: sintered density 0.90-0.95 against 1.01 dense gives 6-12 % void capacity, while Kelvin-radius arithmetic shows humid air cannot fill micrometre voids. Measured diffusivity: PA11 4.95e-13 m2/s (23 C); PA12 not measured in open sources, bounded by my calculation at 3e-13 to 1.4e-12 m2/s; FDM TPU 1.4e-13 to 3.4e-12. With t90 = 0.212 h^2/D, 0.4 / 0.8 / 1.6 mm strips need about 19 / 76 / 305 h (both faces open, D = 4.95e-13; range 7-31 h, 27-126 h, 108-503 h for D 1.4e-12 to 3e-13), 4 times longer with one face sealed. No measured hygroscopic expansion coefficient exists; a vendor figure (0.2 % at 1.4 % uptake) implies 0.1-0.2 % free strain over 30-80 % RH, i.e. bending radii of 130-1000 mm and 1-6 mm tip rise on a 40 mm strip even against an inert partner. Wet/dry modulus sources disagree from -4 % to -52 %. Moisture softening costs at most 3 % of the 3/2 curvature ceiling. A same-powder filled partner gives little (CF fill cut uptake ~16 %); a dissimilar rigid, non-hygroscopic partner is needed. Usable only as a slow (days to weeks), small humidity layer.
fleet.lay_summary: Nylon-type 3D prints take up a little water from the air, much as a wooden spoon does. At normal indoor humidity a printed nylon 12 part holds about half a percent of its weight in water, and at very humid air about one and a third percent. If you dunk a printed part in water it can soak up five to ten percent, but most of that is just water filling the tiny gaps left by the printing process, like a sponge, and not water inside the plastic. Water moves into the plastic itself very slowly: a strip 0.8 mm thick, about as thick as a few sheets of card, needs three to five days to fill most of the way, and a 1.6 mm strip needs two to three weeks. The plastic also grows only about a tenth to a fifth of one percent, so a 40 mm strip glued to a water-proof partner would curl up only a few millimetres, slowly. That makes nylon a possible slow humidity-sensing skin for a building over days or seasons, but not a quick-reacting one, and nobody has yet measured the exact growth, so the first job is a simple bench test.

glossary.plain: Tough plastics made of long chains with water-attracting links; the number is how many carbon atoms sit between the links.
Thermoplastic polyurethane, a rubbery plastic.
A printing method that fuses plastic powder with a laser, layer by layer, leaving tiny gaps inside.
How full of water vapour the air is, as a percentage of the most it can hold.
A curve (or a few points) showing how much water a material holds at each humidity once it has settled.
A number that says how fast water creeps into a material; bigger means faster.
The time to take up 90 percent of the water the strip will eventually hold.
Liquid water sitting in the empty gaps of a sintered part, like water in a sponge; it adds weight but does not make the plastic itself swell.
Water that has actually entered the plastic between its chains; this is what swells and softens it.
How much a material grows in length when it takes up water.
A measure of stiffness; a lower number means the material bends more easily.
Two layers glued together so that if one swells more than the other, the strip curls.
The biggest gap that humid air can fill with liquid water by itself; larger gaps stay dry until they are wetted directly.
The standard maths for steady creeping of a substance into a solid, in which time grows with the square of thickness.

findings.claim: Laser-sintered PA12 (EOS PA 2200 data sheet) takes up 0.52 wt% water at 23 C / 50 % RH, 1.33 wt% at 23 C / 96 % RH and 1.93 wt% when saturated in water at 100 C (DIN 53495 / ISO 62). This is a three-point sorption isotherm for a sintered part. The PDF text layer splits the labels from the numbers; the order of conditions and values is the order printed (monotonic).
findings.evidence_quote: Water absorption 100°C, saturation in water 1,93 | 23°C, 96% RF 1,33 | 23°C, 50% RF 0,52 (pdftotext of EOS 2007/2010 product information; labels and numbers in separate columns)

findings.claim: Dense moulded PA12 (Arkema Rilsamid AESNO MED) absorbs 1.6 % water at equilibrium by immersion at 23 C (ISO 62); density 1.01 g/cm3; tensile modulus 1500 MPa dry (DAM) and 1440 MPa conditioned, i.e. -4 % (conditioning protocol not stated in the sheet).
findings.evidence_quote: Tensile modulus, 23°C (73°F) 1500 / 1440 MPa ISO 527-1/-2 ... Water absorption, at equilibrium at 23°C (73°F) / Immersion 1.6 % ISO 62 ... * DRY / COND

findings.claim: Dense moulded PA11 (Arkema Rilsan BMNO TLD) absorbs 0.8 % at 23 C / 50 % RH and 1.9 % by immersion at equilibrium (ISO 62); density 1.03 g/cm3; conditioned tensile modulus 1250 MPa (dry value not given).
findings.evidence_quote: Water absorption, at equilibrium at 23°C (73°F) / 50%RH 0.8 % ISO 62 ... Water absorption, at equilibrium at 23°C (73°F) / Immersion 1.9 % ISO 62

findings.claim: Hot-pressed PA11 and PA12 sheets (20 x 20 x 4 mm) reached the same saturation after about two months: 1.5 wt% in water and 0.8 wt% at 50 % RH. The authors report no dimension change (qualitative, no number).
findings.value: 1.5 % water; 0.8 % at 50 % RH; l = 4 mm; ~2 months to saturation
findings.evidence_quote: After around two months, both PAs had the same saturation level for water and moisture absorption, i.e., 1.5% and 0.8%, respectively.

findings.claim: Protolabs PA12 laser-sintered (supplier data attributed to EOS PA 2200 Balance): 0.5 +/- 0.2 % water at 20 C / 50 % RH and 2.0 +/- 0.3 % after 24 h in boiling water, DIN EN ISO 62.
findings.evidence_quote: Water absorption, 20 °C, 50% Relative Humidity DIN EN ISO 62 0.5 ± 0.2% Water absorption, 24 hrs. in boiling water 2.0 ± 0.3%

findings.claim: Formlabs printed-part water absorption (ASTM D570, immersion time not stated): Nylon 12 Powder 0.66 %, Nylon 11 Powder 0.07 % (2021 TDS), TPU 90A Powder 0.89 %. Parts were conditioned at 50 % RH and 23 C for 7 days before tests. Nylon 12 tensile modulus 1850 MPa. I could not re-fetch the 0.4 % Nylon 11 figure the earlier agent saw on the current product page, so the two-value disagreement is neither confirmed nor refuted here; the 0.07 % in the 2021 TDS is confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: Water Absorption (printed part) 0.66% 0.66% ASTM D570 (Nylon 12); Water Absorption (printed part) 0.07% ASTM D570 (Nylon 11); Water Absorption (Printed Part) 0.89% ASTM D570 (TPU 90A)

findings.claim: Measured bulk water diffusivity of injection-moulded PA11 at 23 C by immersion: D = 4.95e-13 m2/s (= 1.78e-3 mm2/h), equilibrium uptake 1.43 %; at 40 C D = 22.0e-13 m2/s and uptake 1.58 %. D from the initial-slope Fick formula; the sample thickness L is the ASTM D638 Type I tensile bar (3.2 mm in the standard, not stated in the extracted text: unverified background).

No primary measured water diffusivity for PA12 at 23 C was found in open sources. Two own bounds from published kinetics: (a) Grilamid L25 injection-moulded bars took up 0.91 % in 40 days at 23 C; if the full extra capacity above the ambient state is 1.6 % (Arkema saturation) D = 3.0e-13 m2/s, if only 1.0 % D = 1.0e-12, and if the 0.91 % were itself saturation D >= 4.2e-12 (thickness 4 mm assumed from ISO 527-2 1A, cross-section ~40 mm2); (b) Bahrami's 4 mm hot-pressed PA12/PA11 sheets saturated in about 2 months, giving D = 6.5e-13 (90 %) to 1.4e-12 m2/s (99 %). A secondary aggregator page quotes 1-3e-13 m2/s for nylon 12 (unverified, no primary source). Working range for PA12: 3e-13 to 1.4e-12 m2/s, central about 5e-13 (the measured PA11 value).
findings.evidence_quote: The water uptake of the specimens immersed in water was around 0.91% (interquartile range (IQR) = 0.15).

findings.claim: Laser-sintered PA12 immersed in water reaches saturation in 2 days at 10.49 % weight gain with a diffusion coefficient one order of magnitude greater than the base material, which the authors attribute to porosity. The number itself is not in the abstract (paywalled); I used 10 x the PA11 value (5e-12 m2/s) only as an optimistic bound.
findings.value: 10.49 % at saturation; t_sat ~ 2 d; D ~ 10 x base
findings.evidence_quote: Water absorption reaches saturation after 2 days of immersion with a weight variation of around 10.49% and a resulting diffusion coefficient one order of magnitude greater than the value of the base material, due to the porosity of the samples.

findings.claim: TPU diffusivity (FDM filament TPUs 60A-98A, 2 mm plates, 0.9 % NaCl, 22 C): D from 1.40e-13 to 3.40e-12 m2/s from the 1-6 h initial slope; 96 h uptake 1.18-1.80 %; volume change after 96 h from about 0.6 % (92A) to about 8 % (89A) with no correlation to uptake. This is FDM material in saline, not SLS TPU in humid air.
findings.evidence_quote: Diffusion coefficients ranged from 1.40 × 10−13 to 3.40 × 10−12 m2 s−1, with no monotonic dependence on hardness.

findings.claim: Sorption isotherm of a polyether TPU (Lubrizol Estane 58887, Shore 87A, 1 mm hot-pressed strips), equilibrium water mass fraction versus RH: 0.25 wt% at 20 % RH, 0.53 at 40 %, 0.91 at 60 %, 1.35 at 80 %. Values are quoted from the DVS study of Pichler et al. (Polymer Testing 2023) as tabulated in the follow-up open paper; I could not read the original (publisher 403). Slope through origin 0.0157 wt% per %RH, slightly convex.
