fleet.label: bm-testing-metrology
fleet.topic: How to measure it properly: a reproducible test protocol (free-coupon swelling strain, mass uptake, wet/dry modulus, bilayer curvature)
fleet.summary: PROTOCOL IN ONE PARAGRAPH. Print flat 40 x 10 mm coupons (0.4 and ~1.0 mm thick, n=5 per material and thickness, plus ISO 62 60 x 60 x 1 mm plates, n>=3) with two 0.5 mm backlit fiducial holes about 36 mm apart; dry to constant mass at 50 C (ISO 62 Method 1, 0.1 mg readability, 1-10 days); photograph each coupon edge-flat on a fixed backlit jig with a calibrated camera to get the dry length L0; expose to distilled water at 23.0 +/- 1.0 C (weigh at 2, 6, 24, 48, 96, 192 h, each within 1 min of removal, ISO 62 Method 1) and to saturated-salt jars at 23 C (LiCl 11 %, MgCl2 33 %, Mg(NO3)2 53 %, NaCl 75 %, KCl 84 %, K2SO4 97 %; ASTM E104 / ISO 483); re-dry at the end to catch extracted material (ISO 62 Method 3); image the same coupon at the same time points; strain = L1/L0 - 1 on the SAME coupon; fit Fick's law (ISO 62 clause 7.2) for D and saturation uptake; measure wet and dry modulus by dead-weight 3-point bend (camera) and by DMA/tensile on companion bars tested within minutes of removal with mass recorded before and after; then bond active and passive strips, stand them on their long edge, photograph, fit a circle to the sub-pixel edge, and compare kappa with f(m,n)*d_eps/h using the independently measured d_eps, n and h. THE NUMBERS THAT DECIDE THE EQUIPMENT. 0.2 % of 40 mm is 80 um. To tell the Timoshenko law from a 20 % error at 3 sigma the strain must be known to 6.7 %, i.e. a length-change uncertainty of 5.3 um (3.8 um per reading). A caliper (resolution 10 um, accuracy +/-0.001 in = 25.4 um on the Travers page) has an accuracy equal to 32 % of the signal and cannot do it unless its errors cancel; a calibrated phone image (60 mm over 4000 px = 15 um/px, 0.1 px edge = 1.5 um) gives about 0.005 % strain noise on paper, but I did not measure a real phone, so that is arithmetic not a result. Formlabs' own Form 4 tolerance is +/-0.2 % (floor 0.06 mm) for 31-80 mm features, i.e. the printing scatter equals the whole signal, so only paired before/after measurements on the same coupon are meaningful. Mass: a 40 x 10 x 1 mm coupon weighs about 0.48 g and 1 % uptake is 4.8 mg; a 0.1 mg balance resolves a 1 % uptake to 0.8 % (1 sigma, relative), a 1 mg balance to 8 %, and a kitchen scale (0.1 g or 1 g) cannot see it at all. A 10 um water film left after blotting weighs 9 mg = 1.9 % of the coupon, larger than the signal, so blotting technique is the real mass-measurement error. WHAT I CONTRADICT. The brief (and spec-resin-chemistry) says stock Formlabs resins gain under 1 % in 24 h. That is true on Formlabs' 1 cm cube table, but the Flexible 80A V2 data sheet reports +8 % mass and +3 % volume after 1 day in deionized water (ASTM D471 slab). Both are verbatim from Formlabs; they differ in specimen, method and (probably) resin version, and I could not reconcile them. Flexible 80A V2 should therefore be in the first experiment as the discriminating specimen. WHAT I CONFIRM. Rigid 10K <0.1 % water and <0.1 % IPA, Elastic 50A V2 39.2 % IPA and 0.7 % water (163.9 % is xylene) all reproduce from the Formlabs page; the Grey V5 one-week row (mass 103.23 %, modulus 65.29 %) is now confirmed by text position, not by row order.
fleet.lay_summary: Before building a clever plastic that bends when the air gets damp, we must measure how much the plastic swells and how stiff it gets when wet. The swelling we are hunting for is tiny: about two parts in a thousand, which on a 40 millimetre strip is less than a tenth of a millimetre, roughly the thickness of a human hair. A hardware-store caliper is not precise enough, but a careful photograph taken from the same spot before and after, with a ruler in the picture, can be. Weighing the water the plastic drinks is harder than it sounds, because a thin film of water left on the surface can weigh more than the water that soaked in, so we need a lab balance and a fixed wiping routine. A phone and a kitchen scale can show whether a strip curls and by roughly how much, but they cannot give numbers good enough to prove or disprove the design rule. The full set of proper equipment costs a few thousand dollars, and a credible cheaper set costs about one to two thousand.

glossary.plain: How much longer something gets, as a fraction of its length (0.2 % means 2 mm per metre).
How much heavier the plastic gets from absorbed water, as a percentage of its dry weight.
Stiffness: how hard you must pull or bend to stretch the material a little.
Two layers stuck together; if one swells and the other does not, the strip curls.
How tightly a strip is curled; one divided by the radius of the circle it follows.
Salt stirred into water until no more dissolves; the air above it settles at a known, steady humidity.
How full of water vapour the air is, as a percentage of the most it can hold.
Dynamic mechanical analysis: a machine that gently wiggles a sample to measure its stiffness.
Digital image correlation: software that tracks a speckle pattern between photos to map stretching.
Locating an edge in a photo more finely than one pixel by looking at how the brightness fades across it.
The standard rule for how a dissolved substance such as water creeps into a solid over time.
A number saying how fast water moves through the material.
Two near-identical standard recipes for measuring how much water a plastic absorbs.
A sealed jar with a drying agent, used to cool dry samples without them re-absorbing moisture.
Two 3D-printing methods: curing liquid resin with light, or fusing powder with a laser.
The smallest step a balance's display shows.
A marked reference point put on a sample so it can be measured in photos.

findings.claim: ISO 62:2008 Method 1: dry at 50 C, weigh to 0.1 mg to constant mass, immerse in distilled water at 23.0 C +/- 1.0 C for 24 h, wipe, reweigh to 0.1 mg within 1 min, then continue at 24, 48, 96, 192 h for saturation.
findings.evidence_quote: Reweigh the test specimens to the nearest 0,1 mg within 1 min of removing them from the water (mass m2).

findings.claim: ISO 62 says drying takes 1 to 10 days at 50 C depending on thickness, so the dry reference state is days of work, not hours.
findings.evidence_quote: At 50 C, for instance, a drying period of between one and ten days will be necessary, the exact duration depending on the thickness of the specimens.

findings.claim: ISO 62 Method 3 corrects for extracted material: re-dry after immersion; if the re-dried mass m3 is below the starting dry mass m1, the loss is water-soluble matter and is added to the absorption.
findings.evidence_quote: If this reconditioned mass m3 is less than the conditioned mass m1, the difference shall be considered as the water-soluble matter lost during the immersion test.

findings.claim: ISO 62 Method 4 is the humid-air version (50 % RH only), with the same drying, weighing and time schedule. Other RH values need salt jars (ASTM E104 / ISO 483).
findings.evidence_quote: The equilibrium moisture content is measured by repeating the exposure of the test specimens to 50 % relative humidity

findings.claim: ISO 62 specimen: 1.0 +/- 0.1 mm squares (ISO 294-3), at least three per material; 8 mL water per cm2 and not less than 300 mL per specimen; the standard warns that 1 mm may not give meaningful results for some materials.
findings.evidence_quote: For each material evaluated, test at least three test specimens.

findings.claim: ISO 62 measures MASS in the through-thickness direction; it does not measure dimensional change although its introduction lists swelling as an effect of water. It excludes cellular plastics and powders, so porous SLS nylon needs extra care.
findings.evidence_quote: The results obtained using the methods described in this International Standard are applicable to most plastics but are not applicable to cellular plastics, granulates or powders, which can show additional absorption and capillary effects.

findings.claim: ISO 62 clause 7.2 fits Fick's law for sheets to get saturation content and D without waiting for constant mass; typical D 1e-6 mm2/s gives t70 about 1 day for 1 mm and the fit need not exceed one week. I reproduced the standard's c/cs table with the Crank series (agreement within 0.005).
findings.evidence_quote: Typical values of D for plastics at 23 C are 10-6 mm2/s, which gives a t70 of 105 s (approximately 1 day) with the 1 mm test specimen.

findings.claim: ASTM D570-22 covers relative rate of water absorption by immersion for sheets >=0.13 mm thick and is technically equivalent to ISO 62 when the 6.2 specimen is used. The standard costs USD 64 on the ASTM store page (D570-22).
findings.evidence_quote: This test method and ISO 62 are technically equivalent when the test specimen described in 6.2 is used.

findings.claim: ASTM D638 tensile test: dumbbell specimens up to 14 mm thick; films under 1.0 mm should use D882; D638 and ISO 527-1 cover the same subject but differ in technical content. Store price USD 80 (D638-22), USD 96 (D638-14).
findings.evidence_quote: This standard and ISO 527-1 address the same subject matter, but differ in technical content.

findings.claim: ISO 527 modulus is taken between 0.05 % and 0.25 % strain and the extension must be measured to +/-1 % or about +/-1 um. That window is as small as our 0.2 % swelling signal, so a tensile frame needs an extensometer or DIC; a phone image is not enough for ISO 527 modulus. (Vendor page, not the standard itself.)
findings.evidence_quote: The tensile modulus is determined in the linear portion of the stress-strain curve, between 0.05% and 0.25% elongation.

findings.claim: ASTM D5229 gives procedures to condition coupons to a moisture-free state, to laboratory equilibrium or to an arbitrary environment, and to get through-thickness diffusivity; written for composites but applicable to single-phase Fickian solids. USD 80.
findings.evidence_quote: Also covered are procedures for conditioning test coupons prior to use in other test methods; either to an essentially moisture-free state, to equilibrium in a standard laboratory atmosphere environment, or to equilibrium in a non-laboratory environment.

findings.claim: ASTM D4065 (DMA practice) is valid for materials from 0.5 MPa to 100 GPa and 0.01-1000 Hz, which spans Flexible 80A (about 6 MPa) to Rigid 10K (10 GPa); ASTM D5418 is the dual-cantilever DMA test. Prices USD 72 and 77.
findings.evidence_quote: This practice is intended for materials that have an elastic modulus in the range from 0.5 MPa to 100 GPa

findings.claim: Humidity-controlled DMA (DMA-RH) exists as a commercial technique: isothermal RH ramps and steps on polymer films were reported with sorption and modulus recorded together. I found no price for the accessory.
findings.evidence_quote: A new technology, humidity-controlled dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA-RH) was explored to characterize CaCas/Gly films during isohume temperature (T) ramps and steps, and isothermal RH ramps and steps

findings.claim: ASTM E104-20 describes saturated-salt solutions in small closed containers giving constant RH from dry to near saturation between 0 and 50 C, and warns that saturated salt solutions are corrosive. Price USD 86.
findings.evidence_quote: This practice is applicable for obtaining constant relative humidities ranging from dryness to near saturation at temperatures spanning from 0 to 50C.

findings.claim: ISO 483:2005 covers enclosures under 200 dm3 using saturated salt, glycerol or sulfuric acid solutions to hold RH for conditioning plastics; confirmed current in 2023 per a search summary of the ISO page; I could not fetch the ISO page (HTTP 403).
Greenspan (NBS 1977) evaluated humidity fixed points for 28 saturated salt solutions from about 3 to 98 % RH with uncertainties, from 21 investigations and 1106 measurements.
findings.evidence_quote: an evaluated compilation of equilibrium relative humidities in air versus temperature ... is presented for 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions. The relative humidities of the solutions range from about 3 to 98 percent.

findings.claim: Greenspan Table 2 at 25 C (read from OCR text of the scan): LiCl 11.30 +/- 0.27, MgCl2 32.78 +/- 0.16, K2CO3 43.16 +/- 0.39, Mg(NO3)2 52.89 +/- 0.22, NaCl 75.29 +/- 0.12 %RH. KCl and K2SO4 rows were not legible in the scan OCR; Table 3 gives K2SO4 98.18 (10 C), 97.59 (20 C), 97.00 (30 C), so about 97.3 at 25 C by interpolation.
findings.value: LiCl 11.30; MgCl2 32.78; Mg(NO3)2 52.89; NaCl 75.29 %RH at 25 C

findings.claim: Temperature sensitivity of the salts (own calculation from Greenspan Table 2, 20 to 30 C): Mg(NO3)2 -0.298 %RH/K, MgCl2 -0.063, NaCl -0.038, LiCl -0.003. Hold the jar to +/-1 K; Mg(NO3)2 is the most temperature sensitive, so +/-1 K is +/-0.3 %RH.

A humidity error of 1 %RH changes swelling strain by about 0.003 percentage points if total swelling is 0.3 % over 0-100 %RH (linear assumption) or 0.01 points if 1 %; the Sensirion SHT45 sensor is typically +/-1.0 %RH, enough to log the jars.
findings.evidence_quote: SHT45 RH accuracy1 typ. 1.0 %RH

findings.claim: A published template for exactly this experiment exists (Krueger, Tahouni, Sachse 2021, 4D-printed hygroscopic bilayers): monolayer coupons 75 x 20 x 0.8 mm are measured in water, 80 % RH and 30 % RH at 23 C, two days each; swelling strain from caliper length/width/thickness and weight; Young's modulus from deflection under self-weight; bilayer curvature from photos.
findings.evidence_quote: at 23 C in water submersion for wet, in 80% ambient humidity for humid and in 30% ambient humidity for dry state over two days to reach equilibrium.

findings.claim: Krueger et al. instruments: caliper accuracy 0.02 mm and a scale quoted as 0.001 mg (almost certainly a typo for 0.001 g, since 0.001 mg is below any lab balance). A 0.02 mm caliper on a 75 mm coupon is 0.027 % strain error, fine for their large wood-filament swelling, but 0.05 % on 40 mm, a quarter of our 0.2 % signal.
findings.evidence_quote: using a digital caliper with an accuracy of 0.02 mm and a scale with an accuracy of 0.001 mg.

findings.claim: Krueger et al. curvature method: strips stood on a flat surface parallel to their strong axis to avoid self-weight bending, imaged from above, and radius from a three-point circumcircle in ImageJ; samples measured with passive side up and down and averaged to cancel initial curvature. A least-squares circle fit to many sub-pixel edge points is an improvement I propose (not in the paper).
findings.evidence_quote: Samples were positioned on a flat surface, standing parallel to their strong axis to avoid additional bending due to self-weight. Images were taken from above and analyzed with a script in ImageJ

findings.claim: Krueger et al. found modulus ratio n of 25 to 60 and a roughly 10-fold wet-to-dry modulus change for their active material, showing the modulus has to be measured in the wet and the dry state, not once.
findings.evidence_quote: For Laywood, an approximately 10-fold increase from wet to dry state can be observed

findings.claim: Measurement set of a recent polyamide 6.6 moisture study: dried at 50 C per ISO 62, balance Mettler AE200 +/-0.1 mg, outside micrometer +/-1 um, density by buoyancy, DIC (GOM ARAMIS 3D) for tensile tests; strain defined as L1/L0 - 1 from the dry state; CME 1.814e-4 (x), 1.823e-4 (y), 3.681e-4 (z) m3/kg. Use a PA6.6 or PA6 plate as the method-validation reference.
findings.evidence_quote: the length, width and thickness of the samples was recorded using a digital outside micrometer (Mitutoyo Digimatic, +/-1 um). Secondly, the density and the volume of the samples were measured with the buoyancy method

findings.claim: iDIC Good Practices Guide: speckle/feature size should be 3-5 pixels; 2D-DIC assumes the piece stays planar and perpendicular to the optical axis, so it is invalid for a curling bilayer; do a noise-floor analysis on static images before the test. The guide gives no single strain-resolution number.
findings.evidence_quote: For 2D-DIC, the test piece is assumed to be planar, to remain planar throughout the test, to be perpendicular to the camera optical axis, and to maintain constant SOD throughout the test.

findings.claim: iDIC noise-floor rule I apply to every optical measurement here: image the unexposed coupon repeatedly and treat any length change smaller than that scatter as noise.
findings.evidence_quote: Any of those QOIs measured in the actual mechanical test that are smaller than the QOIs measured from the static images are indistinguishable from the noise.

findings.claim: Printed-part tolerance: Formlabs Form 4 XY tolerance (Grey V5, 100 um layers, three printers) is +/-0.15 % for 1-30 mm (floor 0.02 mm), +/-0.2 % for 31-80 mm (floor 0.06 mm), +/-0.3 % for 81-150 mm. A 40 mm strip therefore varies by +/-0.2 % = 80 um between prints, equal to the entire swelling signal, so strain must be a paired before/after measurement on the same coupon.
findings.evidence_quote: 1-30 mm features: +/-0.15% (lower limit: +/-0.02 mm) 31-80 mm features: +/-0.2% (lower limit: +/-0.06 mm) 81-150 mm features: +/-0.3% (lower limit: +/-0.15 mm)

findings.claim: Formlabs cube method: washed, post-cured 1 cm cubes, weight gain after 24 h. Same table, 24 h water: Flexible 80A Resin 0.7 %, Elastic 50A V2 0.7 %, Rigid 10K <0.1 %; IPA: Elastic 50A V2 39.2 %, Rigid 10K <0.1 %; xylene: Elastic 50A V2 163.9 %. CONFIRMS the earlier agents (and the brief's 39 % vs <0.1 %).
findings.evidence_quote: Results are reported as weight gain percentage after 24 hours of exposure to solvent.

findings.claim: CONTRADICTION with 'every stock resin gains under 1 % in 24 h' (spec-resin-chemistry, repeated in the brief): the Flexible 80A V2 data sheet reports deionized water 1 day: hardness -26 Shore A, mass +8 %, volume +3 %; 1 week: -27, +9 %, +7 % (ASTM D471 slabs wiped dry, no conditioning). The row was rebuilt from text coordinates because the PDF text is scrambled. It agrees with spec-formlabs-materials and conflicts with the 0.7 % cube value for 'Flexible 80A Resin'. Cause unresolved: slab vs cube, thickness, wipe method, or V1 vs V2 chemistry.
findings.evidence_quote: Rectangular slabs, used for hardness, mass, and volume change, are evaluated immediately after wiping dry without a conditioning period.

findings.claim: Mass gain is not volume-additive for Flexible 80A V2: if +8 % mass were all water entering as extra volume, volume should rise by 0.08 x 1.09/1.0 = 8.7 %, but Formlabs reports +3 % (ratio 0.34 at 1 day; 0.07/0.098 = 0.71 at 1 week). Isotropic linear strain at 1 day would be 1.03^(1/3) - 1 = 0.99 %. So the earlier assumption that strain follows mass through volume additivity with an efficiency of 0.54-0.73 is untested and, here, looks too high at 1 day. Measuring this ratio is a stated aim of the protocol.

Grey V5 Type IV tensile bars in DI water (ASTM D543): 1 day mass 101.38 %, modulus 88.63 %, strength 89.21 %; 1 week mass 103.23 %, modulus 65.29 %, strength 67.62 %. I confirmed the earlier agent's row assignment (it called it low confidence) by text position: the unlabeled DI row sits at y=8815 between the 'DI' and 'Water' labels at y=8803 and 8827 on the 1-day page.

Formlabs' wet-modulus test conditions bars for 24 h in air after removal from the liquid before pulling them. Thin bars lose water in that time, so the published 'wet' modulus is likely an overestimate of true wet stiffness. Test wet specimens within minutes and weigh them before and after the pull.
findings.evidence_quote: After removal, exposed samples were washed and conditioned for 24 hours at 22 C before mechanical testing.

findings.claim: Own fit of Fick's law (ISO 62 clause 7.2 form, Crank series) to the three Formlabs Grey V5 water points (bar 1 d 1.38 %, bar 7 d 3.23 %, 1 cm cube 24 h 0.8 %): D = 5.4e-13 m2/s (bar as 3.2 x 6 x 33 mm box, fit residual <=0.02 points) to 1.9e-12 m2/s (faces only, residual 0.29), saturation 4.3-5.9 %. Time to 95 % of saturation: 0.4 mm 6.6-23 h; 0.8 mm 26-93 h; 1.0 mm 41-145 h; 2.0 mm 165-582 h. Assumed geometry (Type IV nominal) makes this order-of-magnitude only; it is the first water diffusion estimate for a Formlabs resin and lies inside the filament range 2.8e-13 to 4.2e-12 m2/s quoted by the earlier agent.

Strain resolution arithmetic: 0.2 % x 40 mm = 80 um. For a 10 % (1 sigma) strain measurement sigma(dL) = 8 um. To distinguish the Timoshenko law from a 20 % error at 3 sigma the strain needs <=6.7 % relative uncertainty = 5.3 um on the length change = 3.8 um per length reading (two readings). This agrees with the earlier agent's '4 um on 40 mm'.

Caliper: resolution 0.01 mm, accuracy +/-0.001 in (25.4 um) on the Travers page for a Mitutoyo 6 in digital caliper (listed there as 500-196-32), USD 190 catalogue. Accuracy is 32 % of the 80 um signal. Pure quantisation of a difference of two readings is 4.1 um (0.010 % strain), so a caliper could work only if its systematic error cancels between dry and wet readings and jaw force on soft wet resin is constant, which is doubtful.
findings.evidence_quote: Accuracy +/-.001"

findings.claim: Camera arithmetic (assumed 12 MP, 4000 px across, which is unverified background): 60 mm field gives 15 um/px; edge localisation 0.1 px = 1.5 um; two edges 2.1 um = 0.005 % strain; at a pessimistic 0.5 px, 0.027 %. Camera tilt of 1 degree foreshortens length by 0.015 %, 2 degrees 0.061 %, 5 degrees 0.38 %, so the jig must hold the coupon flat to <1 degree and the same camera pose for both images. A 1200 dpi flatbed scanner gives 21 um/px.

Lens distortion cancels to first order only if the coupon is photographed at the same pixel position; calibrate the lens with a planar target (Zhang 2000) and keep a printed or etched scale bar in the coupon plane.

Mass arithmetic: 40 x 10 x 1 mm = 0.4 cm3 = 0.484 g (density 1.21, Clear V5) or 0.436 g (1.09, Flexible 80A V2). 1 % uptake = 4.84 mg; 0.1 % = 0.48 mg; 8 % = 38.7 mg. Relative 1-sigma error of an uptake from two quantised readings (readability/sqrt(12) x sqrt(2)): 0.1 mg balance 8.4 % at 0.1 % uptake, 0.8 % at 1 %; 1 mg balance 84 % and 8.4 %; 10 mg scale 843 % and 84 %; 100 mg kitchen scale 8435 % and 843 %. Stacking 40 coupons on a 10 mg scale gives 2.1 % at 1 % uptake and 0.3 % at 8 %; on a 100 mg scale 21 % and 2.6 %.

Surface water: a coupon of 9 cm2 surface carries 0.9 mg per 1 um of residual water film and 9 mg per 10 um, i.e. 0.19 % and 1.9 % of its mass. This blotting error exceeds the 0.1-1 % uptake of rigid resins, so blot with one fixed routine, weigh within 1 min (ISO 62), run a blotted dummy of an inert reference, and cross-check with loss on drying.

Water loss during the 60 s weighing is small for slow materials (1.75 % of the absorbed content for D = 1e-6 mm2/s at 1 mm) but 5.5 % for D = 1e-5 mm2/s, so use a weighing bottle for sub-mm or fast-diffusing specimens (ISO 62 says so for boiling-water tests of thin specimens).

Self-weight deflection is a poor modulus gauge for rigid resin: a 40 mm x 0.8 mm cantilever sags only 0.026 mm (Clear V5 dry, E=2750 MPa) or 0.040 mm (E x 0.653), under 3 pixels, but 11 mm for Flexible 80A V2 (E about 5.8 MPa secant, from the project record). Rigid strips are therefore measured by dead-weight bending, and soft strips lying flat will sag far more than they curl, so measure them on edge (Krueger) or floating in water.

Dead-weight three-point bend (span 30 mm, width 10 mm, thickness 1 mm) deflects Clear V5 by 0.25 mm at 1 N (dry) and 0.38 mm (wet), readable to about 1 % with a 15 um/px image. Error budget of E: deflection 1 %, thickness 1 % (10 um, needs a micrometer, enters as cube), span 0.3 %, force 1 % gives 3.4 %; with a 25 um caliper thickness error (2.5 %) it is 7.7 %. Linear beam theory fails for soft elastomers at these loads, so test Flexible 80A in tension with printed fiducials and small weights.

How exact must the modulus ratio be? Using the project-record f(m,n) with the thickness ratio chosen as m = n_est^(-1/2), a modulus ratio mis-estimated by a factor 2 (either way) costs at most 3.0 % of the 3/2 ceiling (n=2: 3.0 % if n_est is half the truth, 2.7 % if double; n=10: 2.6 % and 1.8 %; n=50: 1.7 % and 1.0 %); a 30 % error costs under 1 %. So modulus needs only +/-30-50 %, and the binding inputs are the free strain d_eps and the thickness h, which enter kappa one-for-one.
findings.value: factor-2 error in n costs <=3.0 % of curvature

findings.claim: Bilayer readout needs: for optimum h=0.8 mm and strain 0.2 %, kappa = 1.5 x 0.002/0.8 mm = 3.75 /m (R = 267 mm), sagitta over a 40 mm chord = 0.75 mm = 50 px at 15 um/px; a 1.5 um edge error is 0.2 % of the sagitta. At 1 % strain: R=53 mm, sagitta 3.75 mm. Converting back, d_eps = kappa h/1.5 has relative error sqrt(dk^2 + dh^2): 2.4 % with 2 % curvature and 10 um thickness error, 3.7 % with a 25 um error.

The earlier agent's bilayer resolution statement (spec-bilayer-physics: thickness to 3 %, free strain to 5 %, i.e. 4 um on 40 mm at 0.2 %) is confirmed by my arithmetic (4 um = 5 % of 80 um); I add that Form 4's own +/-80 um tolerance forces a paired design and that gravity sag of soft strips swamps the signal unless they are measured on edge or floating.

Prices read from fetched pages: Ohaus Pioneer PX124 analytical balance (120 g x 0.1 mg, internal calibration) USD 2,261.11 at Scientific Labs; the PX124/E external-calibration unit AUD 2,219 incl. GST at Wiltronics; Mitutoyo-type 6 in digital caliper USD 190 at Travers.
findings.evidence_quote: Capacity, g 120 Dims, w x d x h, mm 209 x 321 x 309 Pan Dims, mm Pan 90 Readability, mg 0.1

findings.claim: Prices from search-result summaries only (pages not fetched, so low confidence): Ohaus SPX123 (120 g x 0.001 g) about USD 485 to 1,036 across dealers; a sub-USD 15 kitchen scale of 2000 g x 0.1 g was mentioned by a reviewer.

Phone/kitchen-scale limits (own arithmetic, section above): a phone + tripod + backlit jig can measure strain to the order of 0.01-0.03 % and bilayer curvature (R 53-530 mm) well; it cannot give 0.1-1 % mass uptake (needs <=1 mg readability), cannot give rigid-resin modulus better than about 10 % without a thickness gauge good to ~10 um, and cannot do DMA or ISO 527 modulus.

key_claims.claim: ISO 62 (technically equivalent to ASTM D570) is a MASS method: dry at 50 C to constant mass, weigh to 0.1 mg within 1 min of removal, 23.0 +/- 1.0 C water, time series to saturation, re-dry to catch extracted material, and fit Fick's law for D and saturation content. It does not measure swelling strain, so strain, modulus and curvature need add-on methods.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Reweigh the test specimens to the nearest 0,1 mg within 1 min of removing them from the water (mass m2).

key_claims.claim: A 0.2 % strain on a 40 mm strip is 80 um, and distinguishing the bilayer law from a 20 % error at 3 sigma needs the length change known to about 5 um. A caliper (25.4 um accuracy) fails that; a calibrated, fixed-pose photograph (15 um/px, sub-pixel edges) can meet it on paper, and a micrometer (+/-1 um, used on the PA6.6 study) or DIC would be the reference.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Accuracy +/-.001"

key_claims.claim: Formlabs' Form 4 prints 31-80 mm features to only +/-0.2 % (floor +/-0.06 mm), the same size as the swelling signal, so strain must be measured on the same coupon before and after exposure, never against nominal size or against a different print.
key_claims.evidence_quote: 31-80 mm features: +/-0.2% (lower limit: +/-0.06 mm)

key_claims.claim: The brief's 'stock Formlabs resins gain under 1 % in 24 h' holds for the cube table but not for Flexible 80A V2, whose data sheet gives +8 % mass and +3 % volume in deionized water after 1 day (ASTM D471 slab). This resin belongs in the first experiment and is the only catalogue material read so far with a swelling large enough to matter.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Rectangular slabs, used for hardness, mass, and volume change, are evaluated immediately after wiping dry without a conditioning period.

table.name: Step 1 dry reference
table.fields: oven=50 +/-2 C; time=1-10 d to constant mass +/-0.1 mg; cool=desiccator; balance=0.1 mg; image L0, w0, t0 on same coupon

table.name: Step 2 immersion series
table.fields: water=distilled 23.0 +/-1.0 C; >=8 mL/cm2 and >=300 mL per specimen; weigh at 2,6,24,48,96,192 h; each weighing <=1 min after blotting; n>=3 (use 5)

table.name: Step 3 humid series
table.fields: jars at 23 +/-1 C; LiCl 11.30, MgCl2 32.78, Mg(NO3)2 52.89, NaCl 75.29 %RH (25 C values; 20 C: 11.31, 33.07, 54.38, 75.47); log RH with SHT45 (+/-1 %RH typ.); equilibrate ~2 d (Kruger) to 6 d (t95 for 1 mm, own fit)

table.name: Step 4 re-dry
table.fields: re-dry at 50 C to constant mass m3; soluble loss = m1 - m3 added to uptake

table.name: Step 5 swelling strain
table.fields: eps = L1/L0 - 1 on same coupon; budget <=5.3 um on 40 mm (3.8 um per reading); fiducial holes 0.5 mm (Form 4 minimum hole) ~36 mm apart, backlit; camera fixed pose, tilt <1 degree (0.015 %)

table.name: Step 6 modulus
table.fields: dry and wet: 3-point bend by dead weights (span 30 mm: 1 N gives 0.25 mm dry, 0.38 mm wet on Clear V5), plus DMA (ASTM D4065/D5418, 0.5 MPa-100 GPa) or tensile (ASTM D638 / ISO 527: 0.05-0.25 % window, +/-1 um extensometer); test within minutes of removal, weigh before and after

table.name: Step 7 bilayer curvature
table.fields: strip 40 x 5 mm bonded; stand on long edge; photograph; least-squares circle fit to sub-pixel edge; flip and average to cancel initial curvature; compare with f(m,n)*d_eps/h (d_eps from Step 5, n from Step 6, h by micrometer +/-10 um)

table.name: Controls
table.fields: PA6/PA6.6 plate (CME 1.81e-4 m3/kg in-plane, 0.21 % linear per 1 wt % water by own conversion); sealed or Rigid 10K dummy; blotted inert dummy; static-image noise floor (iDIC); temperature log (+/-0.5 K)

table.name: Balance: 0.1 mg analytical (Ohaus PX124)
table.fields: readability=0.1 mg; rel 1-sigma error at 1 % uptake=0.8 %; price=USD 2,261.11 (also AUD 2,219); meets ISO 62

table.name: Balance: 1 mg precision (Ohaus SPX123 class)
table.fields: readability=1 mg; rel error at 1 % uptake=8.4 %, at 8 %=1.1 %; price=USD 485-1,036 (search summaries, low confidence); adequate for Flexible 80A, marginal for rigid resin

table.name: Scale: 0.01 g pocket or 0.1 g kitchen
table.fields: readability=10 or 100 mg; one coupon cannot be used (843 % / 8435 % error at 1 %); 40 coupons stacked: 2.1 % / 21 % at 1 %, 0.3 % / 2.6 % at 8 %; price=under USD 15-30 (unverified background)

table.name: Length: caliper 0.01 mm
table.fields: accuracy=25.4 um (32 % of 80 um signal); quantisation noise of a difference=4.1 um; price=USD 190; jaw force deforms wet soft resin

table.name: Length: outside micrometer +/-1 um

recommendations: Run Experiment 1 in this order: (1) dry and weigh all coupons; (2) photograph dry; (3) immerse and weigh/photograph on the ISO 62 schedule; (4) humid jars; (5) re-dry; (6) wet/dry modulus on companion bars; (7) bond and image bilayers. Expect about four weeks (1-10 d drying, 8 d immersion, 4 jars x ~6 d).

Specimens: Flexible 80A V2 (the +8 % candidate), Grey or Clear V5 and Rigid 10K (stock pair), Tough 2000 V2 optional, plus a PA6.6/PA6 plate as method reference; each at 0.4 and ~1.0 mm; n=5 strips plus n>=3 ISO plates. Print all in one job orientation and record washing and post-cure settings (swelling depends on cure state); pre-extract in water and re-dry once before the baseline so extractables do not masquerade as negative swelling.

Never use the caliper for the strain number. Use fixed-pose calibrated photographs of backlit fiducial holes (or DIC with a 3-5 px speckle if the coupon is flat), reference the same coupon dry vs wet, and run a static-image noise floor first; require noise <=2 um per reading before trusting 0.2 % strain.

Weigh with a 0.1 mg balance (ISO 62), or a 1 mg balance for Flexible 80A only; fix the blotting routine, weigh within 60 s, and check with a re-dry. Do not use kitchen scales for mass uptake of rigid resins.

Report for every material: m(t), eps(t) on one plot, saturation uptake, D from the Fick fit, swelling efficiency (volume change per volume of water taken up), E_dry, E_wet at the same water content, and kappa measured vs kappa predicted = f(m,n) d_eps/h with its uncertainty. The pass criterion for the Lean-checked law is agreement within the combined uncertainty, not a fixed 20 % band.

Resolve the Flexible 80A discrepancy first: print one 1 cm cube and one 40 x 10 x 1 mm slab of the same lot, run both 24 h in distilled water by the Formlabs cube method and the ISO 62 method; if they differ, thickness/wiping is the cause, if not, the cube-table row is a different resin version.
Buy before the first run: 0.1 mg or 1 mg balance, micrometer, SHT45 logger, six salts and sealed tubs. Defer: climate chamber, DMA (use a university core facility).

fleet.label: bm-wood-cellulose-hygromorphs
fleet.topic: Wood and cellulose hygromorphs in architecture: measured benchmarks (curvature, layer ratios, strain, speed, cycles, Timoshenko error) that a new biomaterial must beat
fleet.summary: Fetched and read in full this run: Holstov et al. 2015 (Newcastle open copy), Correa et al. 2015 (MIT open copy, the MIT Self-Assembly Lab / Stuttgart ICD paper), Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015, Gronquist 2018 and 2019, Cheng et al. 2024, Kruger 2021, Dingler 2021, Khoshtinat 2023 (cellulose acetate), Tseo 2025 (bacterial-cellulose preprint), Peng 2023, plus the ICD project pages for HygroSkin and HygroScope. Benchmarks. Wood bilayers reach 4.5-8.7 m^-1 in about 24-48 h at 4.7-8 mm total thickness (Ruggeberg 2015; Gronquist 2018). Printed cellulose/polyketone bilayers reach 15.5 m^-1 at 80% RH, switch fully in 30 min, survive 170 cycles and 13 months on a facade mock-up (Cheng 2024). A 0.23 mm cellulose-acetate/tape bilayer reaches 51.1 m^-1 (Khoshtinat 2023). Veneer elements in HygroSkin close 'within a few minutes' (ICD page; no thickness or curvature published there). Size sets speed: a 1 mm birch veneer on 0.2 mm glass-fibre reaches 80% of its curvature in 2 h 15 min in humid air (Holstov 2015); 4.1 mm beech needs 12.6-18.8 h for 80% moisture change (my recomputation of the ETH data); 15-45 mm mass timber needs 400-900+ h (Gronquist 2019). No measured wood bilayer I could quantify exceeds kappa*h/d_eps = 1.5; the six ETH beech bilayers give 0.91-1.53. Timoshenko accuracy. Within 5-13% for stiff wood bilayers at near-optimal layer ratio, but at 1:1 thickness the model overpredicts by my calculation; +26% for soft cellulose acetate (analytic 0.0645 vs measured 0.0511 mm^-1); about 4x for 6 um polymer films (Dingler 2021); 2.5-9x off in fitted modulus ratio for printed wood-filament (Kruger 2021); and a fitted correction factor C = 1.72 for bacterial-cellulose bilayers (Tseo 2025). Contradiction of the earlier record: the 3/2 ceiling is NOT a new result. Holstov et al. 2015 plotted f(m,n) over many modulus ratios and wrote that its maximum 'remains constant at 1.5'; what is new in this project is the kernel-checked proof and the exact optimum m = n^-1/2. Also: bacterial-cellulose bilayers in the literature I found are driven by heat-drying (90-120 C), not ambient humidity, and the one preprint also moulds its cellulose in Formlabs Rigid 10K printed parts. Hard gaps: HygroSkin/HygroScope layer thicknesses, curvatures and cycle counts are in paywalled papers I could not read.
fleet.lay_summary: Thin strips of wood or paper curl when the air gets damp or dry, because one side swells more than the other. Think of a wet pine cone closing and a dry one opening. Architects at Stuttgart used this to build walls whose holes open and shut with the weather, with no motors. We collected the best measurements to date, so any new material can be compared fairly. A strip of wood a few millimetres thick takes about a day to bend, while a sheet thinner than a sheet of card can bend in under an hour. Printed wood-fibre plastic survived 170 damp-dry rounds and 13 months outside. The simple bending formula from 1925 works within about 10 percent for stiff wood but can be off by a factor of four for soft, thin films. One surprise: the best possible bend for a given swelling was already known as a plotted limit in 2015, so our contribution is the computer-checked proof, not the limit itself.

glossary.plain: A material that changes shape when the air humidity changes.
Two thin layers glued face to face, one that swells and one that does not, so the strip curls.
How tightly a strip bends; 10 per metre means a circle of radius 10 cm.
How much more one layer would swell than the other if they were not glued together.
The 1925 equation that predicts how much a two-layer strip bends from its layer thicknesses, stiffnesses and swelling.
The most a strip can bend is 1.5 times the swelling difference divided by the strip thickness, whatever the stiffnesses.

glossary.term: thickness ratio m, modulus ratio n
glossary.plain: Passive-layer thickness divided by active-layer thickness, and passive stiffness divided by active stiffness.
Time to reach 80 percent of the final bend.
How damp the air is, as a percentage of the most water vapour it can hold.
A very thin sliver of wood, usually under 2 mm.
Fused filament fabrication, the common hobby 3D printer that melts plastic thread.
A wet, felt-like cellulose sheet grown by bacteria in a tray.
A single number for how fast water soaks through a material, worked out from how long a sample took to respond.
The small trusted program that checks a mathematical proof step by step.

findings.claim: The 3/2 ceiling on Timoshenko's coefficient was already stated numerically in the architecture-hygromorph literature in 2015: Holstov et al. plotted f(m,n) for many stiffness ratios and report that its maximum is the same, 1.5, for every ratio, reached at a different thickness ratio each time. Their Figure 11 marks the f=1.5 line as the optimal (m,n) combinations. They did not prove it.
findings.value: max f = 1.5 for all n (plotted, not proved)
findings.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5 and in each case is achieved at single yet different thickness ratio

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS spec-hygromorph-4d.json, which called the bound 'my own derivation rather than a literature finding'. The numerical ceiling is in Holstov 2015, and Dingler 2021 also states 'global maxima'. What remains new is the proof (Lean kernel) and the closed-form optimum m = n^-1/2. The grid check in benchmarks.py (n from 1e-3 to 1e3, m from 1e-3 to 1e3) gives max f = 1.5000000000000002 with the optimum within 2% of n^-1/2 each time; this is a numerical check only.
findings.value: grid max f = 1.5; optimum m = n^-1/2

findings.claim: Holstov's worked example (wood 0.5 GPa across grain, fibreglass 15 GPa) puts the optimum at a passive layer about 5 times thinner than the active one. Recomputed: n = 30, m = 0.2 gives f = 1.498 (99.9% of the ceiling); the n^-1/2 optimum is m = 0.183. At equal thickness f = 0.545, a 64% loss against the paper's 'as much as 60%'.
findings.evidence_quote: If the layers were of equal thickness, for the same overall thickness of the composite the response would be reduced by as much as 60%.

findings.claim: Holstov 2015 measured speed on 150 x 100 mm samples, 1 mm rotary-cut birch active layer with 0.2 mm fibreglass passive layer: 80% of the curvature change in about 30 min when sprayed with liquid water, but about 2 h 15 min when the change is a humid-air step (wetting and drying alike). Curvature values were in figures only and could not be read.
findings.value: t80 = 0.5 h (liquid), 2.25 h (humid air), active layer 1 mm
findings.evidence_quote: 80% of the total curvature change in both the transfer from dry conditions to humid and vice-versa is achieved in approximately 2 hours 15 minutes

findings.claim: Holstov 2015 says quarter-cut veneer, the type used by the Stuttgart HygroScope/HygroSkin work, responds less than plain-cut or rotary-cut veneer, because rotary-cut aligns the tangential (largest) swelling with the plane.
findings.evidence_quote: Hygromorphs with active layers of plain-cut and rotary-cut wood veneer are more responsive than those with quarter-cut veneer active layers.

findings.claim: Holstov 2015 gives two durability constraints that matter for architecture: wood preservatives and fire retardants destroy hygroscopicity, and thin wood layers erode at 2-10 mm per century outdoors (so a 1 mm layer has a short life).
findings.evidence_quote: many wood processing methods, including the application of fire-retardants and coatings and impregnated preservatives aimed to protect wood against weathering, usually result in irreversible loss of its hygroscopicity

findings.claim: Holstov 2015 saw a first-cycle effect: thin wood layers prepared dry shrink below their start size after the first wet-dry cycle, so the dry shape of cycle 1 differs from later cycles. The authors suspect irreversible compressive strain in the veneer.
findings.evidence_quote: composites with thin active wood layers prepared in dry conditions exhibit a difference between the first and the subsequent response cycles

findings.claim: HygroSkin (ICD, 2013): quarter-cut maple veneer composite apertures respond over 30-90% RH; 28 unique components with 1100 apertures; open-to-closed 'within a few minutes' for a rapid RH rise; reversibility verified in 'a large number of long-term tests' with no count, thickness or curvature on the page. The <0.5 mm figure is geometric accuracy of the self-formed plywood shell, not actuator performance.
findings.evidence_quote: In this project the elements change from open to closed within a few minutes given a rapid rise in relative humidity.

findings.claim: HygroScope (ICD, Centre Pompidou 2012): more than 4000 unique elements of quarter-cut maple veneer plus synthetic composites, programmed by five parameters including the humidity at which the element is produced. The page gives no curvature, thickness or time.
findings.evidence_quote: More than 4000 geometrically unique elements are digitally fabricated and the complex substructure is robotically manufactured.

findings.claim: MIT Self-Assembly Lab / ICD printed wood (Correa 2015): a wood-filament sample 20 x 100 mm needs 12 h to transform fully in submersion, with the reverse 15 min to 2 h depending on RH; the wood/ABS net needs 12-24 h in high humidity to saturate and repeated over 30 cycles without visible degradation; the authors state both methods take very long in water vapour compared with submersion.
findings.evidence_quote: A sample of 20 mm by 100 mm will reach full transformation under full submersion after 12 h; the reverse cycle is faster and can range from 15 min to 2 h, depending on the R.H.

findings.claim: Correa 2015 wood/nylon multimaterial prints fold 104-110 degrees in 1.5-12 min but only by water or heat, and the folding angle shrinks with each cycle, so they are not a durable humidity actuator.
findings.value: 104-110 deg in 1.5-2 min (air-dry) or 10-12 min (heat); angle falls per cycle
findings.evidence_quote: However, the folding angle gradually decreases with each transformation cycle

findings.claim: Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015 (beech 4 mm active, spruce 0.2-4 mm passive, 120 mm long, RH 85->35%): curvature up to 8.7e-3 mm^-1 (8.7 m^-1) for spruce up to 1 mm and 1.5e-3 mm^-1 (1.5 m^-1) for 4 mm spruce after 24 h; computed tip angle 59 deg vs measured 55 deg. Confirms the earlier agent's numbers.
findings.value: 8.7 m^-1 and 1.5 m^-1 at 24 h; 59 vs 55 deg
findings.evidence_quote: For bilayers with a thickness of the spruce layer up to 1mm, curvatures up to 8.7*10-3mm-1 were reached, whereas bilayers with a spruce layer of 4mm thickness reached a curvature of 1.5*10-3 mm-1 after 24 hours only.

findings.claim: Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015 Timoshenko error under cycling: +11% and +13% for the 0.2 mm and 0.8 mm spruce bilayers, under 5% for the other two. Confirms the earlier agent.
findings.evidence_quote: For the bilayers with 0.2mm and 0.8mm thick spruce layers, the specific curvatures slightly increased over time and were 11% and 13% higher than the calculated values.

findings.claim: DEEPENS the earlier record: using the paper's own coefficients (beech 3.2e-3, spruce 0.07e-3 per %MC), a moisture drop of 8 points (18 to 10) and n = 10, 20, 30, Timoshenko gives 6.3-7.9 m^-1 for 0.2-1.0 mm spruce (the measured 'up to 8.7' is 10-28% higher) but 1.7-3.1 m^-1 for 4 mm spruce (m = 1) against 1.5 measured, i.e. +14% (n=30) to +108% (n=10). The paper says the 24 h values 'match' in its Fig. 2e, which I could not read, so this is a check of the 'matches' claim, not a refutation. The earlier agent checked only m = 0.2.

Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015 outdoor test: untreated bilayers carrying 100 g and 150 g tip loads ran nine months from July 2013; specific curvature stayed 3-4e-4 mm^-1 per %RH to January 2014, fell to 2-3e-4 in February-April 2014, despite visible splitting and cracking from UV and rain.
findings.evidence_quote: although splitting and cracking of the wood due to the impact of UV-radiation and rain became visible, the amplitude of actuation has only slightly decreased over time.

findings.claim: Gronquist 2018 thin beech bilayers (120 x 20 mm, 35% RH, 48 h): maximum 4.5 m^-1 at r = 0.17 and minimum 1.5 m^-1 at r = 0.49; model error below 10% at r = 0.34, slightly under-predicting at low r and over-predicting at high r.
findings.evidence_quote: A maximum of κd ≈ 4.5 m−1 was reached for r = 0.17 and a minimum of κd ≈ 1.5 m−1 was reached for r = 0.49 after 48 hours in 35% r.h. climate

findings.claim: Recomputed from the ETH data (six beech bilayers, three samples each): kappa*h/d_eps = 1.35, 1.50, 1.53, 1.36, 1.04, 0.91 for r = 0.13-0.49, confirming the earlier scout figures (1.35-1.53 and 0.91). Moisture half-time 2.8-4.8 h, 80% time 12.6-18.8 h for the 4.1 mm active layer; curvature t80 11.9-19.1 h. Caveat: d_eps uses nominal swelling coefficients (0.0019 and 0.0001 per %MC), so 1.53 is within their stated uncertainty of the ceiling.

Gronquist 2019 mass timber: bilayers 15, 30 and 45 mm; moisture about equilibrated at 400 h, but not at 900 h for 45 mm; the model fairly predicts beech but overestimates spruce curvature; adhesive thickness, stiffness and shear modulus do not influence shape.
findings.evidence_quote: WMCs were approximately equilibrated after 400 hours in the dry target climate, except for the bilayer series with a thickness of 45 mm, for which an equilibration is not visible after 900 hours.

findings.claim: Urbach Tower (14 m, ICD/ITKE): panels were made flat at 22% wood moisture and dried to 12% to curve; only the press report gives this, no radius or lamella thickness was found.
findings.evidence_quote: The panels were manufactured flat and with a high wood-moisture content of 22 per cent.

findings.claim: Vailati et al. 2017 (abstract only; full text paywalled): wood bilayers up to half a metre wide curved only along their length, and milling grooves into the active layer sped moisture change and curvature change, especially under cyclic RH.
findings.value: width up to 0.5 m; grooves raise rate
findings.evidence_quote: The milling of grooves increased the moisture change rate substantially compared to the non-milled samples resulting in a higher rate of curvature change.

findings.claim: Peng et al. 2023 (veneer-scale wood bilayers): a 200 um passive layer on a 400 um active layer at 0.6% initial moisture was the most sensitive to RH; hysteresis between adsorption and desorption grows at lower thickness ratio; behaviour repeatable after the first cycle. Numerical curvatures were in figures I did not read.
findings.evidence_quote: the bilayer composed of a 200 μm passive layer and a 400 μm active layer with 0.6% iMC was found to be the most sensitive to RH change

findings.claim: Cheng et al. 2024 (printed cellulose/polyketone bilayers): mean curvature 0.0155 mm^-1 (15.5 m^-1; radius 64.5 mm, own arithmetic 1/0.0155) at 80% RH independent of temperature; 170 cycles between 30% and 90% RH with slight loss only in the first ten; full 30<->90% RH change within 30 min; 13-month facade mock-up; 424 modules, 1.4% replaced after cycle testing. Confirms the earlier agent. Layer thicknesses are only in the supplement, which I did not read, so kappa*h/d_eps cannot be computed.
findings.evidence_quote: At the high RH of 90%, there is some slight reduction in bilayer curvature within the first ten cycles of actuation; in the following 160 cycles, the bilayer curvatures remain generally consistent

findings.claim: CORRECTS a detail in spec-hygromorph-4d.json: for Kruger 2021 (Laywood/PLA) the original Timoshenko model fits only with modulus ratio n = 111.6-286.0, the width-corrected model with n = 299.7-691.2 (Table 2); the earlier '150-690' blends the two. Measured n is 25-60 (dry/humid), not '~40'. The authors say measured curvatures could not be reproduced computationally because non-linear material behaviour is missing.
findings.evidence_quote: Although the observed experimental values could not be reproduced computationally, because the potentially non-linear material behavior is not accounted for in the model

findings.claim: Cellulose acetate on tape (Khoshtinat 2023, open access): h_a 86 um, h_p 145 um, total 0.228 mm, RH 35->80%. Measured curvature 0.0511 mm^-1 (R 19.56 mm), finite element 0.0519 mm^-1, analytic Timoshenko 0.0645 mm^-1 (R 15.5 mm), i.e. +26% over experiment; authors blame moisture-softening of the film. FE saturation time for 86 um from dry, one face open: about 60 min.
findings.evidence_quote: The analytical model, on the other hand, estimates a final curvature of only 0.0645 mm −1 (R = 15.5 mm), resulting in a 3.43 mm difference in bending radius from the experiment.

findings.claim: Own calculation on the cellulose-acetate bilayer using the authors' m = 1.69 and n = 3.84: f = 0.981, only 65% of the 1.5 ceiling; the n^-1/2 optimum would be m = 0.51, so the passive layer is about 3.3 times too thick. Even so the film makes 51.1 m^-1 because it is 0.228 mm thick; the ceiling implies a free differential strain of at least 0.78%.
findings.source: own calculation benchmarks.py using m, n and kappa from https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10570-023-05342-1

findings.claim: Bacterial cellulose, Tseo et al. 2025 preprint (not peer reviewed): BC bimorph strips follow the Timoshenko equation 'adapted for hydrogels' only with a correction factor (C = 1.72, optimised separately for each bimorph); trajectory error 1.9 +/- 0.6 mm. Actuation is dehydration at 120 C (strips) or 90 C (multi-layer figure, 80 min), not ambient humidity.
findings.evidence_quote: comparing observed trajectories with model predictions across all constructed bimorphs yields a consistently low mean-squared error of 1.9 mm ± 0.6 mm

findings.claim: Same preprint: untreated BC pellicles took 1070 min to reach dry weight against 70-90 min for NaOH/BslA-treated ones; a 0.37 g BC gripper held 135 g; the gripper moulds were 3D-printed in Formlabs Rigid 10K and the pellicle grown inside them, a direct Formlabs-resin route for cellulose shaping. No cycle count or curvature in m^-1 is reported.
findings.value: 1070 vs 70-90 min; 0.37 g holds 135 g; Rigid 10K mould
findings.evidence_quote: we first 3D printed molds of the shape out of autoclavable UV cured resin (Formlabs, Rigid 10K)

findings.claim: Paper/CMC bilayers (Seelinger 2024) deviate about 15% from finite-element prediction at 10 wt% CMC, worse above 20 wt%, and miss the start position by 5-6 mm after cycling between 10% and 90% RH. Confirms the earlier agent; curvature numbers are in figures only.
findings.evidence_quote: Here, the deviation from the observed experimental results to the FEA results is approx. 15%.

findings.claim: Dingler 2021 confirmed: 17 um bilayer measured 1.2 mm^-1, 54 um bilayer about three times lower; Timoshenko with measured inputs gives 1.6 mm^-1 for the 54 um film. The paper's own sentence lists its 'global maxima' as 1.7 and 5.4 mm^-1 for '17 and 54 um', which is reversed: 1.5 x 0.061 / 0.017 mm = 5.4 mm^-1 belongs to the 17 um film. The earlier agent's numbers stand.
findings.evidence_quote: The global maxima generally achievable for 17 and 54 µm bilayers would be κ = 1.7 and 5.4 mm–1, respectively.

findings.claim: Apparent diffusivity from response times (slab with one face open, Fourier numbers 0.197, 0.567, 1.129 for 50%, 80%, 95% uptake): Holstov 1 mm birch t80 = 2.25 h gives 0.25 mm^2/h (7e-11 m^2/s) one-sided or 0.063 mm^2/h two-sided; ETH 4.1 mm beech moisture t50 gives 0.24 mm^2/h (two faces) to 0.95 mm^2/h (one face); cellulose acetate 86 um at 95% in 60 min gives 0.0084 mm^2/h. The earlier spec-bilayer-physics.json filament range was 0.001-0.015 mm^2/h, so wood veneer is roughly 4-1000 times faster per unit area than those printed resins. Treat as order of magnitude: moisture t80/t50 in the ETH data is 4.5, not the Fickian 2.9.
findings.source: own calculation benchmarks.py (apparent_diffusivity) from Holstov 2015, the ETH csv and Khoshtinat 2023
findings.value: wood veneer D_app 0.06-0.95 mm^2/h; CA 0.008 mm^2/h

findings.claim: What the benchmarks demand of a new material, via the ceiling d_eps >= (2/3) kappa h: matching wood (8.7 m^-1) at h = 0.8 mm needs a free differential strain of at least 0.46%; matching printed cellulose (15.5 m^-1) needs 0.83% (1.65% at 1.6 mm); matching cellulose acetate (51.1 m^-1) needs 2.73% at 0.8 mm (1.36% at 0.4 mm). Project-record stock Flexible 80A V2 (0.99% immersion strain at 1 day) caps at 18.6 m^-1 at 0.8 mm, so it can just match printed cellulose but only after immersion, not humid air.
findings.source: own calculation benchmarks.py (strain_needed_for_benchmark_curvature); Flexible 80A figure from agents/scout-biomaterial.json (project record)

findings.claim: Across the bilayers with enough data, only designs near n^-1/2 approach the ceiling: Holstov worked example 99.9%, Dingler 98.9%, ETH beech at r=0.17-0.22 100-102%, cellulose acetate 65%, Dingler's measured curvature only 33-37% of the ceiling at its reported 6.1% strain, Ruggeberg m=1 about 47% by theory. A new material's score should be reported as kappa*h/d_eps, not raw curvature.

key_claims.claim: The maximum of Timoshenko's coefficient is 1.5 for every modulus ratio, and was already shown numerically by Holstov et al. 2015, so the project's novelty is the machine-checked proof, not the bound.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5 and in each case is achieved at single yet different thickness ratio

key_claims.claim: Measured curvature benchmarks: wood 4.5-8.7 m^-1 in 24-48 h at 4.7-8 mm; printed cellulose composite 15.5 m^-1, 30 min, 170 cycles, 13 months on a facade; cellulose acetate film 51.1 m^-1 at 0.228 mm.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The bilayers reach a full transformation between two RH extremes of 30% and 90% within 30 minutes

key_claims.claim: Timoshenko error depends on stiffness and softness: +5 to +13% for stiff wood near the optimum, +26% for cellulose acetate, about 4x for thin soft polymer films, fitted modulus ratio 2.5-9x too high for printed wood-filament, and a fitted correction factor 1.72 for bacterial cellulose.
key_claims.evidence_quote: For the other two bilayers differences between experimentally derived and calculated specific curvature were less than 5%.

key_claims.claim: Response time rises steeply with thickness: 30 min (printed, thin), 2 h 15 min (1 mm birch veneer in humid air), 12.6-18.8 h (4.1 mm beech, 80% moisture change), 400-900+ h (15-45 mm timber). Anything meant to beat wood at 1 mm and above must clear about 2 h for 80%.
key_claims.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6744262/ ; own calculation on ETH csv
key_claims.evidence_quote: 80% of the total curvature change in both the transfer from dry conditions to humid and vice-versa is achieved in approximately 2 hours 15 minutes

A hygromorph benchmark measured on a vat-printed (SLA) or powder-bed (SLS) part: none appears in any source read; the nearest Formlabs link is Tseo 2025 using Rigid 10K printed moulds only for growing cellulose, not as an actuator.
Tools not run: no Lean process was started; the 3/2 grid check is Python floating point and is not a proof.
recommendations: Stop describing the 3/2 ceiling as a new result in anything shown to Mamou-Mani or in a paper; cite Holstov et al. 2015 (numerical, plotted) and present the Lean-checked proof plus the optimum m = n^-1/2 as the contribution.

Report every new bilayer as kappa*h/d_eps with d_eps measured on free-swelling coupons of the same print, alongside raw curvature. Literature efficiency spans 0.33 (thin polymer film) to about 1.5 (tuned wood), so raw curvature hides design quality.

Set the bar to beat: curvature >= 15.5 m^-1 at the same RH step as Cheng 2024 (needs d_eps >= 0.83% at 0.8 mm), t80 under 2 h at 1 mm in humid air (Holstov), 170 humid cycles with <10% loss (Cheng), and a Timoshenko prediction within 10% using humidity-dependent moduli.

Choose the passive layer so that m = n^-1/2 (about 0.18 for a 30:1 stiffness ratio) and check that this thickness is printable (0.2 mm minimum wall on Form 4 per the earlier record); the cellulose-acetate bilayer lost 35% of its possible curvature by being 3.3x too thick on the passive side.

Expect Timoshenko to overpredict for soft, thin or highly swelling layers (+26% to 4x in the sources); plan to fit with humidity-dependent modulus and report the error, since the benchmark papers that do so are the ones that agree within 10%.

Keep the active layer thin: wood needs 12-19 h at 4 mm and 400+ h at 15 mm, so thickness, not chemistry, dominates speed; grooves or perforations (Vailati 2017) and one-sided passive layers (Holstov) are the proven speed-ups.

Bacterial cellulose grown in Form 4 Rigid 10K moulds (Tseo 2025) is a low-risk first demonstrator of cellulose shaping on Formlabs hardware, but it needs a humid-air actuation test before it counts as a hygromorph benchmark.

Get the paywalled HygroSkin/HygroScope papers (Reichert 2015; Menges & Reichert 2015) via the practice or a library before claiming to beat the Stuttgart apertures; the public page gives no thickness or cycle data.

lay_summary: Our group wants to write a science paper about changing a tiny see-through fish on purpose, and then checking the changes against rules about living things that a computer has proved are logically correct.
When we looked at the work we already have, none of it is actually about fish yet: it is about dog kidney cells in a dish, bacteria in jelly, bits of DNA circuitry, and spinning plant seeds.
So the paper should really be about our checking machine, with the fish as its first living test, and we say that out loud instead of pretending we already have fish results.
We do already have two useful surprises: when we rebuilt two published computer models, neither one matched the published measurements, and those misses can be the paper's first pictures.

Before touching a single fish, a real fish scientist has to agree the fish lines, ages, measurements and animal rules make sense, and we also have to admit that many of our 'proved' rules are not actually proved yet.

glossary.zebrafish: A small see-through freshwater fish used to study how bodies develop.
glossary.dpf: Days post-fertilisation: how many days old a fish embryo or larva is.
glossary.lumen: The hollow space inside a tube in the body, like a gut or a duct.
glossary.solidity: A shape number: how much of a shape's outline is filled in rather than dented.
glossary.RMSE: Root-mean-square error: the average size of a model's mistakes, in the units of the thing measured.
glossary.vertex model: A computer model that treats cells as polygons meeting at corners and lets them pull on each other.
glossary.MDCK cysts: Hollow balls of dog kidney cells grown in gel, used as a stand-in for a tube in the body.
glossary.Lean: A computer language in which a mathematical statement can be proved, so the proof is machine-checked.
glossary.law set: The frozen, numbered list of biology statements this project treats as its laws.
glossary.pinned law: A law included in a particular numbered law set; it may or may not have an actual proof attached.
glossary.nanopublication: A tiny machine-readable published claim with its evidence and who said it.
glossary.pre-registered prediction: A prediction written down and frozen before the data is looked at, so it cannot be adjusted afterwards.
glossary.reproduction gate: A pass/fail test that a published model must survive on the original data before anyone builds on it.
glossary.Hill coefficient: A number describing how steeply a biological response switches on as its input rises.
glossary.dose-response: The curve relating how much of a signal you give to how much response you get.
glossary.ribosome binding site: The short DNA/RNA stretch that sets how often a gene's message gets translated into protein.
glossary.reporter: A gene added so that cells glow or change colour when something happens, making it visible.
glossary.transgenic line: A strain of animals carrying an added piece of DNA, bred so all of them have it.
glossary.Gal4/UAS: A two-part genetic switch used to turn an added gene on only in chosen cells.
glossary.apical surface: The face of a cell that lines the inside of a tube.
glossary.Laplace pressure: The relation between pressure inside a bubble or tube, its tension, and its curvature.
glossary.diffusion-driven instability: A mechanism where two spreading chemicals at different speeds spontaneously create stripes or spots (also called Turing patterning).
glossary.Fisher-KPP: A classic equation for how a growing population spreads as a travelling front.
glossary.blade-element model: A way of predicting the forces on a wing or fin by adding up thin slices of it.
glossary.clutch: One batch of eggs from one mating; fish from the same clutch are not independent samples.
glossary.confocal: A microscope that takes sharp slices through a thick sample to build a 3D image.
glossary.Crossref DOI: A permanent identifier for a published paper, checkable against a public registry.
glossary.in silico: Done entirely on a computer, with no lab work.
glossary.validity domain: The range of conditions in which a law has actually been shown to hold.

fleet.summary:
Partial result from a 7-minute run. Funding dates were opened today (2026-11-13) and are sourced; the wedges, the 30/60/90 plan and most of the regulatory path are my proposal built on the two briefs and the two earlier agent files, and the fire-standard texts could not be opened (403).

THREE WEDGES
W1. Fire-test triage for bio-based ("green") fire-retardant coatings. First customer: university or design-school materials labs and small coating makers who cannot get test slots (the pain point in the 13 Nov brief). Delphi adds an elimination certificate: a machine-checked statement of which candidates a named test would reject, with the data and assumptions attached, so scarce slots go to survivors. A competitor's simulation or screening score has no checkable proof and no public record. Regulatory path: reaction-to-fire classification of interior finishes (US ASTM E84 classes under the building code; EU EN 13501-1 Euroclasses), done by an accredited lab. The certificate is pre-screening only and never replaces the test. Standard texts not opened in this run.
W2. Law-constrained printed panel, proof of concept on Formlabs. First customer: an architecture practice's fabrication arm; the earlier file shows Fab.Pub has a public material-intake route and a GBP 250 minimum budget. Delphi adds a per-part certificate that the geometry obeys the stated morphology laws within stated bounds, plus a nanopublication record. Regulatory path: for a temporary installation, structural engineer sign-off (the earlier file shows load tests by an independent engineer on a prior piece) plus the venue's fire requirement, which leads back to W1. Permanent building use would need full product certification, out of scope for 90 days.
W3. Zebot and locomotion design certificates. First customer: biobot and soft-robotics research labs, then funders. Delphi adds a pre-registered, frozen prediction (for example a fin or body constraint in a passive glide surrogate) checked against a printed model. Regulatory path: a research tool is not a medical device unless its intended use makes it one (FDA page opened). Any live zebrafish or zebrafish-cell work needs institutional animal-care approval and biosafety review (not opened); a purely mechanical zebrafish-inspired robot needs neither.

30/60/90 (proposal, unsourced)
Day 30: W1, write the pass/fail rule of one fire test as a formal statement, collect published small-scale burn data for 10-20 bio-based coatings, freeze the predictions. W2, pick one Formlabs resin and one law, print coupons. W3, freeze one glide-surrogate prediction.
Day 60: W1, bench-scale burn test on 3-5 candidates at a partner lab (cone calorimeter or small-flame). W2, print one panel and measure it against the certificate. W3, print and drop-test the surrogate.
Day 90: W1, one accredited test on the best survivor, publish the hit/miss table including failures. W2, hand the panel, certificate and report to the practice with a priced pilot offer. W3, short report and funding submission.

- sbir.gov home page listed no open topics; the topic search was not opened. Innovate UK: only one Innovate UK-funded call appeared on page 1 of 4 (critical minerals, closes 7 Jan 2027, not a fit).

fleet.label: gs-statement-expansion-plan
fleet.topic: Pipeline to expand DELPHI to many more biological statements: harvest, formalize in Lean 4, validate on data, publish as nanopublications
fleet.summary:
Design only; nothing in the repo was changed and no Lean was run by me. Schema and 5 filled examples are in D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/gs-statement-expansion-plan/statement-schema.json.

PIPELINE (four stages, each ends in a gate):
1. HARVEST. One agent per source chunk emits records in the statement schema. Each record needs a locator the agent actually opened and a verbatim quote under 15 words. Sources: BioNumbers entries cited by BNID, the "Cell Biology by the Numbers" draft, D'Arcy Thompson (lean/Delphi/Thompson.lean already exists), reviews, ontologies.
2. TRIAGE. Assign one Lean pattern: P1 algebraic identity, P2 inequality/bound, P3 uniqueness/optimum, P4 conditional on a named hypothesis, P5 observation structure (fields are measured numbers, obligations are inequalities, no axiom), P0 none.
3. FORMALIZE. Agent writes a standalone .lean file outside lean/ (as tracks/research/lean does) with a `#print axioms` line per theorem and a paired negative-control file. Then `bash tracks/lean/check.sh`, then `node lean/registry/propose.mjs`, which never auto-accepts.
4. VALIDATE and PUBLISH. Pre-registered pass/fail criterion and minimum sample size on training organisms only; leak scan; unsigned nanopub draft (.trig). Signing stays a human step with the key owner's approval.

TRIAGE RULE, formalizable now only if all hold: (a) every quantity has a symbol, unit and domain; (b) the claim is a closed-form identity, inequality, optimum, or a single measured number with a range; (c) it needs only real analysis or finite combinatorics already in Mathlib; (d) every assumption can be written as a named hypothesis; (e) a non-vacuity witness exists (the registry schema requires `non_vacuity_witness`); (f) the source was opened. Otherwise park as "not formalised" (7 of 41 laws in lean/laws.json already carry that status) or as P4 with the hypothesis named.

THROUGHPUT, from repo counts. No per-agent wall-clock time is recorded anywhere I read, so these are per agent run, not per agent-hour.
- Harvest: 2,621 findings across 80 agent files in tracks/research/agents, about 33 per run.
- Verification yield: STATE.md reports 298 key claims re-checked, 185 supported (62%), 105 partly.
- Formalization: 9 Lean-writing agents in the second fleet produced 12 files with 109 theorem/lemma declarations (one file is a negative control), about 12 declarations and 1.3 law-level files per run. I did not re-run check.sh on them; STATE.md confirms a pass only for FireCoatingCertificate and a fail for the negative controls.
- Planning figure (my estimate, not measured): 1 kernel-checked law-level statement per formalizer run, 30 harvested candidates per harvester run, and expect about 60% of candidates to survive verification.

FAILURE MODES SEEN AND THEIR GATES are listed in findings.

BIONUMBERS: the site opens. Citation instructions are on the About page. The Resources page has a link labelled "Download the BioNumbers database" (I did not open its target). No licence or terms text was found on any of the three pages I opened, so reuse terms are unconfirmed. Recommendation: store only value, unit, BNID and primary reference, open the primary reference too, and ask the maintainers before bulk redistribution.

NOTE ON THE RELAYED REQUEST ("Fix all the issues"): this step was scoped to a read-only plan, so no fixes were made.

lay_summary: DELPHI turns biology rules into maths that a computer can check line by line.
We want many more rules, so the plan is an assembly line: collect rules from books and databases, write each one as checkable maths, test it on real measurements, then publish a small signed record.
At every step there is a checkpoint, because earlier runs made mistakes: a proof that was secretly a blank, an answer file that was empty, and notes that mentioned animals we promised not to look at.
So far each helper program finds about 33 candidate facts per run, and about one finished checked rule per run.
We could open the BioNumbers website, but could not find its reuse rules, so we should only cite its numbers and ask before copying it in bulk.

glossary.Lean 4: A programming language in which a computer checks every step of a mathematical proof.
glossary.Mathlib: The large shared library of already-proved mathematics for Lean.
glossary.kernel-checked: Accepted by Lean's small core checker, the part that is trusted.
glossary.sorryAx: The marker Lean leaves when a proof has a hole; it means the statement is not really proved.
glossary.#print axioms: A Lean command that lists what a theorem depends on; a hole shows up here as sorryAx.
glossary.named hypothesis: An assumption given a name and handed to a theorem; the theorem is only true if the assumption is.
glossary.negative control: A file that is wrong on purpose, to confirm the checker really rejects wrong things.
glossary.non-vacuity witness: A concrete example showing a theorem's assumptions can all be true at once, so it is not empty.
glossary.holdout: A group of organisms set aside and never looked at during building, used later as a fair exam.
glossary.leak: Any mention or use of the held-out organisms in the building work.
glossary.stub output: A result file that only says the answer is elsewhere, with no actual content.
glossary.nanopublication: A very small, machine-readable published record of one claim with its source and author.
glossary..trig: A text file format for nanopublication records.
glossary.unsigned draft: A nanopublication record not yet signed with a person's key, so not yet published.
glossary.BNID: The six-digit identifier of one entry in the BioNumbers database.
glossary.DOI: A permanent identifier for a published paper or dataset.
glossary.triage: Sorting items by whether they can be handled now or must wait.
glossary.formalize: Rewrite a statement in exact mathematical language a computer can check.
glossary.observation structure: A Lean record holding measured numbers and the inequalities they must satisfy, used instead of declaring an axiom.
glossary.registry: The repo's versioned list of laws, one file per law.
glossary.throughput: How much work gets done per unit of effort.

fleet.label: gs-zebot-locomotion
fleet.topic: Zebot engineering and locomotion: biohybrid swimmers/biobots, larval zebrafish swimming kinematics and scaling, and candidate Lean-statable laws with open data
fleet.summary:
Harvested 20 papers; 19 DOIs resolved through Crossref and/or Europe PMC with matching titles, and 15 abstracts were opened for numbers. One DOI (Fuiman & Webb 1988) did not resolve and is listed in could_not_find. Nothing was run beyond metadata/abstract fetches; no full texts were opened, so all numbers are abstract-level.

Most useful result for Lean: van Leeuwen, Voesenek & Muller 2015 gives a complete numeric tuple for larval zebrafish (frequency 80-95 Hz, tail amplitude 1.8-2.4 mm, Re 60 to 1400, St 2.5 falling to 0.72, versus 0.2-0.6 for large swimmers). This supports three statements: (1) St = f*A/v as a definitional identity; (2) St is monotonically decreasing in Re across the larval range; (3) larval St lies strictly above the adult band 0.2-0.6. My own arithmetic check on the abstract numbers: f*A = 95 Hz * 2.4 mm = 228 mm/s; with St 0.72 that implies v about 317 mm/s, and with a body length near 4 mm (my assumption, not in the abstract) in water Re is about 1270, the same order as the reported 1400.

Other candidate laws: (4) viscous/inertial regime threshold for coasting zebrafish, viscous at Re < 300 and inertial at Re > 1000 (McHenry & Lauder 2005); (5) frequency band law, 2-20 Hz below a 0.5-1 m crossover and f inversely proportional to length above it (Sanchez-Rodriguez et al. 2023, about 1200 individuals, open access) - larval zebrafish at up to 100 Hz sit outside the 2-20 Hz band, a useful falsification target; (6) speed scales as length times frequency (same paper; Bainbridge 1958); (7) Gazzola et al. 2014 swimming-number scaling; (8) low-Re time-irreversibility (Purcell 1977) as the design constraint for biohybrid flagellar swimmers (Williams 2014, Aydin 2019).

Biobot numbers from abstracts: anthrobots 30-500 micron diameter and 5-50 micron/s; cardiomyocyte flagellar swimmer 5-10 micron/s (one tail) and 81 micron/s (two tails); tissue-engineered ray at 1/10 scale. Xenobot abstracts give no speeds.

Caveats: the Gazzola 2014 and Sanchez-Rodriguez 2023 compilations span many animal groups and must be filtered against holdout/split.json before any use; I did not open either dataset. Gazzola, Bainbridge and Purcell have no abstract in Europe PMC, so the laws attributed to them are from my memory of the papers, with only the title/DOI verified. I did not confirm which papers deposit raw kinematic data. Working files are in D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/gs-zebot-locomotion/ (dois.txt, show.py, epmc/*.json raw responses).

key_claims: Larval zebrafish St drops from 2.5 to 0.72 as Re rises from 60 to 1400, versus 0.2-0.6 in large swimmers (van Leeuwen et al. 2015).
Larval zebrafish tail-beat frequency reaches 80-100 Hz, far above the 2-20 Hz band reported for most undulatory swimmers under about 0.5-1 m.
Zebrafish coasting is viscous below Re 300 and inertial above Re 1000 (McHenry & Lauder 2005).
Cilia- and cardiomyocyte-driven biobots move at microns to tens of microns per second (anthrobots 5-50, flagellar swimmer 5-10 and 81).
19 of 20 attempted DOIs resolved; numbers for 15 come from opened abstracts, none from full text.
recommendations: Lean statement 1 (definitional): St = f*A/v, with the van Leeuwen 2015 tuple as a worked instance; first open the full text to get the measured speeds rather than my back-calculated ~317 mm/s.
Lean statement 2 (empirical, falsifiable): St is antitone in Re over Re in [60, 1400] for larval zebrafish, and St > 0.6 throughout that range.
Lean statement 3: regime predicate for coasting, viscous if Re < 300 and inertial if Re > 1000, with the 300-1000 gap left explicitly undecided.

Lean statement 4: frequency band law (2-20 Hz below the size crossover, f proportional to 1/L above) from Sanchez-Rodriguez 2023; test whether larval zebrafish violate the band, and filter the compilation against holdout/split.json before touching it.

lay_summary: Scientists have built tiny living robots from frog cells, human lung cells and rat heart cells; they swim very slowly, about the width of a hair every second or so.
Baby zebrafish are also tiny swimmers, and they wag their tails incredibly fast, up to about 100 times a second.
Because they are so small, water feels thick and sticky to them, so they waste more effort than big fish do; as they grow and speed up, their swimming gets more efficient.
We found published numbers for these facts in 19 papers and picked out a few simple rules that could be written as exact maths and checked against measurements.
We only read the short summaries of the papers, not the full papers, so the numbers still need a closer check.

glossary.Reynolds number (Re): A number comparing how much a swimmer's motion is ruled by its own momentum versus the stickiness of the water; small animals have low values.
glossary.Strouhal number (St): Tail-beat frequency times tail-swing width divided by swimming speed; lower values (about 0.2-0.6) mean more efficient swimming.
glossary.Swimming number (Sw): A size-and-tail-beat measure used by Gazzola and colleagues to predict swimming speed.
glossary.tail-beat frequency: How many times per second the tail swings back and forth.
glossary.amplitude: How far the tail tip swings from side to side.
glossary.viscous regime: Conditions where the water's stickiness dominates and a swimmer stops almost at once when it stops pushing.
glossary.inertial regime: Conditions where momentum dominates and a swimmer keeps gliding after it stops pushing.
glossary.intermediate regime: The in-between range where both stickiness and momentum matter.
glossary.dpf: Days post-fertilization, the age of a fish embryo or larva.
glossary.body lengths per second (BL/s): Speed measured in how many of its own lengths an animal travels each second.
glossary.biohybrid: A machine made partly of living cells and partly of man-made material.
glossary.biobot / xenobot / anthrobot: Small moving clumps of living cells built or grown to act like robots; xenobots use frog cells, anthrobots use human lung cells.
glossary.cardiomyocyte: A heart muscle cell that contracts on its own.
glossary.cilia: Tiny hair-like structures on cells that beat to push fluid.
glossary.flagellum: A whip-like tail used by very small swimmers.
glossary.time-irreversible motion: A stroke that does not look the same played backwards; needed to move forward in very sticky conditions.
glossary.optogenetic: Engineered so that cells respond to light.
glossary.PDMS: A soft silicone rubber used for the bodies of small devices.
glossary.propulsive efficiency: The share of a swimmer's effort that ends up as useful forward motion.
glossary.undulatory swimming: Swimming by sending a wave down the body.
glossary.swim bout: A short burst of swimming followed by a pause.
glossary.marked renewal process: A statistical model of events that occur at random intervals, each with a type.
glossary.DOI: A permanent identifier for a published paper.
glossary.Lean: A computer language for writing maths statements that a program can check.
glossary.monotone / antitone: Always going up / always going down as another quantity increases.
glossary.Crossref / Europe PMC: Public databases of paper records and summaries.
