fleet.label: hv-mat-biomaterials
fleet.topic: Biomaterial mixing, foam, water-uptake and bilayer laws for bio-based printable materials: harvest, formal statements, registry overlap, falsifying tests, two validations, one Lean file
fleet.summary:
Ten statements harvested and formalised; three checks run against one open paper (Islam et al. 2017, fungal mycelium, full text opened via Europe PMC); one Lean file passes check.sh with ALL CHECKED on the first run.

Validation results (all from Islam 2017, densities 30-50 kg/m3):
- Stiffness exponent: PASS, loosely. Gibson-Ashby predicts 2; the paper's reported end-point ranges (600-2000 kPa) imply about 2.36. This is my arithmetic on rounded ranges, not a refit of their data; the authors themselves report square scaling.
- Absolute stiffness with prefactor C = 1: FAIL. Using the paper's chitin wall values (2.5 GPa, 1430 kg/m3) the law predicts 1100 and 3056 kPa at 30 and 50 kg/m3; measured is about 600 and 2000 kPa (ratio 0.55-0.65). Using the hyphal wall modulus the paper also quotes (110-140 MPa) it predicts 48-62 kPa at 30 kg/m3, roughly 10 times too low. The scaling holds; the prefactor and the choice of solid modulus do not transfer.
- Yield strength, exponent 1.5: PASS. Predicted 41 and 88 kPa; measured 40-80 kPa. The 0.3 prefactor is the Gibson-Ashby textbook value from memory, not from a source I opened.

Lean: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-mat-biomaterials/HalpinTsaiBounds.lean proves five theorems with standard axioms only. The new content is that the Halpin-Tsai closed form lies between the Reuss and Voigt bounds for any shape factor xi >= 0, and equals Reuss at xi = 0. This is algebra on the closed forms, not a derivation from elasticity. The fifth theorem (doubling density quadruples stiffness) is a trivial identity.

Registry overlap: Voigt-Reuss ordering and equality case already exist (tracks/research/lean/bm-lean-materials-laws__VoigtReuss.lean); the Timoshenko bilayer ceiling already exists (tracks/lean/HygromorphCeiling.lean). Halpin-Tsai has no hit anywhere in lean, tracks/lean or tracks/research. Fickian uptake and Gibson-Ashby are mentioned in tracks/research but I found no Lean theorem for them (file-name grep only; I did not read those files).

Limits: of the primary sources, only Islam 2017 was opened in full text. Voigt 1889, Reuss 1929, Timoshenko 1925, Gibson-Ashby 1982 and Hashin-Shtrikman 1963 were confirmed as Crossref records only; the Halpin-Kardos DOI was confirmed from the Wikipedia reference list; the Hill 1952 and Shen-Springer 1976 Crossref lookups failed. The quantitative forms for those are the standard textbook ones, written from memory. No fibre-composite or water-uptake dataset was fetched, so statements 1-4, 6 and 8-10 are untested here. The "open dataset" named for each of those is a class of data, not a located file.

findings.claim: S1 Voigt upper bound (rule of mixtures, equal strain). Formal: for a two-phase composite with phase moduli E1,E2 > 0 and volume fraction 0 <= f <= 1, E_eff <= f E1 + (1-f) E2. Assumptions: linear elastic, perfectly bonded phases, no porosity. Registry: ALREADY PRESENT as closed-form ordering (reuss_le_voigt in tracks/research/lean/bm-lean-materials-laws__VoigtReuss.lean). Falsifying test: any open table of flax/PLA or wood-flour/PLA printed-filament tensile moduli with fibre volume fraction; fail if a measured modulus exceeds f Ef + (1-f) Em beyond measurement error.
findings.evidence_quote: E_V = fE1 + (1-f)E2 (as extracted from the page)
findings.confidence: high for the form; primary paper not opened; no dataset located or tested

findings.claim: S2 Reuss lower bound (equal stress). Formal: 1/E_R = f/E1 + (1-f)/E2 and E_eff >= E_R. Same assumptions as S1; porosity breaks it. Registry: ALREADY PRESENT (same VoigtReuss.lean, including the equality case reuss_eq_voigt_iff). Falsifying test: same composite tables; a measured modulus below E_R falsifies the no-porosity, perfect-bond assumptions rather than the algebra.
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_mixtures (opened; formula text garbled in extraction); primary Reuss 1929 doi:10.1002/zamm.19290090104 (Crossref record only)
findings.confidence: high for the form; primary not opened; not tested

findings.claim: S3 Halpin-Tsai. Formal: E/Em = (1 + xi eta phi)/(1 - eta phi), eta = (Ef/Em - 1)/(Ef/Em + xi), xi >= 0 a shape factor (commonly 2 L/d for longitudinal modulus of short fibres). Assumptions: aligned fibres, perfect bond, xi fitted or set by geometry. Registry: ABSENT (no grep hit for Halpin in lean, tracks/lean or tracks/research). Falsifying test: short-fibre biocomposite modulus versus fibre aspect ratio at fixed phi; fail if the xi needed to fit the data is negative, i.e. the measured modulus falls outside the Reuss-Voigt interval.
findings.source: Halpin and Kardos 1976, doi:10.1002/pen.760160512 (not opened; citation confirmed on https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halpin-Tsai_model, which gives no equations)
findings.confidence: medium: equation written from memory, the opened page describes the model in words only; the xi = 2L/d convention is also from memory

findings.claim: S4 (new, Lean-checked) Halpin-Tsai is bracketed by the mixture bounds: for Em, Ef > 0, 0 <= phi <= 1, xi >= 0, Reuss <= HT(xi) <= Voigt, and HT(0) = Reuss exactly. Uses the closed form HT = Em (Ef + xi V)/(D + xi Em), V = phi Ef + (1-phi) Em, D = (1-phi) Ef + phi Em. Registry: ABSENT before this file. Falsifying test: none for the algebra; it means a Halpin-Tsai fit can never explain a measurement outside the bounds.
findings.evidence_quote: ALL CHECKED: no errors, no sorryAx
findings.confidence: high for the algebra; the equivalence of the closed form to the eta form was done by hand in a comment, not proved in Lean

findings.claim: S5 Gibson-Ashby open-cell stiffness scaling. Formal: E/Es = C (rho/rho_s)^2 with C about 1, for bending-dominated open cells at low relative density. Registry: mentioned in tracks/research (bm-lean-materials-laws, bm-mycelium-living-materials); no Lean theorem found. Falsifying test: log-log regression of modulus on density for mycelium foams; fail if the slope's confidence interval excludes 2.
findings.source: Islam et al. 2017, Sci Rep, doi:10.1038/s41598-017-13295-2 (full text opened via Europe PMC PMC5638950); primary Gibson and Ashby 1982 doi:10.1098/rspa.1982.0088 (Crossref record only)
findings.evidence_quote: For open cell foams, the exponents are 2 for the elastic modulus
findings.confidence: high for the form as quoted by Islam; C about 1 is from memory; primary not opened

findings.claim: VALIDATION A (exponent): PASS, loosely. Prediction: slope 2. Measured: modulus 600 to 2000 kPa over 30 to 50 kg/m3 gives ln(3.33)/ln(1.667) = 2.36. Authors state square scaling from their own fit.
findings.value: predicted 2; implied from reported ranges about 2.36
findings.evidence_quote: the modulus varies with the square of mycelium density
findings.confidence: medium: my figure uses rounded end-point ranges, assuming the low modulus pairs with the low density; not a refit of the raw points

findings.claim: VALIDATION B (absolute stiffness, C = 1): FAIL. With chitin wall Es = 2.5 GPa and rho_s = 1430 kg/m3 the law predicts 1100 kPa at 30 kg/m3 and 3056 kPa at 50 kg/m3; measured about 600 and 2000 kPa (ratio 0.55 to 0.65). With the hyphal wall modulus 110-140 MPa also quoted in the paper it predicts 48-62 kPa at 30 kg/m3, about 10 times below measurement.
findings.evidence_quote: varies from 600 to 2000 kPa for the given range of density
findings.confidence: medium: solid-phase values are the paper's literature values for chitin, not measured on these samples; a fibre network is not a true cellular foam

findings.claim: S6 / VALIDATION C Gibson-Ashby open-cell strength. Formal: sigma_y = C2 sigma_ys (rho/rho_s)^(3/2), C2 about 0.3. Prediction with sigma_ys = 45 MPa, rho_s = 1430 kg/m3: 41 kPa at 30 kg/m3, 88 kPa at 50 kg/m3. Measured yield 40-80 kPa. PASS. Registry: no Lean theorem found. Falsifying test: same mycelium density series; fail if the strength slope's interval excludes 1.5.
findings.value: predicted 41 to 88 kPa; measured 40 to 80 kPa
findings.evidence_quote: strength varies with an exponent 3/2
findings.confidence: medium: exponent and measured range are quoted; the 0.3 prefactor is from memory, not from an opened source

findings.claim: S7 Timoshenko bilayer curvature. Formal: kappa = 6 (1+m)^2 d_eps / ( h [ 3(1+m)^2 + (1+mn)(m^2 + 1/(mn)) ] ), m = thickness ratio, n = modulus ratio, h = total thickness, d_eps = differential (hygro)expansion strain; maximum 3 d_eps/(2h) when m^2 n = 1. Assumptions: Euler-Bernoulli beam, uniform strain per layer, perfect bond. Registry: ALREADY PRESENT (tracks/lean/HygromorphCeiling.lean: timoshenkoCoefficient_le, bilayerCurvature_optimal, bilayer_rules_out). Falsifying test: printed wood-fibre/PLA hygromorph curvature tables; fail if measured curvature exceeds 3 d_eps/(2h).
findings.confidence: medium: formula from memory, consistent with theorem names in the repo; primary not opened; not tested here

findings.claim: S8 Fickian water uptake, short time. Formal: for a plate of thickness h exposed on both faces, M_t/M_inf = (4/h) sqrt(D t/pi) while M_t/M_inf < about 0.6. Assumptions: constant D, no swelling, one-dimensional diffusion. Registry: Fickian is mentioned in tracks/research (bm-bilayer-theory-verified, bm-building-physics-standards); no Lean theorem found. Falsifying test: mass gain versus sqrt(t) for immersed natural-fibre/PLA coupons; fail if the early curve is not linear in sqrt(t) or D differs across thicknesses.
findings.source: Shen and Springer 1976, J Compos Mater, doi:10.1177/002199767601000101 (Crossref lookup failed; not opened)
findings.confidence: low on the citation (DOI unverified); the formula is the standard one from memory; not tested

findings.claim: S9 Fickian thickness scaling. Formal: time to reach a fixed fractional uptake scales as h^2 (t_half is about 0.049 h^2/D for a plate). Registry: no Lean theorem found. Falsifying test: uptake curves for printed coupons at two thicknesses; fail if the half-time ratio differs from the thickness ratio squared. Natural-fibre composites often swell, so failure is plausible.
findings.source: Standard result of the plate diffusion solution; no source opened
findings.confidence: low: from memory, no source opened, not tested

findings.claim: S10 Hashin-Shtrikman bounds are tighter than Voigt-Reuss for isotropic two-phase composites. Formal (bulk modulus, K2 > K1, G1 the softer shear modulus): K_lower = K1 + f2 / ( 1/(K2-K1) + 3 f1/(3K1 + 4G1) ), with Reuss <= HS_lower <= HS_upper <= Voigt. Assumptions: statistically isotropic, well-ordered phases. Registry: ABSENT (not in VoigtReuss.lean theorem list). Falsifying test: isotropic particulate biocomposite (e.g. wood-flour filled) moduli; fail if a measurement lies outside the HS interval.
findings.source: Hashin and Shtrikman 1963, doi:10.1016/0022-5096(63)90060-7 (Crossref record only)
findings.confidence: medium: formula from memory; primary not opened; not tested

lay_summary: Engineers have simple rules for guessing how stiff a material made of two ingredients will be, how stiff a sponge-like material is, how fast it soaks up water, and how much a two-layer strip curls.
We wrote ten of these rules down precisely and checked which ones the project already has.
We tested the sponge rule on a real mushroom-root material: the rule gets the trend right (denser means much stiffer) but guesses the actual stiffness almost twice too high.
The matching rule for strength landed almost exactly on the measured numbers.
We also got a computer proof checker to confirm that one popular fibre formula can never give an answer outside the two simplest limits.

glossary.Young's modulus (E): How stiff a material is: the force per area needed to stretch it by a given fraction.
glossary.Rule of mixtures: Estimating a blend's property as a weighted average of its ingredients.
glossary.Voigt bound: The highest stiffness a two-ingredient material can have, as if both ingredients stretch equally side by side.
glossary.Reuss bound: The lowest stiffness, as if the ingredients are stacked in series and carry the same load.
glossary.Volume fraction (f, phi): The share of the material's volume taken up by one ingredient.
glossary.Halpin-Tsai: A formula for the stiffness of a plastic filled with short fibres, with a knob for fibre shape.
glossary.Shape factor (xi): The knob in Halpin-Tsai; bigger for longer, thinner fibres.
glossary.Hashin-Shtrikman bounds: Tighter upper and lower stiffness limits for a blend that looks the same in every direction.
glossary.Gibson-Ashby scaling: A rule saying a foam's stiffness goes as its density squared, and its strength as density to the power 1.5.
glossary.Open-cell foam: A sponge-like solid whose pores connect to each other.
glossary.Relative density: Foam density divided by the density of the solid it is made of.
glossary.Prefactor (C): The constant multiplier in front of a scaling rule.
glossary.Yield strength: The stress at which a material stops springing back and deforms permanently.
glossary.Mycelium: The thread-like root network of a fungus.
glossary.Chitin: The stiff natural polymer in fungal cell walls.
glossary.Fickian diffusion: Spreading of a substance (here water) driven only by concentration differences, at a constant rate coefficient.
glossary.Timoshenko bilayer: A formula for how much a two-layer strip curls when one layer expands more than the other.
glossary.Curvature (kappa): How sharply something bends; one over the bend radius.
glossary.Hygromorph: A part that changes shape when it takes up moisture.
glossary.Lean / Mathlib: A computer proof checker and its maths library.
glossary.Axiom: A starting assumption a proof is allowed to rest on.
glossary.sorry: A Lean placeholder meaning 'not actually proved'.
glossary.Crossref: A public index of published papers and their DOIs.
glossary.DOI: A permanent identifier for a published paper.
glossary.kPa, MPa, GPa: Units of stress or stiffness: thousand, million and billion pascals.

fleet.topic: Binding thermodynamics statements (Kd-deltaG, Hill/occupancy bounds, detailed balance, enthalpy-entropy compensation, Cheng-Prusoff)
fleet.summary:
Ten binding-thermodynamics statements harvested and formalized; three validated against published numbers (all pass, with caveats); the Lean file is NOT checked. Both permitted check runs failed at line 1 on reading Mathlib .olean.private files (a different file each time; the first one named exists on disk), so no proof was evaluated and nothing here counts as proved.

Registry status: grep of lean/, tracks/lean/ and tracks/research/ found no law on Kd-deltaG, occupancy, Hill, Cheng-Prusoff, detailed balance or compensation. The files that matched the term grep (Altitude.lean, altitude-coupling.json, bm-diffusion-kinetics scripts) were not opened, so whether they touch binding is unconfirmed.

Validations:
- Kd = koff/kon: 4 abstracts, predicted vs reported 9.03 vs 9.02 nM, 584 vs 580 nM, 3.0 vs ~3.0 uM, 5.31 vs 5.3 nM. Pass, but these Kd values are probably computed from the same rate constants, so the test is weak. The one independent comparison (enzyme-inhibition Ki 18.9 +/- 1.2 nM vs SPR Kd 9.02 +/- 2.3 nM, same protein pair) differs 2.1-fold, outside the quoted errors.
- deltaG = RT ln Kd: KD 197 uM predicts -5.06 kcal/mol at 25 C; reported -5.14. Pass within 0.1 kcal/mol; exact match needs about 30 C, and the abstract does not state the temperature.
- Hill coefficient <= number of sites: haemoglobin nH 1.7-3.2 vs 4 sites. Pass; the site count of 4 is from memory, not from the opened page.
- Residence time: koff 1.2e-3 s^-1 predicts tau 13.9 min and t1/2 9.63 min; reported 13.9 and 9.63. Pass (arithmetic identity).

Citation caveat: four PMIDs I recalled from memory resolved to unrelated papers (Hill-equation review, Sharp compensation paper, Colquhoun microscopic reversibility, Hulme and Trevethick ligand depletion). Those sources are unverified and listed in could_not_find. Cheng and Prusoff 1973 was confirmed by title and DOI only; PubMed has no abstract, so the formula is from memory.

Each statement's formal form, registry status, dataset and falsifying test are in the findings. Open datasets named: BindingDB, PDBbind, ChEMBL, SKEMPI 2.0.

Dataset/test: BindingDB or PDBbind ITC entries reporting both Kd and deltaG with temperature; falsified if |deltaG_reported - RT ln Kd| > 0.1 kcal/mol at the stated T. lay_summary: When a small molecule sticks to a protein, how tightly it sticks can be written as one number, and that number tells you how much energy is released.

We collected ten textbook rules about this sticking, such as 'the fraction of protein that is occupied can never go above 100%' and 'how fast things come apart divided by how fast they join gives the tightness'.

We checked three of the rules against numbers printed in published papers, and the numbers agreed, although some of those checks were easy because the papers probably used the same rule to get their numbers.
One harder check, comparing two different lab methods on the same pair of proteins, gave answers that were twice as far apart as the stated error bars allow.
We also wrote the rules as computer-checkable maths, but the checking program could not load its library on this machine, so those proofs are not confirmed yet.

glossary.Kd (dissociation constant): The ligand concentration at which half the binding sites are filled; smaller means tighter binding.
glossary.Ki (inhibition constant): The Kd of an inhibitor for its target.
glossary.IC50: The inhibitor concentration that cuts a measured signal in half under one particular set of assay conditions.
glossary.Km: The substrate concentration at which an enzyme works at half its top speed.
glossary.deltaG (binding free energy): The energy released on binding that decides how tight it is; more negative means tighter.
glossary.deltaH (enthalpy): The heat given off or taken up on binding.
glossary.T deltaS (entropy term): The part of the binding energy that comes from changes in disorder, multiplied by temperature.
glossary.RT: The gas constant times temperature; about 0.59 kcal/mol at room temperature.
glossary.kon: How fast two molecules join, per unit concentration.
glossary.koff: How fast a bound pair falls apart.
glossary.Residence time: The average time a ligand stays bound; equal to 1/koff.
glossary.Half-life (t1/2): The time for half of the bound pairs to fall apart.
glossary.Occupancy: The fraction of binding sites that have a ligand on them.
glossary.Langmuir / hyperbolic binding: The simplest binding curve, for one kind of site that does not interact with others.
glossary.Hill coefficient (nH): A number describing how steep a binding curve is; above 1 means sites help each other bind.
glossary.Cooperativity: When binding at one site makes binding at another site easier or harder.
glossary.Detailed balance: At equilibrium each step runs forwards and backwards at equal rates, so no net flow goes around a loop.
glossary.Thermodynamic cycle: A closed loop of steps between states; without an energy source the energy changes around it add up to zero.
glossary.Cheng-Prusoff equation: A formula that converts an IC50 into a Ki by correcting for the competing substrate or labelled ligand.
glossary.Competitive inhibitor: A molecule that blocks a target by occupying the same site as the natural partner.
glossary.Enthalpy-entropy compensation: The observation that a gain in heat released is often cancelled by a loss in disorder, leaving tightness almost unchanged.
glossary.ITC (isothermal titration calorimetry): A method that measures the heat of binding directly to get Kd and deltaH.
glossary.SPR (surface plasmon resonance): A method that watches molecules bind to a surface in real time to get kon and koff.
glossary.Ligand: The molecule that binds to a protein or other target.
glossary.Ligand depletion / tight binding: The situation where so much ligand is bound that the free concentration drops, which breaks the simple formulas.
glossary.Ligand efficiency: Binding energy divided by the number of non-hydrogen atoms in the ligand.
glossary.Heavy atom: Any atom in a molecule other than hydrogen.
glossary.Standard state (1 M): The reference concentration used so that Kd can be put inside a logarithm.
glossary.Lean / Mathlib: A computer proof checker and its mathematics library.
glossary.olean file: A compiled library file that Lean must load before it can check anything.

fleet.label: hv-mol-central-dogma
fleet.topic: Quantitative gene-expression statements: steady-state protein = synthesis/degradation, mRNA-protein correlation, burst statistics, Fano factor
fleet.summary:
Harvested 12 quantitative gene-expression statements from primary papers (abstracts opened via PubMed; full text opened for Taniguchi 2010 and Raj 2006). None of them is in the law registry: a grep of lean/**/*.lean, lean/laws.json, lean/registry/laws and tracks/lean for Fano|mRNA|gene expression|transcription returned no matches. tracks/research has hits for 'burst'/'degradation' only in materials and flying-fish agent files, which I did not open one by one.

Validated 5 predictions against reported numbers; 3 failed, 2 passed:
- Poisson mRNA (Fano = 1) vs E. coli: measured about 1.6. FAIL.
- Poisson mRNA vs a mammalian reporter gene: mean about 40, variance about 1,600, so Fano about 40. FAIL (bursty model consistent).
- Deterministic "protein proportional to mRNA" inside a single cell: predicts strong positive correlation; measured r = 0.01 +/- 0.03 (N = 5,447). FAIL at single-cell level.
- The same relation across genes (means): r = 0.77 by FISH (r^2 about 0.59), 0.54 by RNA-seq. PASS as a positive trend, far from exact.
- Gamma-distribution law for protein numbers: 1,009 of 1,018 strains fit (99.1%). PASS.
Also noted: the pure intrinsic gamma model (CV^2 = 1/a, falling without limit) fails at high expression, where noise plateaus at about 0.1.

Lean: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-mol-central-dogma/CentralDogma.lean has 6 theorems (steady state p = k/d; two-stage mean; Poisson Fano = 1; bursty Fano = 1 + b > 1; gamma CV^2 = 1/a and Fano = b; variance proportional to mean iff CV^2 = B/mean). Run 1 failed on an environment error (could not read a Mathlib .olean.private file that does exist on disk; probably another process using the cache). Run 2, same file unchanged: ALL CHECKED, 0 errors, 0 sorryAx, 6/6 axiom lines. These are algebraic identities with the biology as named hypotheses; they do not prove the stochastic models themselves (no probability distributions are formalised).

Limits: the exact formulas for Thattai (Fano = 1 + b), Elowitz (noise decomposition), Paulsson and Schwanhäusser (R^2 about 0.4, model equations) are stated from memory of the papers; only their abstracts were opened, and the abstracts do not contain those formulas. The proposed open datasets (supplementary tables, GEO) were not opened. Based on articles retrieved from PubMed; DOIs are in the findings and citations.

findings.claim: S1. Steady-state protein level = synthesis rate / degradation rate. Formal: dp/dt = k_s - k_d*p; at dp/dt = 0, p* = k_s/k_d (assumes first-order loss, constant rates, dilution folded into k_d). Registry: absent. Falsifier: Schwanhäusser 2011 supplementary table (mRNA and protein copies, half-lives, >5,000 genes, mouse fibroblasts); test = across genes, log protein vs log(mRNA * translation rate * protein half-life) must have slope 1; note the paper derives translation rates from this model, so an independent rate (ribosome profiling) is needed for a real test.
findings.evidence_quote: cellular abundance of proteins is predominantly controlled at the level of translation
findings.confidence: Medium: abstract opened; model equation from memory of the paper; dataset not opened. Lean: steady_state_protein, checked.

findings.claim: S2. Two-stage model mean: m* = k_m/d_m, p* = k_m*k_p/(d_m*d_p). Formal as stated; assumes constant rates, one gene copy. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Li et al. 2014 E. coli ribosome-profiling synthesis rates (GEO, accession not verified by me) vs independent protein abundance; test = synthesis rate / dilution rate predicts copies per cell within a stated fold-error for stable proteins.
findings.evidence_quote: mean and variance of protein concentration can be independently controlled
findings.confidence: Medium: formula is standard, not in the abstract. Lean: two_stage_mean, checked.

findings.claim: S3. Protein Fano factor in the two-stage model: var/mean = 1 + b, with b = k_p/d_m (proteins made per mRNA lifetime), valid when protein lifetime >> mRNA lifetime. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Ozbudak et al. 2002 B. subtilis translation-efficiency mutants; test = Fano rises linearly with translational efficiency and stays flat with transcription rate.
findings.evidence_quote: noise is essentially determined at the translational level
findings.confidence: Medium: exact formula from memory, abstract supports the qualitative claim only. Ozbudak paper not opened. Lean: bursty_fano (algebra only), checked.

findings.claim: S4. Proteins per burst follow a geometric distribution: P(n) = (1-q) q^n, each burst from one mRNA. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Yu et al. 2006 burst-size histogram; test = chi-square goodness of fit of geometric vs Poisson burst sizes.
findings.evidence_quote: protein copy numbers in the bursts follow a geometric distribution
findings.confidence: High for the statement; dataset not opened.

findings.claim: S5. Burst size is exponentially distributed (continuous limit of S4); burst size and frequency recoverable from the steady-state copy-number distribution. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Cai et al. 2006 real-time beta-galactosidase traces; test = burst size and frequency from real-time traces must equal those fitted from the population histogram.
findings.evidence_quote: number of molecules per burst following an exponential distribution
findings.confidence: High for the statement; dataset not opened.

findings.claim: S6. Steady-state protein number is gamma distributed, p(x) = x^(a-1) e^(-x/b) / (Gamma(a) b^a), with a = k1/gamma2 (bursts per cell cycle) and b = k2/gamma1 (burst size); so mean = a*b, CV^2 = 1/a, Fano = b. VALIDATED: 1,009 of 1,018 E. coli strains fit = 99.1%. PASS. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Taniguchi 2010 supplementary per-gene table; test = fraction of genes whose single-cell histogram rejects a gamma fit.
findings.evidence_quote: 1,009 out of the 1,018 strains can be well fit by the gamma distribution
findings.confidence: High; the formula subscripts were partly lost in the page text. Lean: gamma_cv2_fano (moment algebra only), checked.

findings.claim: S7. Constitutive (Poisson) transcription predicts mRNA Fano factor = 1. VALIDATED against E. coli: measured about 1.6. FAIL (mRNA is not Poisson, even in bacteria). Registry: absent. Falsifier: Taniguchi 2010 FISH table for 137 genes (number recalled, not re-read); test = one-sided test that mean Fano > 1.
findings.evidence_quote: mRNA Fano factor values ... are close to ∼1.6
findings.confidence: High for the measured value. Lean: poisson_fano, checked.

findings.claim: S8. In mammalian cells mRNA is made in bursts, so Fano >> 1 (telegraph model: Fano about 1 + mean burst size when the gene is mostly off). VALIDATED: reporter gene mean about 40 mRNA per cell, variance about 1,600, so Fano about 40 against the Poisson prediction of 1. Poisson FAILS; bursty model consistent. A natural gene (RNA polymerase II large subunit) had variance over 50 times the mean. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Raj 2006 single-cell FISH counts; test = variance/mean with bootstrap interval vs 1.
findings.evidence_quote: the variance was roughly 1,600 molecules squared
findings.value: Poisson prediction Fano 1; measured ~40 (1600/40); FAIL for Poisson
findings.confidence: High for the numbers (Fano 40 is my division). The 1 + burst-size formula is from memory; the paper's numeric burst size was only in a figure I could not read.

findings.claim: S9. mRNA and protein copy numbers of the same gene in the same single cell are uncorrelated. Formal: Pearson r(m_i, p_i) about 0 across cells, when protein lifetime >> mRNA lifetime. VALIDATED: a deterministic p proportional to m reading predicts r clearly > 0; measured r = 0.01 +/- 0.03 (SEM, N = 5,447). The proportional reading FAILS at single-cell level; the statement itself passes. Registry: absent. Falsifier: any joint single-cell mRNA + protein count; test = r differs from 0.
findings.evidence_quote: not correlated (r = 0.01 ± 0.03, SEM, N = 5,447)
findings.confidence: High. Golding 2005 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2005.09.031) reports weaker correlation early in the cell cycle, so timing matters.

findings.claim: S10. Across genes, mean protein rises with mean mRNA but far from perfectly. VALIDATED: E. coli r = 0.77 (FISH), 0.54 (RNA-seq), so mRNA explains about 59% and 29% of variance in means. PASS as a positive trend; FAILS as an exact law. Mammalian cells: mRNA and protein levels correlate 'better than previously thought', while half-lives do not correlate. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Schwanhäusser 2011 table; test = R^2 of log protein vs log mRNA and of protein vs mRNA half-life.
findings.evidence_quote: corresponding half-lives showed no correlation
findings.confidence: High for E. coli values. The widely quoted mammalian R^2 of about 0.4 was NOT verified by me.

findings.claim: S11. Protein noise scales inversely with abundance up to a floor: variance proportional to mean (CV^2 = B/mean) in yeast; in E. coli CV^2 proportional to 1/mean below about 10 molecules per cell, then a plateau near 0.1 from extrinsic noise. So the pure intrinsic gamma model (CV^2 = 1/a, falling without limit) FAILS at high expression. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Newman 2006 yeast GFP-library flow cytometry (>2,500 proteins); test = slope of log CV^2 vs log mean equals -1 and no floor.
findings.evidence_quote: the expression variance was approximately proportional to the mean
findings.value: CV^2 = B/mean, floor ~0.1 in E. coli
findings.confidence: High for the statements; datasets not opened. Lean: cv2_inverse_mean, checked.

findings.claim: S12. Total noise splits into intrinsic and extrinsic parts: eta_tot^2 = eta_int^2 + eta_ext^2, with eta_int measured from the difference between two identical reporter genes in one cell. And bursting is not universal: most constitutive yeast genes show small variation consistent with single, separated initiation events (near-Poisson), while PDR5 is bursty. Registry: absent. Falsifier: Zenklusen 2008 single-mRNA counts; test = Fano of constitutive genes vs 1, and PDR5 vs 1.

findings.evidence_quote: rather than by transcriptional bursts
findings.confidence: Medium: the decomposition formula is from memory, not in the abstract.

Within a single cell, mRNA and protein counts of one gene are uncorrelated (r = 0.01), although across genes the means correlate (r = 0.77).

lay_summary: A cell makes a protein by first copying a gene into a message (mRNA) and then building the protein from that message.
The simplest rule says the amount of a protein settles where making it and breaking it down balance, like a bathtub with the tap on and the drain open.
But cells make messages and proteins in random spurts, so two identical cells can hold very different amounts.
We checked the simple 'smooth and steady' rule against published counts and it failed: real cells were 1.6 to 40 times more uneven than the rule allows.
A better rule that includes spurts matched 99 out of every 100 bacterial genes tested, and a computer proof-checker confirmed the algebra behind six of these rules.

glossary.mRNA: The message copied from a gene that tells the cell how to build a protein.
glossary.protein: A molecule that does work in the cell, built from an mRNA message.
glossary.synthesis rate: How many molecules are made per unit of time.
glossary.degradation rate: The fraction of molecules broken down (or diluted by growth) per unit of time.
glossary.steady state: The level at which making and losing balance, so the amount stops changing.
glossary.half-life: The time it takes for half of the molecules to be lost.
glossary.variance: A measure of how spread out the counts are around the average.
glossary.Fano factor: Variance divided by mean; equals 1 for purely random, independent events.
glossary.CV^2 (noise): Variance divided by the mean squared; spread relative to the average.
glossary.Poisson distribution: The pattern of counts you get when events happen independently at a constant rate.
glossary.burst: A short spell in which many molecules are made at once, followed by a quiet spell.
glossary.burst size: The average number of molecules made in one burst.
glossary.geometric distribution: A pattern where each extra molecule in a burst is less likely by a fixed factor.
glossary.exponential distribution: The smooth version of the geometric pattern.
glossary.gamma distribution: A two-number curve (shape a, scale b) that describes protein counts when production is bursty.
glossary.telegraph model: A model where a gene randomly switches between on and off.
glossary.two-stage model: A model with two steps: gene to mRNA, then mRNA to protein.
glossary.intrinsic noise: Randomness from the gene's own chemical steps.
glossary.extrinsic noise: Cell-to-cell differences in shared machinery that affect all genes together.
glossary.correlation coefficient (r): A number from -1 to 1 saying how closely two quantities move together; r^2 is the share of variation explained.
glossary.FISH: A microscope method that lights up and counts individual mRNA molecules.
glossary.RNA-seq: A sequencing method that measures the amounts of all mRNAs.
glossary.ribosome profiling: A method that measures how fast each protein is being made.
glossary.constitutive gene: A gene that is on all the time.
glossary.Lean / Mathlib: A computer proof checker and its maths library.
glossary.axiom: A basic assumption the proof checker accepts without proof.
glossary.named hypothesis: An assumption written openly in a theorem instead of being hidden.
glossary.law registry: The project's list of formal laws already written down.

fleet.label: hv-mol-enhancer-logic
fleet.topic: Enhancer-promoter statements: multiplicative vs. saturating models, rank-order preservation, contact-frequency models (ABC)
fleet.summary:
Harvested 12 statements from 11 primary sources (abstracts via Europe PMC; full text opened only for Fulco 2019 and Zuin 2022) and ran 5 validations against reported values: 3 fail, 2 pass.

FAILS: (a) "Transcription is proportional to enhancer-promoter contact" (Hill exponent h = 1) is rejected by Zuin 2022: fitted h = 2.8, 95% CI 2.4-3.2. (b) The same linear model predicts at most a 2-fold expression change for a sub-2-fold contact change; Xiao 2021 cites about 10-fold. (c) A strict multiplicative model predicts no promoter selectivity; Martinez-Ara 2022 reports more than half of elements selective, and Bergman 2022 reports R2 = 0.82, not 1.

PASSES: (d) The ABC product beats either factor alone (AUPRC 0.65 vs 0.22 and 0.29). (e) A distance^-1 contact proxy does as well as measured Hi-C (AUPRC 0.64 vs 0.65).

Repo coverage: tracks/research/lean/q1-theory-lean__EnhancerPromoterRank.lean already defines Mult, SingleIndexMono, LogAdd, Thermo, General and TwoFactor and proves no rank reversal for monotone single-index models; q1-mechanisms__RankSaturation.lean also exists. A grep for "enhancer" / "ABC score" / "activity-by-contact" hit nothing under lean/ or tracks/lean, so the law registry has none of this. The Bergman and Martinez-Ara numbers are already in tracks/research/agents/q1-literature.json. I did not check whether tracks/research already states the ABC normalisation or the contact-Hill law; the Lean file I read does not.

Suggested next formalisations: (1) ABC as a normalised product, with the lemma that scores for a gene sum to 1 and ranking within a gene is invariant to promoter-side scaling; (2) Hill contact-to-on-rate law, with the lemma that h > 1 amplifies a contact fold-change r to up to r^h (3^2.8 is about 21.7, my arithmetic).

Limits: ran out of time before fetching any raw table, so all validations use numbers reported in the papers, not recomputed. Validations (a) and (b) test a linear contact-to-expression reading; ABC itself only claims a fraction of regulatory input, so they do not falsify ABC as a classifier. The holdout clade is not involved in this topic and no data about it was used.

Files (scripts and fetched text only): D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-mol-enhancer-logic/fetch_abs.py, pull.py, abstracts.json, PMC9021019.txt, PMC6886585.txt

findings.claim: S1 ABC definition. Formal: ABC(E,G) = A_E*C_EG / sum over e within 5 Mb of G of A_e*C_eG; A = geometric mean of DHS and H3K27ac reads, C = KR-normalised Hi-C at 5 kb. Assumption: effect of an element is a fraction of total regulatory input. In repo: not in the Lean file read; not in lean/ or tracks/lean. Falsifier: Fulco CRISPRi-FlowFISH table (>3,500 pairs, 30 genes) - within each gene, Spearman of ABC vs measured effect must be significantly non-zero.
findings.evidence_quote: the fraction of regulatory input to gene G contributed by element E

findings.claim: S2 The product A*C predicts regulatory pairs better than A or C alone. Formal: AUPRC(A*C) > max(AUPRC(A), AUPRC(C)). VALIDATION PASS: predicted product wins; measured 0.65 vs 0.22 (Activity) and 0.29 (Contact); also 0.65 vs 0.39 for genomic distance. In repo: not found. Falsifier: ENCODE-rE2G CRISPR benchmark (10,411 element-gene pairs) - recompute the three AUPRCs; fail if product does not exceed both.
findings.evidence_quote: AUPRC = 0.22 and 0.29, respectively
findings.confidence: high for reported values; not recomputed from raw table

findings.claim: S3 Contact can be replaced by a power law of distance. Formal: C_EG proportional to d(E,G)^-1 gives the same classifier performance as measured Hi-C. VALIDATION PASS: predicted difference about 0; measured AUPRC 0.65 (K562 Hi-C), 0.66 (average Hi-C of 10 cell types), 0.64 (distance^-1). In repo: not found. Falsifier: same CRISPR table; fail if AUPRC drops by more than bootstrap noise when Hi-C is swapped for d^-1.
findings.evidence_quote: AUPRC = 0.65, 0.66, and 0.64 respectively
findings.confidence: high for reported values; no confidence intervals read

findings.claim: S4 ABC score is quantitatively monotone with effect size. Formal: Spearman(ABC, % change in expression on CRISPRi) < 0 among regulatory pairs. Reported rho = -0.63 in K562, -0.30 across 5 other cell types (weaker out of sample). In repo: not found. Falsifier: Gasperini 2019 screen (5,920 candidate enhancers, 664 pairs) - rho not different from 0 would falsify.
findings.evidence_quote: Spearman ρ for regulatory DE-G pairs = –0.63

findings.claim: S5 Multiplicative model. Formal: f(p,e) = a(e)*b(p), b > 0 (equivalently log f additive). Reported R2 = 0.82 in a 1,000 x 1,000 reporter assay in K562. In repo: YES - class Mult in EnhancerPromoterRank.lean and the number in q1-literature.json. Falsifier: GEO GSE184426 (accession taken from the repo notes, not re-opened) - fit additive log model; residual variance beyond replicate noise falsifies exact multiplicativity.
findings.evidence_quote: multiplicatively combine to determine RNA output (R2 = 0.82)

findings.claim: S6 Rank-order preservation. Formal: if f(p,e) = h_p(a(e)) with every h_p monotone, no pair of promoters orders two enhancers in strictly opposite ways; Mult and promoter-specific saturation V_p*a/(K_p+a) are special cases. VALIDATION FAIL of the strict (noise-free multiplicative, zero selectivity) form: predicted 0% selective elements and R2 = 1; measured 'more than half' selective in mouse cells and R2 = 0.82 in K562. The approximate form survives. In repo: YES - theorem no_reversal_of_monotoneOn. Falsifier: GSE186265 (accession from repo notes) - count strict reversals exceeding replicate noise.
findings.evidence_quote: More than half of the tested CREs exhibit significant promoter selectivity
findings.confidence: medium: abstract-level; selectivity beyond noise is not the same as strict rank reversal

findings.claim: S7 Promoter-side saturation. Formal: responsiveness d log f / d log a(e) is lower for promoters with built-in activating motifs (housekeeping class); consistent with f = V_p*a/(K_p+a) with small K_p. Qualitative in the source. In repo: YES - class Thermo and RankSaturation.lean. Falsifier: GSE184426 - regression slope of log output on log enhancer activity must be lower for housekeeping promoters.
findings.evidence_quote: decrease the responsiveness of promoters to distal enhancers

findings.claim: S8 Contact-to-transcription is sigmoidal, not linear. Formal: k_on(p_c) = k0 + (k1-k0) * p_c^h / (c^h + p_c^h), fitted h = 2.8 (95% CI 2.4-3.2). VALIDATION FAIL of the linear model: linear predicts h = 1; measured interval excludes 1. Consequence (my arithmetic): a 3-fold contact drop can cut on-rate up to 3^2.8 = about 21.7-fold. In repo: not in the Lean file read; not in lean/ or tracks/lean. Falsifier: the Zuin enhancer-mobilisation cell lines (eGFP level vs Capture-C contact probability, hundreds of lines) - refit and test h = 1.
findings.evidence_quote: Hill coefficient ( h ) of 2.8 (95% confidence interval = 2.4–3.2
findings.confidence: high for reported fit; one locus, one enhancer-promoter pair in mouse stem cells

findings.claim: S9 Hypersensitivity across domain boundaries. Formal: with r = contact ratio inside/outside a boundary and R = expression ratio, linear model predicts R <= r. VALIDATION FAIL: r < 2 but R about 10. Authors propose a futile-cycle model with bistability. In repo: not found. Falsifier: same Zuin dataset - compare expression ratio to contact ratio across the boundary.
findings.evidence_quote: usually less than 2-fold, even though disruptions of TAD borders can change gene expression by 10-fold
findings.confidence: medium: a summary of other experiments stated in a modelling paper's abstract, not one dataset

findings.claim: S10 Transcription decreases monotonically with enhancer distance. Formal: d1 < d2 implies T(d1) >= T(d2) for the same enhancer-gene pair, other things equal; cohesin needed only for distant, not proximal, activation. In repo: not found. Falsifier: Zuin mobilisation lines - Spearman of expression vs genomic distance inside the domain must be negative.
findings.evidence_quote: gene transcription levels and activity over time reduce with increased enhancer distance

findings.claim: S11 Enhancer-promoter contacts and transcription are robust to acute (3 h) loss of loop-forming proteins. Formal: change in E-P contact and in nascent transcription is about 0 for most genes after depletion; so domain-level structure is not the contact term that matters. Tension with S8/S9, which say small contact changes can matter. In repo: not found. Falsifier: the paper's Micro-C and nascent-transcript data in mouse stem cells - fraction of genes with significant change.
findings.evidence_quote: E-P) interactions are largely insensitive to acute (3-h) depletion

findings.claim: S12 Activity and contact are not sufficient. Formal: adding promoter class and enhancer-enhancer synergy features improves prediction over A*C; benchmark of 10,411 CRISPR element-gene pairs, >13 million predicted interactions in 352 biosamples. Also the thermodynamic background assumption: expression proportional to equilibrium probability that polymerase is bound (Bintu 2005), which is the origin of the saturating form. In repo: Thermo class covers the saturating form; the feature claim not found. Falsifier: the ENCODE-rE2G benchmark - ablate the two features; no AUPRC drop would falsify.
findings.evidence_quote: additional features guide enhancer-promoter communication including promoter class and enhancer-enhancer synergy
findings.confidence: medium: preprint abstract only; no ablation numbers read

key_claims: Linear contact-to-transcription fails: fitted Hill exponent 2.8 (CI 2.4-3.2), not 1 (Zuin 2022)
Strict multiplicative / zero-selectivity fails: R2 0.82 and more than half of elements selective; approximate multiplicativity holds
ABC product beats either factor alone: AUPRC 0.65 vs 0.22 and 0.29 (Fulco 2019)
Distance^-1 is as good a contact proxy as Hi-C: AUPRC 0.64 vs 0.65
Repo already has the rank-order theorem and model classes in tracks/research; nothing on this topic in lean/ or tracks/lean; ABC normalisation and Hill contact law are the gaps
lay_summary: Genes have on-switches called promoters and far-away helper switches called enhancers that turn the gene up.
One simple idea says the gene's output is just the enhancer's strength times the promoter's strength; real measurements show that this is mostly right but not exactly.
Another idea says an enhancer matters in proportion to how strong it is times how often it touches the gene, and that rule does predict real experiments better than either part alone.
But touching does not work like a dimmer: one careful experiment shows it works more like a step, where a small drop in touching can switch the help almost off.
So we found two rules that passed their checks and three simple versions that failed, which tells us which maths to write down next.

glossary.enhancer: A stretch of DNA that raises the activity of a gene, often from far away.
glossary.promoter: The stretch of DNA at the start of a gene where reading of the gene begins.
glossary.multiplicative model: Output equals enhancer strength times promoter strength.
glossary.saturating model: Output rises with input but levels off at a ceiling.
glossary.rank order: The ordering of items from weakest to strongest.
glossary.rank reversal: Two promoters disagreeing on which of two enhancers is stronger.
glossary.contact frequency / contact probability: How often two pieces of DNA are physically close in the cell.
glossary.ABC (activity-by-contact): A score: enhancer activity times contact, divided by the total of that for all nearby elements of the gene.
glossary.Hi-C, Micro-C, Capture-C: Lab methods that measure which pieces of DNA are near each other.
glossary.DHS and H3K27ac: Two lab signals that mark open, active DNA.
glossary.CRISPRi: A method that switches off a chosen piece of DNA to see what changes.
glossary.Hill function / Hill coefficient: An S-shaped curve; the coefficient says how steep the step is (1 means no step).
glossary.AUPRC: A 0-to-1 score of how well a predictor finds true cases without false alarms.
glossary.Spearman correlation: A -1 to 1 measure of whether two lists are in the same order.
glossary.R2: Fraction of the variation in the data that a model explains (1 is perfect).
glossary.TAD / domain boundary: A neighbourhood of DNA that mostly touches itself, and its edge.
glossary.CTCF, cohesin: Proteins that fold DNA into loops and neighbourhoods.
glossary.housekeeping gene: A gene that is on in nearly all cells.
glossary.on rate (k_on): How often a gene switches from off to on.
glossary.reporter assay / STARR-seq: A test where DNA pieces are put next to a readout gene to measure their strength.
glossary.thermodynamic model: A model where gene output follows the chance that the reading machine is bound to the promoter.
glossary.K562: A widely used human blood-cancer cell line.
glossary.fold change: How many times bigger or smaller one value is than another.

fleet.label: hv-mol-evo-popgen
fleet.topic: Population-genetic statements usable as axioms: fixation probability, neutral substitution rate, mutation-selection balance, drift barrier, Haldane cost
fleet.summary:
Ten statements harvested and formalised; two checked against reported numbers. Only 5 of the 10 primary sources were opened (PubMed records, mostly abstracts) in the 7-minute budget; the classical formulas for the other 5 are from memory and are marked so.

Validation 1 (neutral clock, k = mu) FAILS by about 2x under naive assumptions: the pedigree mutation rate 1.20e-8 with ~35 million human-chimpanzee single-nucleotide changes gives a split of 13.0 Myr (generation 25 yr) or 15.5 Myr (29.7 yr), against fossils of 6-7 Myr. The genome length (2.8e9 bp) and generation times are my assumptions, not opened values, and ancestral polymorphism is ignored, so treat this as a real but soft failure.

Validation 2 (Haldane cost) PASSES as a consistency check: a limit of 1 selective substitution per 300 generations allows about 867 adaptive substitutions per lineage in 260,000 generations, against about 17.5 million observed, so at most ~5e-5 of them can be adaptive. The chimpanzee genome abstract independently says fixation is dominated by neutral and slightly deleterious alleles. The 300-generation figure is from memory.

Registry coverage: lean/Delphi/Kimura.lean already has neutral fixation probability (wrightFisher_fixation_one) and the neutral substitution rate (neutral_substitution_rate, _diploid, _tendsto); lean/Delphi/Favored.lean has a lower bound for favoured alleles (wrightFisherSelection_fixation_one_ge) but not Kimura's closed form or Haldane's 2s. A grep for drift barrier, mutation-selection balance, mutational/substitution load, cost of selection, nearly neutral and fixation time found only 4 hits (lean/Delphi/Genotype.lean x2, lean/assessment/inputs.json, lean/assessment/prompts/kimura-substitution-rate.md), which I did not open; no law for these exists in Kimura.lean, Favored.lean or the registry proposals (kimura-heterozygosity, maynardsmith-hitchhiking). tracks/research mentions fixation/Kimura mainly in t6-flyingfish-law.json and t2-patterns-law.json.

Script: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-mol-evo-popgen/validate.py. Nothing was written to the repo. No held-out clade data were used.

findings.claim: S1 Neutral fixation probability. Formal: in a Wright-Fisher population of N diploids, a new neutral mutation (1 copy of 2N) fixes with probability 1/(2N). Assumptions: neutrality, constant N, random mating. Registry: ALREADY PRESENT (lean/Delphi/Kimura.lean, wrightFisher_fixation_one, fixationProbability_eq). Falsifier: experimental-evolution barcode lineage data (e.g. Levy et al. 2015 yeast barcodes): fraction of neutral barcodes reaching fixation must equal starting frequency within binomial error.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/47.6.713 (Kimura 1962; PubMed record opened, no abstract available, formula from memory)
findings.confidence: high for the maths; source text itself not read (PubMed has no abstract)

findings.claim: S2 Fixation probability under selection (Kimura 1962). Formal: u(p) = (1 - exp(-4 Ne s p)) / (1 - exp(-4 Ne s)) for genic selection, initial frequency p; for p = 1/(2N), Ne = N, small s > 0: u ~ 2s (Haldane 1927). Assumptions: diffusion limit, additive selection, constant Ne. Registry: PARTIAL - Favored.lean proves only a lower bound (wrightFisherSelection_fixation_one_ge, fixationProbability_ge); the closed form and the 2s limit are absent. Falsifier: Lenski LTEE / barcode-lineage establishment data: establishment probability of a mutation with measured s must be within a factor ~2 of 2s.
findings.confidence: medium: formula recalled from memory; PubMed record has no abstract and full text was not opened

findings.claim: S3 Neutral substitution rate equals mutation rate. Formal: k = 2N * mu * 1/(2N) = mu per site per generation, independent of N. Assumptions: strict neutrality, constant mu. Registry: ALREADY PRESENT (Kimura.lean neutral_substitution_rate, neutral_substitution_rate_diploid, neutral_substitution_rate_tendsto; assessment prompt kimura-substitution-rate.md). Falsifier: pedigree mutation rate (trio sequencing) vs divergence/(2 x split time in generations) for a fossil-dated species pair; ratio must be ~1.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/217624a0 (Kimura 1968; PubMed record opened, no abstract)
findings.confidence: high for the statement; original text not read

findings.claim: VALIDATION 1 of S3 - FAIL (soft, ~2x). Prediction: split time T = d * g / (2 mu). Inputs: mu = 1.20e-8 (opened), ~35 million single-nucleotide changes (opened), aligned length 2.8e9 bp (ASSUMED), g = 25 or 29.7 yr (ASSUMED). Result: d = 0.0125; T = 13.0 Myr (g=25) or 15.5 Myr (g=29.7). Measured: fossils attributed to the human lineage at 6-7 Myr. Ratio 2.0-2.4. Ancestral polymorphism and a slower ancestral per-year rate are not modelled; Langergraber et al. themselves get 'at least 7-8' Myr.
findings.evidence_quote: average de novo mutation rate is 1.20 × 10(-8) per nucleotide per generation
findings.value: predicted 13.0-15.5 Myr vs fossil 6-7 Myr: FAIL by ~2x
findings.confidence: medium: two inputs (genome length, generation time) are assumptions, not opened values; the published 1.23% divergence figure could not be opened (paywall redirect)

findings.claim: S4 Haldane's cost of selection. Formal: total selective deaths per substitution C ~ -2 ln(p0) x N (about 30N for typical p0); with a tolerable selection intensity of ~0.1 per generation, adaptive substitutions occur at most ~1 per 300 generations per lineage. Assumptions: independent loci, hard selection, constant N. Registry: ABSENT (no 'cost of selection' or 'substitution load' law; Favored.lean has an expectedSubstitutions budget definition only). Falsifier: McDonald-Kreitman adaptive substitution counts (e.g. Drosophila DGRP / PopFly alpha estimates): adaptive substitutions per generation per lineage must not exceed 1/300.
findings.source: Haldane 1957, J. Genet. 55:511-524 (NOT opened; no DOI given because I could not verify one)
findings.confidence: low-medium: figures from memory, primary source not opened

findings.claim: VALIDATION 2 of S4 - PASS (consistency check). With a 6.5 Myr split and g = 25 yr (both assumed mid-values) there are 260,000 generations per lineage; Haldane's limit allows ~867 adaptive substitutions; observed ~17.5 million substitutions per lineage (half of ~35 million) = 67 per generation. So at most 5e-5 of substitutions can be adaptive; the rest must be non-selective. The genome paper's own conclusion agrees. Neutral expectation mu*L = 33.6 per generation vs 67 observed (the same 2x gap as Validation 1).
findings.evidence_quote: dominated by the fixation of neutral and slightly deleterious alleles
findings.value: Haldane max 867 adaptive vs 1.75e7 observed total; max adaptive fraction 4.95e-5: consistent
findings.confidence: medium: a consistency check, not a strict falsification test; the 300-generation limit is from memory

findings.claim: S5 Drift-barrier hypothesis. Formal: selection lowers the per-site mutation rate u until the selective advantage of a further reduction is below ~1/(2Ne) (diploid) or 1/Ne (haploid); hence across species u * Ge (Ge = coding genome size) scales negatively with Ne (log-log slope < 0). Assumptions: mutation-rate modifiers are mostly deleterious-load reducing; Ne estimated from silent diversity pi = 4 Ne u. Registry: ABSENT. Falsifier: mutation-accumulation rate table in Lynch et al. 2016 (Nat Rev Genet) supplementary: regression of log(u*Ge) on log(Ne) must have negative slope; a zero or positive slope falsifies. Note the circularity risk: Ne is derived from pi/u.
findings.evidence_quote: scales negatively with both the effective population size
findings.confidence: high that the source states this; not numerically validated here (could not open a per-species table in time)

findings.claim: S6 Drift barrier limits molecular refinement generally. Formal: a trait improvement with selective advantage s is unreachable by selection when |s| < 1/(2Ne); replication fidelity is the worked case. Assumptions as S5. Registry: ABSENT. Falsifier: same Lynch 2016 table; also error-prone polymerase fidelity vs number of nucleotides replicated per generation.
findings.evidence_quote: ultimate limits to what can be achieved set by the power of random genetic drift
findings.confidence: high for the qualitative statement; the 1/(2Ne) threshold is the standard form, not quoted from the abstract

findings.claim: S7 Mutation-selection balance. Formal: equilibrium frequency of a deleterious allele: q = mu/(h s) if partially dominant (h s >> mu); q = sqrt(mu/s) if fully recessive; for a dominant lethal, incidence at birth = 2 mu. Assumptions: infinite population, random mating, constant mu and s. Registry: ABSENT as a law (grep hits only in Genotype.lean and assessment inputs, not opened). Falsifier: gnomAD constraint table: for haploinsufficient lethal genes, summed loss-of-function allele frequency must be ~ mu_LoF/(h s); or birth incidence of a fully penetrant dominant disorder must equal 2 x per-gene mutation rate from trio data.
findings.confidence: medium: textbook result stated from memory; primary source not opened

findings.claim: S8 Haldane-Muller mutational load principle. Formal: at mutation-selection balance mean fitness is reduced by L = 1 - exp(-U) (multiplicative loci, U = genomic deleterious mutation rate per diploid genome per generation), independent of the selection coefficients. Assumptions: no epistasis, equilibrium. Registry: ABSENT. Falsifier: human trio data (Kong 2012: 1.20e-8 x 2 x 3e9 ~ 70 new mutations per birth) times the constrained fraction of the genome gives U; if U > ~2 the predicted load > 86% conflicts with observed viability unless epistasis/soft selection holds.
findings.source: Haldane 1937, Am. Nat. 71:337 (NOT opened); mutation count from https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11396
findings.confidence: medium: from memory; primary source not opened

findings.claim: S9 Nearly neutral theory (Ohta 1973). Formal: mutations with |Ne s| < ~1 behave as neutral; therefore the ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rate (dN/dS) decreases as Ne increases. Assumptions: most nonsynonymous mutations are slightly deleterious; fixed DFE across species. Registry: ABSENT ('nearly neutral' not found as a law). Falsifier: cross-species dN/dS vs silent diversity pi_S (Ne proxy) in a public comparative set (e.g. Galtier 2016 PLoS Genet animal transcriptomes): Spearman correlation must be negative.
findings.source: Ohta 1973, Nature 246:96 (PubMed title search returned nothing; NOT opened). Indirect support opened: https://doi.org/10.1038/nature04072
findings.evidence_quote: dominated by the fixation of neutral and slightly deleterious alleles

findings.claim: S10 Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutation. Formal: conditional on fixation, a new neutral mutation takes on average 4 Ne generations to fix. Assumptions: diffusion limit, constant Ne. Registry: ABSENT ('fixation time' not found). Falsifier: coalescent depth in resequencing data: mean TMRCA of autosomal neutral loci must be ~4 Ne generations with Ne from pi/(4 mu); e.g. 1000 Genomes pi with trio mu.
findings.source: Kimura & Ohta 1969, Genetics 61:763 (PubMed title search returned nothing; NOT opened)
findings.confidence: medium: from memory; primary source not opened

findings.claim: S11 Paternal-age dependence breaks the constant-mu assumption behind S3. Formal: mu per generation is not constant; de novo count rises ~2 per year of father's age, so k = mu holds per generation only at fixed generation time. This is a marked assumption for any Lean statement of the molecular clock in years.
findings.evidence_quote: The effect is an increase of about two mutations per year
findings.value: +~2 mutations per paternal year; doubling every 16.5 years

key_claims: Already in the Lean registry: neutral fixation probability 1/(2N) and neutral substitution rate k = mu (lean/Delphi/Kimura.lean); a lower bound only for favoured alleles (lean/Delphi/Favored.lean).

Not in the registry as laws: Kimura's closed-form fixation probability and the 2s limit, Haldane's cost of selection, mutation-selection balance, mutational load, drift barrier, nearly neutral dN/dS-Ne relation, 4Ne fixation time.
Validation 1: k = mu with the pedigree rate predicts a human-chimpanzee split of 13.0-15.5 Myr versus fossils at 6-7 Myr - fails by about 2x under naive assumptions.

Validation 2: Haldane's limit allows ~867 adaptive substitutions per lineage versus ~17.5 million observed - consistent only if almost all substitutions are neutral, which the genome paper also concludes.
Five of ten primary sources were not opened; their formulas are from memory and flagged.

lay_summary: Every living thing copies its DNA with small mistakes, and scientists have simple maths rules for what happens to those mistakes over time.
We collected ten of these rules, such as how likely a new mistake is to spread to everyone, and checked which ones the project has already proved by computer.

We tested one rule that says harmless changes should pile up at the same speed as mistakes happen; using real human numbers it predicted humans and chimpanzees split about 13 million years ago, but fossils say 6 to 7 million, so the simple version of the rule is off by about two times.

We tested a second rule that says helpful changes can only spread slowly; it fits the data only if nearly all the DNA differences between humans and chimpanzees are harmless ones, which is what the genome scientists also concluded.
Some of the old original papers could not be opened in the time allowed, so those rules are written from memory and need checking.

glossary.fixation: when a new gene version spreads until every individual in the population has it
glossary.fixation probability: the chance that a new gene version eventually reaches everyone
glossary.neutral mutation: a DNA change that neither helps nor harms its carrier
glossary.mutation rate (mu): how often a DNA letter is copied wrongly, per letter per generation
glossary.substitution rate (k): how fast DNA differences become permanent in a whole species
glossary.N and Ne (effective population size): the number of breeding individuals, adjusted so the maths of chance works as in an ideal population
glossary.selection coefficient (s): how much a gene version raises or lowers the number of offspring, as a fraction
glossary.dominance (h): how much of a gene version's effect shows when only one copy is carried
glossary.genetic drift: random change in how common a gene version is, caused by chance in who has offspring
glossary.Wright-Fisher model: a simple idealised population where each generation is a random draw from the previous one
glossary.diffusion limit: a maths shortcut that treats gene frequencies as changing smoothly in a large population
glossary.mutation-selection balance: the steady level of a harmful gene version, where new mistakes arrive as fast as selection removes them
glossary.mutational load: the drop in average fitness of a population caused by harmful mutations
glossary.Haldane's cost of selection: the number of deaths or failed births needed to replace one gene version by a better one, which limits how fast helpful changes can spread
glossary.drift barrier: the point where an improvement is so small that chance overwhelms selection, so it cannot be perfected further
glossary.nearly neutral theory: the idea that slightly harmful changes act as harmless in small populations
glossary.dN/dS: the rate of protein-changing DNA changes divided by the rate of silent ones
glossary.divergence (d): the fraction of DNA letters that differ between two species
glossary.generation time (g): the average age of parents when their offspring are born
glossary.pedigree or trio sequencing: reading the DNA of parents and child to count new mutations directly
glossary.ancestral polymorphism: differences that already existed in the ancestor population before two species split
glossary.molecular clock: using the steady build-up of DNA differences to date when species split
glossary.McDonald-Kreitman test: a method comparing differences within and between species to estimate how many changes were helpful
glossary.epistasis: when the effect of one gene change depends on other gene changes
glossary.DFE: distribution of fitness effects, the spread of how helpful or harmful new mutations are
glossary.TMRCA: time back to the most recent common ancestor of a set of gene copies
glossary.pi (nucleotide diversity): the average fraction of DNA letters that differ between two individuals of one species

fleet.label: hv-mol-mechanics
fleet.topic: Molecular and cell mechanics statements: motor force-velocity, actomyosin tension, osmotic/turgor pressure, worm-like chain
fleet.summary:
Partial harvest inside the 7-minute budget. 11 statements are listed: 6 rest on PubMed records I opened (Svoboda & Block 1994, Finer 1994, Gittes 1993, Wang 1997, Bell 1978, Peskin 1993; for the last two only the abstract was opened and the formula is from memory), and 5 are stated from memory with no source opened (Hill 1938, Marko-Siggia, the ATP work bound, van't Hoff/turgor, cortical tension). No files were written, and none of the datasets named for falsification tests was opened.

Registry check: grep of lean/*.lean and lean/*.md finds none of force-velocity, worm-like chain, persistence length, turgor, stall force, kinesin, myosin or actomyosin. Only two neighbours exist: Physiology.laplace_pressure_limit (thin-wall stress, proved with no instance) and Perturb.depth_le_isosmotic (osmolyte depth cap). In tracks/, the terms appear only in tracks/research/buehler-corpus.json, tracks/research/corpus/buehler.json and one workflow script (17 hits, contents not read).

Validations (3 run, by hand arithmetic):
- PASS: persistence length = flexural rigidity / kT. From Gittes' rigidities at an assumed 25 C, actin gives 17.8 um against 17.7 um reported, and microtubules 5350 um against 5200 um (2.9% off, inside the 6.4% stated uncertainty). This is a consistency check within one paper, not an independent test.
- PASS, weak: stall force x step <= free energy of one ATP. Kinesin 5-6 pN x 8 nm = 40-48 pN nm; myosin 3-4 pN x 11 nm = 33-44 pN nm; both below roughly 80-100 pN nm. The 8 nm step and the ATP free energy are from memory, not from an opened source.
- FAIL / mixed: 'DNA persistence length is 50 nm'. Wang 1997 reports about 47 nm in 10 mM Na+ (6% low) and about 40 nm with multivalent ions (20% low). The constant is buffer-dependent; a law must carry ionic strength as a parameter.
- FAIL of generalisation (read from an abstract, no calculation): Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve does not carry over to single kinesin, where velocity falls linearly with load.

Three PMIDs I guessed (Visscher 1999, Dogterom & Yanagida 1997, Schnitzer & Block 1997) and one for Deng 2011 resolved to unrelated papers, so those sources are unverified and listed in could_not_find. The holdout clade was not used or named.

findings.claim: S1 Kinesin force-velocity is linear with a stall near 5-6 pN. Formal: v(F) = v0 (1 - F/Fs), 0<=F<=Fs, Fs in [5,6] pN (single molecule, in vitro, bead assay). Registry: absent. Falsifier: digitised single-kinesin force-velocity curves (force-clamp data, e.g. Visscher 1999 figures; dataset not opened); fit linear vs Hill-hyperbolic and reject if the hyperbolic fit wins by AIC > 10 or the fitted Fs falls outside 4-8 pN.
findings.evidence_quote: Velocity decreased linearly with increasing force
findings.confidence: high for the 1994 abstract; later force-clamp work reports a non-linear curve, not opened

findings.claim: S2 A single myosin II head produces about 11 nm steps at low load and 3-4 pN isometric force. Formal: d = 11 nm (low load), F_iso in [3,4] pN. Registry: absent. Falsifier: later single-molecule myosin step-size reports (not opened; smaller steps near 5 nm are claimed in later literature, from memory); reject if the pooled step-size CI excludes 11 nm.
findings.evidence_quote: single force transients averaging 3-4 pN were measured under isometric conditions

findings.claim: S3 Thermodynamic work bound for a stepping motor: F_stall * d <= DeltaG_ATP (one ATP per step, tight coupling assumed). VALIDATION: kinesin 5-6 pN x 8 nm = 40-48 pN nm; myosin 3-4 pN x 11 nm = 33-44 pN nm; bound about 80-100 pN nm. PASS (implied efficiency below about 0.6). Registry: absent. Falsifier: any motor whose measured stall force times step exceeds DeltaG_ATP at the assay's nucleotide concentrations (a BioNumbers motor table would serve; not opened).
findings.evidence_quote: kinesin molecules moved against applied loads of up to 5-6 pN
findings.value: 40-48 and 33-44 pN nm vs bound ~80-100 pN nm: pass
findings.confidence: medium-low: the 8 nm kinesin step and DeltaG_ATP ~80-100 pN nm are from memory, no source opened; myosin force and step were measured under different load conditions, so their product is only an upper estimate of work

findings.claim: S4 Semiflexible filament: persistence length Lp = EI / (kB T). VALIDATION at assumed T = 298 K (kT = 4.11e-21 J): actin 7.3e-26 / 4.11e-21 = 17.8 um vs 17.7 um reported, PASS; microtubule 2.2e-23 / 4.11e-21 = 5350 um vs 5200 um reported, 2.9% off, inside the 6.4% uncertainty, PASS. Registry: absent. Falsifier: independent flexural-rigidity measurements of the same filaments by a non-thermal method (e.g. hydrodynamic or optical-trap bending); reject if EI/kT disagrees with the thermally measured Lp beyond combined error.
findings.evidence_quote: corresponds to a persistence length of 5,200 microns
findings.value: predicted 17.8 um and 5350 um; reported 17.7 um and 5200 um
findings.confidence: high for the numbers; this is internal consistency within one paper, not an independent test; the assay temperature was assumed, not read

findings.claim: S5 Double-stranded DNA is a worm-like chain with Lp about 50 nm (textbook constant). lay_summary: Inside every cell there are tiny machines that pull and push, and stringy molecules like DNA that act like very thin springs.

I collected eleven rules that scientists use to describe how hard these machines pull and how stiff the strings are, and checked whether this project already has them written down as proofs; it mostly does not.
I tested three rules with real published numbers: a stiffness rule for cell 'bones' matched very well, and a rule saying a motor cannot do more work than its fuel allows also held.
One popular number, the stiffness of DNA, turned out not to be a fixed number: it changes with the salt in the water, so the simple rule fails.
Several papers I wanted could not be opened in the time available, and I say clearly which rules are from memory only.

glossary.motor protein: A tiny protein machine that walks along a track inside a cell using chemical fuel.
glossary.kinesin: A motor protein that walks along microtubules carrying cargo.
glossary.myosin: A motor protein that pulls on actin filaments; it powers muscle.
glossary.actomyosin: Actin filaments together with myosin motors, the cell's pulling machinery.
glossary.ATP: The small molecule cells use as fuel; splitting one releases a fixed packet of energy.
glossary.DeltaG_ATP: The usable energy released by splitting one ATP molecule.
glossary.force-velocity relation: How a motor's speed drops as the load it pulls against grows.
glossary.stall force: The load at which a motor stops moving forward.
glossary.pN (piconewton): A millionth of a millionth of a newton; the size of forces single molecules make.
glossary.nm, um: Nanometre (a billionth of a metre) and micrometre (a millionth of a metre).
glossary.kT: The typical energy of random thermal jiggling at a given temperature, about 4.1 pN nm at room temperature.
glossary.worm-like chain: A model of a molecule as a smoothly bendable rod that thermal jiggling keeps crumpling.
glossary.persistence length (Lp): The distance over which a filament stays roughly straight before thermal bending takes over.
glossary.flexural rigidity (EI): How strongly a rod resists being bent.
glossary.microtubule: A stiff hollow protein tube that acts as a cell's girders and tracks.
glossary.actin filament: A thin, more flexible protein filament in the cell skeleton.
glossary.Hill equation: A hyperbolic formula relating muscle force and shortening speed.
glossary.Bell model: A rule that a molecular bond breaks exponentially faster when pulled harder.
glossary.slip bond / catch bond: A bond that breaks sooner under pull (slip) or, unusually, lasts longer under pull (catch).
glossary.Brownian ratchet: Force made by a growing filament that locks in random thermal movements of the thing it pushes.
glossary.osmotic pressure: Pressure created when water moves toward the side with more dissolved particles.
glossary.van't Hoff relation: Osmotic pressure equals gas constant times temperature times the concentration difference, for dilute solutions.
glossary.turgor pressure: The internal pressure pushing a cell's contents against its wall.
glossary.mOsm: A unit for the concentration of dissolved particles.
glossary.Young-Laplace relation: Pressure difference across a curved stretched surface equals twice the tension divided by the radius, for a sphere.
glossary.cortical tension: The pulling tension in the thin actomyosin layer just under a cell's surface.
glossary.ionic strength: How much dissolved salt (charged particles) a solution holds.
glossary.AIC: A score for comparing how well competing formulas fit data, penalising extra parameters.
glossary.in vitro: Done in a dish or tube, outside a living organism.
glossary.registry: This project's list of laws that have been stated and proved in Lean.
