fleet.label: hv-mol-morphogen
fleet.topic: Morphogen gradient statements: exponential decay length sqrt(D/k), scaling with size, positional-information precision bounds, and measured Bicoid / Dpp / Fgf8 numbers
fleet.summary:
Harvested 10 statements, 5 with numbers read from full text (the two Gregor 2007 Cell papers on PMC) and 5 from PubMed abstracts only. Based on articles retrieved from PubMed; DOI links are in citations.

Validation: 4 arithmetic checks against the Gregor 2007 reported values.
- FAIL: decay length = sqrt(D*tau). With lambda ~100 um and FRAP D = 0.30 um^2/s the implied lifetime is 33,333 s (9.3 h), against a gradient established in under 90 min. This is about 6x off and is the known Bicoid diffusion paradox.
- PASS: reaching lambda ~100 um in 90 min needs D of about 1.85 um^2/s; the paper says D must be far above 2.
- PASS: neighbour discrimination. Delta x / lambda = 8/100 = 8%, against the paper's ~10%.
- PASS on arithmetic, FAIL on biology: the Berg-Purcell averaging time comes out at 6,944 s against the paper's ~7,000 s, but that is nearly two hours, longer than the time available, so a single nucleus averaging over time cannot reach 10%.

Registry: none of the 10 statements is in the law registry. Grep of lean/ and tracks/lean finds morphogen only in the two Turing laws (turing-ddi, turing-wavelength). tracks/research mentions morphogens in corpus and agent files, with no decay-length law; 'decay length' / Gregor / Kicheva hit only tracks/research/agents/q1-mechanisms.json, which I did not open.

Lean: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-mol-morphogen/MorphogenGradient.lean has 5 theorems (profile slope, position-independent fold change, lifetime from length, Berg-Purcell time, scaling invariance). It reached ALL CHECKED on the second of two runs, with no sorry. The first run failed with an olean read error on a Mathlib file, not an error in my file. The captured output was cut to the last lines, so the axiom lists show for only two theorems; the counter reports 5/5 axiom lines.

Not done:
- No dataset was downloaded; the falsification tests are named but not run.
- Shh: no number harvested.
- Fgf8 and Dpp: no numeric D, k or lambda, because the abstracts carry none and I did not open the full texts.
- One neural-tube gradient-decoding paper was excluded because its abstract uses a held-out-clade species.
- Houchmandzadeh 2002 could not be located (my PMID guess was wrong).

findings.claim: S1 Exponential profile. Formal: steady state of dc/dt = D c'' - k c with a source at x=0 is c(x) = c0*exp(-x/lambda), lambda = sqrt(D/k) = sqrt(D*tau). Assumptions: 1-D, uniform D and k, steady state, linear degradation. Measured Bicoid lambda ~100 um. Registry: not present. Falsifier: FlyEx (urchin.spbcas.ru/flyex) Bcd intensity profiles; fit log c vs x, reject if residuals are systematically curved or lambda differs from sqrt(D*tau) using independently measured D and tau.
findings.evidence_quote: The observed concentration profiles have λ ~ 100 μm.
findings.confidence: high for the number (read in full text via fetch summary); FlyEx dataset named from memory, not opened

findings.claim: S2 VALIDATION (FAIL). Prediction from S1: tau = lambda^2/D. With lambda = 100 um and FRAP D = 0.30 um^2/s, tau = 10000/0.30 = 33,333 s = 9.3 h. Measured: gradient established in ~1 h (under 90 min). Predicted time is about 6x too long, so simple diffusion-degradation with the FRAP D fails. Registry: not present.
findings.value: predicted 33,333 s vs observed < 5,400 s: FAIL
findings.evidence_quote: the gradient would never reach steady-state with our measured small diffusion constant
findings.confidence: high; arithmetic is mine, inputs are the paper's reported values

findings.claim: S3 VALIDATION (PASS, consistency). Inverse of S2: to reach lambda = 100 um within t = 90 min needs D >= lambda^2/t = 10000/5400 = 1.85 um^2/s. Paper states the requirement as D much greater than 2 um^2/s, an order above the measured 0.30 +/- 0.09.
findings.evidence_quote: a cytoplasmic diffusion constant D = 0.30±0.09 μm2/s
findings.confidence: medium-high; the 'D >> 2' wording comes from the fetch tool's summary of the full text, not a verbatim quote I saw

findings.claim: S4 Competing D by FCS. Bicoid-EGFP diffusion coefficient ~7 um^2/s in cytoplasm during cycles 12-14, large enough for diffusion alone to set up the gradient. Formal: D_FCS >= lambda^2/t_establish. With S3's threshold 1.85 um^2/s, 7 > 1.85 so S1 is rescued if the FCS D is the right one. Registry: not present. Falsifier: repeat FRAP vs FCS on the same Bcd-GFP line; reject if long-range effective D stays under 2 um^2/s.
findings.evidence_quote: with a diffusion coefficient approximately 7 microm(2)/s
findings.confidence: high for the abstract value; full text not opened

findings.claim: S5 VALIDATION (PASS). Neighbour discrimination: for an exponential profile, the fractional concentration difference between nuclei Delta x apart is Delta c / c = Delta x / lambda (small Delta x). Prediction: 8 um / 100 um = 8%. Reported: ~10%. Registry: not present. Falsifier: FlyEx or Gregor-lab Bcd-GFP nuclear intensities; reject if the measured embryo-to-embryo noise at mid-embryo exceeds Delta x / lambda.
findings.value: predicted 8% vs reported ~10%: PASS (same order, within rounding of '~')
findings.evidence_quote: all of these quantities are approximately 10%
findings.confidence: high; 8 um spacing and 100 um length constant read from full text via fetch summary

findings.claim: S6 VALIDATION (arithmetic PASS, biology FAIL). Berg-Purcell limit: delta c / c ~ 1/sqrt(D*a*c*T). With D = 1 um^2/s, a = 3 nm = 0.003 um, c = 4.8 molecules/um^3 and target 0.1: T = 100/(1*0.003*4.8) = 6,944 s. Paper: about 7,000 s, nearly two hours, which exceeds the available time; so one nucleus time-averaging alone cannot reach 10%. Registry: not present. Falsifier: live hunchback transcription readouts (MS2); reject if single-nucleus readout noise reaches 10% in a window far shorter than D*a*c allows without spatial averaging.
findings.evidence_quote: approaching the limits set by basic physical principles
findings.confidence: high for inputs (full text summary); the quote is from the abstract

findings.claim: S7 Positional information in bits. Formal: I(g; x) = mutual information between gap-gene expression g and position x; reported nearly 2 bits per gene, and four gap genes give positional error sigma_x ~1% of egg length, roughly constant along the axis. Assumption: Gaussian noise approximation for the decoder. Registry: not present. Falsifier: the Dubuis/Petkova gap-gene profile data set (Princeton Gregor lab release); recompute sigma_x(x) = sqrt of inverse Fisher information, reject if above ~1 nuclear spacing (about 1.5-2% EL) over most of the axis.
findings.value: ~2 bits per gene; error ~1% egg length
findings.evidence_quote: Individual genes carry nearly two bits of information
findings.confidence: high for abstract values; the abstract text reads 'error bar of ~1' with the percent sign dropped, I read it as 1% EL; dataset location not opened

findings.claim: S8 Scaling across species. Formal: lambda / L = constant across related fly species with different egg length L, while effective D is essentially the same; under S1 this forces tau proportional to L^2 (lifetime adaptation). Registry: not present. Falsifier: Bcd profiles in species of different egg size (data in the paper's figures); regress lambda on L, reject if slope of log lambda vs log L is not near 1, or if tau does not scale as L^2.
findings.value: qualitative: D same, pattern scales with L
findings.evidence_quote: effective diffusion constants are essentially the same in closely related dipteran species
findings.confidence: medium; abstract only, no numeric lambda/L opened

findings.claim: S9 Lifetime sets length (direct test of lambda = sqrt(D*tau)). Bicoid lifetime is 50 min before cycle 14 and 15 min during cellularization; the gradient does not reach steady state; artificially shortening lifetime shortens the gradient. Formal: d lambda / d tau > 0, and under S1 lambda2/lambda1 = sqrt(tau2/tau1). Check against S2: tau = 50 min = 3000 s with lambda = 100 um implies D = lambda^2/tau = 3.3 um^2/s, between the FRAP (0.3) and FCS (7) values. Registry: not present. Falsifier: the Dronpa-Bcd perturbation series in the paper; reject if lambda ratio departs from sqrt of lifetime ratio.
findings.value: tau = 50 min then 15 min; implied D = 3.3 um^2/s (my arithmetic)
findings.evidence_quote: changing from 50 min before mitotic cycle 14 to 15 min during cellularization
findings.confidence: high for lifetimes (abstract); implied D is my calculation mixing two papers' numbers

findings.claim: S10 Other morphogens. (a) Fgf8 in zebrafish: gradient forms by free extracellular diffusion plus a receptor-endocytosis sink, so lambda = sqrt(D/k) with k set by uptake; changing uptake changes gradient shape. (b) Dpp vs Wingless in the fly wing disc: four kinetic parameters (production, effective D, degradation, immobile fraction) were measured and differ, Dpp range longer. (c) Dpp gradient scales with disc size during growth, lambda proportional to L. Registry: not present. Falsifier: Kicheva 2007 supplementary FRAP parameter table; reject if sqrt(D/k) from FRAP differs from the fitted decay length of the same discs beyond reported error.
findings.value: qualitative only; no numeric D, k, lambda in the abstracts
findings.evidence_quote: Both Dpp concentration and signaling gradients scale with tissue size during development
findings.confidence: medium; abstracts only. I did not open full texts, so I report no numeric D or lambda for Fgf8 or Dpp

findings.claim: Registry check. The law registry has no morphogen decay-length, scaling or positional-precision law. 'morphogen' appears in lean/registry only in turing-ddi and turing-wavelength (two-morphogen reaction-diffusion instability), which is a different statement. tracks/research mentions morphogens in corpus and agent files but no sqrt(D/k) law.
findings.evidence_quote: two-morphogen reaction-diffusion system
findings.confidence: high for lean/ and tracks/lean; tracks/research files were counted by grep, not read

findings.claim: Lean file with 5 theorems checked: profile_deriv (slope of c0*exp(-x/lam) is -(c0/lam)*exp(-x/lam)), fold_change (moving d multiplies concentration by exp(-d/lam) at any x), lifetime_from_length (lam^2 = D*tau implies tau = lam^2/D), berg_purcell_time (eps^2*D*a*c*T = 1 implies T = 1/(D*a*c*eps^2)), scaling_invariance (lam = alpha*L makes the profile at relative position s independent of L).
findings.value: ALL CHECKED on run 2 of 2; run 1 failed on an olean read error
findings.evidence_quote: ALL CHECKED: no errors, no sorryAx
findings.confidence: high; these are the algebraic/calculus skeleton only, not the full PDE steady-state uniqueness

key_claims: The textbook law lambda = sqrt(D*tau) FAILS for Bicoid with the FRAP diffusion constant: predicted 9.3 h to steady state vs under 90 min observed.
The same law is consistent if the FCS value (D ~7 um^2/s) or the measured 50 min lifetime (implied D 3.3 um^2/s) is used; the disagreement is about which D is right.
Neighbour-discrimination precision Delta x/lambda = 8% matches the reported ~10%.
Berg-Purcell averaging time recomputes to 6,944 s, matching the paper's ~7,000 s, and is too long for a single nucleus.
None of these statements is in the DELPHI law registry yet; only Turing two-morphogen laws are.
Lean file MorphogenGradient.lean: 5 theorems, ALL CHECKED, no sorry.
lay_summary: A growing embryo tells its cells where they are by using a chemical that is strong at one end and fades toward the other, like the smell of cooking fading as you walk away from the kitchen.
A simple rule says how far the chemical reaches: it depends on how fast it spreads and how long it lasts before it is broken down.
We checked that rule with real fruit-fly measurements and it failed with one way of measuring the spreading speed: the chemical would need over nine hours, but the embryo does it in about one.
Another check passed: next-door cells see about a one-tenth difference in the chemical, which is just what the fading rule predicts.
We also wrote five small maths facts about the rule and a computer proof-checker confirmed them.

glossary.morphogen: A chemical signal whose amount tells a cell where it is in the embryo.
glossary.gradient: A smooth change in amount from high at one place to low further away.
glossary.decay length (lambda): The distance over which the signal drops to about 37% of its starting value.
glossary.D (diffusion constant): How fast molecules spread out by random motion, in square micrometres per second.
glossary.k (degradation rate) and tau (lifetime): How quickly the molecule is destroyed; tau = 1/k is how long a molecule lasts on average.
glossary.steady state: When the pattern stops changing because supply and loss balance.
glossary.SDD model: Synthesis-diffusion-degradation: made at one end, spreads, and is broken down everywhere.
glossary.Bicoid (Bcd): A fruit-fly morphogen that marks the head-to-tail axis of the early embryo.
glossary.Dpp, Wingless, Fgf8, Shh: Other morphogens, in the fly wing (Dpp, Wingless), zebrafish embryo (Fgf8) and vertebrate tissues (Shh).
glossary.FRAP: Bleach a spot with a laser and time how fast fluorescence returns, to measure spreading speed.
glossary.FCS: Watch flickering of a few fluorescent molecules in a tiny spot to measure how fast they move.
glossary.Berg-Purcell limit: The best accuracy a tiny sensor can reach when counting randomly arriving molecules over a set time.
glossary.positional information: How much a cell can know about its location from the signals it reads.
glossary.bit: A unit of information; one bit is one yes/no answer.
glossary.mutual information: How much knowing one quantity reduces uncertainty about another.
glossary.scaling: The pattern keeping the same proportions when the embryo is bigger or smaller.
glossary.egg length (EL): The length of the embryo, used as the ruler for positions.
glossary.nucleus / nuclear cycle: The compartment holding DNA; early fly embryos double their nuclei in numbered rounds.
glossary.hunchback and gap genes: Genes switched on by Bicoid in broad bands along the embryo.
glossary.Lean / Mathlib: A computer program that checks mathematical proofs, and its library of known maths.
glossary.axiom: A starting assumption a proof is allowed to rely on.
glossary.olean: A compiled library file the Lean checker loads.

fleet.topic: Scaling and allometry statements: Kleiber, surface-area/volume, Murray's law for vessels, limb scaling
fleet.summary:
Harvested 11 scaling statements, validated 4 against the AnAge mammal table, and wrote one Lean file that did NOT check.

**Validation (AnAge, mammals only, n=422, 2.4 g to 3.67 t, plain least squares on log10 values):**

| Statement | Prediction | Measured | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kleiber 3/4 law | slope 0.75 | 0.709, 95% CI [0.694, 0.725] | FAIL |
| Surface law 2/3 | slope 0.667 | same fit | FAIL |
| Curvature (not a pure power law) | upper-half slope > lower-half | 0.791 (se 0.015) vs 0.607 (se 0.027) | PASS |
| Mass-specific rate | slope -0.25 | -0.291 | FAIL (same data as row 1) |

The fit has no body-temperature or phylogeny correction, so the two failures are for the naive pooled form only. White & Seymour reached 2/3 only after those corrections.

**Lean:** `AllometryScaling.lean` has three theorems (Kleiber mass-specific form, cube surface-to-volume, Murray cube law from flow = k r^3 plus conservation), no sorry, no axioms. Both allowed check runs FAILED at `import Mathlib` with "failed to read file ... .olean.private" in the shared Mathlib cache, a different file each time. The first file named exists on disk, so this looks environmental (possibly memory or concurrent use), but that is not confirmed. Nothing is proved.

**Registry coverage:**
- **Kleiber:** no hit for "kleiber" in `lean/registry/laws`, `lean/laws.json`, `lean/LAWS.md`, `tracks/lean` or `tracks/research`.
- **Murray:** found only in `tracks/research` (`t3-lumen-law.json` and two bm-* agents), not in the Lean law registry.
- **Present by filename only (contents not opened):** `elastic-similarity`, `scaling-area-law`, `scaling-strength-law`, `scaling-bending-law`, `flight-allometry-law`, `disc-pectoral-length-allometry`.

**Sources not opened:** Kleiber 1932, Alexander 1979 and Savage 2004 were not found on Europe PMC; Murray 1926 and Stahl 1967 returned a title but no abstract. Findings resting on these are marked low confidence.

Files are in D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-morph-allometry/:
- AllometryScaling.lean
- scripts/fit_anage.py
- dl/anage_data.txt

findings.claim: S1 Kleiber's law: basal metabolic rate B = a*M^(3/4). Formal: exists a>0 such that for all species, log B = log a + 0.75 log M + error, error mean zero. Assumptions: basal conditions, single pooled power law. Registry: NOT present (no 'kleiber' hit in lean registry or tracks). Falsifier: AnAge mammal rows, OLS slope of log10(W) on log10(g); reject if 95% CI excludes 0.75. VALIDATED: FAIL.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1126/science.276.5309.122 (statement of the law, abstract opened via Europe PMC); data https://genomics.senescence.info/species/dataset.zip
findings.value: predicted slope 0.75; measured 0.7091 (se 0.0079, 95% CI 0.6936-0.7246, n=422 mammals)
findings.evidence_quote: including the 3/4 power law for metabolic rates
findings.confidence: medium: the fit is my own naive OLS with no temperature or phylogeny correction; Kleiber's 1932 original was not opened

findings.claim: S2 Surface (geometric) law: mammalian BMR proportional to M^(2/3). Formal: slope b = 2/3 in log B = log a + b log M after correcting for body temperature, digestive state and phylogeny. Registry: not present as a metabolic law. Falsifier: same AnAge fit; reject if CI excludes 0.667. VALIDATED on uncorrected data: FAIL (measured slope lies between 2/3 and 3/4).
findings.evidence_quote: finds no support for a metabolic scaling exponent of 3/4
findings.confidence: medium: my test omits the corrections the paper says are needed, so this fails only the uncorrected form

findings.claim: S3 Curvature: log metabolic rate vs log mass is convex, so no single exponent holds. Formal: d^2(log B)/d(log M)^2 > 0; testable as slope(upper mass half) > slope(lower mass half). Registry: not present. Falsifier: AnAge mammals split at median mass; reject if upper slope <= lower slope. VALIDATED: PASS.
findings.value: lower-half slope 0.6065 (se 0.0267, n=211); upper-half slope 0.7909 (se 0.0151, n=211)
findings.evidence_quote: has convex curvature on a logarithmic scale, and is therefore not a pure power law
findings.confidence: medium-high: difference is about 6 standard errors, but a median split is a crude curvature test

findings.claim: S4 Mass-specific metabolic rate B/M = a*M^(-1/4) (algebraic consequence of S1; M>0). Registry: not present. Falsifier: slope of log(B/M) on log M in AnAge mammals; reject if CI excludes -0.25. VALIDATED: FAIL, same data as S1 so not independent.
findings.confidence: medium: the algebra is written in Lean but the Lean file did not check

findings.claim: S5 Murray's law: at a vessel branch, r0^3 = r1^3 + r2^3. Formal: if flow Q_i = k*r_i^3 with common k != 0 (minimum-work condition) and Q0 = Q1 + Q2, then r0^3 = r1^3 + r2^3. Registry: not in lean registry; 'murray' appears only in tracks/research (t3-lumen-law.json, bm-bioinspired-generative-design, bm-diffusion-kinetics). Falsifier: fit exponent x in r0^x = r1^x + r2^x on measured bifurcation radii; reject if CI excludes 3. Candidate dataset: published coronary arterial tree morphometry tables (not opened, not confirmed open).
findings.evidence_quote: cube of the radius of a parent vessel equals the sum of the cubes
findings.confidence: high for the statement; no dataset opened, so not validated. Murray 1926 (doi 10.1073/pnas.12.3.207) record found, title only, no abstract available

findings.claim: S6 West-Brown-Enquist model: 3/4 scaling follows from a space-filling fractal branching network, minimised energy dissipation and size-invariant terminal tubes. Formal: (space-filling) AND (dissipation minimised) AND (terminal tube size independent of M) implies B proportional to M^(3/4). Registry: not present. Falsifier: capillary dimensions vs body mass across mammals; reject the premise if terminal vessel radius scales with exponent significantly different from 0. Also indirectly failed by the curvature result S3.
findings.evidence_quote: the terminal tubes do not vary with body size
findings.confidence: high for the statement; no dataset opened for the premise test. Kolokotrones 2010 abstract says a vascular-architecture model fails the curvature test

findings.claim: S7 Elastic similarity: length scales as diameter^(2/3) in limbs and trunks. Formal: l = c*d^(2/3); with M proportional to l*d^2 this gives l proportional to M^(1/4), d proportional to M^(3/8). Registry: PRESENT by filename (lean/registry/laws/elastic-similarity.json; contents not opened). Falsifier: regress log bone length on log body mass; reject if CI excludes 0.25.
findings.evidence_quote: lengths increase as the (2/3) power of diameter
findings.confidence: high for the statement; the M^(1/4), M^(3/8) forms are my derivation from it

findings.claim: S8 Biological frequencies (heart rate, breathing rate) scale as M^(-1/4). Formal: f = c*M^(-1/4). Registry: not found. Falsifier: resting heart rate vs body mass across mammal species; reject if slope CI excludes -0.25. No open heart-rate table was opened in the time available.
findings.evidence_quote: biological frequencies are predicted to go inversely as body weight to the (1/4) power
findings.confidence: high for the statement; no dataset identified. Stahl 1967 (doi 10.1152/jappl.1967.22.3.453) record found, title only

findings.claim: S9 Body surface area scales as M^(5/8) under elastic similarity, versus M^(2/3) under geometric similarity. Formal: A = c*M^(0.625). Registry: scaling-area-law.json exists by filename (contents not opened; may be the 2/3 form). Falsifier: measured skin area vs mass; the two predictions differ by 0.042 in slope, so the test needs a standard error below about 0.02.
findings.evidence_quote: total body surface areas should correlate with body weight to the (5/8) power
findings.confidence: high for the statement; no dataset opened

findings.claim: S10 Geometric surface-to-volume law: for similar shapes, area proportional to L^2, volume to L^3, so S/V proportional to 1/L and S proportional to V^(2/3); for a cube S/V = 6/L. Registry: PRESENT by filename (scaling-area-law.json, thompson1917-ch02-* entries; contents not opened). Falsifier: pure geometry given the similarity assumption; the biological test is whether organisms are geometrically similar (see S7, S11).
findings.source: Elementary geometry; the registry attributes related entries to Thompson 1917 (not opened by me)
findings.confidence: high for the mathematics; primary source not opened

findings.claim: S11 Limb bone scaling across land mammals: reported exponents are close to geometric similarity (length about M^0.35) and not elastic similarity (M^0.25). Registry: scaling-bending-law.json and scaling-strength-law.json exist by filename (not opened). Falsifier: regress log limb bone length on log mass; elastic similarity rejected if CI excludes 0.25.
findings.source: Alexander et al. 1979, J. Zool. (doi 10.1111/j.1469-7998.1979.tb03964.x) - NOT OPENED, not found on Europe PMC
findings.confidence: low: the 0.35 figure is from memory and unverified; treat as a lead, not a finding

key_claims: In AnAge mammals (n=422) the pooled metabolic slope is 0.709, 95% CI 0.694-0.725: both 3/4 and 2/3 fall outside the interval on uncorrected data.
The slope rises from 0.61 in the lighter half of species to 0.79 in the heavier half, consistent with the published curvature finding.
Kleiber's law is absent from the Lean law registry and from tracks/lean and tracks/research; Murray's law appears only in tracks/research.
The Lean file did not check: both runs failed reading Mathlib cache files, so nothing is proved.

lay_summary: Bigger animals burn more energy, but not in step with their weight: an animal ten times heavier uses only about five times the energy.
Scientists have argued for a century about the exact rule, with one camp saying the power is three quarters and another saying two thirds.
We checked a public table of 422 mammal species and got a number in between (about 0.71), so on raw data neither tidy rule fits exactly.
The line also bends: small mammals follow a shallower rule than large ones, which matches what a 2010 study reported.
We also wrote three small maths proofs about these rules, but the proof checker could not load its library, so they do not count yet.

glossary.allometry: How a body feature changes as overall body size changes.
glossary.basal metabolic rate (BMR): The energy an animal uses per second while resting and not digesting.
glossary.exponent / power law: A rule of the form y = a times x raised to a fixed power; the power is the exponent.
glossary.slope (on a log-log plot): The exponent of a power law, read off as the steepness of a straight line after taking logarithms.
glossary.OLS (ordinary least squares): The standard way of fitting a straight line through scattered points.
glossary.95% confidence interval (CI): The range in which the true value plausibly lies given the data.
glossary.standard error (se): A measure of how uncertain a fitted number is.
glossary.Kleiber's law: The claim that metabolic rate goes as body mass to the 3/4 power.
glossary.surface law: The claim that metabolic rate goes as body mass to the 2/3 power, like skin area.
glossary.mass-specific rate: Energy use per gram of body.
glossary.convex curvature: The line bends upward instead of staying straight.
glossary.Murray's law: At a fork in a blood vessel, the parent radius cubed equals the sum of the branch radii cubed.
glossary.geometric similarity: Big and small animals having the same shape, just scaled up.
glossary.elastic similarity: The idea that bones and trunks get relatively thicker with size so they bend equally under their own weight.
glossary.space-filling fractal network: A branching system of tubes that repeats the same pattern at smaller sizes and reaches every part of the body.
glossary.phylogeny: The family tree of species; related species are not independent data points.
glossary.Lean / Mathlib: A computer program that checks mathematical proofs, and its standard library.
glossary.olean: A compiled library file that Lean must load before checking a proof.
glossary.falsifier: A test whose outcome could show the statement is wrong.

recommendations: Add Kleiber's law, the 2/3 surface law and the curvature statement to the registry as three competing entries with the AnAge mammal test attached; the naive fit already separates them.
Repeat the fit with body-temperature and phylogenetic correction before recording any final verdict on 2/3 versus 3/4.
Rerun check.sh on AllometryScaling.lean when the machine is quiet; if the 'failed to read file' error persists, inspect the shared Mathlib cache at C:\Temp\delphi-lean-lake.
Promote Murray's law from tracks/research into the Lean registry once a bifurcation radius table is located for the exponent test.
Open Alexander 1979 before using the limb-bone exponent; it is unverified here.

fleet.topic: Fish fin and swimming statements: Strouhal number range, elongated-body theory, fin-ray bilayer bending, glide ratio bounds
fleet.summary:
Harvested 10 statements; 7 rest on abstracts or metadata I opened (PubMed, Crossref), 3 are from memory and listed in could_not_find. Three validations ran against reported numbers. (1) The narrow optimal-efficiency Strouhal band 0.25-0.35 FAILS as a description of real swimmers: only 55% of 248 measured cetacean values fall in it, and the mode sits about 20% lower (0.225-0.275). (2) The broad band 0.2-0.4 passes only at species-mean level, with considerable scatter. (3) Flying-fish glide: steady-glide ceiling h*(L/D) = 13.2 m * 4.7 = 62 m against a simulated 45.4 m, a pass, but a weak one because both numbers come from the same CFD paper. A derived point: the two reported kinematic windows (amplitude/length 0.15-0.25, normalised frequency 1-2) only force St into [0.15, 0.5], so the 0.2-0.4 band is extra information, not a consequence of them.

LEAN: NOT PROVED. One file with four theorems (Strouhal factorisation, Strouhal window, Lighthill thrust sign iff wave speed > swim speed, glide range bound) was written at D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-morph-fin-locomotion/FinLocomotion.lean. Both permitted check runs FAILED at line 1 (import Mathlib) with 'failed to read file ... .olean.private', a different Mathlib file each time; the first named file exists on disk, so this looks like an environment or contention fault in the shared Mathlib cache, not a proof error. The proofs themselves were never elaborated, so their correctness is unknown.

Registry overlap (grep only, not read in depth): lift-to-drag is already present (lean/constraints.json lift_to_drag_max; tracks/research/lean/t4-glide-law__MaxLiftToDrag.lean; t4-glide agents). Fin ray appears in tracks/research/agents/pp-fish-biomechanics-morphology.json. Strouhal, elongated-body and Bainbridge terms hit in tracks/research (t4-glide and pp-fish agent files) but I did not confirm any Lean law for Strouhal or Lighthill thrust in lean/ or tracks/lean; treat those as probably new. No file was written to the repo. Based on articles retrieved from PubMed; DOIs are given per finding.

findings.claim: S1 Strouhal band. Formal: St := f*A/U; for cruising lift-based swimmers 0.2 < St < 0.4 (assumption: steady cruise, oscillatory lift-based propulsion). Registry: Strouhal term found in tracks/research agent files, no Lean law confirmed. Falsifier: per-species f, A, U table in Rohr and Fish 2004 (JEB, open); test = fraction of species means outside [0.2,0.4] > 0. VALIDATED: prediction species means in [0.2,0.4]; measured: each species average within range (6 cetacean species, 248 values) -> PASS at mean level, with considerable individual scatter.
findings.evidence_quote: usually peaks within the interval 0.2 < St < 0.4
findings.confidence: high for the statement (abstract opened); validation uses the Rohr and Fish abstract only, not the table

findings.claim: S2 Narrow efficiency optimum. Formal: St in [0.25, 0.35] at maximum propulsive efficiency (oscillating-foil prediction, attributed to Triantafyllou et al. 1993). Registry: not found. Falsifier: same cetacean table; test = share of observations inside [0.25,0.35]. VALIDATED: prediction most values in 0.25-0.35; measured 55% inside, versus 74% in 0.20-0.30 and mode 0.225-0.275 -> FAIL as a tight bound (observed values about 20% lower than predicted).
findings.evidence_quote: between 0.20 and 0.30 (74%) than the 0.25-0.35 (55%) range predicted
findings.confidence: high for the measured shares; the 1993 primary source for the 0.25-0.35 prediction was not opened

findings.claim: S3 Kinematic windows. Formal: k := f*L/U in [1,2] and a := A/L in [0.15,0.25] for toothed cetaceans; then St = a*k (identity) so St in [0.15, 0.5]. This is wider than 0.2-0.4, so the band is not implied by the windows. Registry: not found. Falsifier: same table; test = any animal with k or a outside the window while cruising. Consistency check: midpoint 0.2*1.5 = 0.30, observed mode 0.225-0.275 lies inside [0.15,0.5] -> PASS (weak, necessary only).
findings.evidence_quote: generally restricted from 1 to 2
findings.confidence: high for the windows; the derived interval is my own arithmetic, Lean proof written but unchecked

findings.claim: S4 Elongated-body theory, wave speed. Formal: for a slender fish with body wave h = g(x - V t), mean thrust T = (m/2)*(V^2 - U^2)*g'^2 at the tail (m = added mass per length), so T > 0 iff V > U; recommended V about (5/4)*U for high Froude efficiency. Assumptions: slender body, inviscid, small amplitude. Registry: 'Lighthill'/'elongated' hits in tracks/research only; no Lean law confirmed. Falsifier: any open kinematics table giving body-wave speed V and swim speed U (for example midline kinematics in Dryad swimming datasets); test = any steady swimmer with U/V >= 1. Not validated against data here.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112060001110 (Crossref record opened; abstract seen only as a paraphrase by the fetch tool)
findings.value: V approx 1.25 U; thrust requires V > U
findings.confidence: medium: the 5/4 figure came through a tool paraphrase of the abstract, not a verbatim read; the thrust formula is from my memory of the theory

findings.claim: S5 Fin-ray bilayer stiffness control. Formal: a fin ray is two bending half-rays (hemitrichs) joined along their length; a base offset d between them sets curvature, and effective bending stiffness K(actuated)/K(unactuated) > 10; curvature is concentrated at the base or at the load point. Assumption: linear elasticity. Registry: 'fin ray' appears in tracks/research/agents/pp-fish-biomechanics-morphology.json; no Lean law confirmed. Falsifier: force-displacement curves in the open PMC article (PMC2359861); test = stiffness ratio between actuated and unactuated < 10.
findings.evidence_quote: variation in ray stiffness over more than an order of magnitude
findings.confidence: high for the qualitative bound; exact ratio not read from the full text

findings.claim: S6 Flying-fish glide ratio ceiling. Formal: (L/D)max = 4.7, so minimum steady glide angle = atan(1/4.7) = 12.0 degrees, and steady glide distance x <= h*(L/D)max. Registry: lift_to_drag_max already in lean/constraints.json and tracks/research/lean/t4-glide-law__MaxLiftToDrag.lean (value there not compared). Falsifier: wind-tunnel polar in Park and Choi 2010 (JEB); test = measured L/D max of the fins-spread model exceeds the bound in use. VALIDATED: prediction x <= 13.2 m * 4.7 = 62.0 m; reported glide 45.4 m -> PASS (weak: same CFD paper, and the launch is powered, not a pure steady glide).
findings.evidence_quote: maximum lift-to-drag ratio of 4.7 is achieved
findings.value: L/D max 4.7; CL max 1.03; distance 45.4 m; height 13.2 m
findings.confidence: high for the reported numbers; they are simulation results, not field measurements

findings.claim: S7 Flying-fish polar shape. Formal: argmax over attack angle of L/D is near 0 degrees; argmax of lift coefficient is at 30-35 degrees; L/D rises near the sea surface (ground effect), i.e. L/D(h small) > L/D(h large). Registry: glide content exists in t4-glide agents; these specific angle statements not confirmed there. Falsifier: Park and Choi wind-tunnel tables; test = L/D peak outside about -5..5 degrees, or no L/D gain at small height.
findings.evidence_quote: lift-to-drag ratio was maximum at attack angles of around 0 deg
findings.value: L/D max at about 0 deg; CL max at 30-35 deg
findings.confidence: high for the angles; the abstract gives no L/D number, so I did not quote one

findings.claim: S8 Swimming-number scaling. Formal: with Sw := f*A*L/nu and Re := U*L/nu, Re ~ Sw^(4/3) in the laminar regime and Re ~ Sw in the turbulent regime, which implies St roughly constant (about 0.3) at high Re. Registry: not found. Falsifier: the paper's supplementary table of swimmers (use only non-held-out rows); test = log-log slope of Re on Sw outside 1.0 +/- 0.1 for Re > 1e4.
findings.value: Re ~ Sw^(4/3) laminar; Re ~ Sw turbulent
findings.confidence: low: stated from memory, source not opened this session

findings.claim: S9 Speed proportional to tail-beat frequency. Formal: U/L = (3/4)*(f - 4/3) for f above about 5 Hz, i.e. U = (L/4)*(3f - 4) (dace, trout, goldfish). Registry: 'Bainbridge' hits only in tracks/research agent files. Falsifier: any open f-U-L table for a teleost (for example FishBase swimming-speed table); test = slope of U/L on f differs from 0.75 beyond its confidence interval.
findings.source: Bainbridge 1958, Journal of Experimental Biology 35:109-133 (NOT opened)
findings.confidence: low: from memory, source not opened, coefficients unverified

findings.claim: S10 Optimal Strouhal depends on drag. Formal: the efficiency-optimal St is a function of the drag coefficient and tail aspect, giving a predicted window wider than 0.2-0.4 across animals. Registry: not found. Falsifier: same per-species St tables; test = observed St not ordered by body drag coefficient as predicted.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfluidstructs.2012.02.008 (Crossref metadata opened; no abstract in the record)
findings.confidence: low: only title, author, journal and pages were confirmed; the numeric window is not quoted because I could not read it

key_claims: The narrow 0.25-0.35 Strouhal optimum fails on real cetacean data: only 55% of 248 values fall inside, and the mode is about 20% lower.
The broad 0.2-0.4 Strouhal band holds for species means but not for individual observations.
Amplitude and frequency windows alone only bound St to [0.15, 0.5]; the 0.2-0.4 band is an independent empirical claim.
Flying-fish L/D max of 4.7 gives a minimum steady glide angle of about 12 degrees and a 62 m ceiling from 13.2 m height; the reported 45.4 m is inside it.
The Lean file was written but NOT checked: both check runs failed reading Mathlib build files, so nothing is proved.
lay_summary: A fish pushes itself forward by wagging its tail, and scientists divide how fast and how wide the tail wags by how fast the fish swims to get one number called the Strouhal number.
Many swimming animals keep that number between about 0.2 and 0.4, but when we checked real dolphin and whale measurements, the tighter 'best' range people predicted only fit about half the time.
For a fish to move forward, the wiggle travelling down its body has to go backward faster than the fish goes forward.
Each fin ray is like two thin strips stuck together; sliding one strip against the other makes the ray bend and can make it more than ten times stiffer.

A flying fish gliding in air travels at most about 4.7 metres forward for each metre it drops, and the numbers we found fit that limit. The computer proof file we wrote could not be checked because the proof library failed to load, so it does not count as proved.

glossary.Strouhal number (St): Tail-beat frequency times tail sweep width, divided by swimming speed. A pure number with no units.
glossary.tail-beat frequency (f): How many full tail wags happen each second.
glossary.amplitude (A): How far the tail tip moves side to side in one wag, peak to peak.
glossary.propulsive (Froude) efficiency: The share of the animal's effort that turns into forward motion instead of wasted water movement.
glossary.elongated-body theory: Lighthill's mathematical model of a long thin fish that works out thrust from how the body wave moves.
glossary.body wave speed (V): How fast the wiggle travels backward along the fish's body.
glossary.added mass: The water that has to be pushed aside and so acts like extra weight on the moving body.
glossary.fin ray: One of the thin bony rods that support a fish's fin.
glossary.hemitrich: One of the two half-rods that together make up a fin ray.
glossary.bilayer: Two layers joined together; sliding or stretching one against the other makes the pair bend.
glossary.bending stiffness: How hard something is to bend.
glossary.lift-to-drag ratio (L/D): Upward force divided by slowing force; in a steady glide it equals metres forward per metre dropped.
glossary.glide ratio: Distance travelled forward divided by height lost; equal to L/D in a steady glide.
glossary.glide angle: The downward slope of a glide path.
glossary.angle of attack: The tilt between the body or wing and the oncoming air.
glossary.lift coefficient (CL): A unitless measure of how much lift a wing shape makes.
glossary.ground effect: Extra lift and less drag when gliding very close to a surface such as the sea.
glossary.Reynolds number (Re): Speed times length divided by the fluid's stickiness; tells whether flow is smooth or turbulent.
glossary.swimming number (Sw): Tail frequency times amplitude times body length, divided by the fluid's stickiness.
glossary.laminar / turbulent: Smooth, orderly flow versus messy, swirling flow.
glossary.CFD: Computational fluid dynamics: simulating air or water flow on a computer.
glossary.Lean / Mathlib: A computer program that checks mathematical proofs, and its library of already-proved maths.
glossary.hypothesis (in a proof): An assumption written down by name so the reader can see exactly what the result depends on.
glossary.falsify: To show a statement is wrong by finding data that contradicts it.

fleet.label: hv-morph-lumen-epithelia
fleet.topic: Lumen, tube and epithelial geometry statements (Laplace law, hydraulic lumen coarsening, Kupffer's vesicle, cell packing / Euler rules): harvest, formalize, validate
fleet.summary:
Harvested 10 statements; 8 rest on sources I opened (PubMed abstracts or PMC full text) and 2 (Lewis's law, Aboav-Weaire law) are from memory only and are marked unverified. Three checks were run on fetched numbers.

Validation results:
- Euler mean-six rule: PASS. Fly wing disc counts (N=2172) give a mean of 5.931 sides; a cucumber epidermis sample (N=1000) gives 5.996. Both are within 0.1 of 6.
- Proliferation equilibrium polygon mix: PASS for the fly wing disc (27.9% / 45.7% / 20.1% pentagons / hexagons / heptagons against the quoted approximate 25 / 45 / 20). The pentagon share is about 3 points high, and an onion sample has 41.2% hexagons (marginal). The prediction used is the approximate one quoted in a secondary paper; the exact Markov-model figures in Gibson 2006 were not opened.
- Thin-wall Laplace applicability in the zebrafish inner-ear vesicle: FAIL early, PASS late. Wall thickness over radius is 0.52 at the small stage (20 um wall, 38 um equivalent radius) and 0.069 at the large stage (4 um wall, 58 um radius). The thin-wall formula sigma = PR/2h is therefore not valid early; it gives about 96 Pa early and about 2.2 kPa late. The radii are my equivalent-sphere conversion of reported volumes, and the wall thicknesses are regional values.
- Kupffer's vesicle threshold: consistency only. Wild-type mean lumen area 3127 um^2 is 2.4 times the 1300 um^2 threshold. This is not an independent test.

Registry status: only the Laplace wall-stress law is in the accepted registry (physiology-laplace, lean/Delphi/Physiology.lean). tracks/research holds a proposed lumen-area-ceiling law (t3-lumen-law) and lumen data (t3-lumen-data). Kupffer, Lewis, coarsening and hydraulic terms appear only in tracks/research agent notes, not in lean/ or tracks/lean. Aboav and scutoid appear nowhere.

Files written: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-morph-lumen-epithelia/validate.py and D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-morph-lumen-epithelia/results.json. Nothing in the repo was touched. Literature metadata is from PubMed, with DOI links in the citations.

findings.claim: S1 Euler mean-six rule. Formal: for a planar polygonal tiling with all vertices trivalent, Euler's V-E+F=2 gives mean sides <n> = 6 - 12/F -> 6 as F grows (assumptions: planar sheet, three-cell vertices only, boundary effects negligible). Registry: NOT present in lean/ or tracks/lean (hexagon hits are in tracks/research notes only). Falsifier: any segmented epithelium dataset (e.g. EpiTools wing-disc segmentations, doi 10.1016/j.devcel.2015.12.012); test |mean neighbours - 6| > 0.1 with N > 1000 interior cells and under 1% four-way vertices.
findings.value: VALIDATED: fly wing disc counts 4:64, 5:606, 6:993, 7:437, 8:69, 9:3 (N=2172) -> mean 5.931; cucumber epidermis N=1000 -> mean 5.996. Prediction 6. PASS (tolerance 0.1).
findings.evidence_quote: the average polygonal cell must have exactly six sides in a planar tissue
findings.confidence: high for the arithmetic; counts are as quoted in an opened secondary paper, not re-derived from raw images

findings.claim: S2 Proliferation equilibrium polygon distribution (Gibson et al. 2006). Formal: under a Markov chain on side-number driven by cell division, the side-number distribution converges to a fixed vector p* with roughly 25-29% pentagons, 45-46% hexagons, 20-21% heptagons, independent of the initial condition (assumptions: all cells divide, cleavage plane splits neighbours roughly evenly, no rearrangement or cell loss). Registry: NOT present. Falsifier: polygon histograms from EpiTools or similar; chi-square of observed against p*, reject if hexagon fraction is outside 40-50% in a proliferating simple epithelium with N > 1000.
findings.value: VALIDATED: prediction approx 25/45/20% (5/6/7 sides); measured fly wing disc 27.9/45.7/20.1% (N=2172). PASS on hexagons and heptagons; pentagons about 3 points above the approximate figure. Onion sample 41.2% hexagons (n=500) is marginal (about 1.7 SE below 45%).
findings.evidence_quote: approximately 25% pentagons, 45% hexagons, and 20% heptagons
findings.confidence: medium: the exact Markov-model values in the Nature paper were not opened (paywalled); the approximate prediction is quoted from a secondary source

findings.claim: S3 Laplace law for a pressurised epithelial dome (Latorre et al. 2018). Formal: for a spherical-cap monolayer with radius of curvature R and transmural pressure dP, surface tension sigma = R*dP/2 (assumptions: membrane-like sheet, uniform isotropic tension, static equilibrium). Registry: PRESENT as physiology-laplace (lean/Delphi/Physiology.lean, theorem laplace_pressure_limit) in wall-stress form P r/(2t); the surface-tension form for monolayers is not separately registered. Falsifier: the paper's dome source data (pressure from traction microscopy, R from confocal stacks); test whether sigma computed from 2*sigma = R*dP stays flat (within 30%) between 100% and 300% areal strain.
findings.value: Reported tension about 1 mN/m at small strain, plateau about 2 mN/m up to 300% areal strain. Not numerically validated: no pressure or radius values in the text.
findings.evidence_quote: obeyed Laplace's law 2σ = R Δ P, where Δ P is the transmural pressure
findings.confidence: high for the statement; numeric pressures and radii are only in figures

findings.claim: S4 Thin-shell wall stress in the zebrafish inner-ear (otic) vesicle (Mosaliganti et al. 2019). Formal: sigma = P R / (2 h) for a spherical shell of radius R and wall thickness h (assumption: thin wall, h/R << 1; uniform pressure). Registry: same form as physiology-laplace, PRESENT. Falsifier: the paper's otic vesicle volume, thickness and pressure time series (eLife source data); test whether h/R < 0.1 holds at each stage; where it does not, the thin-wall law must not be applied.
findings.value: VALIDATED (applicability): volume 235 -> 807 pl gives equivalent-sphere R = 38.3 -> 57.8 um; wall 20 -> 4 um; h/R = 0.52 early (FAIL thin-wall), 0.069 late (PASS). sigma = PR/2h gives about 96 Pa at 100 Pa early (not trustworthy) and about 2170 Pa at 300 Pa late.
findings.evidence_quote: the pressure level gradually increases from 100 Pa to upwards of 300 Pa
findings.confidence: medium: R is my equivalent-sphere conversion of reported volume; the 20->4 um thinning is regional (lateral/medial wall), and pairing volumes, thicknesses and pressures by stage is my approximation

findings.claim: S5 Hydraulic negative feedback on lumen growth (Mosaliganti et al. 2019). Formal: dV/dt = J(P) with dJ/dP < 0, and P increasing with wall strain, so a volume perturbation decays back toward the growth trajectory (assumptions: single lumen, flux depends on pressure only). Registry: NOT present in lean/ or tracks/lean. Falsifier: the paper's puncture experiments (source data in eLife); test whether post-puncture growth rate exceeds the unpunctured control rate; no catch-up falsifies it.
findings.evidence_quote: Pressure, in turn, inhibits fluid transport into the lumen
findings.confidence: high for the statement; no numeric test run

findings.claim: S6 Kupffer's vesicle size threshold (Gokey et al. 2016). Formal: P(normal left-right patterning | lumen cross-section area A) is high for A >= A* and falls for A < A*, with A* about 1300 um^2 (bracketed 1300-1700 um^2) at the 8-somite stage; above A* the outcome does not depend on A (assumptions: zebrafish, area measured at the vesicle mid-plane). Registry: NOT present in lean/ or tracks/lean; Kupffer appears in 2 tracks/research files only. Falsifier: the paper's per-embryo table (n=84, lumen area against laterality marker); logistic or step fit; a monotone dose-response with no plateau above 1300 um^2 falsifies the threshold form.
findings.value: Consistency check only: wild-type mean area 3127 um^2 at 8 somites = 2.4 x threshold; cilia mean 52, range 31-88; n=30 (size survey), n=84 (threshold analysis).
findings.evidence_quote: KV must exceed a size threshold of approximately 1300 μm2 for robust LR patterning
findings.confidence: high for the quoted values; the per-embryo table was not fetched

findings.claim: S7 Hydraulic lumen coarsening (Dumortier et al. 2019). Formal: N microlumens connected through the intercellular space, each with Laplace pressure P_i = 2*gamma_i/R_i; fluid flows from high to low P, so small or high-tension lumens shrink and the count N(t) falls monotonically to 1 (Ostwald-ripening analogue); the winner sits where contractility gamma is lowest (assumptions: connected fluid network, conserved or slowly pumped volume). Registry: NOT present in lean/ or tracks/lean (coarsening hits are tracks/research notes). Falsifier: time-lapse of mouse blastocysts from the paper (image data; open deposit not located); test that N(t) is non-increasing and the final lumen sits by the lower-contractility cells in chimeras.
findings.evidence_quote: a process akin to Ostwald ripening, underlying the coarsening of foams
findings.confidence: medium: abstract only; the formal pressure-difference form is the standard model, not checked against the paper's equations

findings.claim: S8 Lumen pressure and cortical tension rise together in the mouse blastocyst (Chan et al. 2019). Formal: by Laplace, T = P R / 2 for the enclosing cell layer, so a twofold rise in P at similar R predicts about a twofold rise in tension; rupture occurs when T exceeds a critical T_c (assumptions: spherical thin shell, quasi-static). Registry: only the generic Laplace law is present. Falsifier: the paper's micropressure-probe and micropipette-aspiration source data; test the tension/pressure ratio against R/2 at each stage.
findings.evidence_quote: there is a twofold increase in lumenal pressure during blastocyst development
findings.confidence: medium: abstract only; absolute pressure values not opened

findings.claim: S9 Hydraulically gated size oscillations (Ruiz-Herrero et al. 2017). Formal: a fluid-permeable shell inflates until wall stress reaches a rupture threshold, leaks, shrinks, reseals and regrows, giving sawtooth R(t) with slow growth and fast collapse; mean size is set by the rupture threshold (assumptions: spherical shell, constant inward pumping). Registry: NOT present in lean/ or tracks/lean. Falsifier: R(t) traces of hollow tissue spheroids or blastocysts; test for asymmetric sawtooth (collapse time much shorter than inflation time); symmetric oscillation or no collapse falsifies.
findings.evidence_quote: shells can relieve internal pressure by bursting intermittently, shrinking and re-growing
findings.confidence: medium: abstract only, no numbers extracted

findings.claim: S10 Scutoids in curved epithelia (Gomez-Galvez et al. 2018). Formal: in a tubular epithelium with basal/apical radius ratio > 1, some cells have different neighbour sets on apical and basal faces (apico-basal intercalation), so the cell is not a prism or frustum; the fraction of such cells rises with the radius ratio (assumption: Voronoi-like packing on both surfaces). Registry: NOT present anywhere in the repo (0 hits). Falsifier: 3D segmentations of fly salivary gland from the paper; test whether the fraction of cells with apical neighbour set different from basal is greater than 0 and increases with curvature.
findings.evidence_quote: forces cells to have different neighbours in their basal and apical surfaces
findings.confidence: medium: abstract only; the monotone dependence on radius ratio is my reading of the model, not a quoted result

findings.claim: S11 (UNVERIFIED, from memory) Lewis's law: mean apical area of n-sided cells is linear in n, A_n/A_mean = (n-2)/4. Aboav-Weaire law: mean side-number of neighbours of an n-sided cell m(n) = 5 + (6+mu2)/n, where mu2 is the variance of n. Registry: Aboav 0 hits; Lewis appears in tracks/research notes only. Falsifier: per-cell area and neighbour tables from EpiTools segmentations; linear regression of A_n on n (Lewis) and of n*m(n) on n (Aboav-Weaire, slope 5).
findings.source: No source opened. Candidate: Kokic et al. 2019, 'Minimisation of surface energy drives apical epithelial organisation and gives rise to Lewis' law' (not found in PubMed search)
findings.value: For a future Aboav-Weaire test, mu2 computed here from the fly counts is 0.738 and from the cucumber counts 0.684.
findings.confidence: low: formulas recalled, not checked against any opened source

findings.claim: Existing repo coverage on this topic: accepted registry has physiology-laplace only; tracks/research has a proposed (not accepted) lumen-area-ceiling law, a = AL/A0 <= (N*la)^2/(4*pi) under the isoperimetric inequality, plus cyst/lumen sphericity data.
findings.evidence_quote: Proposed law `lumen-area-ceiling` (NOT in law set 1.8.1
findings.confidence: high (files read directly); grep was case-insensitive over lean, tracks/lean, tracks/research excluding .lake

key_claims: Euler mean-six rule passes on real counts: 5.931 (fly wing disc, N=2172) and 5.996 (cucumber, N=1000) against a prediction of 6.
Hexagon share in fly wing disc is 45.7% against an approximate prediction of 45%; pentagons 27.9% against about 25%; heptagons 20.1% against about 20%.
Thin-wall Laplace stress formula is not applicable to the early zebrafish inner-ear vesicle (wall/radius about 0.52) but is at the later stage (about 0.069).

Of the harvested statements only the Laplace wall-stress law is in the accepted law registry; mean-six, polygon equilibrium, Kupffer threshold, coarsening, hydraulic feedback, gated oscillations and scutoids are all absent from lean/ and tracks/lean.
Lewis's law and Aboav-Weaire law are listed but unverified (no source opened).
lay_summary: Many body parts start as tiny water-filled balloons made of a single layer of cells, and simple physics rules say how tight the balloon skin gets as the water pressure rises.

We collected ten such rules from published papers, for example that cells in a flat sheet have six neighbours on average, and that a small fluid-filled organ in a fish embryo must be bigger than a certain size to tell left from right.
We checked the six-neighbour rule with real cell counts from a fly wing and a cucumber skin, and it held: the averages were 5.93 and 6.00.
We also checked whether the simple balloon formula can be used for the growing fish ear; it works when the wall is thin but not early on, when the wall is about half as thick as the balloon's radius.
Only one of these rules is already in the project's official list of proven laws, so most of them are new candidates.

glossary.lumen: The fluid-filled space inside a hollow organ or ball of cells.
glossary.epithelium: A sheet of cells stuck side by side, like tiles, that lines or covers organs.
glossary.Laplace law: The rule linking pressure inside a balloon-like shell to the tension in its wall and its radius: bigger radius or pressure means more wall tension.
glossary.thin-wall assumption: Treating the wall as very thin compared with the radius (usually under one tenth); the simple Laplace formula needs this.
glossary.transmural pressure: The pressure difference between the inside and the outside of a wall.
glossary.wall stress: Force per unit area carried inside the wall material.
glossary.surface tension (of a cell sheet): Pulling force per unit length within the sheet, measured in millinewtons per metre.
glossary.Euler's formula: A counting rule for any network drawn on a surface: corners minus edges plus faces equals 2; it forces the six-neighbour average.
glossary.trivalent vertex: A corner where exactly three cells meet.
glossary.polygon distribution: The share of cells with 4, 5, 6, 7 or more sides.
glossary.Markov model: A step-by-step chance model where the next state depends only on the current one.
glossary.Kupffer's vesicle: A small, short-lived fluid-filled ball in the zebrafish embryo whose beating hairs set up left versus right.
glossary.cilia: Tiny hair-like structures on cells that can beat and move fluid.
glossary.left-right patterning: How an embryo decides which organs go on the left and which on the right.
glossary.otic vesicle: The hollow fluid-filled ball that becomes the inner ear.
glossary.blastocyst: An early mammal embryo that is a hollow ball of cells with a fluid cavity.
glossary.microlumen: A very small fluid pocket between two cells.
glossary.coarsening / Ostwald ripening: Many small bubbles or pockets merging into fewer big ones because small ones have higher pressure and drain into large ones.
glossary.hydraulic feedback: Pressure in the fluid slowing down the pumping that created it, which steadies the size.
glossary.hydraulically gated oscillation: Repeated cycle of slow inflation, sudden leak and collapse, then regrowth.
glossary.cortical tension: The tightness of the thin contractile layer just under a cell's surface.
glossary.scutoid: A cell shape whose top and bottom faces touch different sets of neighbours, found in curved cell sheets.
glossary.apical / basal: The two faces of an epithelial cell: apical faces the lumen, basal faces the outside.
glossary.Lewis's law: A rule of thumb that cells with more sides have proportionally larger area.
glossary.Aboav-Weaire law: A rule of thumb that many-sided cells tend to be surrounded by few-sided neighbours.
glossary.isoperimetric inequality: For a given perimeter, a circle encloses the most area.
glossary.mu2: The variance (spread) of the number of sides per cell around six.
glossary.equivalent-sphere radius: The radius a perfect ball would have if it held the same volume.
glossary.falsify: To show a statement is wrong by a test it could have failed.
glossary.law registry: The project's list of accepted, machine-checked laws.

fleet.label: hv-morph-segmentation
fleet.topic: Segmentation and somite statements: clock-and-wavefront (segment length = wavefront speed x clock period) and zebrafish somite numbers
fleet.summary:
Harvested 10 statements on vertebrate segmentation, formalized each, and validated three against numbers fetched in this session; one Lean file passed check.sh on its second run. Sources were PubMed abstracts and the ZFIN staging table, not full texts, so the exact numeric values inside the papers (23.5 min period, hes6 percent change, snake somite count) were NOT opened and are listed in could_not_find.

Registry status: grep for somite / wavefront / "segmentation clock" across lean, tracks/lean and tracks/research found no law for clock-and-wavefront. The only hits are incidental mentions in lean/genotype/dev-certificate.json, the turing-ddi proposal and requirement files, tracks/research/agents/bm-open-hardware-repro.json and tracks/research/doi-resolution.json (I did not open those files to see the context). So all ten statements are new to the registry.

Validation (ZFIN staging table, 28.5 C stage onsets: 1 somite at 10.33 h, 5 at 11.66 h, 10 at 14 h, 14 at 16 h, 20 at 19 h, 26 at 22 h):
- V1, constant clock period (one somite per 30 min throughout): FAIL for the first interval (4 somites in 1.33 h = 3.0 per hour, i.e. a 20 min period), PASS after that (2.14, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0 per hour). A constant-period law holds only from about somite 5-10 onward.
- V2, Lewis 2003 delayed-autoinhibition model, predicted period close to 30 min: PASS against the trunk rate of 2.0 somites per hour (30 min per somite) in the same table. Caveat: the paper itself compared to 30 min, so this is only an independent re-check of the observed value, not a blind test.
- V3, N = D / T for the counted window: from 11.66 h to 22 h (10.34 h) at T = 0.5 h predicts 20.7 somites; the table gives 26 - 5 = 21. PASS (within 2 percent). Stage boundaries are ranges, so precision is about +/- 1 somite.

Qualitative checks from abstracts only (direction, no numbers opened): slowed-clock zebrafish mutant has fewer segments (Schroter & Oates 2010) and Delta-Notch disruption gives longer period and correspondingly longer segments (Herrgen 2010): both agree in sign with S = v*T. Soroldoni 2014 is a stated FAILURE of the naive law: the oscillation period alone does not equal the segmentation period (Doppler contribution from tissue shortening).

Lean: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-morph-segmentation/ClockWavefront.lean, six theorems (segment length and number scaling with period, monotonicity, N = D/T, axis length), standard axioms only. First check run failed with an environment fault ("failed to read file ... CentroidHom.olean", the file exists; probably a concurrent reader); the second run, with the file unchanged, printed ALL CHECKED. These theorems are arithmetic consequences of the model, not evidence that the model is true.

Holdout: one harvested paper (Gomez 2008) compares four species including one from the held-out clade; I used only its snake/zebrafish/mouse statement and no data on the held-out clade. Any future test built on that paper must drop that species.

findings.claim: S1 Clock-and-wavefront core law: segment length S = v * T (v = wavefront speed relative to tissue, T = clock period). Assumptions: v and T constant over one cycle; one boundary per cycle. Registry: absent. Falsifier: per-embryo time-lapse measurements of v, T and S in zebrafish (Herrgen 2010 / Schroter 2008 supplementary tables); fail if S/(v*T) differs from 1 beyond measurement error.
findings.source: Cooke & Zeeman 1976, J Theor Biol, doi:10.1016/S0022-5193(76)80131-2 (NOT opened; statement of the model taken from the Schroter & Oates 2010 abstract, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2010.05.071)
findings.confidence: medium: model form is textbook, primary 1976 paper not opened
findings.evidence_quote: The Clock and Wavefront model for somitogenesis proposes

findings.claim: S2 Total segment number N = D / T, where D is the total duration of presomitic mesoderm growth and T the clock period. Assumption: one segment per cycle, T constant. Registry: absent. Falsifier: ZFIN staging table; fail if somite count over a window differs from window/T by more than 1-2 somites. Validated here (V3): predicted 20.7, table 21, PASS.
findings.value: N = D/T; 10.34 h / 0.5 h = 20.7 vs 21 observed
findings.confidence: high for the statement; validation precision about +/-1 somite
findings.evidence_quote: determined by the period of an oscillator or clock operating in the PSM

findings.claim: S3 Slowing the clock reduces segment number: T' > T with D and axis growth unchanged implies N' < N (N' = N * T/T'). Registry: absent. Falsifier: somite counts in the zebrafish hes6 period mutant versus wild type from the paper's figures; fail if the fractional drop in N does not match the fractional rise in T.
findings.value: direction confirmed; magnitude not in abstract
findings.confidence: high for direction, numbers not opened
findings.evidence_quote: This reduces segment number as predicted

findings.claim: S4 Longer period gives proportionally longer segments: disrupting Delta-Notch coupling raises the somitogenesis period, and segment length and gene-expression wavelength rise correspondingly (S'/S = T'/T at fixed v). Registry: absent. Falsifier: the multiple-embryo time-lapse period and segment-length tables of this paper; fail if the S ratio and T ratio differ beyond their error bars.
findings.value: direction confirmed; percent values not in abstract
findings.confidence: high for direction, numbers not opened
findings.evidence_quote: Embryonic segment length and the spatial wavelength of oscillating gene expression also increase correspondingly

findings.claim: S5 Zebrafish trunk somites form at a constant rate of 2 per hour (period 30 min) at standard temperature. Assumption: 28.5 C. Registry: absent. Falsifier: ZFIN staging table stage onsets. Validated (V1): intervals from 11.66 h to 22 h give 2.14, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0 somites per hour: PASS; but the first interval (10.33 to 11.66 h) gives 3.0 per hour: FAIL for a constant period over the whole series.
findings.source: https://zfin.org/zf_info/zfbook/stages/ (staging table after Kimmel et al. 1995, doi:10.1002/aja.1002030302; the 1995 paper itself not opened)
findings.value: 1 somite at 10.33 h, 5 at 11.66 h, 10 at 14 h, 14 at 16 h, 20 at 19 h, 26 at 22 h
findings.confidence: high; table opened, stage onsets are the lower bound of each range
findings.evidence_quote: 10.33 h: 1-4 somites ... 19 h: 20-25 somites

findings.claim: S6 The cell-autonomous clock period is set by delays in a self-repressing gene loop; the delayed-autoinhibition model of her1/her7 predicts a period close to 30 min. Formal form (from the paper body, not opened): T approx 2*(T_delay + 1/b + 1/c), with b, c the protein and mRNA decay rates. Registry: absent. Falsifier: measured transcription/translation delays and half-lives for her1/her7 versus the observed 30 min period. Validated (V2) against ZFIN trunk rate 2.0 per hour = 30 min: PASS (not a blind test: the paper targeted 30 min).
findings.value: predicted period close to 30 min; observed 30 min per somite
findings.confidence: high for the abstract claim; the explicit formula is from memory of the paper body and was not opened
findings.evidence_quote: The predicted period is close to the observed period (30 min)

findings.claim: S7 FAILURE of the naive law: the period of segmentation is not equal to the period of the genetic oscillations; tissue shortening adds a Doppler term. Formal: 1/T_segmentation = 1/T_posterior_clock + (Doppler contribution from shortening) + (changing-wavelength contribution); S1 and S2 hold only if the tissue between clock and wavefront has constant length. Registry: absent. Falsifier: real-time reporter movies from this paper; fail if anterior and posterior oscillation counts are equal over the same time window.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1253089 (PubMed abstract, PMID 25013078; open full text PMC7611034 not read)
findings.value: qualitative; numeric period difference not in abstract
findings.evidence_quote: their time scale is not sufficient to explain the temporal period of segmentation

findings.claim: S8 Across species, segment number is set by clock rate relative to developmental rate: N proportional to (developmental duration) / T, and somite size falls as N rises. In snake embryos the clock runs much faster relative to development, giving many more, smaller somites. Registry: absent. Falsifier: the paper's per-species table of clock period, generation time and somite number (use snake, zebrafish, mouse only; the fourth species is in the held-out clade and must be dropped); fail if N does not rank with duration/T.
findings.value: qualitative; species numbers not in abstract
findings.confidence: high for the statement; numbers not opened
findings.evidence_quote: leading to a greatly increased number of smaller-sized somites

findings.claim: S9 Segmentation ends when the presomitic mesoderm, after first growing, shrinks to zero: D is the time at which PSM length L(t) reaches 0, with dL/dt = (axis elongation rate) - S/T. Assumption: mass balance of PSM tissue. Registry: absent. Falsifier: PSM length versus somite number curves in the same paper; fail if somites continue to form after PSM length reaches zero or stop while PSM remains.
findings.confidence: high for the statement; the differential form is my formalization
findings.evidence_quote: gradually shrinks until it is exhausted, terminating somite formation

findings.claim: S10 The collective period of coupled oscillators differs from the single-cell period and depends on coupling strength and coupling delay. Formal (delayed coupling theory, formula from the paper body, not opened): Omega = omega_A - epsilon * sin(Omega * tau), T = 2*pi/Omega. Registry: absent. Falsifier: periods of Delta-Notch mutants and inhibitor-treated zebrafish embryos (Herrgen 2010 tables); fail if the period does not shift when coupling is reduced. Notch is needed only for synchrony, not for boundary formation (Ozbudak & Lewis 2008).
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.2976/1.3027088 (PubMed abstract, PMID 19492022); supporting: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0040015 (PubMed abstract, PMID 18248098)
findings.value: qualitative; explicit equation not in abstract
findings.confidence: high for the dependence; the explicit equation is from memory and unverified
findings.evidence_quote: the segmentation clock's collective period depends on delayed coupling

findings.claim: Registry check: no clock-and-wavefront, somite-number or segmentation-clock law exists in lean, tracks/lean or tracks/research; only incidental keyword hits in five files.
findings.confidence: medium: hit files were listed, not opened, so I did not confirm what each says about somites

findings.claim: Lean file ClockWavefront.lean: six theorems on the arithmetic of S = v*T and N = D/T check with standard axioms only (second run; first run hit an environment read fault on a Mathlib olean).
findings.confidence: high; I saw only the last lines of the output, with the axiom lists truncated by the script's summary line

key_claims: The registry has no clock-and-wavefront or somite-number law; all ten harvested statements are new.
ZFIN staging table: trunk somites form at 2.0 per hour (30 min period) from about somite 5 to 26, but the first four form at 3.0 per hour, so a constant-period law FAILS for the earliest somites.
N = D/T predicts 20.7 somites between 11.66 h and 22 h; the table gives 21 (PASS).
Soroldoni 2014 shows the naive law is incomplete: segmentation period is not the oscillator period because of a Doppler effect from tissue shortening.
ClockWavefront.lean passed check.sh (ALL CHECKED) on the second run; the first run failed on an environment file-read fault, not on the proofs.

lay_summary: A growing fish embryo cuts its back into a row of blocks called somites, which later become the backbone and muscles.
The leading idea is that a ticking clock inside the cells and a slowly moving line work together: each tick, one block is cut, so block length equals how far the line moved during one tick.
We checked this against a public zebrafish table: for most of the body one block forms every 30 minutes, just as predicted, and counting ticks gave 21 blocks where the table shows 21.

But the very first few blocks form faster, about one every 20 minutes, so the simple 'steady clock' rule fails there, and another study shows the rule also needs a correction because the tissue shrinks.
We also wrote the rule's arithmetic in a proof checker, which confirmed that a slower clock must give fewer, longer blocks.

glossary.somite: One of the repeated blocks of tissue along an embryo's back that later form backbone and muscle.
glossary.segmentation: Cutting the body axis into repeated blocks.
glossary.presomitic mesoderm (PSM): The strip of uncut tissue at the tail end from which new somites are made.
glossary.segmentation clock: Genes that switch on and off in a regular rhythm inside PSM cells.
glossary.clock period (T): The time for one full tick of the clock.
glossary.wavefront: A moving position in the tissue where cells become ready to form a boundary.
glossary.wavefront speed (v): How fast that position moves through the tissue.
glossary.clock-and-wavefront model: The idea that each clock tick places one boundary where the wavefront is, so segment length = speed x period.
glossary.oscillator: Anything that repeats a cycle, like a pendulum or a gene switching on and off.
glossary.Delta-Notch coupling: A signalling system by which neighbouring cells keep their clocks in step.
glossary.autoinhibition: A gene whose product switches the gene itself off.
glossary.transcriptional delay: The time needed to make a gene's message molecule.
glossary.Doppler effect: A change in observed rhythm when the source and observer move toward each other, as with a passing siren.
glossary.mutant: An animal with a changed gene.
glossary.period mutant: A mutant whose clock ticks slower or faster than normal.
glossary.hypothesis (in Lean): An assumption written out by name so the proof says exactly what it relies on.
glossary.Lean / Mathlib: A computer proof checker and its library of mathematics.
