fleet.label: hv-morph-turing
fleet.topic: Reaction-diffusion (Turing) pattern statements: onset wavelength, activator/inhibitor diffusivity, stripe insertion with growth, digit number vs. wavelength and domain size
fleet.summary:
Harvested 11 statements; 2 validated against fetched numbers (both pass); the Lean file was written but NOT checked (both allowed check runs failed on a missing Mathlib build file, an environment error, not a reported proof error), so nothing here counts as proved.

Registry status: `turing-ddi` and `turing-wavelength` (both v1.1.0, status candidate) already cover the instability condition and the onset wavenumber on an unbounded domain. `turing-wavelength` explicitly lists finite-domain mode quantisation as NOT established; that gap is what the new statements (S8-S10) and the unchecked Lean file target. Grep of lean/ and tracks/lean showed no other law ids on this topic; tracks/research has hits in phase2/verify-t2-patterns-*.json which I did not open.

Validations (article details according to PubMed; numbers read from the PMC full texts):
- V1 PASS. Prediction (turing-ddi: inhibitor must diffuse faster than activator). Measured in zebrafish embryo (Muller 2012, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1221920): Cyclops 0.7 +/- 0.2, Squint 3.2 +/- 0.5 (activators); Lefty1 11.1 +/- 0.6, Lefty2 18.9 +/- 3.0 um^2/s (inhibitors). All four inhibitor/activator ratios exceed 1 (3.5, 5.9, 15.9, 27.0, my arithmetic). Caveat: this tests only the necessary inequality, not the full Turing inequality, which needs the kinetic Jacobian.
- V2 PASS (ordinal only). Prediction (S9: at fixed handplate width, shorter wavelength gives at least as many digits, so digit count is non-decreasing as distal Hox dose falls). Measured (Sheth 2012, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1226804): 7-9, then 8-9, then 9-11, then at least 12-14 digits; authors state the increase did not rely on larger handplate size. Monotone, as predicted. Caveat: digit period values are only in figures (1C, 4B, 4C), so the quantitative form (period x count = width) is untested; the Hoxa13-null class (7-8 condensations, count "could not be precisely determined") was left out of the ordering.

Not verified today: Turing 1952 itself (cited via the registry files only), the marine angelfish stripe-insertion paper and the Kondo-Miura 2010 review (my PMIDs for both were wrong and returned unrelated papers), and any measured stripe spacing in zebrafish. S4, S6, S7, S10, S11 are untested.

Files: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-morph-turing/TuringFiniteDomain.lean (unchecked). The folder also has src/PMC3525670.xml and src/PMC4486416.xml, two 150-byte failed downloads that can be deleted.

findings.claim: S1 Diffusion-driven instability. Formal: for u_t=f+Du*lap u, v_t=g+Dv*lap v with fu+gv<0, det J>0, a spatial mode is unstable iff Dv*fu+Du*gv > 2*sqrt(Du*Dv*det J); this forces Du != Dv. Assumptions: two species, linearisation, fixed domain. ALREADY IN REGISTRY as turing-ddi v1.1.0 (candidate). Falsifying test: measured D of an identified activator/inhibitor pair with inhibitor not faster (see S3).
findings.evidence_quote: the two diffusivities are necessarily unequal
findings.confidence: high for registry status; primary paper not opened in this run

findings.claim: S2 Onset wavelength. Formal: k_c^2 = sqrt(det J/(Du*Dv)), lambda_c = 2*pi/k_c; scaling both D by m multiplies lambda_c by sqrt(m); tissue size does not appear. Assumptions: onset, unbounded domain. ALREADY IN REGISTRY as turing-wavelength v1.1.0 (candidate, constraint TURINGLAMBDA1). Falsifying test: pattern spacing vs. measured sqrt(D) across perturbations in a system with measured D and kinetics; no single open dataset with all inputs found.
findings.evidence_quote: the critical wavelength grows as the square root of the diffusivity scale

findings.claim: S3 (VALIDATED, PASS) In the zebrafish Nodal/Lefty activator/inhibitor pair the inhibitor has the higher effective diffusion coefficient. Formal: D_Lefty > D_Nodal. Not in registry as a data row (turing-ddi has empty observations). Dataset: FRAP values in Muller et al. 2012 (PMC3525670). Test: any inhibitor/activator ratio <= 1 within error falsifies. Result: ratios 3.5 to 27, all > 1.
findings.evidence_quote: 11.1 ± 0.6 μm2/s for Lefty1-GFP, and 18.9 ± 3.0 μm2/s for Lefty2-GFP
findings.confidence: high (numbers read from full text via fetch tool; ratios are my arithmetic)

findings.claim: S4 Signalling range follows diffusivity when clearance is similar. Formal: gradient length = sqrt(D/k); with equal k, range_Lefty/range_Nodal = sqrt(D_L/D_N), e.g. sqrt(18.9/3.2) = 2.43 for Lefty2 vs Squint. Assumption: steady-state exponential gradient, uniform clearance. Not in registry. Dataset: gradient profiles and half-lives in the same paper's supplement. Test: measured range ratio outside the predicted ratio's error band. UNTESTED: I did not fetch the measured ranges or half-lives.
findings.evidence_quote: Nodals and Leftys have similar clearance kinetics
findings.confidence: medium; prediction computed, measurement not fetched

findings.claim: S5 (VALIDATED, PASS, ordinal) Digit number rises as distal Hox dose falls in the Gli3-null mouse limb, without a larger handplate: read as Hox dose setting the Turing wavelength. Formal: N(dose) non-increasing in dose at fixed width L; with N = floor(L/lambda), lambda falls with dose. Not in registry (the Sheth DOI is only a see_also of turing-wavelength). Dataset: genotype digit counts and Fig 1C digit periods in Sheth et al. 2012. Test: a lower-dose genotype with fewer digits at equal width falsifies. Result: 7-9 -> 8-9 -> 9-11 -> at least 12-14, monotone.
findings.evidence_quote: to at least 12 to 14 digits when only one copy of Hoxa13 remained
findings.confidence: medium-high; counts read from text; wavelength values are in figures only and were not extracted; Hoxa13-null class excluded (count not precisely determinable)

findings.claim: S6 Digit patterning is driven by a three-component Bmp-Sox9-Wnt Turing network modulated by morphogen gradients. Formal: periodic Sox9(x) along the anterior-posterior axis with period set by network parameters; gradients modulate wavelength along the proximo-distal axis. Not in registry (DOI is a see_also only). Dataset: Sox9 limb-bud expression images from the paper / eMouseAtlas (not opened). Test: Bmp or Wnt inhibition failing to change Sox9 stripe period in the predicted direction. UNTESTED.
findings.evidence_quote: a Turing network implemented by Bmp, Sox9, and Wnt drives digit specification
findings.confidence: medium; abstract only, no numbers extracted

findings.claim: S7 Zebrafish stripe cells satisfy the Turing sign structure: short-range mutual exclusion of melanophores and xanthophores, long-range support of melanophores by xanthophores. Formal: interaction kernel w(r) < 0 for r < r1 and > 0 for r1 < r < r2 (local inhibition, lateral activation of the other type), equivalent to short-range activation with long-range inhibition. Not in registry. Dataset: laser-ablation outcomes in Nakamasu et al. 2009 (PMC2689028, not opened in full). Test: ablating distant xanthophores not reducing melanophore survival falsifies. UNTESTED; no stripe spacing number obtained.
findings.evidence_quote: the local effect of these cells is opposite to that of their effects long range

findings.claim: S8 Stripe insertion with growth: new palate ridges (Shh stripes) appear where the gap between existing ridges has widened; FGF and Shh act as activator and inhibitor. Formal: at fixed lambda, stripe count n with n*lambda <= L < (n+1)*lambda is non-decreasing in L (theorem count_mono_in_size in my Lean file, UNCHECKED). Not in registry (finite-domain behaviour is listed as not established). Dataset: ruga-spacing time series in Economou et al. 2012 (PMC3303118, not opened in full). Test: gap at insertion not near twice the baseline spacing, or count decreasing with growth.
findings.evidence_quote: appear at two growth zones where the space between previously laid rugae increases
findings.confidence: medium; abstract only; Lean statement not machine-checked

findings.claim: S9 Fixed domain, shorter wavelength, at least as many repeats. Formal: if n*lam <= L < (m+1)*lam' with 0 < lam and lam' <= lam then n <= m (theorem count_mono_in_wavelength, UNCHECKED). This is the arithmetic behind S5. Not in registry. Dataset and test: as S5, plus the quantitative version period x count = handplate width using Fig 1C values.
findings.evidence_quote: the dose of distal Hox genes modulates the digit period or wavelength
findings.confidence: low as a proved result (file failed to check); the mathematics is elementary

findings.claim: S10 Minimum domain size. Formal: with no-flux boundaries the admissible wavenumbers are n*pi/L; if the unstable band ends at k_hi and L*k_hi < pi, no mode n >= 1 is unstable, so no pattern forms below L_min = pi/k_hi (theorem no_mode_below_critical_size, UNCHECKED). Standard textbook consequence of S1; I did not open a primary source for it. Not in registry. Dataset: none identified; a test needs pattern onset size in a growing tissue plus an independent wavelength estimate. UNTESTED.
findings.confidence: low: no primary source opened, Lean file not checked

findings.claim: S11 Inhibitor dose sets spacing in mouse skin: overexpressing the inhibitor DKK lowers hair follicle density, and moderate WNT suppression clusters follicles. Formal: follicle density is non-increasing in inhibitor production rate. Not in registry. Dataset: follicle density counts in Sick et al. 2006 (full text not opened). Test: DKK overexpression line with unchanged or higher follicle density. UNTESTED.
findings.evidence_quote: Transgenic DKK overexpression reduces overall appendage density

key_claims: Registry already holds turing-ddi and turing-wavelength (both candidate); finite-domain mode quantisation is explicitly not covered and is the gap worth filling.
V1 pass: measured inhibitor (Lefty) diffusion coefficients exceed activator (Nodal) ones by 3.5x to 27x, as the instability condition requires.
V2 pass (ordinal): digit count rises monotonically 7-9, 8-9, 9-11, >=12-14 as distal Hox dose falls with no larger handplate.
The Lean file TuringFiniteDomain.lean did NOT check: both runs failed reading a Mathlib .olean.private file (a different file each run), so no theorem in it is proved.

lay_summary: Some animal patterns, like stripes and the row of fingers, may form because two chemicals spread through tissue at different speeds: one switches things on nearby, the other switches things off farther away.
The maths says the 'off' chemical must spread faster, and a zebrafish experiment we looked up found exactly that: it spreads about 3 to 27 times faster.

The maths also says that if the repeat distance gets shorter while the space stays the same, more repeats fit; mice with fewer copies of certain genes grew more and thinner digits, from about 8 up to 12-14, which matches.
We wrote a computer-checked proof of the 'more repeats fit' idea, but the proof checker on this machine was broken, so it has not been confirmed yet.
Several other statements were collected but not yet tested against numbers.

glossary.reaction-diffusion (Turing) system: Two or more chemicals that react with each other and spread through tissue, which can make repeating patterns by themselves.
glossary.activator: A chemical that increases its own production and that of the inhibitor nearby.
glossary.inhibitor: A chemical that shuts the activator down and spreads farther.
glossary.diffusion coefficient (D): How fast a substance spreads, in square micrometres per second.
glossary.wavelength / period: The distance from one stripe or digit to the next.
glossary.wavenumber (k): 2*pi divided by the wavelength; a bigger k means tighter stripes.
glossary.Jacobian (J), det J: The table of how each chemical's rate changes with each chemical's amount; det J is one number computed from it.
glossary.onset: The point where the even, pattern-free state just becomes unstable.
glossary.no-flux boundary: An edge that chemicals cannot cross.
glossary.mode: One allowed wave shape that fits in the tissue.
glossary.Nodal, Lefty: A signalling protein (activator) and its blocker (inhibitor) in early fish embryos; Cyclops and Squint are two Nodal proteins.
glossary.Hox genes, Gli3: Genes that control body and limb layout; removing them here changes digit number.
glossary.handplate: The flat paddle at the end of an embryonic limb where digits form.
glossary.Sox9, Bmp, Wnt, Shh, FGF, DKK: Signalling molecules or markers used by cells in developing tissue; DKK blocks Wnt.
glossary.melanophore, xanthophore: Black and yellow pigment cells in fish skin.
glossary.rugae: Ridges on the roof of the mouth.
glossary.FRAP: A microscope method that bleaches a glowing spot and times how fast glow returns, to measure spreading speed.
glossary.clearance: How quickly a molecule is removed.
glossary.Lean / Mathlib: A program that checks mathematical proofs, and its library of known mathematics.
glossary.named hypothesis: An assumption written out explicitly in a proof instead of being hidden.
glossary.ordinal test: A test of order only (more or fewer), not of exact amounts.

fleet.label: hv-nanopub-format
fleet.topic: How a harvested biological statement should be written as an unsigned nanopublication (assertion / provenance / pubinfo), with a template and three filled examples
fleet.summary:
Wrote one unsigned template and three filled example .trig files, but none has been parsed by an RDF parser (rdflib is not installed), and the harvest is short of the 8-12 asked for. The only check on the files was a count of four graph blocks each and a search confirming no ORCID.

**What was harvested.** Four format rules from the nanopub guidelines and three base-count statements, seven in total. No Kleiber, Hardy-Weinberg or other laws were harvested, because I did not open a primary source for them in the time available.

**Validation 1: Chargaff's second parity rule (one strand has A about equal to T and G about equal to C).** I fetched three genomes from NCBI and counted bases. The 5% tolerance is my own choice, not from a source.

| Genome | Accession | A/T | G/C | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phage lambda | NC_001416.1 | 1.029 | 1.128 | Fail (A/T passes, G/C does not) |
| Phage phiX174 | NC_001422.1 | 0.767 | 1.084 | Fail (single-stranded virion, so out of the rule's scope) |
| Human mitochondrion | NC_012920.1 | 1.252 | 0.419 | Fail |

These are three small genomes; they say nothing about large chromosomes.

**Validation 2: format rules against the existing drafts.** The 10 files in `holdout/nanopubs/unsigned` each have the four named graphs and no ORCID line: pass. The 21 files in `math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned` did not match my graph-name pattern and each has 2 ORCID lines. I did not open them, so whether that is a real problem or just different graph naming is unknown.

**Registry check.** Grep for "chargaff" or "parity rule" in `lean`, `tracks/lean` and `tracks/research` returned no files, so the rule is not in the law registry or research track.

**Known gaps in the files.**
- The template is example 1 with the claim id, slug and accession swapped for placeholders; it still carries the lambda numbers and label.
- `delphi:formalStatement`, `delphi:Hypothesis` and `delphi:Evidence` are my guesses at ontology terms; I did not check them against the Delphi ontology.
- `dct:created` is date-only precision (midnight placeholder).
- The claim's primary paper (Rudner, Karkas and Chargaff, 1968) was not opened, so the .trig files cite only the NCBI records.

The repo was not edited; nothing was signed, published or sent.

Files are in D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-nanopub-format:
- template-unsigned.trig
- example-1-lambda.trig
- example-2-phix174.trig
- example-3-human-mito.trig
- gen.sh

findings.claim: Format rule: a nanopublication head contains exactly one typing quad and one link each to assertion, provenance and publication info. Formal: |{q in H : q = (N, rdf:type, np:Nanopublication)}| = 1, likewise for np:hasAssertion, np:hasProvenance, np:hasPublicationInfo. Falsifying test: count those four predicates in the Head graph of every draft; any count != 1 fails.
findings.evidence_quote: There is exactly one quad of the form '[N] rdf:type np:Nanopublication [H]'.
findings.value: The 10 drafts in holdout/nanopubs/unsigned each show the 4 named graphs (grep count only): pass. The 21 math-bio-theorems drafts did not match my grep pattern: not assessed.
findings.confidence: high for the rule (page opened via WebFetch summary); medium for the check (regex, not an RDF parser)

findings.claim: Format rule: the provenance graph must refer to the assertion graph. Formal: exists a triple in P whose subject or object is the assertion IRI A. Test: parse each draft and check P mentions A.
findings.evidence_quote: Triples in [P] have at least one reference to [A].
findings.value: My four files each have 'sub:assertion prov:wasAttributedTo ...' in sub:provenance (by construction, not parser-checked).

findings.claim: Format rule: the publication-info graph must refer to the nanopublication IRI; attribution and timestamp are SHOULD, not MUST. Formal: exists a triple in I mentioning N. Test: parse and check; also flag drafts lacking dct:created or dct:creator.
findings.evidence_quote: MUST be the nanopublication URI and SHOULD contain attribution and timestamp
findings.value: My files carry dct:created and dct:creator (a software agent, no human ORCID).
findings.confidence: high for the rule; the quote is as relayed by the fetch tool's summary

findings.claim: Format rule: trusty URIs are recommended, not part of well-formedness, so an unsigned draft with a temp URI is still a well-formed nanopublication.
findings.evidence_quote: are the recommended way of assigning integrity keys to nanopublications
findings.value: All four files use http://purl.org/nanopub/temp/... URIs, with no hash and no signature.
findings.confidence: medium (quote is a fragment relayed by the fetch summary)

findings.claim: Chargaff's second parity rule on phage lambda. Formal: on the deposited strand, |nA/nT - 1| <= 0.05 and |nG/nC - 1| <= 0.05 (assumptions: double-stranded genome; the 0.05 tolerance is mine). Prediction: both ratios within 5% of 1. Measured: A 12334, C 11362, G 12820, T 11986; A/T = 1.029, G/C = 1.128. FAIL (A/T passes, G/C does not). Not in the repo: grep for 'chargaff|parity rule' in lean, tracks/lean, tracks/research returned no files. Open dataset: NCBI RefSeq genomes; test: per-genome single-strand base counts against the tolerance.
findings.evidence_quote: NC_001416.1 Enterobacteria phage lambda, complete genome
findings.confidence: high for the counts; the tolerance is an arbitrary choice

findings.claim: Chargaff's second parity rule on phage phiX174. Same formal statement. Prediction: both ratios within 5% of 1. Measured: A 1291, C 1157, G 1254, T 1684; A/T = 0.767, G/C = 1.084. FAIL on both. The virion DNA is single-stranded, so the rule's double-strand assumption is not met; recorded as out of scope rather than a refutation.
findings.evidence_quote: NC_001422.1 Escherichia phage phiX174, complete genome
findings.confidence: high for the counts; the single-stranded scope note is from my own knowledge, not a source opened in this run

findings.claim: Chargaff's second parity rule on the human mitochondrial genome. Same formal statement. Prediction: both ratios within 5% of 1. Measured: A 5124, C 5181, G 2169, T 4094, plus one N excluded; A/T = 1.252, G/C = 0.419. FAIL on both. Says nothing about nuclear chromosomes.
findings.evidence_quote: NC_012920.1 Homo sapiens mitochondrion, complete genome

findings.claim: Existing drafts: the 21 files under math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned each contain 2 lines matching 'orcid.org/0' and none of my four graph-name patterns; the 10 holdout drafts contain 4 graph blocks and 0 ORCID lines.
findings.value: 21 files: 0 graph-pattern matches, 2 ORCID lines each. 10 files: 4 graph blocks, 0 ORCID lines.
findings.confidence: low on what it means: I did not open any math-bio-theorems draft, so the ORCID lines could be legitimate citations and the graphs may simply be named differently

key_claims: Four unsigned .trig files were written (one template, three examples); none was parsed by an RDF parser.
Chargaff's second parity rule fails a 5% tolerance on all three small genomes tested; phiX174 is out of the rule's scope because it is single-stranded.
The 10 holdout drafts match the four-graph structure and carry no ORCID; the 21 math-bio-theorems drafts were not assessed beyond a grep.
Chargaff's rule is not in lean, tracks/lean or tracks/research.
Only 7 statements were harvested, not the 8-12 asked for.
lay_summary: A nanopublication is a tiny digital note with three parts: what is claimed, where it came from, and who wrote the note and when.
I wrote a blank form for such notes and filled it in three times, without signing or publishing anything.
To have something real to write down, I tested an old rule that says one strand of DNA has about as many A letters as T letters, and as many G as C.
I counted the letters in three small genomes and the rule did not hold within 5 percent in any of them, which is a useful thing to record honestly.
My files have not yet been checked by a proper reading program, so they might still contain typing mistakes.

glossary.nanopublication: A very small machine-readable record of one claim, with its source and its author information attached.
glossary.assertion: The part of the record that states the claim itself.
glossary.provenance: The part that says where the claim came from and how it was made.
glossary.pubinfo: The part that says who made the record, when, and under what licence.
glossary.head: The part that ties the other three parts together into one record.
glossary.TriG / .trig: A text file format for writing linked data split into named groups.
glossary.RDF: A standard way to write facts as subject-verb-object triples that computers can read.
glossary.quad: A triple plus the name of the group (graph) it belongs to.
glossary.graph: A named group of triples inside the file.
glossary.IRI / URI: A web-style address used as a unique name for a thing.
glossary.trusty URI: An address that includes a fingerprint of the content, so changes can be detected.
glossary.unsigned: Not stamped with anyone's digital key, so nobody has vouched for it.
glossary.ORCID: A personal ID number for researchers.
glossary.software agent: A program, not a person, named as the maker of a record.
glossary.Chargaff's second parity rule: The observation that within a single DNA strand, A and T counts are roughly equal, and G and C counts are roughly equal.
glossary.genome: The full DNA sequence of an organism or virus.

fleet.label: hv-zebrafish-data
fleet.topic: Open zebrafish datasets (ZFIN, Zebrahub, DANIO-CODE, single-cell atlases, FishBase) that can validate morphological and molecular statements: access, size, licence, what each can test
fleet.summary:
Ten statements harvested and three checked against live data. Two passed and one failed its strict form.

- FAIL (strict): Howe 2013 says 71.4% of human genes have a zebrafish orthologue. The ZFIN curated orthology table downloaded today gives 13,749 distinct human genes, which is 67.1% of Howe's 20,479. It passes only the abstract's looser "approximately 70%". ZFIN's curated orthology and Howe's Ensembl-based method differ, so this is a method gap, not a refutation.
- PASS: somites form at 2 per hour at 28.5 C. The ZFIN stage table gives 14 somites at 16 h, 20 at 19 h and 26 at 22 h, exactly 2.0 per hour. The first few form at 3.0 per hour.
- PASS: body growth is isometric (b = 3). FishBase gives b = 3.04 (2.84 - 3.24).

Registry check: a grep of lean/laws.json for somite, ortholog, cis-regulatory and cell atlas found only the flying-fish length-weight entry, so none of the ten statements appears there as a zebrafish law. Zebrafish terms do occur across 112 files under lean/, tracks/lean and tracks/research (551 hits, mostly lean/genotype and FinDevelopment), but I did not open those files, so statement-level overlap is unchecked.

Licences are unconfirmed for every dataset: the FishBase and Zebrahub pages I opened state none, and I did not open the ZFIN or DANIO-CODE terms. The Zebrahub data page rendered without its dataset lists, so its cell counts come from the Zebrahub-Multiome preprint only.

Files are in D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-zebrafish-data/:
- validation.md
- epmc.txt
- dl/human_orthos.txt

findings.claim: S1. About 71.4% of human protein-coding genes have at least one zebrafish orthologue. Formal: |{h in H : exists z, orth(h,z)}| / |H| = 0.714, with |H| = 20,479. Assumption: orthology as called by Ensembl Compara. In registry: not found in lean/laws.json. Falsifying test: count distinct human genes in ZFIN human_orthos.txt; reject if the fraction is outside 0.714 +/- 0.01.
findings.evidence_quote: 71.4% of human genes have at least one zebrafish orthologue
findings.value: VALIDATED TODAY: predicted 14,622 human genes; measured 13,749 (67.1%) in ZFIN table. Strict FAIL; passes only the abstract's 'approximately 70%' at +/-5 points.
findings.confidence: high for the measured count; medium for the comparison, because ZFIN curated orthology and Ensembl Compara use different methods and denominators

findings.claim: S2. About 69% of zebrafish protein-coding genes (26,206) have at least one human orthologue. Formal: |{z in Z : exists h, orth(z,h)}| / |Z| = 0.69. In registry: not found. Falsifying test: distinct ZFIN gene IDs in human_orthos.txt divided by 26,206.
findings.evidence_quote: 69% of zebrafish genes have at least one human orthologue
findings.value: VALIDATED TODAY: predicted 18,082; measured 17,180 (65.6%). Strict FAIL, loose pass.
findings.confidence: medium; the ZFIN gene set today is not the 2013 Zv9 gene set

findings.claim: S3. After the first few somites, zebrafish somites form at a constant 2 per hour at 28.5 C (period 30 min). Formal: N(t) = N0 + 2(t - t0) for t in [16 h, 22 h]. Assumption: standard temperature 28.5 C. In registry: 'somite' not found in lean/laws.json. Falsifying test: ZFIN staging table, slope of somite number against hours; reject if slope is outside 2.0 +/- 0.25.
findings.evidence_quote: h = hours of development at 28.5°C
findings.value: VALIDATED TODAY: 14 somites at 16 h, 20 at 19 h, 26 at 22 h gives slope 2.0 per hour. PASS. Early somites: 1 at 10.33 h to 5 at 11.66 h gives 3.0 per hour.
findings.confidence: high for the table values; the rate sentence in Kimmel 1995 itself was not opened (segment page returned 404), so the 2-per-hour wording is from memory and the table

findings.claim: S4. Zebrafish grow isometrically: weight W = a L^b with b = 3. Formal: b in the 95% interval of the fitted exponent. In registry: lean/laws.json has a length-weight entry, but for flying-fish species only (line 1001-1009), not zebrafish. Falsifying test: FishBase Bayesian length-weight estimate for Danio rerio; reject if the interval excludes 3.
findings.value: VALIDATED TODAY: interval 2.84-3.24 contains 3. PASS (not falsified). Note this is a Bayesian estimate from related species, not a field fit.
findings.confidence: medium; a weak test because the interval is wide

findings.claim: S5. Adult vertebral count is 31-32 and maximum standard length is 3.8 cm. Formal: V in {31, 32}; SL_max = 3.8 cm. In registry: not found. Falsifying test: count vertebrae in an open micro-CT or cleared-and-stained zebrafish series; reject if the modal count is outside 31-32.
findings.evidence_quote: Vertebrae 31-32.
findings.value: FishBase: vertebrae 31-32; max length 3.8 cm SL; branched anal fin rays 10-12
findings.confidence: high that FishBase states this; not independently tested

findings.claim: S6. The zebrafish genome has over 140,000 developmental cis-regulatory elements, drawn from 1,802 genomic data sets. Formal: |CRE| >= 140,000 across the profiled stages. In registry: 'cis-regulatory' not found in lean/laws.json. Falsifying test: count rows in the DANIO-CODE consensus regulatory-element track at danio-code.zfin.org; reject if below 140,000.
findings.evidence_quote: We identified over 140,000 cis-regulatory elements throughout development
findings.value: 1,802 data sets; >140,000 elements; access route https://danio-code.zfin.org
findings.confidence: high for the quoted abstract; portal itself not opened, size and licence not checked

findings.claim: S7. A single-cell multiome atlas of 94,562 cells over six stages (10-24 hours post-fertilization) yields 640,000 regulatory elements in 402 modules. Formal: |CRE_multiome| = 640,000. This is 4.6 times the DANIO-CODE count, so the two element definitions cannot both be 'the' regulatory set. In registry: not found. Falsifying test: overlap the Zebrahub-Multiome peak set with DANIO-CODE elements; reject 'DANIO-CODE is complete' if under half of the multiome peaks overlap.
findings.source: doi 10.1101/2024.10.18.618987 (preprint, abstract read via Europe PMC)
findings.evidence_quote: 94,562 cells across six stages of zebrafish embryogenesis
findings.value: 94,562 cells; 6 stages; 640,000 elements; 402 modules; portal zebrahub.org/epigenomics

findings.claim: S8. Over 92,000 cells from the first day of development form a single connected cell-state landscape, and clonally related cells stay restricted within it. Formal: for clone pairs (c1, c2), graph distance d(c1, c2) is smaller than for random pairs. In registry: 'cell atlas' not found. Falsifying test: Wagner 2018 TracerSeq data (GEO); permutation test of clone-pair state distance against random pairs.
findings.evidence_quote: single-cell RNA sequencing to >92,000 cells from zebrafish embryos
findings.confidence: high for the abstract; GEO accession not opened

findings.claim: S9. 38,731 cells resolve into trajectories of 25 cell types through early somitogenesis. Formal: the trajectory tree has 25 leaves. In registry: not found. Falsifying test: recluster the Farrell 2018 expression matrix; reject if a stable clustering gives far fewer or more than 25 terminal types at the same stage.
findings.evidence_quote: identified the trajectories of 25 cell types through early somitogenesis
findings.confidence: high for the abstract; data portal not opened

findings.claim: S10. 82% of human disease (OMIM morbid) genes, 2,601 genes, have at least one zebrafish orthologue; 47% of human genes have a one-to-one zebrafish orthologue. Formal: |M with orthologue| / |M| = 0.82. In registry: not found. Falsifying test: join ZFIN human_orthos.txt column 6 (OMIM id) against the OMIM morbid list; reject if outside 0.82 +/- 0.03.
findings.evidence_quote: 2,601 (82%) can be related to at least one zebrafish orthologue
findings.confidence: high for the quote; not tested (needs the OMIM morbid list, which requires registration)

findings.claim: Dataset access: ZFIN bulk downloads are open flat files with no login; the human orthology table is 9.7 MB and 44,346 rows.
findings.value: 9,739,225 bytes; 44,346 rows; 17,180 distinct zebrafish genes; 13,749 distinct human genes
findings.confidence: high (downloaded and counted); ZFIN licence page not opened

findings.claim: Dataset access: Zebrahub imaging is in OME-Zarr over HTTP, with copies on Google Drive and figshare, and raw reads at NIH SRA under BioProject PRJNA940501. The data page states no licence and its dataset lists rendered empty.

findings.confidence: medium; page content was only partly rendered

lay_summary: Zebrafish are small fish that scientists study a lot, and much of the data about them is free to download.
We collected ten exact claims about zebrafish, such as how fast the body segments form and how many of their genes match human genes.
We checked three of them against real numbers today.
The body segments really do form at two per hour, and the fish's weight grows with the cube of its length, as claimed.
The gene-matching claim came out a bit lower than the famous paper says (67 in 100 instead of 71 in 100), probably because the two lists were made in different ways.

glossary.orthologue: A gene in one species that matches a gene in another species because both came from the same ancestor gene.
glossary.somite: One of the repeated blocks of tissue along an embryo's back that later become backbone and muscle.
glossary.hours post-fertilization (hpf): How many hours have passed since the egg was fertilized.
glossary.cis-regulatory element: A stretch of DNA near a gene that acts like a switch, turning the gene on or off.
glossary.isometric growth: Growing while keeping the same shape, so weight goes up with length cubed.
glossary.length-weight exponent (b): The power in the formula weight = a x length^b; b = 3 means the shape stays the same.
glossary.standard length (SL): A fish's length from snout tip to the base of the tail fin.
glossary.single-cell RNA sequencing: A method that reads which genes are switched on in each individual cell.
glossary.multiome: Measuring two things from the same cell at once, here gene activity and which DNA is open.
glossary.cell atlas: A catalogue of all the cell types in an animal, built from single-cell measurements.
glossary.OME-Zarr: A file format for very large microscope images that can be read in pieces over the internet.
glossary.light-sheet microscopy: A microscope that lights a thin slice of a living embryo at a time, so whole embryos can be filmed.
glossary.lineage: The family tree of cells: which cell divided to make which.
glossary.Ensembl Compara: A computer pipeline that works out which genes match across species.
glossary.curated: Checked and entered by human experts rather than only by a computer.
glossary.OMIM morbid gene: A human gene listed in the OMIM catalogue as causing a disease.
glossary.Bayesian estimate: An estimate that combines data with prior knowledge, here from related species.
glossary.nanopublication: A tiny, machine-readable published statement with its source attached.
glossary.preprint: A paper posted online before other scientists have formally reviewed it.
glossary.falsify: To show a claim is wrong by a test it could have failed.

lay_summary: Scientists build tiny genetic switches in bacteria, and one idea says you can change how easily a switch flips without changing how sharply it flips.
We tested that idea on a public parts list and it mostly held, but one pair of switches changed sharpness more than the limit we had set, so the honest score is a fail.
For the bacteria-spreading project, we confirmed that the two maths rules it needs are already in the project's rule book.
One project still needs someone to redo an earlier calculation, which we did not have time for.
The last two need real objects to be 3D-printed and weighed or measured, which only a person in a lab can do.

glossary.RBS (ribosome binding site): A short stretch of DNA that sets how much protein a gene makes.
glossary.Repressor: A protein that switches another gene off.
glossary.Hill coefficient (n): A number for how sharply a genetic switch flips from on to off.
glossary.Threshold (K): The input level at which the switch is half flipped.
glossary.Steepness drift (dn): How much the sharpness number differs between two switches, as a fraction of their average.
glossary.UCF: User constraints file: the public Cello parts list with measured switch numbers.
glossary.sha256: A digital fingerprint that proves a file is exactly the one that was downloaded.
glossary.Frozen bound / pre-registration: A limit or prediction written down before looking at the test data.
glossary.Declared-not-blind: A test where the answer had already been seen, said openly.
glossary.Lean theorem: A maths statement checked by a computer proof program.
glossary.Law set: The project's versioned list of rules, here version 1.8.1.
glossary.Candidate: A rule that has a checked statement but is not yet fully accepted.
glossary.Vertex model: A computer model that draws cells as polygons to predict tissue shape.
glossary.RMSE: A single number for how far predictions are from measurements on average.
glossary.Autorotating fruit: A winged seed that spins as it falls.
glossary.Immersed weight: How heavy an object is while under water.
glossary.Swelling strain: The fraction by which a material grows when it soaks up water.
glossary.Bilayer: A strip of two bonded layers that bends when one layer swells more.
glossary.Coupon: A small test piece of a material.

glossary.Lean: A computer language for writing maths proofs that a program checks line by line.
glossary.kernel: The small trusted core of Lean that decides whether a proof is really correct.
glossary.theorem: A statement that has been proved.
glossary.elimination certificate (rules_out theor: A proof that a particular design cannot work because it would break a known law.
glossary.law set: A numbered, frozen list of the laws the project currently relies on (for example 1.8.1).
glossary.pinned law: A law that is included in a given law set.
glossary.registry: The folder of records describing each law and where its proof lives.
glossary.axiom audit: A check of which basic assumptions a proof depends on; it exposes unfinished proofs.
glossary.sorryAx: Lean's marker for a proof with a hole in it.
glossary.Timoshenko ceiling: The upper limit on how much a two-layer strip can curl when one layer swells more than the other.
glossary.hygromorph: A material that changes shape when it gets damp or dry.
glossary.induced drag: The air resistance a wing pays for making lift.
glossary.aspect ratio: How long and narrow a wing or fin is.
glossary.elastic similarity: A rule for how the thickness of supports should grow with length so they bend the same amount.
glossary.enhancer: A stretch of DNA that turns a gene's activity up.
glossary.promoter: The stretch of DNA where reading of a gene starts.
glossary.rank reversal: Two things swapping places in an ordered list when conditions change.
glossary.monotone: Always going the same direction: more input never gives less output.
glossary.MPRA / STARR-seq: Lab methods that measure the strength of thousands of DNA switches at once.
glossary.null rate: How often something appears by chance alone, with no real effect.
glossary.source of truth: The one copy that everyone else is meant to follow.
glossary.Mathlib: The large shared library of maths already proved in Lean.

lay_summary: Five open questions on the project's public list needed answers, and I worked on each one.

For the drug question, I checked how much two labs disagree when they measure the same drug on the same protein. They disagree enough that even a perfect computer guess could never match the lab numbers exactly.
Two questions can only be finished by the project lead, because each needs one fact only he knows: which partner was meant, and where a number of 'tokens' came from.
For the 3D-printing plastics, nobody has published how much they grow when wet, so I wrote down a simple soak-and-measure test to find out.
For the organism file format, I checked that it has no way to say 'when light hits here, move there', and I wrote a draft of how to add that.

glossary.binding affinity: How tightly a drug molecule sticks to its protein target.
glossary.Ki / pKi: A lab number for binding strength; pKi is its negative logarithm, so one unit means ten times tighter.
glossary.pChEMBL: ChEMBL's standard negative-log scale for potency numbers such as Ki.
glossary.ChEMBL: A free public database of measured drug-protein activities.
glossary.EGFR, factor Xa: Two well-studied human proteins used here as example drug targets.
glossary.SD (standard deviation): A measure of how spread out a set of numbers is.
glossary.noise floor: The size of the disagreement between repeat measurements of the same thing.
glossary.attenuation ceiling: The best correlation any predictor can reach when the answers it is scored against are themselves noisy.
glossary.Pearson r: A score from -1 to 1 for how well two lists of numbers rise and fall together.
glossary.variance split (between/within target): How much of the spread in the data comes from differences between proteins versus differences among drugs on one protein.
glossary.leakage: When test examples are too similar to training examples, so a model looks better than it is.
glossary.clean split: A way of dividing data so the test set is not similar to the training set.
glossary.cycle consistency: The rule that energy differences added around a closed loop of molecules must sum to zero.
glossary.Lean: A computer program that checks mathematical proofs line by line.
glossary.theorem: A statement proved from stated assumptions.
glossary.pinned law / registry placeholder: A law listed in the project's fixed list that has a name but no checked proof yet.
glossary.hygroscopic expansion coefficient: How much a material grows in length for each percent of water it soaks up.
glossary.water diffusivity: How fast water spreads into a material.
glossary.Fickian uptake: The standard simple model of water soaking in by diffusion.
glossary.ASTM D471: A standard test for how much a rubbery material changes after soaking in a liquid.
glossary.bilayer: Two layers glued together; if one swells and the other does not, the strip bends.
glossary.PLA / PETG: Two common plastics used in 3D printing.
glossary.Fuse powder / Form 4 resin: Formlabs materials for its powder-fusing printers and its liquid-resin printers.
glossary..life / .organism format: The project's file formats for describing a designed organism, where every value says whether it was measured, assumed or unknown.
glossary.kind and scope: The format's required labels on every value: how it is known, and what it does and does not apply to.
glossary.not-established: The format's label for a value that was looked for and does not exist yet.
glossary.sensor / actuator: A part that detects something (here light) and a part that moves in response.
glossary.xenobot: A tiny living machine built from frog cells.
glossary.token: The unit of text an AI model reads or writes; grants may be counted in tokens.
glossary.grep: A tool that searches files for words.

fleet.label: lf-fire-regs
fleet.topic: How a new bio-based fire-retardant coating or material is tested against fire regulations (EU, UK, US, intumescent practice), evidence that finding testers is a bottleneck, and bio-based flame-retardant chemistry numbers
fleet.summary: Fetch date for every item below is 2026-11-13. Many publisher pages (iso.org, astm.org, ANSI/BSI previews) returned HTTP 403, so for ISO/ASTM/EN standards the paywalled text and in several cases the edition status could NOT be confirmed from a fetched page. What was read: the Euroclass table (EN 13501-1 Table 1, via legislation.gov.uk copy of Reg 2016/364), UK gov.uk Approved Document B page, ICC 2027 cycle notice, Genorma/DIN/EVS catalogue pages for EN 16623, EN 13381-8 and ISO 5660-1, Intertek E84 page, a UL 94 explainer, and several open-access papers. Pass criteria in numbers were obtained for Euroclasses A1-E, ASTM E84 classes, UL 94 V ratings. Not obtained: numeric pass criteria and sample counts for ISO 1182 beyond the Euroclass table, ISO 1716 sample count, EN 13823 specimen count, NFPA 285 numeric limits, ASTM E119 end-point numbers, E2768 criteria, EN 13381-8 specimen count, ISO 5660 sample size. Bottleneck evidence is real but qualitative: UKAS-accredited capacity shortage stated by Warringtonfire (2024), long waiting times stated by a Danish lab (CFPA-E), a USD 0.5-1M cost for one full-scale mass-timber apartment fire test program (ENR 2017). No count of accredited fire labs for any region, no queue times in weeks and no per-test price were found. Bio-based chemistry: phytic-acid layer-by-layer coatings on cotton raise LOI from 18% to 26-31% and cut pHRR by ~57-63%; mycelium composites peak near 180-200 kW/m2 at 50 kW/m2 flux versus roughly 200 for the substrate; phytic-acid treated wood LOI 31.8-37.2% (as quoted in a review). Most lab-scale numbers are LOI, cone or MCC on textile or foam, which are NOT the tests the building regulations use (SBI, E84, E119), a key gap for any Lean/Delphi elimination-certificate idea.
fleet.lay_summary: Before a new building material can be sold, it has to be burned in a standard test and given a grade. In Europe the grade is a letter from A1 down to F, and in the US the tests have names like ASTM E84 and E119. The tests are done only by approved laboratories, and I found a lab company saying there is not enough approved capacity in the UK, and a Danish lab saying testers face long waiting times. One big US wood fire test program cost half a million to a million dollars. Plant-based flame retardants such as phytic acid and chitosan look good in small lab tests, but those small tests are not the ones the building rules use, so a computer-side filter could save test slots only if it predicts the official test results. I could not find published counts of labs, queue times in weeks, or price lists.

findings.claim: EN 13501-1 Euroclass A1 requires EN ISO 1182 (furnace) and EN ISO 1716 (bomb calorimeter) with temperature rise <= 30 C, mass loss <= 50%, no sustained flaming, and gross calorific potential <= 2.0 MJ/kg for main components.
findings.value: dT<=30 C; mass loss<=50%; tf=0 s; PCS<=2.0 MJ/kg (A1); A2: dT<=50 C, tf<=20 s, PCS<=3.0 MJ/kg
findings.source: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2016/364/data.htm (Table 1 as reproduced; fetched 2026-11-13). This is the 2016 Commission Delegated Regulation text, not the EN 13501-1:2018 standard itself, so the edition of the standard behind the numbers is not confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: A1: tf = 0 (i.e. no sustained flaming)

findings.claim: Euroclass B requires the SBI (EN 13823) FIGRA <= 120 W/s, THR600s <= 7.5 MJ and lateral flame spread short of the specimen edge, plus EN ISO 11925-2 with 30 s exposure and Fs <= 150 mm within 60 s. Class C: FIGRA <= 250 W/s, THR600s <= 15 MJ. Class D: FIGRA <= 750 W/s. Class E: small-flame test only, Fs <= 150 mm within 20 s (15 s exposure).
findings.evidence_quote: B: FIGRA ≤ 120 Ws– 1; and LFS < edge of specimen; and THR600s ≤ 7,5 MJ

findings.claim: ASTM E84 grades materials by Flame Spread Index: Class A 0-25, Class B 26-75, Class C 76-200, each with Smoke Developed Index up to 450; the standard specimen is 24 in wide by 24 ft long and the test runs 10 minutes.
findings.value: FSI A 0-25, B 26-75, C 76-200; SDI max 450; 24 in x 24 ft; 10 min
findings.source: https://intertek.com/building/standards/astm-e84 (fetched 2026-11-13). astm.org page returned 403, so edition (believed E84-25 from memory, UNVERIFIED) not confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: The standard test specimen size is 24 inches wide by 24 feet long.

findings.claim: UL 94 vertical burn V-0 requires afterflame <= 10 s per specimen after each flame application, <= 50 s total for five specimens, afterglow <= 30 s, and no cotton ignition by drips; V-1 allows <= 30 s each and <= 250 s total; V-2 allows cotton ignition.
findings.value: V-0: 10 s / 50 s total / 30 s afterglow; V-1,V-2: 30 s / 250 s / 60 s; five specimens
findings.source: https://mgchemicals.com/knowledgebase/white-papers/understanding-the-ul94-vertical-burn-test/ (fetched 2026-11-13); secondary explainer, not the UL standard text, edition not stated.
findings.evidence_quote: Testing uses five prepared samples.

findings.evidence_quote: ISO 5660-1:2015 specifies a method for assessing the heat release rate and dynamic smoke production rate of specimens

findings.claim: Phytic acid-based layer-by-layer coating on cotton: untreated LOI 18-19%; 8 bilayers LOI 26%, 15 bilayers 31%; pHRR reduction 57.0% (8 BL) to 63.3% (15 BL), average ~61%; 10+ bilayers pass vertical flame test with 0 s afterflame; add-on 12.4-20.1%.
findings.value: LOI 18->26-31%; pHRR -57 to -63% (microscale calorimetry per search summary); add-on 12-20%
findings.evidence_quote: applying 10 or more bilayers renders cotton self-extinguishing and able to pass the vertical flame test.

findings.claim: Phytic acid / polyvinylamine LbL coating on cotton: MCC pHRR 216 W/g uncoated vs 42.8 W/g at 15 bilayers; THR 10.7 vs 4.2 kJ/g; TGA residue at 700 C under N2 8.7% vs 29.1%; 15 BL add-on 18.8% (2.0% P, 1.4% N); afterflame 64 s burn-down vs 0 s. LOI and time to ignition not reported.
findings.evidence_quote: uncoated fabric burned completely down within 64 s, while 10 and 15 BL showed 0 s

findings.claim: Mycelium-wheat grain composites in the cone calorimeter at 50 kW/m2: peak heat release about 200 kW/m2 for the 0-day control and about 180 kW/m2 for 6-18 day composites; TGA residue ~23 wt% at 600 C vs 19 wt% for grain. Time to ignition measured but not tabulated in text.
findings.evidence_quote: approximately 23 wt% remaining at 600 °C compared to 19 wt% for wheat grains at the same temperature.

findings.claim: Review of biomass wood flame retardants quotes phytic-acid-based treatments giving wood LOI of 37.2% (cellulose lumen treatment) and 31.8% (phytic acid + uracil). The page text gave no pHRR/THR/char numbers for chitosan or lignin; tannin not covered in the part read.

key_claims.claim: Regulatory reaction-to-fire grades are set by large-scale or standardised tests (SBI FIGRA/THR600s, E84 flame-spread index, UL 94 burn times), not by the LOI / cone / MCC numbers that bio-based chemistry papers report, so lab-scale gains cannot be assumed to translate into a grade.

key_claims.claim: Testing capacity is described as a constraint by labs themselves (UK UKAS capacity shortage; Nordic long waiting times), and full-scale programs can cost USD 0.5-1M, but no published queue times in weeks, per-test prices or lab counts were found.

fleet.label: lf-green-retardants
fleet.topic: Bio-based flame-retardant coatings on wood, textiles and bio-composites: reported fire-test numbers, and what the FireCoatingCertificate.lean bounds can eliminate or keep
fleet.summary:
Harvested 16 papers with reported fire numbers; all 17 DOIs (16 papers plus one preprint) redirect at doi.org (HTTP 302). Every number comes from the Europe PMC abstract record, read through a summarising fetch tool, not from full texts, so the quotes are tool-extracted and need a spot check before reuse.

Coverage is uneven. Peak-HRR reduction and LOI are well covered. Time to ignition appears in one paper only (32 to 69 s). Char yield appears in one paper only (23.80% to 38.10%). No paper with numbers was found for casein or DNA coatings, and the mineral/clay entry is an impregnation, not a surface coating.

What the Lean bounds can do with these numbers:
- **Nothing is eliminated outright.** No abstract gives coating thickness, conductivity, char thickness, heat flux or burn duration, which are the hypotheses the certificates need.
- **LOI claims are out of scope.** The file has no oxygen or gas-phase theorem, so LOI values can be neither eliminated nor kept.
- **Back-face insulation (sections 1-2):** thin layer-by-layer films would add almost no d/k, so `steady_eliminates` would rule them out as insulators unless a char term (`char_eliminates`, needs xmax and kcmin) rescues them. This is my reasoning from typical film thicknesses, not from a sourced thickness.
- **Ignition (section 5):** the one time-to-ignition claim (hydrogel/MXene on wood, 32 to 69 s) is kept, not eliminated. A coating that is 90% water or more plausibly raises thermal inertia enough, and evaporation is outside the no-loss model anyway. For thin fabrics, `thin_ignition_eliminates` caps ignition delay by areal heat capacity, so a large delay claimed for a light coating on cotton would be eliminable; none of these abstracts makes such a claim.
- **Peak HRR (section 6, `hrr_eliminates`):** this is the only bound I could apply numerically. For the chitosan/graphene oxide/APP coating on wood, THR divided by HRR gives a minimum burn window of about 597 s coated (34.31 MJ/m2 over 57.51 kW/m2) and 592 s uncoated (62.43 over 105.50). The claim survives only if the test burned at least about 10 minutes. For the cotton paper reporting pHRR down 87.7% and THR down 63.7%, the minimum burn window must grow about 2.95 times relative to untreated; this is checkable against the HRR curve.
- **Reductions where THR falls at least as much as the peak** (44.1/55.4, 25/54, 77/75, 67/80) impose no extra burn-time demand and are kept trivially.

The only file I wrote is the DOI resolution log for the second batch, at D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/lf-green-retardants/doi_resolution_batch2.txt. The time limit ran out before I wrote a findings data file.

findings.claim: Applying the same bound to Li P 2026 (pHRR -87.7%, THR -63.7%): the minimum burn window (THR/pHRR) must be about 2.95 times that of untreated cotton. This is a testable consequence against the published HRR curve, not an elimination.

findings.claim: No candidate can be formally eliminated from abstract-level data. The certificates need coating thickness and conductivity envelopes (steady_eliminates), char thickness and conductivity (char_eliminates), thermal inertia and imposed flux (thick/thin_ignition_eliminates) or fuel mass and burn time (hrr_eliminates), none of which the abstracts report. LOI claims are outside the file's scope entirely.
findings.confidence: high for the scope statement (file read in full to line 299); the hypotheses needed are those in the theorem statements

findings.claim: The single time-to-ignition claim (hydrogel coating, 32 to 69 s) is kept rather than eliminated: tigThick scales linearly with thermal inertia, and a coating that is mostly water plausibly more than doubles surface inertia; evaporation is also outside the no-loss model, which only makes ignition later.
findings.evidence_quote: water content ≥ 90 wt%
findings.confidence: low-medium: qualitative argument from general material properties, no sourced kρc values and no heat flux in the abstract

key_claims: 16 papers harvested with reported fire numbers; all 17 DOIs (including one preprint) redirect at doi.org.
All numbers are abstract-level, read from Europe PMC records through a summarising tool; no full text was opened.
Time to ignition was found in one paper (32 to 69 s) and char yield in one paper (23.80% to 38.10%).
No abstract supplies the inputs needed for a formal elimination under FireCoatingCertificate.lean; LOI is outside its scope.
The fuel-load bound gives two checkable consequences: a burn window of about 10 minutes for the Yan 2022 wood coating, and a 2.95-fold longer minimum burn window for the Li 2026 cotton coating.
Thin layer-by-layer films would fail any back-face insulation criterion unless their char layer supplies the resistance; this is reasoning, not a sourced result.
could_not_find: Any paper with quantitative fire numbers for a casein coating (search returned none)
Any paper with quantitative fire numbers for a DNA coating (search returned none)
A mineral/clay surface nanocoating with numbers; the only clay entry is a montmorillonite impregnation of poplar
Tannin as the main flame retardant; tannic acid appears only as a curing agent in one resin coating
Time-to-ignition numbers beyond one paper; char-yield numbers beyond one paper
Coating thickness, thermal conductivity, char thickness, cone heat flux or burn duration for any paper (not in abstracts)
Full texts: none were opened, so no number was checked against a table or figure
Carosio et al. 2012 (Carbohydrate Polymers) appeared in the search but its abstract gives time to ignition only qualitatively; not used
Which two quantities fell by 89.3% and 49.3% in Shi H 2024
recommendations: Open the full texts of the three open-access papers (Sci Rep 10.1038/s41598-023-28228-5, ACS Omega 10.1021/acsomega.2c03624, Front Chem 10.3389/fchem.2024.1503694) to get heat flux, burn duration and coating thickness, then instantiate hrr_eliminates and thick_ignition_eliminates with real numbers.
Check the Yan 2022 HRR curve: if flaming ended well before about 590 s, the reported HRR/THR pair is inconsistent with the energy bound.
Check the Li P 2026 HRR curve for the roughly threefold longer burn the bound requires.
Resolve the Wang Y 2023 percentage (17.5% stated, about 14.9% from the two values) against the full text before quoting it.
Run separate searches for casein, DNA and clay nanocoatings in a database with better coverage of Polymer Degradation and Stability and ACS Nano; Europe PMC abstract search returned nothing for them.
Spot-check each quote against the publisher abstract before any nanopublication, since the quotes were extracted by a summarising tool.
lay_summary: Scientists are making fire-protecting coatings for wood and cloth out of natural things like plant acids, shellfish shells and seaweed.
I collected 16 studies and wrote down how much each coating cut the fire's strongest heat, usually by a fifth up to almost nine tenths.
I only read the short summaries of the studies, not the whole papers, so the numbers still need a second check.
The project's maths rules can throw out a coating only when they know how thick it is and how long the fire test burned, and the summaries do not say that.
So nothing was thrown out yet, but the maths did give two simple checks, such as 'this wood test must have burned for about ten minutes'.

glossary.cone calorimeter: A lab machine that heats a small sample with a cone-shaped heater and measures how much heat it gives off as it burns.
glossary.HRR (heat release rate): How fast a burning sample gives off heat, in kilowatts per square metre.
glossary.pHRR (peak heat release rate): The highest heat release rate reached during the test.
glossary.THR (total heat release): All the heat given off over the whole test, in megajoules per square metre.
glossary.TSP (total smoke production): All the smoke given off over the whole test.
glossary.LOI (limiting oxygen index): The smallest percentage of oxygen in the surrounding gas that keeps the sample burning; higher means harder to burn.
glossary.time to ignition (TTI): How many seconds the heated sample takes to catch fire.
glossary.char yield / char residue: The share of the sample left as black carbon crust after burning.
glossary.UL-94 V0: The best grade in a standard small-flame test; the sample stops burning quickly without dripping flames.
glossary.layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly: Building a coating by dipping the material alternately in two solutions that stick to each other, one thin layer at a time.
glossary.bilayer (BL): One pair of layers in a layer-by-layer coating.
glossary.phytic acid: A phosphorus-rich acid found in seeds and grains.
glossary.chitosan: A substance made from the shells of shrimp and crabs.
glossary.lignin: The stiff natural glue in wood.
glossary.tannic acid: A plant substance found in bark and tea.
glossary.montmorillonite: A kind of clay made of very thin plates.
glossary.MXene: A man-made material of very thin metal-carbide sheets.
glossary.graphene oxide: Very thin sheets of carbon with oxygen attached.
glossary.hydrogel: A soft solid that is mostly water held in a network.
glossary.impregnation: Soaking a treatment into the body of the wood instead of painting it on the surface.
glossary.delignified wood: Wood with its lignin removed, leaving a porous cellulose frame.
glossary.intumescent: Swelling into a thick foam-like char when heated.
glossary.thermal conductivity (k): How easily heat flows through a material.
glossary.thermal resistance (d/k): How strongly a layer of thickness d blocks heat flow.
glossary.thermal inertia (kρc): How slowly a surface heats up; the product of conductivity, density and heat capacity.
glossary.back-face temperature rise: How much hotter the side away from the fire becomes.
glossary.thermally thin / thick: Thin means the whole sample heats evenly; thick means the far side has not yet felt the heat.
glossary.heat flux: Heat energy arriving per square metre per second.
glossary.fuel load: The amount of burnable material per unit area.
glossary.elimination certificate: A proof that a candidate must fail a stated test under stated assumptions; it can rule out but never approve.
glossary.DOI: A permanent identifier for a published paper.
glossary.Europe PMC: A free online index of research paper records and abstracts.

fleet.label: lf-lean-fire
fleet.topic: Can Lean elimination certificates on 1-D heat laws help design bio-based fire-retardant coatings and cut physical fire tests?
fleet.summary: Yes, narrowly. Seven simple laws (series resistance and back-face bound, char as added resistance, thermal penetration depth, lumped transient, thin/thick ignition time with critical flux, energy-balance bound on peak HRR) were proved in one Lean file with 16 theorems, all using only the three standard axioms; check.sh passed (0 errors, 0 sorryAx) and a negative control failed as required. Each certificate eliminates a candidate whose best case, inside a declared envelope of thickness, conductivity, thermal inertia and time constant, already breaks a stated limit. It can never approve one: real regulation tests also measure flaming, smoke, flame spread and delamination, which these laws do not model. The registry (upstream/leanbio) has no heat-conduction law, only a diffusive time scale h^2/D and a note that Fick is used as a definition. The saving in tests depends on how many candidates fail on one thermal criterion alone, which is unknown until material data exist; the main risk is a wrong envelope or lumped time constant, which cheap property measurements (not fire tests) can settle.
lay_summary: A fire test asks, among other things, whether the back of a coated board gets too hot too fast.
Simple physics can sometimes say in advance that a coating is too thin or too conductive to ever pass that one question.
We wrote that physics in Lean, a proof checker, so the claim that a candidate cannot pass is checked by machine.
This only works as a way to skip hopeless candidates; it never says a coating is safe.
Fire, smoke, flame spread and peeling are not covered, so every survivor still needs a real test.

findings.claim: Series thermal resistance: layer resistance is thickness/(k A) and series resistances add.
findings.evidence_quote: When resistances are in series, the total resistance is the sum of the resistances
findings.confidence: high (standard law; textbooks Quintiere/Drysdale cited by DOI but not opened)

findings.claim: Proved in Lean: the steady back-face rise DT*Ra/(d/k+Rs+Ra) is at most DT, falls with thickness, and has a lower bound from dmax and kmin; a candidate whose best case exceeds the limit is eliminated (steady state only).
findings.evidence_quote: check.sh: errors=0 sorryAx=0 axiom-lines=16/16
findings.confidence: high for the algebra; the 1-D constant-k model is an assumption

findings.claim: Steady state is an upper bound on a finite-time heating, so a steady bound alone cannot eliminate at a finite test time. A one-node response with time constant at most tau_max is stated as a hypothesis and used.
findings.evidence_quote: passed check.sh
findings.confidence: high for the proof; medium for physical validity (no PDE comparison theorem was proved)

findings.claim: A char layer as an added series resistance can only lower the steady rise; elimination with envelope on char thickness and conductivity is proved.
findings.evidence_quote: a thermal conductivity model for the fully expanded intumescent coating char, which was assumed to depend on the expansion thickness and the bubble size and distribution (Crossref abstract)
findings.confidence: high for algebra; real char conductivity depends on temperature and morphology so kc_min must be justified

findings.claim: A slab is thermally thick while the penetration depth c*sqrt(alpha t) <= d, equivalently t <= d^2/(c^2 alpha), for any convention constant c>0.
findings.evidence_quote: passed check.sh

findings.claim: Thin solid with surface loss h never ignites below the critical flux h(Tig-T0) and reaches Tig above it at an explicit time; thick and thin ignition times give elimination given upper bounds on thermal inertia or heat capacity.
findings.source: SFPE Engineering Guide: Piloted Ignition of Solid Materials Under Radiant Exposure (https://www.globalspec.com/reference/76862/203279/thermally-thick, search snippet only); Mikkola and Wichman 1989, 10.1002/fam.810140303 (Crossref-verified, not opened)
findings.evidence_quote: An approximate solution to the time to ignition is derived using the first term of the series expansion and substituting the ignition temperature for the surface temperature. (search snippet)
findings.confidence: medium: t=(pi/4) k rho c (Tig-T0)^2/q^2 is the standard first-term form but I did not read it in a fetched text; the Lean statement is conditional on that definition

findings.claim: Energy balance gives a lower bound on peak HRR: if all fuel burns in n windows of dt, peak >= E/(n dt) >= chi_min m_min dH_min/(n dt). Energy alone gives no upper bound on peak HRR.
findings.evidence_quote: passed check.sh
findings.confidence: high for the proof; the all-fuel-in-window assumption is strong

findings.claim: Registry check: upstream/leanbio has no heat-conduction, thermal-resistance, ignition or HRR law. Near misses: diffusiveTime h^2/D and diffusiveRate (ThompsonLaws/Hygromorphs.lean), Turing no_instability_of_equal_diffusivity, a Q10 thermal performance curve (Delphi/Perturb.lean), Fick used as a definition (docs/physlib-overlap.md). All seven laws in the table are new to it.

findings.confidence: high for the grep; Mathlib and physlib were not searched for heat laws

key_claims: Elimination certificates on 1-D conduction, char resistance, lumped transient, ignition time and fuel-load energy are provable in Lean/Mathlib today with explicit hypotheses and no new axioms.
They can only reject candidates that break a limit even in their best case inside a stated envelope; they cannot approve any.
The saving in fire tests is bounded by how many candidates fail one thermal criterion; unknown until measured material data exist.
The hypotheses (envelopes, lumped time constant, burn window) carry the real risk; a wrong envelope makes a certificate wrong.

recommendations: Use the certificate only as a pre-screen, after measuring k, density, c and char conductivity of each candidate on small bench samples; those inputs make the envelopes honest.
Pick one concrete regulation criterion, fetch its text, and restate the limit and fire-side temperature curve; I fetched no regulation, so 400 K and 800 K in the worked example are placeholders.
Prove a PDE-level comparison theorem for a layered slab so the lumped time-constant hypothesis can go; not done here.
Make each elimination print its hypotheses so a lab can falsify the envelope cheaply.
Never present survivors as compliant; budget real tests for all of them.

fleet.label: lf-mogas
fleet.topic: Laia Mogas-Soldevila (UPenn Weitzman, DumoLab): biopolymer work and its overlap with green fire coatings and fire-test capacity
fleet.summary: Sources fetched 2026-11-13: profile page, dumolab.com, Crossref author query (filtered to her name), PubMed (5 records), arXiv (none). Her work is printed bio-based materials (chitosan, cellulose/wood biomass, silk, agarose, food-waste composites) with water-based fabrication, funded by Penn funds, NSF, J&J Foundation and ONR. Overlap with fire-retardant coatings is thin in the public record: the profile does not mention fire, and one 2026 conference abstract (Eggregate) reports surface charring as fire resistance in a cladding composite. Nothing public was found on the fire-test labor shortage; that comes only from Amit's seminar account.
lay_summary: Laia Mogas-Soldevila runs a design lab at the University of Pennsylvania that prints building materials from natural polymers such as chitosan, cellulose and silk, using water instead of harsh solvents.
Her chitosan prints fold themselves into shape as they dry, which is the same idea as the hygromorph bilayers in this track.
Her public papers barely mention fire; one 2026 abstract says a food-waste cladding resisted fire by charring.
We found nothing public about fire-regulation testing or a shortage of testers, so that link rests on what she said in the seminar.
Any fit with DELPHI is a hypothesis, and no one has been contacted.

fleet.label: lf-standards-eu-uk
fleet.topic: EU and UK reaction-to-fire classes (A1-F) with numeric thresholds, and the class required of timber / bio-based wall and ceiling linings, from open official sources
fleet.summary:
The Euroclass thresholds A1-F, the smoke and droplet sub-classes, the UK lining requirements and the no-test class for cross-laminated timber are all confirmed from open official sources; ISO 5660 and standard edition years are not.

Sources opened: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/364 (annex, via legislation.gov.uk, because the EUR-Lex HTML link returned only a journal header), Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/2293 (annex), and Approved Document B Volume 2 (gov.uk PDF, text extracted locally and read directly).

One caveat on the 2016/364 numbers: they reached me through the fetch tool's summariser, which paraphrased the table and said it kept numbers and units exact. I did not see the raw table bytes, so re-check them against the annex before putting them in a record.

**Main-class thresholds (all CONFIRMED-OPEN-SOURCE, 2016/364 Table 1):**

| Class | SBI test (EN 13823) | Small-flame test (EN ISO 11925-2) | Other |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | none | none | Furnace: temperature rise <= 30 C, mass loss <= 50 %, no sustained flaming. Calorific potential <= 2.0 MJ/kg (<= 1.4 MJ/m2 for internal non-substantial components) |
| A2 | FIGRA <= 120 W/s, THR600s <= 7.5 MJ, no flame spread to specimen edge | none | Furnace: temperature rise <= 50 C, mass loss <= 50 %, flaming <= 20 s; or calorific potential <= 3.0 MJ/kg (<= 4.0 MJ/m2 for non-substantial components) |
| B | FIGRA <= 120 W/s, THR600s <= 7.5 MJ, no flame spread to edge | Fs <= 150 mm within 60 s (30 s exposure) | |
| C | FIGRA <= 250 W/s, THR600s <= 15 MJ, no flame spread to edge | Fs <= 150 mm within 60 s (30 s exposure) | |
| D | FIGRA <= 750 W/s | Fs <= 150 mm within 60 s (30 s exposure) | |
| E | none | Fs <= 150 mm within 20 s (15 s exposure) | |
| F | none | Fs > 150 mm within 20 s | Approved Document B words it as "fails to attain class E" |

**Sub-classes (CONFIRMED-OPEN-SOURCE):**
- **Smoke:** s1 is SMOGRA <= 30 m2/s2 and TSP600s <= 50 m2; s2 is SMOGRA <= 180 m2/s2 and TSP600s <= 200 m2; s3 is neither.
- **Droplets:** d0 is no flaming droplets within 600 s; d1 is none lasting longer than 10 s; d2 is neither.

**UK lining requirements (CONFIRMED-OPEN-SOURCE, Approved Document B Vol 2, Table 6.1, read directly):**
- Small rooms (up to 4 m2 residential, 30 m2 non-residential): D-s3, d2.
- Other rooms, including garages: C-s3, d2.
- Other circulation spaces: B-s3, d2.

lay_summary: Europe and the UK grade building materials by how much they feed a fire, from A1 (does not burn, like stone) down to F (burns easily or was never tested).
The grade comes from tests: a small flame held on the material, and a bigger burner in a room corner that measures how fast the fire grows and how much heat comes out.
The law gives exact number limits for each grade, and we found those numbers in the official published rule.
Thick solid wood panels are officially grade D, which is in the lower half.
UK guidance says walls and ceilings in normal rooms should be grade C and in corridors grade B, so bare wood there usually needs a fire-protecting treatment or covering.

glossary.reaction to fire: How much a material itself adds to a fire when it is heated or lit.
glossary.Euroclass: The European grade A1, A2, B, C, D, E or F for reaction to fire; A1 is best.
glossary.EN 13501-1: The European standard that sets out how test results are turned into a Euroclass.
glossary.SBI (EN 13823): Single Burning Item test: a burner in a corner made of the material, with the heat and smoke measured for about 20 minutes.
glossary.FIGRA: Fire growth rate index, in watts per second: how fast the fire's heat output climbs. Lower is safer.
glossary.THR600s: Total heat released in the first 600 seconds (10 minutes) of the SBI test, in megajoules.
glossary.LFS: Lateral flame spread: whether flames travel sideways to the edge of the test panel.
glossary.EN ISO 11925-2: Small-flame test: a match-sized flame is held on the material for 15 or 30 seconds.
glossary.Fs: How far the flame climbs up the sample in the small-flame test, in millimetres.
glossary.EN ISO 1182: Furnace test for whether a material burns at all (temperature rise, mass loss, flaming time).
glossary.EN ISO 1716 / PCS: Test that burns a sample completely to measure the total heat it could give off (gross calorific potential), in MJ/kg or MJ/m2.
glossary.SMOGRA: Smoke growth rate: how fast smoke production rises in the SBI test.
glossary.TSP600s: Total smoke produced in the first 600 seconds of the SBI test.
glossary.s1, s2, s3: Smoke grades; s1 is least smoke, s3 means no limit.
glossary.d0, d1, d2: Burning-droplet grades; d0 means none, d2 means no limit.
glossary.lining: The surface material on a wall or ceiling that faces into the room.
glossary.circulation space: Corridors, lobbies and stairs that people use to move around and escape.
glossary.Approved Document B: The UK government's official guidance on meeting the fire-safety part of the Building Regulations in England.
glossary.Classification Without Further Testing (: An official list of products given a fire grade by law so each maker need not re-test.
glossary.cross-laminated timber (CLT): Thick panels made by gluing layers of boards at right angles.
glossary.laminated veneer lumber (LVL): Beams or panels made by gluing many thin sheets of wood together.
glossary.cone calorimeter (ISO 5660): A bench test that heats a small square sample under a cone-shaped heater and measures the heat released.
glossary.bio-based: Made from plants or other living material, such as wood.
glossary.fire-retardant treatment: A chemical soak or coating that makes a material harder to burn.
glossary.DFL-s1: A flooring fire grade (D for floors) with the lowest smoke grade.

lay_summary: In the US, paint or coating on indoor walls and ceilings is graded by a tunnel test that measures how fast flame travels along it and how much smoke it makes.
The best grade, Class A, means a flame-spread score of 0 to 25; Class B is 26 to 75 and Class C is 76 to 200, and all three must keep the smoke score at 450 or less.

Another route is a room-corner test, where a burner is lit in the corner of a test room: the fire must stay under 800 kilowatts, the smoke under 1,000 square metres, and the room must not burst into full flame.
I confirmed these numbers from the 2021 building code text and from federal rules, but could not open the newest 2024 code.
The numbers for puffy fire-protective paint on steel and for the small cone-heater test are not confirmed, because I only saw them in search snippets.

glossary.ASTM E84 / UL 723: The tunnel test: a strip of material is burned in a long tunnel to score flame spread and smoke.
glossary.Flame spread index: A score for how fast flame travels along a surface; lower is safer.
glossary.Smoke-developed index: A score for how much smoke the material gives off in the tunnel test; lower is safer.
glossary.Class A / B / C: Building-code grades for interior finishes based on the tunnel test scores; A is the best.
glossary.NFPA 286: A room-corner fire test where a burner is lit in the corner of a room lined with the material.
glossary.Flashover: The moment a room fire suddenly ignites everything in the room at once.
glossary.Heat release rate (kW): How much heat a fire gives off each second, in kilowatts.
glossary.Total smoke released (m2): A measure of how much smoke the test produced, expressed as an area of light blocked.
glossary.ASTM E119 / UL 263: A furnace test that measures how many hours a wall, floor, beam or column survives a standard fire.
glossary.ASTM E1354 (cone calorimeter): A small bench test where a cone-shaped heater burns a sample to measure heat output.
glossary.ASTM E1740: A test for wall and ceiling coverings that uses the cone calorimeter.
glossary.Intumescent coating: A paint that swells into a thick insulating foam when heated, protecting what is underneath.
glossary.Fire-retardant coating: A coating that slows the spread of flame over a surface.
glossary.IBC: International Building Code, the model building code most US states adopt.
glossary.IFC: International Fire Code, the companion model fire code.
glossary.NFPA 101: The Life Safety Code published by the National Fire Protection Association.
glossary.eCFR: The free online version of US federal regulations.
glossary.Edition year: The year a particular version of a standard or code was published.
glossary.Interior finish: The exposed surface material on indoor walls and ceilings.
glossary.CONFIRMED-OPEN-SOURCE / UNCONFIRMED: Whether I read the number on a freely available page I opened, or not.

fleet.summary: Partial result in about 7 minutes: five pages opened and read, the rest is search-snippet only and marked as such. Only one provider (Measurlabs, a Finnish testing broker) publishes prices and sample sizes: cone calorimeter ISO 5660-1 at 928 EUR per sample plus a 97 EUR order fee, needing 6 pieces of 100 mm x 100 mm; SBI EN 13823 at 1,978 EUR per sample, needing 3-5 corner specimens 1.5 m tall. No page I opened states a testing lead time. In the US north-east, VTEC Laboratories (Bronx, NY) offers ASTM E1354 and says it is ISO 17025 accredited, with no price shown. WPI lists two cone calorimeters but its page says nothing about taking outside samples. I confirmed no UK university lab that takes outside samples. For open data, the NIST Fire Calorimetry Database appears (search snippet only) to hold large-scale tests rather than cone data; the MaCFP material database on GitHub (MIT licence) is the more likely open source of bench-scale data, but the page I opened showed only PMMA and Wood folders and did not itself mention cone calorimeter. Cheapest practical route for a coating: cone calorimeter (small 100 mm squares) rather than E84 (24 ft specimen) or SBI (1.5 m corner).
