lay_summary: To show a new coating is safe in a fire, a lab burns pieces of it and measures how much heat and smoke come off.
The smallest test needs only six squares about the size of a coaster, and one company lists it at about 928 euros per sample.
The bigger tests need a piece as tall as a door or as long as a bus, so they cost more and need much more material.
We found a lab in New York that does the small test and a university in Massachusetts that owns the machines, but neither says its price or how long it takes.
There is some free burn-test data online, but we could not confirm it has the right kind of test for a coating.

glossary.cone calorimeter: A bench-top machine that heats a small flat sample with a cone-shaped heater and measures how much heat and smoke it gives off as it burns.
glossary.ISO 5660-1 / ASTM E1354: The international and American written rules for how to run a cone calorimeter test.
glossary.ASTM E84 (tunnel test): An American test that burns a long strip of material along the ceiling of a tunnel to see how fast flame spreads and how much smoke is made.
glossary.ASTM D3806: A small 2-foot version of the tunnel test used to screen fire-retardant paints.
glossary.SBI / EN 13823: Single Burning Item: a European test that burns a room-corner-shaped specimen to rate building products.
glossary.accredited: Checked by an official body to confirm the lab runs a test properly.
glossary.ISO 17025: The international standard a testing lab is checked against to be called accredited.
glossary.UKAS: The United Kingdom's official body that accredits labs; its 'schedule' lists exactly which tests a lab is approved for.
glossary.specimen: One piece of material prepared for a test.
glossary.lead time: How long you wait between sending a sample and getting results.
glossary.heat release rate: How fast a burning material gives off heat; the main number a cone calorimeter reports.
glossary.NIST FCD: Fire Calorimetry Database of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, a public collection of fire experiment measurements.
glossary.MaCFP: Measurement and Computation of Fire Phenomena, a research group that shares burn-test data openly.
glossary.PMMA: Acrylic plastic (Perspex), a standard reference material in fire tests.
glossary.bio-based coating: A paint-like layer made from biological materials rather than petroleum.
glossary.MIT licence: A permissive licence that lets anyone reuse the data or code freely.
glossary.VAT: Value-added tax, a sales tax added to the listed price in Europe.

fleet.label: lf-verify-lean
fleet.topic: Independent re-check of lf-lean-fire.json and FireCoatingCertificate.lean: are the heat formulas right, and does each theorem say what its docstring claims?
fleet.summary:
The formulas are the standard ones, but three of the elimination theorems are unsafe as physical certificates. The two ignition eliminations use no-loss ignition times, which are lower bounds on the real ignition time, so "formula time < treq" does not show the material ignites before treq. The finite-time elimination has no hypothesis linking the one-node curve to the real back face, although its docstring says it does. I did not run Lean (7-minute budget), so this is a read of the statements, not a re-check of the proofs. I wrote no files and changed nothing in the repo; the fixes are listed as recommendations.

Sources: I opened one page (Wikipedia, Lumped-element model), which confirms series resistance, the lumped transient and its time constant. The thick-ignition formula and the penetration depth are not confirmed from an opened text: the SFPE guide page and a UCL paper both returned HTTP 403.

Verdict per claim:
- CONFIRMED: series resistance R = d/k + Rs + Ra and the steady back-face rise algebra (backRise_le_ΔT, backRise_antitone_thickness, backRise_lower, steady_eliminates, char_lowers_rise, char_eliminates). Caveat: there is no fire-side film resistance, so ΔT must be the coating-surface temperature minus ambient; using gas temperature overstates the rise.
- CONFIRMED: lumped transient Tss(1 - exp(-t/τ)) with τ = C/h, and relax_ode. The Biot-number validity condition (< 0.1) appears nowhere in the file.
- CONFIRMED (algebra only): thick_iff_time matches its docstring exactly. The sqrt(αt) depth itself was not found in an opened source.
- CONFIRMED: thin solid with loss (thinTemp, thin_never_ignites, critical flux h(Tig - T0)).
- WEAKER: thin_reaches_Tig shows the temperature equals Tig at t*, but not that t* is positive or the first such time.
- UNVERIFIED-SOURCE: tigThick = (π/4)·kρc·ΔT²/q². It agrees with the semi-infinite constant-flux solution as I recall it, but I opened no text containing it.
- WEAKER and UNSAFE: thick_ignition_eliminates and thin_ignition_eliminates. Docstring: "prove ignition happens before the required non-ignition time". Statement: only that the no-loss formula value is below treq. Inside the file's own lossy thin model, t* = -(C/h)·ln(1 - x) ≥ C·ΔT/q, so real ignition is later than tigThin. Neither theorem requires the thick or thin regime (no link to thick_iff_time), and ΔTig ≥ 0 is not required in the thick one.
- DIFFERENT: transient_eliminates. Docstring calls the one-node response a "hypothesis, not axiom"; in fact the conclusion is about relax(backRise…) itself. A one-node curve starts rising at once, while a real slab's back face lags, so the bound can overstate early-time rise.
- OVERSTATED: worked_example docstring says "eliminated before any test", but it is steady-state only, which section 1 itself says proves nothing at a finite test time. The arithmetic is right (447.6 K bound, 490.8 K actual).
- CONFIRMED: peak_ge_mean and hrr_eliminates match their docstrings; hχ, hm, hH are unused.
- MINOR (JSON): it says "16 theorems"; the file has 19, with 16 #print axioms lines. Its finding 4 says "passed check.sh" for physics that check.sh cannot test. The section 5 title mentions critical flux, but no critical flux appears in that section.

findings.claim: CONFIRMED: series thermal resistance. Slab resistance is L/(kA), film resistance 1/(hA), and layers in series add; totalR = d/k + Rs + Ra is the per-unit-area form.
findings.evidence_quote: the equivalent resistance is the sum of the resistances of the components
findings.confidence: high. Caveat: the model has no fire-side film resistance, so ΔT must be coating-surface minus ambient; if gas temperature is used the rise is overstated and an elimination is not conservative.

findings.claim: CONFIRMED: lumped transient. The first-order solution is exponential with time constant C/(hA); relax and thinTemp (τ = C/h per unit area) match, and relax_ode states the ODE identity for every t.
findings.evidence_quote: Thus, in thermal systems, t0=C/hA.
findings.confidence: high for the formula. The file never states the validity condition; the same page says the Biot number must generally be less than 0.1.

findings.claim: DIFFERENT from docstring: transient_eliminates. The docstring says the one-node response is a 'hypothesis, not axiom', but no hypothesis ties any physical temperature to relax; the conclusion is literally about relax (backRise ...) τ t.
findings.value: conclusion: limit < relax (backRise ΔT d k Rs Ra) τ t
findings.evidence_quote: Model assumption (hypothesis, not axiom): the back-face rise follows the one-node response
findings.confidence: high for the statement mismatch. Medium for the physical concern (a one-node curve rises immediately while a slab's back face lags, so the bound can overstate early rise); that is my own reasoning, with no source opened.

findings.claim: WEAKER and physically UNSAFE: thin_ignition_eliminates and thick_ignition_eliminates. They prove only that the no-loss formula value is below treq, not that ignition happens before treq. In the file's own lossy thin model t* = -(C/h) ln(1-x) with x = h(Tig-T0)/q, and -ln(1-x) >= x gives t* >= C(Tig-T0)/q = tigThin, so real ignition is later than the formula.
findings.value: tigThin is a lower bound on the lossy ignition time; the eliminations need the opposite direction
findings.evidence_quote: enough to prove ignition happens before the required non-ignition time
findings.confidence: high for the thin case (algebra from the file's own definitions). Medium for the thick case (same direction expected by standard reasoning, not derived or sourced here).

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED-SOURCE: thick ignition time t = (π/4)·kρc·(Tig-T0)²/q². It matches the semi-infinite constant-flux surface solution Ts-T0 = 2q·sqrt(t/(π kρc)) as I recall it, but I opened no text containing the formula.
findings.source: https://www.globalspec.com/reference/76862/203279/thermally-thick (HTTP 403, NOT opened); web-search result summary only
findings.confidence: medium: from memory plus a search summary saying the thick exponent on flux is 2 and the thin is 1. The original report's own 'medium' was fair.

findings.claim: CONFIRMED (algebra only): thick_iff_time states exactly what its docstring says, pdepth c α t <= d iff t <= d²/(c²α), for any c > 0.
findings.evidence_quote: exactly while `t ≤ d² / (c² α)`
findings.confidence: high for statement vs docstring. The sqrt(αt) depth was not found in an opened source (Wikipedia Thermal diffusivity and Thermal effusivity do not state it cleanly). The thick/thin test is never used as a hypothesis by the ignition theorems.

findings.claim: CONFIRMED: thin solid with loss. Critical flux h(Tig-T0) and thin_never_ignites match their docstrings. WEAKER: thin_reaches_Tig shows the temperature equals Tig at t* but does not prove t* > 0 or that it is the first crossing (both true, just unstated).
findings.evidence_quote: T(t)=Tenv+(T(0)−Tenv) e−rt
findings.confidence: high. The linear loss h(T-T0) is a linearisation; real surface loss includes radiation.

findings.claim: OVERSTATED docstring: worked_example says the candidate is 'eliminated before any test', but it applies steady_eliminates only, which the file itself says proves nothing at a finite test time. The arithmetic is right.
findings.evidence_quote: Says nothing about a finite test time: see section 5.
findings.confidence: high. That pointer is also wrong: the finite-time material is in section 4, not section 5.

findings.claim: CONFIRMED: steady and char theorems (backRise_le_ΔT, backRise_antitone_thickness, backRise_lower, steady_eliminates, char_lowers_rise, char_eliminates) and the energy theorems (peak_ge_mean, hrr_eliminates) state what their docstrings say.
findings.value: hχ, hm, hH unused in hrr_eliminates; ht, hC unused in thin_never_ignites
findings.evidence_quote: A char layer (thickness `xc ≥ 0`, conductivity `kc > 0`) can only lower the steady rise.
findings.confidence: high by reading; Lean was not re-run. Keeping the full virgin thickness d plus the char overstates resistance, which is the safe direction for elimination.

findings.claim: MINOR, JSON vs file: the report says '16 theorems', but the file has 19 theorem declarations and 16 #print axioms lines (totalR_pos, backRise_lower, relax_lower are not printed, though they are dependencies of printed ones). Section 5's title mentions critical flux but no critical flux appears there. The report's Wikipedia Thermal_resistance quote was not re-opened by me.

key_claims: The formulas for series resistance, lumped transient, thin solid with loss and critical flux are stated correctly; one opened source supports the first two.

thin_ignition_eliminates and thick_ignition_eliminates point the wrong way for a physical elimination: no-loss ignition times are lower bounds on the real ignition time (shown for the thin case from the file's own lossy model).
transient_eliminates has no hypothesis linking a real temperature to the one-node curve, although its docstring says it does.
The worked-example docstring overstates: it is a steady-state result, not an elimination 'before any test'.
The thick-ignition formula and the penetration depth are not confirmed from an opened text; Lean was not re-run.
recommendations: Restate the ignition eliminations with a model that includes loss: the thin case can use thinTemp and thin_reaches_Tig directly; for the thick case add an explicit hypothesis that losses are negligible, or use net flux q - q_cr.
Add the regime as a hypothesis: thick_ignition_eliminates should require pdepth <= d at the ignition time, thin_ignition_eliminates the opposite or a Biot-number bound.

Rewrite transient_eliminates to take a real temperature function Tb with hypothesis Tb t >= relax (...) τ t, so the model assumption is visibly a hypothesis; or change the docstring to say the theorem is about the model curve only.
Add a fire-side film resistance to totalR, or state in the docstring that ΔT is coating-surface temperature minus ambient.
Change the worked_example docstring to 'steady-state rise exceeds the limit', drop 'eliminated before any test', and fix the 'see section 5' pointer to section 4.
Add the two small lemmas missing from thin_reaches_Tig: t* > 0, and thinTemp < Tig for t < t*.
Correct the JSON count to 19 theorems (16 axiom checks) and keep the thick-ignition formula marked unverified until a text is opened (Quintiere 2006 ch. 7 or the SFPE guide, via library access).
lay_summary: Another agent wrote maths rules about how heat moves through a painted board and had a computer check the maths.
I checked whether those rules match the physics pages I could open, and whether each rule really says what its label says.
The basic heat rules are right.
But two rules about when something catches fire ignore heat escaping, so they say fire starts sooner than it really would, which makes them unsafe for ruling out a paint.
One rule about how fast the back of the board warms up is labelled as resting on an assumption that is not actually written into it.

glossary.thermal resistance: how strongly a layer holds back heat flow; thickness divided by conductivity
glossary.series resistance: layers stacked one after another, whose resistances add up
glossary.film resistance: the resistance of the thin air layer at a surface, equal to 1/h
glossary.back-face rise: how much hotter the unheated side of the board gets than the room
glossary.steady state: the final condition after temperatures stop changing
glossary.lumped (one-node) model: treating a whole object as one temperature with a single time constant
glossary.time constant: the time for a warming object to cover about 63% of the way to its final temperature
glossary.Biot number: a ratio that says whether an object is uniform enough inside for the lumped model to hold
glossary.penetration depth: how far into a solid a heating pulse has reached, growing like the square root of time
glossary.thermal diffusivity: how fast temperature changes spread through a material (α)
glossary.thermally thick: the heat pulse has not yet reached the back of the layer
glossary.thermally thin: the layer is so thin that it has nearly one temperature throughout
glossary.thermal inertia: the product kρc; high values mean the surface heats slowly
glossary.heat flux: heating power per unit area hitting the surface
glossary.critical flux: the heating level below which the surface never gets hot enough to ignite
glossary.ignition time: how long heating takes for the surface to reach its ignition temperature
glossary.lower bound: a value the true answer cannot be below
glossary.elimination certificate: a proof that a candidate must fail a stated limit under stated assumptions
glossary.docstring: the plain-language comment written above a theorem
glossary.hypothesis: an assumption written into a theorem that must hold for it to apply
glossary.HRR: heat release rate, the power a burning material gives off
glossary.char: the burnt carbon layer that forms on a heated coating and insulates it

fleet.summary: All three key claims hold on re-fetch (2026-11-13), with two caveats. (1) Chitosan self-folding: SUPPORTED; the quoted sentence is verbatim in both the PubMed and Crossref abstracts. (2) "Only fire-related result": PARTLY; the Eggregate abstract quote is verbatim, but "only" is weaker than it reads, because 17 of her 32 Crossref records carry no abstract and no full text was read. fleet.topic: Independent re-check of the key claims in tracks/research/agents/lf-fire-regs.json (fire-test regulations, test-capacity bottleneck, bio-based flame-retardant numbers)
fleet.summary: I re-fetched 12 of the cited sources on 2026-11-13 and compared them with the claims. Ten claims are SUPPORTED as written: Euroclass thresholds A1 to E, ASTM E84 classes, UL 94 V ratings, ISO 5660-1 status, EN 16623 stage, the UK capacity shortage, the USD 0.5-1M test program, both phytic-acid cotton papers' headline numbers and the mycelium cone numbers. Two are PARTLY supported. (1) The UK Approved Document B claim is out of date against the gov.uk page as I read it: the page now lists the 2019 edition incorporating 2020, 2022, 2025 AND 2026 amendments, collated with the 2029 amendments, and says withdrawal of the national classes (BS 476) "is concluded"; the original said the 2026 amendments were not yet collated and that withdrawal was still in transition. (2) In the Magovac phytic-acid paper the 57.0% pHRR reduction for 8 bilayers was not confirmed in my fetch; the page extract gave 59.5% (10 BL), 62.3% (12 BL), 63.3% (15 BL) and the text '~61%'. The instrument is microscale combustion calorimetry, not a cone calorimeter, which the original states only in the value field. One further caveat: in Zilke et al. the uncoated MCC pHRR of 216 W/g equals the HRC figure in the same table and may be a typo in the paper. Not re-checked for lack of time: DIN EN 13381-8 page, NFPA 285 article, NAHB page, CFPA-E notice, European Accreditation page, the Liang 2023 review, and all snippet-only claims (these stay unverified). All fetches went through a summarising fetch tool, so quotes are as returned by that tool, not from raw page bytes. No files were written.

key_claims: Of 13 claims re-fetched, 11 are supported as written and 2 are partly supported; none were contradicted outright.
The UK Approved Document B entry is stale: the gov.uk page now shows the 2026 amendments incorporated and collated with 2029, and the BS 476 national-class withdrawal described as concluded.
The 57.0% pHRR reduction at 8 bilayers (Magovac 2020) was not confirmed; the confirmed range is 59.5-63.3% for 10-15 bilayers, measured by microscale calorimetry, not cone.
The bottleneck evidence is real but thin: one provider's own press statement and one cost figure for a single program from 2017.
Seven sources and all snippet-only numbers were not re-checked and remain unverified by this pass.
lay_summary: I opened twelve of the web pages the first report relied on and checked whether they really say what the report claimed.
Almost everything matched: the fire-grade numbers for Europe and the US, the lab company saying there are not enough approved test slots in the UK, and the plant-based coating results on cotton.
Two things did not fully match: the UK building guidance page has been updated since the wording in the report, and one percentage for a thin coating could not be found on the page.
Some pages I did not have time to open, so those claims are still unchecked.
The plant-based results are from tiny lab tests, which are not the tests that building rules use.

glossary.Euroclass: The European letter grade (A1 best, F worst) for how a building material reacts to fire.
glossary.FIGRA: Fire growth rate from the European corner test, in watts per second; lower is better.
glossary.THR600s: Total heat given off in the first 600 seconds of that corner test.
glossary.LFS: Lateral flame spread: how far sideways the flame travels across the test panel.
glossary.Fs: Flame spread height in the small-flame test, in millimetres.
glossary.PCS: Gross calorific potential: how much heat a kilogram of material can release when fully burned.
glossary.SBI: Single Burning Item test (EN 13823): a corner of two panels lit by a gas burner.
glossary.ASTM E84: US tunnel test that gives a flame spread index and a smoke index for surface materials.
glossary.FSI / SDI: Flame Spread Index and Smoke Developed Index, the two scores from ASTM E84.
glossary.UL 94: A small vertical burn test for plastics; V-0 is the strictest of the V ratings.
glossary.Afterflame / afterglow: How long a sample keeps flaming or glowing after the test flame is taken away.
glossary.LOI: Limiting oxygen index: the lowest oxygen percentage at which a material keeps burning; higher is safer.
glossary.pHRR: Peak heat release rate: the highest rate at which a burning sample gives off heat.
glossary.THR: Total heat released by a sample during a test.
glossary.HRC: Heat release capacity, another number from the microscale test, in different units from pHRR.
glossary.MCC: Microscale combustion calorimetry: a heat-release test on a few milligrams of material.
glossary.Cone calorimeter: A bench test (ISO 5660) that heats a small square of material and measures the heat it gives off.
glossary.TGA residue: What fraction of a sample is left after slow heating in a furnace balance; more residue means more char.
glossary.Layer-by-layer (LbL) / bilayer (BL): A coating built by dipping fabric alternately in two solutions; each pair of dips is one bilayer.
glossary.Add-on: How much weight the coating adds to the fabric, as a percentage.
glossary.Phytic acid: A phosphorus-rich compound from seeds and grains used as a plant-based flame retardant.
glossary.Mycelium: The root-like body of a fungus, grown through grain or straw to make a material.
glossary.UKAS: The UK body that officially approves test laboratories.
glossary.ISO/IEC 17025 and 17065: International rule sets for approved test labs (17025) and for product certification bodies (17065).
glossary.Approved Document B: The official fire-safety guidance for buildings in England.
glossary.BS 476: The older British fire test standards that the Euroclass system replaces.
glossary.Stage 90.20: A standards-body status code meaning the standard is under its routine periodic review.
glossary.Collated: Amendments merged into one combined document.

fleet.lay_summary: We looked for scientists tied to the Broad Institute, a Boston-area research centre, who study fish. We found three who mainly work on zebrafish, a small see-through fish used as a living window into how bodies form. One studies skin cancer and blood, one studies the liver and skull cartilage, and one maps which genes switch on where in a growing embryo, like a street map of a tiny city. We did not find Broad people working on cave fish, killifish or sticklebacks. Any link to our own projects is only an idea to test, not a sign anyone wants to work with us.

fleet.topic: Contracts: how a small team gets paid for a verified design pipeline
fleet.summary: Source-backed: SBIR/STTR is reauthorized to 30 Sep 2031 (Crowell); SBIR Phase I ceiling $335,937 and Phase II $2,239,578 without SBA approval (sbir.gov/about); awardees can keep title to inventions with a government licence (35 USC 202); universities usually offer an option to negotiate rather than an outright licence (UT System); Lean 4 and mathlib4 are Apache-2.0. Innovate UK 2026 terms could not be confirmed from a primary page. Pilot shapes, IP-ownership recommendations and price points below are general knowledge, not sourced. Not legal advice.
fleet.lay_summary: A small research team usually gets paid in one of three ways. It can sell a short paid study to a company, apply for a government innovation grant, or work through a university office that signs deals for it. In the US the main grant scheme has just been renewed until 2031, and early grants are in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars. A good first paid job is small: check one real design with the proof tool and hand over a report, like paying an inspector to certify one bridge before ordering a hundred. Who owns the proofs, the design files and the measurements must be written down before work starts. Free software parts used along the way come with a licence that allows commercial use but has a few attribution rules.

fleet.summary: Boston-area experts verified: Lauder (Harvard OEB/MCZ; fin and body mechanics; 3 verified recent papers), Harris (HMS/Boston Children's; fin development incl. a 2021 Current Biology flying-fish paper; 3 verified papers), Triantafyllou (MIT; biomimetic fish robots; only a 2000 paper verified, no recent fish paper found). fleet.lay_summary: We looked for scientists who study how fish fins work and grow. Near Boston, George Lauder at Harvard studies how fish swim, often with robot fish. Matthew Harris at Harvard Medical School studies the genes that set fin shape, including how flying fish got long wing-like fins. At MIT, Michael Triantafyllou builds robot fish. Each paper was checked against a public records database. Every idea of working together is only a guess, such as asking whether a simple unpowered glider model can show if a fin shape could glide at all.

fleet.topic: Funding and institutions in bioelectricity and organism design, including the Levin ecosystem; and the idea of an optogenetic xenobot
fleet.summary: Money behind xenobots/anthrobots traces to four verifiable streams: the Paul G. Allen Frontiers Group / Allen Family Foundation (Allen Discovery Center at Tufts, announced March 2016), DARPA (award HR0011-18-2-0022, the Lifelong-Learning-Machines-era contract number as printed in Crossref funder metadata), NSF, and for the 2023 anthrobot paper the John Templeton Foundation (award 62212) and NIH (S10 OD021624). The Wyss Institute (Harvard) is a Levin affiliation funded mainly by gifts from Hansjorg Wyss (USD 125M 2009, 125M 2013, 131M 2019, 350M 2022 per Harvard Magazine / Crimson). The Institute for Computationally Designed Organisms (icdorgs.org) is a two-site collaboration (Tufts Allen Center + UVM) whose own site does not state its funding. I could not find a dedicated 'bioelectricity foundation' with fetched evidence. Optogenetics in this field: published peer-reviewed optogenetic work on epidermal multiciliated cells (Yasunaga 2022, phytochrome PHYB/PIF) controls rootlet anchoring, not beating; the only light-gated beating claim I saw (ChR2 in ciliated biobots) came from a search-engine snippet of a US patent (12215344) that I could not open (USPTO PDF came back corrupt), so it is unverified. The closest peer-reviewed light-driven contractile biohybrid is Park 2016 (Science, optogenetic cardiomyocyte stingray). A computation-only first step is a design/simulation study (not run here).
fleet.lay_summary: Most of the money behind the 'living robots' made from frog cells came from a private foundation set up by Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, from the US military research agency DARPA, and from the US National Science Foundation. The later robots made from human lung cells were also backed by the John Templeton Foundation and the NIH. Harvard's Wyss Institute, which is paid for mostly by gifts from one Swiss billionaire, is a partner. The idea of steering these robots with light means giving their hair-like cilia a light switch, like adding a remote control to a tiny rowing crew. I found one patent claim that this works, but I could not open it, so I treat it as unconfirmed. A sensible first step would be to simulate the design on a computer before touching any cells.

recommendations: Computation-only first step: (1) in silico design of an optogenetic xenobot: a voxel/cilia-patch model (as in the Kriegman 2020 design pipeline) where each ciliated patch has a light-gated on/off state and a light field is the only input; (2) use evolutionary search to find patch layouts and light patterns that give steerable swimming and test robustness to noise in channel expression and light attenuation; (3) pre-register predicted velocities before any wet work; (4) use published ChR2 kinetics and Yasunaga/cilia-beat data as parameters (requires fetching, not done here).

What would be new: closed-loop-free light steering of ciliated Xenopus-derived biobots (no imaging, no manipulation) with peer-reviewed data; the patent claim, if real, may already cover open-loop ChR2 velocity increase, so freedom-to-operate and prior art must be checked after obtaining the full text.
Obtain patent 12215344 text via a working source and verify the ChR2 claim before relying on it.

Not read or no extractable terms: Schmidt open calls, DARPA, Sloan, Moore, CZI/Biohub, HHMI, NHGRI/NICHD specifics, OpenAI, Google, NVIDIA, Simons deadlines, and award sizes for MIRA, HFSP, Templeton. Fit ratings are my own judgement.
fleet.lay_summary: We looked up who pays for research that uses maths and computers to understand how living things get their shape. Think of it as a list of doors you could knock on. The surest open doors are two US National Science Foundation programmes, a UK charity called Wellcome that takes applications at any time, and a few groups that fund open tools. Nobody we read has a scheme for proving biology results with software proof checkers, so that idea would need pitching as maths-and-biology or as a shared tool. Several big funders could not be read from their websites, and we say so instead of guessing.

Most plausible readings: Formlabs = a shortlist of ~10 printable resins from a 72-material catalogue; woolly mammoth = Colossal Biosciences (no public 'mammoth' AI travel product found, so the link is undetermined); Anthropic = likely the AI for Science API-credit program (up to $20,000 / 6 months, so '3 million tokens' is not that figure); Mamou-Mani = bioplastic-pellet printing practice, no Formlabs link found; .life already carries genome edit list + staged cell geometry/mechanics/lineage but has NO vocabulary at all for locomotion, sensors, actuation or light; Levin 'optogenetic xenobots' has no located paper, only EosFP light-memory xenobots and a stated 'next step' for light-evoked behaviour in neurobots. No source for 'license your patent', '500 papers', 'non profit Bioelectricity' or '3 million tokens' was found.
fleet.lay_summary: The notes are shorthand from a meeting, a bit like a shopping list written in a hurry. We matched each line to public facts and to the team's own file format. Some lines have an obvious reading, like Formlabs being a maker of resin 3D printers. Others, like the woolly mammoth line, could mean several things and we did not guess. The team's file format can describe a creature's DNA and how its cells change over time, but it has no way yet to say 'this cell senses light and so the body moves'. That is like having a recipe book with ingredients and photos but no step that says 'when the oven beeps, take it out'.

fleet.label: pp-sentry-agent-platform
fleet.topic: Sentry as a platform for agents to communicate
fleet.summary: I could not identify an agent-to-agent communication platform called Sentry. The well-known Sentry (sentry.io) is error monitoring. It offers a hosted MCP server (https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp, OAuth login) that lets an AI assistant query a Sentry account, and agent observability features (agent tracing, Conversations beta), but I found no feature that routes messages between agents. Separate, unaffiliated products do agent-to-agent messaging: AgentDM (MCP-based, CLI creates an agent and API key) and MCP Agent Mail (open-source, per-agent inboxes). Repo search of delphisci found only ISSUES.md line 164 (an open "identify Sentry" issue, blocked) and a helper script mention; replies.md has no mention. Nothing was logged into or created. Note: the minimal JSON written to the output path is a stub; this structured return is the full result.
fleet.lay_summary: You said Sentry is a place where agents talk to each other. I could not find that. The famous Sentry is a tool that records software crashes, a bit like a flight recorder for programs. It can be plugged into an AI assistant so the assistant can read those crash reports, but that is the assistant looking things up, not agents chatting. Other products really are like a mailbox for AI agents, and one of them may be what you remember. I did not sign up or log in to anything. One question from you will settle which it is.

fleet.label: q1-critic
fleet.topic: Q1 enhancer-promoter specificity: adversarial review of "rank reversals prove interaction"
fleet.summary: Under a strictly multiplicative (additive-in-log) model with NO enhancer x promoter interaction, measurement noise alone produces large fractions of discordant enhancer pairs. In my simulation (100 enhancers, 4950 pairs, 200 sims per cell) the discordant-pair fraction ranges from 1.3% (spread SD 2 log2, replicate noise SD 0.1, 3 replicates) to 43.7% (spread 0.5, noise 1.0, 1 replicate), and matches the closed form arccos(rho)/pi within 0.003. So a raw count of reversals is uninformative unless compared with the null at the study's own noise/spread ratio. Pairs that are individually significantly ordered in opposite directions on both promoters (uncorrected alpha=0.05) still occur at 0.1-5.3 per library of 100 enhancers under the null; with Bonferroni across all 4950 pairs the null count is ~0. Regression to the mean: top-10 enhancers on promoter A land at only the 59th-95th percentile on promoter B under the null. Saturating (ceiling) readout compresses spread and so raises noise-driven reversals (disc 0.030 to 0.170 for noise 0.1 to 0.6) without any true interaction. Literature: the largest human ExP STARR-seq study found multiplicative combination (R2=0.82) with only subtle class-specific preferences, while a mouse CRE x promoter study reported more than half of CREs selective and a Drosophila study found two enhancer classes with core-promoter specificity; the referee conclusion is that reversals support interaction only when (i) they exceed the noise-matched null, (ii) replicate across independent library/barcode/context, and (iii) survive a monotone-transform (ceiling/scale) explanation. Not done: no real dataset was reanalysed, the Lean registry was not read, and the multiplicity/barcode/episomal points are argued, not simulated.
fleet.lay_summary: Imagine ranking 100 runners by their times on two different tracks. Even if every runner is just a fixed amount slower on the second track, timing errors will shuffle the order of some runners. We simulated exactly this for enhancers (DNA switches that turn genes up) on two promoters (the gene's start switch), with no real interaction at all. With noisy measurements, up to four in ten pairs swapped order by chance alone. So seeing swaps does not prove the enhancer and promoter interact. Swaps only count if there are clearly more of them than this chance baseline predicts.

findings.claim: Under a purely multiplicative model, the fraction of enhancer pairs whose order differs between two promoters spans 0.013 to 0.437 across tested noise/spread settings (N=100, 200 sims/cell).
Simulated discordant fraction equals the analytic value arccos(rho)/pi, rho = 2s^2/(2s^2+2e^2/r), to within 0.003 in all 24 cells.

Discordance depends on the ratio of per-pair noise to spread: halving spread at fixed noise roughly doubles it; averaging 3 replicates cuts it by about 1/sqrt(3) in the SD, e.g. 0.236 to 0.148 at s=1,e=0.6.
Spearman rank correlation between promoters under the null falls to 0.18-0.40 when replicate noise SD is 1.0 log2 with spread 0.5, despite zero interaction.

Pairs significantly ordered in opposite directions on both promoters (two-sided z, alpha 0.05 each, uncorrected) still occur under the null: 0.1 to 5.3 pairs per 100-enhancer library; with Bonferroni over 4950 pairs the mean is 0.00 in every cell.
Regression to the mean: the top 10 enhancers selected on promoter A rank at only the 0.59-0.95 percentile (mean) on promoter B under the null.

A monotone saturating readout on one promoter (ceiling 4x median, s=1, r=3) creates no true reversal but raises measured discordance from 0.030 to 0.170 as noise rises 0.1 to 0.6, i.e. ceiling/floor effects act through compressed spread plus noise.

ExP STARR-seq of 1,000 enhancers x 1,000 promoters in K562 found most enhancers activate all promoters by similar amounts and activities combine multiplicatively (R2=0.82), with two classes showing subtle preferential effects.
findings.evidence_quote: most enhancers activate all promoters by similar amounts, and intrinsic enhancer and promoter activities multiplicatively combine to determine RNA output (R2 = 0.82)

findings.claim: A mouse CRE x promoter combinatorial reporter study reports more than half of tested CREs have significant promoter selectivity.
findings.evidence_quote: More than half of the tested CREs exhibit significant promoter selectivity.

findings.claim: Drosophila S2/OSC enhancers show marked specificity to one of two core promoters (housekeeping vs developmental).
findings.evidence_quote: thousands of enhancers in Drosophila melanogaster S2 and ovarian somatic cells (OSCs) exhibit a marked specificity to one of two core promoters

findings.claim: The two mammalian studies disagree in emphasis (mostly multiplicative/promiscuous vs more than half selective); the difference may reflect noise thresholds, library design, or cell type, which I could not resolve here.
findings.source: comparison of the two abstracts above

findings.claim: Reasoned (not simulated) artefact risks: barcode/plasmid-context effects and episomal vs genomic differences can add promoter-specific, non-biological variance that inflates reversals; multiplicity over thousands of pairs inflates false reversals unless corrected.

key_claims.claim: With zero interaction, noise alone makes 1.3% to 43.7% of enhancer pairs change order between promoters, depending on replicate noise, replicate count and enhancer spread; any observed reversal fraction must be compared with this noise-matched null.
key_claims.source: own simulation: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/q1-critic/null_reversals.py; confirmed by closed form arccos(rho)/pi

key_claims.claim: Significant-in-both-directions reversals appear under the null at uncorrected alpha 0.05 (0.1-5.3 per 100 enhancers) but essentially vanish under Bonferroni, so a reversal claim needs multiplicity correction and replication.
The best human dataset cited reports multiplicative combination (R2=0.82) with only subtle class effects, so interaction is not the default expectation.
key_claims.evidence_quote: intrinsic enhancer and promoter activities multiplicatively combine to determine RNA output (R2 = 0.82)

fleet.label: q1-data
fleet.topic: Q1 enhancer-promoter specificity: public data and a first analysis (GSE186265, Martinez-Ara et al. 2022, mouse ES cells)
fleet.summary: Dataset: GEO GSE186265 (Martinez-Ara, van Steensel lab, Mol Cell 2022): combinatorial reporter assay of DHS-centred candidate CREs ('enhancers') x promoters from three mouse loci, 3 biological replicates, upstream placement. After pooling orientations/locus libraries to one value per replicate per (enhancer, promoter) cell, 232 enhancers x 31 promoters, 3747 cells (52% filled). Analysed the largest complete block found by a deterministic greedy rule: 98 enhancers x 15 promoters (105 promoter pairs). log2(activity+0.01). Noise = pooled replicate SD in deciles of cell mean (about 1.0 log2 for the weakest 40% of cells, 0.16-0.20 for the strongest 30%). Results (point estimate, bootstrap 95% interval where stated): (1) rank agreement between promoters is weak and variable: Spearman median 0.38 (range -0.29 to 0.72 over the 105 pairs), Kendall tau-b median 0.27 (range -0.19 to 0.52). A purely multiplicative model with the same replicate noise predicts Spearman median 0.81, so all 105 pairs fall below the null's 95% lower bound; per-promoter replicate reliability is high (median 0.96, min 0.72), so this is not replicate noise. (2) Among enhancer pairs whose order is significant (|z|>2) on both promoters of a promoter pair, a median 26.5% (range 9.6-63.5%) are in opposite order; summed over the 105 pairs 65,174 of 224,658 doubly-significant comparisons reverse, against 368 (95% 196-624) expected from noise under a multiplicative model; at |z|>3, 43,854 vs 4.4. The mean size of a reversal (min of the two absolute log2 differences) has median 1.33 log2 over pairs (max 2.52). The most extreme pair, P007 vs P021, has Spearman -0.29 (enhancer+replicate bootstrap -0.47 to -0.10). (3) Spectrum: on the linear matrix the best rank-one fit explains 71.3% of the sum of squares (rep-bootstrap 70.8-71.6%, enhancer+rep 67.2-76.2%); on the log2 matrix 75.7% (uncentered) and 61.6% (grand-mean centred). Because a multiplicative model is rank one on the LINEAR scale and ADDITIVE (row+column effects, not rank one) on the log scale, the more telling log-scale split is: additive row+column effects 73.3% of variance, interaction 26.7% (enh+rep 23.8-30.1%), interaction 11.9x the size expected from replicate noise alone (10.7-13.4), 25.0% after subtracting noise; the best rank-one fit of that interaction captures 38.5% of it (31.7-44.6%); additive + rank-one interaction = 83.6%. Conclusion: in this dataset multiplicativity is a good first approximation for about three quarters of the variance but is rejected as an exact model; the order of enhancer strengths changes materially between promoters (promoter-specific interaction), beyond measurement noise, and the interaction has more than one dimension. Caveats: cCREs are DHS fragments not validated enhancers; promoter-pair correlations are strongly structured (clusters such as P013/P014/P021 correlate ~0.7); orientations and locus libraries pooled; one dataset, one cell type; this is mouse ES cells not human.
fleet.lay_summary: Imagine 98 loudspeakers (enhancers) each wired to 15 different light bulbs (promoters), and we record how bright each bulb gets. If every speaker simply multiplied every bulb's brightness by a fixed amount, the speakers would rank the same way for every bulb. We found they do not: for typical pairs of bulbs, the speakers' ranking agrees only weakly, and in about a quarter of the clear-cut comparisons the order is flipped. Simple multiplication still explains roughly three quarters of the variation, but the rest is a real bulb-specific effect, about twelve times larger than measurement noise. So an enhancer is not just 'strong' or 'weak'; how strong it looks depends on which promoter it is paired with.

findings.claim: Largest complete block (greedy, deterministic) is 98 enhancers x 15 promoters, giving 105 promoter pairs.
Spearman correlation between promoters over the 98 shared enhancers: median 0.382, range -0.286 to 0.715 across 105 pairs (log2(activity+0.01)).
Kendall tau-b between promoters: median 0.269, range -0.190 to 0.522.

Bootstrap intervals for the extreme pairs: P014 vs P021 Spearman 0.715 (replicate bootstrap 0.675-0.746; enhancer+replicate 0.563-0.808); P007 vs P021 Spearman -0.286 (replicate bootstrap -0.317 to -0.259; enhancer+replicate -0.471 to -0.095). Interval for every pair is in panel_pairs_main.json (B=1000).

Replicate noise alone cannot explain the weak agreement: under a purely multiplicative (log-additive) model with the estimated replicate noise, the median pair Spearman would be 0.812; all 105 observed pair Spearmans lie below the null 95% lower bound. Per-promoter replicate reliability median 0.962, min 0.722 (P015).
findings.source: own calculation: summary_main.json (null_rho_median_of_pairs, promoter_reliability_spearman); 500 null simulations

findings.claim: Rank reversals (|z|>2 on both promoters, opposite sign): 65,174 of 224,658 doubly-significant enhancer-pair comparisons summed over 105 promoter pairs (29.0%; per-pair median fraction 26.5%, range 9.6-63.5%). Null expectation under multiplicative model + noise: 368 (95% 196-624). At |z|>3: 43,854 observed vs 4.4 expected.

Typical reversal magnitude: mean over reversed enhancer pairs of min(|log2 difference on promoter a|, |on promoter b|) has median 1.33 log2 across promoter pairs (max 2.52, i.e. about 5.7-fold at both promoters).

Best rank-one fit explains 71.3% of the sum of squares of the linear-scale 98x15 matrix (replicate bootstrap 70.8-71.6%; enhancer+replicate bootstrap 67.2-76.2%). Linear singular values: 79.9, 37.8, 20.9, 19.2, 11.1, 8.5, 6.9, 6.5, 5.2, 2.8, 2.3, 2.2, 1.9, 1.7, 1.4.

On log2 scale: best rank-one fit explains 75.7% (uncentered) / 61.6% (grand-mean centred) of the sum of squares; additive row+column effects explain 73.3% of variance about the grand mean, the row x column interaction 26.7% (enh+rep CI 23.8-30.1%). Uncentered log singular values: 91.3, 28.6, 26.5, 15.6, 13.0, ... 4.1.

Interaction sum of squares is 11.9x the amount expected from replicate noise alone (replicate bootstrap 12.0-12.4; enhancer+replicate 10.7-13.4); 25.0% of variance after subtracting the noise expectation. Best rank-one fit of the interaction explains 38.5% of it (31.7-44.6%); additive plus rank-one interaction explains 83.6%.
findings.source: own calculation: summary_main.json (svd.interaction_ss_over_noise etc.). Noise expectation = mean SE^2 x (nE-1)(nP-1) assumes homoscedastic-like errors; approximate.

findings.claim: Results are robust to the pseudocount and threshold: pseudocount 0.03 gives Spearman median 0.378, reversal fraction 0.265, interaction/noise 17.3; pseudocount 0.003 gives 0.378, 0.263, 8.8; z=3 gives reversal fraction 0.222. Linear rank-one share 0.713 in all.
Restricting to the more active enhancers does not restore agreement: top 50% by mean activity (n=49) Spearman median 0.355; top 25% (n=25) 0.385.

All 363 promoter pairs with at least 20 shared enhancers (pairwise-complete, all 31 promoters): Spearman median 0.312 (range -0.574 to 0.838), median reversal fraction 0.252. Per-pair table in allpairs_main.csv (point estimates only, no bootstrap).
The original authors report that more than half of the tested CREs show significant promoter selectivity (independent support for promoter-specific enhancer effects).
findings.evidence_quote: By systematic reporter assays of thousands of CRE – promoter pairs from three Mb-sized genomic regions in mouse cells, we found that CREs vary substantially in their promoter compatibility, with more than half showing significant selectivity.

findings.claim: Martinez-Ara et al. note that Bergman et al. (human K562) proposed multiplicative combination of enhancer and promoter activity while both datasets also show selectivity.
findings.evidence_quote: Based on mathematical modeling of their data, the authors proposed that intrinsic cCRE and P activities generally combine multiplicatively to determine reporter activity.

fleet.label: q1-literature
fleet.topic: Q1 enhancer-promoter specificity: the literature
fleet.summary: Crossed-design reporter assays give two pictures. Human K562 ExP STARR-seq (1000x1000, GSE184426) finds a multiplicative model with R2=0.82 and high rank agreement across promoters (mean Spearman 0.81 across promoter pairs, 0.72 across enhancer pairs), with a structured minority of deviations (E1 enhancers favour P1 promoters 1.93-fold) and a saturating response at strong, housekeeping-like promoters. Drosophila core-promoter studies (Zabidi 2015) find far stronger specificity: 72% of 11,364 enhancers prefer one of two core promoters by at least 2-fold, and cofactor screens (Haberle 2019) link this to promoter class. Mouse ES-cell MPRAs (Martinez-Ara 2022, 2024) find that over half of enhancers are selective, that strong promoters are boosted less (saturation-like), and that promoters transform summed enhancer input non-linearly. Martinez-Ara's re-analysis of the Bergman data and Bergman's text differ in emphasis, not in data. No study I read gives a per-promoter-pair rank statistic beyond Bergman's means; that would need re-analysis of the GEO tables, which I did not download, so no files were kept.
fleet.lay_summary: Think of an enhancer as a volume knob and a promoter as an amplifier. If you try many knobs on one amplifier and then another, the loudest knob is usually still the loudest. A large human experiment found this: about four fifths of the variation fits a simple multiplication of knob times amplifier. In fruit flies, though, most knobs work much better on one of two kinds of amplifier, so the order of strength flips. Mouse studies sit in between: weak amplifiers gain most, strong ones hit a ceiling, and some knobs are picky. So the order mostly changes when promoters belong to different classes, or when a ceiling squashes the strongest enhancers.

key_claims.claim: Even in the multiplicative human data a structured minority deviates (E1/P1 1.93-fold), and the same K562 data show selectivity beyond noise by another group's test (90.46% of cCREs).

key_claims.claim: Promoter strength rescales enhancer input non-linearly (weak promoters boosted most; saturation at strong promoters and strongest enhancers), a mechanism that can reorder enhancers across promoters.

fleet.label: q1-mechanisms
fleet.topic: Q1 enhancer-promoter specificity: mechanisms that break the ranking
fleet.summary: Mechanisms that can change enhancer rank order are those adding a second hidden dimension beyond one enhancer strength: core-promoter motif compatibility (TATA, DPE, Inr, CpG; housekeeping versus developmental), cofactor-promoter compatibility, and TF preferences. Saturation, power-law responsiveness and promoter-independent distance or contact effects are monotone functions of one strength; a compiled core-Lean theorem (Q1.no_reversal) shows they can create ties but never reversals, although with noise they lower the raw rank correlation (simulated raw Spearman 0.76-0.83 with no true change). The literature disagrees: Martinez-Ara 2022 (mouse) finds over half of CREs promoter-selective; Bergman 2022 (human) finds multiplicative combination (R2 0.82) with subtle class effects; the Tan 2026 preprint finds similar rank order with promoter-specific power-law exponents. Our re-analysis of Martinez-Ara GEO GSE186265 gives noise-corrected between-promoter Spearman medians of 0.56, 0.83 and 0.62 for three loci (saturation alone predicts 1.0), so a rank-changing component exists there, with the caveats listed. One added experiment (2 contrasting promoters x 48-192 enhancers x 1-8 tandem copies x 3 replicates, scored by noise-corrected Spearman) separates the one-strength class (predicted about 1.0, flat in dose) from the compatibility class (predicted about 0.6-0.8, flat in dose). It does not separate motif from cofactor from TF compatibility, and does not test topology or promoter competition.
fleet.lay_summary: Think of an enhancer as a volume knob and a promoter as an amplifier. If every amplifier turns the same knob setting into more or less loudness, the loudest knob on one amplifier is also the loudest on the others, even if one amplifier clips at high volume. If different amplifiers listen for different things, the order of the knobs can truly flip. We proved on a computer that clipping alone can make two knobs tie but never swap places. In published mouse-cell data the order shifts by more than measurement noise allows, though studies disagree on how much. One extra experiment would tell the stories apart: turn each enhancer up in steps on two contrasting promoters and repeat every measurement three times.

findings.claim: In vivo, some Drosophila enhancers are specific for DPE-containing versus TATA-containing core promoters (position-matched reporter lines).
findings.evidence_quote: These studies revealed transcriptional enhancers that are specific for promoters that contain either DPE or TATA box elements.

findings.claim: Thousands of Drosophila enhancers show marked specificity for one of two core promoters (a ribosomal-protein-gene promoter versus a developmentally regulated TF promoter).
findings.evidence_quote: thousands of enhancers in Drosophila melanogaster S2 and ovarian somatic cells (OSCs) exhibit a marked specificity to one of two core promoters

findings.claim: The housekeeping/developmental enhancer split is linked to different transcription factors: Dref activates housekeeping, Trl developmental enhancers.
findings.evidence_quote: we identify two transcription factors--Dref and Trl--that bind and activate housekeeping versus developmental enhancers, respectively.

findings.claim: Core-promoter responsiveness to one strong enhancer spans several orders of magnitude across Drosophila sequences (a promoter-side axis).
findings.evidence_quote: In the presence of a single strong enhancer, the enhancer responsiveness of different sequences differs by several orders of magnitude

findings.claim: Transcriptional cofactors differ in which core-promoter types they activate (cofactor-promoter compatibility).
findings.evidence_quote: We observe differential activation of CPs, indicating distinct regulatory preferences or 'compatibilities' between COFs and specific types of CPs.

findings.claim: In human K562 ExP STARR-seq (1,000 enhancers x 1,000 promoters), enhancer and promoter activities combine multiplicatively; most enhancers activate all promoters by similar amounts.
findings.evidence_quote: most enhancers activate all promoters by similar amounts, and intrinsic enhancer and promoter activities multiplicatively combine to determine RNA output (R2 = 0.82).

findings.claim: Bergman et al.: housekeeping promoters carry built-in activating motifs (GABPA, YY1) that lower responsiveness to distal enhancers (a ceiling-like promoter-side effect).
findings.evidence_quote: Promoters of housekeeping genes contain built-in activating motifs for factors such as GABPA and YY1, which decrease the responsiveness of promoters to distal enhancers.

findings.claim: Martinez-Ara et al. (mouse cells, thousands of CRE-promoter pairs) emphasise the opposite: most CREs are promoter-selective.
findings.evidence_quote: More than half of the tested CREs exhibit significant promoter selectivity.

findings.claim: Martinez-Ara et al.: selectivity does not track native looping, so compatibility and folding are separate axes.
findings.evidence_quote: CRE-promoter selectivity does not correlate with looping interactions in the native genomic context

findings.claim: Martinez-Ara et al. note a saturation-like pattern and say it cannot be told apart from lower enhancer dependence of high-basal promoters.
findings.evidence_quote: This suggests a saturation effect, or it could indicate that promoters with high basal activity are less dependent on distal enhancers.

findings.claim: Martinez-Ara et al.: strong boosting occurs mostly at low-basal promoters.
findings.evidence_quote: Strong boosting occurred primarily at promoters with low basal activities, while highly active promoters were more difficult to boost

findings.claim: Tan et al. 2026 preprint says earlier reporter assays disagree because of assay confounders and finds a similar enhancer rank order across promoters (abstract only; full text blocked by HTTP 429).
findings.evidence_quote: Promoters differ in their responsiveness to enhancers (>100-fold versus 1.1-fold activation) while enhancers activate all promoters in a similar rank order.

findings.claim: Tan et al.: promoter output follows a power law in enhancer activity with a promoter-specific exponent (a promoter-specific monotone response, rank-preserving by construction).
findings.evidence_quote: Promoter output scales with enhancer activity following a power law, with the exponent varying across promoters.

findings.claim: Tan et al.: responsiveness is modulated by core-promoter TF motifs.
findings.evidence_quote: Responsiveness is modulated by transcription factor motifs in the core promoter.

findings.claim: Enhancer effect depends nonlinearly on enhancer-promoter contact probability.
findings.evidence_quote: the transcriptional effect of an enhancer depends on its contact probabilities with the promoter through a nonlinear relationship.

findings.claim: Zuin et al. best-fit Hill coefficient for burst frequency versus contact probability is 2.8.
findings.evidence_quote: Hill coefficient ( h ) of 2.8 (95% confidence interval = 2.4-3.2

findings.claim: Enhancer needs cohesin only for activating distant genes (distance/topology axis).
findings.evidence_quote: It requires cohesin exclusively for the activation of distant genes, not of proximal genes

findings.claim: SPIE-seq (preprint): enhancer influence decays with distance with similar average scaling for all enhancers.
findings.evidence_quote: enhancer influence declines with genomic distance, following similar average distance-decay scaling across all tested enhancers

findings.claim: SPIE-seq: promoter skipping grows as competitors accumulate, so promoters do not respond independently (invisible in single-promoter reporters).
findings.evidence_quote: Promoter skipping is common and increases as competitors accumulate

findings.claim: Strong enhancers behave sub-additively because of competition with the target promoter; weak ones additively (Drosophila embryo).
findings.evidence_quote: weakly active enhancers function additively while strong enhancers behave sub-additively due to competition with the target promoter.

findings.claim: A product of activity and contact (ABC) predicts CRISPRi enhancer-gene links better than earlier methods (a one-strength-times-contact model).
findings.evidence_quote: a simple activity-by-contact model substantially outperformed previous methods at predicting the complex connections in our CRISPR dataset.

findings.claim: In mouse ESC loci, developmental genes insulate regulatory domains partly by promoter competition rather than enhancer blocking.
findings.evidence_quote: developmental genes preferentially contribute to regulatory insulation through non-structural mechanisms involving promoter competition rather than enhancer blocking.

findings.claim: Theory: burst frequency and burst size rise with E-P communication strength as power laws.
findings.evidence_quote: burst frequency and burst size are up-regulated by E-P communication strength, following power laws with positive exponents.

findings.claim: A native-locus enhancer (eNMU) shows a hierarchy: autonomous enhancer e1 dominates facilitators and the promoter.
findings.evidence_quote: The autonomous enhancer e1 is functionally hierarchical to e2, additional facilitators, and the NMU promoter

findings.claim: Lean 4 (core only, no Mathlib, v4.35.0), compiled with exit 0: if every promoter responds to one enhancer strength through a non-decreasing function (any saturation, Hill, power law), a strict order on one promoter can never become the opposite strict order on another (Q1.no_reversal); with strictly increasing responses strict order is kept (Q1.strict_preserved); a two-latent model reverses order (Q1.two_latent_reverses). So saturation alone creates ties, never reversals.

findings.claim: Re-analysis of Martinez-Ara GSE186265 upstream EP matrix, locus Klf2 (69 cCREs x 22 promoters, 1344 observed cells): replicate-disattenuated Spearman between promoter pairs has median 0.56 (10-90% 0.37-0.83; raw median 0.36; 231 promoter pairs). Pure saturation predicts 1.0. 5-fold CV R2 on log10 activity: additive 0.938; one-latent+per-promoter-monotone 0.923; additive+rank1 interaction 0.943; rank2 0.942; replicate-noise ceiling 0.968; gap additive-to-ceiling 0.030.

Re-analysis of Martinez-Ara GSE186265 upstream EP matrix, locus Nanog (29 cCREs x 11 promoters, 294 observed cells): replicate-disattenuated Spearman between promoter pairs has median 0.83 (10-90% 0.51-1.00; raw median 0.60; 29 promoter pairs). Pure saturation predicts 1.0. 5-fold CV R2 on log10 activity: additive 0.859; one-latent+per-promoter-monotone 0.845; additive+rank1 interaction 0.862; rank2 0.869; replicate-noise ceiling 0.930; gap additive-to-ceiling 0.071.

Re-analysis of Martinez-Ara GSE186265 upstream EP matrix, locus Tfcp2l1 (145 cCREs x 21 promoters, 2304 observed cells): replicate-disattenuated Spearman between promoter pairs has median 0.62 (10-90% 0.42-0.74; raw median 0.49; 190 promoter pairs). Pure saturation predicts 1.0. 5-fold CV R2 on log10 activity: additive 0.842; one-latent+per-promoter-monotone 0.855; additive+rank1 interaction 0.860; rank2 0.856; replicate-noise ceiling 0.985; gap additive-to-ceiling 0.144.

Simulation (assumed: SD of log10 enhancer strength 0.5; noise 0.10 log10 on a 3-replicate mean; promoter A Hill K=10^1.5, basal 1, headroom 100x; promoter B basal 30, headroom 10x, K=1; 48 enhancers; 1,2,4,8 copies): saturation-only gives RAW Spearman between promoters 0.76 [0.60,0.87] / 0.82 [0.71,0.90] / 0.82 [0.71,0.90] / 0.77 [0.62,0.88] at 1/2/4/8 copies (mean [95% interval]) although no order changes, but replicate-disattenuated Spearman 1.00 [0.85,1.16] / 0.99 [0.87,1.10] / 0.99 [0.87,1.10] / 0.98 [0.82,1.15]. Two-latent models at 2 copies give disattenuated 0.82 [0.60,0.98] (latent r=cos34deg=0.83) and 0.58 [0.30,0.83] (r=cos53deg=0.60). So saturation can mimic a low raw rank correlation; it cannot mimic a low disattenuated one.

recommendations: Run the proposed experiment: 2 contrasting promoters x at least 48 enhancers (192 to resolve a mild rank change) x 1,2,4,8 tandem copies x 3 independent replicates, same backbone, position and cell type; score with replicate-disattenuated Spearman, not raw Spearman (saturation alone gives raw 0.76-0.83 in simulation).

Decision rule: a disattenuated Spearman whose 95% interval includes 1.0 and is flat in copy number supports one strength plus a monotone promoter response (saturation, responsiveness, power law, promoter-independent distance or contact). A value clearly below 1 (0.6-0.8 in the Martinez-Ara re-analysis) that is flat in dose supports compatibility (motif, cofactor, TF).

To split compatibility sub-mechanisms (outside the one experiment): an arm that swaps or mutates TATA, DPE, Inr or CpG content in the same promoters, and a cofactor-degron arm (Mediator, BRD4 or p300 depletion). Predictions for these are qualitative only here.

To test topology and competition (also outside the one experiment): vary spacing for the same enhancers on one promoter, and add a second promoter in cis. SPIE-seq predicts similar average decay for all enhancers (no reorder) and context-dependent competition.

Reconcile the literature before relying on one study: Martinez-Ara (mouse, over half of CREs selective), Bergman (human, mostly multiplicative), Tan 2026 (similar rank order, promoter-specific exponent). Our re-analysis finds a rank-changing component in the mouse data but cannot exclude the assay confounders Tan et al. describe.

fleet.label: q1-theory-lean
fleet.topic: Which enhancer-promoter model classes can change the rank order of enhancers, as Lean 4 theorems
fleet.summary: One self-contained Mathlib file (EnhancerPromoterRank.lean, 14 #print axioms checks) passes check.sh with "ALL CHECKED: no errors, no sorryAx". Axioms used: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only. Proved: (1) any model f p e = h_p(a e) with every h_p merely monotone (not only strictly) has no strict rank reversal. This covers (a) multiplicative with b_p>0, (c) additive on a log scale, and (d) thermodynamic V*x/(K+x) with promoter-specific V and K, each proved to be a special case. (2) Elimination certificates: one strict reversal RankReversal f p q e e' refutes classes a, b (weak and strict), c and d together, whatever the latent a and whatever the monotone h_p (certificate_all, certificate_pair). (3) A noise-robust form: if observations are within eps of truth, a reversal in the data with margin 2*eps on both promoters is a true reversal. (4) Exact characterisation: promoter q is a monotone function of promoter p on the measured enhancers iff there is no weak reversal (a pair p orders as <= and q orders strictly the other way), so ties broken differently by q also break class (b). (5) Limits of the inference: a negative promoter factor, a non-monotone (biphasic) single-index response, or a two-feature model with promoter-specific weights can each reverse ranks; the general interaction class is vacuous (every matrix is in it). So a reversal proves the effect is not a monotone function of one enhancer-intrinsic latent; it does not by itself prove two independent features, since a non-monotone single-index response also explains it. Also proved: promoter-specific saturation changes fold change (1.5x vs 2.5x in the worked case) without changing order. Not done: no data test, no literature search or citations (not requested for this theory task), no probabilistic or noise-model theory beyond the bounded-error certificate. Only a deprecation warning for push_neg remains.
fleet.lay_summary: Imagine ranking enhancers (DNA switches that turn genes up) by strength on one gene, then on another. If every gene just turns the same underlying strength dial up or down, or squashes it at a ceiling, the ranking cannot flip. We proved that with a computer proof checker, for several kinds of model including ones where each gene saturates at its own level. So if real data show two enhancers swapping places on two genes, those simple models are ruled out. We also proved what that swap does not tell you: it could come from two different enhancer properties read differently by each gene, or from one property that a gene responds to in a rise-then-fall way. The proof file and its check command are saved so anyone can rerun them.

findings.claim: Monotone single-index models f p e = h_p(a e), with every h_p only Monotone (not strict), admit no strict rank reversal (no_reversal_of_monotone, via no_reversal_of_monotoneOn on a set S).

recommendations: For data tests, apply noisy_certificate with a replicate-based eps and require margin 2*eps on both promoters before calling a reversal real.
Use pair_monotone_iff_no_weak_reversal to test class (b) between each promoter pair: fit the isotonic map and report the discordant enhancer pairs.

Treat a confirmed reversal as evidence for either a multi-feature enhancer code or a non-monotone response (e.g. squelching or biphasic), and design a follow-up (dose titration of one enhancer on one promoter) to separate them; the theory alone cannot.
If exact ties matter, use WeakReversal; strict reversal alone is the weaker certificate.

fleet.label: q2-critic
fleet.topic: Q2 binding-affinity prediction: adversarial review
fleet.summary: Verdict: the noise-ceiling story is real but weak as the main explanation. Published noise estimates imply a ceiling of Pearson r about 0.85-0.95, above the r about 0.75-0.80 that leakage-free models reach on CASF2016, and well above the gap between leaky and clean splits. Leakage inflates scores and clean splits expose the drop (Graber 2025, Volkov 2022); a simulation with stated noise shows split choice moves r by 0.7 while noise of 0.8 log units moves it by under 0.05. Cleaner splits do not restore performance, they reveal it. Caveat: the ceiling can bind at the level of per-assay agreement (Landrum 2024) and in narrow-range datasets, and my simulation has a large label SD (2.64) which makes noise look cheap.
fleet.lay_summary: Many people say binding-prediction programs fail because the lab measurements they learn from are noisy. We checked. The noise is real, but it only caps a perfect program at a score of about 0.85 to 0.95 out of 1, while today's honest programs get about 0.75 to 0.80. The bigger problem is that benchmark tests often contain near-copies of the training examples, like a student who has seen the exam questions. In our simulated experiment, a program scored 0.90 when tested on look-alikes of what it had studied and about 0.19 on truly new proteins and molecules, and adding measurement noise barely changed that. A fairer test does not make programs better; it shows how good they really are.

findings.claim: Mean experimental error between independent ChEMBL Ki measurements is 0.44 pKi units (SD 0.54, median 0.34); max achievable squared Pearson R on large datasets estimated 0.81 (r about 0.90, my sqrt).
findings.evidence_quote: The maximum possible squared Pearson correlation coefficient (R(2)) on large data sets is estimated to be 0.81.

findings.claim: Cross-assay IC50 agreement in ChEMBL is poor: minimal curation Kendall tau 0.51, 65% of points differ >0.3 log; maximal curation tau 0.71, 48% differ >0.3 log.
findings.evidence_quote: almost 65% of the points differ by more than 0.3 log units, 27% differ by more than one log unit, and the correlation between the assays, as measured by Kendall's τ, is only 0.51.

findings.claim: Converting Landrum tau to Pearson via r=sin(pi*tau/2) (bivariate normal assumption) gives between-assay r 0.718 (minimal) and 0.898 (maximal); a perfect predictor then correlates sqrt(r) = 0.847 / 0.948 with a single assay, assuming equal reliability.

Using Kramer SD 0.54 as per-measurement noise and assumed label SD 1.4-2.2 (assumption, not sourced) gives ceiling r 0.92-0.97; if 0.54 is a pair-difference SD, per-measurement sigma is 0.38 and ceiling is higher.

Mixing public IC50 data adds only moderate noise: SD of IC50 pairs is only 25% larger than SD of Ki pairs (Kalliokoski). Disagrees in emphasis with Landrum 2024, which finds substantially poorer agreement under minimal curation.
findings.evidence_quote: The standard deviation of IC50 data is only 25% larger than the standard deviation of Ki data

findings.claim: A trivial nearest-neighbour search (mean label of 5 most similar training complexes) reaches CASF2016 Pearson 0.716 on original PDBbind; ligand-only similarity search 0.707. On CleanSplit these fall to 0.653 and 0.625.
findings.evidence_quote: Averaging the affinity label of the five most similar training complexes resulted in an r.m.s.e. of 1.648 and a Pearson correlation of 0.653.

findings.claim: Trained on CleanSplit, GEMS reaches CASF2016 Pearson 0.803 (RMSE 1.308), GenScore 0.780, Pafnucy 0.746: clean-split performance is about 0.75-0.80, below the 0.85-0.95 noise ceilings, so the ceiling is not what binds on CASF. Pafnucy dropped substantially on CleanSplit, GenScore much less.
findings.evidence_quote: With a prediction r.m.s.e. of 1.308 and a Pearson correlation of 0.803, GEMS considerably outperforms Pafnucy (r.m.s.e. = 1.484, Pearson R = 0.746) and GenScore (r.m.s.e. = 1.362, Pearson R = 0.780)

findings.claim: Original-split Pafnucy retrained on PDBbind 2020 had CASF RMSE 1.046; its Pearson was in a figure/table I did not read. So the leaky-to-clean RMSE change is 1.046 -> 1.484.
findings.evidence_quote: This increased Pafnucy’s CASF performance to an r.m.s.e. of 1.046, making it the best-performing binding affinity prediction models evaluated on the complete CASF2016 dataset

findings.claim: Memorisation dominates in deep affinity models; explicit interaction description gives no advantage over ligand or protein descriptors.
findings.evidence_quote: Simple models, inferring binding affinities of test samples from that of the closest ligands or proteins in the training set, already exhibit good performances, suggesting that memorization largely dominates true learning

findings.claim: Simulation: RF on ligand+protein descriptors, noise SD 0.4 log units: r vs noisy labels 0.904 (random pair split), 0.797 (series held out), 0.581 (protein family held out), 0.200 (both held out). Split choice changes r by 0.70; noise 0 -> 0.8 changes r by at most 0.045 (random split 0.916 -> 0.871).
Simulation: reported r vs noisy labels is always at or below the ceiling and the ceiling is never binding: reported/ceiling is 0.91 under random split and 0.20 under strict split at sigma 0.4.
Simulation: a ligand-only model scores r=0.265 on random pair split, falling to -0.10 under both-held-out, illustrating that memorisable series/protein offsets, not noise, create apparent skill.

Limit of the simulation: true-value SD is 2.64 (world seed 0), larger than real pKd spreads, so noise SD 0.8 costs little; the ceiling would bind harder in narrow-range sets (e.g. a congeneric series with SD about 0.7 and noise 0.5 gives r_max about 0.82 by sqrt(1-0.25/0.49)). DGP is built by me, so it demonstrates mechanism only, not real-world magnitudes.

Better splits do not restore performance: in both the literature (CleanSplit lowers the scores of retrained models) and the simulation (held-out splits lower r). Restoration came only from model/architecture changes (GEMS 0.803 on CleanSplit per authors).
findings.evidence_quote: Retraining current top-performing models on CleanSplit caused their benchmark performance to drop substantially, indicating that the performance of existing models is largely driven by data leakage.

key_claims.claim: Published noise estimates (Kramer R2max 0.81; Landrum tau 0.51-0.71) imply a ceiling of r about 0.85-0.95, above what leakage-free models reach on CASF2016 (r 0.75-0.80); so noise is not the binding constraint on that benchmark.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The maximum possible squared Pearson correlation coefficient (R(2)) on large data sets is estimated to be 0.81.

key_claims.claim: Leakage between PDBbind and CASF inflates scores: 49% of CASF complexes have near-duplicates, and a similarity-lookup gets r 0.716 with no learning.
key_claims.evidence_quote: involving 49% of all CASF complexes. These findings reveal a clear train–test data leakage

key_claims.claim: In a controlled simulation, split type changes reported r from 0.90 to 0.20 while 0.8 log-unit label noise changes it by under 0.05.

recommendations: State the Lean claim as a conditional: reported r <= sqrt(reliability) of the labels, and note it is slack (not binding) for CASF-type benchmarks; pair it with a leakage lemma (test items with train neighbour at similarity above threshold) rather than treating ceiling as the explanation.
Always report a nearest-neighbour baseline and a ligand-only baseline next to any model; if they come within 0.1 r of the model, the split is leaky.
Use label-noise ceilings per dataset (assay-matched, Landrum maximal curation) rather than a global 0.81.
Next test: estimate the CASF2016 label SD from the data file and compute its specific ceiling (I could not do so without downloading it).

fleet.label: q2-data
fleet.topic: Q2 binding-affinity prediction: public data and a first analysis
fleet.summary: Data: 80 ChEMBL_37 REST downloads (Ki and IC50, pChEMBL, relation '=', biochemical assays, 40 hand-picked well-studied targets, 39 returned data; ~95 MB). (1) Noise: pooled SD between independent documents for the same compound-target pair is 0.61 pKi (CI [0.588, 0.637]) and 0.84 pIC50 (CI [0.805, 0.870]); a robust MAD estimate is lower (0.32, 0.55) because errors are heavy-tailed (16% of Ki pairs and 23% of IC50 pairs differ by more than 1 log). (2) Between-target share of variance in pooled data is 7.7% (Ki) and 14.7% (IC50); the rest is within-target. (3) A predictor knowing only the target reaches pooled Pearson r=0.28 (Ki) / 0.38 (IC50) with zero within-target correlation. (4) Attenuation ceiling for a perfect predictor scored against one noisy measurement: pooled r <= 0.88 (Ki) / 0.77 (IC50); within-target r <= 0.87 / 0.72 (robust-noise ceilings 0.96 / 0.89). So noise caps achievable correlation but leaves large headroom; it does not by itself explain poor within-target performance, and it matters more for IC50. Caveats: targets are a hand-picked set, not a random ChEMBL sample; two IC50 targets were capped at 12,000 rows; the Lean registry was not opened.
fleet.lay_summary: People build computer programs to guess how tightly a drug sticks to a protein. We asked how much of their shortfall can be blamed on the measurements they learn from. When different labs measure the same drug on the same protein, answers typically differ by about 0.6 on a scale where one unit is a ten-fold change, and sometimes by ten-fold or more. That noise puts a ceiling on how well any program can score, like marking a spelling test against an answer key that has typos. The ceiling is fairly high (about 0.87 out of 1 for the best-case correlation), so noise explains only part of the problem. Also, knowing only which protein is involved explains under a sixth of the variation, so the hard part is ranking similar drugs for the same protein.

fleet.label: q2-literature
fleet.topic: Q2 binding-affinity prediction: the literature on why it fails
fleet.summary: Verified literature (Crossref + Europe PMC/PMC full text, fetched 2026-11-12) gives three converging explanations. (1) Leakage: Graber et al. (Nat Mach Intell 2025) find nearly 600 train-test similarities involving 49% of CASF complexes; a lookup baseline averaging the labels of the 5 most similar training complexes gets CASF2016 Pearson 0.716 / RMSE 1.517 trained on PDBbind but 0.653 / 1.648 on CleanSplit. (2) Shortcuts: Volkov 2022 report that nearest-neighbour lookups on ligands or proteins do well ('memorization largely dominates'); Durant 2025 show ligand-only (r 0.76) and protein-only (0.75) baselines near five ML scoring functions (0.74-0.82) on CASF2016, and all models fall to r 0.17-0.37 on a peptide holdout / ligand-bias-free set. (3) Noise floor: Kramer 2012 estimate mean error 0.44 pKi (SD 0.54), max R2 0.81 (r about 0.90, own sqrt) on large ChEMBL Ki sets; Landrum & Riniker 2024 find about 65% of cross-assay IC50 pairs differ by >0.3 log units (Kendall tau 0.51); Ross 2023 give pairwise experimental RMSE 0.91 kcal/mol vs FEP+ 1.25. LP-PDBBind (Li 2026) shows retraining on a leak-proof split changes scores and that original test performance was over-estimated. PLINDER (2024) and PLABench (2026 preprint) abstracts confirm the leakage framing but gave no readable key numbers. Caveats: Pafnucy/GenScore before/after numbers exist only in a figure; Volkov, Kramer, Brown and Wang full texts are paywalled so only abstract numbers are used.
fleet.lay_summary: Computer programs that guess how tightly a drug sticks to a protein look great on the standard tests. But many test cases are near-copies of the examples the programs learned from, like a student who saw the exam questions in advance. When researchers removed the copies, scores fell, and even simple lookup tricks that ignore the physics did almost as well as fancy AI. On top of that, the lab measurements used as the answer key are themselves fuzzy: two labs measuring the same drug often disagree by a few-fold. That fuzziness sets a ceiling no program can beat, much as nobody can read a blurry ruler more precisely than its blur.
