fleet.label: t2-patterns-deep
fleet.topic: Track 2 deep literature: chemotactic range-expansion front of E. coli in soft agar (Cremer 2019, Narla 2021)
fleet.summary:
STATE OF THE ART, Track 2 (chemotactic range-expansion front of E. coli in soft agar). Each step is tagged MEASURED (seen in an experiment I read), DERIVED (follows by mathematics from stated assumptions) or ASSUMED.

1. What the system is. [MEASURED] Motile E. coli placed at the centre of a 0.25 percent agar plate with a plentiful carbon source and a little amino-acid attractant (aspartate or serine, 100 uM) grow, and a visible ring moves outward at a steady speed. Classic papers saw this: Adler 1966 (bands made by cells that create their own gradient), Wolfe and Berg 1989 (soft agar also lets non-chemotactic, tumbling cells swarm), Croze 2011 (speed is weakly dependent on agar below 0.25 percent and drops sharply above).
2. The baseline with no steering. [DERIVED] A population that only grows and diffuses advances as a Fisher-KPP wave at c_F = 2 sqrt(D r), D the cell diffusivity, r the growth rate (Fisher 1937; Aronson-Weinberger 1978 is the rigorous source cited by the law library). [MEASURED] Non-chemotactic E. coli follow this wave with no adjustable parameters (Cremer 2019). [ASSUMED] In the law library the diffusivity is taken from run-and-tumble motion: D about 50 um^2/s in agar.
3. Why chemotaxis speeds it up. [MEASURED] Cells eat the attractant, which makes a gradient that points outward; cells at the front drift up it ('pioneers'), cells behind mostly grow ('settlers'). With an abundant carbon source plus 100 uM attractant the front moved about 3 to 4.3 mm/h in minimal media (source data, own table below). [MEASURED, own arithmetic] That is 4.4 to 5.4 times the Fisher speed computed with D = 50.2 um^2/s and the measured growth rate for the six wild-type carbon sources.
4. The model. [ASSUMED] Growth-Expansion (GE) model: logistic growth plus diffusion plus drift velocity chi0 grad(a)/(a + a_m), with attractant consumed by Michaelis-Menten uptake. It is the Keller-Segel (1971) model plus growth, the 'Patlak-Keller-Segel with growth' family. Keller-Segel alone needs a_m = 0 to be stable (Narla 2021).
5. Closed form. [DERIVED] Narla, Cremer, Hwa 2021: c = (chi0 - D) sqrt( r (a0/a_m) / (chi0 - D + D_a) ), valid when a0/a_m >> 1 + D_a/(chi0 - D). So c grows as sqrt(r) and sqrt(a0/a_m), does not depend on the uptake rate, and equals more than the Fisher speed; the Fisher speed is the lower bound. The derivation is a heuristic ansatz checked against numerical solutions, not a theorem.
6. How well it fits. [MEASURED + own calc] With Cremer's published parameters (chi0 = 315, D = 50.2, D_a = 800 um^2/s, a0/a_m = 100) the closed form is 7 to 32 percent above the six wild-type speeds (ratios 1.07 to 1.32). A single-coefficient square-root law u^2 = k r fitted on those six rows (k = 16.9 mm^2/h) misses titrated-uptake strains by 10 to 64 percent. Inside an uptake-titration series the log-log slope of u on r is 1.12 (0.89 without the zero-inducer point), not 0.5, so the sqrt(r) law is a statement about varying r with other parameters fixed; Cremer 2019 says the observed trend needs growth-rate-dependent parameters in the full model.
7. Dependence on attractant. [MEASURED] Speed rises with attractant concentration then falls: on glucose it peaks at 1000 uM (4.65 mm/h) and drops to 2.10 mm/h at 10 mM; on glycerol it peaks at 100 uM (3.67) and drops to 1.32 at 10 mM. The log-log slope over 10 to 100 uM is 0.30 (glucose) and 0.28 (glycerol), not 0.5. [DERIVED] The sqrt(a0) law cannot make a peak by itself. A peak needs an extra ingredient: the published simulation parameter file has an upper sensing limit of 30 uM (weber_offsetmax_1, read from the file), and Narla 2021 has a carrying-capacity correction (Eq 24 to 25) that I did not read myself, only through the earlier design report.
8. Contested and unsettled. (a) The Patlak-Keller-Segel form itself: Phan 2024 measured the attractant directly in a microchannel and found it fails at high cell density (consumption and chemotaxis both suppressed); the soft-agar GE model has not been tested that way. (b) Whether cell motility depends on growth rate: Cremer found flat swimming speed and diffusion in exponential growth; Ni 2020 found motility gene expression rising linearly as growth rate falls. (c) Pushed versus pulled front: Bai 2021 argues the band is a pushed wave because drift velocities fall from back to front. (d) Cell-to-cell variability: Fu 2018, Salek 2019, Keegstra 2017 show large clonal differences yet the band holds together, which a single chi0 ignores. (e) The 1971 Keller-Segel instability and finite-time blow-up of some variants (Hillen and Painter 2009).
9. Beyond the single ring. [MEASURED] Other microbial patterns on the same medium: Budrene-Berg spots and stripes from excreted attractant (1991); stripes from engineered density-dependent motility (Liu 2011); density-dependent motility with logistic growth gives spots without chemotaxis (Cates 2010); sectors from genetic drift at the edge (Hallatschek 2007). [DERIVED] The Turing law in the library (linear instability of a stationary mode) does not describe the travelling front.
10. Evolutionary reading. [MEASURED] Liu 2019: after 50 cycles (about 600 generations) the optimal expansion speed depends on habitat size, with a stable strategy of speed = growth rate x habitat size.
11. Law library (set 1.8.1, 2026-11-01). Only fisher-kpp-speed 1.1.0 (candidate, non-binding; constraint KPP1: c^2 >= 4 s D) and turing-ddi 1.1.0 (candidate) are pinned; turing-wavelength 1.1.0 is a candidate not yet pinned. The earlier law-mapper looked at 1.6.0 and found only the Turing law. There is no law for Keller-Segel or chemotactic fronts. Over the 23 aspartate/serine rows of the source data, speed over Fisher speed is between 2.49 and 7.09, so KPP1 holds in every row (own calculation, Fisher speed computed with the single D = 50.2 um^2/s for every strain, which is an approximation for the engineered strains).
OPEN PROBLEMS. (i) A direct measurement of the attractant field and density in agar to test whether the PKS closure holds at the colony density, as Phan did in a channel. (ii) A reconciled growth-rate story: how chi0, D and uptake change with r, and whether the 0.5 exponent or about 1 is right across a titration. (iii) Unifying the sensing-limit ceiling (Cremer code, 30 uM upper limit in my reading of the published parameter file) with the closed form. (iv) Prediction in new conditions (mixtures of attractants, other strains, other gel stiffnesses) from single-cell parameters alone. (v) 2D and 3D front stability, finite-time blow-up and cell-density effects beyond the 1D wave. (vi) A Lean statement that fits the actual claim: only the arithmetic of c^2 >= 4 s D is proved; the chemotactic closed form is not.
fleet.lay_summary: Imagine dropping bacteria in the middle of a dish of soft jelly with food. As they eat, they use up a little amino acid, which leaves a slope of less amino acid near them; the bacteria then swim up that slope, so a ring of cells races outward. Plain spreading by growing and wandering would move that ring only about one millimetre an hour, but the measured ring moves three to four and a half millimetres an hour. A short equation from the 1970s was improved in 2019 and 2021 to explain this, and it says the speed grows with the square root of how fast the cells divide. That rule fits roughly but not exactly, and a 2024 study shows the old equation fails when cells are very crowded. So the main picture is well supported, but the exact rule for how fast the ring moves is still being argued about.

glossary.plain: Swimming up (or down) a chemical slope by changing how often the cell tumbles.
A chemical, such as an amino acid, that cells swim towards.
A very watery jelly (0.25 percent agar) that cells can swim through.
A population spreading into empty territory.
The moving edge of the population, seen as a ring on a plate.
How fast the cells multiply, in doublings-per-time units (here per hour).
How quickly random motion spreads cells out, in square micrometres per second.
The speed of a front driven only by growth plus random spreading: 2 times the square root of D times r.
Equations that describe cells following a chemical slope that they themselves make.
The Keller-Segel model plus cell growth, used by Cremer and Narla.
A shape that moves at constant speed without changing form.
How strongly the slope of attractant pushes cells.
The attractant level below which cells hardly sense a slope, about 1 micromolar for aspartate.
Cells at the front that move forward, and cells behind that stay and grow.
A stationary spotty or stripy pattern that arises from two spreading chemicals; different from the travelling ring.
A pulled front is led by the few cells at its tip; a pushed one is driven by the bulk behind.
A formally checked statement in the project library that is listed but not yet binding.
Cloudiness of a culture at 600 nanometres, used as a stand-in for cell density.

findings.claim: Classic observation: motile E. coli placed in a capillary or on agar migrate out as visible bands (rings on plates) because the cells themselves create a gradient of oxygen or an energy source and then move up it.
findings.evidence_quote: The essence of the matter is that the bacteria create a gradient of oxygen or of an energy source, and then they move preferentially in the direction of the higher concentration of the chemical.

findings.claim: A different pattern, not a travelling front: E. coli on semi-solid agar with TCA-cycle intermediates form stationary spots or stripes that arise sequentially, driven by an attractant the cells excrete themselves.
findings.evidence_quote: they form symmetrical arrays of spots or stripes that arise sequentially.

findings.claim: Keller and Segel gave the first mathematical travelling-wave account of the bands, but their model neglected cell growth.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: The first attempt to understand these migrating bands mathematically was made by Keller and Segel, who recovered a traveling-wave solution using a pair of reaction–diffusion–convection equations
findings.value: 1971 model; the original paper has no abstract in Europe PMC and was not read by me, this is Narla 2021 reporting it

findings.claim: The Keller-Segel stable wave needs infinitely sensitive sensing (a_m = 0); with a finite threshold the part of the band with a < a_m cannot keep up and the band decays and slows.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: The latter assumption of the KS model is necessary for stable traveling waves

findings.claim: Cremer 2019 also states that the original Keller-Segel front is unstable given a realistic limit of chemotactic sensitivity.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: The original Keller–Segel front was unstable given a realistic limit of chemotactic sensitivity

findings.claim: Mathematical review: Keller-Segel-type chemotaxis models are a cornerstone of the field, but some formulations show finite-time blow-up (a density spike forming in finite time).
findings.evidence_quote: This phenomenon has been shown to lead to finite-time blow-up under certain formulations of the model

findings.claim: Review of the molecular side: the E. coli signalling pathway (phosphorylated regulator acting on the flagellar motor) is a paradigm for sensory systems.
findings.evidence_quote: This simple pathway has provided a paradigm for sensory systems in general.

findings.claim: In soft agar non-chemotactic cells also swarm; tumbling lets cells back away from obstructions, and cells that tumble more formed larger swarms, so a large colony alone does not prove chemotaxis.
findings.evidence_quote: Surprisingly, the higher the tumble frequency, the larger the swarms.

findings.claim: Agar concentration matters: front speed is weakly dependent on agar concentration below 0.25 percent (w/v) but falls sharply above it.
findings.evidence_quote: The migration front speed is weakly dependent on agar concentration at C < 0.25%, but decreases sharply above this value.

findings.claim: At 0.35 percent agar the bacteria migrate as broad growth/diffusion bands because the gel suppresses chemotaxis.
findings.evidence_quote: These are growth/diffusion waves arising because of suppression of chemotaxis by the agar

findings.claim: Central claim of the chosen system: chemotaxis along self-generated gradients of a low-dose attractant, with an abundant primary carbon source, speeds up population expansion before nutrients run out.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: Chemotaxis in nutrient-replete conditions promotes the expansion of bacterial populations into unoccupied territories well before nutrients run out in the current environment.

findings.claim: Navigated expansion beats unguided Fisher-Kolmogorov expansion in speed and population gain.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: This navigated range expansion process spreads faster and yields larger population gains than unguided expansion following the canonical Fisher-Kolmogorov dynamics

findings.claim: Measured: expansion speed increases with the batch growth rate across carbon sources, for aspartate or serine as attractant, and for two other motile E. coli strains.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: The measured expansion speeds follow a common increasing trend with the batch culture growth rate in the respective medium

findings.claim: Without a supplemented attractant, or in a Delta-tar mutant that cannot sense aspartate, expansion is much slower.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: In contrast, the expansion became much slower in the absence of a supplemented attractant

findings.claim: Measured: swimming speed and run duration showed no substantial variation with growth rate during steady exponential growth, so cell diffusion is nearly growth-rate independent in that study.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: neither swimming speed nor run duration showed substantial variation at different growth rates

findings.claim: Reference condition (glycerol + aspartate, confocal run): the front bulge advanced at about 3.2 mm/h, followed by a broad exponentially rising density behind it.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: the advance of the front bulge (~3.2 mm / h ) is steadily followed by a trailing region with a broad, exponentially increasing density profile
findings.value: 3.2 mm/h here; the source-data table gives 3.675 mm/h for the same medium (different plates), a 13 percent gap

findings.claim: Without chemotaxis the populations follow the Fisher-Kolmogorov solution with no adjustable parameters.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: Detailed quantitative analysis established that bacterial dynamics in these cases are indeed described by the FK solution without adjustable parameters

findings.claim: Growth-Expansion model: only one parameter, the chemotactic coefficient chi0, was left free, fixed by matching the asymptotic speed in the reference condition; the others came from independent experiments or literature.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: only one parameter remained unknown, the chemotactic coefficient χ 0

findings.claim: Model prediction confirmed: changing the attractant uptake rate hardly changed the expansion, although uptake is what builds the gradient.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: changing the uptake rate hardly affected the expansion dynamics, in agreement with model prediction

findings.claim: A simple scaling analysis gives the square-root growth-rate dependence; the authors say the full model with growth-rate-dependent parameters describes the data with no adjustable parameters.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: a simple scaling analysis captures the square-root form of the growth-rate dependence

findings.claim: Speed versus attractant concentration peaks at a moderate level (long known), reproduced by the model.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: The model also adequately accounted for the dependence of the expansion speed on the attractant concentration, long known to peak at a moderate level

findings.claim: Pioneers and settlers: cells in the front bulge drift forward; cells behind drift little and only grow, seeding the territory the front passed.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
findings.evidence_quote: cells in the front bulge region have positive drift velocities and move forward on average; they are the ‘pioneers’ of the population.

findings.claim: At chi0 = 0 the GE model reduces to Fisher-KPP, whose speed 2 sqrt(D_rho r) is the minimum expansion speed of the system.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: In the absence of chemotaxis ( χ 0 = 0 ), the GE model reduces to the Fisher–Kolmogorov–Petrovsky–Piskunov (F-KPP) equation

findings.claim: Derived (heuristic ansatz, checked against numerical solutions): speed is proportional to sqrt(growth rate r).
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: First, there is a square root dependence on the growth rate r
findings.value: Eq 21: c = (chi0 - D_rho) sqrt( r (a0/a_m) / (chi0 - D_rho + D_a) )

findings.claim: Derived: speed rises with the square root of relative attractant a0/a_m.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: The expansion speed is further increased by the square root of the relative background attractant concentration

findings.claim: Derived: speed is independent of attractant uptake rate mu (bulge size is inversely proportional to mu so mu cancels).
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: the expansion speed c does not depend on the specific rate of attractant uptake μ

findings.claim: Validity condition of the closed form: a0/a_m much greater than 1 + D_a/(chi0 - D_rho); independent of r.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.value: Eq 22; equation is garbled in the PMC XML so no verbatim quote; read from extracted symbols

findings.claim: Parameter ranges: D_rho about 50 um^2/s in soft agar vs 300 to 1000 um^2/s in liquid; sensitivity phi = (chi0 - D_rho)/D_rho between 2 and 8 (cited); aspartate uptake and sensing constants about 1 uM (assumed equal, a_k = a_m).
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: D ρ ∼ 50 μ m 2 / s for E. coli swimming in soft agar ( 39 ) and D ρ ∼ 300 to 1 , 000 μ m 2 / s in liquid media

findings.claim: Predicted boost: speeds can exceed the Fisher speed by orders of magnitude when environmental attractant is high relative to the sensing limit.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: expansion speeds can be boosted by orders of magnitude when the environmental availability of chemicals relative to the cellular limits of chemical sensing is high

findings.claim: Earlier growth-including models restored stability but did not reproduce fast speeds or the rising density trailing the band.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: they fail to reproduce experimental observations such as fast expansion speeds and a trailing region of increasing bacterial density behind the migrating band

findings.claim: Contested: the standard Patlak-Keller-Segel model with growth was never directly verified; direct fluorescent measurement of the aspartate gradient shows it fits low-density waves but diverges at high cell density.
findings.evidence_quote: While the model agreed well with our data at low cell densities, it diverged at high cell densities.
findings.value: peak OD 0.6 (fits) vs 4.6 (fails); microchannel, not agar

findings.claim: Phan 2024 proposes that attractant consumption and chemotaxis are both suppressed at higher cell densities.
findings.evidence_quote: in which both attractant consumption and bacterial chemotaxis are suppressed at higher cell densities

findings.claim: Phan 2024 low-density fit: growth rate 0.38 +/- 0.02 per h; consumption 0.51 +/- 0.05; half-saturation 7.6 +/- 3.7 uM; D_B 400 +/- 100; chi 3300 +/- 230 (the XML prints the diffusion units as uM^2/s, which I read as um^2/s).
findings.evidence_quote: These PDEs fit the data well for low cell density bacterial waves

findings.claim: Phan 2024 wave speed 4.4 um/s at low density is 15.8 mm/h by my arithmetic (4.4 x 3.6), about four times the 3 to 5 mm/h of soft agar, so it is a different regime (assuming the XML symbol means um).
findings.source: own calculation, script D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/t2-patterns-deep/calc.py on Cremer 2019 source data MOESM11/MOESM22

findings.claim: Contested or at least unreconciled: motility gene expression rises linearly as growth rate falls on poorer carbon sources (anticipatory investment), whereas Cremer 2019 found swimming speed and run time flat against growth rate in steady exponential growth.
findings.evidence_quote: the expression of motility genes increases linearly with the decrease of growth rate on poorer carbon sources
findings.value: different quantity (gene expression vs measured swimming); not a direct contradiction

findings.claim: Ni 2020: E. coli invests more in motility in poor media, in proportion to the fitness advantage of following gradients.
findings.evidence_quote: in poor nutritional conditions, Escherichia coli increases its investment in motility in proportion to the reproductive fitness advantage provided by the ability to follow nutrient gradients

findings.claim: Evolution at the front: an optimal expansion speed exists for a given habitat size; the stable strategy is speed equal to growth rate times habitat size.
findings.evidence_quote: to expand at a speed given by the product of the growth rate and habitat size

findings.claim: Experimental evolution (50 cycles, about 600 generations, 0.25 percent TB agar): ancestor speed about 6 mm/h; samples from 15 mm from the centre stayed at ancestor speed.
findings.evidence_quote: (position C, with distance X C = 15 mm) at which the expansion speed of the evolved populations fluctuated around that of the ancestor (~6 mm/h)
findings.value: 6 mm/h in rich TB vs 3 to 4.3 mm/h in minimal medium (Cremer)

findings.claim: Within a travelling band, clonal cells of very different chemotactic ability stay together by sorting along the gradient.
findings.evidence_quote: despite substantial differences in individual chemotactic abilities, the cells are able to migrate as a coherent group by spontaneously sorting themselves within the moving band

findings.claim: In the microchannel higher aspartate gave a slower band, consistent with the peak-then-fall dose curve in agar.
findings.evidence_quote: as the concentration of Asp increased, the speed of the band decreased

findings.claim: Individual drift velocity decreases from back to front of the band, so the band is a pushed wave front.
findings.evidence_quote: enables the bacterial population to migrate as a pushed wave front

findings.claim: Clonal E. coli differ strongly in chemotactic sensitivity (pathway gain).
findings.evidence_quote: strong heterogeneity in the chemotactic sensitivity coefficient exists even within clonal populations of bacteria

findings.claim: Signalling is variable across and within single cells (FRET).
findings.evidence_quote: pervasive signaling variability, both across cells in isogenic populations and within individual cells over time

findings.claim: Directional persistence of runs is larger up the gradient inside a travelling wave, improving collective migration.
findings.evidence_quote: not only the mean run length is longer in the direction of propagation, but also that the directional persistence is larger compared to the opposite direction

findings.claim: Information limit: E. coli climb gradients within a factor of two of a theoretical bound.
findings.evidence_quote: Despite these limitations, E. coli climb gradients at speeds within a factor of two of the theoretical bound.

findings.claim: Populations can smooth out large-scale perturbations of the front in a 3D porous medium through spatial variation of sensing.
findings.evidence_quote: bacterial populations autonomously smooth out large-scale perturbations in their overall morphology

findings.claim: Alternative route to stable spots and rings without chemotaxis: density-dependent motility with logistic growth (arrested phase separation).
findings.evidence_quote: No chemotaxis is assumed in the model, yet it predicts the formation of patterns strikingly similar to some of those believed to result from chemotactic behavior.

findings.claim: Engineered stripes: a synthetic circuit coupling cell density to motility makes E. coli form periodic stripes in an expanding population.
findings.evidence_quote: This system enabled programmed Escherichia coli cells to form periodic stripes of high and low cell densities sequentially and autonomously.

findings.claim: Genetic sectoring at the edge of expanding colonies is driven by fluctuations in a thin band of pioneers.
findings.evidence_quote: The formation of these regions is driven by random fluctuations that originate in a thin band of pioneers at the expanding frontier.

findings.claim: Law set 1.8.1 pins two relevant laws, fisher-kpp-speed 1.1.0 and turing-ddi 1.1.0, both status candidate (advisory, non-binding). turing-wavelength exists as an unpinned candidate. No law covers chemotactic fronts or Keller-Segel (grep of the lean tree found none).
findings.evidence_quote: Fisher-KPP: c^2 = 4sD is the minimum of the linear speed relation, attained at one decay rate

findings.claim: The Fisher-KPP law explicitly does not prove a wave exists or that organisms disperse diffusively; its checkable direction is the lower bound c^2 >= 4 s D (constraint KPP1).
findings.evidence_quote: it does not establish that a travelling wave exists, that compactly supported initial data converge to it, or that any population disperses diffusively.

findings.claim: The Turing law gives linear instability of a spatial mode only, not a pattern; it does not describe the chemotactic front, which is a growth-and-drift travelling wave.
findings.evidence_quote: Establishes linear instability of a spatial mode, not that a pattern forms

findings.claim: Narla states the Fisher speed is the minimum expansion speed of the GE system, so KPP1 (c^2 >= 4 s D with s = r, D = D_rho) is a testable lower bound for this track.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
findings.evidence_quote: The green dashed line represents the stable Fisher speed, c F = 2 D ρ r , the minimum expansion speed of our system.
findings.value: link between Narla and the law is my mapping

key_claims.claim: Chemotaxis along a self-made gradient of a low-dose attractant, with an abundant carbon source, makes the E. coli front in soft agar faster than the Fisher-Kolmogorov front; speed rises with growth rate.
key_claims.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1733-y (full text via Europe PMC PMC6883170)
key_claims.evidence_quote: This navigated range expansion process spreads faster and yields larger population gains than unguided expansion following the canonical Fisher-Kolmogorov dynamics

key_claims.claim: Narla 2021 gives a closed-form speed for the Growth-Expansion model: proportional to sqrt(r) and sqrt(a0/a_m), independent of uptake rate; at chi0 = 0 it is the Fisher-KPP wave.
key_claims.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2105138118 (full text via Europe PMC PMC8640786)
key_claims.evidence_quote: The expansion speed is further increased by the square root of the relative background attractant concentration

key_claims.claim: The Patlak-Keller-Segel closure underneath the model is not directly verified in agar and fails at high cell density in a channel; the dependence of the front on growth rate beyond sqrt(r) is therefore the main open point.
key_claims.evidence_quote: While the model agreed well with our data at low cell densities, it diverged at high cell densities.

key_claims.claim: The law library (set 1.8.1) has no chemotactic-front law; fisher-kpp-speed (candidate, non-binding) gives only the lower bound c^2 >= 4 s D, and turing-ddi is not the right mechanism for a travelling front.
key_claims.evidence_quote: it does not establish that a travelling wave exists, that compactly supported initial data converge to it, or that any population disperses diffusively.

fleet.label: t2-patterns-law
fleet.topic: Track 2 (E. coli chemotactic range-expansion front) mapped against law set 1.8.1, with a new checked Lean law
fleet.summary: Law set 1.8.1 (59 pinned laws: 36 accepted, 10 candidate, 7 proposed, 3 retired, 3 contested; 14 have no theorem) contains NO accepted law about spatial patterns or fronts. Directly relevant are two pinned candidates, fisher-kpp-speed (Delphi.LeanBio.Round2.KppSpeed.kpp_min_speed) and turing-ddi (Delphi.LeanBio.Round2.TuringDDI.turing_instability). turing-wavelength has a registry file but is NOT pinned in 1.8.1. The older map (laws-patterns.json, read at 1.6.0 from the split-out leanbio copy) cites Delphi/Turing.lean and Delphi/CellGeometry.lean, which do not exist in the application repo; it listed Fisher-KPP speed as missing, but it is now pinned as a candidate. The older map missed the Narla closed form and every law a chemotactic front actually needs. I wrote and checked NarlaSpeed.lean (namespace Delphi.Track2.ChemotaxisFront): from the Narla closed form c^2 (X+Da) = X^2 r A it proves that front speed goes as the square root of growth rate (ratio law, strict monotonicity, quadrupling doubles speed, log-log slope exactly 1/2) and an elimination lemma (a 1.5-fold faster front cannot come from at most 2-fold faster growth at fixed X, Da, A). Checker: errors=0, sorryAx=0, axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] for all 10 theorems; a sorry-mutated copy was correctly rejected.
fleet.lay_summary: We have a library of mathematical rules that a computer has checked line by line. Almost none of them talk about colonies of bacteria spreading across a plate, so the library was nearly blind to this track. The nearest rule says how fast a wave of growth plus random wandering can spread, and it gives only a slow baseline: the real chemotactic front is about five times faster. I added one new checked rule. It says that if bacteria steer toward food, the front speed should grow like the square root of how fast they multiply, so doubling the growth rate should speed the front by only about 41 percent. Earlier lab numbers on this project suggest the real exponent is closer to one, which means the simple rule may fail, and that is exactly what a good test should be able to show.

glossary.plain: A proof-checking program: a statement counts only if the computer verifies every step.
The hidden placeholder Lean uses when a proof has a gap; its presence means the proof is not finished.
A frozen, numbered list of the rules the project trusts at a given moment.
Registry stages: candidate is machine-checked but not human-approved; accepted is approved; proposed is only an idea with no proof.
A registry entry that names a topic but has no proved theorem behind it.
The moving edge where a colony spreads into fresh territory.
Cells steering up a gradient of a food chemical.
A front driven by growth plus random spreading, moving at a fixed speed.
Spots or stripes that appear when two chemicals spread at different rates.
How many percent one quantity changes when another changes by one percent.
A theorem that says a stated combination of numbers is impossible, so a design that commits to it can be rejected.

So KPP1 would not be violated but is nowhere near binding. Inputs are taken from design-patterns.json (not re-fetched by me).

findings.claim: The older map cites lean/Delphi/Turing.lean (turing_instability_iff, no_instability_of_equal_diffusivity, trace_neg_of_wellMixed, exists_pos_growth_of_D_neg), lean/Delphi/CellGeometry.lean (tripleJunction_120, hexagon_of_120, etc.) and registry ids turing-ddi-linear-condition and seven cell-geometry ids. None of these files or ids exist in the application repo at 1.8.1: lean/Delphi has no Turing.lean or CellGeometry.lean (only Altitude, Audit, Blueprint, Certificates, Constraints, Empirical, Favored, Fisher, Flight, Genotype, Hydrostatics, Kimura, MaynardSmith, Perturb, Physiology, Scaling, Thompson), there is no ThompsonLaws or DarwinLaws library, and the registry has turing-ddi (a different, weaker theorem: one direction, hypothesis-form) instead. Those files do exist in the older split-out copy upstream/leanbio/lean/Delphi/ (Turing.lean, CellGeometry.lean, Crystals.lean listed). So the older map's strongest law (the iff characterisation) is not available to this application's checker.

The older map listed 'Fisher-KPP front speed' as a missing law. It now exists in 1.8.1 as the pinned candidate fisher-kpp-speed (introduced 1.8.0), but only as the algebraic minimum of the linear speed relation under hypothesis c^2 = 4sD; it does not prove travelling-wave existence and has nothing on chemotaxis.
findings.evidence_quote: it does not establish that a travelling wave exists, that compactly supported initial data converge to it, or that any population disperses diffusively.

findings.claim: Other pinned laws touching the track only marginally: maynardsmith-hitchhiking (candidate, Delphi.LeanBio.Hitchhiking.hitchhiking_relHet, lean/registry/proposals/maynardsmith-hitchhiking/law.lean) and kimura-fixation-probability (accepted, Delphi.NeutralChain.fixedBy_tendsto, lean/Delphi/Kimura.lean) and favored-fixation-lower-bound (accepted, Delphi.FavoredChain.fixationProbability_ge, lean/Delphi/Favored.lean) for edge sectoring/genetic drift at the front (the scout's runner-up); physiology-q10 (accepted, Delphi.Physiology.q10_ratio, lean/Delphi/Physiology.lean) for temperature scaling of growth and motility; development-growth-asymptote (candidate, von Bertalanffy, Exocoetidae-scoped, binds nothing) is NOT a fit for logistic colony growth.

What the older map missed (relative to 1.8.1 and to the chosen system): (1) it mapped the wrong library version, so it names files and ids absent from 1.8.1; (2) it never mentions turing-ddi, turing-wavelength or fisher-kpp-speed by their real registry ids; (3) it has no law for the Narla/Keller-Segel closed form that the design's frozen predictions F1 to F3 actually use; (4) it contains no check of the square-root-of-growth-rate law, which is the control law the design says the data already contradict.
findings.source: laws-patterns.json keys (existing, missing, elimination_pattern, changes_since_october) read in this run

findings.claim: Narla et al. state a square-root dependence of the expansion speed on growth rate and on the relative attractant concentration, and that speed does not depend on the uptake rate.
findings.source: Europe PMC full text PMC8640786, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8640786/fullTextXML (fetched in this run, 315460 bytes, sha256 17ca8bac191814334ace7abe484087836bbfdb141c5b960d6628b22965424054, saved scratch/t2-patterns-law/narla.xml)
findings.evidence_quote: there is a square root dependence on the growth rate r, as validated by numerical results in Fig. 2A.

findings.claim: I did NOT independently re-derive or re-read Narla Eq. 21 from the MathML; the closed form c = X sqrt(r A/(X+Da)) is taken from the design file's transcription, with only the sqrt-in-r dependence confirmed from the paper text. The Lean law is therefore a theorem about the stated form, labelled as a named hypothesis.

Using the design's fitted X = 0.7874 mm^2/h, Da = 2.88 mm^2/h, A = 100, r = 0.9985 /h, Eq 21 gives c = 4.109 mm/h and c^2/r = 16.906 mm^2/h, matching the design's fitted k = 16.907 (the fit was to this relation) and 5.2 percent below the measured 4.335 mm/h.

fleet.label: t2-patterns-lay
fleet.topic: Track 2 plain-language explanation: the chemotactic range-expansion front of E. coli in soft agar (Cremer 2019 data, Narla 2021 travelling-wave law), checked against law set 1.8.1
fleet.summary:
PLAIN-LANGUAGE PACK FOR TRACK 2. Bracketed tags like [F6] point to the numbered findings in this file (claim text begins with the same tag). Reading level about 9th grade.

A. WHAT ARE WE DOING AND WHY (one paragraph). Some bacteria spread across a dish as a moving ring that can run several times faster than ordinary spreading [F1][F2][F7]. Two published papers describe this ring with data and with a formula [F8][F9][F10]. We are using it as a test case for a bigger question: when a scientist writes down a rule for how a living pattern forms, can the rule be checked honestly against measurements that were not used to build it? We will first write down what the rule predicts and only then open the measurements, so nobody (including us) can quietly adjust the rule afterwards [F22]. The aim is not a new discovery about bacteria. It is a fair, repeatable check of a named rule, and an honest record of where it holds and where it breaks [F12][F13].

B. HOW, STEP BY STEP (each step has an everyday comparison).
1. Pick the system. We study the common gut bacterium E. coli spreading from a spot in a dish of soft agar, a jelly so loose that cells can swim through it [F3]. Comparison: a drop of ink spreading in a thin gel, except the ink is alive and steers.
2. Name what we measure. The first number is how fast the outer edge of the colony moves outward, in millimetres per hour; the second is how fast the cells double, in doublings-rate per hour [F6]. Comparison: the speed of a spreading crowd and how quickly the crowd is having babies.
3. Understand the effect being explained. When the jelly holds a little attractant (a food-like smell), the cells form a travelling ring at the edge and move much faster than cells that only wander and multiply [F1][F2][F4][F7]. Comparison: a crowd that follows a smell trail it is itself laying down, instead of wandering at random.
4. Write down the formula. One paper gives a formula in which the edge speed grows with the square root of the growth rate and with the square root of how strong the attractant is compared with the weakest level the cells can sense, and does not depend on how fast cells eat the attractant [F8][F9][F10]. Comparison: a recipe card that says which dials matter and which do not.
5. Set the simple baseline. We fit one number to six ordinary-cell measurements, so that speed squared is a fixed multiple of growth rate [F12]. Comparison: a rule of thumb that has no biology in it, used as the bar to beat.
6. Write predictions before opening new data. The earlier design lists six predictions with pass and fail lines, kept in a dated file that is not edited afterwards [F22]. Comparison: sealing your guess in an envelope before the race.
7. Open the held-out measurements. These are cells with modified food uptake, a mixture of two attractants, and measurements of single swimming cells, none of which were used to set the formula [F22]. Comparison: the exam questions you did not see while studying.
8. Score each prediction as passed, failed or inconclusive. A failure is kept and reported, never removed [F22]. Comparison: a referee who writes down every foul.
9. Check the formula against the law library. The project's law library (version 1.8.1) holds a related candidate law about the minimum speed of a spreading wave, and nothing about chemotactic waves [F17][F18]. Comparison: asking whether a building code already covers the thing we are building.
10. Report the map of what held and what did not. The result is a list of which dependencies in the formula survived the checks, with the conditions under which each holds [F22]. Comparison: a road map with the closed roads marked.

C. WHAT WOULD COUNT AS BEING WRONG (plain words). The design proposes these tests; none has been run yet [F22]. (1) If the formula is right that speed does not depend on how fast cells eat the attractant, strains that eat it at different rates should front at about the same speed; a clear trend would show it is wrong. (2) The formula says the density of cells in the ring should go down in proportion to how fast they eat the attractant, so a strain that eats about three times slower should have about three times denser rings; if the density does not follow within the stated range, the formula is wrong there. (3) The formula says the cell density behind the ring rises smoothly with a length equal to speed divided by growth rate; a measured length more than 30 percent off would count as wrong. (4) If the single-cell swimming data cannot explain why speed rises faster than the square root of growth rate in the food-uptake series, that explanation is dropped. Already seen, so not blind: the square-root-of-growth rule is already known to miss many modified strains [F13][F14], and the dependence on attractant strength is already known to look weaker than square-root in the seen data (design-patterns.json, own calculation).

D. WHAT COULD GO WRONG. (1) Our guess can be partly leaked: the published figures show the data we call unseen, so only the numeric files are unopened [design-patterns.json risks]. (2) The formula was copied from a computer-readable version of the paper by an earlier agent and must be checked against the PDF before any freeze [design-patterns.json risks]. (3) Some conditions have only one or two repeats, so averages are shaky [F6 table]. (4) The standard chemotaxis model can fail at high cell density, which the formula may inherit [F16]. (5) The jelly dish is not a gut or soil, so the result says little about wild settings by itself. (6) The related library law is a candidate, not accepted, and only proves arithmetic about a formula, not that a colony obeys it [F17]. (7) We have no wet lab here, so nothing new is grown; 'new' means new to our fit.

E. GLOSSARY: see the glossary field (ten terms).

F. THREE QUESTIONS A LAYPERSON WOULD ASK.
Q1. Why does a formula for a bacteria ring matter? Honest answer: on its own, little outside this system. It matters here as a clean test of whether a rule, checked on conditions it was not built from, keeps working. Where it breaks is as informative as where it holds [F12][F13].
Q2. Is this proving that bacteria smell their way across a dish? Honest answer: that finding comes from the Cremer paper, which reports that chemotaxis in food-rich conditions speeds up expansion [F1][F2]. Our work does not re-prove it. We test whether a formula for the speed holds up.
Q3. If the simple rule already fits the normal cells, why bother with the rest? Honest answer: because it fits only six measurements, then misses most of the other seventeen we checked, by 8 to 94 percent [F12][F13]. A rule that works only where it was tuned is not yet a law.
fleet.lay_summary: Imagine a drop of living ink spreading in a dish of clear jelly. Bacteria called E. coli do not just drift outward. They follow a faint smell of food that they themselves use up, and this makes a ring at the edge that moves several times faster than plain wandering [F1][F2][F7]. Scientists have a formula for how fast the ring should move [F8][F9][F10]. We are checking that formula on measurements it was not tuned on, and we write down our predictions first so we cannot cheat. A very simple rule fits six normal measurements within about 11 percent but misses most of the others, so the formula still has to prove itself [F12][F13].

findings.claim: [F1] In a Cremer et al. 2019 Nature paper, chemotaxis (directed movement along chemical gradients) in nutrient-rich conditions makes E. coli populations expand into empty territory.
findings.evidence_quote: Chemotaxis in nutrient-replete conditions promotes the expansion of bacterial populations into unoccupied territories well before nutrients run out in the current environment.

findings.claim: [F2] Low attractant levels act as 'aroma-like cues' that set the direction and raise the speed of population movement along self-generated attractant gradients; this is faster than unguided Fisher-Kolmogorov expansion.
findings.evidence_quote: Low levels of chemoattractants act as aroma-like cues in this process, establishing the direction and enhancing the speed of population movement along the self-generated attractant gradients.

findings.claim: [F3] Expansion speeds were measured on soft-agar plates containing 0.25 percent agar.
findings.evidence_quote: Expansion speeds were measured using soft-agar plates containing 0.25% agar and growth media resembled to the liquid culture conditions introduced above.

findings.claim: [F4] The moving ring shows up as a bulge in the cell-density profile just behind a steep exponential rise at the front.
findings.evidence_quote: The chemotactic ring is seen as a bulge in the density profile following the steep (exponential) increase at the front

findings.claim: [F5] In one example (glycerol as food, a low amount of aspartate as attractant) the front bulge advanced at about 3.2 mm per hour, followed by a broad exponentially increasing density behind it.
findings.evidence_quote: Strikingly, the advance of the front bulge (~3.2 mm / h ) is steadily followed by a trailing region with a broad, exponentially increasing density profile

findings.claim: [F6] Wild-type E. coli (strain HE206) on 20 mM glucose with 100 uM aspartate in 0.25 percent agar: mean expansion speed 4.335 mm/h (n=5) and growth rate 0.9985 per hour; on 40 mM glycerol: 3.675 mm/h and 0.7735 per hour.

findings.claim: [F8] Narla, Cremer and Hwa (2021) report that the front speed of the growth-expansion model depends on the square root of the growth rate.
findings.evidence_quote: First, there is a square root dependence on the growth rate r , as validated by numerical results in Fig. 2 A .

findings.claim: [F9] The same paper reports that speed increases with the square root of the relative background attractant concentration a0/am.
findings.evidence_quote: The expansion speed is further increased by the square root of the relative background attractant concentration, a 0 / a m ( Fig. 2 B ).

findings.claim: [F10] The same paper reports that speed does not depend on the attractant uptake rate or on the starting population size.

findings.claim: [F11] The paper's abstract says speeds can be boosted by orders of magnitude when the environment's chemical availability is high relative to the cells' sensing limits.

findings.claim: [F12] A one-number baseline u^2 = k*r (least squares through the origin) fitted on the six wild-type aspartate rows gives k = 16.904 mm^2/h and reproduces those six rows within -9.6 to +11.1 percent. (An earlier agent reported 16.907; the difference is rounding in the fit.)

findings.claim: [F16] Phan et al. 2024 (PNAS) report that the standard Patlak-Keller-Segel model of collective chemotactic migration breaks down at high cell densities, using a fluorescent aspartate sensor. fleet.label: t3-lumen-alt
fleet.topic: Track 3 alternatives and neighbours: lumen geometry (MDCK cyst lumen shape, Vasquez 2021)
fleet.summary: Keep MDCK (Vasquez 2021) as the primary system. Seven further candidates were screened beyond the four the scout already ranked (blastocyst, pancreatic organoids, zebrafish otic vesicle, bile canaliculus): zebrafish Kupffer's vesicle, ascidian notochord tube, intestinal organoids, a phase-field organoid model, Hydra spheroids, kidney-cell fluid pumps, and electrically inflated kidneyoids. None of the new ones is a better primary. Only the notochord (21.2 GB of images, MATLAB code with no licence field) and the kidney pump (source data in the article, plotting code on GitHub) have public material bearing on lumen mechanics, and neither pairs per-sample shape tables with a model sweep the way Vasquez does. Strongest competing explanation: pressure-dominated lumens (Laplace sphere, hydraulic inflation), refined by Mukenhirn 2024 into a pressure versus junctional-tension force balance in MDCK-II cysts. It is not independent of the chosen model: Vasquez's own model includes pressure and covers the pressure-dominated case, and Mukenhirn also reports excess apical area aiding lumen opening. The discriminating prediction is non-sphericity at low pressure, which a pure Laplace model cannot produce. I found no public per-cyst data for the Mukenhirn model, so it can be run only as a model arm on Vasquez data. Run alongside: the scout's pancreatic organoid tables (a higher-pressure regime where the rival should do better) as a regime check; do not add a dataset from this report as a gate. Registry note: law set 1.8.1 contains physiology-laplace (accepted) and no cell-geometry or lumen law; the seven cell-geometry candidates the earlier law-mapper cited are not in this tree.
fleet.lay_summary: Scientists want to know why the hollow centre of a tiny ball of kidney cells has the shape it has. One idea is that fluid pressure inflates it like a balloon, so it should be round. The chosen study found the shapes are often irregular, because the cells have a fixed amount of inner surface that they must fit around. I looked for other living systems that could test the same question, such as a fish embryo organ, the tube inside a sea squirt, and gut organoids. Each is either too large to download, has no public measurements, or is only a computer model, so I recommend keeping the kidney-cell balls as the main test. The balloon idea stays as the rival to beat, and a data set from pancreas organoids, where pressure matters more, is the best companion run.

findings.claim: Vasquez 2021 reports MDCK lumen shape reflects cell geometry tied to polarity, and its model includes both geometry and pressure.
findings.evidence_quote: We find that in this system, lumen shape reflects basic geometrical considerations tied to the establishment of apico-basal polarity. A physical model incorporating both cell geometry and intraluminal pressure can account for our observations

findings.claim: The pressure-dominated view is the competing explanation, supported by the mouse blastocyst.
findings.evidence_quote: Hydrostatic pressure has been proposed to drive lumen expansion, a view that is supported by experiments in the mouse blastocyst.

findings.claim: Mukenhirn 2024 (MDCK-II cysts) explains lumen morphologies from a pressure versus tension force balance and suggests excess apical area helps lumen opening, so the rival partly agrees with the chosen model.
findings.evidence_quote: enabled us to explain lumen morphologies from the pressure-tension force balance.

findings.claim: Mukenhirn 2024: ZO depletion collapses the lumen and folds apical membrane; claudin ion barrier is not required for inflation.
findings.evidence_quote: the depletion of the zonula occludens scaffold resulted in lumen collapse and folding of apical membranes

findings.claim: Kupffer vesicle: cell volume and shape changes are separable from lumen forces, so it argues against pressure alone controlling cell shape.
findings.evidence_quote: asymmetric changes in KV cell volume and shape occur normally when KV lumen growth fails due to leaky cell adhesions

findings.claim: The eLife record for the Kupffer vesicle paper lists no data files: additionalFiles holds only a transparent reporting form.
Ascidian notochord paper builds a conservation-law tube-expansion theory with asymmetric cortex tension and tight-junction gating, and predicts growth kinetics under different conditions.
findings.evidence_quote: a conservation-laws-based tube expansion theory was developed

findings.claim: Notochord images on Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.15005334 total 21,226,936,940 bytes in 6 files under CC-BY-4.0, far above the 150 MB cap.
Notochord code is the public GitHub repo WenjieShi8514/Physics_tube, 11 files, MATLAB and Mathematica, no licence reported by the API.
Intestinal organoid paper: feedback between cellular tension and fluid pressure gives bulged versus budded crypt bistability.
findings.evidence_quote: bistability arising from feedback between cellular tensions and fluid pressure could be a general mechanism that coordinates multicellular shape changes in developing systems.

findings.claim: Intestinal organoid data statement: Source Data with the paper; code from an earlier MIT-licensed repo.

findings.evidence_quote: construct phase diagrams and show their dependencies on proliferation time and lumen pressure.

findings.evidence_quote: periodic osmotically driven inflation and deflation cycles generate mechanical stimuli in the form of tissue stretching

findings.claim: Kidney epithelial pumps: flux falls with hydraulic pressure until a stall pressure; ADPKD cells reverse flux direction.
findings.evidence_quote: The fluidic flux declines with increasing hydraulic pressure until a stall pressure, in a manner similar to mechanical fluid pumps.

findings.claim: Kidney pump data: source data with the paper, remainder on request.

recommendations: Keep MDCK (Vasquez 2021) as the primary Track 3 system; none of the seven new candidates has per-sample shape tables plus a model sweep.

Implement the pressure-only Laplace sphere and a pressure-plus-junctional-tension variant as explicit rival model arms scored on the same Vasquez data; the pressure-tension arm needs per-cyst pressure, which Vasquez does not provide, so it must use a genotype-level pressure constant.
Run the scout pancreatic organoid tables alongside as a regime check (higher pressure, where the rival should do better); a model that wins in MDCK and loses there is a coherent result.

Do not add the notochord (21.2 GB), Hydra (186.7 MB, expression data) or Kupffer vesicle (no public data) to the gate. Optionally pull the kidney-pump Source Data (small) to put a pressure scale on the Laplace arm.
Ask the registry owner why the seven cell-geometry candidate laws are absent from 1.8.1: any lumen certificate would currently rest on physiology-laplace alone, which has no instance.
Try to obtain Mukenhirn 2024 per-cyst pressure and tension values (Dev Cell data statement not read); this is the single most valuable missing item.

fleet.label: t3-lumen-crit
fleet.topic: Track 3 adversarial critique of the frozen MDCK lumen-shape design (design-lumen.json)
fleet.summary: Recomputed every checkable number in design-lumen.json from the Vasquez 2021 source tables. RIGHT: WT counts (52 with N, 43 in N 3..10, 7 above 10), M2 line 0.6703+0.0261 N, RMSEs 0.124/0.106/0.212, N ceiling 12.64, Spearman 0.008 and 0.525, P2 critical rho 0.276 and 0.396, the four sha256 hashes, held-out N coverage (44/7 and 22/2/1), the rerun-grid counts, and all five scalloped-polygon solidities (also checked by numerical area). WRONG: the second 'identity' (a = (N l_b)^2/(4 pi IPQ_cyst) - N) has IPQ_cyst in the wrong place (max error 3.23 on 52 WT rows; the corrected form is exact to 1.8e-14); and 'once N, l_a, l_b are measured lumen IPQ is fixed' also needs a or IPQ_cyst. STRUCTURAL PROBLEMS not in the design: genotype is fully confounded with imaging session (WT 7 sessions 2017-18; Rab11a 3 sessions in 2020; Cldn-qKO ONE session, 3 fields); WT residuals differ by session (ANOVA p=0.0025, ICC 0.36, SD of session means 0.074), larger than the +-0.05 and -0.03 thresholds, so P3 and P4 cannot cleanly test genotype. POWER: P2 has 56 percent power against a true rho of 0.3 (n=51) and 30 percent (n=25); P4's RMSE<=0.16 clause almost cannot fail and its mean clause false-fails 2.6 percent with no batch effect but about 52 percent with a WT-sized one; P3 full-support probability is 25 to 84 percent for assumed shifts of 0.03 to 0.08; P5 has SE(RMSE)=0.022 on n=15 and its WT part is now seen; P6 has no data (Zenodo holds example images only). Thresholds 0.124, 0.106, 0.16, +-0.05 were set from the same WT data; the P1 gate beats a constant, not the size-only line. RECOMMENDATION: keep P1 (revised: leave-session-out, versus M2), keep P2 for Rab11a only with an equivalence-style bound, demote P3/P4 to exploratory, DROP P5 and P6, keep the physical build with a tighter tolerance. DISCLOSURE: I read WT lumens with N>10 (7 rows) and held-out N counts and filenames only; I read NO held-out solidity, l_a or area values.
fleet.lay_summary: The plan predicts the shape of tiny fluid-filled balls of kidney-type cells using a computer model. I redid the sums from the published data. Most numbers check out, but one formula was written upside down and several tests are too weak to ever say no. The biggest problem is that each cell type was photographed on different days, so a difference between cell types cannot be told apart from a difference between days. It is like comparing exam marks from two different schools in two different years. I suggest keeping three tests in a stricter form and dropping two that have no usable data.

glossary.plain: the fluid-filled hollow space in the middle of a ball of cells
a shape area divided by the area of the smallest dent-free outline around it; 1 means no dents
a computer model that draws each cell as a polygon and moves its corners to lower an energy
the typical size of a prediction error, in the units of the thing predicted
a number from -1 to 1 saying whether two things rise together, using ranks only
the chance that a test notices an effect that is really there
a test that tries to show two things are the same within a stated margin
differences caused by when and how a group was photographed, not by what is being studied
fit on all imaging days but one, test on the left-out day, repeat
isoperimetric quotient, 4 pi times area over perimeter squared; 1 for a circle
1 minus the squared error of the new model divided by that of the baseline; above 0 means better

recommendations: P1: keep as the only hard gate, changed. Compare M3 to the size-only line M2, not the constant; use leave-one-session-out CV (measured: line 0.121, constant 0.140); pass if M3 LOSO RMSE <= 0.121 and a session-blocked paired bootstrap does not show it worse than M2. Treat the published sweep as an expected-fail check (best N-curve RMSE 0.192), not a gate. Fix the threshold from training sessions only.

P2: keep for Rab11a-GFP only. Replace 'rho within +-0.28' with: report Spearman rho and slope with a 90 percent bootstrap CI resampled by session; call l_a size-independent only if the CI upper bound is below +0.30 (n=51 gives 0.56 power against rho 0.3; say so). Drop the Cldn-qKO arm (n=25, one session, power 0.30). Also report N 3..10 only, where WT rho is -0.277 rather than 0.008.

P3: demote to exploratory. Three Rab11a sessions cannot support a session-clustered bootstrap and genotype shift is not separable from session. If kept, report power (0.25 to 0.84 by shift) and require SS>0 under session-blocked resampling; delete the mean-residual < -0.03 clause (sign already known; smaller than session SD 0.074).

P4: demote to an exploratory equivalence estimate. Use a TOST margin of +-0.09 on mean residual (power 0.97 at n=22 with no batch effect) and report the 90 percent CI; delete the RMSE<=0.16 clause (cannot fail) and compare M3 to M2 by paired squared-error difference. State that Cldn_qKO is one imaging day, so a null cannot be read as genotype insensitivity.
P5: drop. n=15 over three genotypes, SE of RMSE 0.022, M2 clipped at 1 is a strawman, and the 7 WT rows are now seen. Keep N>10 simulation convergence as a code-health check only.

P6: drop as a prediction; send the author data request now. If ever scored, use SE (0.106/sqrt(n)) plus a between-lab term, not the lumen SD, and replace the 'explains half the deficit' ratio (unstable at 5 lumens) with a plot.
Fix the data map: identity 2 must read a = (N l_b)^2 IPQ_cyst/(4 pi) - N, and lumen IPQ needs a or IPQ_cyst besides N, l_a, l_b. Both identities are sound Lean candidates once corrected.

Add session to every model: fit M2 with a session random effect on WT and report any held-out genotype shift with variance including the session SD (0.074). Without a same-session WT control, genotype claims are descriptive.

Physical build: keep (arithmetic right). Measure wall slack to +-0.005 and set the refutation band at 0.03 in S, or use slacks 1.02, 1.08, 1.14 to widen spacing. A slack wall has no unique zero-pressure shape; the symmetric scalloped form is one equilibrium among buckled alternatives.
Log in the blindness ledger that WT N>10 outcomes (7 rows) have been read by this critique.

fleet.topic: Track 3 data and reproducibility: MDCK cyst lumen shape (Vasquez et al 2021 Source Data, vertex-model sweep, authors' code)
fleet.summary: Downloaded the Vasquez et al 2021 Source Data (1.9 MB zip, six workbooks, sha256 recorded), the authors' lumen_vm.py (31,238 bytes) and the independent-lab Zenodo files (7.5 MB images plus 76 KB intensity tables). Wrote and ran 02_reproduce.py, which reproduced every checkable number from the scout (sphericity, surface area per cell, solidity by condition, Fig 3 ratios, 15,030 sweep rows) and every checkable number from the design (WT counts, medians, Spearman values, five RMSE baselines, WT size-only line 0.6703+0.0261N, ceiling at N=12.6, best published-sweep setting solidity RMSE 0.229 and IPQ RMSE 0.298, log-area 1.06 vs 1.03 vs 0.35, both sweep-direction examples, the data-map identity). Two differences in wording, no differences in value: the design's '99 non-physical rows' needs four filters (negative area, area-per-cell at or below 0, solidity outside 0..1, IPQ above 1), not the two it names (which give 61); and 291 settings is the count after the filter (292 before). The authors' code does NOT run as documented: it lacks 'import os', fails on NumPy 2.x (np.cross on 2-vectors), and with the README's default jitter=0 never leaves its initial-condition loop (A0 is NaN every time). With a NumPy shim and jitter=0.05 (my choice) one 3-to-10-cell growth run took 102 s but its IPQ fell inside the published replicate range at only 2 of 8 cell numbers and lumen areas were about 0.000 to 0.001, so reproducing the simulation could not be established. Held-out genotype outcomes (Rab11a-GFP, Cldn-qKO) were deliberately not read; only cell counts and filename joins were.
fleet.lay_summary: Earlier AI helpers studied how the hollow centre of a tiny ball of kidney cells takes its shape, and they quoted many numbers from one published data set. We downloaded that same data set and recomputed their numbers from scratch. Every number we could check came out the same, to the digit. Think of it as re-adding a shopping receipt and getting the same total. The authors' computer simulation, though, would not run as published, and when we patched it, one run did not clearly match their published runs. We kept the 'exam answers' for two cell types sealed, so the planned test stays fair.

glossary.plain: The hollow space in the middle of a ball of cells.
A small hollow ball grown from dog kidney cells in the lab.
How filled-in a shape is compared with its smooth outer wrapping; 1 is a smooth blob, lower means dented.
A roundness score: 1 for a perfect circle, smaller for wiggly shapes.
A computer model that draws each cell as a corner-to-corner polygon and finds the arrangement with the least stored energy.
A fingerprint of a file; if one byte changes, the fingerprint changes.
A typical size of the miss between predicted and measured values.
A score from -1 to 1 for whether two lists rise and fall together, using only their ranks.
A cell line whose results are kept unseen until the prediction is locked.
Many simulation runs over a grid of settings.

fleet.label: t3-lumen-deep
fleet.topic: Track 3 deep literature: MDCK cyst lumen shape (Vasquez et al 2021) and the physics of lumen geometry
fleet.summary:
STATE OF THE ART, MDCK CYST LUMEN SHAPE (Track 3). Written 2026-11-12; 21 distinct papers cited (plus the published DOI of one preprint and the bioRxiv version of another); 13 were read in full text (two only in the sections searched) and 8 as abstract only, as stated per paper in citations.how_verified.

GROUND-UP EXPLANATION (each step tagged M measured, D derived, A assumed)
1. A lumen is the fluid-filled hollow inside a ring or ball of epithelial cells. MDCK (dog kidney) cells grown in Matrigel form such balls ('cysts' or 'spheroids') with one lumen within about a day. [M: Vasquez 2021]
2. Each cell becomes polarised: one face (apical) faces the lumen, the opposite (basal) faces the gel, the sides (lateral) touch neighbours. The apical face is built by delivering membrane and polarity proteins (PTEN/PIP2, Cdc42, aPKC, Rab11a-Rab8a-exocyst, an AMIS site). [M: Martin-Belmonte 2007, Bryant 2010]
3. The apical faces are non-sticky (the two sides of a young lumen sit 200-300 nm apart), so a gap stays open. [M for the gap; A that non-adhesion is the cause]
4. Classical physics view: if cells pump salt and water into the gap, the fluid pushes outward with pressure P. A skin with tension T enclosing pressure P obeys Young-Laplace, P = T x (sum of the two curvatures); for a sphere of radius R, P = 2T/R. [D: textbook law; A: uniform tension, single P] A pressurised lumen should therefore be convex everywhere. [D]
5. Measurement: MDCK lumens are not round. Sphericity (1 is a perfect sphere) is 0.3-0.7 and 13-48 percent of the lumen surface is concave (bowed into the lumen) while the outer cyst surface stays almost spherical. [M: Vasquez; own recomputation n=35] A single-pressure, uniform-tension lumen cannot do that. [D]
6. Perturbations: making the junctions leaky (claudin knockout) should lose pressure yet shape is unchanged; drugs that change fluid pumping or acutely wreck the cytoskeleton change lumen shape little by the authors' reading. [M] Their conclusion is that apical area per cell, regulated by trafficking, dominates shape while pressure only adds roundness. [D, model-based]
7. Their model: a 2D vertex model (cells as polygons) with a preferred apical length l_a, a preferred basal length, a stringency k and a lumen-area/pressure term; run from 3 to 10 cells. Larger l_a lowers solidity at low pressure; pressure raises it; solidity rises with size even at zero pressure. [D] Pressure is dimensionless there and never measured in those cysts. [M: absence verified]
8. Counter-evidence and refinements: an independent lab measures 65 Pa in MDCK cysts and sees lumen number/fusion governed by pressure [M: Lu 2025]; Mukenhirn 2024 and Guha Ray 2026 show tight junctions control lumen opening/buckling through pressure-tension balance, with lateral and basal tensions also modulated [M, abstract-level]. Mouse blastocyst and zebrafish ear are the strongly pressure-driven cases (hundreds of Pa) [M].
9. Laws in the library (law set 1.8.1): only the thin-wall Laplace bound (physiology-laplace) applies; it needs a wall strength and thickness no one has supplied here. The richer Young-Laplace / Plateau theorems live only in the older leanbio tree. [library fact]

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED WITH NUMBERS: lumen sphericity 0.3-0.7; concave fraction 13-48 percent (own, n=35); WT/qKO solidity 0.865 vs 0.893 (p=0.88); pressure 65 Pa MDCK cysts (n=27), 100-300 Pa zebrafish ear; MDCK dome tension 1-2 mN/m.
WHAT IS CONTESTED: (a) role of pressure (Vasquez no; Lu, Mukenhirn yes, in different conditions/sizes); (b) whether Rab11a lowers solidity at matched size (paper yes; my simple tests find no significant difference, unconfirmed); (c) whether ddAVP changes shape (paper modest; day-3 medians 0.552 vs 0.881 in the source table, size-confounded); (d) constancy of apical length per cell (paper/Guha Ray constant; own l_a vs N rho 0.01, -0.44, +0.61 across genotypes; lumen area per cell CV 0.50); (e) tension scale (Lu model 0.1 mN/m vs dome 1-2 mN/m).
KEY EXPERIMENTS/MODELS IN ORDER: 2007 PTEN-PIP2-Cdc42 apical identity; 2008 Cdc42 spindle orientation (Caco-2); 2010 Rab11a-Rabin8-Rab8a AMIS; 2012 confinement; 2013 Cerruti non-equilibrium multilumen model; 2014/2017 vertex-model reviews; 2017 Ruiz-Herrero hydraulic oscillations; 2018 Dasgupta lumen growth physics and Latorre superelasticity; 2019 Chan, Dumortier, Mosaliganti hydraulics; 2021 Vasquez geometry model and Le Verge-Serandour coarsening theory, Torres-Sanchez review; 2023 Bebelman bulkheads; 2024 Mukenhirn tight junctions; 2025-26 Lu (65 Pa) and Guha Ray (3D vertex model).
BEST REVIEWS: Torres-Sanchez/Kerr Winter/Salbreux 2021 (tissue hydraulics); Navis and Bagnat 2015; Fletcher et al. 2014 and Alt et al. 2017 (vertex models).
OPEN PROBLEMS: how apical area is set and why it follows a per-cell constant; 3D rather than 2D vertex models matched to the same cysts; a joint dataset with pressure, tension and 3D shape in the same cyst; reconciling the 0.1 vs 1-2 mN/m tension scales; mapping dimensionless p to pascals; why the model sweep does not beat a constant on WT solidity (earlier design pilot, not re-run by me).
fleet.lay_summary: Many organs are made of tubes and sacs with a hollow space inside, called a lumen. Kidney-cell clumps grown in the lab make such a hollow, and you might expect it to be round like a water balloon, because fluid pressure pushes evenly on the wall. Measurements show it is not round: up to about half of its inner surface dents inwards, like a half-deflated beach ball. A 2021 study argued that the shape is set mainly by how much inner-facing skin each cell makes and by how many cells there are, with pressure adding only some roundness. Other labs measured a real pressure of about 65 pascals in these clumps and say pressure matters more, so the question is still open. The numbers I recomputed from the published tables agree with the dents but do not confirm every claim in the paper.

findings.claim: [MEASURED] MDCK cells embedded in Matrigel spontaneously form hollow spheroids within 24 h; at 18-24 h the two opposing apical cortices of a young lumen are 200-300 nm apart by lattice light-sheet imaging. The authors infer apical surfaces are intrinsically non-adhesive (an inference, not measured).
findings.evidence_quote: MDCK cells spontaneously form hollow spheroids within 24 h

findings.claim: [MEASURED] A positive luminal pressure with uniform surface tension should give convex (outward-bowed) lumen walls; Vasquez et al. state this as the premise they test, citing blastocyst and bile canaliculus as cases where convex curvature is documented.
findings.evidence_quote: Importantly, a positive luminal pressure should produce convex lumen surfaces that bow outwards toward the surrounding cells.

findings.claim: [MEASURED] Lumens of 35 MDCK spheroids (7-30 cells in the intermediate set) are irregular: sphericity runs from about 0.70 down to about 0.3, less spherical than a cube (0.81).
findings.value: 0.3-0.70 (paper); own recomputation median 0.484, min 0.276, max 0.712, n=35
findings.evidence_quote: The sphericity of lumens ranged from Ψ ~ 0.70 to very far from spherical ( Ψ ~ 0.3)

findings.claim: [MEASURED] The fraction of lumen surface with negative (concave) mean curvature is 10 percent to over 50 percent in the paper; the basal (outer) surface is almost fully convex. My recomputation from the per-cyst table gives 13.3 to 48.1 percent (median 33.8) for the lumen and median 11.4 percent for the whole-cyst surface, a small disagreement with the paper wording.
findings.evidence_quote: The percent of the total lumen surface area with negative mean curvature varied from 10% to over 50%

findings.claim: [MEASURED] The outer (basal) cyst surface is nearly spherical while the lumen is not, so the irregularity belongs to the lumen. Own check: whole-cyst sphericity median 0.732, min 0.615.
findings.evidence_quote: the sphericity and percent concavity of the basal surfaces of the spheroids were close to 1 and 0%, respectively

findings.claim: [MEASURED, own] Sphericity formula check: recomputing psi = pi^(1/3)(6V)^(2/3)/A from the file columns vol_lumen and SA_lumen reproduces spher_lumen to within 0.0000 (max abs diff).

findings.claim: [MEASURED] Pressure-pharmacology: ddAVP (fluid secretion up) and ouabain (Na/K-ATPase inhibitor) did not strongly change 2D lumen solidity for lumens of about four to tens of cells, in the authors reading.

findings.claim: [MEASURED, own] That reading is size-dependent. At day 3 the median solidity is 0.881 (control, n=23), 0.552 (ddAVP, n=20), 0.881 (ouabain, n=19); at day 7 all three are 0.989-0.996. A crude linear size adjustment (solidity ~ normalised radius + treated) gives treated minus control of -0.255 (p=0.0013) for ddAVP and -0.247 (p=0.0042) for ouabain at day 3, but solidity vs size is a sharp step, not a line, so this adjustment is only a flag, not a test. The paper used a 2D Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, which I did not run.
