fleet.topic: Track 4 deep literature: passive-glide surrogate, 3D-printed double-winged autorotating fruits and the published blade-element model
fleet.summary:
SCOPE. System: 3D-printed double-winged autorotating fruits (Fauli, Rabault, Carlson, Oslo) plus their blade-element model. Question: does a body or fin constraint (here: fixed wing mass and length, only curvature free) set how slowly a passive body can sink, and can a published model say how before anything is built? Note the limit: a spinning fruit is a SINK-RATE surrogate, not a forward glide. For forward glide the closest model is the quasi-steady plate glider (Li 2022; Pomerenk and Ristroph 2025), covered in section 6.

1. THE SCIENCE FROM THE GROUND UP
1.1 A body falling through air or water speeds up until drag and lift on it balance its weight; then it moves at a steady terminal speed. [A: definition]
1.2 Most of the weight a surface can hold up comes from how much fluid it pushes down. A big light wing falls slowly. The simple rule: speed U goes as the square root of (weight / swept area), called wing loading. [D: momentum argument stated in Fauli 2019 and Rabault 2019; M: wild fruits follow it as groups]
1.3 A wing that spins (autorotates) keeps moving through the fluid even while the body drops slowly, so its wing tips meet fast flow and give lift. Near the axis the lift tilts forward and pushes the spin; near the tip drag brakes it. Spin settles where these torques cancel. [D: blade-element argument, PRE section 'Blade element model']
1.4 Why a spinning wing lifts more than a flat plate: a stable vortex sits on its leading edge and adds lift (the leading-edge vortex, LEV). [M: robotic-model flow measurements, Lentink 2009 abstract]
1.5 Two dimensionless numbers describe the motion. Reynolds number Re = U L / nu compares inertia to viscosity; Strouhal number St = f L / U compares spin speed to sink speed. A water tank can imitate air if Re and St match. Fruits: Re about 2400-14000, St 0.35-0.82. [M: PRE Table I; D: I recomputed Re and found one table entry (14000) does not follow from its own speed range (12000)]
1.6 The blade-element model cuts each wing into thin strips. Each strip sees a wind made from the sink speed and the spin speed, at an angle of attack; lift and drag coefficients from earlier robot-wing work give the force. Setting total vertical force = weight and total spin torque = 0 gives U and f. Because the coefficients do not depend on Re in this model, torque balance fixes St from geometry alone, and U goes as the square root of weight. [D: PRE; M: measured St is constant per geometry within about 5 percent (PRE); an earlier agent reported U-squared linear in lead mass with R-squared 0.992-0.997 in 10 of 11 series, which I did not recheck]
1.7 The geometry knob is the fold angle KL (wing length times curvature, radians). Too flat: wing tips lie at a steep angle and make little lift. Too curled: the lifting part moves toward the axis where the wind is slow. In between is a minimum sink speed. [D/M: PRE, PRL] The base angle psi (wing root tilt from vertical) moves the optimum: larger psi, smaller best KL. [M: tank optimum about 2.3 at psi=0, about 1.2 at psi=35]

2. WHAT IS ESTABLISHED WITH NUMBERS
- Tank optimum fold angle about 2.3 (psi=0) and about 1.2 (psi=35) [M, PRE]. Re-read from the public data file at the 2.16 g lead key: psi=35 speed 0.0676 (KL 1.20), 0.0674 (1.33), 0.0693 (1.50), 0.0710 (1.71), 0.126 m/s (KL 0.06); psi=0: 0.1011 m/s at KL 2.31 against 0.1137 (1.71), 0.1258 (3.00), 0.1678 (0.92) [M, own script analyze_repo.py].
- Model optimum: KL 2.05 (psi=0), 1.80 (psi=15), 1.31 (psi=35); minimum Re 4709, 4352, 3900 [M: stored model files]. The psi=15 case has never been run in a tank, as far as I found.
- Wild whirling fruits have mean fold angle 1.8 with 10 percent image error, n=27 [M, PRL], i.e. equal to the model optimum for psi=15 (1.80) and above the one for psi=35 (1.31); the paper does not report each fruit's base angle, so the match is not tested per fruit.
- Maple-type samaras: printed copies match natural descent within one standard deviation (1.28 vs 1.10 m/s), descent factor DF about 3 [M, Nave 2021]; my recomputation gives DF 2.82 (natural) and 3.17 (printed) at assumed air density 1.225 kg/m3 [D].
- Plate glider: maximum glide ratio 3.8 at centre of equilibrium about 0.22 chord [M: model output reported by Pomerenk and Ristroph; this is a model number, not an experiment]; arctan(1/3.8) = 14.7 deg [D].
- Field dispersal of 13 dipterocarp species from a 30 m tower: median 4 m, 90 percent within 10.5 m [M, Smith 2015].

3. KEY EXPERIMENTS AND MODELS IN ORDER
1973 Norberg: momentum theorem plus blade-element analysis of single-winged fruits; flat-plate tests at Re about 2000 show pitch stability for centre of mass 27-35 percent of chord behind the leading edge [M, abstract only]. 1986 Augspurger: terminal velocities of wind-dispersed fruits of neotropical trees (the dataset the dipterocarp work leans on; not read). 1987 Azuma and Okuno: Alsomitra seed flight (not read; its 0.3-0.7 m/s glide descent rate is quoted second-hand). 1997 Yasuda and Azuma: autorotation boundary (not read). 1999 Dickinson, Lehmann, Sane: three unsteady mechanisms of insect wings (delayed stall, rotational circulation, wake capture). 2004 Wang, Birch, Dickinson: 2D computation versus robotic-wing forces, the source of the CL, CD fits the fruit model reuses. 2009 Lentink et al.: LEV on dynamically scaled maple and hornbeam seeds. 2010 Ulrich et al.: robotic samara. 2014 Looy and Stevenson: autorotating seeds in Permian conifers. 2015 Smith et al.: field dispersal of dipterocarps. 2015 Sunada et al.: lift-drag ratio controls descent factor. 2019 Fauli et al. and Rabault et al.: the system studied here. 2021 Nave et al.: printed maple samaras. 2022 Li et al.: plate with moving centre of mass flutters, tumbles, glides, dives. 2023 Jung and Rezgui: blade-element-momentum model of samaras with LEV lift models. 2024-2025: origami fruits with folding and flexibility (Cai et al., not read), number of wings (Liu et al.), linden stalk (Cazaubiel and Carlson), falling bent plates (Loo and Alben), plate equilibria and stability (Pomerenk and Ristroph).

4. WHAT IS CONTESTED OR UNRESOLVED (both sides stated)
(a) Lift law. The Letter (PRL) says CL = 2 sin(alpha) adjusted for intermediate Re; the long paper (PRE) and the code use a hovering-wing fit CL = 0.225 + 1.58 sin(2.13 alpha - 7.2 deg). The code's own comment says the formula in the source paper may have a sign error. A stall-type parametrization in the PRE supplement gives reasonable Re but worse St. [M]
(b) The model is partly tuned. The authors halve the published drag to match experiment (PRE), and the 'mass loading' of 1.2 g in the model is not the lead key in the data (2.16 g), so absolute speed is not independently predicted. [M]
(c) Between-angle offset. Model best-speed ratio psi=0 over psi=35 is 4709/3900 = 1.21; tank data give 0.1011/0.0676 = 1.50 [D]. An earlier agent found the same disagreement with a different method (design-glide.json: 1.22 vs 1.40-1.50).
(d) Lab range. Table I says Re up to 14000; its own speed range gives 12000 [D]. Unknown which is right.
(e) Error bars in the paper are 5 standard deviations and n is 3 at psi=35; the minimum is flat over KL 1.2-1.5 so the optimum location is uncertain by at least 0.2-0.3 [D from the data file].
(f) Is slowest descent what selection favours? Smith 2015 finds dispersal distance depends on wing loading and wind, but the simple drift model (wind x height / sink speed) over-predicts the fitted-model distances by 4.1-8.0 times (median 6.9) [D from Smith Table 3; the tabulated drift model uses regression descent speeds from Augspurger 1986 and a constant wind]. Fold angle has not been linked to field dispersal.
(g) LEV lift model for rotating wings: normal-force versus Polhamus forms are both used (Jung and Rezgui 2023, abstract only).

5. OPEN PROBLEMS
Blade-element model with induced inflow (no public version tested); full 3D numerical flow for double-winged fruit at Re 2000-14000; psi=15 and psi=55 and pitch variations (the PRE-fixed pitch 15 deg and camber 2.5 deg are 'inspired by' wild fruits but could not be measured, they dry and curl); flexibility (Cai 2024, not read); stalk and centre-of-mass control of the onset of autorotation (Cazaubiel and Carlson 2025, preprint); relation of fold angle to field dispersal; stability of the autorotating state at large psi (coning, tumbling).

6. FORWARD-GLIDE LINK (the body/fin constraint proper)
For a surrogate that must glide forward, the best-supported model is the 2D quasi-steady plate glider of Li 2022 / Pomerenk and Ristroph 2025: centre of equilibrium about 0.1-0.3 chord glides, beyond about 0.3 dives, max glide ratio 3.8 [M model output]; it is 2D and tested for slenderness 0.001-0.1 [M]. Engineered Javan-cucumber-inspired gliders reached 9.5-13.6 deg glide angles = glide ratios 4.1-6.0 [D from Wiesemuller Table 2]. I found no raw public trajectories for either.

7. LAW LIBRARY (set 1.8.1, read only)
flight-climb-glide-law (glide range <= h x (L/D)max; hash identical to 1.6.0), perturb-wind-glide (needs horizontal airspeed > 0), [claim id withheld] (vmin_le), flight-allometry-law, scaling laws. None covers autorotation. vmin_le applied naively to a samara with the model's peak CL 1.805 is violated (1.37 vs 1.10 m/s) because an autorotating wing is not in steady freestream flight: the law must not be used as a cut here without an effective CL,max near the descent factor 2.8-3.2 [D]. Law E1 is flying-fish only and internally inconsistent (2.981 - 1.834 = 1.147 vs 1.236). A wind-drift identity range = w h / s survives (22 m for h=30, w=1.72, s=2.35) but is loose by about 5.7x for the species tested [D].

8. WHAT THIS ADDS TO THE EARLIER SCOUT, DESIGNER AND LAW-MAPPER
Newer literature (2024-2025); field-ecology anchor (Smith 2015) with a computed bound-looseness; the 14000 vs 12000 Re discrepancy; the CL-law disagreement between the two papers; samara descent factor recomputed; law set 1.8.1 check (flight laws unchanged from 1.6.0) and the vmin_le scope failure; E1 inconsistency; independent re-reading of the public data.
fleet.lay_summary: Some tree fruits have two curved wings and spin like a helicopter blade as they fall, which slows their fall so wind can carry them away. Researchers in Oslo 3D-printed copies of such fruits and dropped them in a tall tank of water, where the flow behaves like fast air. They found that the wings fall slowest when they are curved by a particular amount, and that real tropical fruits are curved by about that amount. A simple computer model that cuts each wing into thin strips predicts this best curve fairly well, but it is partly tuned and it misses the size of the change when the wing root is tilted. Think of a sycamore seed: too flat and it plummets, too curled and its lifting part sits near the middle where the air is slow. This is a test of how slowly something can sink, not how far it can glide sideways, and the field data show real fruits land much closer to the tree than a simple wind-drift sum predicts.

findings.source: script derived.py block F on the Europe PMC XML (sha256 506cfbbb...cff)
findings.evidence_quote: Dipterocarpus humeratus 9.29 (± 0.27) 326.37 4.25 21.93

findings.claim: Dipterocarp fruits are called poor dispersers despite large wings, and wing loading is the standard single predictor; the water-tank fold-angle work targets descent speed, not distance, so the link from fold angle to field dispersal has not been measured.
findings.evidence_quote: Dipterocarp dispersal is generally considered to be poor given their large, gyration-dispersed fruits.

findings.claim: Law set 1.8.1 pins flight-climb-glide-law (accepted, physical, v1.0.0): no-thrust steady glide from height h covers at most h*(L/D)max; with drag cut by a fraction delta near a surface, at most h*(L/D)max/(1-delta). Its content hash 6ac1beea70e5 is identical in the older leanbio copy (1.6.0), so the earlier law-mapper conclusions for this law stand.
findings.evidence_quote: A steady glide with no thrust, lift equal to weight and L/D ≤ (L/D)max from height h covers at most h (L/D)max horizontally

findings.claim: perturb-wind-glide (accepted, v1.0.0, constraint P4b): ground range of a steady glide in a tailwind w is (u+w)h/s = (L/D)h(1+w/u). Its Lean theorem requires horizontal airspeed u > 0, so it does not apply directly to a vertical autorotator; with u = 0 only the kinematic identity range = w h / s remains.
findings.evidence_quote: the glide lasts `h / s` and covers `(u + w) h / s`, which is

findings.claim: DERIVED: the autorotator drift identity w h / s with h = 30 m, w = 1.72 m/s and s = 2.35 m/s (the descent speed implied by the ballistic row for D. humeratus) is 22 m, matching the tabulated 21.93 m; the measured median is 3.84 m, so the law-derived bound is respected but loose by about 5.7x for that species (21.93/3.84).
findings.source: script derived.py blocks F and G
findings.value: 22.0 m bound vs 3.84 m measured median

findings.claim: DERIVED SCOPE TEST: the registry law vmin_le (v >= sqrt(2W/(rho S CL,max)), [claim id withheld]) applied naively with S = wing area and the repo model peak CL = 1.805 gives a minimum speed 1.37 m/s for the natural maple samara (W/S = 2.09 N/m2), above the measured 1.10 m/s; for the printed one 1.70 versus 1.28 m/s. The law is about steady freestream lift; an autorotating wing sees far higher local flow, so it must not be used as a cut on autorotation without an effective CL,max of about 2.8-3.2 (the DF values).
findings.source: script derived.py block I; law file registry/laws/[claim id withheld].json

findings.claim: Law E1 (accepted, Exocoetidae only) holds within-species flying-fish exponents: mass 2.981, fin area 1.834, wing loading 1.236. Its own text warns these are separate regressions that are NOT mutually consistent (2.981 - 1.834 = 1.147 versus 1.236). So the minimum-speed exponent (bW-bS)/2 the earlier law-mapper quoted is 0.5735 from the first two but 0.618 (= 1.236/2) from the fitted wing loading, both versus 0.5 for isometry. It is a fish statement and does not transfer to a fruit surrogate.
findings.evidence_quote: NOT mutually consistent: 2.981 - 1.834 = 1.147 against the fitted 1.236.

findings.claim: Law set 1.8.1 is the current set (previous 1.8.0); the three flight laws above (flight-climb-glide-law, perturb-wind-glide, [claim id withheld]) have the same content hashes in 1.6.0, so 1.8.1 adds no new glide or autorotation law. No law in the registry covers autorotation, descent factor or blade-element balance.
findings.evidence_quote: "version": "1.8.1"

key_claims.claim: In 3D-printed double-winged fruits dropped in water, terminal descent speed has a minimum at an intermediate fold angle KL: about 2.3 at base angle 0 and about 1.2 at base angle 35 deg (shipped data re-read: 0.1011 m/s at KL 2.31 for psi=0; 0.0674-0.0676 m/s at KL 1.2-1.33 for psi=35).
key_claims.evidence_quote: we notice that the optimal fold angle has decreased, with a minimum terminal descent velocity obtained near KL  1.2.

key_claims.claim: The blade-element model is partly tuned, not parameter-free: the published drag is halved to match tank data, and the model loading (1.2 g) differs from the data key (2.16 g); the model also gives a psi=0/psi=35 best-speed ratio of 1.21 where the data give 1.50.
key_claims.evidence_quote: we reduce the value of the drag coefficient to obtain good agreement with our experiments

key_claims.claim: Wild whirling fruits have mean fold angle 1.8 (10 percent image error, 27 fruits), at the model optimum for base angle 15 deg; the base angle of each fruit is not reported.
key_claims.evidence_quote: which is illustrated by the errorbar from mean(KL) = 1.8

key_claims.claim: A simple wind-drift bound (distance = wind x height / sink speed) is respected but loose for real dipterocarp fruits: 4.1-8.0 times (median 6.9) above the fitted field distances, so slow descent alone does not set dispersal distance.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Dipterocarpus humeratus 9.29 (± 0.27) 326.37 4.25 21.93

recommendations: Build the psi=15 and psi=55 fruits only after freezing both the blade-element prediction and the disk-area rival (see design-glide.json); this report shows the model already misses the psi=0 to psi=35 offset (1.21 versus 1.50), so a psi=15 test is a real discrimination, not a rubber stamp.
Weigh each fruit immersed and record lead mass, so the unresolved 1.2 g versus 2.16 g loading question is removed before analysis.
Do not use vmin_le as an elimination rule on any autorotating body without declaring an effective CL,max near the descent factor (about 3); treat law hits there as scope warnings.
Anchor any ecology claim to Smith 2015: slow descent is necessary but the field bound is loose by about 7x, so claim descent speed, not dispersal distance.
Check law E1 before reusing its exponents: its own text says they are not mutually consistent (1.147 vs 1.236), and it is fish-only.
Re-fetch the 2024-2025 papers (Cai, Liu, Cazaubiel) when a licence-clean full text exists; the stalk result may add a second knob (centre of mass) worth a test.

fleet.label: t4-glide-law
fleet.topic: Track 4 law map against law set 1.8.1, with one new checked Lean law
fleet.summary: Mapped Track 4 (passive glide, printed autorotating-fruit design) onto law set 1.8.1 of the application repo (59 pinned laws, 14 placeholders with no theorem). Registered glide laws: glide_range_le, wind_glide_rules_out, vmin_le/vmin_ratio and the allometry and scaling theorems; all take L/D as a committed number. The most valuable easy missing law is max L/D from aspect ratio on a parabolic polar, composed with glide_range_le. I wrote it as MaxLiftToDrag.lean and it checks with no errors and no sorryAx. fleet.lay_summary: The project keeps a library of rules that a design must obey, each backed by a computer-checked proof. I looked up which rules apply to a small printed glider. They cap how far it can travel from a given height, but only if you already know its best glide ratio. That ratio depends on how long and thin the wings are, and no rule linked the two. I wrote and machine-checked that missing rule: long, thin wings glide further, but never past a limit set by their shape. Think of a paper dart: a longer wingspan helps, but only up to a point. The rule assumes a simple standard model of drag, so it is a limit under that assumption, not a measurement.

fleet.label: t4-glide-lay
fleet.topic: Track 4 plain-language explanation: printed double-winged autorotating fruits and the blade-element model
fleet.summary:
Some tree fruits have two curved wings and spin like a helicopter blade as they fall, which slows the fall so the wind can carry them farther [S1]. Researchers 3D-printed copies of such fruits, dropped them in a water tank, and wrote a computer model that predicts how fast each shape sinks [S1, S3]. We plan to reuse their free design files and code [S3], and to write down, before printing anything, exact numbers that the published model and a much simpler rival rule predict for new shapes, including a wing-base angle of 15 degrees that the papers did not test in experiments [S1, S5]. Then we print 21 fruits, drop them, and see which rule holds up, or whether both fail [S5]. The point is that a design rule is only worth trusting if a test it was not tuned on could have shown it wrong. This is a test of sinking speed, not of forward gliding, so it is a stand-in for fin and body limits in a glide, not a glide itself [S5]. The files I read describe this as a plan; I found no results from it.

HOW
1. Write the guesses down first. We save the model, its code and every predicted number in a file before any fruit exists, like handing in a betting slip before the race [S5].
2. Check the model on old data. The earlier designer rewrote the model in modern Python, and my re-run shows it matches the authors' stored results to within 0.17 percent, like checking a new calculator on sums whose answers you already know [S5, my re-run].
3. Build the video-measuring tool and test it on recorded paths. The tool follows the fruit's lowest point and its spin from side video, like testing a stopwatch on a race you already have on tape [S1, S5].
4. Print 21 fruits from one recipe. In the CAD file we change only three numbers (base angle, curve, wing tilt), like baking cookies from one recipe with one setting changed each time. A batch of 3 takes about 5 hours [S1, S5].
5. Make them equally heavy underwater. We add small metal shot into each hollow body until it weighs 2.60 g plus or minus 0.05 g in water, like loading coins into paper boats until they float alike [S5].
6. Run sanity checks with the control fruits. Three identical copies must agree within 8 percent, or the whole test is void, like making sure a scale reads zero before weighing anything [S5].
7. Drop and film. Each fruit is released fully under water and dropped 10 times in random order while a side camera films at 30 frames per second or faster, like timing runners in several heats [S1, S5].
8. Score against the written guesses with the saved code, then publish every drop, including the bad ones, like opening the sealed envelope and showing all the ballots [S5].
9. Ask a different person to compare wild fruits with the rule that curl should shrink as base angle grows, using pictures only, so nothing needs printing [S5].
10. Turn the result into a formal check. In the project's math-proof library, a short statement says what a body of this kind cannot do, so shapes that break it are ruled out by a computer-checked rule, like a spell-checker for physics claims [S5, S6a].

WHAT WOULD COUNT AS WRONG
- The published model is wrong about base angle if the best 15-degree fruit's speed, as a share of the control's, is not near 1.11, or if the 0-degree fruits come out at 1.31 or more [S5].
- The simple disk rule is wrong if the 15-degree result is not near 1.18, or if the 0-degree fruits come out below 1.31 [S5].
- Both are wrong about the 55-degree fruits if the best one is not between 0.80 and 0.97 of the control's speed, or if they tumble in more than 2 of 10 drops [S5].
- Pitch: the model is wrong if the 5-degree tilt does not slow the fruit to about 0.64 (it fails if it is above 0.80), and the disk rule is wrong if either tilt changes speed by more than 12 percent [S5].
- The result does not count if three identical controls differ by more than 8 percent, and it is called inconclusive, not a pass, if the 15-degree result is too noisy to separate the two rules [S5].
- My own note: on public data the 0-degree speed ratio is 1.50 measured against 1.22 from the model, so the model may already fail one of these tests [S4, S5].

WHAT COULD GO WRONG
- Sinking is not gliding. A spinning fruit does not travel forward, so what we learn about fins and bodies is limited [S5].
- The two rules differ by only about 6.5 percent at 15 degrees (1.111 versus 1.183), and public drop-to-drop scatter is 0.3 to 7.5 percent, so noise could hide the difference [S5].
- The container may be too narrow. The original tank was 25 cm across and the widest fruits would be about 14 cm across, so the walls could slow them. The plan uses 40 cm or wider [S1, S5].
- We do not know exactly what the paper's '1.2 g' loading means. The designer inferred it and built a test to settle it, but the reading is unconfirmed [S5].
- Printing can warp the wings and change the curve or tilt, so each fruit is measured and excluded if out of tolerance [S5].
- The CAD file is for FreeCAD 0.17 and newer versions may break it, so we may have to rebuild the wing from its numbers [S3r, S5].
- A 5-degree wing may not start spinning, which would also count against the model [S5].
- Someone may already have done this. One 2024 paper on folded winged fruits had no readable abstract and was not read [S5].

QUESTIONS
Q: Why drop the fruits in water instead of air?
A: The authors chose water so the flow behaves like a wild fruit falling through air. They say they set it up so two flow numbers (Reynolds and Strouhal) match nature [S1]. Water makes the motion slow enough to film at 30 frames per second [S1]. Matching those numbers does not prove that every detail carries over.
Q: If the papers already tested this, why do it again?
A: They tested base angles of 0 and 35 degrees only [S1]. We would test 15 and 55 degrees and two wing tilts. The designer checked citing papers and found none varying these on printed fruits, but one paper could not be read, so this is not certain [S5]. We also use their model as a rival rather than a given.
Q: Does this tell us how animals glide?
A: No, not directly. A spinning fruit sinks straight down, and the project's glide-distance rule does not apply to it [S5, S6b]. It tests whether a simple body-and-wing rule holds up in a printed object. A true gliding test would be a follow-up [S5].

Source tags: S1 arXiv 1811.12221; S2 arXiv 1902.08038; S3 MIT repo jerabaul29/EffectFoldAngleAutorotatingSeeds; S4 repo pickle dump (my re-run); S5 delphi-work/agents/design-glide.json (earlier designer, partly re-run); S6a/S6b law set 1.8.1 Scaling.lean / Flight.lean.

findings.claim: The work combines 3D printing, a model and experiments to find the shape that falls slowest (arXiv abstract).
findings.evidence_quote: combines 3D-printing, a minimal theoretical model and experiments to determine the shape of multi-winged autorotating seeds, fruits and other diaspores that provide them with the optimal wind dispersion potential i.e. minimal terminal descent velocity

findings.claim: The printed fruits were made on a Formlabs Form 2 resin printer; about 5 hours per batch of 3.
findings.evidence_quote: The synthetic fruits are produced by using the Form 2 3D-printer from Formlabs [42], relying on the stereolithography technique with a print time of about 5 hours for a batch of 3 fruits.

findings.claim: The fruit is a hollow sphere so its weight can change while its volume stays fixed.
findings.evidence_quote: the fruit itself is designed as a hollow sphere with two holes, allowing us to vary its weight in experiments while keeping the volume fixed.

findings.claim: The original tank was 1.2 m tall and 25 cm across.
findings.evidence_quote: Experiments were performed in a cylindrical water tank of a height 1.2 m and a diameter 25 cm.

findings.claim: Each fruit is released fully under the water surface.
findings.evidence_quote: The fruit is fully immersed under the water surface before it is released.

findings.claim: Video was recorded from the side at 30 Hz.
findings.evidence_quote: from the side of the tank at a frequency of 30Hz and a resolution of 864 × 480 pixels.

findings.claim: The water test was designed to match the flow regime of wild fruits in air (Reynolds and Strouhal numbers).
findings.evidence_quote: We design our experiments so that both the Reynolds number (Re) and the Strouhal number (St) are in direct correspondence to fruit flight in Nature.

findings.claim: For a given wing shape, a heavier fruit sinks faster, with speed growing like the square root of weight.
findings.evidence_quote: for each individual wing geometry the terminal descent velocity scales as ∼√mg, consistent with experiments on wild fruits

findings.claim: The paper tuned the model's drag number to match its own experiments.
findings.evidence_quote: we reduce the value of the drag coefficient to obtain good agreement with our experiments.

findings.claim: The paper tested two base angles only: 0 and 35 degrees.
findings.evidence_quote: The angle ψ between the base of the wing and the vertical direction is chosen equal to ψ = 0 ◦ or ψ = 35◦

findings.claim: At base angle 35 degrees the best fold angle is lower than at 0 degrees, near KL about 1.2.
findings.evidence_quote: the optimal fold angle has decreased, with a minimum terminal descent velocity obtained near KL≈ 1.2.

findings.claim: The stroboscopic test at base angle 0 put the slowest-falling fold angle near KL 2.3, in line with the model.
findings.evidence_quote: the minimum terminal descent velocity is around KL ≈ 2.3, in accordance with predictions of the blade element model

findings.claim: 27 wild species have a mean fold angle KL = 1.8 +/- 0.18, close to the optimum.
findings.evidence_quote: 27 species that reside in Africa, Asia, and the Americas where they were collected in the wild, which are found to have a fold angle mean(KL) = 1.8 ± 0.18, close to the optimum.

findings.claim: The companion letter reports an optimal fold angle for maximal flight time, and a similar angle in wild fruits.
findings.evidence_quote: to produce a maximal flight time there is an optimal fold angle for the desiccated sepals. A similar sepal fold angle is found for a wide range of whirling fruits collected in the wild

glossary.plain: Spinning on its own as air or water flows past, the way a maple seed twirls as it falls.
The steady speed a falling object settles at, when the upward push of the fluid balances its weight.
How strongly the wing is curved: wing length divided by the radius of its curve, in radians (about 57 degrees each).
The angle at which each wing leaves the body, measured from straight up.
The tilt of the wing surface against the flow, like tilting your hand out of a car window.
A computer method that slices each wing into thin strips, adds up the push on each strip, and finds the speed where forces balance.
A simple rival rule: sinking speed depends only on weight divided by the circle the spinning wings sweep out.
A number that says whether flow is smooth and syrupy or swirly; matching it makes a water test behave like air.
A number linking how fast something spins to how fast it moves; the model says it stays fixed for a given wing shape.
A copy of the reference shape that every other fruit is compared against, as in a taste test with one standard recipe.
Saving the guesses in a file with a fingerprint (hash) before the test, so they cannot be changed afterward.
Printing by shining light into liquid resin so it hardens layer by layer.
A stand-in that is easy to build and measure, used to test an idea meant for something harder.

fleet.label: t6-flyingfish-alt
fleet.topic: Track 6 alternatives and neighbours: other systems that could play the flying-fish role in the elimination-certificate framework, and the strongest competing explanation
fleet.summary: Law set 1.8.1 is current in the application repo (registry/lawsets/current.json); the glide lemmas (glide_range_le, glide_range_le_groundEffect, vmin_le, wind_glide_rules_out, glide_range_rules_out, vmin_rules_out, aerobic_flight_rules_out) all exist there; I ran no Lean. The strongest competing explanation for the main phenomenon (long flying-fish flights) is thrust-supported surface taxiing, not a longer pure glide. Davenport 2003 argues the accepted 'extended ballistic leap' model of how flight evolved is flawed and taxiing in half-beak-like ancestors came first; Davenport 1994 describes free flight 'prolonged by further taxiing'; Chen 2026 CFD finds large caudal thrust and lift while taxiing. The library already knows this: Flight.lean says taxiing thrust is outside the glide bound 'which is why the field glide distances exceed the bound', and the registry holds an unformalised proposed law taxiing-thrust 1.0.0. So the chosen glide energy-height certificate cannot fairly judge field distances that include taxiing; it can only judge a single thrust-free glide. Eight alternatives or neighbours are assessed (flying snake, gliding mammals, Draco lizards, flying squid, ballistic-jumper fishes as a negative control, Alsomitra seed with a CC BY CFD dataset, a bat ground-effect dataset, engineered tail-beat gliders). The cheapest and best companion is the flying snake: a thrust-free drop of 9.62 m with 3-D tracked glides. My own arithmetic (scripts/t6-flyingfish-alt/snake_bound.py) gives a range bound of 12.2 m with the 2-D section L/D of 2.7 after subtracting kinetic energy at 10 m/s, against an observed mean 10.14 m (sd 2.69): consistent on average, but mean+1 sd (12.83 m) exceeds it, so whole-animal L/D would be needed before any verdict. Recommendation: keep the flying fish as the host system but restrict its certificate to thrust-free glides; add the snake as a no-thrust control and formalise taxiing-thrust as the rival model to run alongside; use squirrel non-equilibrium glides only as a scope test of the lift=weight hypothesis.
fleet.lay_summary: A flying fish does not just glide; before and during a flight it beats its tail on the water, which can push it along and lengthen the flight. One respected researcher argues that this tail-on-water skimming, not leaping, is how flying fish first learned to fly. Our test asks whether a claimed flight distance is more than a pure glide could give from the height and speed available. That test is fair for a fish only if the tail is not pushing. A flying snake is a cleaner test case: it drops from a branch 9.6 metres up with nothing pushing it, so the same sums apply without argument. We should keep the fish, add the snake as a fair-play check, and write down the tail-push idea as a rival to be tested rather than ignored.

glossary.plain: Moving forward through air while falling slowly, with no engine or flapping pushing the animal.
How many metres forward a glider can travel per metre it drops, in steady flight.
Skimming along the water surface with the tail beating in the water while the fins are held out, before or between glides.
A jump that follows a simple arc under gravity, with the wings giving no real lift.
The drag reduction a wing gets when flying very close to a surface such as the sea.
A short machine-checked proof that a claimed design or number contradicts a proved law, so it can be thrown out.
A glide in which speed and lift keep changing, so lift does not equal weight at each instant.
The frozen version of the project's list of proved and candidate laws that verdicts are stamped against.
A number that says whether a flow is smooth or turbulent for a given size and speed.
Computer simulation of air or water flow.
The skin membrane that serves as a gliding wing in some mammals and lizards.
A case where the test should give the 'no' answer, used to show the test is not saying yes to everything.

findings.claim: Davenport 2003 argues the accepted model that flight in flying fishes evolved by extension of ballistic leaps is flawed, and proposes lift-supported surface taxiing in half-beaks with enlarged pectoral fins (enhanced by ground effect) as an essential preliminary step.

findings.claim: Davenport 1994 describes take-off by taxiing with the tail beating in the water at up to 50 beats per second, and a free flight that may be prolonged by further taxiing.
findings.evidence_quote: accelerate to take-off speed by taxiing with the lateral fins expanded and the tail beating in the water at up to 50 beats s -1 , and enter a free flight that may be prolonged by further taxiing.

findings.claim: Davenport 1994 concludes flying fish fly mainly to escape predators (dolphin-fishes and ommastrephid squid) and says an alternative energy-conservation hypothesis is rejected; other ideas such as migration between food-poor and food-rich areas have limited support.
findings.evidence_quote: Flying fish probably fly mainly to escape from predators, particularly dolphin-fishes ( Coryphaena hippurus ) and ommastrephid squid. An alternative hypothesis of energy conservation is rejected

findings.claim: Davenport 1994 estimates ground effect gives significant drag reduction below about 0.5 m height for a 0.3 m standard-length flying fish.
findings.evidence_quote: significant reduction of drag by ground effect will take place at heights below about 0.5 m, prolonging flights and helping take-off.

findings.claim: A 2026 CFD study of a four-winged flying fish finds the caudal fin makes substantial thrust while taxiing (CT about 1.22) where deep-water swimming gives a negative value (about -3.79), and lift while taxiing (CL about 2.15) is far above aerial gliding (CL about 0.57); the caudal fin supplies over 60% of lift when taxiing and the pectoral fins 85% in glide. These are simulation results, not measurements.
findings.evidence_quote: free-surface taxiing exhibits a markedly higher lift (CL≈2.15) compared to aerial gliding (CL≈0.57).

findings.claim: Own calculation: with h = 9.62 m, L/D 2.7, x <= h*L/D = 25.97 m; subtracting kinetic height v^2/2g = 10.0^2/19.62 = 5.097 m at the reported 10.0 m/s gives x <= (9.62-5.097)*2.7 = 12.21 m; with L/D = cot(13 deg) = 4.331 the same bound is 19.59 m. Observed mean 10.14 m is under all of these; mean + 1 sd = 12.83 m exceeds the 12.21 m figure. The 10.0 m/s is the speed 'reached', not shown to be the final speed, and the 2-D L/D is not a whole-animal value, so this is an illustration, not a certificate verdict.

Northern flying squirrels do not glide at equilibrium: velocities and force coefficients change continuously and lift exceeds weight, so the lift = weight hypothesis of glide_range_le does not hold for short inter-tree glides.
findings.evidence_quote: flying squirrels do not glide at equilibrium, and instead demonstrate continuously changing velocities, forces and force coefficients, and generate more lift than needed to balance body weight.

findings.claim: Parallel genetics: Daane 2021 found convergent genetic signatures for larger paired fins and aerial gliding in 35 flying-fish and relatives, with lat4a and kcnh2a regulating fin proportion; Moreno 2024 found Emx2 regulation underlies the patagium in marsupial gliders. Gliding membranes in mammals are therefore a genetics-level neighbour of the disc-flying-fish-fin-ratio-gap law.

Davenport 1992 (Exocoetus obtusirostris) reports wing loading rising with standard length (b = 1.236), fin area b = 1.834, mass b = 2.981, and the cap that pectoral fin length cannot exceed 78-79% of standard length; these are the numbers the disc-* laws are compared against.
findings.evidence_quote: Exocoetus obtusirostris shows negatively allometric growth in relation to standard length in terms of body mass (b =2·981), and lateral fin area (b =1·834).

findings.claim: Searches of DataCite (resource-type dataset) for flying fish, Exocoetidae, flying snake, Chrysopelea, Draco, colugo, squid flight and gliding mammals returned no public raw glide-trajectory dataset for any of those animals; the only relevant open sets were the bat and Alsomitra sets above.

key_claims.claim: The strongest rival to 'long flights are long pure glides' is thrust-supported surface taxiing, and the existing certificate's lemma explicitly excludes it, so field distances can legitimately exceed the glide bound without any law being wrong.
key_claims.evidence_quote: (ground effect, updraft and taxiing thrust are outside, which is why the field glide distances exceed the bound)

key_claims.claim: Davenport 2003 holds the accepted ballistic-leap route to flight is flawed and taxiing-in-half-beaks came first.
key_claims.evidence_quote: These data indicate that the accepted model of evolution of flight in flying fishes (by extension of ballistic leaps) is flawed

key_claims.claim: The flying snake is the cheapest thrust-free companion: 9.62 m drop, 14 tracked glides, mean 10.14 m horizontal; with the 2-D L/D of 2.7 and kinetic height subtracted my bound is 12.21 m, so no elimination on average, but the L/D is not whole-animal and the upper tail exceeds it.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Snakes traveled a horizontal distance of 10.14+/-2.69 m (mean +/-s.d.) while reaching an airspeed of 10.0+/-0.9 m s(-1)

key_claims.claim: No public raw trajectory dataset for any gliding animal in this list was found, so every alternative that needs fresh numbers has a data-acquisition cost; only the Alsomitra CFD set (CC BY 4.0) and the oversized bat set (CC0, 6.7 GB) are open.

recommendations: KEEP the flying fish as the host system for Track 6. It is the only candidate with a measured polar (Park and Choi 2010), the ground-effect lemma, the four disc-* laws and the Daane 2021 genetic link already in the library. Replace nothing.

RESTRICT what its certificate claims: a verdict of 'eliminated' applies to a single thrust-free glide only. A field distance that may include taxiing must return 'cannot rule', and that rule should be written in the pre-registration, because Flight.lean already says taxiing thrust is outside the bound.

RUN ALONGSIDE (1): a flying-snake certificate (Socha 2005, h = 9.62 m, Holden 2014 L/D). It is thrust-free with a known start, needs one new candidate file and no new Lean. Treat the 2.7 as a section value; add a whole-animal L/D source or report 'cannot rule'. Stamp with law set 1.8.1 and the Lean commit.

RUN ALONGSIDE (2): formalise taxiing-thrust (currently proposed, not formalised) as the rival model, with a minimal thrust-energy term, so 'glide only' and 'glide plus taxiing' are two competing certificates on the same field distances. Inputs available: Chen 2026 coefficients (simulation), Davenport 1994 tail-beat rate (up to 50 per second).

USE AS A SCOPE TEST (3): northern flying squirrel non-equilibrium glides (Bahlman 2013) to check whether lift = weight can be dropped; if raw glides can be obtained, this is the real test of the lemma's hypothesis. Needs raw data, which is not public as far as I found.

USE AS NEGATIVE CONTROL (4): hatchetfish and guppy jumps must come out as ballistic, never as eliminated glides; this checks the certificate does not say yes to everything. Cost: choose a projectile-motion model, small.

DO NOT RUN: flying squid (thrust-powered by design, only photographs, no speed numbers read) and the 6.7 GB bat set (flapping power, over the 150 MB cap); cite them as scope limits. The Alsomitra CFD set is a cheap optional engineered-body cross-check only after a size check, since its listed size is empty.
LAW SET: the earlier law-mapper used 1.6.0; the application repo is 1.8.1 and should be the stamp for anything new.

fleet.label: t6-flyingfish-crit
fleet.topic: Track 6 adversarial critique of the frozen flying-fish glide-energy design (design-flyingfish.json)
fleet.summary: Referee verdict on P1-P6. Arithmetic is right: every number I could recompute from the cited equations matches (vmin 9.854 m/s, bounds 0.65/28.49/67.47 m, 17.03 m/s for 50 m, Cheilopogon T=0.500 s, reach 2.37 m). The scientific problems are elsewhere. (1) The headline novelty, the stall floor in M3, is false outside steady lift=W glide: in a point-mass simulation with the same L3 polar, pitch-up launches beat the floor bound by 13-58% for the printed glider (and 19.7x at 10 m/s for the fish), while the plain no-floor energy bound held (ratios 0.57-0.80). P5's 1.10 allowance would fail at low launch speeds, and P5 never freezes its three speeds. (2) P2 is implied by P1 and cannot fail independently; its 0.30 floor equals an unreachable 25 m/s launch. (3) P1's threshold ignores apex speed (should be 17.8-18.2, not 16.1 m/s). (4) P3's 0.50 s threshold is only 20% above pure ballistic time, so a 5-10 degree angle error refutes it 96-100% of the time under the ballistic null; use about 1.0 s with per-leap measured angle. (5) P4 and P6 test software and a checker scope rule, not nature; P6's 1.8.1 arm passes by construction and its 1.6.0 arm likely will not reproduce. (6) P5 speed-gate error (about 10% on the bound) equals its allowance, and the 30 flights share one calibration. Law set 1.6.0 versus 1.8.1 makes no difference to the laws this track uses. Recommend: drop P2 and P6 as predictions; relabel P4; rewrite P1, P3, P5 as in recommendations.
fleet.lay_summary: The earlier plan predicted how far a flying fish, or a 3D-printed model of one, can glide from a given launch speed. I rechecked the sums and they are correct. The trouble is that the main distance limit only holds for a smooth, level glide, and a glider thrown upward in an arc can beat it, as my simple computer model shows. Think of throwing a paper plane up and then letting it float: it travels further than a rule that assumed it never climbed. Several of the planned tests also could not really fail, or would fail for a trivial reason such as a slightly wrong launch angle. I suggest dropping two tests, relabelling one as a software check, and rewriting three with sturdier thresholds.

glossary.plain: The slowest speed at which the wings can still hold the weight up.
How many metres a glider can travel forward per metre of height it loses, in still air.
A ceiling on distance set by how much height and speed energy the glider starts with.
A launch angled upward so the body climbs before gliding down.
Flying like a thrown stone, with almost no help from wings.
The highest point of a flight path.
The table linking a wing's lift to its drag at each angle.
Running a made-up experiment many times on a computer to see how often a rule would fail by chance.
The chance that a test catches a real effect of a given size.
A numbered, frozen list of checked rules that a design is judged against.
A computer model that treats the whole animal or glider as a single dot with weight, lift and drag.

findings.claim: Design arithmetic for model L3 is correct: S=0.012688 m2, W=0.5886 N, W/S=46.39 N/m2, vmin^2=97.10, vmin=9.854 m/s.
findings.evidence_quote: Table 1 model L3; Table 2 ... CL_max 0.78 at 35 deg attack; LD_max 4.37 at 0 deg; CD_min 0.055 at -10 deg; coefficients use reference area A1+A2+A3

findings.claim: Level-launch bounds recompute exactly: 0.65 m (10 m/s), 28.49 m (15), 67.47 (20); with delta 0.14: 0.75, 33.12, 78.45; 50 m needs 17.03 m/s (delta 0.14) or 17.93 (delta 0). All design figures are right.

P1 threshold 16.09 m/s = sqrt(2 g 13.2) is arithmetically right, but assumes zero speed at the apex. A gliding trajectory at apex must still fly at >= vmin; adding that term gives 17.8-18.2 m/s (W/S 37.0-46.4 N/m2, CLmax 1.03).

P2 is logically implied by P1 for the headline trajectory: ratio=45.4/(4.7 v0^2/2g) is 0.731 at v0=16.1 and falls as v0 rises; ratio>1 needs v0<13.77, which contradicts P1 (v0>=16.1). The lower floor 0.30 equals v0=25.1 m/s, above every speed in the project data (field 15-20 m/s).
P2 denominator (4.7 v0^2/2g) drops both h0 and the stall floor, so P2 does not test the wrapper M3 that P4 and P5 rely on.
findings.source: design-flyingfish.json frozen_predictions P2 vs model M3

findings.claim: The stall-floor bound M3 is violated by lofted flight in a point-mass model using the L3 polar (parabolic fit CD=0.055+0.238 CL^2, CLmax 0.78): fish L3 from 10 m/s, h0=0, best flight 12.7 m versus M3 bound 0.65 m (19.7x); from 15 m/s 37.5 m vs 28.5 m (1.32x).

For the 30 g printed-glider placeholder (h0=1 m, vmin 6.96 m/s) best simulated flights exceed M3 by 58% at 7.5 m/s, 44% at 8, 25% at 10, 13% at 12. P5 1.10 allowance would fail at every speed for an optimal pitch-up launch.

Even constant-CL launches (no control) exceed M3 at low speed: ratio 1.43 at 7.5 m/s, 1.26 at 8, 0.95 at 10, 0.81 at 12. The P5 outcome therefore depends on the three launch speeds, which P5 does not state.
The plain energy bound without stall floor, (L/D)max (h0+v0^2/2g), was not exceeded in any simulated case (ratios 0.57-0.80), so it is the defensible P5 upper bound.

The registry scope for flight-climb-glide-law already says the lemma covers a single steady glide with no thrust and lift equal to weight. A P2/P5 failure on lofted launches would therefore not narrow the law, contrary to the design paper claim; it would show misapplication.
findings.evidence_quote: A single steady glide with no thrust and lift equal to weight; taxiing, repeated touch-and-go, wind and updrafts are outside the model.

findings.claim: Minimum launch speed for a 50 m flight, h0=0, no ground effect: design formula 17.93 m/s; point-mass search about 17.2 m/s (49.2 m at 17, 53.7 at 17.9); no-floor energy bound 14.98 m/s. The 17.0 m/s requirement is a model statement with about +-1 m/s spread.

P4 verdict (e) 0.65 m from 10 m/s consistent is hypersensitive: v0^2-vmin^2 = 2.9 m2/s2 (3% of v0^2). CLmax 0.80 gives 1.19 m, 0.90 gives 3.53 m, 1.03 gives 5.89 m. Verdicts (a),(b) stay eliminated for CLmax up to 2.0 (15 m/s bound 48.5 m at CLmax 2.0).

P4 is a pipeline/arithmetic unit test: (c) and (e) are consistent with any claim below the bound, (d) is cannot-rule, (f) is a mutant. None can fail on nature; the design says so itself (a failure is a bug report).

P3 threshold 0.50 s is arithmetically correct (T=0.500 s at 5.15 m/s, 23.3 deg, f=0.170, vmin 12.50 m/s) but only 20% above the no-lift ballistic time (0.415 s). At 30 deg (field value cited in takeoff-data.csv) T=0.632 s; at 45 deg 0.894 s. It fails on launch-angle error, not on gliding.
findings.evidence_quote: pitch angle at leaping (captive),20.0 +- 3.3,degrees ... previous field studies cited there give about 30 deg

findings.claim: P3 rule no leap > 0.50 s over n=10 leaps (13 fish, repeated measures): Monte Carlo under a pure-ballistic null gives refutation probability 26% (path angle = pitch), 47% (+3 deg extra sd), 96% (path angle 5 deg above pitch), 100% (+10 deg, sd 5). At a 1.0 s threshold it is 0% in all four scenarios; at 0.80 s, 8.5% in the worst.
Body pitch (20.0 +- 3.3 deg, accelerometer) is not the flight-path angle, and leap speed 3.87-5.15 m/s is itself an estimate from tail-beat 21.2 Hz by Wardle formula, not a measurement.
findings.evidence_quote: captive aquarium with 3-axis accelerometer; leap speed estimated from tail-beat frequency 21.2 Hz by Wardle's formula

findings.claim: P5 launch-speed gate error alone is as large as the allowance: a 0.5 m gate at 240 fps is 10-16 frames; +-0.5 frame timing at each edge gives speed sd 2.6-4.1% and bound sd 9.6-10.5%, about one sd equal to the 10% allowance, before vmin and L/D fit errors.

P5 refutation rule (>=2 of 30 above 1.10 bound) has power 0.23 at a true per-flight exceedance of 3%, 0.45 at 5%, 0.82 at 10% if flights were independent; they are not, since one calibration (10 drop glides) sets the bound for all 30.

P6 cannot fail on its 1.8.1 arm: the 1.7.0 fix was wording-only, the checker returns out-of-scope for a candidate declaring flight_mode glide, and a standing registry test asserts no accepted law is violated by a real organism. The 1.6.0 arm is doubtful: the out-of-scope rule for E3 is in checker code (browser-check.mjs lines 1827-1828), not in the law-set file, so the current checker run with lawset 1.6.0 would probably not turn red.
findings.evidence_quote: the checker now returns out-of-scope for a declared unpowered glide, and a standing registry test asserts no accepted law is violated by a real organism making a realistic claim.

findings.claim: Law-set difference for this track is nil: flight-climb-glide-law is 1.0.0 accepted in both 1.6.0 and 1.8.1; perturb-wind-glide 1.0.0 both. thompson1917-ch02-10 (vmin) is 1.1.0 in 1.8.1 with scope text unchanged from 1.0.0. Only E3 (2.0.0 to 2.1.0), fick-principle (1.1.0 to 1.3.0), scaling-area-law and scaling-strength-law (1.0.0 to 1.1.0) changed.

Deng 2019 simulated height 13.2 m exceeds the 8 m maximum recorded field flight height in the project data by 1.65x; Deng morphology mimics Park and Choi model L3, so P1/P2 are not independent of the calibration polar and test a simulation, not a fish.

findings.claim: Ground-effect delta 0.14 was measured only for h/b <= 0.97 with b the half pectoral span (0.1305 m for L3, so h <= 0.127 m); applying it to the whole 50 m path is generous, and the design correctly uses delta 0 for P5 (rail 1.0 m).

recommendations: DROP P2 (implied by P1; thresholds 0.30/1.00 map to v0 of 25.1 and 13.8 m/s, neither reachable if P1 holds). Keep only the Deng row as an input-reading check.
DROP P6 as a prediction. Keep it as a regression test and run the 1.6.0 arm with a checker build from before the 1.7.0 commit, or state that the arm is not reproducible with the current checker.

RELABEL P4 as a pipeline unit test, not a prediction. Replace verdict (e) 10 m/s by 12 m/s, since the 10 m/s result swings 0.65 to 5.89 m as CLmax goes 0.78 to 1.03. Report bounds as a range over CLmax 0.78-1.03 and state wind w=0.

REVISE P1: v0 >= sqrt(2 g 13.2 + vmin^2) = 17.8-18.2 m/s (vmin from Deng's own W/S and CLmax 1.03, falling back to L3 W/S 37.0-46.4); refuted if any reported launch speed is below that minus 2%. State the number of trajectories n in advance (unknown to me).

REVISE P3: per-leap rule T_obs <= 1.0 s, or T_obs <= T_M5(v_i, theta_i + 10 deg) + 0.1 s using that leap's own measured pitch. The threshold must exceed the 45 deg ballistic-with-lift time at 5.15 m/s (0.894 s) so only genuine gliding (above about 1.5 s) refutes. If per-leap airborne durations are not tabulated, record cannot-test before opening results.

REWRITE P5: freeze the three launch speeds (suggest 9, 11, 13 m/s so v0^2 - vmin^2 is at least 30 m2/s2 and gate error stays near 10% of the bound); use the no-floor bound (L/D)max_measured (h0 + v0^2/2g) as the upper bound; pre-register the integrator band 0.55-0.80 of it as a two-sided prediction for the best flight per speed; refute at 1.15 x bound with more than 1 of 30 above; use the floor bound M3 only for steady drop glides. Pre-register the integrator parameters and seed before building.

Do not claim a law is narrowed by a P2/P5 failure: the registered scope of flight-climb-glide-law already restricts it to steady lift=W glide. State the claim as the stall-floor wrapper is rejected for lofted launches, which my simulation already predicts.
Stamp verdicts with the law set, but note it makes no difference here: flight-climb-glide-law 1.0.0 and perturb-wind-glide 1.0.0 are identical in 1.6.0 and 1.8.1.
Treat shared calibration explicitly: report the 30 flights as a clustered sample under one bound, and give the bound's own uncertainty from the 10 drop glides before FREEZE 2.

fleet.label: t6-flyingfish-data
fleet.topic: Track 6 data and reproducibility: flying-fish glide energy certificate
fleet.summary: Downloaded Deng 2019 (Zenodo, md5 matches the record) and Makiguchi 2013 (publisher open PDF); read Park and Choi 2010 and Daane 2021 Data S1 from the project's cached copies because both refuse automated download. repro.py ran 67 checks: 65 reproduce. Every headline number of the scout and design agents reproduces (energy-bound ranges 22.3/50.1/89.1 m, vmin 9.85 m/s, stall-floor bounds 0.65/28.5/67.5 m, 49 flying fish with pectoral/SL 0.406-0.823, 14 adults 0.656-0.757, 3 above 0.76, 2 above 0.79). The data overturn three readings: (1) Deng's abstract 45.4 m and 13.2 m come from two different runs (alpha0=0 deg, gamma=25 deg gives 45.4 m in 3.5 s; 13.2 m is the apex of the alpha0=10 deg, gamma=40 deg run, whose range peak is 41.5 m), and every run launches at a fixed 20 m/s, so the design's P1 launch-speed premise (v0 >= 16.1 m/s) is satisfied by construction; (2) on those Deng runs the distance is 0.43-0.47 of the no-stall-floor energy bound (0.56-0.61 with the stall floor), inside the design's P2 window [0.30, 1.00], but this is Deng's own quasi-steady model, not an independent flight; (3) Makiguchi 2013 reports no per-leap airborne time (its 'duration' is the tail-acceleration phase), so design prediction P3 is untestable from this paper. Also found: the project's glide-data.csv says the Makiguchi mean length 325.0 mm and mass 227.7 g are 'over 13 fish'; Table 1 shows they are the mean of the ten 2010 fish only (all 13 give 312.8 mm, 221.6 g).
fleet.lay_summary: Earlier helpers claimed numbers about how far a flying fish can glide. We downloaded the original papers and measurements and redid the arithmetic with a short program anyone can rerun. Almost every number came out the same. A fish gliding is like a cyclist coasting off a hill: the speed it starts with can be traded for distance, but only down to the speed at which its wings stop holding it up. When we opened the computer-simulation paper, we found its two headline figures, a 45.4 m glide and a 13.2 m climb, came from two different simulated flights, and that every simulated flight started at 20 metres per second. We also found the aquarium paper never records how long each leap lasted, so one planned test cannot be done from it.

glossary.plain: How many metres a glider moves forward for each metre it drops; higher is a better glider.
The slowest speed at which the wings can still hold the weight up.
Body weight divided by wing area, in newtons per square metre; heavier for the same wing means a higher stall speed.
A ceiling on glide distance set by the launch height plus the launch speed turned into height.
A computer model that tracks a flyer's forward, up-down and pitching motion in a flat slice.
Computer simulation of air flowing around a shape.
A fingerprint of a file; any change to the file changes the fingerprint.
The large side fin behind the gill cover, used as a wing in flying fish.
Body length from snout to the end of the backbone, not counting the tail fin.
The angle above horizontal at which the fish leaves the water.
