No Lean build was run (not needed for the data task); the wrapper glide_energy_range_rules_out is not in the application repo's Delphi/*.lean.
The cached CSV extract and xlsx came from the project, so independent reproduction of Daane covers the parsing and arithmetic, not the publisher's file identity.
recommendations: Correct the design's P1/P2 text: Deng launches at a fixed 20 m/s and the abstract's two figures are different runs; restate P2 as distance/bound = 0.43-0.47 (0.56-0.61 with the stall floor) and say it is a model self-consistency check.
Mark P3 'cannot test from Makiguchi 2013' now and look for a source with airborne times, or drop it.
Carry the Park and Choi mass rounding into the certificate: use vmin as an interval 9.43-10.26 m/s, since the 10 m/s launch verdict (a) sits inside it.
Fix the 'over 13 fish' note in the project's glide-data.csv: the mean is of ten fish.
Put Deng's CLmax 1.03 (area A1 only) and Park and Choi's 0.78 (area A1+A2+A3) on one reference area before mixing them in any certificate.

fleet.label: t6-flyingfish-deep
fleet.topic: Track 6 deep literature: the flying fish glide and its elimination-certificate evaluation framework
fleet.summary:
STATE OF THE ART: FLYING FISH GLIDE, AND WHAT AN ELIMINATION-CERTIFICATE FRAMEWORK CAN AND CANNOT SAY ABOUT IT
(Tags: [M] measured in a source I read, [D] derived by arithmetic I did and saved in analysis.py, [A] assumed. Where I could only read an abstract or a second-hand quotation I say so.)

1. THE QUESTION. Can a 20-30 cm fish, which has no wings in the usual sense, cover tens of metres through air, and what do the laws of motion allow or forbid? The framework in the application repo answers the second half by writing each law as a Lean theorem and each candidate claim as a certificate that concludes False if the claim and the law cannot both hold.

2. THE SCIENCE FROM THE GROUND UP.
Step 1 [M]. Flying fishes are the family Exocoetidae. Adults are 150-500 mm long (Davenport 1994). Two-winged forms (Exocoetus) enlarge only the chest (pectoral) fins; four-winged forms (Cypselurus, Hirundichthys) enlarge the belly (pelvic) fins too.
Step 2 [M]. A glide is a trade of energy: height and speed are spent to pay for drag. For a steady glide with lift equal to weight, distance forward per metre of descent equals the lift-to-drag ratio L/D. [D] This is textbook mechanics; in the repo it is Delphi.glide_range_le.
Step 3 [M]. The only direct force measurement on flying-fish bodies is Park and Choi 2010: stuffed Cypselurus hiraii models in a 12 m/s wind tunnel, Reynolds number about 2e4. Best model: L/D 4.37 at about 0 degrees, CLmax 0.78 at 35 degrees, CDmin 0.055. Pelvic fins add more than 20 percent lift and make pitch more stable. Flying within 0.33 half-spans of water cuts drag by 14 percent (9 percent over a solid surface).
Step 4 [M, simulation]. Deng 2019 CFD gives L/D 4.7 and CLmax 1.03 for a differently built model. Its glide-distance numbers depend on an ASSUMED 20 m/s launch speed; see the contested list.
Step 5 [D]. Stall speed: the wings can hold weight only above v_min = sqrt(2W/(rho S CLmax)). For model L3 (0.06 kg, 0.012688 m2) this is 9.85 m/s. A fish leaving the water at 3.9-5.2 m/s (Makiguchi 2013, aquarium) is at 0.39-0.52 of that, so it cannot be gliding on lift alone; it is on a ballistic hop (apex 0.8-1.4 m, reach 1.5-2.7 m at 45 degrees by my arithmetic).
Step 6 [D]. Energy-height bound for a level lifting glide: x <= (L/D)(v0^2 - v_min^2)/(2g)/(1-delta). A 50 m glide at L/D 4.37 needs launch airspeed >= 17.9 m/s, or 17.0 with 14 percent ground effect. [A] The bound is a theorem only if lift equals weight; ballistic arcs, wind, updrafts and repeated taxiing are outside it.
Step 7 [M, second-hand]. Reported field behaviour: leap at about 10 m/s, glide up to 50 m at 15-20 m/s air speed, up to 400 m in 30 s with repeated taxiing, maximum recorded height 8 m. All from older film work I could not read (Hertel 1966, Edgerton and Breder 1941, Davenport 1990).
Step 8 [M]. Davenport's flight sequence: approach below the surface at under 30 body lengths per second, leap at a shallow angle, accelerate by taxiing with the tail beating up to 50 times a second, then glide. Red (aerobic) axial muscle is no more than a fast-cruising mackerel-type fish carries, so acceleration to take-off speed probably uses anaerobic white muscle (Davenport 1992, stated as probable, not measured).
Step 9 [D from E3]. Sustained powered level flight at L/D 4.37 needs 1.33 W at v_min for the 0.06 kg reference fish against an aerobic ceiling of 0.0833 W (registry law E3 2.1.0): a factor 16. So flight must be unpowered glide plus burst power. [A] The ceiling is built from zebrafish oxygen data (Palstra 2010: 82.18 umol O2 per g per hour = 2629.6 mg per kg per hour by my unit conversion) taken from 0.43 g fish; this is extrapolated across a 140-fold mass difference.
Step 10 [M]. Why they fly is unresolved: predator escape (Davenport 1994: dolphinfish and squid) versus energy saving (rejected by Davenport; listed as open by Park and Choi).
Step 11 [M]. Evolution: extant Exocoetidae have no fossils older than the Eocene (Xu 2013); the Triassic thoracopterids (Ladinian, 235-242 Ma) glided convergently, with a gradual four-stage sequence (Xu 2015). Molecular phylogeny supports a progressive two-wing to four-wing transition and a non-monophyletic Cheilopogon (Lewallen 2010). Genomics (Daane 2021, 35 species) finds convergent changes in fin, balance and muscle genes, and zebrafish alleles of lat4a and kcnh2a that together reproduce flying-fish fin proportions.

3. WHAT IS ESTABLISHED WITH NUMBERS. L/D 4.37 and CLmax 0.78 (tunnel, dead models); ground-effect drag cuts 9-14 percent; pectoral fin length exponent 1.058 [1.017, 1.099] across 49 museum fish (my recomputation); pectoral/SL 0.406-0.823 in flying fishes against at most 0.388 in other beloniforms in one 3-species dataset; wing loading 37-46 N/m2 on four models; fin and geometry limits 24 percent and 76 percent of standard length; 50 tail beats per second.

4. WHAT IS CONTESTED. (a) Real L/D: 4.37 measured, 4.7 CFD, 15.7 in Kawachi 1993 (3.6 times higher; I could not read it). (b) Deng's headline pairs 45.4 m from the 0-degree run with 13.2 m from the 10-degree run (whose best is 41.5 m), uses coefficients from 10 m/s but launches at 20 m/s. (c) Why they fly. (d) Pelvic fins: extra lift (Park and Choi) versus tailplane (Davenport). (e) Origin of flight: extension of ballistic leaps versus lift-supported taxiing first (Davenport 2003) versus progressive two-to-four-wing sequence (Lewallen). (f) Species count 50 versus 80. (g) Davenport 1992 wing-loading exponent 1.236 versus the 1.147 implied by its own mass and area exponents.

5. THE FRAMEWORK, AND WHAT THIS REVIEW CHANGES. The application repo is at law set 1.8.1 and has the four *_rules_out lemmas (vmin, aerobic flight, glide range, climb) that the 1.6.0 upstream copy lacks. The 50 m, 8 m field certificate treats 8 m as the only energy and so eliminates a claim the physics allows once launch kinetic energy is counted (20 m/s launch gives a 67.5 m bound). The stall-floor plus kinetic-energy wrapper is the missing piece. The fin-ratio gap law rests on three flying-fish species. The aerobic ceiling rests on zebrafish. I did not compile any Lean.

6. OPEN PROBLEMS. A modern tracked data set of wild glides (launch speed, height, distance, wind). Live-fish force measurements. Deng's free-flight CFD with the polar tied to the actual speed. Taxiing power measured not simulated. Whether the pelvic fins are lift or stability. Functional test of lat4a and kcnh2a in a flying fish. A flying-fish aerobic ceiling measured on flying fish.
fleet.lay_summary: Flying fish do not fly like insects. They launch themselves out of the sea and glide, rather like a paper plane that can swim. The best force measurements we have come from dead, stuffed fish held in a wind tunnel, and they say a fish can travel about four metres forward for every metre it drops. That is far better than a plain body but nowhere near a sailplane. Reported glides of 50 metres therefore need a very fast start, which the fish gets by skimming the water and beating its tail up to 50 times a second. Nobody has yet filmed and measured a wild glide end to end with modern tools, so the speeds and distances people quote are second-hand. Our contribution is to turn those few measurements into simple limits that a computer can check, and to show where those limits are loose, wrong, or silent.

findings.claim: [measured] Wind-tunnel force measurements on stuffed Cypselurus hiraii (a four-winged flying fish) give a best lift-to-drag ratio of 4.37, reached at an angle of attack near 0 degrees, for the best model (L3).

[measured] Same table: maximum lift coefficient 0.78 at 35 degrees; minimum drag coefficient 0.055 (the sign of the angle is lost in text extraction; the project reads -10 deg). Coefficients use the sum of pectoral, pelvic and body planform area as reference area.
[measured] Lift is largest near 30-35 degrees, which matches the angle at which flying fish are seen to leave the sea; the lift curve stays high after stall (thin-airfoil stall).
findings.evidence_quote: the lift coefficient is largest at attack angles around

findings.claim: [measured] Enlarged pelvic fins raise lift (by more than 20 percent at 0 degrees compared with the pectoral-only model M) and improve pitch stability; the paper explains this by a jet-like accelerated flow between pectoral and pelvic fins (smoke-wire flow visualisation).
findings.evidence_quote: The role of the pelvic fins was found to increase the lift force and lift-to-drag ratio

findings.claim: [measured] Tunnel speed 12 m/s, chord Reynolds number about 2e4 (Table 2 gives 2.0e4 for the flying-fish row), measured on models with SL about 200 mm; 150-500 mm is the quoted adult size range.
findings.evidence_quote: the standard lengths (SL) of the present models are about 200mm

findings.claim: [measured] Caveat on the polar: the models were dead fish, stuffed within a day, with fins spread and fixed, a thin nylon cloth glued on the upper fin surface, and the dihedral angle of three models deliberately set to 22, 12 and 7 degrees; model mass and wind-tunnel lift agreed well for two of three models (about 30 percent off for model L2), so the shapes did not shrink much.
findings.evidence_quote: Five fish of similar sizes were selected and stuffed in the appropriate gliding positions

findings.claim: [derived] Induced drag from strong wing-tip vortices is judged one of the dominant drag components at this Reynolds number (an inference from flow visualisation and from aircraft practice, not a measured drag split).
findings.evidence_quote: induced drag is one of the dominant drag

findings.claim: [measured] Ground effect: flying close to water cut drag by up to 14 percent (at height/half-span 0.33) and by 9 percent over a solid surface (at 0.21) for the full model; the body alone gave 7 and 4 percent. The authors note the tunnel water surface did not move with the airflow, so the true gain should be larger.
findings.evidence_quote: maximum reduction of the drag by 14% was obtained at

findings.claim: [contested] The paper itself says the reason flying fish fly is still unclear: escape from underwater predators or saving transport cost are the two suggestions it lists.
findings.evidence_quote: the exact reason is still not clear

findings.claim: [derived] CFD on a flying-fish model built to mimic the Park and Choi pectoral fins gives maximum lift coefficient 1.03 and maximum lift-to-drag 4.7 (against 0.78 and 4.37 measured). My arithmetic: 4.7/4.37 = 1.075 and 1.03/0.78 = 1.32, so CFD is 7 percent higher on L/D and 32 percent higher on CLmax. The Deng fins are flat 1 mm plates and model A has no pelvic fins, so it is not the same body as the stuffed fish.
findings.evidence_quote: The maximum lift force coefficient of 1.03 is reached at the angle of attack

findings.claim: [assumed] The 3-degree-of-freedom trajectory model fixes the take-off speed at 20 m/s for all runs. This is an input assumption, not a result.
findings.evidence_quote: The take-off speed is fixed at 20 m

findings.claim: [measured+derived] The two headline numbers in the Deng abstract come from different runs: 45.4 m (endurance 3.5 s) is the best distance with initial angle of attack 0 degrees; the 13.2 m apex is reached in the run with initial angle of attack 10 degrees, whose best distance is 41.5 m. The abstract states them together as "a distance up to 45.4 m, and reach a height of 13.2 m".
findings.evidence_quote: distance and its endurance are 41.5 m and 3.47 s

findings.claim: [contested] Deng computes the aerodynamic coefficients at 10 m/s (Re = 2.6e4) but launches the trajectory at 20 m/s; the authors call their model a preliminary approximation and say a free-flight model would be more suitable.
findings.evidence_quote: Clearly, a fixed velocity of 10 m s

findings.claim: [derived] With launch at 20 m/s the energy height v0^2/2g is 20.4 m; the loose bound 4.7 x 20.4 = 95.8 m is about twice the 45.4 m simulated (ratio 0.47), and the 13.2 m apex is 0.65 of the energy height. So Deng's trajectories do not violate an energy-height range bound; they sit inside it by a factor of about two.

[reported-second-hand] Deng cites Hertel for a four-winged fish of 0.38 kg that could reach 48 m given 20 m/s free flight and 10 m/s head wind, and a maximum recorded flight height of 8 m; and Kawachi, Inada and Azuma for a model of a 0.226 kg fish with maximum lift-to-drag around 15.7 giving a maximum distance of 80 m. I could read neither original.
findings.evidence_quote: They reported a maximum distance of 80 m

findings.claim: [contested] Kawachi's assumed maximum L/D of 15.7 is 3.6 times the measured 4.37 and 3.3 times Deng's CFD 4.7 (my arithmetic). Whether the real fish's lift-to-drag is nearer 4.4 or far higher is therefore a live disagreement between a 1993 analytical model and the 2010 and 2019 data; the wind-tunnel models were dead and fixed, so neither side is a live-fish measurement.

[measured] Makiguchi and colleagues put miniature 3-axis accelerometers on Cypselurus heterurus doederleini in a controlled aquarium and estimated leap speeds of 3.9 to 5.2 m/s, which they say is 38.7 to 51.5 percent of earlier reported maximum swimming speeds.
findings.evidence_quote: leap from the water surface at speeds of 3.9 to 5.2 m s

findings.claim: [derived] The leap speed is not measured directly: it is predicted from stroke-cycle frequency by a swimming-speed relationship (3.87 to 5.15 m/s), and the authors speculate that the fish were not performing maximally because the aquarium was small.
findings.evidence_quote: maximum swimming speed would have been predicted to reach 3.87 to 5.15 m s

findings.claim: [reported-second-hand] Typical field numbers are quoted second-hand in Makiguchi: leap speed about 10 m/s, glides up to 50 m, air speed 15-20 m/s, from older stroboscopic film work; the primary film papers (Edgerton and Breder 1941; Davenport 1990) were not read by me.
findings.evidence_quote: flying fish leap from the water surface at a speed of about 10 m s

findings.claim: [reported-second-hand] Park and Choi quote glides totalling as much as 400 m in 30 s through repeated taxiing, with maximum flight speed 10-20 m/s (Hertel; Fish; Davenport).
findings.evidence_quote: The flying fish glides over a total distance of as much as 400m in 30s

findings.claim: [reported-second-hand] Davenport's review describes the flight sequence: swim to the surface at very high speed (under 30 body lengths per second) with fins furled, leap at a shallow angle, accelerate by taxiing with the tail beating at up to 50 beats per second, then free flight that may be prolonged by more taxiing.
findings.evidence_quote: accelerate to take-off speed by taxiing with the lateral fins expanded and the tail beating in the water at up to 50 beats

findings.claim: [contested] Davenport judges flying fish "probably fly mainly to escape from predators, particularly dolphin-fishes (Coryphaena hippurus) and ommastrephid squid" and explicitly rejects the energy-conservation alternative; Park and Choi list both as unresolved.
findings.evidence_quote: Flying fish probably fly mainly to escape from predators, particularly dolphin-fishes

findings.claim: [reported-second-hand] Davenport: for a 0.3 m standard-length fish, significant drag reduction by ground effect occurs below about 0.5 m height; fish start to show flight at about 50 mm length; and flight is unlikely below 20-23 C water because of muscle limits.
findings.evidence_quote: For a flying fish of 0.3 m standard length, significant reduction of drag by ground effect will take place at heights below about 0.5 m

findings.claim: [contested] Davenport on pelvic fins in four-winged species: they act as stabilising tailplane, with area 20-35 percent of total lateral fin area, not as extra lifting area. Park and Choi (wind tunnel) found the pelvic fins do add lift; both can hold at once (the Saro-Cortes robot paper finds a lift-stability trade-off).
findings.evidence_quote: The expanded, flat pelvic fins of four-wingers have evolved, not to increase wing area, but to function as

findings.claim: [reported-second-hand] Davenport 1992 (Exocoetus obtusirostris): body mass exponent 2.981 and lateral fin area exponent 1.834 against standard length; wing loading rises with exponent 1.236; pectoral fin length cannot exceed 78-79 percent of standard length.
findings.evidence_quote: wing-loading rises in positive allometric fashion with standard length

findings.claim: [contested] Internal check: mass exponent minus area exponent is 2.981 - 1.834 = 1.147, not the reported 1.236. The abstract does not say how the 1.236 was fitted (probably a direct regression on specimen loadings); I could not read the tables to resolve the 0.089 gap.

[reported-second-hand] Davenport 2003: pectoral leading edge fixed at 24 percent of standard length from the snout, wing length cannot exceed 76 percent of SL, heavier fish need faster flight and better L/D, so larger fish have their centre of mass further behind the centre of wing pressure; this limits the size of two-winged species and the pelvic fins of four-winged species act as stabilising tailplane.
findings.evidence_quote: the leading edge of the pectoral fin

findings.claim: [contested] Davenport 2003 also argues the traditional model of flight evolution (by extension of ballistic leaps) is flawed and proposes lift-supported surface taxiing in halfbeaks with enlarged pectoral fins as an essential preliminary.
findings.evidence_quote: the accepted model of evolution of flight in flying fishes (by extension of ballistic leaps) is flawed

findings.claim: [reported-second-hand] Davenport 1992: the flightless flying halfbeak Oxyporhamphus micropterus cannot fly mainly because its centre of gravity is so far behind the pectoral fins that stalling on take-off would be inevitable; and acceleration to take-off speed "probably" needs anaerobic white muscle.
findings.evidence_quote: acceleration to take-off speed in flying fish requires use of anaerobic white muscles

findings.claim: [reported-second-hand] Fish 1990 (six genera): fin area and span rise with body mass, the pectoral share of wing area and the hypocaudal-lobe share of caudal area stay constant, and the flight is a high-speed glide with a relatively flat trajectory. The abstract gives no numbers.
findings.evidence_quote: The flight performance of flying fish is a high

findings.claim: [derived] CFD preprint (not peer reviewed in the record I have): a 0.25 m, 0.191 kg fish needs 350 W to swim underwater at 10 m/s but only 36 W to taxi at 10 m/s; with 350 W of flapping power it reaches 16.5 m/s. The ratio is 350/36 = 9.7 (my arithmetic).
findings.evidence_quote: the minimum power required for a stead-state locomotion at 10 m s

findings.claim: [derived] A 2026 CFD study of a four-winged fish finds that during free-surface taxiing the caudal fin yields thrust (mean coefficient about 1.22) where deep-water swimming gives -3.79, that the caudal fin supplies over 60 percent of lift while taxiing, and that the pectoral fins supply 85 percent of lift in aerial glide; whole-body lift coefficient is about 2.15 taxiing against 0.57 gliding.
findings.evidence_quote: the caudal fin yields substantial thrust

findings.claim: [derived] Taxiing power per kilogram from the CFD preprint is 36/0.191 = 188 W/kg; the registry aerobic ceiling E3 v2 is 0.0833/0.06 = 1.39 W/kg; the ratio is 136 (my arithmetic). If the CFD is right, taxiing cannot be aerobic, which agrees with Davenport's anaerobic white-muscle suggestion and with the registry 1.7.0 rescoping of E3 (burst effort on white-muscle stores is out of scope).

[assumed] Mass-scaling caveat on the ratio above: the CFD fish (0.191 kg) and the registry reference fish (0.06 kg) differ by a factor of 3.2; I compared per kilogram, which assumes power scales linearly with mass.

[measured] Daane 2021 sequenced targeted regions (over 300,000 loci) pooled from 35 beloniform species and measured fin length against standard length across the clade; the pectoral fin allometry was identical across two- and four-winged flying fishes, and the two gliding halfbeak genera are intermediate.
findings.evidence_quote: The allometric relationship between body size and pectoral fin length was identical across the two- and four-wing flying fishes

findings.claim: [measured] Convergent evolution: 44 amino-acid substitutions present only within all three gliding lineages, against 14-28 in control comparisons; accelerated sequence evolution in gliding branches for fin development, semicircular canal, vestibular, muscle-hypertrophy and fear-circuit gene groups.
findings.evidence_quote: Compared with 14

findings.claim: [measured] Zebrafish genetics: the dominant mutation nr21 is a T200K change in the amino-acid transporter lat4a (small fins; gain of function), and the classic longfin mutant is an inversion that raises kcnh2a expression in the fin; combining alleles in zebrafish closely phenocopies flying-fish fin proportions.
findings.evidence_quote: interaction between these genetic loci in zebrafish closely phenocopies the observed fin proportions of flying fishes

findings.claim: [contested] Caveat: lat4a and kcnh2a are candidate regulators supported by convergence signals plus zebrafish phenocopy; no flying-fish gene was edited and the paper reports no flying-fish functional test. This is an inference, and the grounded part is the zebrafish result.

[measured] Independent confirmation that kcnh2a controls fin size: in the longfin zebrafish, ectopic kcnh2a expression acts autonomously in the fin intra-ray mesenchyme and tunes the outgrowth period rather than positional information.
findings.evidence_quote: ion signaling within the growth-determining mesenchyme lineage controls fin size by tuning outgrowth periods

findings.claim: [measured] Phylogeny: a cytochrome b and RAG2 tree supports the progressive transition from two-wing to four-wing gliding, and shows the largest genus Cheilopogon is not monophyletic.
findings.evidence_quote: The results support the progressive transition from two

findings.claim: [contested] Species count disagrees across sources: Xu 2013 says "some 50 species of extant flying fishes" and a 2026 cytogenetics paper says four subfamilies, seven genera and 80 species (citing Fricke et al.). Counting depends on the taxonomy used; I did not resolve it.
findings.evidence_quote: Some 50 species of extant flying fishes are classified in the Exocoetidae

findings.claim: [measured] Fossils: the Triassic thoracopterids convergently evolved over-water gliding; the earliest evidence reported in 2013 was Middle Triassic of China, and Wushaichthys and Peripeltopleurus (Ladinian, 235-242 Ma) are described as the oldest and most primitive thoracopterids, with a gradual four-stage sequence cranial specialisation, asymmetrical caudal fin, enlarged paired fins, scale reduction.
findings.evidence_quote: the evolution of overwater gliding of thoracopterids was gradual in nature

findings.claim: [measured] Extant Exocoetidae have a fossil record no older than the Eocene (Xu 2013), so Triassic and modern flying fish are convergent, not ancestral.
findings.evidence_quote: which have a fossil record no older than the Eocene

findings.claim: [measured] A 2026 cytogenetic study of three Atlantic species reports all share 2n = 48 chromosomes, with structural karyotype divergence between populations, genera and congeners.
findings.evidence_quote: All the flying fish species and populations analyzed share 2n = 48 chromosomes

findings.claim: [measured] Robot flying fish studies: Saro-Cortes 2022 ran a modular robot model in a wind tunnel at Reynolds number 30,000 and found a trade-off between lift and pitch stability for the pelvic fins; Chen 2023 built a robot that exits water at 1.55 m/s (5.9 body lengths/s) in 0.233 s and a reinforcement-learning fin-morphing controller that lengthened simulated glide by 7.2 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: there is a clear a trade-off between stability and lift generation

findings.claim: [derived] Stall floor: with the Park and Choi L3 numbers (mass 0.06 kg, reference area 0.012688 m2 from the project's reading of Table 1, CLmax 0.78, air density 1.225) v_min = sqrt(2W/(rho S CLmax)) = 9.85 m/s. A lift-equals-weight glide cannot go slower; with Deng's CLmax 1.03 it is 8.58 m/s.

[derived] Energy-height range bound, level lifting glide: x <= (L/D) (v0^2 - v_min^2)/(2g) / (1 - delta). For 50 m with L/D 4.37 the launch airspeed must be at least 17.9 m/s (no ground effect) or 17.0 m/s (14 percent drag cut). At 15 m/s the bound is 28.5 m, at 20 m/s it is 67.5 m (no ground effect).

[assumed] Scope of that bound: it is a theorem only while lift equals weight. A lofted ballistic arc has unloaded wings, and at 10 m/s the parasitic drag (about 0.043 N with CDmin 0.055) is 14 times smaller than the weight (0.589 N), a ratio above 4.37; so field flights with a ballistic phase can legitimately beat it, and the bound is a modelling claim for them.

[derived] The earlier (prior-agent) pure-glide certificate eliminate 50 m from 8 m at L/D 4.37 treats the 8 m height as the only energy; it is a compiled certificate (elim_pure_glide_field_distance_C15 in lean/Delphi/Certificates/Eliminations.lean, read not built by me). Once launch kinetic energy is counted (20 m/s launch gives 67.5 m of bound) the 50 m field glide is not eliminated, so that certificate removes a candidate that the physics does not forbid.

[derived] Powered aerobic level flight at L/D 4.37 needs W v / (L/D) = 1.33 W at 9.85 m/s (2.02 W at 15 m/s) for the 0.06 kg reference fish, 16 times (24 times) the registry E3 v2 aerobic ceiling of 0.0833 W; so a sustained powered flight is ruled out and flight must be unpowered or burst-powered, as the project's earlier 16x figure also says.

[derived] Provenance check on the E3 v2 input: Palstra 2010 reports maximal oxygen consumption at Ucrit of 82.18 +/- 6.50 micromol O2 per g per hour for zebrafish; times 31.998 g/mol this is 2629.6 mg O2 per kg per hour, matching the 2630 quoted in the registry changelog. The fish measured were about 3 cm and 0.43 g, so using them to bound a 60 g flying fish is an extrapolation across body size and clade.
findings.evidence_quote: a maximal oxygen consumption at Ucrit of 82.18

findings.claim: [measured] Registry state read from the application repo changelog: law set 1.7.0 rescoped E3 and fick-principle so they no longer fire on unpowered glide, 1.8.0 narrowed five scopes for a third wild-type false positive and moved C14 to aerobic-power-bound, and 1.8.1 retired a loop-test law; current set is 1.8.1.

[measured] The application repo Constraints.lean defines vmin_rules_out, aerobic_flight_rules_out, glide_range_rules_out and climb_rules_out (grep). The earlier law-mapper reported them missing because it read the 1.6.0 upstream copy; they are present at 1.8.1. I did not compile.

[derived] Fin-ratio gap check, from the project's cached CSV of Daane Data S1A: pectoral/SL for 49 flying fish ranges 0.406-0.823 (median 0.687); 19 flying halfbeaks 0.175-0.388; 22 halfbeaks 0.115-0.177; 19 needlefish 0.071-0.106. The ">= 0.406 vs <= 0.389" gap holds in this file, but the flying-fish group has only three species (Cheilopogon furcatus, Exocoetus volitans, Hirundichthys rondeleti) and the CSV carries a spreadsheet float artifact (a pelvic ratio of 2.4e-16), so the gap is a three-species museum observation, not a clade law.

[derived] Pectoral length versus standard length, log-log fit over the 49 flying-fish rows: exponent 1.058, 95 percent interval 1.017-1.099, r2 0.983 (my recomputation, matches the registry). An exponent above 1 means pectoral fins grow slightly faster than the body, i.e. positive allometry.

[contested] The 2023 Biology Open review of gliding locomotion (covering 2022 work) concludes gliding is a sophisticated behaviour resulting from interdependent morphology, sensing, environment and selective pressure; it says new techniques should make it possible to study flying fish gliding in open water, which it calls understudied (the paucity of studies).
findings.evidence_quote: addressing the paucity of studies in each system

key_claims.claim: Measured: stuffed Cypselurus hiraii models in a 12 m/s wind tunnel (Re about 2e4) reach a lift-to-drag ratio of at most 4.37 and a lift coefficient of at most 0.78; this polar is the only direct force measurement on flying-fish bodies and underlies every range bound below.

Assumed, not found: the Deng 2019 CFD headline (45.4 m glide, 13.2 m apex) rests on a take-off speed fixed at 20 m/s, uses coefficients computed at 10 m/s, and pairs a distance from the 0-degree run with an apex from the 10-degree run (whose best distance is 41.5 m).
key_claims.evidence_quote: The take-off speed is fixed at 20 m

key_claims.claim: Measured then derived: in an aquarium, Cypselurus heterurus doederleini leaped at an estimated 3.9-5.2 m/s, well below the 9.85 m/s stall speed I derive for the L3 body; the quoted field values (leap 10 m/s, glide 50 m, air speed 15-20 m/s) are second-hand from older film work.
key_claims.evidence_quote: leap from the water surface at speeds of 3.9 to 5.2 m s

key_claims.claim: Derived (lift equals weight assumed): a single level lifting glide of 50 m at L/D 4.37 needs launch airspeed of at least 17.9 m/s (17.0 with a 14 percent ground-effect drag cut) once the stall floor is respected; the bound is a theorem for lift = weight only, so lofted ballistic phases and repeated taxiing fall outside it.

glossary.plain: moving through air with no engine or wing-flapping, trading height and speed for distance
how many metres forward a glider travels for each metre it sinks; higher is better
body weight divided by wing area; a high number means the animal must fly faster to stay up
the slowest speed at which the wings can still hold the body up
skimming along the water surface with the tail flicking in the water to gain speed before and between glides
extra efficiency a wing gets when it flies very close to a surface such as the sea
a tube with moving air used to measure the forces on a model held still
a computer simulation of how air or water flows around an object
a number comparing speed, size and air stickiness that tells you whether two flows behave alike
powered by muscle that burns oxygen continuously, as in steady cruising
muscle that gives short bursts of power from stored fuel without needing oxygen at that moment
how a body part grows relative to the whole body as the animal gets bigger
a computer-checked proof that a stated design or claim breaks a stated law and so cannot be true
the height you would need to start from, with no speed, to have the same total energy as a given height and speed
unrelated groups independently evolving the same trait
flying fish with only enlarged chest fins versus those with enlarged chest and belly fins

recommendations: Replace the pure-glide field certificate (8 m, 50 m, L/D 4.37) with the stall-floor energy-height wrapper: x <= (L/D)(v0^2 - vmin^2)/(2g)/(1-delta); a 50 m single-glide claim is then consistent only if launch airspeed is at least 17.0-17.9 m/s, and the certificate must carry the scope hypothesis lift = weight.

Stamp every verdict with law set 1.8.1 and note that the upstream 1.6.0 pin lacks vmin_rules_out, aerobic_flight_rules_out and the glide/climb lemmas (present in the application repo Constraints.lean at lines 243, 316, 324, 331).
Use the Makiguchi leaps as a falsification test of the stall-floor logic: any logged leap that is both airborne beyond about 0.5 s and below 9.85 m/s would contradict a lift-equals-weight reading.
Treat Deng 2019 launch conditions as inputs: re-run with the coefficients at the launch Reynolds number before using 45.4 m or 13.2 m as targets, and never cite the two numbers as one trajectory.
Mark the Palstra-derived aerobic ceiling as extrapolated from a 0.43 g fish; seek flying-fish or similar-size pelagic MO2max before relying on the 16x shortfall as more than order-of-magnitude.
Label the fin-ratio gap law with its three-species base and the spreadsheet float artifact in the cached CSV; do not promote past candidate until more Exocoetidae species are measured.

fleet.topic: Track 6 law map against law set 1.8.1 with a checked Lean law (parabolic drag polar L/D bound)
fleet.summary: Mapped Track 6 against the application repo's law set 1.8.1 (59 pinned laws; 45 with a Lean theorem verified present in the named module, 14 placeholders with none). 48 relevant laws are in 'table' with registry id, version, status, theorem and module. The older map used leanbio 1.6.0: its versions are stale (E3 2.0.0, fick 1.1.0), its 'broken reference' finding does not hold in the application repo (vmin_rules_out etc. are defined in Constraints.lean), and it missed physiology, Hydro, altitude helpers, froude and the growth-asymptote candidate. Chosen missing law: the parabolic drag polar bound C_L/C_D <= (1/2) sqrt(pi e AR / C_D0), which closes the registry gap aspect-ratio-induced-drag. It is in DragPolarBound.lean, composed with Delphi.glide_range_le, and passes check.sh with no errors and no sorryAx (first attempt failed, then fixed). It is a theorem about a MODEL (the parabolic polar is a hypothesis); no flying-fish C_D0, e or AR was measured here, so it is not yet an empirical test.
fleet.lay_summary: A flying fish glides because its long fins give lift, but the fins also cause drag. Engineers know a rule: the longer and thinner the wing, the better the glide ratio, up to a limit. The project's rulebook had this rule only as a note saying 'not written down yet'. I wrote it as a short mathematical proof, and a computer proof-checker confirmed every step. On a simple drag model, the glide ratio can never beat half the square root of a number built from the wing shape. The proof links to the existing rule on how far a glide can go from a given height. It only holds if the fish's real drag follows that simple model, which nobody has measured yet.

fleet.label: t6-flyingfish-lay
fleet.topic: Track 6 plain-language explanation material
fleet.summary:
What we are doing and why: we are building a referee for biological and engineering claims. Each claim is written as exact numbers and compared with physical rules that a proof-checking program (Lean) has verified. We use the flying fish as the practice case because its wings were measured in a wind tunnel, simulated on computers, and its leaps recorded in an aquarium. The aim is a reusable kit that can say 'this claim breaks a rule', 'this claim is not ruled out', or 'we cannot tell', and that is honest about the difference between the last two. The kit is then to be reused for the project's other five tracks. The next step, still a plan, adds the energy a fish carries when it leaves the water, plus the minimum speed a wing needs, and states predictions before looking at new data.

STEPS:
1. Pick a claim to test, such as 'a flying fish can glide 50 metres'. Think of a referee who says: show me the numbers first. [framework: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/.antigravity-ide/ScienceClaw/delphisci/lean/eliminate/README.md]
2. Write down a few simple physical rules that cannot be broken, like 'you cannot get more glide distance than the energy you start with'. It is like knowing you cannot bake more cookies than your dough allows. Each rule is written in a proof language called Lean so a computer can check it. [D:/Users/ashenoy00000/.antigravity-ide/ScienceClaw/delphisci/lean/eliminate/README.md]
3. Measure the animal. Researchers put a model fish in a wind tunnel and measured its lift and drag. We use those measurements for the weight, wing area, and best glide ratio of 4.37. [Park and Choi 2010; physics/glide-data.csv]
4. Add the stall floor. Like a bicycle that tips over below a certain speed, a wing cannot hold up the weight below a minimum speed. For the model fish that speed works out to about 9.85 m/s. [calc.py]
5. Write the claim down as exact numbers, with a range if unsure. The program does not guess. If a needed number is missing, it says 'cannot rule' rather than 'fine'. [D:/Users/ashenoy00000/.antigravity-ide/ScienceClaw/delphisci/lean/eliminate/README.md]
6. Let the computer look for a contradiction. If the claim and the rules cannot both be true, Lean checks the proof and the answer is 'eliminated'. If none is found the answer is only 'consistent', meaning 'not ruled out', like an alibi that has not been broken, which is not proof of innocence. [D:/Users/ashenoy00000/.antigravity-ide/ScienceClaw/delphisci/lean/eliminate/README.md]
7. Fix the predictions in writing before looking at new data, like a bet placed before the race. The plan has six predictions, for example that a simulated glide with a 13.2 m peak starts no slower than 16.1 m/s. [design-flyingfish.json]
8. Check against real or simulated results: the simulation paper's tracks, the aquarium leaps of live fish, and later a 3D-printed glider thrown at measured speeds. [design-flyingfish.json; Deng 2019; Makiguchi 2013]
9. Check the checker. Run it on real animals that are known to behave normally. If it flags one, the rules are too strict, as happened with law set 1.6.0, and the rules get fixed in a new version. [CHANGELOG 1.7.0 and 1.8.0]
10. Publish all results, including failures, and reuse the same kit for the other five tracks. [design-flyingfish.json step 10]

WHAT WOULD COUNT AS WRONG:
- The idea that the energy limit holds even for launches that fly up and arc is wrong if any simulated or measured flight goes farther than the limit (ratio above 1.00). Then the rule is narrowed to level glides only. [design P2]
- Wrong if a simulated glide with a 13.2 m peak turns out to start slower than 16.1 m/s, or if any peak exceeds the speed-based limit by more than 2%. [design P1]
- Wrong if any aquarium leap is in the air longer than 0.5 s, because the plan says these slow leaps are short hops, not glides. If the paper does not list times, the answer is 'cannot test'. [design P3]
- Wrong if more than 1 of 30 thrown printed gliders lands farther than 1.10 times the limit, or if the best flight at every speed reaches under half the limit (true but useless). [design P5]
- The pipeline itself is wrong if a certificate fails to compile or a verdict differs from the six listed in advance. That is a bug report, not a fact about fish. [design P4]
- The rules are wrong if they flag a healthy, normally gliding flying fish as impossible. [design P6; CHANGELOG 1.7.0]

WHAT COULD GO WRONG:
- Repairs may be needed: in the older upstream copy (1.6.0) some certificate files call lemmas that are not defined there. I did not run a Lean build. [scout]
- The model fish is one preserved specimen in a tunnel at 12 m/s; a live fish with flexible fins may lift better. At C_Lmax 1.03 the stall speed falls from 9.85 to about 8.6 m/s, so the 0.65 m figure would be about 6 m. [calc.py; design risks]
- Field distances and speeds (50 m, 10 m/s, 15 to 20 m/s) are quoted second-hand and no public raw trajectory data was found. [scout]
- The energy-limit lemma is proved only for steady glides where lift equals weight. A launch with a nearly weightless arc might beat it, which is exactly what prediction P2 tests. [design M3]
- Two law-set versions (1.6.0 upstream, 1.8.1 here) give different verdicts on some real fish, so results must say which was used. [CHANGELOG]
- A proof holds only under its stated assumptions. 'Eliminated' means 'inconsistent with these rules', not 'impossible in nature'. [ELIM README limits]
- A printed resin glider is heavy and brittle; if its stall speed is above about 8 m/s the test needs a long hall and may be underpowered. [design risks]
- Many answers are 'cannot rule': 23 of 44 open-problem candidates were untouched by any theorem. [ledger.open-problems.json]

QUESTIONS A LAYPERSON WOULD ASK:
Q: Why a flying fish and not something more useful?
A: It is a test case with real measurements (wind tunnel, simulation, live-fish leaps) and a clear physical limit, so the method can be checked before it is used on harder problems such as new materials. The same kit is meant to be reused for the other tracks. [design-flyingfish.json step 10; tracks/BRIEF-2026-11-12.md]
Q: Does the computer prove that flying fish fly?
A: No. Everyone knows they glide. What the work does is check whether specific numbers people claim, such as distance or power, fit the physical rules. Powered, aerobic flight is ruled out in all 3 ledger cases, while a normal glide is not. 'Not ruled out' is never 'proved'. [ledger.physiology.json; ELIM README; CHANGELOG 1.7.0]
Q: Has this already been tested and passed?
A: Not the new glide test. The framework exists and its examples are checked by Lean (13 of 18 sample claims eliminated). The new energy-based glide test is a written plan with predictions fixed in advance, and has no result yet. Also, the data on real glides is mostly second-hand. [design-flyingfish.json; scout could_not_find]
fleet.lay_summary: We are testing a way to check animal and design claims with computer-checked math. Think of a referee who will not accept 'the fish glided 50 metres' until the numbers fit physical rules, like not getting more cookies than the dough allows. The test case is the flying fish, because its wings have been measured in a wind tunnel and in simulations. The checker says 'ruled out', 'not ruled out', or 'cannot tell', and it never says 'proved'. The framework works and is checked by a proof program, but the newest glide test is still a plan with predictions written down in advance, so it has no result yet.

extraExplain.label: explain2-leanbio-enhancers
extraExplain.one_line: We test whether a DNA switch has one fixed strength or a strength that changes with its partner, and how to tell that apart from chance.
extraExplain.what: Cells have DNA switches called enhancers. DNA is the long molecule that stores a cell's instructions. An enhancer turns up a gene, which is one recipe in that book. It does this through a second switch next to the gene, called a promoter. We ask a simple question. Line up enhancers from weakest to strongest on one promoter. Is the line-up the same on another promoter? If yes, each enhancer has just one strength. If no, strength depends on the pairing. We reread a public set of mouse measurements. It covers 98 enhancers on 15 promoters. We also ran a computer simulation of pure chance. And we wrote a proof that a computer checked, line by line, about what simple models allow.
extraExplain.why: Doctors and engineers want to design DNA switches that work in a chosen gene. That is easier if an enhancer has one fixed strength. It is harder if strength depends on the partner. Past studies disagree. So a clear test helps. We do not claim a final answer here. We claim only a sharper way to ask the question.

steps.text: We read the main papers on this question. A large human study found a simple pattern. In it, each enhancer has one strength, and each promoter scales that strength up or down by a fixed amount. Fruit fly and mouse studies found pickier pairings.
steps.picture: Reading three reviews of the same restaurant before you eat there.

steps.text: We took a public set of measurements from mouse cells. It has 98 enhancers. Each was measured on 15 promoters. Every measurement was done 3 times.
steps.picture: Timing 98 runners on 15 different tracks, three times each.

steps.text: For each pair of promoters we asked how well the two line-ups of enhancers agree. We used a score called the Spearman score. It runs from -1 to 1. A score of 1 means the same order. A score of 0 means no link. Our middle score was 0.382. That is a weak link.
steps.picture: Comparing two teachers' grade lists for the same class. Most students move up or down the list.

steps.text: We counted pairs of enhancers whose order flips between promoters. We only counted pairs where the gap was large enough to trust on both promoters. Then we compared the count with what measurement noise alone would give. Noise is the small random error that makes repeat measurements differ.
steps.picture: Checking if a coin that landed heads 60 times in 100 is really unfair.

steps.text: We fitted the simplest pattern. Each enhancer gets one strength, and each promoter multiplies it by a fixed number. Then we measured how much of the data was left unexplained.
steps.picture: Laying a straight ruler along a curved line and measuring the gap.

steps.text: We ran a computer simulation with no real pairing effect at all. It shows how often noise alone swaps the order of two enhancers. We call this the chance baseline.
steps.picture: Shuffling a deck many times to see what luck looks like.

steps.text: We wrote a proof about simple models and had a computer check each step. The proof is about a ceiling, a top level that output cannot pass. A ceiling squashes strong enhancers to the same top level. Squashed enhancers end up equal. Equal is a tie. A ceiling cannot make a weaker one beat a stronger one. So a ceiling makes ties but never swaps.
steps.picture: A speed limit can make two cars tie at 65 miles an hour. It never makes the slower car win.

steps.text: We also proved what a flip does not tell you. Several different causes could give the same flip.
steps.picture: A wet street can mean rain, a hose or a passing truck.

steps.text: We suggest one extra experiment. Turn each enhancer up in steps, from weak to strong. Do this on two very different promoters. Repeat every measurement three times. If the enhancers only tie at the top, a ceiling is the cause. If they truly swap, the pairing is the cause.
steps.picture: Turning a volume knob in steps on two different speakers, to see if both just max out or if one really sounds different.

extraExplain.wrong_if: Our bet, written down before we looked, is this. In real data, enhancer order flips between promoters more often than noise alone predicts. If flips were no more common than that chance baseline, we are wrong. Then one fixed strength per enhancer would be enough.
could_go_wrong: The 98 enhancers are DNA stretches that look like switches. Nobody tested each one on its own.
We had only 3 repeats per measurement. So our estimate of noise is rough.
Our chance simulation assumes tidy, even noise. Real counts are messier, especially for weak enhancers.
We could not read the large human data set. So we did not rerun that analysis ourselves.
Two of the sources are early drafts. Other scientists have not yet reviewed them. We read only their summaries.
The extra experiment we suggest is a prediction from a simulation. It is not a result from a lab.
We have not compared the real flip counts with the range from our own chance simulation. That final step is still undone.
Studies disagree, and their different designs may explain some of the gap.

questions.q: How do you know?
questions.a: We reran public data and got the numbers in the check list below. A second set of checkers confirmed most of the key claims. Some were only partly confirmed, and we say so.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We did not rerun the large human data set. We did not test each enhancer in a lab. We did not compare real flip counts with the range from our own chance simulation. We do not know how big the effect is in most human cells.

questions.q: Is the answer yes or no?
questions.a: We do not know. The mouse data show real pairing effects. The big human study found a mostly simple pattern. Both can be partly true.

questions.q: What is a flip?
questions.a: Take two enhancers, A and B. On one promoter A is stronger. On another promoter B is stronger. That swap of places is a flip.

questions.q: How big is the pairing effect in the mouse data?
questions.a: Think of all the ups and downs in the 98 by 15 table. The one-strength pattern explains about 71 out of every 100 parts of them. The part it misses is the pairing effect. That leftover is about 12 times bigger than the leftover we would expect from measurement noise alone. So the leftover is far too big to be just noise.

questions.q: Do the real flips beat chance?
questions.a: In the mouse table, 65,174 of 224,658 clear-cut pairs flipped. That is about 29 out of every 100. A simple noise model in the same analysis expected only about 368 flips, which is far fewer. But our separate chance simulation gives a wide range, and we have not yet set the real rate against that range. So we call this a strong hint, not a final answer.

questions.q: Why is the chance range so wide, 1.3 to 43.7 percent?
questions.a: Noise matters more when enhancers are close in strength. If enhancers are far apart, noise rarely swaps them. If they are bunched together, noise swaps many. Fewer repeats also mean more noise. Our simulation tried many settings of noise, repeats and spread. At the calm end, 1.3 in 100 pairs swapped. At the noisy end, 43.7 in 100 swapped. So a raw count of flips proves little until you match it to the noise level.

questions.q: What would a flip prove?
questions.a: A flip rules out the simple models we proved things about. Those models say each enhancer has one strength and a ceiling. A flip does not say which other cause is true. Several different causes give the same flip.

questions.q: Why does a ceiling make ties but not swaps?
questions.a: A ceiling squashes strong enhancers to the same top level. Two squashed enhancers become equal, which is a tie. The ceiling treats a stronger enhancer at least as well as a weaker one. So it can never put the weaker one ahead.

questions.q: What would settle it?
questions.a: Test each enhancer at several strengths on two very different promoters, with three repeats. If enhancers only tie at the top, that points to a ceiling. If they really swap places, that points to a true mismatch. We do not yet know which one the real data show.

extraExplain.label: explain2-leanbio-binding
extraExplain.one_line: Computer programs that guess how tightly a drug grips a protein score lower than hoped. Our reading so far: messy lab numbers play a small part, and tests that are too easy play a bigger one.
extraExplain.what:
The finding first. Programs that guess how tightly a drug grips a protein do worse than people hoped. We looked at two reasons. One is that the lab measurements are messy. The other is that the tests are too easy. We lean towards the second reason, but we do not call it settled.

What is being guessed? It is a single number for each drug and protein pair. The number says how tightly the drug sticks to the protein. We call this "stickiness". Labs write it on a scale where one step up means ten times tighter.

How do we judge a program? We compare its guesses with the lab numbers. The score is called a correlation. It runs from 0 to 1. A score of 1 means the guesses rise and fall exactly with the lab numbers.

Here is a worked example of a "ceiling". Say you are guessing the heights of children. The true heights differ by about 0.7 units from child to child. Your tape measure is off by about 0.5 units each time. Even a perfect guesser then cannot score above about 0.82, because the answer key itself wobbles. That 0.82 is the ceiling. We worked out this example from numbers in one of our reports. For real drug data, we estimate the ceiling at about 0.85 to 0.95.

We also wrote four facts about noise as maths proofs. A computer checks every step of each proof. That part is explained in the steps below.
extraExplain.why: A program that ranks drug candidates wrongly wastes months of lab work. If the cause is messy data, we need better measurements. If the cause is easy tests, we need fairer tests. These are different fixes, so the cause matters. Our reading is that messy data is real but is not the main story. We do not claim this is settled.

steps.text: Read the papers on lab noise and on test cases that leak. Check each number against the paper itself.
steps.picture: Like checking a news story against the original report, not a friend's retelling.

steps.text: Download real measurements from a free public drug database. Look for cases where different labs measured the same drug on the same protein.
steps.picture: Like collecting two bathroom scales that weigh the same person, then comparing the readings.

steps.text: Measure how far apart those repeat readings are. Then work out the best score any program could reach. That best score is the ceiling.
steps.picture: Like marking a spelling test against an answer key that has a few typos. Even a perfect student loses marks.

steps.text: Split the spread of the numbers into two parts. Part one is the gap between different proteins. Part two is the gap between different drugs on the same protein.
steps.picture: Like prices in shops. Some of the price gap is because one shop is dearer than another. The rest is because items inside one shop cost different amounts.

steps.text: Run a made-up experiment on a computer. Test a program on look-alike cases, then on truly new cases. Add noise and see what changes.
steps.picture: Like giving a student last year's exam, then a brand new one.

steps.text: Write four facts as proofs. First, noisy lab numbers set a ceiling that no program can beat. Second, a program that knows only the protein cannot rank drugs for that protein. Third, energy changes around a closed loop of steps must add up to zero. Fourth, any claim of a score above the ceiling must be wrong for that noise level. A computer program checks every step.
steps.picture: Like a referee who will not let any move pass without a rule to back it. It is also like walking round a block and ending where you began: your total height change must be zero.

steps.text: Compare the ceiling with the scores that fair tests really give. See which gap is bigger.
steps.picture: Like comparing a speed limit with how fast cars really go on a rough road.

steps.text: List what we could not check, so no one reads more into the result than it holds.
steps.picture: Like a map with the unexplored edges marked.

extraExplain.wrong_if: Our bet, written down before looking, is that noise alone does not explain the poor scores. We are wrong in two cases. The first is a fair test with no look-alike cases that scores right at the ceiling. The second is cleaning out look-alikes and finding that scores stay the same. So far the opposite has happened. Scores fell when look-alikes were removed. But we have not tested this on the main benchmark's own lab numbers.
could_go_wrong: Our ceiling of about 0.85 to 0.95 out of 1 is our own conversion from published noise figures. It assumes errors are mostly small and rarely big, equally on both sides, like adult heights. Real errors have some big misses: 16 percent of repeat pairs for one measure differ by more than one full unit, which is ten times in stickiness. So the true ceiling may be lower.

In the made-up experiment, the true values were spread very widely, more than in real data. When true values differ a lot, a little noise barely hides them. So noise looked cheap there. In a narrow set, like our child-height example, noise bites harder. The experiment shows how the mechanism works. It does not show the real size.
The drug database sample uses 40 hand-picked, well-studied proteins, so it is not a fair random sample.
Repeat readings from different papers may differ for reasons other than noise, such as different test conditions. We do not know how much of the gap is real noise.
We did not work out the ceiling for the main benchmark itself, because we did not download its lab numbers.
Some key papers were behind a paywall, so we read only their summaries.

The proofs cover a small, tidy case: a limited list of examples. Real data is messier. They also assume the program never saw the lab's measurement errors. If a program copies the noisy readings, it can score a perfect 1, and the ceiling no longer applies.
No proof was tested against real data in this round.

questions.q: What exactly is being predicted?
questions.a: One number per drug and protein pair: how tightly the drug sticks. Labs write it on a scale where each step up means ten times tighter.

questions.q: Is the lab noise real?
questions.a: Yes. When different papers measure the same drug on the same protein, results typically differ by about 0.6 units. One unit is a ten-fold change in stickiness, so 0.6 units is roughly a four-fold change.

questions.q: What is the ceiling, and how does it compare with real scores?
questions.a: It is the best score any program could get when the lab numbers themselves wobble. We estimate it at about 0.85 to 0.95. Programs score about 0.75 to 0.80 on a fair test. So noise leaves room, though it is not zero.

questions.q: Then why not blame the noise?
questions.a: Real scores sit below the ceiling, so noise alone does not explain them. The gap between easy and fair tests is also large. That points more to the tests than to the noise.

questions.q: What is the 'look-alike' problem?
questions.a: About half of the standard test cases (49 percent) have a near-twin in the training set. The training set is the examples a program studies before the test. A simple lookup of similar cases, with no learning, scored 0.716 out of 1 on the original split.

questions.q: What happened when the twins were removed?
questions.a: The lookup trick dropped to 0.653. Researchers reported that scores fell for other programs too.

questions.q: Can simple tricks match fancy programs?
questions.a: On the standard test, a program that looks only at the drug scored 0.76. One that looks only at the protein scored 0.75. Published learning programs scored 0.74 to 0.82. So the fancy programs barely beat the simple tricks.

questions.q: Does knowing the protein help?
questions.a: A little. In our sample, which protein it was explained only about 8 to 15 percent of the spread. The hard part is ranking similar drugs for one protein. A program that knows only the protein can guess that protein's average, and nothing more.

questions.q: What do the proofs add?
questions.a: They show that the ceiling is a matter of arithmetic and not just a hunch. They also show that a program that knows only the protein cannot rank drugs on that protein. The proofs only hold if the program never saw the lab's errors.

questions.q: What score did your own program reach?
questions.a: None. We trained no learning program ourselves.

questions.q: Which proteins did the lookup trick do best on?
questions.a: We do not know. Our sources do not say.

questions.q: How do you know?
questions.a: We checked numbers against the papers' full text or summaries and re-ran our own scripts. A second group of checkers confirmed most claims. Some were only partly confirmed, and we say so in the left-out list.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We have not worked out the ceiling for the main benchmark. We trained no learning program ourselves. We did not use a second database. We also do not know how much of the repeat-reading gap is real noise.

Recalling answers seen before instead of working them out.
Careful cleaning and selecting of data.
Two ways labs write stickiness on the ten-fold scale. A higher number means tighter. The names are lab shorthand.
A score for how well two rankings agree. A 1 means the same order. Papers report it for repeat lab measurements.

A free public database of drug measurements taken from papers.
The proof-checking language we used. A program that accepts a proof only if every step is valid.
A loop of changes that ends where it started, so the energy changes must add up to zero.
The weakening of a link between two things because one of them is measured with noise. A wobbly ruler makes a real match look weaker.
Having no straight-line link: when one list goes up, the other does not tend to go up or down.
A standard formula for converting between two ways of reporting stickiness. It is not needed to follow the main story.
The share of a measurement that is real signal rather than noise.
A typical size of spread around the average.
A starting rule a proof is allowed to assume without proving it.
A marker the proof checker leaves where a proof has a gap. Zero markers means no gaps.
A tool that makes a long fingerprint of a file. If the file changes at all, the fingerprint changes.

extraExplain.label: explain2-people-funding
extraExplain.one_line: We looked up who might fund, advise or hire our work on fish, tiny living robots and computer-checked maths, and we mark every idea as a guess.
extraExplain.what: Our project uses computers to study how living bodies are built and how they move. It looks at fish fins, including the fins of flying fish that glide above water. It looks at tiny living robots made from frog cells. It also uses a free program called Lean, which checks maths proofs step by step, to test the project's own claims. The notes here map the people and money around that work. We looked for fish scientists near Boston who might help. We looked for grants that could pay for it. We looked at how a small team could be paid by a company. We also decoded a hurried set of meeting notes. Last, we tried to find out what "Sentry" is, a tool someone remembered. Nothing here is a deal or a promise. Every link to a person or funder is an idea to test. These notes do not state one single research question, so we do not invent one.
extraExplain.why: A project needs people who know fish, and money to keep going. Without a map, we might knock on the wrong doors. Some funders have open doors today and some have shut ones. A hurried meeting note can mislead us if we build on it too fast. Checking each claim now saves time later. We say "we do not know" where that is true.

steps.text: We searched the Broad Institute's public list of members for people who study fish. The Broad Institute is a large research centre near Boston. Then we checked their papers in Crossref, a public database that lists scientific papers.
steps.picture: Like looking up a plumber's licence before you let them in.

steps.text: We searched for Boston experts on how fish fins grow and move. We checked each paper by its DOI. A DOI is a permanent web code that points to one paper.
steps.picture: Like checking a receipt against the shop's own records.

steps.text: We read the pages of funders to see who backed the living robots made from frog cells. We also read what the pages say about money for maths-and-biology work.
steps.picture: Like reading the sign on each shop door for its opening hours.

steps.text: We read public rules for small-business grants, university deals and free software licences. These rules say who owns what.
steps.picture: Like reading the lease before you rent a flat.

steps.text: We matched each line of the hurried meeting notes to public facts and to our own file format. Our file format is the set of rules we use to write down a creature's design in a file.
steps.picture: Like turning a shopping list written in a rush into real items.

steps.text: We searched for a product called Sentry that lets software agents message each other. An agent is a computer program, often an AI, that does tasks on its own. We did not sign up or log in anywhere.
steps.picture: Like looking for a shop by name on the map before you drive there.

steps.text: Two checkers then re-read the key claims. We kept only claims they backed. We marked partial ones.
steps.picture: Like a second proofreader marking your homework.

steps.text: We wrote down what we could not find. That way no gap gets filled with a guess.
steps.picture: Like leaving a blank on a form instead of making up an answer.

extraExplain.wrong_if: Our bet, written before looking: at least one Boston-area fish group fits our questions, and at least one open funding door exists. We are wrong if the listed people do not work on fish now. We are also wrong if every funder page we trust turns out shut. And we are wrong if any person says our reading of their work is off.
could_go_wrong: Web pages change. A deadline we read today may be out of date next month.
Some pages were read through a summary tool. A few quotes may be loose paraphrase.
A person listed as linked to the Broad Institute may have moved. One scientist is now at a Swiss university, and we could not confirm his Broad role.
We could not read many funders' pages at all. So the list of open doors is partial.
The grant rules and ownership rules here are not legal advice.
The meeting-note readings are our best guesses. Several lines have no source.
We could not tell which Sentry was meant. We may have searched for the wrong thing.
We checked only a few papers per scientist. We may have missed better matches.

questions.q: What does the project actually do, and why do fish, maths proofs and frog robots belong together?
questions.a: The project uses computers to study how living bodies are designed and how they move. Fish fins and flying-fish gliding are about body shape and motion. The frog-cell robots are living machines that people design on a computer. Lean, a free program that checks maths proofs, is used to test our own claims. Beyond that, these notes do not state one exact research question, so we do not know how to put it more tightly.

questions.q: How do you know?
questions.a: Each paper was looked up in a public records database by its web code. Each funding rule was read on the funder's own page. A second set of checkers re-read the key claims. We kept only those they backed.

questions.q: What have you not checked?
questions.a: We did not read many big funders' pages, such as several large foundations and a US military research agency. We did not confirm any prices for paid pilot work. We did not open one patent that may matter. We also could not show that no funder pays for proof-checking of biology. We only found no page that does, and our search was not complete.

questions.q: Does anyone want to work with us?
questions.a: We do not know. We found people whose work is near ours. We have not contacted anyone. No one has agreed to anything.

questions.q: Who paid for the frog-cell living robots?
questions.a: The records show a private foundation set up by Paul Allen, the US military research agency DARPA, and the US National Science Foundation. The later robots made from human lung cells also list the John Templeton Foundation and the US National Institutes of Health. A Harvard institute called the Wyss Institute is a partner. It is paid for mostly by gifts from one Swiss donor.

questions.q: Which grants look open right now?
questions.a: A US National Science Foundation core biology call takes proposals at any time. The Wellcome charity's Discovery Awards have no deadline. They average about 3.5 million pounds, which is roughly the price of a few big houses. One US maths-and-biology call has a March 1 date. Its page is marked archived, so check before relying on it.

questions.q: Can a small team keep what it invents under a US small-business grant?
questions.a: Yes. Under US law a small business can usually keep ownership of inventions made with federal money. The government gets a free, permanent right to use those inventions itself. A university deal is often different. We read only one source on that, a checklist from a single university system. We do not know how other universities handle it.

questions.q: What is Sentry?
questions.a: We could not tell. The well-known Sentry records software crashes. It also lets an AI assistant read those crash records. We found no Sentry feature that passes messages between agents. We read only two pages, so that does not prove none exists. Other, separate products do that job.

questions.q: What do the meeting notes say, and why do Formlabs and Sentry appear?
questions.a: The notes are hurried shorthand from a meeting. We matched each line to public facts. Formlabs makes 3D printers that use liquid plastic. Its store lists 72 materials, so we read the note's "10 materials" as a shortlist. Sentry was a tool someone remembered, and we could not pin it down. Some lines have no source at all: 'license your patent', '500 papers', 'non profit Bioelectricity' and '3 million tokens'. We do not know what those mean.

questions.q: Why not just guess where the notes are unclear?
questions.a: A wrong guess can send weeks of work the wrong way. One question to the note-taker is cheaper.
